Tuesday, 6th March, 1928.
The Fourth Session of the Second
Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet 6th March, 1928, in the
Eighteenth year of the Reign of King
George V, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.P.)
in person.
The House met at Ten minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.)
in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.), was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

the Standing Orders have been complied
with in the following cases:

SESSIONAL ORDERS
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
Sessional Orders
King's Speech
6 MARCH 1928
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
"for the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries" read the First
time and ordered to be read a Second
time.
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate to hear His
Grace's Speech on behalf of the
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament;
of which I have for greater accuracy
obtained a copy.
The Speech is as
follows:
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I am much gratified by the knowledge
that industrial peace continues to prevail throughout Northern Ireland.
Trade disputes wherever they have
occurred have proved gravely detrimental to national progress and
prosperity.
The unemployment position this year
has improved considerably as compared
with the corresponding period of 1927,
and I hope that even greater
improvement will develop during the
remainder of the year, and as time
proceeds.
I am pleased to observe that under
those provisions of the Contributory
Pensions Act which came into operation
on the Second of January last 8,900
persons who have attained the age of
65 years have received Old Age
Debate on the Address 8
King's Speech
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Pensions, increasing the total number of
men, women and children, enjoying
the benefits of Pensions, contributory
and non-contributory, to 78,000.
In view of the success which has
attended the operations of the Loans
Guarantee Acts, my Government propose to extend for a further period the
power of giving facilities to industry.
A Measure will be submitted modifying in certain respects the financial
provisions of the Constabulary Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922, and amending the provisions of that Act dealing
with the contributions payable by local
authorities for additional Police forces
stationed in their respective areas.
Proposals will also be laid before you
regarding the registration of Nursing
and Maternity Homes and for the
better regulation of street trading in
our towns.
It
found impracticable last
Session to consider proposals relative to
the improvement of roads by local
authorities and the acquisition of land
for road purposes. A Bill dealing with
these matters will be submitted forthwith for your consideration.
Other Measures will be laid before
you dealing with:
:-
Unemployment Insurance.
National Health Insurance.
The adoption of children.
Legitimacy.
The storage and transport of
Petroleum.
Superannuation and other Trust
Funds.
The amendment of the law relating
to Fisheries.
The amendment of the law relating
to Bankruptcy.
and the amendment of the existing
Game Laws.
Members of the House of Commons.
The results which have attended the
publicity campaign carried out by the
Linen Industry in the United States
during the past two years have been
sufficiently encouraging to warrant its
continuance for a further period and its
extension to a wider market. You will
accordingly be asked to vote an
additional sum towards this object for
the year 1928-29.
The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I am glad to learn that my
Government have under consideration
measures directed to the further
alleviation of the present depressed conditions with which those engaged in
Agriculture are faced, and I earnestly
trust that the general improvement in
other industries will react beneficially
on farming generally.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty
God may rest upon your labours.
Debate on the Address.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL (in morning dress): I beg to move:
"That an humble address be presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland, as followeth-
Debate on the Address

6 MARCH 1928
Debate on the Address
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to Your Grace for the Speech which
Your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."
I would like to thank the Government
for allowing me to move this Address. 1
have one special reason for this and that
is that it gives me the opportunity, how-.
ever inadequate my words may be, of letting those who sent me to this House to
represent them know that I am fulfilling
the trust impcsed upon me, and which I
willingly accepted, of loyally supporting
our present Prime Minister and Government.
Everyone will, I am sure, welcome the
fact that the revised old-age pensions
scheme is now in work, and the numbers
show how far-reaching are the benefits.
It is very gratifying to learn that the
Government have decided to extend the
working of the Loans Guarantee Act, because I am satisfied that the facilities
accorded by that Act have contributed
very largely towards providing employment, and I hope that as a result of their
taking their courage in their hands, and
continuing it, they will reap the benefit
of seeing much less unemployment in the
future.
We see in the newspapers that Workman, Clark & Co. have been bought up.
We can only hope that whoever may now
become responsible for the working of the
firm will soon get orders for ships, and,
if necessary, avail themselves of the
Loans Guarantee Act, so that, ere long,
the yards will again be in full swing, and
so provide a still greater amount of
employment.
((
It is satisfactory to learn that what one
might almost have called the strained
relations" existing between the local
authorities and the Government on the
question of the charges for additional
police have, as we hope, now been satisfactorily settled.
Mr. KYLE: No, no.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: We will see.
The Government must be congratulated
on taking up the question of nursing and
maternity homes. While there are a
large number of these institutions which
are as near perfection as possible, and
which, I am sure, will not be interfered
with in any way, yet one cannot deny that
there are places in the Province which
certainly need supervision in order that
they may be made more fit and proper for
those who have to make use of them.

In dealing with the acquisition of land
for road purposes, I can't think that the
local authorities have had any large number of cases where the owner of land has
taken up the position of trying to "salt"
the local authority. I don't think that
is a trait in the character of the people of
Northern Ireland. At the same time
there are sure to be some such cases, and
it is only fair to the community at large
that where land is required for the general
good and safety that the authority should
have power to acquire it, and, at the
same time, be compelled to pay a fair and
just price for it. The improvement of
the roads has become a very serious problem, but, unfortunately, it is by no
means a simple one. All sorts of interests have to be considered. It is a
problem which has only come into existence in its present acute form within the
last few years, and, like all new problems,
the correct solution will only be arrived
at as the result of experience.
In bringing in a Bill to amend the
laws on bankruptcy, the Government is,
at least, bringing forward a Measure
which has long been needed, and which
will be of very valuable service to the
commercial community if it is, as I am
sure it, will be, a Bill to do away with
some of the blatant absurdities which
exist at present. For example, a person
may get through his bankruptcy with the
payment of 6d in the £, and he can set
up the next day in his wife's name, or
in an assumed name, without any penalty.
That is simply putting a premium on
the dishonest trader and a heavy handicap on the honest trader who is trying
to carry on his business in a fair manner.
Also the delays which were entailed were
quite unnecessary. We have heard of
the law's delays," and certainly the
Bankruptcy laws were by no means
behindhand in showing the truth of that
saying.
I see that the Government proposes to
deal with the laws relating to Fisheries
11 Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Debate on the Address
[Mr. Lloyd Campbell]
and Game. Doubtless some people will
say that the preservation of game, etc.,
is merely pandering to the rich. Such is
by no means the case. Fish and game
are two very valuable assets to a community from a financial point of view,
provided these assets are properly utilized.
In the past there has been no proper
control, and what little control existed
has been very poorly exercised. If the
laws were good and were properly enforced the money which would accrue
from the pursuit and sale of game, etc.,
in Northern Ireland would be a very
welcome asset indeed to the Chancellor
of the Exchequer, and would also bring
a large amount of money into the pockets
of all those concerned, either rectly or
indirectly, in what would with. t doubt
become a very fair-sized and valuable
business. As things are to-day, the
amount of money lost through want of
proper control is large, but if proper laws
and control were instituted and carried
out, then I am satisfied that the financial
benefit would be indeed great.
The Wild Fowl, Game and Fish Preservation Society, two years ago, distributed in small lots amongst farmers over
5,000 pheasant eggs, and the result has
proved in many places quite satisfactory.
During the past year I understand that
the Ministry of Commerce have taken
considerable interest in the exhibitions
arranged by the Empire Marketing
Board. During the last year I believe
they took part in some eight displays, and
I can only hope that during the present
year that number will be doubled or
trebled. One of the first essentials for
getting a market for one's goods is to get
into touch with the consumer,
and
already, through these exhibitions, the
products of Northern Ireland have been
brought directly home to the consumer.
These exhibitions fulfil a twofold purpose. Firstly, they bring home to many
people the fact that we all-Northern
Ireland, Australia, Canada, and all the
other units are members of one great
Commonwealth-the British Empire.
Secondly, these exhibitions show us that it
is to our mutual benefit to buy from those
who buy from us. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The housewife learns that she can
buy Empire products, such as flour,
raisins, meat and many other things
cheaper and better than if she bought
those articles outside the Empire.
What man would not prefer to wear a
suit of clothes which was made from
Empire-grown wool and manufactured
throughout within the Empire rather
than go to some foreign country which
often heavily taxes our imports? I
believe that if the Empire had a ring
fence round it and no internal barriers,
that it could be self-consuming and selfproducing to its full capacity. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) That may be an
ideal view, but at anyrate it is a worthy
ideal, and one well worth aiming at.
Some people seem to think that the
grant which has been given to the
publicity campaign for the linen industry
has been in the nature of a subsidy. Such
is by no means the case. By far the
largest industry-by that I mean the industry that affects, directly or indirectly,
the largest number of persons in North
Ireland, is the linen industry. If it could
be brought back to its former state it
would mean a very much larger circulation of money in the Province, and that
in its turn would mean that the butcher,
the baker, the candlestick maker-not
forgetting agriculture-would benefit very
largely by the revival of the linen trade.
In the past two years the Government
has contributed 10s. for every £1 which
has been subscribed by the trade, and the
propaganda has proved so successful, although confined to one country, viz., the
U.S.A., that the trade feel justified in
"Use
wanting to spread the gospel of
Irish Linen" further afield, and try to
make an equal success in other countries.
I am glad the Government have seen it
in this light, and that they express their
willingness to carry on a grant for a
further period.
I am not a pessimist, far from it.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) At the
same time I do not believe in undue
optimism. Optimism if carried to excess,
like anything else, becomes a danger, but
if properly handled is a very great tonic.
I believe that trade is reviving, slowly
One of the chief
perhaps, but surely.
factors that are helping on that general
revival is the feeling of mutual trust and
confidence, which is every day becoming
stronger, between all those engaged in
industry; the realization that each and
every one of us is dependent on his neighbour; that we must all work for the common good, whatever our task may be.

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Davison]
The Government cannot possibly engage upon any task of greater importance
to the community at large. The farmers
are the backbone of Ulster. If we allow
them to go down or be driven out of the
country by stress of circumstances we can
never make good the loss. No success in
any other sphere of labour or commerce
would compensate Ulster for the loss of
her farmers. At present agriculture is
facing a crisis, and there appcars no sign
of immediate improvement. The prices
of farm produce of all kinds have gone
down and down, but the prices of all that
the farmer has to buy have kept up.
He
buys cattle at the beginning of the season,
feeds them and cares for them, and at the
end of the season he is offered less than
he paid for them. It is the same with
almost everything else. The fruit crop,
which used to be the mainstay of many a
County Armagh farmer, has ceased to be
profitable.
Over and above this great inducements
are offered to the young men of the farming class to emigrate. We must see that
there are inducements for them to stay
here and work the farms of Ulster. The
first step is to realize the serious state of
affairs we have got so far. The Government, as we read in the King's Speech,
are alive to the present depressed conditions. The next thing is to take steps
to improve these conditions.
We are
promised this. In its consideration of
the necessary steps the Government ought
to have the support of every Member of
this House regardless of what constituency
he represents, whether urban or rural,
and regardless of what his politics may
be. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
This ought to be above party. I know
the Government are in earnest to do all in
their power for the farming community.
The farmer does not want charity or
doles. Anything that we could do or
have the money to do in that way would
be very little good. Short of this the
Government can help the farmer in many
ways, and, indeed, has been helping him in
some of them. The pace must be speeded
up. The Government may help the
farmer with loans at low rates of interest
to tide over the bad times. It may help
him to get new and more productive
varieties of seeds. It may give him
advice as to his methods so that the results of the latest scientific research may
be at his disposal. It may advise him as
to the marketing of his produce and help
him to secure the most profitable markets.
It may encourage co-operation among
farmers so that both in buying aud
selling he may be in a stronger position.
Above all it may see that all possible
economies are effected both in central and
local government, so that the burden of
taxation may be lessened and life eased
not only for the farmer but for all who
have to contribute.
Again, the Ministry of Agriculture may
suggest new lines upon which the farmer
may develop, whether by way of new crops
for his land or the adoption of new or
the improvement of old sources of
revenue. Egg production and poultry
rearing are examples where the Ministry
has done much and may do more. The
markets for cattle are changing. It is
the duty of the Government to help our
farmers to accommodate themselves to
the change. Drainage measures ought
to have immediate and generous help.
The situation is beyond all question
serious. The only comfort is that the
Government realize it and has promised
to deal with it.
The keynote of the King's Speech is
peace. We have passed through the storms
and we have now political and industrial
peace. No big contentious Measures are
foreshadowed, and we do not need them.
I often think that Acts of Parliament are
to the nation what drugs and medicine
are to the individual. Sometimes they
may be necessary, but the fewer taken the
better. The habit in the case of either
is fatal. All the same, Acts of Parliament are sometime necessary, and I congratulate the Government upon the moderation of their programme in general and
upon the objects of those Measures
which they propose to introduce.
In one of these I am particularly interested, namely, the Roads Improvement
Bill.
Our traffic tends to go more and
more upon the roads, and for the new
traffic our roads are more or less unsuited.
They were designed for horse vehicles,
and are not fit for our fast motor traffic.
Speedy and cheap compulsory powers are
wanted by our road authorities if the
necessary alterations and improvements
The law in this respect
are to be made.
has been left substantially unaltered since
the Grand Jury (Ireland) Act, 1836. I
do not agree with the hon. Member for

North Belfast (Mr. Lloyd Campbell)
that attempts would not be made,

companies are acquiring land or local

very utmost exacted that can be exacted.
The Bill to be submitted will, I believe,

in this respect.
May I suggest that a greater share should
be borne by taxes as distinguished
from rates of the burden of road
maintenance and improvement. Roads
are no longer for merely local
traffic. One can go from one, end
of Northern Ireland to another in
3 hours. It is really the motors of the
towns that use the roads most.
It is unfair to the country districts to lay so
inuch of the burden of their maintenance upon the ratepayers of those
districts who use the roads so little and
whose vehicles do so little damage. We
need good modern roads built upon the
best engineering principles. It is hardly
to be expected that a body of farmers
will lay upon themselves the cost of providing for the benefit of others roads any
better than their own necessities dictate.
It is not human nature. The Government, I suggest, should accept more of the
burden. Again, this is another way in
which the farming community may be
benefited.
Looking back over the years since this
Parliament was set up, the Government
have no reason to be ashamed of their record. They have faced every difficulty
not with high-sounding phrases or empty
boasts, but in a business style and with
common sense. We on this side of the
House have confidence that they
will win through in the end. I beg to
second the Motion for the presentation of
the Address.
Mr. KYLE: I desire to congratulate
the mover and the seconder of the Address
on the very able speeches they have delivered to this House. I noticed that
both hon. Gentlemen thought fit to do
what some of us here will do in perhaps
a slightly different way, that is, to instruct the Government as to what they
ought to do in regard to the various
matters that are mentioned in the Speech
from the Throne. The Speech seems to
breath self-complacency in every line, the

of the Government and of the Government party. They have no conception
of how the great mass of the people who
are employed in agriculture, or in industry in the city of Belfast, live, and
move, and have their being.
The hon. Gentleman (Mr. Lloyd
Campbell) who moved the Address stated
that he was a Free Trader, but would like
to be a Protectionist. Some of us on this
side of the House are neither Free Traders
nor Protectionists, but are solely concerned about the lives and well-being of
the people whom we represent. It has
seemingly become the fashion on the
other side of the House to quote Labour
leaders, and we are delighted to see that
right hon. and hon. Gentlemen opposite
read carefully the speeches and homilies
that are delivered from time to time by
members of the Labour party on the
other side of the water. We are hopeful
that if they continue to read these
speeches they may become converted to
the ideas of the gentlemen who make
those speeches. The hon. Member inferred that the Members on his side of
the House were the only people interested
in the development of the individuality
of the citizens of this part of the country,
just as the Rt. Hon. Philip Snowden
spoke of the development of the individuality of the people at the Whitefield's Tabernacle.
We here on this side of the House,
equally with right hon. and hon. Gentlemen opposite, are very much concerned
about the development of the individuality of everybody, and we feel compelled
from time to time to utter criticisms of

that system crushes the individual. If
the hon. Member had quoted the entire

he would have seen that it was a criticism to a very considerable extent of the
present system of society. I want to ask
right hon, and hon. Gentlemen opposite
what chance is there to develop individuality in the spinning room, or the
weaving factory, or the engineering shop,
or the shipyards.

Mr. KYLE: What chance is there to
develop individuality when the workers.
are there from half-past eight in the

they are sacked, and then the Ministry of
Labour turns them down at the Employment Exchange because they have been
dismissed for unsatisfactory service.
The Speech does not mention a thing
that it was formerly a very common
practice to mention, namely, economy.
I am sure I will be supported by the hon.
Gentleman (Sir Robert Lynn), who sits
behind the Government front bench, in
regard to this particular matter, and
that when we make our proposals for
economy we shall have the support of the
hon. Member for West Belfast, who in
days gone by led the attack on the
Government in matters of economy.
Not
a word of economy has been mentioned in
the Speech. Surely when our agricultural industry is in the condition described
by the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Lloyd
Campbell) who moved the Address, which
was corroborated by the hon. and learned
Gentleman (Mr. Davison) who seconded
in a very able speech, and the linen industry is in a deplorable, but not so
parlous, state, it is time for the Government to attempt to exercise some economy
in regard to administration, in regard to
the officials of this House, and in regard
to everything in connection with this
House. Surely it is time they were
thinking about economy in these very
important things. That would show the
people of the Six Counties that the
Government themselves were in earnest
so far as economical administration is
concerned.
The Speech from the Throne begins by
speaking about industrial peace. All the
Members on this side of the House
equally with those on the other side desire
to see nothing that will mar the harmony
that exists so far as workpeople and employers are concerned. But we can have
peace at too dear a price. Is it the intention of the Government or of hon.
Members opposite to say they are in
favour of peace at any price? We on
this side I speak for myself and for some
of my colleagues are not in favour of
peace at any price. If we are going to
have peace at any price, at the price of
half-starved workpeople, if we are going
to have peace at the price of 37/6 for a
47-hour week in the shipyards, or if we
are to have peace at the price of 20/- or
25/- a week in our spinning mills and
weaving factories, some of us think peace
is rather too dear at that price.
With regard to the gratification expressed at the absence of trade disputes,
trade disputes are sometimes very necessary to compel members of the employing class to see that their workpeople
cannot for ever live on the verge of starvation as they are doing in our shipbuilding and engineering and linen industries
to-day. The linen trade has been built
up and has reached its zenith in this
country of ours. Ulster is looked upon
all over the world as the home of the
linen industry, and yet the workers are
worse paid than the workers in the linen
trade in Great Britain, where it is only
a very minor and subsidiary trade. This
is a state of affairs that nobody with a
heart or a conscience can view with the
equanimity with which the Government
apparently views it, as is evidenced by
this Speech to-day.
With regard to the suggestions that
are made for the present Session in reference to unemployment insurance, I
want to say quite definitely to the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), after
his dismissal from unemployment insurance benefit of a great number workpeople, that I suppose now the Government are going to add infamy to
infamy by proposing to reduce the
amount of benefit that is to be granted to
a certain class of workpeople. It is
absolutely monstrous to suggest that
young men of twenty-one should have a
lesser amount than is being paid to them
from the unemployment exchanges.
So far as the Loans Guarantee Acts
are concerned, we do not oppose Loans
Guarantees, nor have we ever done so
since they were first introduced into this
House, or rather since we became
Members of this House. We have never

think from what one can gather as to the

going to be compelled still to make that
criticism-that when we guarantee a loan
there ought to be some measure of public
control, so far as the firm that is getting
the advantage of that guaranteed loan is
concerned, of the wages of the workpeople
employed by such firm which enjoys public

I would have liked if someone could

affairs is not likely to be remedied in the

Then again there is no reference in the

curring problem-has everflowed

to say all is right with the world, everything in the garden is beautiful, there is
no need to worry about these farming

(Mr. Davison) says, are the basis of all

prosperity for our industries; and despite
all this unparalleled depression, right
hon. and hon. Gentlemen sit in their

We had a Local Government Commission quite recently and, while
suppose the Prime Minister would say
that one or two of these Measures that
are going to be laid before us arise out of
the Report of that Commission, yet, so far

Commission are concerned, there is no
mention of them at all. For example,
the Local Govenment Commission suggested the abolition of Poor-law Guardians
in all places outside Belfast. No legislation along that line is suggested at all.
Apparently the Government are only
awakening now at the opening of Parliament. I am sure they think it is a bore
to have to discuss these matters at all.
They would rather do as apparently they
used to do, namely, put a rubber stamp on
the English Acts and make them apply to
Northern Ireland automatically.
In the Report of that Local Government Commission there were some very

Another reform mentioned by the

The Prime Minister in his tour of the
Northern area about a year ago stated in
the County Tyrone that he would introduce public health legislation, but that
public health legislation is not materialising. Where it it? Search the Speech,
and find out where is this public health
Amendment that the Prime Minister
promised to introduce. It is admitted
by everybody, I think, that there is much
to be done so far as public health legislation is concerned. Our death-rate in
Belfast and the North of Ireland is too
high. I think that that is recognised.
Just fancy, the death rate in Belfast is
higher than that of London, and if you
do not want to take London, the death
rate in Belfast is higher than that of
Dublin. That is a state of affairs that
ought not to be.
Again, take the subject of infantile
mortality, a matter which should be the
especial care of the Government from the
point of view of public health. We find
that the rate of infantile mortality has
gone up and is going up. With these
facts before the Government, I think we
are quite justified in expecting much
more public health legislation than they
have seen fit to introduce.
Then there is the question of scarlet fever.

day that scarlet fever has become endemic

All this leads up to what we on these

medical service. It is probably the only
solution of the problem, and it is the
only one that I can see, after having given

bring about any far-reaching reforms, so

The whole Speech, if I may say so without desiring to give offence, is so complacent, so self-satisfied, that it is
extremely difficult to speak in moderate
language of those responsible for framing
it. Instead of saying that the first duty
of the Government is to see that the
people of the Six Counties are fed,
clothed and housed, the Speech deals with
the reform of the game laws, something
that may interest right hon. and hon.
Gentlemen opposite, but has very little to
do with the lives and the well-being of
the great mass of the people. I wish the
Government well in their attempt to put
before the House the Measures they have
outlined in the King's Speech. I hope
that in the coming Session they will treat
the Opposition with a little more courtesy,
with a little more respect, and with more
feeling than they have done in the past.
If they do that, perhaps some good may
come out of the amendments and suggestions that are put forward from time
to time from this side of the House. They
should not continue to treat us as helots,
as hewers of wood and drawers of water.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): My first and most pleasant
duty is to tender very hearty congratulations to the mover and seconder of the
Motion now before the House. In the
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Lloyd
Campbell), I have always found a true
and trusted Friend, and it was with
especial pleasure, therefore, that the duty
was placed upon him of moving the Resolution to-day.
With regard to the hon. and learned
Member for the County of Armagh (Mr.
Davison), I can only say that he fulfilled
his duty in a way which brings honour to
a distinguished member of the Northern.
Bar.
I think, if I am right, this is the
seventh occasion on which our present
Governor has delivered the Gracious
Speech to both Houses of our Parliament,
and I feel that perhaps it might be fitting
if I were to refer to the pleasure that
everyone here experienced on the
marriage between his eldest son and the
daughter of a distinguished family in our
area. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It
was, I am sure, doubly pleasant to some of
us who had the honour of witnessing the
marriage ceremony, and we wish the
young couple as great honour, and as
great a position in life, as their distinguished parents have earned in the service.
of the Ulster people. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Then, I think I would be interpreting
the feeling of all the Members of this
House if I referred to the sad loss sustained by the Senate through the death.
of Senator Greer, who was one of the
original Members of that House, and who
the longer he was known was the better
liked. Personally, I knew his brother,
Sir Francis, better than I knew him, but
I do not think there was any man in
Northern Ireland more respected than
Senator Greer. We feel his loss very
much, and we tender to his widow
and the other relatives our sincerest
sympathy.
The Leader of the Opposition, as far
as I can gather, has found some objection
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
6 MARCH 1928
to the Speech delivered to-day, because
there does not seem to him to be enough
matter in it to irritate him sufficiently
so that he can tear it about during the
Session. It is purposely so. I have said
before, and I state here to-day, that what
Ulster requires, and what I think Great
Britain-indeed the whole world-requires is that there should be as little
contentious legislation as possible introduced, because we want, if we can, to
settle down to real work and progress.
Therefore if there is nothing of outstanding brilliancy or importance in the
Gracious Speech of to-day, at all events
it will ensure that we will be able to give
the most careful consideration to such
Measures as are mentioned, and I hope
we will be able to carry through a very
profitable Session.
The hon. Member, the Leader of the
Opposition, seemed to object to the
paucity of information given. I would
remind him that the time to discuss
Measures, and to elicit from Members of
the Government their intentions in
regard to legislation, is when the specific
Bills are introduced into the House.
Then all information can be ascertained,
and criticisms can be fitly made. He
mentioned that there was an omission of
reference to the Commission on Local
Government and the question of the
drainage of the River Bann, and he
seemed to throw out the suggestion that
those matters were not constantly in the
minds of the Government. Nothing could
be further from the truth, and if he had
only read the local Press he would have
observed that a very short time ago my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, addressed a communication to
all the local authorities concerned with
regard to the question of the drainage of
the River Bann. There the matter stands
at the moment. It is a very big and a
very important question. It requires consideration from every angle, and nothing
is lost by any delay there has been in
making even further inquiries into what
is required by the local authorities.
I would like to say while on this subject that I do hope no narrow view will
be taken on this great question. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The Government are satisfied that something should
be done and can be safely done. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). We started out
by explaining to the public how nervous
we were about the squandering of any
public money, and how necessary it was
to be absolutely sure that every pound
put into the development of the drainage
of the River Bann should bear full fruit.
Well, I think my right hou. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) is satisfied that the inquiries
that have been made have elicited the fact
that this can be safely done. The matter
is now before the local authorities, and I
earnestly hope that before any of the
local authorities turn down the very
generous offer made by the Government
they will all meet my colleagues and myself at Stormont to discuss the question
in its broadest aspect. It would be most
regrettable if through any little misunderstanding local authorities stood out from
carrying through a great scheme which
should be of immense assistance practically
to the whole of the catchment area of
Lough Neagh. Therefore, I hope that
within a reasonable time we will be able
to make progress with this ameliorative
Measure.

With regard to the matter of the
reform of local government in our midst,
that is occupying the constant attention
of my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Rates). No one who understands local
government and all its intricacies can
expect a Bill to be introduced so soon
after the issue of the Report which itself,
I think, took two and a half or three
years to prepare. No time will be lost,
and I am hopeful that good will result.
I am most hopeful that the life of the
whole of the people of Ulster will be
greatly benefited by the outcome of the
consideration that the Home Office have
given to the Report.
I think we may congratulate ourselves
after the expiration of another twelve
months that law and order are maintained
in our midst (hon. Members: Hear,
hear) and that we can give due credit
to the members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary who are so actively engaged in
protecting life and property, and in
guiding the affairs entrusted to their
hands. The longer I have observed the
activities and growth of our new force
the prouder I am of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Then it is also a great gratification to
me to be able to pay a tribute to the
smooth working of the various Departments. I think we may say that
they are now established upon a basis

The Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) said that no mention was made in
the Speech in regard to economy. There
is no necessity whatever to refer to that

"efficiency
and economy.' (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Efficiency has
been our aim and it is
economy that my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) has
accomplished. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We are quite satisfied that there
is no waste, and we are quite satisfied
that the public get full value from the
establishments that have been set up.
I now come to the outlook for the
coming year, and in regard to that I
would like to follow what the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Lloyd
Campbell) said as to the industry with
which he is principally associated-I
refer to linen. It is some satisfaction at
all events to see the fruits of a little
labour I expended when I had the
pleasure of meeting the Prime Minister
of Canada in Ottawa after his election
about eighteen months ago. He was
kind enough to invite me to give an expression of opinion on the subject of our
linen industry. In the conversation
which took place I was able to point out
that in Canada it is almost impossible to
manufacture linen such as we can make
in Belfast, that there was no necessity in
Canada to have protection from the point
of view of protecting the industry, and
that so far as revenue was concerned
Canada could well afford to give us in
the North of Ireland, from which so many
of her sons have gone to people that
great Dominion, a helping hand.
I was pleased indeed to see just a few
days ago in the public Press an announcement that a reduction would also be made
in the British preferential rates on the
finer grades of linen. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) That coupled with the
work being done to further advertise our
goods not only in the United States of
America but also elsewhere will, I hope,
assist in the return, if I may call it, of
the prosperity which has shown itself in
that great industry.
With regard to shipbuilding, of course
we are all delighted to see that what is
known as "the little yard" has been
acquired by those to whom we wish every
possible success in their efforts to bring
back the old prosperity to that side of
the Lough. I need hardly say that there
is no body of men rejoices more than my
colleagues and myself do when we find
that the numbers of those unemployed
are steadily decreasing. I am glad to
hear from my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) that during the past week the
figures are considerably better. I think
he said they were 1,400 down since the
last return was made. That shows an
improvement.
The next point to which I desire to
refer is the tourist traffic. I am delighted
to observe that the Ulster Tourist
Development Association is working on
exactly the lines we would all like them to
work. There is no portion of tourist development that they do not inquire into
and take charge of in a most able
inanner, and our thanks are due to those
who devote themselves voluntarily to
helping to attract to our area those who
undoubtedly bring with them money to
our hotels, to our railways, to our motor
cars, and to our lodging houses. This
coming year will be greatly helped, I
have no doubt, by the fact that the Grand
Prix, if I may use that term in connection with the great motor race, is to
take place in the Ulster area. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I think it is a
feather in our cap that we have
been able to secure the premier race of
the season for our area. I hope that
everything will pass off without any untoward accident and that those who come
to our shores will benefit from their visit.

I myself was, I must say, astounded by
the few facts that came to my notice a
day or two ago. From the census of
agricultural production recently taken
throughout the Six Counties it is to be
observed that the cutput of our area in

for that year
output in cattle
£3,500,000. Our poultry industry is
therefore almost as valuable as our cattle
industry. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
In 1923 our poultry population was
6,682,000, and in 1927 it was 7,896,000, an
increase of slightly over 1,000,000 birds.
We have a much larger poultry population
per acre in Northern Ireland than in any
other part of the British Isles. In this
connection the following figures may be
of interest. The number of poultry of
all kinds per 100 acres of crops and
pasture in Northern Ireland is 321; in
the Irish Free State 176; in England and
Wales 133; and in Scotland 121. Our
poultry industry-and this is what I wish
to emphasize especially for consumption
throughout our area-is capable of a
very much further expansion. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The population
might easily be increased by 50 per cent.
Our County Committees of Agriculture
are doing a great deal through their
schemes to encourage poultry keeping,
and the poultry industry could be developed much more rapidly if further funds
were made available for the purpose.
The development of this industry has
three important advantages. Production
can be increased at a much more rapid
rate than in the case of any other agricultural product, the capital cost involved is
relatively very small and the market
in the British Isles is almost unlimited. Great Britain imports annually
£20,000,000 worth of eggs excluding the
£1,250,000 which have been received
from Northern Ireland.

I say that there is a tale that reflects

Members: Hear, hear). If that can be
done in one small industry of that sort
the outlook is unlimited as far as other

is undoubtedly a fact that no matter

As an earnest of our practical sympathy

Mr. MCALLISTER: I would like to

With regard to the Speech itself, I

Instead of being a source of inspiration

was in a most fruitful and progressive

now considering, after seven years of

most particular of those was to find the

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I would like to
join with those who have spoken in congratulating the mover and seconder of
the Address in reply to the Gracious
Speech from the Throne. They have
done their work remarkably well. Those
of us who have listened to many such

debates outside controversy are very dull.
In this case, both speeches have been interesting and helpful.
I was particularly struck with one part
of the speech of the seconder, in which
he dealt with the question of roads, because nearly seven years ago I suggested
in this House that the main roads in
Northern Ireland should be a national
and not a local charge. Our whole
system of transportation has changed in
the last 25 or 30 years, and it is most
unfair that local people should be asked
to maintain the local roads which are
now used far more by people outside than
by people who live inside their districts.
I hope the Government will give this
matter earnest and serious consideration.
I think, on the whole, you will find that
the thing will work out much better; it
is really a question for the Government
to go into, and I am quite sure they will
do so.
I wanted to deal specially with the
speech of the Leader of the Opposition,
and I am sorry to see that he is not in
his place. On the whole, it is a speech
that we on this side of the House could
not take much exception to. I object to
his conclusions, but I must say that he
puts his arguments forward with the
great ability that he always shows, with
great courtesy, and with consideration
for political opponents. But I think he
was scarcely fair to us on this side of the
House when he spoke of our self-complacency and of our ignorance of the
conditions under which the masses of the
people in this Province live. I venture
to say there is not one of us on this side
of the House who is not just as anxious
to help the masses of the people as the
members of the Socialist party and the
Opposition generally are, and we give
them full credit for their sincerity in this
matter. Then he twitted us with reading Socialist speeches, but surely that is
not a great offence. If you want to be
correct yourself you always want to see
what the failures of your opponents are
like, and I make it a point to read every
Socialist speech I can lay my hands on,
because I find it most useful as a corrective, and as something that keeps me
from making economic blunders.
The Leader of the Opposition pointed
out that the great object of Socialism was
to develop individuality. I never came
across such a contradiction in terms in my
lifetime, because how individuality can be
developed under the system of Socialism
passes my comprehension. He asked
what opportunity is there for one in a
spinning mill or factory to develop his
individuality. I would like to ask him
this. Suppose all the spinning mills and
factories in Northern Ireland were
taken over and run by the Government, and that Government a
Socialist Government, what greater opportunity would those engaged in the
spinning mills and factories have for developing their individuality than they
have to-day? Surely, there is nothing
more absurd than to say that the present system crushes any hope of individuality being developed. On the
contrary, it gives us every chance of extending and developing the individuality
of the people.
Then, I am very glad to find that in
the Leader of the Opposition I have got
an able recruit in the cause of economy.
I believe that all Governments and all
public bodies are the better for being
criticised with regard to their expenditure, and that we should see on every
occasion that we get twenty shillings
worth of value for every twenty shillings
we spend. But I did not know until now
that one of the objects of Socialism was
economy. On the contrary, I have
always looked on Socialism as a very extravagant system, and have always found

the Socialists very anxious to spend the

I
The Leader of the Opposition spoke
with regard to peace in industry.
have no desire to do him an injustice, and
I am quite sure, that so far as he is

working together in harmony, that we can

We all deplore the depression in the

Leader of the Opposition or any of his
friends who may be following in this

for any of us to criticise, but let us get

particular industry-I do not care whether
linen, shipbuilding, or any other.
Just for a moment the Leader of the
Opposition-I will not say exactly that he
lost his temper-almost lost his temper
with regard to the Bill that is to be
brought in regarding Unemployment Insurance. May I point out to him in that
connection that the Bill that has been
passed by the Imperial Parliament is one
that has been founded upon the Blanesburgh Report, that two of the members
of that Committee were two distinguished
members of the Socialist party, and that
the Report of that Committee was a unanimous one? Why, therefore, he should
lash himself into a fury over the proposal
of the Government in this matter is something that I fail to understand.
I was pleased to note that he has
given full expression, as the hon.
Member who has just sat down (Mr.
McAllister) has also done, co his desire to
encourage the Government in the matter
of the Loans Guarantee Act. Under that
Act good service has been rendered to the
cause of employment in Northern Ireland
during very trying times, and I think it
augurs well for the future that all parties
in the House are agreed to unite and to
work together harmoniously for the good
of the Province, and in order to press
forward anything that may be for our
mutual advantage.
The Leader of the Opposition referred,
and I think rightly, to the great development that has taken place in the artificial
silk industry. Here the Government has
helped one factory that has been set up
outside Ballymena, but in Great Britain
at the present time a good many important companies are being established to
manufacture artificial silk, and I can say
this from personal experience, that they
find no difficulty whatever in getting the
necessary capital. There are certain
conditions that are necessary for the
manufacture of artificial silk, and if suitable sites are to be found in different parts
of Northern Ireland, it ought to be possible to encourage those people to come
here. Personally, I think that Northern
Ireland especially the rural districts in
Northern Ireland-is in some ways much
better suited for manufacturing artificial
silk than industrial areas in Great
Britain.
I am quite sure that what has been
said in this debate to-day will help to rivet
attention to this matter, and people like
myself who spend a good deal of time on
the other side of the Channel will not fail
to bring to the notice of people interested
in this industry the fact that all parties
in this House are combined in their
anxiety to help industry in every possible
way.
With regard to the franchise for
women, speaking for myself, I can only
say that I have supported the franchise
for women for over thirty years, and that
I have always advocated it inside this
House as well as outside. I believe that
women should be put on exactly the same
standing as men. I see no reason whatever why there should be any differentiation, and when the time comes to deal
with this question I am quite sure that
this House will follow the example of
Great Britain and do the right thing by
putting women on exactly the same electoral basis as men.

My hon. Friend the Leader of the

I need not refer to the Bann except

With regard to electrical development

only deal with this question by applying

We can only deal with it in that way, and

do agree with the words of the Prime

Home Affairs whether he can state the
total licence duty paid by public service

1927, and the amount paid in rates by the

period.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The total
Road Fund Licence Duty paid in respect
of Public Service Vehicles of all kinds,
including taxis, hackney motor cars and
omnibuses during the year was £60,461.
Of this sum the heavier motor omnibus, i.e., those over 2 tons weight, paid
£20,987 6s 8d.
I have not complete returns of the

1927, and it would take some little time

can, however, give the hon. Member an

I
Railways wholly within Northern Ireland paid about £20,000 in rates.
Railways partly in Northern Ireland
and partly in the Free State paid altogether £66,087. If this total is appor
tioned on the basis of mileage, it would
give a sum of £38,000 paid in Northern

The total rates paid in Northern Ireland by railways may, therefore, be

Mr. KYLE: Are the figures the
right hon. Gentleman gave us the figures
for Northern Ireland Railways only, or

Sir DAWSON BATES: No. They are

State. I gave the total amount paid, and

£38,000 estimated as the rates paid in
Northern Ireland on a mileage basis.
WOODEN BUNGALOWS IN
NEWTOWNARDS.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received
a report of the discussion at the Newtownards Rural District Council, on the
25th February, on the subject of wooden
bungalows for city workers; whether he
is prepared to issue instructions to this
body to the end that city workers may
still retain their bungalows and thereby
gain in health by having the advantage of
a home by the sea or in the country.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen a
report of the proceedings of the Newtownards Rural District Council, on the
25th February.
That Council had before it a motion
proposing that the further erection of
temporary structures for human habitation be not approved. This motion was
not adopted, but the Council decided to
consider the question of amending the
conditions to be complied with, in the
erection of temporary dwellings for human
habitation.
It will be seen, therefore, that the
Council has not prohibited the erection of
temporary houses, and it is very desirable
that they should (as proposed) frame
rules ensuring that these dwellings are
erected with due regard to the requirements of Public Health.

Mr. McHUGH: At the close of the debate last night I was endeavouring to
impress upon the Government how
essential it is that they should come to
the rescue of the small farmers of
Northern Ireland; otherwise they are
down and out. I must respectfully submit that the grant the Government have
given is entirely inadequate,
and
that it is
is practically of no value
whatever to the small tenant farmers.
I would ask the Minister of Agriculture,
who is thoroughly conversant with the
farmers of County Fermanagh, to scan the
situation. The amount of money which
each tenant will derive from the special
grant given by the Government is 4d. in
the £, and the County Council of Fermanagh has this year raised the rates 3d.
in the £. Therefore, if you take a small
farm of £5 valuation, what does the
occupier receive? The large sum of 5d.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Is the hon. Member in favour
of the withdrawal of that grant to the
farmers?
Mr. McHUGH: What I am in favour
of is that you confine the grant to tenant
farmers with a valuation of under £20.
You will see quite clearly that the grant
at present is of no assistance to these poor
people. I am speaking of farmers of
three and four-acre holdings, who are in
a state of bankruptcy at the present time.
If they are called upon to pay their liabilities the only course open to their creditors
would be to turn these people out. This
state of affairs arose solely through the
terrible disease known as abortion of
cattle, and I attribute that solely to the
Government rushing through this House
the Scrub Bull or Improvement of Cattle
Bill. The moment you passed that Bill
you put it into operation, and you compelled a farmer to keep only a registered
bull. Then you intimidated him by
telling him distinctly that if he did not
have this animal registered, and if it was
not of a certain quality he would be
liable to a severe penalty.
The result was that small farmers along
the mountain sides sold their cattle. For
three long years the Government were
dreaming, and never passed a Bill for the
purpose of enabling farmers to replace the
cattle they had sold. I know of my own
knowledge that people had to travel
almost five miles with their cattle to have
them served with bulls that were approved
by the Ministry of Agriculture, and when
they arrived there was no less than eight
or nine animals waiting to be served. The
result of that was that this terrible disease
became prevalent throughout Northern
Ireland, and I regret to say it is prevalent along the mountain sides at the
present moment. I am surprised that
when faced with a charge of indifference
and apathy the Government did not
immediately bring in a relief Bill to try
to do away with what is known as the
"scrub" bull.
I trust the Government will take into
consideration the question I have just
put before them that this special grant
will be given solely to the small tenant
farmers, and that no person will receive
it whose valuation is over £20. That
will prevent the well-to-do farmer and
the landlord from receiving any benefit.

what I am about to state now is not borrowed from the opinions of others, but is
the result of my own experience. I have
been selling farms for the last twenty
years, both in Northern Ireland and in
the Free State, and I find no difference

Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Contributory Pensions.

But humbly regret that no mention

the Widows', Orphans' and Old Age
Contributory Pensions Act in the direction of correcting the inadequacy of

It will be remembered that when this
Measure was passing through the House
I made a speech on behalf of my colleagues, in the course of which I stated
that I believed no basis to a Pensions Act
could be satisfactory unless that basis was
a non-contributory one. The widows'
and orphans' portion of this Act has
been in operation for a period of two
years, and during that time I have seen
nothing to alter the view I expressed on
that occasion. In point of fact, I have
seen much to confirm my view, because I
know of my own personal experience that
dozens of people have been denied pensions
on one pretext or another, pretexts which
to me appear to be flimsy and unsatisfactory. I am satisfied that had our
advice been accepted on that occasion
a larger number of people would be in
receipt of widows', and orphans', and
old-age pensions than the number in
receipt of those pensions at the present
time.
Contributory Pensions 156
Debate on the Address-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
I am sure every member of the House,
regardless of the seat he occupies, has
been importuned by many of his constitutents to see if it would be possible to
have pensions conceded where they had
been refused by the Department of the
Minister of Labour. I have dealt with
a large number of cases personally.
Many of them I have taken up with the
two heads of the Department, and if I
have not been able to get satisfaction, I do
not attribute that shortcoming to either
of the heads of the department. I blame
the limitations of the Act for disqualifying those people from receiving
pensions.
One case that came to my own personal observation was that of a lady
whose husband died at 11-30 p.m. on 3rd
January, 1926, half-an-hour before the
time the Act came into operation.
In
this case the husband died half an
hour too soon, or the lady was
too truthful in not
recording the
death as having taken place thirtyone minues later, because had the husband either died thirty-one minutes
later, or had the lady registered the death
as having taken place thirty-one minutes
later she would have been entitled to a
pension of 10s a week for life. I think
that lady is as much entitled to a pension
as is any widow whose husband dies after
4th January, 1926.
that
There is a further shortcoming as far
as this Act is concerned in regard to
women whose husbands died before the
operation of the Act. Surely the Government do not mean to contend
a lady whose husband dies before 4th
January, 1926, is not as much entitled
to a widow's pension as one whose husband dies after that date. Many glaring
anomalies can be pointed out so far as
the working of this Act is concerned.
A case has been cited to me-I have not
personal experience of this case, but
have reason to believe the circumstances
are absolutely correct-of a man who attained the age of 70 years before 2nd
January, 1928. He had been paying
health benefit since the year 1912 up to
a few days before 2nd January, 1928.
He paid approximately sixteen years, and
because he became 70 a few days prior to
2nd January of this year his wife, who
is just 65 years of age, was denied the
old-age contributory pension.
I believe there is a great deal of hardship entailed in the case I am citing, because the man had been paying both health
and unemployment contributions for a
period of sixteen years. In point of fact,
he had been paying for approximately two
years for the purposes of qualifying, and
simply because he had attained the age of
70 before 2nd January, 1928, his wife,
who is 65 years of age, is denied that oldage pension. A pathetic circumstance in
this case, as stated to me, is that within
the past few weeks the husband has been
discharged from his employment, and the
only income the old couple have to keep
body and soul together is 10s a week.
I think that if I ceased at this juncture
and did not utter another word I should
have proved beyond the shadow of a
doubt that it is now necessary to amend
the Act. Further anomalies can be
pointed out. A grave objection I would
offer against the Act is this: that a person
who has not been able to satisfy the
statutory conditions, and who has attained the age of 65, has no further
opportunities of qualifying. Perhaps
some Members of the House are not as
familiar with the working of this Act as
are some of us who come into actual contact with it. I think I am right in observing that for the receipt of the
widows', and orphans' and old-age contributory pensions there are three main
tests. The first test is that the male
parent is required to have five years' continuous membership. In the event of
this membership lapsing he has subsequently to pay 104 contributions. In
addition to these two conditions it is
necessary in the two years immediately
preceding the date of his claim to maintain an average level of 36 stamps in one
case and 26 in the other.
Take the case of a man who has attained
the age of 65 years who, through a prolonged period of unemployment or possibly of illness, has been unable to pay
those 104 contributions. The Act at the
present time states that having attained
the age of 65 he is no longer eligible to
pay either health insurance or unemployment insurance. The man might be
physically fit and might be as able to do
a hard day's work as a person twenty
years younger, but as the Act stands at
present it is absolutely impossible for that.
man to qualify even if he is fully employed. The Parliamentary Secretary
(Mr. Gordon) shakes his head. I am
proceeding from the particular to the
general, because I had a case of this kind
157 Debate on the Address-
Contributory Pensions 158
8 MARCH 1928
which I took up with the Parliamentary
Secretary, and unless my memory is
playing me tricks, which it seldom does,
the statement contained in the letter from
the Parliamentary Secretary was that
this man was unable to have his cards
stamped any more because he had attained the age of 65.
I know an employer is compelled to
stamp the card of a person who has
reached 65 years
of age,
and I agree with
that principle, because if it was not
adopted the probability is that an
employer would give a preference in some
degree to a man who had attained 65
years, because he would escape payment
of a contribution in respect of that
person. But while the employer has
failed to pay his own portion, and in
many cases where the man is willing to
pay his own portion, this Act restricts his
right to pay his contribution, and incidentally to qualify to obtain old age
pension. I hope I am wrong in that
statement.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): You are wrong.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I am glad to
have that information. If the Minister
is right in the statement he makes, and
I am wrong, I certainly will reopen the
case with them that has been turned
down by the Department.
I think a further hardship is inflicted
where the wives of men who have attained
the age of 70 years are not allowed to
draw the old-age pension.
I think a
grave hardship has been inflicted here,
because the income has been substantially
reduced in the home, and where the husband has been paying for a number of
years I do not think the wife should be
precluded from drawing the old age
pension through her husband's insurance.
i believe a very grave omission in regard
to this Act has been this, that a safeguardng clause of some kind was not inserted
to prevent unscrupulous employers from
taking advantage of this Act I do not
offer this objection primarily or principally against this Act in particular. I
know very wel!, and I am prepared to
acknowledge it if the Act was placed on
a non-contributory basis, unscrupulous
employers would be prepared to take
advantage of the men's pension whether
that pension was given as a contributory
or a non-contributory one.
was
But I have noticed in the Press,
particularly the Labour Press of England,
where many employers have taken advantage of the payment of the pension
at 65 for the purpose of reducing the
wages of the men. I think in the main
that has been done by Tory employers
and Tory Lords, and if I wanted to take
up the time of the House I could give a
long recital of the names, particularly
of Tory landlords in England, who have
taken the benefit and advantage of this
alleged beneficent Act-that has been
noticed by the Tory Government of Great
Britain-for the purpose of reducing the
men's wages.
And when I use this
argument it will show that if the Act
on a non-contributory basis,
all the employers would not believe
they had as reasonable a case to
make the deduction as they have
when the Act is contributory, because
when one of these gentlemen was called
upon to try to justify his action in reducing the men's wages, he said he had
a perfect right to do so because he was
paying the employers' portion of the contribution. That excuse, to me, is not
satisfactory by any means at all. I do
not believe advantage should be taken of
the Act. I do not believe a person being
in receipt of 10s a week would justify an
employer, under any circumstances, in
attempting to reduce that person's wages.
But when the employer is paying his
portion it lends colour to his argument
which would not be there if it was placed
on a non-contributory basis. I hope that
if the Government propose to introduce
an Amending Bill of any kind that this
point will not be overlooked, and any employer who attempts to take advantage of
the operation of the Act for the purpose
of reducing wages will be penalized, because I do not believe it ever was the intention of the Government to introduce
a Bill of this character to permit employers to take advantage of it for the
purpose of reducing wages. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Of course it would
be possible, had I desired, to multiply the
cases I have cited indefinitely.

I think this Amendment, as it stands
on the Order Paper, asks that the amount
should be made more adequate than it
is at present. In that connection I would
like to make the point of the men being
forced out of industry, and I believe
there is a great deal of substance in this
point, because I am told on fairly reliable
Debate on the Address-
Contributory Pensions
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. W. McMullen]
authority, although I did not read the
speech myself, that the Minister of
Labour thought he was called upon to
address a rebuke to a number of employers in Northern Ireland for taking
advantage of the pensions the men were
in receipt of. There must have been
some substance in the grievance when the
Minister of Labour felt called upon to
make a speech. And, therefore, if the
statement is true that a large number of
people have been disemployed as a result
of receiving the pension, then I hold the
amount is absolutely inadequate for the
purpose of maintaining a man and his
wife and possibly a dependant of some
kind, although there may not be a large
number of dependants. I am aware of the
fact that people in the neighbourhood of
65 or 70 years of age are not likely to
have many dependants, unless they are
physically incapable in some direction.
Even to maintain the man and his wife
the sum is hopelessly inadequate.
If this Act had not been put on a contributory basis I imagine it would be possible
for a person to receive unemployment
benefit up to 70 years of age, thereby
removing a great many of the hardships
inflicted on the people at the present time
by unemployment benefit being stopped
on their becoming 65 and their being compelled to exist on 10s. per week. It is
not my intention to weary the House. As
I pointed out, I could multiply these cases
indefinitely. I believe I have said suffi
cient. If not, the experience of every
Member of this House has been such since
this Act operated as to prove conclusively
that there are many defects and shortcomings under it. I want to ask the
Government to remedy these defects and,
if possible, to adopt the suggestion, even
at this late stage, which we made two
years ago, instead of its being contributory to make it non-contributory. If you
do that you will have a much more satisfactory basis than at the present time.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have pleasure in
congratulating the hon. Member on the
very clear and reasonable way he has put
his views before the House. I do not
agree with all he has said, but at the same
time I admit that in any scheme of this
kind, whether contributory or non-conuributory, there are bound to be border-line
cases and consequently cases of hardship.
When you come to deal with the question
of pensions you must have a test of some
kind unless Parliament is prepared to give
pensions to everyone, to those who do not
require them as well as to those who do, to
the rich as well as to the poor. Under the
scheme I do not think that that was the
intention of Parliament. In connection
with our non-contributory scheme which
the hon. Member has advocated he is just
as well aware as I am that there are necessarily border-line cases. There the test is
a means test, and a very difficult test it is
to administer, because where persons do
not keep a profit and loss account it is extremely difficult to estimate what their
means are for instance, what the value
of a small holding is under existing conditions.
Now, this, in my opinion, is a great
measure. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
It is worthy, in my opinion, to be placed
alongside those other great measures of
social reform, which have made the
United Kingdom distinguished throughout the world. The hon. Member has
cited cases of hardship. The one about
the women's husband dying a few hours
before the appointed day is a case in
point.
the
There, undoubtedly, if
husband had lived a few hours longer she
would have been entitled to a pension.
But the case is not as hard as it would
appear in the first instance, because if
the woman had had children dependent
upon her, that is, of school age, she would
have received the pension, notwithstanding the fact that her husband had
died, admittedly, a few hours before the
appointed day. Now, as a matter of fact,
I would like the House to realize the
great benefit that this Bill has been to
our industrial classes in Northern Ireland
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear), and how
generous it is in the main, because although insurance is the test applied, it
has been applied in a most generous way.
There is one misunderstanding which
I am glad to have the opportunity of removing. It is thought by many because
persons have contributed to our Health
Insurance schemes that, therefore, because
the Act has been tacked on in a measure
to that scheme, they have contributed to
this pension scheme. Of course nothing
of the kind is the fact. They only begin
to contribute to this pension scheme when
they begin to pay contributions, and,
obviously, when these persons contributed
to the Health Insurance scheme they only
contributed in order to obtain the benefits
which that particular Act gave these contributors, namely, sickness benefit, disable-
Debate on the Address-
Contributory Pensions
8 MARCH 1928
ment benefit, maternity benefit, and sanitorium benefit, and they did not contribute, as I have said, in order to obtain
widows' and orphans' and old-age contributory pensions at 65. The Health
Insurance Measure is simply a test of
whether the person has been an insured
person within the four corners of the Act
or not.
Everyone who is entitled under the
provisions of the Act to get benefit, I
am glad to be in a position to say, has
already obtained it. If it can be shown
that a wrong has been done to anyone,
and if any hon. Member will bring that
particular case before either the Parliamentary Secretary or myself we will be
glad to have the case reinvestigated. But
I would point out that the House left us
no discretionary power in connection with
the matter. But what the Act did do was
this, that it allowed the benefit to be paid
to a great number of persons who really,
strictly speaking, were never entitled
to it at all. For instance, already
no fewer than 3,569 widows, who are
termed pre-Act widows and whose
husbands never contributed a penny
in order to obtain the advantages of this
Act for their wives, have obtained pensions. Surely that cannot be described
as a cruel provision. Again, allowances
have been paid to no less than 8,000
children of widows whose husbands
never contributed anything in order to
obtain allowances for their children.
Further, 452 pre-Act orphans have obtained pensions under similar circumstances.
Mr. KYLE: How many widows have
been denied?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have not the information as to how many widows have
been denied, but I am in a position to say
that no widow has been denied who is
entitled to receive the money.
Mr. KYLE: It is not a widow's
pension.
Mr. ANDREWS: No less than 8,885
old people have obtained these contributory pensions at 65, and a great advantage, admittedly, it has been to them.
Again, 9,046 persons have obtained pensions at 70 free of certain restrictions as
to means under this Act. In other words
there are 36,000 persons in our midst
benefiting by this Act alone. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). And yet hon.
Members opposite very frequently in their
speeches on public platforms instead of
giving credit where credit is due seem to
confine their remarks to the extent of saying that the Act is defective, cruel, and
all the rest of it. One point that is made
with considerable frequency is that 10s is
not sufficient.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: I never said it was,
but 10s is better than nothing. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). Besides, what
you have to remember is this, that as regards the widows the 10s as a rule does
not stand by itself. Take the average
workman with a wife and three children,
the 10s as long as those children are of
school age is changed into 21s, not a bad
beginning to build upon. Then let us
look at this side of the picture. Hon.
Members know just as I do that before
this Widows' and Orphans' Act came in
at all there were a great many charitable
associations connected with our churches,
connected with our political parties and
connected with other organizations.
These, I understand, continue to
function. They may not be distributing
the funds in the same way, but they are
continuing to function and to give an
enormous amount of relief which is added
to this sum which this Act gives. Then,
again, in most instances there is nothing
to prevent a person receiving benefits
continuing to work, so that they have an
opportunity themselves of adding to the
pension. Therefore, I say without
hesitation that what may be described
as an insufficiency itself can be turned
into a reasonable sufficiency.
Now, I want to go one step further.
Hon. Members forget that in scheme
any
of the kind you have got to balance
between contributions on the one hand
and benefits on the other. Are hon.
Members advocating increased benefits at
the expense of increased contributions?
The matter must be based upon an
actuarial foundation or else of course it
would mean disaster. Therefore, for
those reasons and for many others I have
no hesitation in saying that this is a
great Measure of social reform. I am not
going to say that it is the last word in
connection with the matter. (Hon.
Debate on the Address-

Members: Hear, hear). It is the beginning, and as years go on we may have
to build upon this Measure a greater
Measure, but many of those hardships to
which hon. Members have referred are
due, as they will admit, to the bringing
into operation of the Act and they will
disappear without any amendment of the
Act in the course of a very short time.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Therefore, I would appeal to hon.
Members to give the Act an opportunity

one and inseparable.

It is like the argument which was
used yesterday with regard to lard purchase by the hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone (Mr. Elliott) with the same
grace and exquisite skill which we associate with the hippopotamus. That argument was effectively answered by the only

Mr. KYLE: Instead of that you take

insurance scheme and link it

[Mr. Kyle]
Act consists of very little else but defects
to those people who have been denied

Like the hon. Member (Mr. William.
McMullen) who moved this Amendment,
I have had some pitifui cases brought to

woman who worked in a weaving factory
from she was thirteen years of age.
She
is now 66. During the war she inherited
some little money, and she and her sister
bought a little shop. As a result of the

She went
back to work two years ago, and has

(Mr. William McMullen) pointed out.

this
