Debate on the Address-
Leasehold Tenure
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gyle]
debate because there was a matter rather
personal to me at that time. Since that
time the thing I then referred to has
taken place. The lease expired on some
property I was interested in and I was
landed out. I was not able to come to
any terms with my landlord. That is the
danger I think most leaseholders are in.
The landlord has an exaggerated idea of
the value of the premises-
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. GYLE--and instead of coming
to terms, instead of having a fair rent
court set up so that we would be enabled
to arrive at the real value as between
landlord and tenant the landlord has an
exaggerated idea and insists on having
possession of his premises. After getting
possession of the premises and putting
them on the market he very often finds
that the tenant was correct, and that the
landlord was entirely out as regards the
value.
I know of many instances in Northern
Ireland at the present time where the
leases are running out and where offers
have been made to the landlord in which
in my opinion and in the opinion of many
people well able to judge were equitable
and have been refused by the landlord,
and these tenants and leaseholders are
going to be put to a considerable amount
of expense simply because we have not
got a fair rents court so far as leaseholders
are concerned. I wish to impress on the
Government the necessity of expediting
this Committee so that we may have their
report as soon as possible, and after
getting the report we will have the matter
turned into law so that many leaseholders
whose leases are running out at the
present time may not be put to unnecessary expense. I have great pleasure now
in supporting the Amendment and hope
the Government may see their way to
agree to something.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think hon.
Members will agree that the subject
raised is one of the greatest possible difficulty, and it was for that reason a committee was set up. The Committee is
presided over by a most eminent lawyer

is rather ridiculous for the hon. Member

Government have set up this Committee

From what I know of the chairman of
that Committee and I may add that my

Sir DAWSON BATES: My point is
this, that I imagine that these gentlemen who are giving valuable time-and
their time is valuable-if they thought

moment take part in a pure farce.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: They do not know
the Government.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I point
out that this Committee was set up to

Friend, the Member for East Belfast,

the difficulties are far greater than he

I understand they are proposing to hold

inonth. They have already asked various

I really cannot see what more the Government can do in the meantime. After
this assurance that the Government were

see the futility of moving this Amendment.

Sir DAWSON BATES: It may shorten
discussion if I state to my hon. Friend
that it is sometimes difficult to get suitable people to serve, especially gentlemen
engaged in the law. I tried to get the
best Committee, and I am sure the House
will agree it is a most excellent one.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I
think the promise was made this time
last year that a Committee would be set
up to inquire into the subject. I really
have no fault to find with the composition
of the Committee. I think it is constituted in a way that will probably give
confidence to the people generally of
Northern Ireland. But I do feel this is
a question of great urgency. I am not
going to labour at all the point of the
necessity for this, because I think the
fact that the Government have set up a
Committee to inquire is proof that they
themselves feel that a case has been made
out and that legislation is needed. Therefore, I do not propose to go into the
merits of this question to any extent
to-day.
I have the feeling myself that the cause
of this delay might have been that the
Government of Northern Ireland wanted
to see really what would occur in connection with the Bill before the Imperial
Parliament. It was stated here, I think
it was in the speech of the Prime Minister
two years ago when this question was discussed, that if legislation was passed by
the Imperial Parliament this Parliament
would be delighted to follow on similar
lines. I do not know if that was the
reason for the delay in setting up this
Committee. They wanted to see how
the cat would jump in regard to the Bill
before the Imperial House, and to see what
would really happen when this Bill came
before the Lords. Very strong opposition was put up to this Bill. Lord
Carson proposed an Amendment in the
House of Lords that would have been
fatal to the Bill. For some time the
fate of the Bill in the Imperial House
was hanging in the balance. Fortunately
it got through. While that Bill is a
faulty Measure in some respects, it lays
down great principles and foundations on
which will be built a structure that will
give even-handed justice between two
sections of the community, and it has
rung the death knell of the present
system of landlords in England.
We are not out to advocate that the
landlord should be penalized. Landlords
are just like other classes of the community. I suppose there are good, bad
and indifferent among them. What we
are out against is the present system, a
system that gives a class a monopoly, a
system that puts the power in the hands
of a class to confiscate the property
created by the business capacity, ingenuity
and energy of another class. I confine
myself largely to the urgency of this
question. We will take the opinion here
of Bushmills. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Mr. P. O'NEILL: You would rather
have Comber.
Mr GEORGE HENDERSON: I hope
it will not develop into a licensing debate. (Laughter). At a public meeting
at Portrush the case of Bushmills was put
forward. It appeared in the public
papers. "That the inhabitants of Bushmills were loyal law-abiding citizens"
Nobody will dispute that.

"That all
they asked from the landlord was fair
terms and a straight deal. Their
landlords' terms were, in their opinion,
monstrously unfair and unjust.
""
Their
leases were for 99 years and the unexpired
term ran from two months to round about
six years.'
That is to say very much property would revert into the landlords'
hands in April next. Surely that is
proof of the urgency of this question,
because every day this question is delayed injustices are happening over the
Province.
Just another instance of what is going
on in Bushmills. "They instanced two
cases of landlord tyranny in Bushmills.
In one case, where the lease was not up
till April, the property was sold six
months before over the tenant and this
landlord never spent to the extent of a
bucket of whitewash on this property.
The ground rent accruing to that landlord from houses in Bushmills amounted
to £52. He has made a valuation, has
offered the property for sale, and the
price asked for this income of £52 is
£9,870. That would bring him an income
of almost £500 a year at five per cent.
This landlord has never spent a single
shilling to increase the letting value of
these premises. I think you will agree
that that is unfair.
Why could not this Committee have
been set up last year, and why could not
their report have been ready for this

cannot create the land, he has to take

is stated, in fact, that the rates are a

Mr. HANNA indicated dissent.
Mr. LEEKE: If the Parliamentary
Secretary denies it I accept his denial of
course, though I am afraid the Portrush
people would not agree with him. What
I believe the Government will do is that
they will get this Commission to sit, carry
on to the end of this Session, and the

go to the country, and in their next manifesto they will state that they are going to
introduce legislation affecting the town
tenants. I would suggest that if they

Bill retrospective for five years. That
would cover all the interests and safeguard
those whose leases are rapidly expiring.
There is a great deal of interest taken
in this particular Measure. Everyone
in places like Portrush, which is a famous
place for it-indeed I might say that
Portrush was the pioneer town in this particular movement is interested in it. It
affects all the rural areas, the small towns
and villages throughout the Six Counties,
it affects the larger towns and cities, and
it even affects the capital of the Six
Counties, the city of Belfast. There was
a meeting held in Ballymena recently and
said
one of the speakers, a Mr. Morrow,
that he had discovered that all over
Ballymena there had been large increases
in ground rents on renewal, and he instanced a case where the rent was increased from £2 15s 9d to £50.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Shame.
Mr. LEEKE: What sort of a landlord was he who increased the rent from
£2 15s 9d to £50? Do the Government
not honestly believe that it is time such
a tyrant was controlled?
The land movement and the fight of the farmers of
Ireland to get some fixity of tenure began
away back in 1881. It is continuing to
this day, and the fight is not finished yet.
I hope the Government will not place us
in the same position in this fight for
security of tenure for the town tenants.
I hope they will face the question in a
practical way. The landlords of to-day
are mostly shrewd business men, and they
well understand that this movement is a
popular movement, and that eventually
the demand must be agreed to. They
well know that the best way is to
have it dealt with immediately. If the
Government, as I say, are sincere in this
matter then when the Commission has sat
and has issued its report, if they want
to show the people of Northern Ireland
that they really wish to carry out the
views expressed therein let them call a
conference of landlords and tenants, put
before them the evidence of the Commission, ask them do they agree, and then
introduce legislation, and carry it into
effect immediately. That will save all the
strife, all the recrimination, and all the
bitterness which unfortunately held Ireland and split the country in twain for
many years.
Here is a movement, which is a popular
movement, backed by the whole people
of the Six Counties, or ninety per cent.
of them. There is no question of that. It
cannot be denied. Particularly in the
constituency from which the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna) comes everybody is enthusiastic about it. There is
no cause for delay, and I fail to see why
the Government should not carry a
Measure into effect immediately. In the
town of Portrush-and I am not blaming
Lord Antrim-I have known him deal
with many cases in a generous manner.
I want to be fair to the landlords. Nobody wants to take anything from them
that is unfair, but rather that the case
should be dealt with in a fair manner.
But in Portrush there are other landlords
than Lord Antrim. There was a case
which came before the courts yesterday
where the landlord bought at £1,200 and
sold in a few days at £1,900 to the
occupying tenant. There should be some
check put on that form of speculation.
Of course yesterday there was a check
put in this particular case, but I think
the Government should put some broad
check on this sort of thing.
I know another case of a poor man who
came into the town and by his enterprise
built up a very fine business. He took
a place at £20, and to-day that man is
paying £50 for a house for which he
originally paid £20. He built up the
business in it and made it valuable, and
the landlord took advantage of his enterprise.
That should be stopped. As I
said at the beginning of my speech, I hope
it will be more widely advertised that
witnesses are invited to attend before
this Committee, because people are not
quite sure where the Commission is sitting. This would give them an opportunity of putting their cases clearly before the Commission. I hope further that
when this Commission has reported the

(Mr. Archdale): My attention has been

Northern Ireland farmers to grow

PRICE OF LIME.
the
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked
Minister of Agriculture whether his attention has been drawn to the disadvantage which farmers are subject to, owing
to the prohibitive price of lime, and
whether he will consider the introduction
of some scheme that would reduce the
price of this mineral, which is so much
required by the farming community.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am aware of the
fact that the price of lime has considerably increased since 1914, due largely
to the increased cost of labour and the
increased price of coal.
Lime is undoubtedly of benefit when
applied to land which is being cultivated,
especially land of a stiff clay character
and peaty land; but practically all the
experiments carried out for the last ten
years throughout Great Britain and
Ireland indicate that when lime is applied.
to grass land it has little or no effect,
and that much better results can be procured from the application of phosphatic
manures, such as basic slag, superphosphate, mineral phosphates, etc.
I am prepared to consider applications
from owners of lime quarries for loans to
enable them to procure grinding
machinery so that lime could be applied
to land without having to be burnt in a
lime kiln.

BELFAST ELECTRICAL SUB-
STATION.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has seen the proposal of the Belfast Corporation to buy
a piece of land for the erection of an
electrical sub-station; whether he can
state the price that it is proposed to pay
for this property, who is the owner of it,
and whether he is satisfied that the Belfast citizens are not being overcharged.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am aware of the proposal to which the hon. Member refers.
I should explain, however, that the matter is one which lies primarily within the
discretion of the Electricity Commissioners for Northern Ireland, who have
power to grant, or to withhold, sanction
for a loan to cover the expenditure involved. I am informed that in the present case the Electricity Commissioners,
after satisfying themselves as to the
merits of the proposal, have granted the
loan sanction for £1,000 for the purchase
of the site from the trustees of the late
W. W. Kennedy.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman prepared to make representations to
the Electricity Commissioners, in view of
the fact that it has been estimated that
the value of the land, or at least the
price given, is going to be £8,500 an acre.
Is he prepared to make representations to
the Electricity Commissioners to have a
further investigation before they authorise this absolutely inordinate price to be
expended on land for this purpose.
Mr. BARBOUR: No. So far as the
papers which I have gone through reveal,
the ordinary procedure in this connection
has been gone through by the regular
authority. The selection of the land, in
the first instance, is a matter for the Belfast Corporation, and thereafter it is submitted to the Electricity Commissioners,
who are
a semi-independent body, and
they review it in the light of the suitability of the site itself, the purpose intended, and, naturally, in the case of
electricity, in relation to the load which
exists in the neighbourhood which will be
supplied from that station. Having regard to all the circumstances I have not
seen anything of an irregular character,
or any matter that would call for my
intervention, if indeed, it would be appropriate for me to intervene in the
matter.
Mr. KYLE: Do I gather that the
right hon. Gentleman states that he is
prepared to accept responsibility on behalf of the Government for the purchase
of this land at this inordinate price?
Mr. SPEAKER: I understand from
the Minister that it is a matter over which
the Government has no control. Again,
I must remind the hon. Member that he
must not get into the habit of criticising
the action of other elected bodies, whether
the Belfast Corporation or the Board of
Guardians, when the responsibility is
theirs.
Mr. KYLE: I have no desire to criticise other elected bodies, except that we.
as a Parliament, are responsible to some
extent, or have been held responsible, for
the activities of some of the local authorities, and particularly the Belfast Corporation. I was only wanting, if I
could, to see whether or not the Government were prepared to be responsible for
the purchase of this land.
Mr. SPEAKER: That would raise a
very large question. If the Government
became responsible for the deeds and misdeeds of local authorities who are elected
bodies we should be in an impossible
position, and I gather that the Electricity
Commissioners are also not responsible to
the Government.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is quite open to
the ratepayers, if they think fit, to call
for an inquiry into this matter.

of management by Mr. Armour.
On
investigation it appeared that the
signatories to this letter had constituted
themselves a School Committee," and
had not the right to demand the resignation of the manager. As, however, it

there had in fact been a School Committee, the Ministry took steps to have a

[Mr. Robb]
The reply to the question as to whether
the Chief Inspector, who conducted the
inquiry, reported that none of the unsigned and anonymous charges were upheld and substantiated by evidence is in
the negative.
The reply to the question "whether the
Minister of Education then decided to dismiss the case" is also in the negative.
The Ministry as referee, named in the
agreement executed between the manager
and the teacher, having fully considered
the report of the inquiry held by its Chief

May, 1927, that it was prepared to concur should he decide to give the teacher
three months' notice for the purpose of
terminating his employment under the
agreement. The Ministry's concurrence
was granted, as I have pointed out, as a
result of the findings of the inquiry, and
was based upon these alone.

TEACHERS' PENSIONS-TIME AND
MEANS BARRIER.
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has received a copy
of resolutions passed at the recent meeting
of the Northern Retired Teachers' Union,
asking for the removal of the time and
means barrier from the Pensions (Increase) Acts; the increase of pensions
below £50 to that sum; pensionable recognition of service in workhouse schools;
the non-devaluation for pension purposes
of the services of junior assistant mistresses; the allocation of pensions to those
who retired before the 1st January, 1922;
and the appointment of a committee of
inquiry into the system of superannuating
teachers, and what action he proposes to
take in those matters.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The resolutions in question have
been brought to my notice. I will reply
seriatim:
Firstly, the object of the Pensions Increase Acts was to alleviate hardships in
the case of persons drawing small prewar pensions; the Acts apply not only to
teachers, but to all other types of public
servants; the time and means barrier is
an essential feature, which could not with
any propriety be removed.
Secondly, in regard to the suggestion
that pensions below £50 should be increased to that sum, I would refer my
hon. Friend to the reply to a similar
question asked by him on the 30th
November, 1926.
Thirdly, the question of recognising
service in workhouse schools as pensionable is at present under consideration.
Fourthly, the concession under which
non-pensionable teaching service has been
allowed to count in part for pension is
one which was applied to teachers of
various grades by the Government of
Northern Ireland, and I regret that I
can see no grounds for placing junior assistant mistresses in a more favourable
position than the others.
Fifthly, it would be impossible for this
Government to undertake to grant pensions to teachers who retired before the
Service came under its control.
Sixthly, I see no grounds for the appointment of a Committee of Inquiry into
the system of superannuating teachers.

It is undoubtedly difficult to adjust
Trade Board Rates of Wages to the conditions under which retail trades are carried
on in country districts. Trade Boards, as
the hon. Lady knows, have been set up to
prevent what are known as "sweated"
rates of wages, and but for these Boards
very low wages might be paid in some
districts. On the other hand, if the
wages fixed by the Boards are uneconomic,
employers may be faced with the competition of the self-employed person or the
cheap factory-made article, and may be
unable to continue to give employment at
all.
It is between these difficulties that
the Boards, in determining the rates, have
to strike a proper balance.

Trade Board, representations have been
made recently that separate Trade Board
machinery should be established to advise
the Board as regards country rates, and
the Department has replied to these representations in a favourable sense.

over a year ago, the House passed the
Motor Traffic Act, which, as hon.

the object of removing and abating the

offences, such as drunkenness in charge of
a vehicle for exceeding the prescribed
speed limit in certain cases, driving to
the danger of the public, at the same
time the Measure reduced the then existing penalties for what might be
described as technical breaches of the law,
such as breaches of the law in regard to
the lighting regulations. But one of
the most important provisions of this
Measure was the fact that it set up for
the first time in Northern Ireland a
central system, controlling the licensing
of motor omnibuses and motor hackney
vehicles.
It might interest the House to know
that this system only exists in Northern
Ireland, and exists in no other place in
the Three Kingdoms, although attempts
have been made to bring about that
condition of affairs in England and
Scotland.
During the progress of the Act I have
referred to through the House, I was
careful to explain that the necessity
for this Measure was justified by the
appalling number of motor accidents on
our roads involving loss of life and

I then made it clear that while that
Measure provided for the control of
traffic as such, that of itself was not
sufficient and much remained to be done,
and that I hoped before long to introduce
Measure which would have as its
object the improvement of our road
system, so as to make them safer and more
adapted to modern traffic conditions,
and therefore the present Bill is the
logical sequel to the Motor raffic Act

Before dealing with the provisions of
the Bill, I think it might be of advantage

these particulars will show to the House
that the Traffic Act of 1926, no matter

When dealing with the Traffic Bill of
1926 I quoted figures which showed that
during the year ending 1925 there were
no fewer than 1,300 accidents in which
motor vehicles were concerned, involving

and in 759 other cases they resulted in
serious injury to individuals.
I cannot but think when hon. Members
realize the appalling increase in casualties on our roads, they will agree with me
that this House should leave no stone
unturned to do something to lessen the
risks which the public have to take on
our roads.
During the year 1927, there were no
fewer than 1,438 accidents on our roads,
and out of these, fatalities occurred in
no fewer than 100 cases, involving the loss
of 102 lives, while 1,530 persons received
injuries of a more or less serious character.
I might point out that in one month alone
20 people were killed and in another month
10 people. Hon. Members will thus realize
that notwithstanding the restrictions
that have been put on motorists, and notwithstanding the activities of the police.
in endeavouring to enforce the observance of the law, the number of fatal
accidents on our roads has doubled itself
in one year.
I recollect very well that during the
passing of the Motor Traffic Act certain

strict a character, and it is indeed true
that since that Bill became law. I have,
from time to time, received resolutions
of protest from various quarters and
from well-intentioned individuals who
have no axe to grind, but who, unfortunately, have not studied the question,

At the time the Act of 1926 was
passed the maximum speed limit for
heavy motor vehicles was only 12 miles
an hour, and that speed limit still exists
in England and Scotland to-day. At that

The enforcing of the law in regard to

but the pedestrian public, who, after all,

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The other reason, which I think will
appeal to Hon. Members who are in the
position of having to pay rates for the
maintenance of the roads, is the damage
which these vehicles, going at a high
speed, do to the roads.
The
Government have, again and
again, been accused of introducing restrictive Measures in regard to omnibuses
for the sole purpose of driving the
omnibus off our roads. There is not a
grain of foundation for such a statement.
On the contrary, the Government realize
that buses have come to stay, and that
buses have conferred an undoubted
benefit on the whole community by
opening up new districts which were
hitherto untouched, and the view that the
Government take is that every facility
within reason and equity should be given
to these machines. But if the bus traffic
is to develop along proper lines and be
of use to the community, the first thing
that has to be considered is the provision
of proper and suitable and, above all
things, safe roads.
When the Government took over
control in 1921 the roads in Northern
Ireland were in an appalling condition,
and since that time the Government,
realizing that to allow the roads to remain in this condition would be to retard
the natural progress and the development
of the motor industry in Northern
Ireland, assisted the road authorities in
every possible way to bring their roads
up to modern requirements, and, at the
risk of wearying this House, I would like
to indicate what the Government have
done towards bringing about the improvement of roads in Northern Ireland.
I find that in the year 1913 the total
expenditure on roads in Northern
Ireland amounted to the sum of £361,093,
of which the Government expended a sum
of £11,185. In 1921, when we took over
control, the total expenditure had risen
to £843,299, and towards that amount
this Government contributed £173,075;
and from that time on there was a continual increase in the total expenditure
and in the amount contributed by the
Government until we find that in 1926-27
the total sum spent on the roads amounted
to no less a sum than £1,411,723, that
is to say, four times the amount that had
been spent in 1913, and of this sum the
Government contributed £578,726-in
other words, more than 50 times the
amount contributed by the Government
in 1915.
In 1927-28, however, I find that the
total estimated expenditure is reduced to
a sum of £1,320,000, of which it is
estimated that £609,601-almost half
the amount has or will be contributed by
the Government, but the amount contributed by local authorities will be
substantially less than in the previous
year.
May I remind the House that the
Government have used all the Road Fund
for the development of road traffic, and
no part of that Fund has gone into the
Exchequer for general purposes-a different policy from that which has been
adopted elsewhere.
I believe that the Government are
right in the course they took and are
taking, and I believe if that policy had not
been adopted it would have been impossible for the bus traffic to develop in
Northern Ireland to the extent it has
done, and, therefore, I cannot think
how anybody who studies these figures
can suggest, with any degree of truth,
that because the Government bring in
Measures which have for their sole object
the safety of the community, the
Government wish to prevent the development of this bus traffic which has done so
much to meet the needs of the community.
But the local authorities are daily
explaining that their ratepayers cannot
stand the terrible burden imposed upon
them for the maintenance of the roads.
The figures, as you have seen, go to show
that while the Government grant towards
the maintenance of the roads has increased the expenditure by the local
authorities has decreased.
Again and
again I have complaints from the road
authorities as to the inordinate damage
done by buses and other heavy motor
vehicles on roads which are constructed
with such a surface that they are not
fit for these vehicles to go on at a high
speed. I am advised on the highest
authority that the wear and tear on a
road due to a particular vehicle increases
in the ratio of the square of the speed,
in other words the damage done to a road
by a heavy motor vehicle travelling at
20 miles an hour is four times the
damage which would be done by the same
vehicle at 10 miles an hour. Similarly
the damage done by the same vehicle at
30 miles an hour would be nine times
greater than the damage done at 10 miles.
an hour.

As I have already indicated, the
Measure which is now before the House
is more to ensure that the roads will be
safer for the use of motor traffic. None
of our roads were built for the purpose
of carrying motor traffic, and the result
of that in many cases is that they are
positively dangerous when so used.
In 1921 we had 11,700 motor vehicles
licensed in Northern Ireland, while for
1926 the number was increased to no
less a sum than 30,000, while for 1927
that number was increased to no less a
In
figure than 31,400. In other words, out
of a population of 1,254,000 we have one
vehicle for every 40 inhabitants, as contrasted with England where there is one
vehicle to every 22.
But what has made
it all the more necessary that further
steps should be taken to make the roads
safer for motor traffic has been the
enormous increase in the bus traffic.
1924 we had only 346 motor omnibuses
licensed in Northern Ireland, and in the
corresponding month of 1927 the number
had increased to 719. For some time
past it has been felt that the powers
which are now vested in the local authorities were entirely inadequate to deal with
the present situation. We feel that the
road authorities should be invested with
the fullest possible powers to widen the
roads, remove corners, and remove all
obstacles which obstruct the driver's view.
But in some countries the policy of the
Government has been to encourage the
making of new roads. Anybody who has
studied the road question in Northern
Ireland must realize that one of the difficulties with which local authorities are
confronted is that there are too many
roads; but, on the other hand, it is quite
clear that many of the existing roads are
entirely unsuitable for any traffic except
that of the ordinary horse and cart.
Much has been done during the past six
or seven years to improve our roads, and
many of them are equal to the best roads
in England and Scotland, and when I
say this I would like to bear testimony to
the enterprise and foresight of so many
of our road authorities.
Without being too invidious, may I
refer particularly to some of the roads in
Down, Antrim, and Armagh. One of the
difficulties which our road authorities
have met with has been the difficulty and
expense in acquiring land, and while it
is perfectly true that many have shown a
great deal of patriotism in agreeing to
give land for widening purposes, at the
same time others have taken another view,
and, as the law now stands, the present
system under which land can be compulsorily acquired for this purpose is of such
a complicated nature that it is practically
impossible for any local authority to avail
themselves of these powers, and many
schemes which would otherwise have been
undertaken by road contractors have had
to be abandoned as a consequence.
Another matter which is very often the
cause of road accidents is the difficulty
which drivers experience in avoiding
accidents owing to the presence of high
walls, fences, trees, haystacks and other
obstructions along the roadside. We
propose under this Bill, the particulars
of which I will explain afterwards, to
deal with this matter also.
Another feature of the Bill is the
question of the restriction of certain
traffic on our roads. At the present time,
before a road can be closed for traffic,
the road authorities have to apply to the
Ministry, when an inquiry is held, and,
therefore, a great deal of time may
elapse before an Order is actually made,
and during that time a great deal of unnecessary damage can be done to a road,
and, therefore, in certain limited cases,
which I will explain to the House later,
we propose to give the authorities greater
power in regard to closing a certain class
of a road to a certain class of traffic
where damage may result to the road.
Dealing with the various Clauses of
the Measure, hon. Members will see that
the first Clause gives general power to
the road authority to acquire compulsorily such land as may be necessary for
the purpose of improving or widening
existing roads or streets, or for making
new streets or roads. Our aim in framing
this Clause, which must be read in conjunction with the Schedule to the Bill, is
to provide a procedure which will be both
speedy and inexpensive and, at the same
time, afford all reasonable protection to
the owners whose land must, of necessity,
be taken compulsorily.
I think hon. Members who have studied
the subject will agree that this is necessary, because in the majority of cases the
amount to be taken from any one owner
will be very small, and the whole object

where the amount awarded exceeds £100
an appeal is given to the County Court
Judge.
As I have already pointed out, the

land in the ordinary way. The costs in

Members will appreciate, out of all proportion to the amount of compensation,
and we propose under this Measure to
make the process as inexpensive and as

With regard to small cases, that is
where the amount does not exceed £100,
we have adopted the procedure which
already exists under the Labourers
Acts, and in such cases instead of asking
the owner to prove his title for many
years back, it has been found to be advantageous to allow the local authorities
to take a little risk, and to accept as
evidence of title the fact that the
claimant for a period of not less than six
years immediately prior to the vesting
Order was in possession, either by himself
or his predecessor, or in receipt of the
rents. This particular matter is dealt
with in Paragraph 18 of the Schedule.
Should another claimant turn up within
six years after the vesting Order and prove
that he, and not the original claimant,
was entitled to the money, the local
authority would have to pay twice.
While this may appear rather a big risk
to take, the system has been in operation
for about 22 years under the Labourers
Acts, and it is very seldom found that a
second claim has been made, and the
saving effected fully compensates for any
risk taken. Where the compensation
exceeds £100, the title of course will have
to be investigated in the ordinary way by
the legal advisers of the local authorities
concerned.

he open then to the local authority to pay

that, subject to the over-riding authority
of the Ministry in the case of classified
roads, to which I will refer later, we propose that a local authority may, by
resolution, prescribe the frontage line for
the building in respect of either side of
any part of a road maintainable by them,
but before making an Order following the
passing of the resolution we provide that
the local authority must give public
notice of their intention to do so, and
they must then consider any objection
received by interested parties.
If an interested party is able to prove
that his property has been injuriously
affected by the prescription of such a line,
he will be entitled to recover compensation
from the local authority. Such compensation will be fixed by the official
arbitrator under the Acquisition of Land
Act, but we have expressly provided that
no claimant will be able to recover compensation in respect of anything done by
him after the date of the service of the
notice of the intention to prescribe the
building line.
We have put in another provision here
which is perhaps novel so far as this
country is concerned. We have provided
that in fixing the amount of compensation
the arbitrator is to be entitled to take
into consideration as a set-off any benefit
Roads Improvement Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
accruing to the claimant by reason of any
improvement made or about to be made
on the road. Hon. Members will appreciate the reason for that. When once
the building line has been prescribed no
one may erect any new building except,
of course, a boundary wall, nearer the
centre of the road than the line prescribed
without the consent of the local authority.
I stated earlier that we did not propose
to interfere with the existing rights of
corporations or urban councils under any
of their special Acts of Parliament, but
this is qualified by sub-clause (b) of the
Bill. Hon. Members will appreciate that
a case may arise where a local authority
wishes to prescribe a building line on a
road near that authority's boundary, and
I think hon. Members will agree that it
is obviously desirable that the adjoining
local authority should be consulted, so
that the road running in the two areas
may have a common building line, and,
therefore, we propose that in the event
of the two local authorities being unable
to arrive at an agreement the Ministry is
to decide the matter. I imagine, however, that the local authorities will
always settle their own differences.
Clause 5 enables a local authority
to make an Order closing any 3rd-class
road against any class of traffic and to
close any 1st or 2nd-class road against
traffic other than pneumatic-tyred
vehicles. If any parties interested in the
matter desire to object to such an Order
they can appeal to the Ministry against
the making of the Order when, if
necessary, an inquiry will be held into
the matter.
As I have already pointed out, many
of the roads are entirely unfit to carry
heavy traffic. Imagine the case of a
heavy boiler or other heavy machinery
traversing certain roads in the county.
Before that boiler, weighing perhaps 20
tons, gets to its destination, thousands of
pounds worth of damage may be done to
the road, which will only have to be paid
by the ratepayer. While our 3rd class
roads are improving, there can be no
question that, under certain conditions, it
would be absolutely ruinous for the ratepayers to permit these heavy machines,
whether they have pneumatic tyres or
not, to traverse these roads. Hon.
Members will appreciate that there
is an appeal in every case against any
unreasonable attitude on the part of the
road authority.
As regards 1st and 2nd-class roads,
before any of these roads can be closed to
machines which are shod with pneumatic
tyres the old procedure must be adopted,
that is, application must be made to the
Ministry, and then an inquiry is held.
Coming to Clause 6, under which we
seek to do something to relieve the congestion of traffic in urban areas, hon.
Members are aware that a great deal of
inconvenience is caused by cars being left
for an indefinite period at the sides of
streets, but, on the other hand, considerable inconvenience and hardships are
caused to the owners when prosecutions
follow. Sometimes, where the streets
are broad, it has been found possible to
assign parking places for cars, but in
other towns where the streets are narrow
this has been found quite impossible, and
under this Clause we have thought it
right to authorize county boroughs and
urban districts to provide parking places,
either in streets or in places specially
assigned to them, and for that purpose to
acquire land.
We propose that the local authorities
will have power to make by-laws, regulating the use of such special parking
places, and to charge reasonable sums for
the use as a compensation as against the
cost which such road authority will have
to incur by acquiring the land. Of
course, this right will not apply to the use
of a street, but only to land specially
acquired as parking places.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Why not?
Hon.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sure my
hon. Friend can make arguments on the
other side when he comes to speak.
Members will, of course, appreciate that
before these by-laws can become
operative they must be approved of by
the Ministry, after public inquiry if
necessary.
Coming to Clause 7, this deals with the
very vexed question of petrol pumps. As
the law now stands, local authorities have
no power to allow owners of garages to
erect petrol pumps on the footpath of the
public street. Some local authorities
take the view that the place is better
without petrol pumps. Others take the
view that they should have a discretionary power to give permission in suitable
places.
Roads Improvement Bill-

3,

e
At all events all of us will agree that
these petrol pumps are a great convenience to members of the public using
motor vehicles, provided they are placed
in suitable places, and, accordingly, we
propose to confer on local authorities the
right, if they think fit, of authorising the
erection of these pumps on any road,
street or footpath under their jurisdiction.
We also provide that before any pumps
can be erected a licence must be obtained
from the local authority, which will be
empowered to charge a fee for the
privilege.
Clause 8 I do not think requires very
much explanation. As the law now
stands, the road authority is precluded
from expending a greater sum than
£1 in the erection of milestones
or
direction posts in any one case. I think
hon. Members will agree with me when I
say that it is most desirable, with a view
to encouraging the development of the
tourist traffic, that suitable direction
posts and milestones should be erected.
Accordingly, we propose to enable the
local authority to incur reasonable expenditure in this direction, and also
extend the power to urban districts. We
also take power to enable the Ministry to
assist the local authorities out of the
Road Fund towards this very necessary
expenditure.
Clause 9 prevents any person from
affixing on any road any overhead rail
without the consent of the local authority.
Clause 10 will be appreciated by most
hon. Members. It simply compels the
owner of premises adjoining a street or
road to maintain such down pipes or
gutters as will prevent the water running
off the roof of the premises on to the footpath of the road or street.
Clause 11 will require the owner of
any lands abutting on a road or street to
fence off his land, so as to prevent soil
or refuse from such lands being washed
or carried into the road. Hon. Members
will, I am sure, appreciate the cases
where a great deal of unnecessary expense
devolves on the road authority through
the carelessness of the adjoining owner.
Clause 12 deals with the question of
projections, and I do not think requires
any explanation.
Coming to Clause 13, as Hon. Members are aware, road construction has
developed to an enormous extent during
the last three or four years, and the
methods which we re-adopted 10 or 15
years ago are entirely unsuitable now.
New methods of construction have been
adopted, but one of the main difficulties we
are faced with in reconstructing our roads
is the enormous expense involved, and
the whole tendency of inventors is to try
to discover a system of reconstruction
of roads by a method of a less expensive
character.

are

Local authorities, of course,
somewhat reluctant to conduct these experiments and to run the risk of incurring
the expense of using materials which
have not been fully proved. The Clause,
therefore, empowers the Ministry of
Home Affairs, either by itself
through any authority or organization
approved by the Ministry, to conduct
experiments or trials for the improvement
of the construction of roads, or for testing
the effect of various classes of vehicles on
various types of road, and for this purpose
may construct such roads as may be
necessary and subject to the approval of
the Ministry, incur expenditure for this.
purpose.

I do not think it is necessary to detain
this House in going further into the remainder of the Clauses. Most of them
are consequential on the Clauses which I
have already dealt with. They provide
for such matters as the holding of inquiries, the making of by-laws, and the
preservation of Crown rights. I regret I
have taken up the time of the House for
so long, but I think the importance of
this Measure affords me some justification
for doing so. I beg to move.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I think every
Member of the House will be in entire
sympathy with the object which this Bill
purports to fulfil. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) In the first place I would
like to take exception to and to condemn
in the strongest possible terms the
methods by which this Bill has been
introduced. It was presented and
circulated on last Thursday, and now we
have the Second Reading taken in the
House to-day. I seriously suggest to the
Government that that does not give the
people of Northern Ireland, the people
who are affected by this Bill, the slightest
chance of investigating how their interests
231 Roads Improvement Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. McAllister]
are to be affected by any Clause contained in the Bill. This Bill may have
more far-reaching consequences than any
of us can foresee in the way that it may
affect various classes of landowners, in
Northern Ireland. Therefore, I do protest as a Member of this House, but more
particularly in the public interest, against
this method of bringing in this Bill by
circulating it on Thursday and taking the
Second Reading to-day.
There is one principle in the Bill that
I heartily welcome, and that is the departure from the very obnoxious and
expensive principle of the minimum fine
which has been embodied in every Bill
recently introduced into this House. We
have all seen in the public Press the
almost universal condemnation by Courts
or Summary Jurisdiction of the insertion
of this principle of the minimum fine in
the various Bills which have passed
this House. Magistrates have been
compelled to inflict what they considered an injust penalty. When they
found that the merest nominal technical
offence was committed they have been
compelled to inflict penalties which they
felt were out of proportion to the offence
committed, and were a grave injustice to
the people on whom they were inflicted.
With regard to this and all other Bills,
I take exception, and will offer the most
strenuous opposition to giving a free hand
to any Government Department to franie
Regulations. If you take the recent
Motor Bill, it was drastic in the extreme.
but the Regulations are ten times more
drastic than the original Bill, and we had
no opportunity of dealing with those
Regulations in this House. They were
formulated in the office of the Minister
of Home Affairs and they were inflicted
on the people of Northern Ireland without
the Parliament of Northern Ireland
having an opportunity of determining
the justice or merits of those Regulations.
They alter the face, they alter the context, and they alter the principle of the
original Bill, and they are to all intents
and purposes a new and a more onerous
Bill than the original Motor Bill. Therefore I for one will offer the most strenuous
opposition to giving a free hand to the
Ministry to formulate Regulations under
this Bill.
There is also another principle
embodied in the Bill. I will endeavour
during the Committee stage to secure
that the public will be protected in all
instances by the right of appeal to the
court. I do not see why, for instance,
when damage is done to any person
under this Bill the Ministry of Home
Affairs, who are responsible for that
damage, should have the right to fix the
compensation for the damage they have
inflicted. I believe it is the right of
every citizen to have an appeal to an
impartial tribunal, and when the
Government is affected that impartial
tribunal can only be the court. There
is another principle in this Bill to which
I am very much opposed, and it is this.
As I understand it, the Bill vests che
interest of the owner of the property in
the local authority before they pay to the
owner of the property the amount of the
compensation he is entitled to. I object
to that for this reason. At the present
time I know local authorities who, under
the Labourers Act, over a year ago
entered into possession of people's land
and refused to pay them on the ground
that it would be simpler and cheaper and
easier for them to pay them when the
lands are vested under the Land Purchase Act I say that is indefensible.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Why do you
not sue them?
Mr. MCALLISTER: Does the right

out. I think that when these people's

With regard to Clause 3, I think that

Mrs. CHICHESTER: This Bill will

continually find fault with the Government on any and every subject. The hon.
Member who has just sat down made a

I was very interested in the figures
which were put before the House by the

Bill, and who gave a great many figures
dealing with the Road Fund, and of the
amount which the roads in the Six
Counties cost to keep up from 1913 to the
present day. He gave those figures in
demonstrating the necessity for this Bill.
I am not quite sure that I was able to
follow the right hon. Gentleman all the
time, but I do think he demonstrated
one thing which I would like to emphasize, though perhaps in a somewhat different manner. I think he told us that
this year the total cost of the upkeep of
roads in the Six Counties was about
£1,300,000, and that towards that
amount the Government were contributing about £690,000. I presume that he
meant that the Road Fund, made up
of money received from the owners of
motor vehicles, was contributing £690,000
towards the upkeep of the roads. Of
course £690,000 is a very large sum, but,
as has been mentioned here to-day, I do
not think that we who represent rural
districts can quite allow those remarks to
pass without pointing out that half the
amount for the upkeep of the roads with
which we are dealing has to be provided
by the ratepayers of the Province, quite
apart from the amount received from the
owners of motor cars who use the roads.
I do want to take this opportunity of
asking the Government if it is altogether
fair that the ratepayers, and I am speaking especially for the farmers, should
have to pay this very large amount.

I want particularly to deal with Clause

because they are in this Clause recognizing
the damaging effects on roads not constructed for heavy motor traffic by this
extremely heavy bus and lorry traffic.
They are enabling a local authority to

the case of a district road which has been

Idealt with if circumstances should arise

Committee
Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order, No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the
Loans Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922-1927, by extending to the
31st day of March, 1929, the period
within which the Ministry of Finance
may give guarantees under the Loans
Guarantee Act (Northern Ireland),
1922." (Governor's Recommendation
signified)-(Mr. Pollock.)
Mr. BARBOUR: I would like to remind the Committee that this is only the
Money Resolution which is the forerunner
of a Bill which will be promoted in due
time, in order to give proper Statutory
effect to the policy indicated in the Resolution which has just been read.
The
policy is merely to extend the operation
of the Loans Guarantee Acts for the
further period of one year, otherwise by
the time limit included in the last Loans
Guarantee Act the operation of the
Loans Guarantee Acts would be brought
to a close on 31st March of the present
year, although the amount of money
authorized to be guaranteed under these
Acts is not exhausted. The aggregate
capital amount of the loans that may be
guaranteed was increased by the Act of
1927 from £9,000,000 to £10,500,000,
and the position at the present time is
that guarantees have been issued to the
extent of about £8,770,867, leaving a
margin of approximately £1,700,000
which is still available for further guarantees. The Government feel that this unexhausted margin is probably sufficient
to cover any new application which may
be granted, more especially as we are all
glad to know that the biggest shipyard
in Belfast is likely to be fully occupied
during the year by work already on hand.
Hon. Members may perhaps remember
that when the last extension of the Loans.
Guarantee Act was being moved, the
hope was expressed that it would be possible to withdraw these facilities at the
end of the present financial year, and in
expressing that hope the Government had
particularly in mind the fact that the
British Trades Facilities Act had already
been allowed to lapse. The Government,
however, are of opinion that our circumstances here, with our limited number of
major occupations, are not wholly analagous to the wider basis of British
industry. Accordingly, the Committee is
asked to agree to a further extension of
time, but not of the amount, provided for
by this Resolution. I beg to move.
Mr. BEATTIE: Can I get the information on this Money Resolution as to
how much of the money that is being
asked for here is covered by guarantees.
The CHAIRMAN: I should point out
that no money is being asked for by this

expedient to amend the Loans Guarantee

1929," and so on. No sum is asked for.

of the loans guaranteed is now covering
new works in Harland & Wolff's?

widened strip now vested in the county
council, a rather curious situation from
the legal point of view.

Mr. DAVISON: It is quite true there
is in existence a precedure for acquiring
land for the purpose of widening a road.
I think it could be done more satisfactorily
and avoid the necessity of making vesting
orders and vesting the land in the county
council, which is unnecessary; if it simply
purported to give the county council power
to widen the road, and the works could be
specified if necessary. That is, the order,
by whomsoever it should be made, would
authorize certain works marked out on the
order to be done, setting back fences or
altering corners so as to widen the road.
The authority of Parliament to widen
the road makes that part widened part of
the public highway, and gives authority
to the user who would be authorized to
trespass to that extent on the adjoining
land, and the same authority that gave
power should estimate the damage done
to the adjoining land, and by the exercise
of these powers the money would be
there as compensation for the authorized
trespass upon the land for distribution
among those concerned. That would
appear to me to be be a more satisfactory
method of dealing with the question than
the proposed system which really is in
effect the system of procedure for the
acquisition of land for the purpose of
labourers' cottages.
Also this Section does not make any
provision for the acquisition of easements
or giving authority to county councils to
do acts upon the land's adjoining the
roads which are necessary sometimes a
considerable distance from the road.
Take the question of drainage which is a
very important matter in several lowlying portions of the country. Drainage
operations may necessitate going on ad-
That is one respect in
joining lands.
which county councils have very extended
powers, for the purpose of draining
roads. That would not necessitate the
acquisition of any land, but simply give
authority to enter upon adjoining lands
for some distance from the road for the
purpose of properly draining the road.
There is in existence at the present time
power to do that, but it is limited to adjoining lands. It is very doubtful if the
county council has the right. I think it
is under the Grand Jury Act of 1836
embodied in the Adaptation of Irish
Enactments Order, 1899. There is a long
list of classes of property which cannot
be entered upon, deerpark, bleachgreens,
orchards, walled gardens, haggards or
yards. There is a long list.
It is on that the difficulty of the
county councils or road authorities arose.
When the county council proposed to
enter upon land for the purpose of constructing a drain it is nearly always said
to be an orchard. I have known cases
where a few trees planted along the drain
on the farmers' land were held to be an
orchard and the county council had no
power to enter upon it. It might be
considered by the Minister in charge of
the Bill whether the provisions of the
Grand Jury Act should not be improved
and extended so that the county council
should have wider and more convenient
powers for draining a road.
Then I am inclined to think that the
proposed procedure is too cumbrous for
what it is intended to meet. In these cases
the land that would be affected would be
very small and of comparatively little
value. Take the case of country roads
being improved. A bad corner had to be
straightened up. That means cutting of
on
the
a little bit of the corner and setting back
the fence. That is not a very big thing.
Probably £10 would cover it so far as
the real damage to the adjoining land is
concerned. Yet what will this procedure
drive the council to do to get that land
if the owner objects. They will first
have to publish advertisements. They
will make application to the Ministry of
Home Affairs on the prescribed form.
They will have to serve the notice in the
prescribed manner both by advertisement
in the locality and on the owners,
lessees, and occupiers, also
Government Departments. After the
expiration of one month and the Ministry
have considered the objections made to
the scheme I am now assuming that the
owner is objecting and fighting to the
bitter end-a Local Government Board
inquiry will be held and advertisements
published for the holding of it. The
Local Government Board inspector will
have to come down. He will have to sit
there to hear objections and his expenses
will have to be paid for by the local
authorities. Then the Ministry of Home
Affairs if satisfied can make a vesting
order vesting that land at once in the
county council.
Then after that is done the question of
payment for the lands will arise, and
that procedure begins afresh just as
under the Housing of the Working
Classes Acts. The Housing of the Work-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Davison]
ing Classes Act has embodied in it this
procedure. Maps and schedules of the
land will have to be lodged. The names
of owners or reputed owners will have to
be lodged with these schedules. These
will have to be deposited with the confirming authority. The confirming
authority will appoint an arbitrator.
The arbitrator will have to take the
oath. The maps and plans must be
sent to the arbitrator. Notice must be
given in three successive weeks of the
appointment of the arbitrator by advertisement and by bills posted near the land,
and sending by post notices to owners and
occupiers. Notice will have to be given.
of the time and place of the arbitration.
The arbitrator hears and decides and
then issues the award. All that will have
to be gone through, because the county
council want to get a little bit of land to
straighten a corner which will be of about
£10 value.
There is in existence at the present time
a method of dealing with the acquiring
of land by the county council for the purpose of widening a road. It is Section 10
of the Local Government Act, 1898. The
county council can acquire compulsorily
land, but the procedure is rather troublesome. But there is a short procedure prescribed by that section for acquiring land
for the specific purpose of making a road
by a single petition to a judge of Assize.
It has already been exercised in some
cases. It is a very good, cheap, and expeditious method. It has the advantage
that the authority that deals with it is
one of our courts, and that is not done by
some official in a Government Department. There always has been a certain
amount of objection to leaving a question
of this kind where rights of property are
involved and private owners are being
interfered with to the uncontrolled discretion of someone that is unknown and
has no personal responsibility for his
action. And in almost every case up to
the present where power has been given
to a Government Department to deal with
rights of property, the rights of individuals of this kind, provision for appeal
or for control by the courts of the acts of
that Department was made. Here there
is no such provision. There is no power
to control what the Ministry of Home
Affairs may do in his interference with
the right of private property. I think
the Government ought to consider
seriously whether it would not be an advantage to go back to the recognized
practice of giving the right of appeal to
the judge of assize. Even under the Act
which provides for the right of appeal to
the judge of assize, Parliament gave the
right of appeal from the judge of assize
to the Privy Council.
There is one other matter that I would
suggest for the consideration of the
Government, and that is with regard to
the powers given to road authorities to do
acts such as the lopping of hedges against
the will of the owner. Again you have
existing powers in previous Acts. In
no case has the road authority been empowered to enter upon lands against the
will of the owner, except under the
authority of a magistrate's order. Clearly
the reason for that is, that it is likely to
lead to a breach of the peace as between
an unwilling owner and a county official
who wants to enter upon land for the purpose of lopping trees or doing whatever
is necessary to be done.
Parliament has always said, if the
owner objects, you must go to the magistrate and get an order to do these acts.
I think that is worthy of consideration.
To sum up, I would suggest that a rather
cheaper method ought to be adopted for
the purpose of enabling road authorities
to improve the roads, in cases where the
amount involved is small; second, this
should be done under the direction of the
courts of the country, and should not be
left entirely to any Government Department; lastly, the road authorities should
not be empowered to enter upon lands
against the will of the owner, unless under
some authority of the courts.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: There
is one point to which I desire to draw the
attention of the House. During the
course of a very comprehensive review
given yesterday, the Minister of Home
Affairs stated a number of problems, and
I am in some doubt as to whether he will
adumbrate a solution of some of the problems that he stated. In regard to the
number of fatalities that occurred during
the year 1927 as compared with 1926, I
am of the opinion that the Bill that is
before the House at the present moment
is scarcely going to obviate that appalling
number of fatalities. I am trying to
think whether the improvements that are
likely to be made in the roads will have
the effect of reducing the number of
fatalities. I am forced to the conclusion
Roads Improvement Bill-
14 MARCH 1928
Second Reading
that the improvements that are likely to
take place by the rounding of corners and
alterations are not likely to achieve it,
uniess there have been a very large
number of accidents last
year at the
corners of roads.
For the purpose of illustrating what I
mean, I should point out that so far as
I know the roads are in precisely the same
position in 1927 as they were in 1926.
During the course of 1926, 59 fatal accidents occurred; during 1927, 102 fatal
accidents occurred. The only alteration
that has taken place in the meantime is
that heavy vehicles have been allowed to
travel at 20 miles an hour instead of 12.
Superficially, that would lead one to the
conclusion that the reason for the increase
in the number of fatalities is the fact that
those vehicles are allowed to travel at a
greater speed than they were allowed to
travel at before the Motor Act was
introduced.
If that is the position, I am rather
inclined to think that the suggested
improvements in this Bill are not going
to decrease the number of accidents that
have taken place. Has there been a
meticulous examination in connection
with all these fatalities so far as the
Ministry of Home Affairs is concerned?
I notice that in July there were 20 fatal
accidents. In August there were 10 fatal
accidents. That would appear to indicate
that during the month of July, when
there is a large volume of traffic-
Mr. ANDREWS: The Twelfth.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Yes,
the Twelfth included-there was a larger
number of accidents than in any other
month of the year. That may be due to
increased traffic. What I would like some
information about is this, the time at
which these accidents take place. You
are attempting to legislate for a number
of things, and it appears to me you are
making a very great mistake so far as one
aspect of the matter is concerned. You
have discussed this Bill from many
aspects, but you have not taken into consideration the human element that is
employed for the purpose of driving these
vehicles. I have not got the information
-I want to get it as to the hour of the
day at which these accidents occur,
whether it is late in the evening. If it is
late in the evening, the presumption is
that the accidents are due to the fact that
the motor drivers are fatigued after a
very long and weary day, and are not as
efficient as they are early in the day. On
that point I would like some information.
I would further like some information
in regard to the statement made yesterday
by the Minister of Home Affairs. I
understood him to say-and he is reported
in the Press as having said that a
vehicle that travels at 20 miles an hour
will damage the roads four times as
much as a vehicle travelling at 10
miles an hour, and that a vehicle travelling at 30 miles an hour would do nine
times the amount of damage that it would
do if it were travelling at 10 miles an hour.
It is quite obvious from that statement
---if that statement is true-that it is
the heavy type of vehicle that is playing
havoc with the roads. I am told that
extra taxation has been imposed on those
heavy vehicles, but it would appear to be
a fair thing that if this heavy type of
vehicle is responsible for the whole of the
damage to the road-four times greater
when it is travelling at 20 miles an hour
than when it is travelling at 10, and nine
times greater when it is travelling at 30
than when it is travelling at 10-the
owners of those heavy vehicles should be
asked to pay taxation commensurate with
the amount of damage that the vehicles
do to the roads. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I understand that there has been
additional taxation imposed upon them,
but has it been commensurate with the
amount of damage that these heavy
vehicles are doing to the roads?
On those two points I desire to get information. I would urge that the
Ministry of Home Affairs should go very
carefully into the whole question, and
find out precisely what was responsible for
the great increase in the number of deaths
in 1927 as compared with 1926, and I
would like to be quite sure that the legislation that is now before the House is
likely to have the effect of obviating the
large number of fatalities that occur.

The procedure for the carrying out of
the object of Section 1 is set out in the

Gentleman, or any other Member of this

Having given notice then to a person
""
that his interests are to be affected, why

cannot conceive of a more simple procedure than that. The hon. and learned
I
Gentleman says, "Let him go to the

that they have been unmindful of their
duties in regard to matters pertaining
to the roads. The figures given by my
right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
yesterday, starting away back a few
years ago in humble thousands and now
showing that a million and a half is being
spent to make the roads safe, are surely
sufficient answer to that. We have been
asked to give some more money out of
the Road Fund. There is nobody on this
side of the House, and no Member of the
Government whom I have had the pleasure of meeting yet, who can bring more
rabbits out of the hat than were in it
when he started. What we have been
trying to do is to bring the last penny
out of the Road Fund and to apply it for
the purpose of making these roads
efficient and suitable for their purpose.
Now, I think I have dealt with all the
points that have been raised in regard to
the Bill, and I hope the House will show
its appreciation of the fact that an honest
effort is now being made for the purpose
of rendering our roads safer by allowing
the Second Reading to pass.

Question put, and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time and committed
to a Committee of the Whole House for
to-morrow.

Supplementary Estimates, 1927-28.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLASS VI. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £23,995 be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending on the
31st of March, 1928, to defray the
Expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture
in respect of Agricultural Education and
Research, Improvement of Live Stock,
Agricultural Development, Agricultural
Statistics, Afforestation and Diseases of
Animals, including sundry Grants in Aid
and certain capital expenditure.
""
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): It will be within the
recollection of the Committee that an
arrangement was made by Parliament in
connection with the Hillsborough Research Station and Experimental Farm
that there was to be an endowment fund
of £60,000, which it is calculated will
yield an income of £3,000 per annum for
the upkeep of the station. Pending the
completion of the Endowment Fund an
interim grant was to be made by Parliament each year of such amount as, with
the interest payable on sums already
accumulated in the Endowment Fund,
would give an income of £3,000 a year
for its upkeep. This was originally proposed to be done in five years at £12,000
a year, but at the request of the Ministry
of Finance we have this year increased the
grant so as to make it up to the £60,000
at the earliest possible date. It is found
that it would be much more to the interest
of the Ministry of Finance to complete
the sum of £60,000 instead of waiting for
five years.
It is now proposed to add
£12,000 this year so as to hasten the
completion of the Endowment Fund.
The next sum of £1,000 is for the
Ulster Dairy School at Cookstown.
During the 20 years and more which have
elapsed since the school was first acquired
for its present purpose the buildings have
been very considerably enlarged and
adapted so as to render them suitable for
use
One
as an educational institution.
result of these alterations has been that
the heating arrangements have become
out of date and inadequate for their purpose. Numerous fires, stoves and boilers
have had to be kept going hitherto to provide the necessary heat and
for
power
classrooms, dormitories, living rooms,
laundries, and so on. Notwithstanding
all this expenditure of fuel the conditions
have been unsatisfactory. There has also
been excessive outlay for the maintenance
of heating apparatus and for labour employed in tending fires and boilers.
Although due economy has been exercised
in the use of fuel the results obtained
have not been commensurate with the
quantity consumed. The installation of a
central heating system as now proposed
is, in short, essential from the point of
view of efficient and economic organization. The total cost of the scheme is estimated at £1,100, of which £100 will fall
on the Vote for 1928-29, leaving £1,000 to
be met this financial year.
As regards the replacement of livestock, it will be within the recollection
of hon. Members that, owing to the great
losses farmers had sustained through the
deaths of their cattle, we granted some
1,600 loans to the total amount of
£76,000. Those were granted in the year
1925 for three years. The Ministry have
been able, with the assistance of the
Ministry of Finance, to make it easier for
the farmers to pay off these loans by
spreading the period of repayment over
five years instead of over three as originally provided. We have ample evidence
that the livestock replacement loans have
been of the greatest value to the small
farmers in many districts who were so unfortunate as to lose animals through
disease due to recent inclement seasons.
if
The amount next before us is for the
forestry unemployment relief scheme.
The House is fully acquainted also with
this scheme which, in addition to advancing the Ministry's efforts to deal
adequately with the re-afforestation of
Northern Ireland, has also helped,
only in a small way, to reduce unemployment. During the past year some 50 men
were employed under the scheme, and it
is hoped that during the coming year
this number may be doubled. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). With this end
in view we are asking for an additional
£750 with £200 for extra materials.

Supplementary Estimates
14 MARCH 1928
The Committee will be pleased to learn
that the efforts of the Ministry to extend
its afforestation activities are proving
successful. Prior to the present financial
year the Ministry had 5,076 acres of land
under forestry. We have now acquired
an additional 6,135 acres, making a total
of 11,211 acres. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). We are at present in negotiation
with a view to the acquisition of
additional lands. The average number of
acres planted each year in the past six
years has been 350. We hope to double
this next year. I beg to move.

CONTRIBUTORY PENSIONS
1.
Mr.
ACT.
WILLIAM MCMULLEN
asked the Minister of Labour whether it
is a fact that a number of employers have
taken advantage of the ten shillings per
week which is paid to old-age pensioners
under the Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Contributory Pensions
Pensions Act, to
reduce the wages of their employees, and
whether he would state if the Government will introduce an Amending Act to
put an end to this practice.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Cases in which the facts were
similar to those mentioned by the hon.
Member have been reported to me, but I
think they are of rare occurrence, and
I am glad to be able to say that in
certain instances where retrenchments
had taken place or where wages had been
reduced the matter has been rectified.
I made, as I think the hon. Member
knows, a very definite public statement,
when the matter was first brought to my
notice, to the effect that I felt that employers ought only to take into consideration efficiency, and that they should not
take advantage of the Contributory
Pensions Act in order either to reduce
wages or discharge their employees.
On the other hand, I feel that legislation to fix the wages to be paid to such
persons and to make it compulsory for
employers to employ them, or to compel
them to work for certain employers would,
for very obvious reasons, prove to be ineffective and the Government does not,
therefore, propose to promote such legisiation.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would
the right hon. Gentleman be prepared
to promote an Amending Bill to penalize
employers who are guilty of this practice
of reducing men's wages on the ground
that they are receiving pensions?
Mr. ANDREWS: No, Sir. I would
imagine the hon. Member knows, from
his knowledge of industrial relations, that
such a scheme would not be workable in
practice.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Is the
right hon. Gentleman aware that a
number of cases of this kind have occurred
since he made the speech referred to, and
under those circumstances is he prepared
to make another speech importuning employers not to take advantage of men in
this way?
Mr. ANDREWS: I think the answer
I have given to the question will be sufficient for the purpose.

whatever premises were necessary to set
them off upon their new lives. When the
matter had been gone into for some time,
I pointed out to the British Cabinet of the
day that owing to the high cost of building
at that time it would place Northern Ireland in a very serious financial position to
have to provide these buildings as compared with the position in which Southern
Ireland was at the time with its buildings
complete and fit for Government offices,
and for carrying on administration in
every direction. Owing to that we here
in Northern Ireland would be placed in a
very prejudicial position.
In consequence of those representations His Majesty's Government of the
day altered that Clause in the Act of 1920,
and undertook to put Northern Ireland
in full possession of a House of Parliament and the necessary administrative
buildings, to be equipped properly without any charge to the taxpayers of
Northern Ireland. I think I have made
that perfectly clear. I am only a passing

I am extremely anxious that there
should be no unnecessary expense in connection with it for many years to come,
and I myself have taken the opportunity,
from time to time, to point out where

was in a very bad way indeed, and there
was also the fencing. With regard to

Government that they had handed over
the place in a rather incomplete manner,
and after a considerable amount of
negotiation they very generously said
they would contribute the sum of
£10,000. The whole of that amount was
available for doing these various things.
The fencing on the drive is being put up.
If I may digress for one moment in
connection with that, I may say that my
colleagues and I, even in a small thing
thing like fencing, asked the British
Government to be kind enough to allow
us to have it made of our local Magheranourne cement and to employ as much
local labour as possible. Otherwise the
work might have been given to some firm
across the water and our local workmen
might not have had any benefit. We
take that precaution in order to see that
the money the British Government allocate to us is spent to the best possible
advantage.
I hope the Committee will not misunderstand me. It is just possible that all
these works may not be covered by the

appears in the book. It is quite proper

I think that with that explanation hon.

exception to the Estimates placed before
the Committee to-day.

Downing Street is by no means an unmixed advantage to the occupant of

Prime Minister who had experience of
it as I had would, if he were offered
the choice, rather not live in it at all.
The Prime Minister here has given expression to exactly the same views, that
if it were a matter of his own volition
and he had not to occupy the very important position of Prime Minister he

was given something in the nature of a

regard to the fact that it is not only the

CLASS I. VOTE 2.
CABINET OFFICES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£2,326 be granted to His Majesty for the
service of the year ending the 31st March
to defray the salaries of the Department
of the Prime Minister, the salaries of
the Cabinet and of the Cabinet secretariat
and other expenses in connection therewith including the expenses of the Privy
Council Office (15 and 16 Geo. V, c. 3,
s. 4 (N.I.).
Mr. BARBOUR: It may seem strange
to some Members of the Committee that
these items should be presented afresh
immediately after the discussion upon
them, so I would like to remind some of
them of the general construction of our
accounts, and the object aimed at in presenting the accounts in this particular
way. In the first place we divide our
accounts into different Departments and
endeavour to show as nearly as we can
the cost of conducting each Ministry and
each activity of that Ministry, and where
the nature of that activity permits two
separate accounts are kept in respect
thereof. And then in order that hon.
Members may be in a position to criticize
the work being done by the Public Works
Department, all the expenditure falling
under that head is brought forward into
an account by itself entitled Public Works
and Buildings. So that while hon.
Members may see, as just for instance in
the case of this particular item, there is
an item down there of £75 for fuel that
might be difficult to criticize in itself. if
