Oral Answers to Questions.
PRESERVATIVES IN CREAM.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he is
aware that the recent Order of the Imperial Government prohibiting the use of
preservatives in cream has killed the import of cream from Northern Ireland to
England and Scotland; and whether he
will make representations to the Ministry
of Health to have this Order revoked.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to reply to this question.
I understand that the recent Order
made by the Ministry of Health, Whitehall, on the subject of preservatives in
cream has undoubtedly adversely affected
the export of preserved cream from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain
At the same time I should explain to
the hon. Member that the Order referred
to was made by the Minister of Health
after the most careful consideration of
specific recommendations made to him
by a Committee of experts appointed to
consider the question of the injurious
effect on public health of certain preservatives in food.
The Minister of Health was SO
concerned at the representations and recommendations made by this expert
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
19 MARCH 1928
-t
Committee that he has steadfastly re
fused, in spite of repeated applications,
to consider the question of revoking or
amending these Regulations.
I may add further, that the Minister
of Home Affairs, as the Minister of
Health for Northern Ireland, concurs in
the principles which actuated the Minister
of Health regarding the dangers to
public health from preservatives in
foods, and proposes to issue a similar
Order next year applying in Northern
Ireland.
In these circumstances there can be no
question of any representations such as
the hon. Member suggests being made to
the Minister of Health.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Is the
hon. and learned Member aware that an
English daily paper, on Saturday, referred to this Order in the following
terms:
Another series of regulations has
banned even the least objectionable and
safest preservatives in milk and cream,
so that large quantities of these valuable foodstuffs are going sour and being
lost.
That is how an English daily referred to
this Order. Would not that strengthen
the hands of the Minister of Home Affairs
in making representation to the English
Department with regard to the evil effects
of this Order?
Mr. HANNA: I have not seen the report the hon. Member has referred me to,
and I would advise him to follow my
own example and not pay too much attention to what appears in a newspaper.
HIGHER RATES FOR DUTY ON
MOTOR LORRIES AND CARS.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Finance whether the higher
rates charged for duty on motor lorries
and cars, when the duty is paid quarterly
instead of yearly, is not a discouragement
to the occasional user and also a penalty
on the poorer owner; and whether he
would reconsider this matter and issue
quarterly licences at the same rate as that
paid for annual licences, these payments
being made in advance and involving no
cost for collection.
Mr. HANNA: I have been asked to
reply to this question.
The higher rates of duty charged for
quarterly licences in respect of motor
vehicles are not a discouragement to the
occasional user of such vehicles. On the
contrary, it has been found that the privilege of being able to obtain such licences
even at such higher rate is very much
appreciated, particularly as it enables
owners who desire to do so to put their
cars out of use during the winter quarter.
on
The granting of quarterly licences
entails a considerable amount of extra
work and expense
the licensing
authorities, and it is for this reason that
the small extra charge of one-tenth the
amount of duty is made.
This extra charge is only half that
made for quarterly licences prior to 1st
January, 1925, when an extra 20 per
cent. was charged for the privilege.
The reduction from 20 per cent. to 10
per cent. so increased the popularity of
quarterly licences that it is obvious that
were the surcharge to be still further reduced, no annual licences would be taken
out, and considerable unnecessary additional work would devolve on licensing
authorities, necessitating substantially increased staffs.
INSTRUCTIONS TO APPEALS
OFFICERS.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether it is a fact that instructions have been sent out to Appeals
Officers in Northern Ireland, informing
them that in future they will be expected
to take orders from the Chief Insurance
Officer; and whether, in view of the fact
that the Court of Referees is a statutory
body and is supposed to be independent
of the Exchange and Ministry officials, he
will take immediate steps to cancel these
instructions.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): It has always been the practice
of my Department, as in Great Britain,
to keep the officers of the Ministry, who
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
act as Appeals Officers or Clerks to Courts
of Referees, informed of the point of view
of the Chief Insurance Officer and the
Umpire on general questions of the interpretation and application of the statutory
conditions for unemployment benefit, in
order to assist them in their duty of
bringing in impartially before the Courts
all the salient considerations. No change
in this practice has been made or is in

Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that

CLERICAL. WORK OF ORANGE
ORGANIZATIONS.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that the
clerical work of the Junior Orange Association of Ireland, the Loyal Enniskillen
Memorial Orphan Society, and the County
Grand Lodge of Belfast, is all being done
by the staff of the Orange and Protestant
Friendly Society of Great Britain and
Ireland, in their Belfast office, 12 Donegall Square West, and can he state
whether it is a fact that the members of
the Orange and Protestant Society are
deprived of benefits to-day owing to work
done for the above Associations.
Mr. ANDREWS: Societies approved
for the purposes of National Health Insurance are entitled to make their own
office arrangements and the approval of
my Ministry is not required.
If specific cases of delay in payment of
benefit are brought to my notice I will
be glad to have inquiries made and the
matter rectified.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman has apparently misread the intention
of my question. It was that the Junior
Orange Association, of Ireland, the Loyal
Enniskillen Memorial Orphan Society
and the County Grand Lodge of Belfast
are engaged in work which is performed
by officials of the Ministry of Health or
by officials of the Orange and Protestant
Friendly Society. I want to know is it
desirable that that should be so?
Mr. ANDREWS: I have no knowledge that this is taking place, nor have
I any control over the approved societies
in this connection.
FORESTRY SCHEME-NUMBER OF
WORKERS EMPLOYED.
6. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. W.
McMullen) asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he can state the number
of workers employed in the Forestry
Scheme under his Department, and the
rates of wages paid.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): By reason of a sad bereavement in the family of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr.
Archdale) I am empowered to take this
question. The number of labourers employed on the Ministry's forestry operations is 83, and their wages range from
24s per week to 35s per week according
to district--the rate paid being based on
the current local wage for agricultural
labourers. There are also eight foremen
and assistant foremen employed at wages
ranging from 33s to 55s per week.
In certain cases workmen are provided
with cottages free of rent. I may say
that all men on 24s a week have free
cottages.
Seventeen boys are also employed at
wages of
from 15s to 23s per week
according to age. These boys are chiefly
engaged on work connected with the
Ministry's forestry nurseries.

Mr. BEATTIE: On a point of Order.
I would like to ask through you, Mr.
Moles, what rights Members of this House
have in regard to getting Forms or Regulations authorized by this Parliament. I
was in the unhappy position ten minutes
ago of going, on the instructions of my
leader, to ask for a copy of the Form U.I.
85.
The Gentleman who was in possession
of that Form, a civil servant who is highly
paid, refused to hand it to me. I went
to the Minister in charge of the Department concerned, and without any reluctance on his part he handed me a
copy of the Form which was in his
possession. Are the Members of this
House entitled to receive the Forms they
ask for or are they not?
Mr. ANDREWS: Perhaps, Mr. Moles,
before you answer the question I should
give an explanation in the matter. My
private secretary was asked for the Form.
He felt that he ought to keep the Form
for the Member who asked the question.
The hon. Member who has just spoken
did not make it clear to my private
secretary that he wanted it for the
Member who was asking the question, and
therefore he felt justified in refusing it.
When the hon. Member mentioned the
matter to me I handed him the Form,
leaving the other Form for the hon..
Member who asked the question, and
leaving myself without any Form at all.
I cannot see how any ground for complaint can be raised.
Mr. KYLE: On a point of Order. The
point of order I gather is: Is a Member
of the House entitled to get a copy of any
Form issued by the Ministry, which is not
private and confidential-any document
printed and published at the public
expense?
The CHAIRMAN: In the first place,
this is not a question which ought to be
addressed to me as Chairman of Committees. It ought to have been addressed
to Mr. Spearker. The second observation
I have to make about it is this: There is
a stipulated form of procedure in respect
of all such documents which does not
appear to me to have been complied with
in the present instance, except when the
request was made to the Minister.
There is a regular and recognized form by
which documents are made available for
Members, whatever quarter they come
from.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am a Member of this
House, and according to that ruling I
take it I am entitled to all publications
and public documents, except when they
are private and confidential. I asked in
a courteous manner for this document,
not for myself but for another Member.
I was bluntly refused, and I certainly resent that refusal by a highly paid civil
servant very much.
The CHAIRMAN: We may pass from
the incident. As I stated a moment ago,
the point of Order should have been
directed to Mr. Speaker when he was in
the Chair. In the second instance, if the
Minister had been approached I have not
the slightest doubt, from what he said,
that he would at once have handed the
hon. Member the Form. I can readily
understand what occurred in this matter.
There is procedure by which such documents can be demanded as of right by
Members.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move a reduction
of £1,000 in this Vote on Account, in
order to call attention to the state of the
administration in the Ministry of Labour.
I have given notice of this to the right
hon. Gentleman's private secretary. The
first matter I want to deal with is the
question of the Courts of Referees.
Courts of Referees are set up under Act
of Parliament, and the chairmen of them
are appointed by the Ministry of Labour.
They are supposed to be persons independent of the Ministry or of the Government. What I want to suggest is that in
G
Supply-
Vote on Account
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
future these appointments ought to be
made by the Crown and not by the
Ministry, because we have had an answer
from the Minister of Labour to-day, in
which he states that his Department has
issued instructions to the Courts of
Referees that they are to be a channel of
communication for giving instructions to
these appeals officers.
I want to submit to this Committee
that the Ministry of Labour has no right
under the Act of Parliament to issue
instructions to the Courts of Referees.
The Courts of Referees being statutory
bodies the Ministry has no right to interfere with their working or to prejudice
their decisions in any way. What happens
at the present moment is that when a man
or woman makes a claim to benefit at the
local Employment Exchange the Exchange officials put a series of questions,
with which they are no doubt provided
by the Department, quite legitimate
questions, asking the persons where they
have been looking for work, and if they
have been genuinely seeking employment.
To the average man with ordinary
intelligence those questions present no
difficulty, but a very great number of
people when they appear before Government officials seem to lose their heads.
They cannot answer the questions in a
straightforward manner, with the result
that when their claims are submitted to
the Court of Referees they are prejudiced
by the answers given to the questions submitted by the Exchange officials. In
other words the Exchange officials set a
trap for the unemployed persons, and the
applicants when they appear before the
Court of Referees fall into the trap set for
them. The result is that the Minister
can then declare that so many more people
have ceased to be unemployed.
Further, I want to know by what right
the Minister of Labour has defined what
is not defined in the Act of Parliament.
He says in this Form, issued under the
heading "Ministry of Labour," that one
of the disqualifications for an insured
contributor is misconduct. He goes on to
define what misconduct is. He has no
right to do so; that should be determined
by the Court of Referees. The Minister
defines misconduct as including breaches
of discipline, and conduct inconsistent
with conditions of service, or rendering a
worker incapable of performing his work
efficiently.
the
If a worker is sick that renders him incapable of performing his work efficiently,
and all his employer has got to do is to
write on the Form the Ministry sends him
that the person was guilty of misconduct
and the application for benefit is treated
accordingly by the Court of Referees.
The employer who signs this Form is not
expected to attend the Court of Referees
to allow either the applicant or
applicant's representative to ask him
questions regarding the manner in which
the worker performed his work. In fact,
it is stated specifically in this Form that
the information which the employer gives
will be treated confidentially. I protest
against this method of denying people
unemployment insurance benefit, because
I hold it is unfair. It is entirely against
all the traditions of fair play which I
always fondly assumed were in operation
in this country as well as in Great Britain.
I may say I never received such shocks
as I have during the past year or two.
Being a member of this Committee I
realize how the working people are liable
to suffer loss of benefit which they have
paid for through the wiles of Governments
who see a circular of this character filled
in.
That these Forms should be a means
of disqualifying a person from benefit is
something that no fair-minded person can
defend, particularly in view of the fact
that the employer's word is accepted in
99 cases out of 100, and the workman who
is examined by the Court of Referees does
not count for a snap of the fingers.
The workman appears before the chairman of the Court of Referees and before
the representative of the employers and
the representative of the workers and is
quizzed right, left and centre as to how
he left his employment. He is put
through the third degree before the Court,
yet the employer has nothing to do but
write anything he likes, and that reply
by the employer is treated as confidential
and used to the detriment of the workman.
Again, I say that is surely a state of
affairs that no right-minded person could
defend. The employer, if he gets evidence against a workman and writes that
evidence on this U.I.85 Form should,
equally with the workman, be summoned
to attend the Court of Referees before an
applicant is disqualified.
When an applicant for benefit makes his
claim at the Ministry of Labour in Corporation Street, Belfast, or at the

ge
Exchanges throughout the country, the
clerks have to put a certain number of

Belfast Exchange the clerks are expected
to attend to no fewer than 500 cases a

readily be seen how impossible it is for
either the clerk in the Exchange or the
applicant to do himself justice. Five
hundred cases per day work out at something like 60 per hour, or one per minute.
I want to submit that that state of affairs
ought to be remedied. A clerk is supposed to ask the applicant whether he
has been looking for work, where he has
been looking for work, and if he has beer
working any time since he had last signed
at the Exchange.
Further, the applicant for benefit is
supposed to sign a Form which is submitted to him by the clerk of the
Exchange. I submit to this Committee
that it is utterly impossible for that work
to be done at the present rate, and to be
done efficiently. Remember, too, that in
those cases in which the clerk gets the
signatures of the applicants, the signatures may be used in a court of law as
evidence against the workmen. The
clerk is supposed to remember every one
of those 500 cases that he deals with each
day, and to swear in a court of law that
such-and-such a person signed this document on such-and-such a day. I submit
that by compelling these Exchange people
to swear what it is obvious they could
not know is making a farce of the law.
It is impossible for a person to deal with
500 cases in a day, and to remember that
John Jones was the person who signed a
particular Form on a particular day. The
Ministry of Labour needs a very great
overhauling from the Minister down.

With my own eyes I have seen the police
marshalling people on a building job in
the outskirts of Belfast, and on the same
day I have seen the same men turned
down by Local Employment Committees
and Courts of Referees on the ground that
they were not genuinely seeking work.
There is something wrong with the administration of a Department in which
a situation like that can develop. My
colleagues and I know that hundreds of
decent working people in the city of
Belfast have been disqualified for not
genuinely seeking work. I want to
protest as strongly as I can against the
administration of the Ministry of Labour
in this connection.
I want to compare some of the figures
in this Vote on Account. I see that we
are spending £853,073 on police, in
contradistinction to £146,405 on agriculture. As has often been said in this
House, agriculture is the basic industry
of this area, and there is a tremendous
difference between the amount that we
spend on the police force and the amount
that we pay so far as agriculture is
concerned, much to the detriment of the
country. And on the same Vote on
Account we are spending £33,390 on
commercial services at a time when industry and commerce have never been
worse. I think that the Government
itself should reconsider the point of
view that was expressed the other day
by the Minister of Finance when he stated
that the Government were not company
promoters, and were not prepared to be
engaged in what he termed a highly
speculative industry such as the manufacture of artificial silk. Now, I am sure
hon. and right hon. Members opposite
have read with interest the Times trade
supplement this week end. In regard to
artificial silk they will see borne out by
the supplement the statement I made the
other day in this House, that the demand
for this article is such that the present
source of supplies are totally inadequate.
Now, I do not see at all why when
unemployment is rife as it is that the
Government should not be prepared to
engage in this highly speculative industry. I am not at all particular
whether the Government do it directly
themselves or do it indirectly, but I think
this industry, which apparently is a
coming one, should be established in the
North of Ireland to a greater extent than
it has been up to now. Whether it needs
Government subsidies or Government
assistance or Government credits it should
be done. We have here in the North of
Ireland, in Belfast particularly, a population that is accustomed to textile works
--a huge number of people who are
accustomed to working textile machinery,

Parliamentary institutions, they have

confronting those industries at the present
time are to be surmounted.

suggest that it is time to give politics a

Mr. KYLE: I put a question to the
Minister of Labour to-day, to which he
replied, and I raised the matter on the
Vote on Account. I thought the Minister
would have an opportunity of replying to
several of the criticizms I then made, and
of explaining to the House in Committee
the answer to the question I put down.
The question I asked the right hon.
Gentleman was:-
HOUSE OF COMMONS Instructions to Appeals Officers 448
Adjournment-
[Mr. Kyle]
Whether it is a fact that instructions
have been sent out to Appeals Officers
in Northern Ireland, informing them
that in future they will be expected to
take orders from the Chief Insurance
Officer; and whether, in view of the
fact that the Court of Referees is a
statutory body and is supposed to be
independent of the Exchange and
Ministry officials, he will take immediate steps to cancel these instructions.
The Minister of Labour, in his reply,
stated that his Department was following
on parallel lines with Great Britain, but
at the end of his reply he said:
No change in this practice has been
made or is in contemplation other than
as regards the channel of communication as to administrative convenience.
I am glad he has stated that so far as he
is concerned he is now prepared to say
that the Appeals Officers and Courts of
Referees are an independent body, and
are independent gentlemen so far as the
Ministry of Labour is concerned, and that
they are not supposed to take instructions
from the Chief Insurance Officer, who is
merely a salaried official responsible to the
Minister of Labour, who is responsible to
this House. But the sting of this answer
is in the tail, where he states there
is a change in contemplation. For reasons
best known to himself he has not yet made
it clear to the House, though he had an
opportunity, why this change is being
made. Without a definite reply from the
Minister of Labour it is impossible to
criticize the proposed change, but if it is
a fact that the change that is contemplated is that Appeals officers and Courts
of Referees are to take instructions from
the managers of local Exchanges, which
I rather think is the change that is contemplated, it is one that I would ask
this House to refuse to agree to.
I am afraid that Members on the opposite of the House are not perhaps as much
concerned about the rights and privileges
of Members of the House as some of us
on this side are. You think these matters are only raised for pure cussedness,
or from the point of view of making it
awkward for the Government. Perhaps
that does arise to some extent, and I
think it is quite right that it should; but
in addition to that, there is the fundamental question that ought to interest
Members on the other side, equally with
Members on this side, as to whether it is
right and proper for a Minister to have
the right to appoint from time to time
certain Courts of Referees. A Court of
Referees is a statutory body, and the
gentlemen who preside over those Courts
ought to be appointed by the Crown, and
be independent of any Minister.
I have pointed that out, and I cannot
see for the life of me that as Constitutionalists we can get away from that point
and allow the Minister of Labour, although he is a Minister of the Crown, to
take upon himself the right to appoint
persons, and then in addition to appointing those persons to instruct a junior
official of the Ministry of Labour, or any
official, to issue an order, or to issue instructions to a Court of Referees, which
is a statutory body, to determine applicants' claims to benefit. That is a position
which this Parliament ought not to allow
the Government to take up. The Government are not, or ought not to be, all
powerful. The Government are only a
part of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, and the Parliament of Northern
Ireland should not stand idly by and see
Ministers usurp powers which it was never
intended they should have.
I want to know from the Minister of
Labour what change in this practice is
contemplated in regard to this channel of
communication, as he puts it. I know
that Ministers are in the habit of not
being very explanatory in reply to Memthan
bers-I could put it much worse
that and that being the case I am at a
loss to understand why there is a necessity for the Minister of Labour to instruct his officials to change a method of
imparting information to chairmen and
officials of Courts of Referees.
I am
very anxious for the Minister to give the
House the information he did not give
in his reply to my question.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I fear it is inevitable that I
should speak with considerable frequency
in this House owing to the fact that the
Ministry of Labour is charged with the
administering of those services included
in our social code which means so much
to our industrial classes. It will be admitted that I have always endeavoured to
make my remarks as brief and as direct
as possible, but on this occasion I will
have to ask for the sympathy and the forbearance of hon. Members for a longer
period than I am accustomed to do.
My
453 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

20 MARCH 1928
Second Reading
justification is two-fold. In the first
place, this is a most important Measure
affecting not only our insured persons, but
also their employers and the general taxpayers to a very substantial extent; and,
in the second place, it is a somewhat complicated Measure.
Lord Carson in the House of Lords described it as a Measure of great difficulty
due to the fact that it referred to so many
previous Acts. I must say at this stage
that I feel personally very grateful to
our Parliamentary draftsman for the pains
he has taken and the skill he has displayed in effecting a considerable amount
of consolidation work in connection with
this Measure, which will make my task
much lighter to-day. Of course, all the
provisions of the Act, of which this is
in effect the counterpart, have been preserved; at the same time he has, by means
of the consolidation he has carried out,
removed the necessity of having so many
references in the Bill to earlier Measures.
The study of the evolution of unemployment insurance is a very interesting
one, because it shows how narrow and
small beginnings can lead to greater
things through an aroused social
conscience prompted by all the best instincts.
of the human heart. The genesis of unemployment insurance is to be found in
the action of
of the friendly societies
and the trade unions-all honour to them
-dating as far back as 1905. At that time
122 Friendly Societies, with a membership
of 75,000, paid benefit or allowances to
unemployed members and also gave expenses allowances to those members who
were unemployed and who sought employment at places considerably distant
from their home. In the same year 81
trade unions did what was tantamount to
the same thing. They gave benefits on
the average ranging from 10s to 12s to
to unemployed members for short periods.
It is interesting to remember that they
also introduced waiting periods and gaps
of considerable length.
It was not until 1911 that the State
first recognized its responsibility in this
direction. The Act of 1911 was a compulsory Insurance Act. It was financially successful, due to several causes
to which I will refer later. It
covered two and a quarter million
workers engaged in seven industries which
were considered to be those industries
most likely to be affected by industrial
depression. These industries were shipbuilding, mechanical engineering, construction works, vehicle works, iron
foundries, building and saw milling. The
Measure was of a modest kind. The contributions from the employer
employer only
amounted to 2d, from the worker 2d,
and 1 2-3d from the State. The benefits
given under this Measure were 7s to
adults and 3s 6d to persons between 17
and 18 years of age. One week's benefit
was given for every five contributions paid,
and only 15 weeks benefit was payable
during the year. No extended benefit, or
uncovenanted benefit as it was called,
was paid at that time.
In 1916 this Measure was extended to
cover munition workers and those trades
which it was felt were likely to be affected
when hostilities ended. Again in 1916
changes were made, and in 1918 this
Measure included four million workers in
the United Kingdom, but it was found
that that was insufficient to deal with the
industrial crisis which developed shortly
after the war, and between November,
1918, and November, 1919, out of work
donations amounting to £22,000,000
were paid to civilian workers, and
£40,000,000 in the same time was paid
to unemployed ex-Service men. This
Measure had really nothing to do with the
Unemployment Act to which I have referred except that it was a great help to
it, as this vast sum of £62,000,000 was
paid without encroaching upon the Unemployment Fund proper.
In 1919 benefit was raised to 11s. for
adults and 5s. 6d. for boys and girls.
Again in 1920 a new Measure was introduced, which is one of great importance
and has been looked upon as the principal
Act ever since. It covered all employees
employed in manual work and those whose
salaries were under £250, except agricultural workers and domestic servants.
In all eleven million workers were covered
by this Measure. The contributions were
raised to 4d from the employer, 4d
from the worker and 2d. from the State,
and the benefit payable was 15s. to men
and 12s. to women. There was a three
days waiting period. One week's benefit
was paid for six contributions. Again
only standard benefit was given and only
for a period not exceeding 15 weeks in
any year. Applications for benefit
determined by the insurance
were
455 Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Andrews]
officer, the courts of referees, and in
certain instances, on appeal, by the
umpire.
There were between that date and the
present no fewer than 16 Unemployment
Insurance Acts passed. They modified
and extended the original provisions and
did many other things as well. In 1921
three Acts were passed. These Acts
altered both the rates of benefit and rates
of contribution. They maintained, however, the one-in-six rule, but increased
the maximum amount of benefit payable
in any one year from 15 to 26 weeks.
Further, for the first time in 1921 uncovenanted benefit, as it was called at
that time, was introduced. Extended
benefit as we know it now was never intended to be more than an emergency provision.
In addition to that, one of these
Acts of 1921 introduced what is
known as dependants' benefit, and
I take especial interest in that provision,
because I am not likely to forget that my
first official duty in connection with the
work of the Ministry of Labour was
associated with having all the benefits of
that Act extended to Northern Ireland
between the time that our Parliament
came into existence and we took over our
powers in 1922. It is not necessary
that I should tell the story of those
negotiations, but they are interesting from
the standpoint of showing how political
opponents at a time of great political
controversy can set aside, for a few
hours at any rate, their various differences in order that the right thing
may be done to their fellow countrymen.
I now wish to refer to the Act of 1924,
which hon. Members will recollect was introduced by the Socialist Government
during the time they were in office.
Benefits were raised to 18s for men, and
15s for women.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: Refunds were, however, terminated, and a new first statutory condition was introduced, very
similar to the one which it is proposed to
include in this Measure. Later Acts prolonged the duration of extended benefit,
altered the rates of benefit, varied the
waiting period and the contributions payable, and the Contributory Pensions Act
prescribed that the payment of benefit and
the workers' share of contributions would
cease at 65.
The Imperial Minister of Labour came
to the conclusion that unemployment insurance legislation had got into a very unsatisfactory condition. One temporary
Measure after another, as I have tried
to show, was added to the Statute Book
without, perhaps, a great deal of regard
having been paid to the ultimate goal.
Moreover, it was felt that two forms of
benefit were objectionable from many
standpoints. I think the hon. Members
from both sides of the House will agree
with that view. I certainly do. Standard benefit was received as a right, and
extended benefit was purely discretionary.
Mr. BEATTIE: No.
If
of
Mr. ANDREWS: There was a statutory right of appeal in one instance and
none in the other. It was not altogether
to be wondered at that claimants were
frequently dissatisfied, and felt that an
injustice was being done to them.
they had understood all the circumstances
they would have formed a different
opinion. The Imperial Minister
Labour with great wisdom, in my opinion,
if I may say so, set up what is known as
the Blanesburgh Committee in 1925, to
consider, in the light of experience
gained in the working of the Unemployment Insurance scheme, what change
in the scheme, if any, ought to
be made. This Committee was presided over by a very distinguished
nobleman, whose name the Committee
bears, and it will interest hon. Members
in this House to recollect that the Secretary to the Committee was Mr. John A.
Dale, who for four years was the Permanent Secretary to the Ministry of Labour
here. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
It is gratifying to know that after having
faithfully and to the great advantage of
the people of Northern Ireland served us
here, he has already played an important part in connection with framing
social legislation in Great Britain, notwithstanding the fact that he is still,
comparatively speaking, a very young
man.
On that Committee there were many
representative employers, also representatives of the general community and
prominent Labour leaders. Amongst
the number was Miss Margaret Bondfield,
who was Under Secretary of the Ministry
of Labour during the Socialist term of
office. There were also Mr. Hodges and
Mr. Holmes, who, as hon. Members know.
457 Unemployment Insurance Bill-

20 MARCH 1928
Second Reading
are men greatly respected not only in
trade union circles, but also outside the
orbit of trade unions. This Committee
considered this problem for about two
years, and they received evidence from
employers' associations and trade unions,
from local authorities, and, in fact, from
everybody who was willing to give evidence which would help to solve a
very difficult problem. The Committee
brought in a unanimous report during
last and I think it should be rememyear,
bered that it was unanimous, notwithstanding that the interests represented
on the Committee were of very various
kinds.
The chief findings of the Committee,
briefly stated, are as follows: That a compulsory contributory scheme is necessary;
that there should be only one form of
benefit; that there should be a single
form of procedure for the adjudication of
claims by the insurance officer, the Courts
of Referees, and the umpire; that the
arbitrary restrictions imposed by the onein-six rule and the 26-weeks rule should
be removed, and instead of that claims
should be examined every 13 weeks; that
the scheme should be wide in its scope;
and that contracting-out should not be
permitted. Certain changes were also
suggested as regards rates of benefit, as
regards contributions and dependants'
allowances and the classes of dependants
which should be included. And with
that preliminary statement I now come
to the present Bill.
The counterpart of this Measure was
introduced at Westminster in August
last, and it was based, in practically every
particular, upon the report of the Blanesburgh Committee, with the exception of
its financial provisions, to which I will
refer later. The Bill was passed in Great
Britain last autumn, and it will come into
operation upon the 19th of next
month. It is
necessary that we
should keep our scheme on parallel
lines with the British one
account of our reinsurance agreement
with Great Britain, which has been such
a tremendous advantage (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)--to our working people
in Northern Ireland-it has actually
brought to our Unemployment Fund no
less a sum that £3,000,000, contributed
in part by the British Treasury and in
part by my right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance. When I speak of keeping on parallel lines with Great Britain
on
I have behind me a considerable weight of
authority, because I feel, whatever hon.
Members opposite may at times say, the
vast majority of our people in Northern
Ireland desire that we should do so.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And
further, a few months after we took over
our powers in Northern Ireland, I appointed what was called the Shillington
Committee, presided over by my hon. and
gallant Friend who sits behind me. This
Committee was also composed of men of
all classes and of all creeds in Northern
Ireland, and it also, it is worth noting,
brought in a unanimous report, which
was to the effect that we should in
Northern Ireland, in connection with
Unemployment Insurance, keep in step
with Great Britain.
This Bill requires that all persons engaged in manual work and those whose
salaries are under £250 a year, except
agricultural workers and domestic servents, should be insured. The contributions remain as at present-8d from the
employer, 7d from the worker, and 6d
from the State. I am only giving the
weekly contributions payable by men as an
example. The total contributions it will
be seen therefore amount to 21d. Now,
this is the departure from the Blanesburgh
Committee's report to which I have referred. The Blanesburgh Committee suggested that the contributions should be
equal as between the employer, the worker,
and the State and that 5d should be contributed by each, making a total of 15d.
But having regard to the fact that the
British fund is overdrawn at the present
time to the extent of over £22,000,000our suspense debt is even heavier in proportion-it was felt that the contributions
suggested by the report would not be
sufficient to restore solvency to the fund
by a repayment of the debt. Now, a
great deal was made of this departure at
Westminster, due to the fact that it was
considered that the State was not contributing its fair share.
Well, whatever grounds there may have
been for that complaint in Great Britain
there are no such grounds here, and for
this reason. When we take into account
the ordinary statutory contribution from
the State and the equalization payment
from the Imperial Treasury, and also the
equalization payment from our own
Treasury, we find that instead of the State
contributing one-third of the total amount

There will be no means test, and,

modified in such a way as to be of very

person. For instance, at the present

after six weeks, employment has been

waiting period; employment for less than

periods of unemployment without

further waiting period. Again a very
considerable concession is made as regards

they were in such subsidiary employment
before they became unemployed. Now
they can accept employment of this kind
and if the wages paid do not exceed
3s 4d per day for the work done they
can draw benefit notwithstanding.
I really do feel that hon. Members

remind hon. Members that it abolishes

this is a very considerable concession.

Mr. ANDREWS: I think it is a very
great concession, and I think those whom

removes the one-in-six rule and the

work a much greater sense of security
than they have ever had before; it enlarges the category of dependants; it
makes a fairer adjustment between the

to the married claimants; it authorizes
more liberal application of the continuity
rule; it extends to claimants greater
opportunities for carrying on subsidiary
work without loss of benefit; it gives the
applicant in all cases a statutory right
to benefit and of appeal from the insurance officer's decision; and it provides for
financial assistance towards the training of
unemployed juveniles. I had the
privilege yesterday of launching a new
Juvenile Committee for this city. The
old Juvenile Committee, which did most
excellent work, were cramped in their
efforts in two directions.
The first direction was that there was a
shortage of schools. That is being made
right under the provisions of the Londonderry Education Act. The other cramping influence was that the Education
Ministry had not sufficient money at their
disposal to deal with the question of continuation classes for juveniles. Under
one of the provisions of this Measure it
will be permissible to take certain sums
from the unemployment fund in order to
train and assist these unemployed
juveniles, and I do not think hon. Members opposite will object to that provision.
But over and above all that, this Measure
keeps us in step with Great Britain, and
therefore it allows us, as I have already
explained, to get the benefits of our
re-insurance agreement.

purposes the Six Counties are an uneconomic unit. That is recognized by the
insurance scheme. Can the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Andrews) defend this.
state of affairs, that workpeople who reside in the Maiden City of Derry, and
who work in the Free State, do not get
the benefit for the stamps which are put
on their cards by their Free State employers, or vice versa? Take the border,
which you were going to defend to the last
ditch. You were never going to surrender an inch. This talk, this tosh-if
that is not an unparliamentary word-is
the burden of their song outside.
We
do not hear so much of it in this House,
perhaps because we would reply to it
here. We read this sort of stuff delivered by hon. and right hon. Gentlemen
outside.
Take the case of the poor worker who
lives across the border, in the Irish Free
State, and who works in the Belleek
Pottery in Northern Ireland. Deductions are made from his wages for unemployment insurance and other purposes.
If the Belleek Pottery shuts down, as it
has done occasionally, that worker is not
entitled to unemployment insurance, despite the fact that contributions have been
deducted from his pay. In other words,
that worker is being robbed, and his employer is also being robbed in the same
way. Can that state of affairs be defended by the hon. or right hon. Gentlemen opposite? If it could be, it would be
very interesting to hear the defence.
Something may be said about the difference in social benefits, the fact that
the unemployment benefit in the Free
State is different from the unemployment
benefit paid here, the fact that there are
no widows' pensions in the Free State,
and that there are widows' pensions here.
All those things may be said.
Mr. GORDON: That is the answer.
Mr. KYLE: But that does not answer
the fact that I, as a worker, have certain
deductions made from my wages to insure
me against unemployment, and when I am
unemployed and require the money that
I have paid from time to time, the insurance company-in this case the Government-refuses to meet its liabilities. I
think that is a perfectly prepostrous, and
perfectly scandalous, bit of business.
Both the Government of the Free State
and the Government of Northern Ireland
are to blame, and, of course, being here
as Members of this Parliament and not
of the Dail, we obviously want to denounce the people here for this iniquitous
state of affairs, which should be remedied
at once.
No satisfactory basis of insurance can
be laid down without recognizing that
point. The right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) in the course of his speech misrepresented me to some extent, as well as
some of my colleagues, in regard to the
Court of Referees and the gentlemen who
adjudicate in those Courts of Referees. He
quoted something that was said yesterday,
and did not quote it correctly, as usual.
What I was getting at yesterday, and
what I repeat to-day, is that the Court
of Referees, as a statutory body, ought
not to receive instructions from the
Minister of Lahour or the Ministry of
Labour. The right hon. Gentleman has
recognized to some extent the strict
legality of that position, but he says that
a change is being made in regard to the
method by which information-I call
it instructions-is imparted to the
court. When the Minister of Labour appoints a man to act in this capacity-
I do not want to say one word against
these men; nor have I-I contend, and I
think rightly contend, that it is wrong
for the Minister of Labour, through his
officials, to send information as he calls it
-instructions, as I insist-to the Court of
Referees that he shall adjudicate according
to this, that, or the other thing. That
is the point I want to stress in this regard.
In regard to the differentiation of
benefit, which has been referred to by
the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr.
William McMullen), and by the right
hon. Gentleman himself, I
may say that

There are many things in this Bill

I think we are at a loss to

Clause 5, page 6, lines 32 and 33,

(ii) after the lapse of such an interval

I have yet to hear definition of what is

ment insurance benefit. That will happen

always believed, he never has to appear

perience of them, I agree with almost

It seems to me that if in the future

491 Unemployment Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Kyle]
If you have 3,000 cases to be got through,
as in many weeks at present there have
to be 3,000 cases disposed of, one can
easily understand it will be a physical impossibility, unless there are several of these
Courts sitting at the same time, to get
through that number of cases per week,
if they are to receive any consideration at
all. The Member for West Belfast told
us in this House yesterday that he had
to wait about an hour for a decision on
a case by a Court of Referees, and if that
is so in regard to one or two cases how
on earth is it going to be possible to get
through the number of cases we will have
in the city of Belfast under this Bill. I
think there is very considerable room for
amendment in this Bill, particularly in
that connection.
I do not want to minimize the right hon.
Gentleman's speech, because it was very
good so far as it went. The only criticizm
I have to make is that it did not go far
enough, because the Minister did not
make it at all clear whether every application for benefit must be submitted to
a Court of Referees at once, or whether
an Insurance Officer is to adjudicate on
the case in the first instance, so that the
applicant might then have a chance to
appeal from the decision of the Chief Insurance Officer to the Court of Referees.
I suggest that if the right hon. Gentleman
has not considered that point he ought to
do so, so that an applicant for benefit
might have at least two sources of appeal
open to him.
What I mean is that an
applicant's claim for benefit should, in
the first instance, be examined by the
Chief Insurance Officer, or his representative, and if he says it is a straightforward claim it should be admitted without having to go to the Court of Referees.
If, on the other hand, the Chief Insurance Officer thinks it is not a good claim,
then the applicant should have the right
of appeal, as he has to-day, to the Court
of Referees, and if the Court of Referees
do not decide in the applicant's favour he
should have the right, under certain circumstances, to appeal to the Umpire.
As far as I have read the Bill, which is,
as the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Wm. McMullen) described it, one
of the worst examples of legislation by
reference ever submitted to this House, it
does not seem to be very clear as to what
the machinery is going to be. As far as
I have been able to understand the Bill,
it seems that every application has to be
submitted automatically to the Court of
Referees. I want the Minister to consider that point between now and the
Committee stage, so that we may have an
opportunity of going into it a little bit
more carefully.
On page 8, line 3, of the Bill it states
that an applicant for benefit may not
have his claim to benefit reviewed, except
at intervals of not less than six weeks.
You will notice the significance of that
word "less." It means that an applicant for benefit who was not able to
satisfy the Chief Insurance Officer or the
Court of Referees that he was genuinely
seeking work is turned down for a period
of not less than six weeks. In my own
experience I have known cases where a
person's application for benefit was
turned down on the ground that he was
not genuinely seeking work, and within
a week he has actually found work, which
shows that he must have been looking for
it.
Again, if a person looks for work every
day from the time he is disqualified, surely
there should be discretionary power given
to the Court of Referees to read, instead
of the word "less," the word "more,'
so that that statutory body would have
power to say "owing to the peculiar circumstances of this case we will only disallow you for two or three weeks." They
can do that to-day, but if this Bill goes
through without Amendment, no one will
have power to disqualify an applicant for
benefit for a less period than six weeks,
no matter what the circumstances may
be. That part of the Bill requires
amendment.
As the hon. Member for West Belfast
has said, no doubt we shall have an opportunity on the further stages of the
Bill to go into these and other points
more carefully than we can on the
Second Reading debate. As the hon.
Member has also said, there are several
things in the Bill that are a welcome
change. The criticizms we have to offer
are all helpful from the point of view
that this Bill is not a satisfactory basis
on which to build Unemployment Insurance, particularly bearing in mind the
fact that unemployment in Northern Ireland is in a higher ratio than unemployment in Great Britain. Taking that into
consideration, we do not think this Measure has been as carefully thought out as
it ought to have been, or that it is a
proper and adequate basis for Unemployment Insurance.

Mr. GRANT: In rising to support the
Second Reading of this Bill I would like
to congratulate the Minister of Labour on
the very clear statement he made to the
House. There are quite a number of
things in the Bill that I do not like, and
I am sure that if the Minister gave his
own private opinion he would admit there
are a lot of things in the Bill that he does
not like. But we have got to reconcile
ourselves to this fact: that it is the best
possible Bill we can get under existing
circumstances, and therefore we ought to
accept it.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) used what, to my mind, was a
very peculiar argument, and he emphasized it in his last sentence. He stated
that the Six County area is a noneconomic unit, and then he went on to
point out that the relative number of
unemployed in Great Britain was from 8
to 10 per cent. against 15 to 18 per cent.
in Northern Ireland. He did admit that
our reinsurance scheme was a good one.
As he has put forward that argument, I
cannot see how he can consistently oppose
this Bill, because if Great Britain, with
an average of from 8 to 10 per cent. unemployed, are prepared to allow us, under
our reinsurance scheme from 15 to 18 per
cent unemployed, and to give the same
benefits for the same contributions, I
think we ought to welcome this Bill with
open arms. I am sure the Member for
North Belfast, if he did not occupy the
position of Leader of the Opposition, and
was speaking to a meeting of unemployed
outside this House, would honestly tell
them that the people of Northern Ireland
were being well served by the Minister of
Labour and his Department under this
reinsurance scheme.
I quite agree with the Leader of the
Opposition that some of the benefits to
be given under this Bill are not as great
as I would like to see. He pointed out
the different treatment meted out to persons between 18 and 19 years of age, and
persons of 21 years of age. The only
advice I can give to young men of 18 and
19 is to get married, in order to obtain
this extra 7s a week dependants benefit.
I am prepared to admit the wisdom of
some of the arguments of the Minister of
Labour. I know quite a lot of cases of
boys of 18 and 19 who left their work
deliberately to get unemployment benefit,
and hon. Members on the opposite side of
the House know of similar cases.
We have been told many times to-day
that Appeals Officers do not give fair consideration to claimants, but we have
never been told what we are bound to
admit is a fact, namely, that claimants
have got benefit through other people not
carrying out the Regulations. Claimants
have got a certificate from employers
that they were out of employment when,
as a matter of fact, they have been
so unsatisfactory to their employers that
the latter have been only too glad to
get rid of them at any price, and they
have been able to draw the unemployment
benefit as a result. This Bill will abolish
claims of that sort. I have a couple of
boys at home who are about this age, and
I know it takes more to keep them than
it does to keep me, and I quite
realize that it is going to be very
hard for mothers and fathers
to keep their boys, who are
genuinely unemployed, on the rates of
benefit proposed in this Bill. At the
same time, unemployment insurance was
never intended to keep families, and
under these circumstances I am prepared
to welcome the Bill.
With regard to the number af contributions to qualify for benefit, I entirely
agree with the proposal in the Bill, and
I would like to thank the Minister for
introducing the particular part of the
Measure dealing with the qualifying contributions of ex-servicemen. We all
know how difficult it is for these men to
find employment at any time, and employers are not always as sympathetic towards them as we would like them to be.
It is difficult for disabled ex-servicemen
to qualify on the same basis as ordinary
workers, and I am glad that this special
provision has been made for them.
Thousands of people will welcome the fact
that the family-income test has been
abolished, because it has been a source of
great trouble to people in Northern Ireland when they had other people prying
into their personal affairs. I wish the
Minister of Labour would just as easily
abolish this other bogey of G. S. W.
There is one particular part of the Bill
I am specially delighted with, and that
is Clause 5, Section 6, which has been
referred to by Members of the Opposition.
That is the Clause which lays it down
that a person must have been resident
in the United Kingdom for three years
immediately preceding the date on which
application for benefit is made. I think

into the Consolidated Fund in the form
of penalties recovered under the provisions of Section 5 of the Act, which
empowers local authorities to prohibit or

This procedure, viz., the passing of moneys to

instead of paying them direct into the
Road Fund is a continuance of the procedure governing all payments into the

Fund or to the Exchequer, should go into
the Road Fund and so be available for

estimate what sum will accrue to the Road
Fund by reason of this provision.

Sir DAWSON BATES: My right hon.

It is the intention of the Government
that the next General Election for the

Member.
On the other hand, the Government do

heavy expense involved.

Therefore, I arranged, and I think it
was in the interests of Ulster-and that is
what I have always had in my mind, and
nothing else (hon. Members: Hear,

advancement of Ulster the best brains

There were a few cases-a number of

have any clash whatever in their own

has no business whatever to inquire. It is a
personal matter which touches the highest
honour of all my colleagues, and I think
the Ulster people are the best judges of

dealing with large sums of money are
not to be subjected to review, and are
not to be re-discussed.
I, as I say, oppose this Vote, not on
this particular issue alone, but principally
on the ground that the whole expenditure in Northern Ireland is on a wrong
basis; that our foundations are laid on
far too big a scale, and that our establishments, not only those included in this
Vote, but the whole Government of
Northern Ireland, are set upon a basis
of revenue Northern Ireland cannot possibly support. If the country were
prosperous, if industry revived, and if
commerce were re-established we might
be able to hold on our way; but with a
small population of a million and a
quarter people it will always be impossible
to develop fully the resources of the
country and, at the same time, carry on
Government on the basis on which we are
doing at the present time.

Order for Second Reading read.

Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think it is
necessary that I should go in very great
detail into the terms of this Bill, which
is only really a provision to continue the
operation of the original Bill for another
year, but, as there was some criticizm
when the Money Resolution pertaining
to the Bill was before the Committee, it
is right that I should speak as shortly as
may be in regard to some of the features
which did not seem to be perfectly clear to
hon. Members opposite who spoke of it
in terms of criticizm. The hon. Member
for Down (Mr. Patrick O'Neill), who I
am sorry to see is not here at the moment,
particularly was under grave misapprehension in regard not only to the objects
for which the Act was brought into existence, but also in regard to the operation
of the machinery by which the Act was
worked.
In order to remove any misapprehension, may I say that the object of the
original Measure and, of course, the object continues was to create employment. I cannot too strongly emphasize
that expression. It was found that,
under conditions such as obtained some
years ago, something was required in
order that we might resuscitate the normal shipbuilding conditions that had obtained in the past. From conditions that
had arisen out of the Great War, so much
capital having been destroyed, shipowners, finding the business of the world
in rather a parlous state, and not having
sufficient loose capital at their command,
were indisposed to continue their building
programmes. As our conditions
unemployment were severe the Government came to the conclusion that it was
necessary to provide some artificial
inethod by which shipowners especially
could be induced to continue and develop
whatever building programmes they had
in mind, and which they were unable to
undertake because of the scarcity of immediate capital.
of
Therefore, the Act was devised in such
a way that accommodation would be provided to enable them to repay the cost of
their building operations over such a term
of years as was mutually arranged, and
perhaps I should read the main condition
of the principal Act which it is the purpose of this Measure I am now discussing
to continue, in order that hon. Members
may clearly understand the gravamen of
the conditions under which it was brought
into existence and the particular objects
for which it was devised.
If the Ministry of Finance for Northern Ireland, after consultation with
an advisory committee nominated by
the Minister of Finance for Northern
Ireland for the purposes of this Act, is
satisfied that the proceeds of any loan
proposed to be raised by any public
authority, or any corporation or other

I
Loans Guarantee Bill-
Second Reading
21 MARCH 1928

body of persons, are to be applied towards, or in connection with, the
carrying out of any capital undertaking, and the application of the loan
in the manner proposed is calculated
to promote employment in Northern
Ireland, the Ministry may, subject to
the provisions of this Act, guarantee
in such a manner and form and on such
terms and conditions as the Ministry
thinks proper, the payment of
the interest and principal of the loan
or of either interest or principal.
Now, that single section of the original
Act clearly sets out the objects in view
and the methods by which the loans advanced to those prepared to engage in
capital undertakings may be guaranteed
by the Government. Now, we found in
the operation of this Act that although
we had in mind at the same time that our
principal industry, shipbuilding, being in
a parlous state, was the one that required
immediate attention, and it was the one
for which, in the main, this Act was
brought into operation, there were other
industries under this heading that could
naturally benefit by its operation. That
is to say, any body of persons engaging
in any capital undertaking calculated to
promote the employment of these unemployed could, by application to the Minisiry of Finance, have the repayment of
capital which was lent guaranteed by the
Government.
Therefore, it has been the case, that
although the major portion of the guarantees have been given in respect of shipbuilding, still there were several other
cases where capital was required for the
provision of industries where the Act itself operated. The principal advantage
that accrued from it from the point
of view of those borrowing-and I still
limit my survey to the shipowners, because it is really our method of dealing
with the shipowners that has been criticized. In the case of the shipowners
the purpose of the guarantee was to enable the shipowner to extend the payment
for the ship over a certain number of
years, and, at the same time, insure that
our yards should be fully occupied if that
were possible.
In the result our principal yard
has been fully occupied, and if hon.
Members will consult the printed form
which is issued from time to time they
will, without the necessity of asking any
see
| questions indeed, be able to know exactly
the amount of the guarantees offered
by the Government, and the character
of such guarantees. They will
that a sum of money up to something
like £8,000,000 has been guaranteed.
Some of that has been paid off, and, of
course, as years go on it will be paid off
from year to year, so that it will lower
the Government's liability, and finally it
will be extinguished.
The hon. Member for Down (Mr. P.
O'Neill) spoke of the limitation of the
Government guarantee to a term of two
years when the Money Resolution came
on. I said something in reply, pointing
that the construction of such large ships
as are built in our principal yard required almost two years at any rate,
and that, therefore, a guarantee limited
to two years would be of no earthly use
to any shipowner, because in the majority
of cases the shipbuilder only received his
money from the shipowner at the end of
the construction of the ship. Therefore,
you will see how perfectly absurd it would
be to place limits such as the hon. Member had in mind. It would have no
value to them, and could have no efficacy
if such limits were imposed. As a matter
of fact, insurance companies, who advance
the major portion of the money in these
cases, are perfectly satisfied to continue
the security to a term of 10 or 12 years.
Of course, repayment is made from year
to year, as the shipowner is able from the
earnings of the ship to repay.
a
As to results, no one can decry them.
We have succeeded by the operation of
this Measure in keeping our principal
shipyard fully employed. We have been
able to assist in the introduction of a new
industry, a textile industry, in Northern
Ireland. We have advanced money for
other purposes, electric light work,
weaving factory, and such like. All these
things, of course, have been directed to
the one purpose to which I have referred,
that is, the creation of employment. I
think the Government can congratulate
itself to this extent, that it has succeeded
in providing employment for a very large
number of men that would otherwise have
been walking the streets. It has been
one of the most useful Acts, and one of
the simplest, and, to some extent, one of
the least troublesome that the Government has passed during the seven years
of its existence. At any rate I, myself,
feel that the small committee which was

the Government may feel, at
any rate,
that it has contributed no little to the
continuance of employment in Northern
Ireland which otherwise would not have
existed. I beg to move.

Mr. BARBOUR: The necessity for this
Money Resolution may be explained
briefly. The Economy Act of 1926 in
Great Britain and our own Economy
(Exchequer Relief) Act of 1926 did not
provide for payment of similar rates of
contributions from public moneys in
respect of Unemployment Insurance of
exempt persons as from the 1st January
of this year.
It is essential for the purpose of the re-insurance agreement that
these rates should be identical. Accordingly, it will be necessary to insert a
Clause for this purpose in the present
Bill. The effect of the Clause will be to
substitute the rates set out in the text of
the Money Resolution in the case of exempt persons as from the 1st January
this year to the end of the extended
period for the rates, which were laid
down in the Second Schedule to the
Economy (Exchequer Relief) Act, 1926.
The additional charge on public moneys
will be very small, probably not more
than £70 per annum. I beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
STANDARD OF MARKING IN
GEOGRAPHY.
1. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
why a difference was made in the standard
of marking between boys' and girls'
answers in geography at the June, 1927,
certificate examination; if it was made in
any subject other than geography; if it
was made with the sanction of the
Ministry, and, if so, on which of the
official "Regulations for the Secondary
School Certificate Examinations" the
Ministry's sanction was based.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The following paragraph appears in the report of
the examiner in geography:
:-
"When the teaching of the subject is
not on a high level, it usually happens
that the girls do worse than the boys.
This is decidedly the case in geography
in many cases, and though the examiner
deliberately marked girls very easily,
the proportion of failures among them
is very high. In the senior examination, 66 out of 98 boys, but only 21 out
of 82 girls passed.”
The Ministry knows of no difference in
the standard of marking between boys and
girls in other subjects. The standards to
be adopted in marking the answers of
candidates are left to the discretion of the
examiners, and no specific instructions on
this subject are issued by the Ministry,
but the examiners are informed that the
papers are to be so set as to be suitable for
the average student reasonably well
taught, and that they should be marked
accordingly.
JUNIOR CERTIFICATE EXAMINA-
TION.-NEW REGULATION
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether candidates at the junior certificate examination, in June, 1928, who

Mr. ROBB: The answer to the first

There are separate regulations for the

passing the junior examination do not

which was issued to the schools in September last, and which is in the following
terms:
-

drawn to Regulation 20 of the Regulations for the Secondary School Certificate Examinations (1928). Under
former regulations history and geography formed a composite subject

Payment of Members of the Senate.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That, in the opinion of this House,
and as from 1st April, 1928, provision
should be made for the payment at the
rate of £100 per annum to each Member
of the Senate who, having subscribed to
the necessary Oath and taken his seat,
has made a declaration on the prescribed
form that owing to insufficiency of means
the provision made by Resolution of the
House of Commons on 18th March, 1924,
is insufficient to permit him to devote
adequate time to the performance of his
duties in the Senate, and such payment
shall be in addition to the provision made
hy the aforesaid Resolution.
""
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It will be within the recollection of hon. Members that a Resolution

was passed by this House on the 18th

ac-
Select Committees of the Senate or Joint

that as the principle of payment of

cepted it could only be considered equitable that a similar principle should be

reason for basing the payment in their
case on attendance instead of adopting

It has now been found that the arrangement does not meet the necessities of
every case, and this Resolution proposes
that, in addition to the payments made
in pursuance of the existing Resolution,
there should be paid an annual flat amount
of £100 to such Senators as make a signed
declaration to the effect that owing to insufficiency of means the normal scale of
payment for attendances in the Senate
does not enable him to devote his time
adequately to his duties in the Senate.
The Government are confident that this
Resolution will commend itself to the
Committee and, in these circumstances,
I do not propose to comment further save
to say that provision will, of course, be
made in the forthcoming Estimates for
the few payments which it is anticipated
will arise. It is proposed that the
arrangement should take effect as from
the first of next month. I beg to move.

CLAUSE 5 (Amendment as to statutory conditions for receipt of benefit).
The following Section shall be substituted for section seven of the principal
Act:-
-
7.-(1) The statutory conditions
for the receipt of unemployment benefit by a person insured under this Act
(in this Act referred to as "an insured
contributor") are—
(i) That not less than thirty contributions have been paid in respect of
him as an insured contributor in respect of the two years immediately
preceding the date on which application for benefit is made;
(vi) that he has, except as may be
otherwise prescribed by regulations
made under this Act, been resident
in the United Kingdom for a period
of three years immediately preceding
the date on which application for
benefit is made:

Free State. I desire to protect Northern

What I want to substitute is this: That 30 will be the qualifying number of stamps. In the event

before he

into the matter. The foundations for

storm which was accompanied by torrential rain. The hon. Member will recall
that this storm caused serious damage
throughout the British Isles. The extra
expense which may be involved is estimated to be in the region of £200.

ESCAPES FROM BELFAST PRISON.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Kyle)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of prisoners who have escaped from Belfast
Prison during the last four years; whether
an inquiry has been held regarding these
escapes; and, if so, on whom has the responsibility been placed and the penalty inflicted in each case; who was the Governor
of the prison on each occasion, and the number of new Governors appointed during
the same period; whether it is true that
the defence of the Governor on the recent escape of four convicts was based
on the disloyalty of the staff, and if he
considers that a Governor who has not
the confidence of his staff is a fit and
proper person to be in charge of a prison; whether he is aware that, previous
to the opening of Belfast as a convict
prison, it was reported to the Governor
by an old and experienced officer then
serving at the prison that the existing
cell locks were unsuitable for the safe
custody of convicts; what steps, if any,
were taken to remedy this defect;
whether he is prepared to place the file
containing the Governor's report on the
matter on the Table of the House; and
L
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
whether the only punishment inflicted
on the Governor for his neglect of duty
in the matter of these escapes was to
grant him three months' leave of absence at the public expense.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
the
(Sir Dawson Bates): During
last four years prisoners have escaped
on three occasions from Belfast Prison.
One prisoner escaped on each of the first
two occasions, but the prisoners in question were immediately recaptured. On
the last occasion four prisoners escaped,
of whom two have been recaptured.
Sworn inquiries were held in each case.
As a result of the inquiry into the first
of these escapes two warders were punished by being fined, and a principal
warder was reprimanded on the grounds
of negligence.
In the other cases it was found impossible, after very full inquiry, to attach
blame to any particular officer connected
with the prison.
On the occasion of the first escape,
Captain Stephenson was acting as
Governor of the Prison in the absence of
Major Long, who was seconded for special
duty at the Home Office, but at the actual
time of the escape Captain Stephenson
was absent on leave, and the chief
warder was in charge.
At the time of the subsequent escapes,
Major Long was in charge of the Prison.
With regard to the remaining part of
the question, I should like to make it clear
at once that the Governor was in no sense
called upon to make a defence, but was
in the ordinary way required to give evidence at the inquiry.
It would be impossible for me, for reasons which should be obvious, to disclose
any particulars of the evidence given at
these inquiries, but, at any rate, I cannot
for one moment admit the suggestion
made by the hon. Member that the Governor has not the confidence of his staff
or of the Ministry, or that he is unfitted
in any way for the responsible position
which he occupies.
As regards the question of the locks on
the cells, this matter as been the subject
of earnest consideration by the Ministry,
but it would not be in the public interest
to enter into any details regarding the
steps which have been taken in the
matter.
For a similar reason I am not prepared to disclose any information or to
publish any reports which have been sub-
Imitted in this connection.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I must deprecate, in the strongest possible terms, the
suggestion in the question that any
punishment was inflicted on the Governor, or that there was any obvious neglect
of duty on his part.
The facts of the case in regard to his
leave of absence are as follow:
Prior to the recent escapes, he had
submitted to the Ministry an application for sick leave, and his application
had been approved, but, following on
the escapes, the Governor very properly intimated that he did not wish
to go on leave until all the circumstances has been fully inquired into,
and, in point of fact, he did not take
his leave until the inquiries had been
completed.
In conclusion, I must once again say
that I have entire confidence in the
Governnor of Belfast Prison, and that I H
deprecate in the strongest possible terms
reflections as those contained in the question being cast on the character of this
officer, or, indeed, of the prison staff
generally.

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to
the first part of the hon. Member's question, I am advised that the police did not,
as suggested, prevent the distribution of
handbills outside the premises of Messrs.
Charley & Co.
I have no information in regard to the
second part of the question, and I see no
reason for holding an inquiry into the
case.
With reference to the last part of the
question, there is no objection to the
distribution of handbills, provided the law
is not thereby infringed.
ULSTER SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
-DEMOBILIZED MEMBERS.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
nature of the arrangements made, if any,
between the Northern Government and
Dominion or Colonial Governments, with
a view to absorbing the demobilized
members of the Special Constabulary who
are desirous of taking up occupations
overseas, and whether these arrangements
are still in force.
Sir DAWSON BATES: On the disbandment of the Special Constabulary,
in the early months of 1926, arrangements were made by my Ministry, in cooperation with the Ministry of Labour,
through the instrumentality of the
accredited shipping agents in Northern
Ireland, to draw the special attention of
disbanded members of the Force to the
facilities afforded by the British and
Dominion Governments in regard to
emigration to certain of His Majesty's
dominions.
I may also say that, at the same time,
the Australian and Canadian emigration
authorities were approached with a view
to granting special consideration, within.
the ambit of the various assisted-passages
schemes, to disbanded members of the
Special Constabulary.
These arrangements are still in force.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if the demobilized members of the
Special Constabulary had special facilities
or had they the ordinary facilities that
were open to the general public?
Sir DAWSON BATES: They had the
facilities open to the general public and
they had other facilities. By reason of
the fact that they were members of the
Special Constabulary they received special
consideration.
Colonel WOODS: How many, if any,
availed themselves of those facilities?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot tell.

Secondly, although amounts are paid

The hon. Member must recall that

from year to year the liability of the
Government is getting less and less as

be under any apprehension whatever
that the Government is running any considerable risk. We have not lost any

as I visualize it, a most wonderful work.
I am not speaking of what the Government but what the Act has accomplished.

House, some thousands of men have been
kept at work who otherwise would have
been walking the streets of Belfast, and

of this Act without any expense of a
