Mr. BEATTIE: I really did think
that the Minister of Labour would prove
that there was some power left to this
Parliament to make alterations where alterations were necessary. But through
the Second Reading and Committee Stage,
which was very short owing to the reasons
given by the Minister, he said he had no
power to alter one letter of the Act. I
want at this late hour of the day to ask
this House if it is not within our power
to change a portion of the Act as it
stands. I question very much if under
the regulations when they are made
we will not find that Australia and
Canada are within the British Empire
and that the Free State is outside
it. We will see benefit given to the man
from the Australian bush and the same
conditions will not apply to the man from
the Free State-the man from Belleek.
That is an absurdity. I think it is a
monstrosity to ask the House to pass the
section contained in the Bill asking for
the three-year qualification.
I question very much whether the
Minister knows the real effect of that on
the workers of Northern Ireland, and it
is from the point of view of the Northern
Ireland workers I am speaking. I am as
jealous of the Northern Ireland Fund as
any other Member in this House. But I
do not want Northern Ireland workers to
be deprived of a Fund that they are entitled to participate in. The point I want
to ask the Minister is, is he really serious
in asking the House to pass a Bill with
a schedule in which certain scales are
attached according to the varying ages.
Will he say that a boy or girl of 18 is not
as hard to maintain as a boy or girl of
21? Surely there is something in the
minds of hon. Members when they base
their calculations on the opinions expressed by a Committee who were
altogether in a different atmosphere from
the atmosphere we are in in Northern
Ireland. Northern Ireland is not in the
same position as Great Britain. When
these scales of benefit were agreed to by
the Blanesburgh Committee I stated before in this House they based their calculations on the fact that there was
another authority outside the Unemployinent Insurance Fund that was also
granting assistance to unemployed
workers. That cannot be claimed for
Northern Ireland. The unemployed
worker here is solely dependent upon the
Unemployment Insurance Fund for his
existence. In Great Britain that does not
apply.
We would be justitied, therefore, in
raising the scale of benefit above the
standard set by the Blanesburgh Committee. We could justify that to the
Imperial Treasury on the step-by-step
policy. I may be told by the Minister
of Finance that that would be dangerous.
I say it would not. In many things we
have not followed the step-by-step policy,
and where explanations are given, and I
know the Minister of Finance can give
explanations just as well as any Members
of this House, I am sure the money
people across the Channel, the Government, would accept the explanations and
allow our scales to be on a different
basis to what they are proposing. I think
many serious aspects of this thing could
be put forward in this House. I have
had many different points of view expressed to me. It was only within the
past week I was considering a claim, and
when I saw the plight of the applicant,
who is now in receipt of 15s a week, I
started to look into the future when the
same applicant would only have 10s, and
I wondered what her position would be
at that period. Will her moral be upheld. The hon. Member may smile, but
this is serious from the point of
view especially of the urphan girl,
and in particular the girls coming in from the country who are
in lodgings. I do not want to explain
what we all know. Money has got to be
provided for the upkeep of modern
fashion. They have got to pay lodging.
From that point of view it rests upon
this House to try to give the Opposition
some little bit of consideration in regard
to that schedule. Now you have made
special concessions to young fellows,
where disablement is in the home as far
as the parents are concerned, to get
the same scale. In the same way
you might have a girl whose circumstances would warrant you in
giving her sufficient to maintain her
in her lodgings and to keep her in a
district where she is likely to get employment. Do you not think that such

coming to that job. Those men will have
to pay stamps in Northern Ireland, and
the Newry Navigation or Harbour Trust

a thing for which they were not responsible,

are contributing stamps to this unemployment insurance fund. That does not
affect County Antrim or many of the
other counties, but it does affect these
men who are living on the immediate
border.

men.

it like a man with a stick trying to beat

by a statutory court. Consequently, all

Roads Improvement Bill 676
[Mr. Andrews]
There is only one other matter to which I
need refer, that is the point raised by the
hon. Member for County Down (Mr.
Patrick O'Neill), in regard to bank clerks.
Here again, I think there is a good deal
of misunderstanding. The Bill definitely
lays down that there shall not be contracting out in the future. The reason for that .
is obvious. No insurance scheme can
exist for long if it only takes the bad lives
and does not take the good lives. For
instance, if an insurance company were
to take all the houses that were liable to
be burned and to leave out those that
were not liable to be burned, it would not
be long before that insurance company
would become bankrupt. Therefore, this
Bill lays it down that certain industries
less liable than others to unemployment
shall not be allowed to contract out.
It is rather a strange thing that these
young men or their representatives could
have asked to be permitted to contract
out of the scheme since the principal Act
was passed in 1920, but that during all
the time the door was open they never
took advantage of it. Now when the door
is going to be shut they say some injustice is being done to them. Again, the
hon. Member for County Down (Mr.
Patrick O'Neill) is under a misapprehension. He says it is not possible for those
young persons to get benefit. He will be
glad to know that some of them have got
benefit in days gone by. They can get
benefit in two ways. It is quite true that
if they are dismissed or if they leave of
their own accord they will not get benefit
for six weeks, but after six weeks they
can put in a claim, and if they can show
they are looking for work, and are qualified in other ways, they are entitled to
benefit in the same way as other people
are. Again, at the end of fifteen years
they may be paid off in the natural course
of their employment. If they get a pension from their employers, unless it brings
their income up to £250 a year, which, I
think, is very unlikely, it will not disqualify them from getting unemployment
benefit. I really fail to see how,
this Clause any more than under any
other Clause, an injustice is being done
to the insured persons.

Mr. P. O'NEILL, What I desire to
know from the Minister of Home Affairs
in connection with this Clause is: will it
empower the local authorities also to
widen roads for the purpose of widening
the footpaths? I need hardly point out
that the condition of the footpaths on
many roads in Northern Ireland is a
shame, and they are also quite dangerous.
In former years the paths were kept in
such a condition that they were quite safe
for pedestrians. In consequence of the
narrowness of many roads, and the present heavy traffic on them, the footpaths
have now been merged into the roads.
They have been neglected altogether, with
the result that there is no protection in
nany places for pedestrians and those
who use the side of the roads.
In addition to that, may I point out
to the Committee that the roads which
are now tar bound are much easier to
walk on than the paths which are gravelled and hardly even. The result is
that pedestrians use the roads, and this is
a danger to themselves as well as a trouble
in many instances to the traffic on them.
It would be a good thing if the footpaths
could be restored to what they were
formerly. I do not know but we should
compel local authorities to put footpaths
alongside all roads.

what might conceivably be a very onerous

CLAUSE 3 (Lopping of hedges overhanging roads)-
(1) Where any hedge overhangs any
road, street or footpath so as to obstruct
or interfere with the light from any
public lamp, or to endanger or obstruct
the passage of vehicles or foot passengers or to obstruct the view of drivers
of vehicles, the local authority may
serve a notice on the owner of the hedge
or on the occupier of the premises on
which such hedge is growing, requiring
him to cut or lop the hedge within fourteen days, so as to prevent such obstruction or interference, and in default of
compliance the local authority may
themselves carry out the requisition of
their notice, doing no unnecessary
damage, and may recover the cost in
the county court as a debt due by the
owner or occupier upon whom the
notice was served.
(2) Any person aggrieved by any requirement of a local authority under
this section may appeal to a court of
summary jurisdiction within fourteen
days after the service of the notice
aforesaid, and the following provisions
shall have effect with respect to any
such appeal:-
(a) Notice in writing of the appeal
and of the grounds thereof shall be
given by the appellant to the clerk
of the local authority;
(b) The court may make such order
in the matter as they consider
reasonable, and may award costs
to be recoverable as costs in cases
of a civil nature are recoverable
under section twenty-two of the
Petty Sessions (Ireland) Act,
1851;
(c) No proceeding shall be taken by
the local authority, or work executed, until after the determination or abandonment of the
appeal;
(d) Notice of the right of appeal
shall be endorsed on the notice
communicating the requirement of
the local authority.

Tuesday, 27th March, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
COST OF ELECTORS AND JURORS'
LISTS.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will grant a return showing the total amount of money
expended in the preparation, revising,
and printing of the lists of Parliamentary and Local Government Electors and
Jurors' Lists in each County and County
Borough in Northern Ireland for the
Registers 1923-24 and 1926-27 respectively, and whether he will undertake to
show the contribution in relief of rates
paid in each County and County Borough
for the same periods; whether he can state
if such contributions or grants in relief
come before Parliament year by year on
the Estimates, and under what heading;
and whether he will state if any money is
paid directly by the Imperial Government,
or if it is a grant-in-aid after the full
amount is paid by the local authorities,
or only half the cost of printing is paid.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A contribution equal
to half the amounts expended in the preparation and printing of the Parliamentary and Local Government electors' lists
is made by the Imperial Government.
The grant is forwarded to the Ministry
of Finance, who act as agents for the Imperial Government in this matter, and
that Ministry distributes it amongst the
County and County Boroughs Councils
after the full amounts have been paid by
them. The grant appears in the Imperial but not in the Northern Ireland
Estimates.
No grant is made in respect of the
jurors' lists. I will ask the hon. Member's permission to circulate with the
Official Report a return showing the
figures asked for in his question.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
RURAL COUNCILS-CIRCULAR
LETTER, P.P. No. 84.
2. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that the recent circular letter, P.P.
No. 84, which was issued to Rural District
Councils by his Ministry, will (especially
in view of the request for the issue of bylaws dealing with factories employing
forty persons or less) throw a greatly increased volume of work upon the Councils,
necessitating the appointment of additional inspectors and increasing the burden upon the rates; and whether the
Government will introduce legislation to
amend Sections 14, 15, and 16 of the
Factory and Workshops Act, 1901, and
so place the duty of inspection of fire
escape methods upon the existing factory
inspectors, who would then be able to do
this work in the course of their ordinary
duties without unnecessary duplication of
inspection and responsibilities.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member is. I think, under a misapprehension with regard to this circular.
The circular does not throw any new
duties on local authorities, but merely
calls attention to the duties of local
authorities under the Factory and Workshops Act, 1901, an Act which has been
in force for 27 years.
It has been brought to the notice of the
Ministry that the provisions of this Act,
with regard to providing proper means of
escape from factories in case of fire were
not being enforced, and the Ministry consider it desirable, in view of the dangers
which might arise from want of proper
means of escape in case of fire, to call the
attention of local authorities to their
responsibilities in the matter.
The provision of fire escapes has to do
with the construction of the buildings, a
matter over which local authorities have
certain powers of control.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if it is not possible
to consider an amendment of the Act?
If the local authorities are to carry out
their duties as they should be carried out.
the Act will have to be amended. Will
he consider the amendment of Sections
14 and 16 Could the duty of inspection
not possibly be placed upon the existing
factory inspectors?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will be very
happy to discuss the matter with hon.
my
Friend, and consider it still further.
ESTABLISHMENT OF CIVIL SER-
VICE MESSENGERS.
3. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that the greater number of the messenger
staff of the Civil Service are still on a
temporary basis; whether most of these
men have been employed for some years;
and whether, as the number so employed
is practically stable, does he not think
that these ex-Servicemen should be placed
on a permanent basis so as to qualify
for pension rights before being debarred
by age.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the first and
second parts of the hon. Member's
question are in the affirmative.
As regards the third part, it has not
up to the present been the practice to
grant established status to manipulative
or quasi-manipulative staff other than
those performing supervisory or specially
responsible duties, and I see no adequate reason for departing from that
practice.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask if it is
not the practice of the Imperial Governnient to have the Government messengers
on a permanent basis?
Mr. POLLOCK: I understand that
is not so.
NORTHERN IRELAND LAND ACT,
1925.
4. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Lloyd
Campbell) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he can give any information regarding the large number of estates which
have not yet been dealt with under the
Northern Ireland Land Act of 1925;
whether he is aware that it seems likely
that a number of tenants will not receive
the benefits of the Act within the period
originally contemplated; and to inquire
whether the Government has brought
this matter to the notice of the Imperial
Government, and, if so, whether
reply has been received to these represen
tations.
any
Roads Improvement Bill- 718
Oral Answers
27 MARCH 1928
Mr. POLLOCK: As I have so often
stated in this House, the administration
of Land Purchase is entirely a matter for
the Imperial Government, which has its
own officers in Belfast over whom we have
no jurisdiction whatever.
Our Government has for some time past
been in communication with the Imperial
Government on this subject, and has indicated that there would be a considerable
hardship inflicted on those tenants who
will not in the ordinary course receive
the benefits of the Act within the period
originally contemplated. The Imperial
Government has received these representations very sympathetically, and is at
the moment considering what steps are
possible to improve the position of those
tenants whose estates would normally be
dealt with after May, 1929. I am hopeful that the proposals of the Imperial
Government will be known shortly after
the Easter Recess.
BANN DRAINAGE-ATTITUDE OF
ARMAGH COUNTY COUNCIL.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private
notice) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he has received any communication from the Armagh County Council
forwarding copy of a Resolution recently adopted by the Council declining
to support the Government's proposal
that the Council should make an annual
contribution from the rates towards the
cost of the proposed Bann Drainage
Scheme, and whether he proposes to take
any further steps in the matter.
Mr. POLLOCK: The reply to the
first part of the hon. Member's question
is in the affirmative. I propose to
address a further communication to the
Armagh County Council, inviting them,
and also the Portadown Urban District
Council, to confer with the Government in
order that there may be a fuller discussion of the details of the Scheme.

[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
CLAUSE 5 (Power of local authorities
to prohibit or restrict driving of vehicles
on roads).
(1) A local authority may, by order,
prohibit or restrict, subject to such
exceptions or conditions as to occasional user or otherwise as may be
specified in the order, the driving of
vehicles of any specified class on any
specified road within the area of the
local authority, in any case in which it
appears to the local authority that the
road is unsuitable for use by a vehicle
of that class and would be damaged if
used by such vehicle:
Provided that a local authority shall
not make an order prohibiting or restricting the driving of any vehicle,
whose wheels are fitted with pneumatic
tyres on a road classified under subsection (2) of section seventeen of the
Ministry of Transport Act, 1919, as a
first-class or second-class road.
(2) A person aggrieved by an order
made by a local authority under this
section may, within such time and in
such manner as may be prescribed by
regulations of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, appeal to that Ministry against
the order, and the decision of that
Ministry on the appeal shall be binding
upon the local authority, and shall not
be subject to appeal to any court.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I think my
hon. Friend who has moved this Amendment has entirely forgotten the effect of
the Roads Act of 1920. We do not
propose to take away the power given
under that Act. I may remind him
what those powers are.
These powers
apply to either first-class or second-class
or third-class roads, and shortly they are
these. If a local authority thinks any
of its roads should be closed by reason
that they are unsuitable owing to
structure, and that damage may result
therefrom, or by reason of the width, it
is open to them to apply to the Ministry
of Home Affairs when the Ministry will
look into the matter and hold an inquiry.
at which everybody-interested parties
such as bus owners or ratepayers can
attend and lodge an objection. The only
thing this Bill does is that in certain cases
it avoids the necessity of having an inquiry. The real meaning of this Bill is
that it is designed to put an end to
damage being done to roads.
I will give a case in point. Assume
for a moment that a third-class road is
unsuitable and a great many of the thirdclass roads are unsuitable for heavy traffic.
It might carry a 10 cwt. vehicle, but it
would be entirely unsuitable to carry a
heavy class vehicle. Or again, supposing
it comes to the knowledge of a county
council that it is proposed to drag a large
boiler to some mill. Perhaps that boiler
may weigh 15 or 16 tons, and irreparable
damage may be done unless the local
authority is placed in the position to deal
with it. So far as this Bill is concerned
we propose to give the local authority
power to close any third-class road in
respect of any class of vehicle, but to limit
that immediate power-that is of the local
authority-to closing first and second-class
roads where the vehicle is shod with metal
tyres. Under this Bill it will not be open
to the local authority to close either first
or second-class roads against rubber tyred
machines unless by going through the old
process under the existing law, that is the
1920 Act, under which they must apply
to the Ministry for an order to close the
road. What we feel is that there is no
great urgency in the case of the first and
second-class roads in respect of vehicles
shod with pneumatic tyres, but there is
immediate urgency in the case of first,
second and third-class roads where the
vehicle passing over them is shod say with
iron tyres.
My hon. Friend (Mr.
Crawford) after hearing this explanation
will perhaps agree with me that it would
be unreasonable that the power should
be placed in the hands of local authorities
to at once close roads against all classes
of traffic.

big interest. The Minister of Home

third-class road with a really sound clay
or rock bottom. To make a flat distinction all over might not be really
practicable. I think that this Amendment would involve no hardship.

CLAUSE 7 (Erection and use of petrol
pumps along roads).
(1) The local authority may, if
they think fit, grant to any person a
licence to erect, construct or place and
maintain, in or under any road, street
or footpath in their area, pumps, pipes
or other appliances for supplying motor
spirit to mechanically propelled vehicles
drawn up in such road or street, and
may by by-laws-
(a) prescribe the period for which,
and conditions upon which, such
licence may be granted or withdrawn,
and the conditions to be observed in
connection with the use and construction of such pumps; and
(b) require the payment, in respect of a licence, of such annual
fees as may be fixed by the by-laws;
and
(c) impose penalties for the erection or use of pumps, pipes or other
appliances without a licence under
this section.

The object of amending Sections 69 and
70 of the Towns Improvement Act is to
prevent projections in towns that are
liable to cause obstruction. Take, for example, a signpost. Under the Towns
Improvement Act, a signpost, if it is sufficiently high, cannot be objected to
even if it is in danger of coming down.

that projects, whether it is an obstruction
or not, if it is not in a safe condition
shall be regarded as an obstruction within the meaning of the Towns Improvement
Clauses Act, 1847. To carry out what
the hon. Member wishes would be absolutely impracticable. It would need an

NEW CLAUSE (Restrictions on repairing roads)—
(1) It shall not be lawful for any
county surveyor, deputy surveyor, assistant surveyor, or any other person,
to break or granulate any road material
within thirty feet of the centre of any
road; nor, in remaking or repairing
any road, to work on more than half
the width of the road at a time, nor
when working on one width of the road
to block the other side or the footpath
with material or machinery, and it shall
be no defence for a person prosecuted
for acting in contravention of this
Section to plead that he was authorized
so to do by the local authority or any
of its officers.

Mr. MILLER: I beg to move, "That
the Clause be read a Second time."
This is a Clause to prevent the county
surveyors doing what they will not allow
other people to do. If I want to break
stones within 30 feet of the public road
I would be prosecuted by the police.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Hear, hear.
Mr. MILLER: But the county surveyor can take up half the road and break
stones on it and nobody says a word. I
think we should have some power under
this Bill to prevent the county surveyors
doing what they will not allow anyone
else to do. I have driven on a first-class
road-the main road between Belfast and
Derry, and at one place I could not pass
along the road at all. On one side men
were breaking stones, and on the other
side they had the machinery. I wanted
to pass a man with a load of broken
stones, and I asked him to get out of the

load of stones into the centre of the road.
I had to wait there until he had levelled
these stones down before I would be

I think the county

There is nothing there to prevent a county

New CLAUSE (Precautions for horse
traffic).
In the repair, remaking, resurfacing
of roads it shall be obligatory on the
local authority to make and maintain
a condition reasonably safe for horse
traffic, and in neglect of this provision
the local authority shall be liable for
damages for accidents to horse traffic
caused by the surface of the roads
being left in a slippery and unsafe
condition for such traffic.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg
to move,
"That the Clause be now read
a Second time."
This New Clause raises a very difficult
problem involved in the change that has
taken place in our transport system. In
their efforts to secure a solution of the
problem as to the best material to bear
motor transport, the local authorities, to
some extent, seem to have met with
another very big problem, that is, the
problem of making the roads reasonably
safe for horse traffic. If we had been told
four or five years ago that such a question
would arise we would not have believed it.
759 Roads Improvement Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMUNS
ebook 760
[Mr. G. Henderson]
Many of our main roads have been left in
a condition that they cannot be used for
horse traffic without serious danger of
accident. Now, our farmers are the men
who have largely made these roads and
largely maintained them, and the present
policy seems to be an entire disregard
of the rights of these users, and in the
reconstruction of these roads the only
interests that are being considered are
those of the motor users.
This circumstance will involve a double
tax on the farmer, because the remaking
and resurfacing has increased the upkeep
of these roads and increased the rates
to an incredible degree.
The Chairman of the County Antrim
Finance Committee this year in introducing the estimates said, even despite
the grant now made from the Road Fund,
the County Antrim Rates were £100,000
more this year than they were in 1914.
He said also, that £99,000 of that rate
was raised on agricultural land, so that
on account of creating these new roads
and resurfacing these roads, the farmers
are heavily taxed. They are taxed also
in this way, that they cannot use these
roads for their horses, and a great many
of them have to resort to paying motor
lorries to convey their produce to the
market.
Now, we hear a great deal at the present time about the advisability of a more
direct service from the producer to the
consumer, but if these roads are left in
such a condition by the local authorities
that the farmers cannot use their horses
it puts the farmer more and more into
the hands of the middlemen. If they
cannot market their own produce with
their own horses they have to sell their
produce to the middlemen and cannot
get into contact directly with the consumer. Therefore, I hold by both these
counts the farmers are doubly taxed.
Besides that, they are forced to make detours from these roads and go roundabouts
that add miles to their journey.
these people the right of user over these
roads?

who wants to use a horse. I know it is

1;
Now everyone knows the asphalt road.
I think the greatest danger is where the
road is rounded and is left too convex.
The great danger is when the horse comes
to the bump, especially when it is a bit
damp. The horse has no chance at all
he is nearly sure to go down. While it
is necessary in a water-bound road that
the road should be convex to throw off
the water, I hold that in the asphalt road,
being waterproof, there is not the same
necessity. A very slight fall in the road
would be sufficient, and would to some
extent obviate the danger created by
these surfaces. That is one point where
I think the local authorities might have
shown some consideration for horse traffic
in the reconstruction of these roads.
It is interesting that the Minister of
Home Affairs has taken powers under this
Bill to experiment in the remaking and
resurfacing of roads, and it surely should
not be beyond the range of science to produce material for road surface that would
bear motor traffic and be waterproof, and
at the same time not be slippery for
horses like the asphalt or cement road.
It may be said that this will involve local
authorities in lawsuits. But if it is
necessary for the community that these
roads should be left in this condition
that is unsafe for horse traffic, and if a
farmer ventures his horse on these roads
and gets his property damaged I say,
should there not be redress. I have been
told of cases where valuable horses had to
be destroyed through accidents happening on slippery roads, and I do feel that

very anxious to arrive at some suitable
road that will stand up to modern traffic
and at the same time meet horse traffic.
In the Clause proposed, if the horse
user on the road suffers any damage because the horse slips he can recover damages from the local authority. There
again there will be more costs. I do not
know whether or not when I say this my
hon. Friend will not think I am dealing
lightly with the problem raised-I hope
he will find a solution in better class
roads, but at the same time I was greatly
struck the other day by an article which
appeared in a certain paper suggesting
that the farmers themselves, by adopting
another method of shoeing might do a
great deal to meet the difficulty. I myself-and I think the hon. Member-have
seen cavalry trotting up Regent Street
which is a fairly steep street and very
slippery. You will find that all over
London where I do not think there is
a single street that is not slippery. The
horses have got accustomed to it and I
understand this newer method of shoeing
helps. I was struck by the remarks made
by the veterinary surgeon attached to
the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty
to Animals. With your permision I
would like to quote from some of the remarks given in the report.

Mr. Coleman, the honorary farrier
adviser to the Society, had taken much
trouble in an endeavour to persuade
farmers to abandon the old methods
of shoeing and instead to have their
horses shod in such a manner that they
can travel in perfect safety on the
smoothest surfaces. In his opinion,
the frog of the foot should take its
natural share of the road pressure, not
only to prevent slipping, but because
in other ways such conditions tend to
prolong the working life of the animal.
The frog is Nature's perfect provision
against slipping and concussion, and
too frequently the frog is deliberately
cut out to enable rubber pads to be
fitted.
Mr. Coleman added that if
the Farmers' Union would take up the
matter the Society for the Prevention
of Cruelty to Animals, jointly with the
Master Farriers' Association would
gladly arrange for demonstrations of
rational shoeing to be given throughout
the country."
I suggest that not as a counter proposal to what my hon. Friend has put
forward, but only because, as being responsible for the road authorities, we are doing
our best to try to arrive at some solution
of a road for both motor and horse traffic.
Something might be done by my hon.
Friend's friends, the Farmers' Union,
with a view to showing whether or nou
the method of shoeing suggested by this
gentleman might not do something to
meet the difficulty the farmers are in at
the present time. I hope my hon. Friend
will not press this Clause which would be
an impossible one to carry out. At all
events, I hope my hon. Friend will accept
the assurance that the Government and,.

1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

ANCE
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

It is not, therefore, possible to state the

barracks involved.

prior to the installation of the Governinent-owned sets is possible, seeing that

2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether his
attention has been drawn to the correspondence between his Department and
the Antrim County Council, with reference to the transfer of the duties of the
Glenariffe Drainage Authority to the
County Council; whether he has seen the
report of the engineer of the County
Council who, after examination of the
river, has reported that an estimated expenditure of £4,000 will be required to
make good the damage caused by the
neglect of the authorities responsible for
the drainage of the river up to the passing of the Drainage Act, 1925; whether
he is aware that the County Council is
prepared to maintain the works in good
order, but declines to involve the ratepayers in the additional expense necessary to make good the damage done
owing to past neglect; and whether the
Government will have these defects
remedied before the business of the old
Drainage Authority is transferred to the
County Council.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have seen the
correspondence between my Department
and the Antrim County Council with
reference to the transfer of the duties of
the Glenariffe Drainage Authority to the
County Council, and I have also seen a
copy of the report of the County Surveyor
with regard to the matter.
Section 15 of the Drainage Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925, which provides
for the transfer to county councils of the
business of drainage authorities arising
within their areas enacts that councils to
whom such business is transferred shall
have not merely the powers but also the
duties of such authorities. It is, therefore, apparent that in its application to
the present case the Act requires that the
County Council should undertake the
repair and maintenance of the Glenariffe
River drainage works which were under
the jurisdiction of the former drainage
authority. The local drainage trustees
appear to have ceased to carry out any
work or to levy any rates since 1905. It
is regrettable that the former authority
did not carry out their duties and maintain these works in a proper condition,
hut I regret that I can see no ground on
which the Government would be justified
in asking Parliament to make a grant-inaid of these works.
the
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of
the answer of the right hon. Gentleman, is it not a fact that the old
drainage authority allowed the course of
this river to get badly blocked up, that
they spent no money and did nothing in
way of maintenance or repairs for the
last fifty years; and does he consider it
fair or reasonable that the cost of making
good the neglect of a Government Department should fall on the ratepayers of
County Antrim? Further, is it not a fact
that sub-Section (1) of Section 16 of the
Drainage Act only requires a county
council to prepare a scheme for maintaining such drainage works as become maintainable by them, and can the right hon.
Gentleman say by what authority the
Secretary of the Ministry states in his
letter of 9th March that it is the duty of
the council to repair the existing works?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I might
correct the remark my hon. Friend made
to the effect that this drainage authority
was a Government Department.
It was
a statutory body set up with power to levy
rates from the area affected, and to maintain these works. For my part I am
really not in a position to interpret the
Act of Parliament at the present moment,
but my hon. Friend, I think, is wrong in
his interpretation of the Drainage Act.
CRAWFORD: Is a statutory
body not under the control of the Government?
Mr.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.
These of course were drainage authorities

done since 1896.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry's
Medical Inspector has visited Downpatrick

the County Council cannot be expected
to embark on a scheme of this magnitude
without careful consideration.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Constabulary Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill has
for its object the amending of the Constabulary Act, 1922. Hon. Members will
recollect that under this Act we continued the old principle contained in the
Royal Irish Constabulary Acts of having
what is known as a free quota. For the
information of hon. Members, I might
tell them that the free quota is the
number of men allocated, free of all cost,
to each local authority. If any area required a number, over and above the free
quota the local authority concerned had
one-half the cost of the extra men.
pay
The free quota was to be fixed by the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
to
As a result of the practical working
of that principle it was found that the
free quota was never exceeded so far as regards areas outside Belfast. From this it
resulted that the Belfast Corporation felt
that they were not being treated fairly,
and a certain amount of friction arose
in regard to the matter, and they complained that, because the local authorities
were not called upon to pay anything,
that they should not be asked to pay.
As a result of negotiations which extended for some considerable time between
myself and the Belfast Corporation, an
arrangement has been arrived at which
is embodied in the present Measure.
The Belfast Corporation quite properly
recognized that, as a capital city, it is
only reasonable and proper that they
should contribute a sum for the upkeep
of the force allocated in their area. The
arrangement is that Belfast should pay a
sum of £25,000 per annum for a period
of seven years, terminating in 1933. In
I
return for that the city will be entitled
to have as many police as the circumstances may require from time to time,
without having to pay anything further.
I think hon. Members will agree with me,
that is those who have studied the question, that this is a satisfactory arrangement. It puts an end to friction that has
been going on, I venture to say, for the
last. 20 or 30 years between former
Governments and the Belfast Corporation. At the same time I would also like
to point out that the other areas in the
counties will also get, without having to
pay anything, as many police as they
require, and I hope that number will be
small. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
During a considerable period, hon.
Members are aware, a large force of
Special Constabulary were employed in
the city of Belfast for the protection of
persons and property, and, as the liability
for any injuries that might be sustained.
in respect of persons or property would
fall upon the ratepayers under the
Malicious Injury Acts it was only
reasonable and proper that the Corporation should contribute something towards
that amount. An arrangement had been
arrived at under which the Corporation
agreed to pay towards the cost of the
Special Constabulary-an arrangement
which I think every hon. Member will
agree was only reasonable and proper.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Another item
dealt with in this Bill has to do with
weights and measures.
As the law now
stands that work is carried out by
sergeants of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. There is a different system
in England. We appoint twelve sergeants of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
who have to undergo a similar examination to that which their colleagues
undergo in England to qualify as weights
and measures inspectors. These men
receive a bonus of £20 a year over and
abcve their normal pay. As against
that, fees are paid by traders whose
machines are examined from time to time.
The total amount thus received-about
£12,000—is paid into what is known as
the Reward Fund of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary.
The Reward Fund is a fund into which
certain fines are paid for the purpose of
giving rewards from time to time to men
for good service, and can only be used
for the benefit of men who are actually in
the Force at the time. It is felt, however, that it is unreasonable that the
Exchequer, which bears all the cost of
the men's pay, amounting to over £4,000
a year, should not have the benefit of the
receipts from these fees, and therefore, in
the future, after certain expenses have
been paid, the money will go into the
Exchequer as an appropriation-in-aid.
The Reward Fund was also established in
connection with the Special Constabulary.
The same remark applies to that Reward
Fund as to the Reward Fund of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. The money
only be paid out for the benefit of the
en who are actually serving at the time.
can
When the Special Constabulary was demobilised-of course, I am referring to
the "A" Special Constabulary, that is,
the whole-time men, and not to the "B's,'
who were only a part-time force a very
considerable sum had to be paid by the
Government by way of compensation for
the ordinary damage done to barracks.
In the case of the regular police force
that would be deducted from the pay of
the men, but we felt that it was inequitable that these men should be asked to
pay this amount for the reason that when
demobilization took place a great many
of them had not been in the barracks at
the time the damage took place. It was
felt, therefore, that a portion of the
Reward Fund should be handed over to
the Exchequer to relieve the general
funds.
Another Clause in the Bill deals with
the vesting of property. A technical
difficulty has arisen as to the individual
in whom the property of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is vested. At the present
time it is vested in the Receiver, who is
the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs. I am advised that on
his death the legal ownership of the
property would pass to his personal representatives, and we propose to make it
perfectly clear that in future instead of
the property resting in an individual,
who, after all, only lives for a certain
period of years, it shall rest in the
Ministry, who have what one might call
perpetual succession, although the holders
of the office may not be perpetual.
The last Clause deals with the giving
of power to the Government to acquire
land compulsorily for barracks. In the
last Act that power was only given for
a period of five years, and it is thought
advisable that the Government should
have those powers to exercise from time
to time when erecting new barracks.
These are the main points in the Bill. I
beg to move.

The PRIME MINISTER: My colleagues and I feel that before the debate
concludes it would be only fitting that I
should say a word or two on account of
the feeling of gratitude we have to the
Lord Mayor of the city of Belfast for the
long, anxious, and able way in which he
has contributed to the consideration of
this question of getting rid of the old
scheme of quota. Eventually, as my
right hon. Friends, the Minister of
Finance and the Minister of Home
Affairs, suggested, a satisfactory arrangement for all purposes was arrived at. I
would like to say that this matter occupied
the attention of the Lord Mayor and ourselves for a very considerable time; and
when I remind the House that there is a
considerable difference between the situation in the great capital city like Belfast
and isolated parts of country districts,
they will realize that some special arrangement had to be reached, and this arrangement which is embodied in the Bill to-day
is the outcome of those efforts.
When one looks back to the period
during which the Special Constabulary
guarded the lives and property of the
citizens of Belfast, it must be borne in
mind that the danger to property is very
much greater in a big city like Belfast
than in a country district. It has also to
be borne in mind that the responsibilities
of the police themselves in the narrow
thoroughfares of the city, in out-of-the
way streets and dens, are much more difficult than they are in a country district.
One must take into consideration the
fact that all the large cities and boroughs
in England have to pay a very considerable sum of money for the protection of
the lives and property in their midst.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, reminds me that they have to
pay 50 per cent. of the total cost of the
Constabulary in Great Britain. Here a
reasonable sum, and what we consider a
fair sum, has been fixed upon, in full
agreement, by the Belfast Corporation
and by the Government.
I have always endeavoured to impress
upon people in our area the great importance of friendly negotiations in
matters of this kind. After all, the city
of Belfast, with regard to population,
and with regard to the value of its property, and in many other respects, is
equal to about one-half of the State that
we govern, and consequently it would be
unseemly, and I think quite unnecessary,
to have any differences when matters of
this kind arise. and I am most hopeful
that the fruition of the efforts of my colleagues in this case will be the precursor
of many settlements that may occur from
time to time.
My right hon. Friend has asked me to
clear up what may be a misapprehension.
The sum mentioned in the agreement.
£66,000-to cover the cost of the Specials
during an extended period has already
been provided by the City. It does not
mean that there will be special rating in
any way in order to pay the Government.
The sum, I understand, was raised some
five years ago.
It was raised in the ordinary way through the rating of the city,
and was only held by the Corporation
pending a final settlement of the whole
matter. Therefore, there will be no cost
thrown upon the citizens in order to meet
the bill, but rather the other way, because I understand that the result to the
citizens of this settlement means that
this year there will be a saving of 5d in
the £ as compared with last year.
consequence is that, the Government

EDUCATION AND REGIONAL
EDUCATION COMMITTEES.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether a deputation from the
Education Board of the General Assembly
recently waited on the Minister of Education, urging that ministers of religion
should be appointed to seats on the Education and Regional Education Committees; whether resolutions from Presbyteries or Committees thereof to the same
effect were received by the Ministry;
whether he is aware that, besides
ministers of religion, other persons such
as ladies interested in the welfare of the
young and retired teachers, might with
advantage be appointed to these Committees; and what steps the Ministry propose
to take in the matter.
Mr. ROBB: A deputation from the
Education Board of the General Assembly
interviewed the Minister on the question
of the desirability of appointing ministers
of religion on Regional Committees on
25th October, 1927. Resolutions on the
same subject were received from the same
Board. On every Regional Committee
except four there are lady members. I
have no information as to how many of
the members of Regional Committees are
retired teachers, but the fact of a person
being a retired teacher is not, I should
think, a disqualification for election.
The question of the individuals to be
appointed to serve on education committees is one for the county and district
councils in each area, and it is not competent for the Ministry to prescribe to
those bodies how they should exercise
their right of appointment, seeing that
Parliament has deliberately conferred
these powers on the councils so that the
control of education, so far as it is delegated to education committees, may be in
the hands of elected representatives of the
ratepayers. The Ministry would regret the
exclusion of the ministers of the various
religious denominations from the committees in view of the great services rendered
by these gentlemen, both at present and
in the past, to the cause of education,
but it is by no means the case that
ministers are invariably excluded from
these committees. A number of the committees contain ministers of religion
amongst their members and the clergy are
almost always to be found on the district
sub-committees and school committees appointed under the terms of Section 3 of
the Education Act for the local management of schools. The Minister is watching carefully the administration of the
Act by the local education authorities
throughout the Province and he is not
convinced that the circumstances,
known to him at present, would warrant
his asking Parliament to enlarge his
powers of control over the exercise by the
councils of their powers of appointment
to education committees.

MOTOR VEHICLES, PORTADOWN.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if it is a fact that no police
prosecutions have been brought forward
for reckless driving of motor vehicles and
overcrowding of omnibuses at Portadown ;
whether numerous accidents have occurred
during the past fourteen months; and,
if so, whether any action has been taken;
and whether he considers it necessary to
hold an inquiry into the whole matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a fact
that no police prosecutions have been
brought forward for reckless driving of
motor vehicles and overcrowding of omnibuses at Portadown. On the contrary,
there have been 45 prosecutions for reckless driving and 29 prosecutions for overcrowding since the 1st January, 1927.
There have been 32 accidents to motor
vehicles in the same period, and in eight
cases prosecutions were instituted. The
circumstances of the remaining cases were
fully investigated, but it was found that
they were not such as to warrant prosecutions.
I am fully satisfied that there are no
grounds whatever for the suggestion that
the police are in any way remiss in the
discharge of their duties with regard to
this matter, and I do not therefore propose to hold any inquiry.

that we expect of it, at least is an honest

to bring our roads into such a condition
that they will be fit and convenient for
the purposes for which they are now required. If it goes any considerable
length in that direction, I think it should
have the Third Reading in our Parliament at the earliest possible moment.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
George Henderson) has raised some points
in regard to this Bill, and I hope there
will be no risk of our misunderstanding
one another when I say that he brought
not only his eloquence but his intelligence
to bear upon the subject, as he always

authorities in our area are all men who
are embued with a high public spirit,
and who are desirous of making our roads
fit for all the purposes that modern traffic
now demands. I think that in connection with this Bill and its administration.
they will invest all their efforts and
activities with the vigour and wisdom
that have characterized their activities in

while they will be convenient for motorists
they will also be in a very great degree
safer for pedestrains and members of the

Superannuation and Other Trust Funds
(Validation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

877 Superannuation Funds Bill-

18 APRIL 1928
Second Reading
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Bill to which
I now ask the House to give a
Second Reading follows closely the
provisions of the Superannuation and
Other Trust Funds (Validation) Act
passed by the Imperial Parliament last
year. That Measure gave effect to the recommendations of a Departmental Committee appointed to inquire into the
effect of the rule of law against perpetuities in its application to certain
superannuation funds and funds with
analogous purposes. The Committee
found that many funds were placed under
disabilities by reason of the rule of law
against perpetuities, and that the only
satisfactory method of removing such disabilities was by way of legislation.
The public policy upon which the rules
of law against perpetuities are founded
was stated by the Master of the Rolls so
far back as 1732 to be
"the mischief that would arise to the
public from estates remaining for ever
or for a long time inalienable or untransferable from one hand to another,
being a damp to industry and prejudice
to trade, to which may be added the inconvenience and distress that would be
brought on families whose estates are so
fettered."
What the Government seek to accomplish
by means of this Bill is to ensure that any
trust funds set up, or to be set up hereafter, for the purpose of providing a
superannuation to the employees of banks,
insurance companies or industrial concerns, or pensions and allowances for the
widows and orphans of such employees
shall have the means of freedom from any
disability arising out of the application of
the rule of law against perpetuities.
It will readily be appreciated that the
success of any superannuation fund depends greatly upon its stability and permanency, and upon the existence of a
continuous stream of entrants and beneficiaries, with, of course, the necessary
safeguard of periodic actuarial valuation.
The Bill lays down certain conditions
to be complied with, the principal one
being the registration of the Fund and its
Rules with the Registrar of Friendly
Societies, who must be satisfied that the
Fund is qualified for registration. The
Trustees must prepare each year a state.
ment of accounts and balance sheet which
must be audited by an auditor, and a
quinquennial investigation and report by
an actuary as to the financial condition of
the Fund is required to be furnished to
the Registrar.
I am not in a position to say how many
Funds exist in Northern Ireland which
require validation by means of this Bill
as the facts and figures concerning any
Fund are usually treated as of a somewhat
private and confidential character. I
have, however, sought the views of leading
industrial concerns, banks, and representative associations as to the desirability
of introducing legislation on similar lines
to that recently passed in the United
Kingdom, and the replies which I have
received satisfy me they are almost
unanimous in their desire that similar
legislation should be passed for the benefit of such funds in Northern Ireland.
Question put and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed to a Committee of the whole House
for to-morrow.

of the Ministry of Finance for the issue

a new method of assessment of an existing
licence duty-I refer to a provision de-

As is customary with Finance Bills

Oral Answers
19 APRIL, 1928
Oral Answers to Questions.
SPIRITS RETAINED FOR CONSUMP-
TION IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
1. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number
of gallons of spirits retained for consumption in Northern Ireland in each of the
three years ending 31st March, 1926, 1927
and 1928.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I regret that, as the information
sought relates to a matter controlled by
an Imperial Department, I am not in a
position to supply particulars, but I will
endeavour to obtain the desired information, and will communicate with the hon.
Member in due course.
DOGS ACT-ADMINISTRATION
EXPENSES.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will state
the reason for the increase of £1,000 in
the administration expenses under the
Dogs Act for 1926 over that of 1925.
Had
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The apparent increase of £1,000 in the administrative
expenses in 1926 as compared with the
figure shown in 1925 is due to the fact
that certain payments which were included in 1925 in the Fines and Fees
Account are more appropriately shown
under the heading Administrative expenses in the Dogs Act in 1926.
these expenses, however, been shown in
926 in the Fines and Fees Account, a
corresponding amount would have been
withdrawn from the Dogs Act Account to
meet the annual deficit on the former
Account. The amount ultimately distributed to the local authorities was,
therefore, not in any way diminished by
the amount shown under the heading of
Administrative expenses.
The Administrative expenses for 1925
and 1926 were approximately the same.
BELFAST HARBOUR COMMISSION-
ERS-AGE OF EMPLOYEES.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that the
Belfast Harbour Commissioners have laid
down as a rule that no man is to be
taken on in their employment over the
age of 55 years; and whether he will use
his influence to have this rule or order
rescinded.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, to reply.
The Minister has been informed that
the rule to which the hon. Member refers
is applied to those members only of the
Commissioners' staff who are engaged for
employment of a regular nature and it
does not affect the engagement of suitable
men over 55 for ordinary day to day employment. The rule came into operation
in November, 1926, in consequence of
men who had entered the Commissioners'
employment at a late age expecting to
be pensioned after a few years' service on
reaching the retiring age of 70, and the
Commissioners feel that it is reasonable
that the service of their regular employees
should, in consequence, begin at an age
not later than 55. In these circumstances, the Minister considers that he
would not be justified in suggesting to
the Commissioners that the present
arrangement should be altered.
Mr. KYLE: Would the hon. Gentleman use his influence with the Government, in view of the fact that this very
important body in Belfast has decided
not to employ men 55 years of age, to
have the pension age reduced to that age
in order to enable these people to have
something to live on?
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think that
arises out of the question.

next. (Captain Dixon.)

Northern Ireland should abolish sinecures.

[The Prime Minister]
Then we come to the general question
whether the office or my salary is excessive under the circumstances. Well,
I can only repeat in this House what I
said on former occasions that no one who
has not filled the position can realize the
cost that it entails upon one's own
private means. I can assure the House,
and I think everybody will believe me
when I say that when I lay down the
reins of office as Prime Minister I will
be an infinitely poorer man than when I
took them up.
But that is one of those
delicate matters into which one does not
care to go. I am sure nobody in the
House will press any further in the
matter. They will find out in time that
generous and all as it appears on paper,
and generous and all as Members of all
quarters of the House feel in regard to
the treatment of myself and my colleagues, there is not one of us who will
not retire from office without feeling very
much poorer in this world's goods than
when they took office. I wish that to be
quite understood in the House, so that
they will not think any one of us is
occupying the position we do for the
purpose of personal gain. I hope that is
not suggested by anyone.
This is a very costly affair. The
position is a very great one and a very
high one, and I am determined to keep
up the dignity of the office. I am not
going to allow anything to interfere with
the dignity of the Prime Minister's Department of Northern Ireland or to
allow of its sinking down in any degree
whatever. We have distinguished visitors
here from all over the world from time to
time. We are in constant communication with people of great distinction and
great weight. If we were in any way to
allow a depreciation of our own position
if ever that came about through any
fault of our own we would be taken up
at that value. That would irretrievably
damage Ulster as a whole. By keeping
up and maintaining the high office as we
are determined to do, I believe in the
long run greater benefit will arise to
Ulster than by talking about a few
hundred pounds here or there. I hope
with that explanation the Committee will
be satisfied.

Mr. POLLOCK: Although this Vote
is the smallest Estimate presented to Parliament, it has invariably provoked very
considerable discussion. Discussion of
broad principles is in itself eminently desirable, and in moving this Estimate I
desire to refer to what is the one important principle underlying the expenditure of this money: It is that the money
must be used in the public interest.
As was stated by the Prime Minister
during a recent debate, the responsibility
for the administration of this Fund rests
upon the Minister of Finance, and I am
personally accountable to Parliament for
the payments which are made.
Hon. Members may not be aware that
the administration of the corresponding
Fund in Great Britain is similarly left.
in the hands of a Minister of the Crown,
subject only to consultation with the
Treasury in exceptional circumstances,
and that it is not customary for Parliament to question, on every possible
Supply-
19 APRIL, 1928
Committee

occasion the manner in which he discharges this public duty. I had hoped
that this House would have extended to
me the same degree of trust, but in view
of the controversy which this Estimate invariably encites, I propose to take this
opportunity of stating as succinctly as
possible the principles upon which my
decisions are based, and to allay any
doubts Hon. Members opposite may
cherish as to my actions.
Hon. Members will not quarrel with me
in saying that it is in the interests of
our Province that its name, its products
and manufactures should be known in
every part of the globe, and that opportunities should be created for an interchange of views between representative
bodies of other areas and of this area,
whether in the realm of public affairs or
of such matters as agriculture, education
and public health. The Government
cannot directly benefit individual commercial undertakings or influence the world
of thought and research, but it can, and
I think it should, create opportunities
for visits to be paid by public men and
representative public bodies from Great
Britain and from overseas, or make use
of these visits, when arranged by other
bodies, to create an atmosphere of goodwill and friendship. A great deal of good
has already been done in this way to
further the progress of the Province.
I have no hesitation, therefore, in
authorizing the entertainment of persons
or associations whose visits here may in
some degree contribute to the material
prosperity of the people, and almost the
whole of the expenditure charged to the
Fund has been incurred in this way.
There is no secrecy about the expenditure;
the objects are all fully set out in a note
to the Appropriation Accounts when
these are published after the close of each
Financial Year. One or two examples
of contemplated expenditure in the current year will clarify the position:-
The Government has been able to assist
in arranging for an International Motor
Race to be run in Ulster during
the coming summer, and we
propose to entertain some of those concerned to dinner on the evening of the
race; or, again, my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Agriculture, has suggested to
me the desirability of entertaing the delegates to the World's Dairy Congress
which will be holding a Session here in
July.
Most of the expenditure from the Hospitality Fund is incurred in entertainments
such as these, and in general I restrict the
scope of the Fund to affording hospitality
on the occasion of important visits. But
instances may possibly occur when the
Fund should be used for some more local
purposes. The forthcoming ceremony of
the Laying of the Foundation Stone at
Stormont is an example of what I have
in mind. Similarly, if, in the interests
of the Province as a whole, an important
conference is summoned, I do not regard
it as improper that time should be saved,
and a friendly atmosphere created, by
arranging some slight hospitality for those
taking part.
In conclusion, I would suggest to hon.
Members that it is somewhat invidious
to bring individual entertainments under
discussion. Hospitality, whether public
or private, must be given graciously, and
anything in the nature of a public dispute concerning the recipients of the
hospitality offered by the State must defeat the end to be achieved. I beg to
move.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sure that everyone on this side of the House has the same
confidence in the Minister of Finance as

PROVISION OF J.W.S. FLAXSEED.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
quantity of J.W.S. flaxseed which will be
available for farmers for sowing this year,
and whether any other varieties are recommended by his Department for sowing.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
In all some 110 tons
(Mr. Archdale):
of J.W.S. flaxseed were available for sowing by Northern Ireland farmers this
season.
The Ministry publishes at the commencement of each sowing season a leaflet intended to guide farmers who contemplate the sowing of flaxseed. This
leaflet contains information as to the
various varieties of seed available for
sowing. I am having a copy of this leaflet sent to the hon. Member.

Government and from the

MENTALLY DEFICIENT CHILDREN
IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether any steps have yet
been taken to ascertain the number of
mentally deficient children resident in
Northern Ireland, and, if not, when it is
proposed to put that part of the 1923
Education Act into operation.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The Education Act imposes upon Education
Authorities the duty of ascertaining what
children in their respective areas are
afflicted children within the meaning of
the Act.
Until schemes of medical inspection are
in full working order in every area it will
not be practicable to deal fully with the
question, but the Ministry has communicated by circular with each Education Authority inquiring what steps
have been taken in the matter, and pointing out that if proceedings have not yet
commenced this duty should be taken in
hand at the earliest possible date.
Several of the Regional Committees
have already reported the presence of
mentally deficient children in their areas
and have taken steps, so far as circumstances permit, to provide for their
education.

Education whether it is a fact that the

equally good quality could have been procured at a cheaper rate in the town of

Mr. ROBB: The cost (including carriage) of the Killough bricks used in the
case referred to by the hon. Member exceeded the cost (including cartage) of

for use in this case.

OBSERVATION OF RULE 55a.
7. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education,
whether he is aware that in almost all nontransferred schools Rule 55a of the Code is
not being observed, and what steps his
Department is prepared to take to see that
managers carry out their duty to make
every school comfortable by having it properly furnished, lighted, cleaned, ventilated and adequately heated in cold
weather.
Mr. ROBB: The Ministry is not aware
that there is any general neglect of the
provisions of Rule 55a of the Code in nontransferred schools.
Where the attention of the Ministry is
drawn to cases where adequate provision is
not made for the health and comfort of the
pupils and teachers, representations are
made to the manager of the school with a
view to such steps being taken as may be
necessary and feasible, having regard to
the circumstances of the case.
In extreme cases in which such definite
improvements as the Ministry thinks proper are not effected, grants are suspended
until the Ministry is satisfied that the
defects have been remedied.
Mr. KYLE: Is the hon. and learned
Gentleman not aware that many teachers
in Belfast and the Six Counties are almost
compelled by the managers of their schools
to heat and light the schools, and, as I
have irrefutable evidence that that is so,
will he not compel the managers of the
schools to carry out their duties under the
Code?
Mr. ROBB: I do not admit the assumption on which the hon. Member has based
his question, but if he will give me particulars I will have inquiries made.
CIVIL SERVICE COMMITTEE.
8. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
nature of the functions of the Civil Service Committee for Northern Ireland in
relation to employees of local authorities,
transferred Civil servants, and employees
of the Queen's University; whether the
Committee will cease to function at the
conclusion of the transitional period of
seven years mentioned in the Government of Ireland Act; who
who are the
members of the Committee, and by whom
is each appointed.
Mr. BARBOUR: In reply to the first
part of his question, I have to inform
the hon. Member that the functions referred to are described, as regards employees of Local Authorities, in Section 8
of the Local Government (Ireland) Act,
1919, as amended by Section 68 (2) of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920; as
regards transferred Civil Servants, in
Sections 55, 56 and 58 of the lastmentioned Act and the Eighth Schedule
thereto; and as regards employees of
Queen's University, Belfast, in Section 16
(2) of the Government of Ireland Act. It
would not be practicable within the
normal limits of an answer to a Parliamentary question to describe them in detail, but it may suffice for me to inform
the hon. Member that they involve, generally, the protection of the superannuation rights of employees of Local
Authorities who held pensionable offices
on the 3rd June, 1919; of Civil Servants
transferred under the operation of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, from
Irish Departments to the Government of
Northern Ireland; and of University employees who held pensionable offices at
the date of the commencement of the
Irish Universities Act, 1908. Furthermore, as regards the local offices and
Civil Servants referred to, the Committee
have power to award compensation where
they are satisfied that the conditions of
service of such officers have, since the
passing of the Local Government (Ireland) Act, 1919, or the transfer of the
officers to the Government of Northern
Ireland, respectively, been materially
altered to their detriment.
The reply to the second part of the
question is in the negative. After the
expiry of the transitional period, although
the right of officers to make application
to the Committee to retire voluntarily
without being required to show adequate
reasons will cease, the responsibilities of
the Committee will continue to exist so
long as any of the employees in respect of
whom their functions are exercisable continue in employment.
In reply to the last part of the question, the members of the Committee are
as follows:

CLOSING OF CO. TYRONE POLICE
BARRACKS LAHEY AND ROCK.
10. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he has received
a memorial from the residents in Killyman district, Co. Tyrone, viewing with
alarm the proposal to close Lahey Police
Barracks, and whether he is prepared to
reconsider his decision.
The following question also stood upon
the Order Paper:
11. Mr. ELLIOTT to ask the Minister
of Home Affairs whether, before deciding
to close the Police Barracks in Rock, Co.
Tyrone, due consideration was given to
the representation put forward by lawabiding residents in that area, who are
afraid that the time has not yet come
when the barracks referred to are
longer necessary.

Mr. HANNA: With the hon.
Members' permission, I propose to take
the two questions regarding the closing
of Lahey and Rock R.U.C. Barracks
together.
The whole question of the distribution
of police barracks in Northern Ireland
has been investigated by a Departmental
Committee consisting of the Inspector-
General, a representative of the Ministry
of Finance and a representative of my
own Department, and the decision to
close the barracks referred to in this question has been arrived at as a result of
the recommendations of that Committee.
The most careful consideration has
been given to the representations which
have been made by the residents in the
districts affected, but as the police
authorities are satisfied that the closing
of these barracks will not prevent the
efficient policing of the districts now
served by these stations, the Government
has decided, in the interests of economy,
that the arrangements already made for
the evacuation of these barracks should
proceed.
I need hardly say that the decision to
close any barrack is given with reluctance, and only after the fullest consideration, but the hon. Member will realize
that the imperative necessity for economy
and the reductions which are being effected in the strength of the Force leave
no other course open in cases where, in
the opinion of the responsible police
authorities, the area concerned can, without material loss of police efficiency, be
merged in adjoining areas.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: May I ask
the hon. and learned Gentleman if he is
aware of the fact that in this district
of Lahey very recently witches have appeared, and if he removes the police from
this district it would take
away all protection from the friends of the Member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott).
Mr. ELLIOTT: And Warrenpoint.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: May I also say in
connection with this question that since
the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Elliott) came to reside in
Belfast there does not appear to be much
necessity for a police barracks in Coagh.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
EASTER ARRESTS-WEARING
FREE STATE COLOURS.
12. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that a
number of young men were arrested at
Easter in consequence of their wearing the
colours of the Irish Free State in their
button holes; can he state the date on which
it became illegal to wear the colours of a
constituent part of the British Commonwealth of Nations; whether it is a fact
that these young men are still incarcerated with no charge preferred against
them; whether he is aware that some of
them have lost their employment in consequence of their arrest, and will he
order their immediate release.
Mr. HANNA: The facts regarding the
incident referred to in the question are
as follows:-
On the 25th ult. posters were exhibited
announcing an "Easter Week Commemoration" to be held at Milltown
Cemetery on Easter Sunday. These
posters set out that an oration would be
delivered at the "Republican" plot in
the cemetery bv "a prominent Republican," and the poster concluded with
the words "God bless the clay where rest
to-day the felons of our land.'
In connection with this demonstration,
arrangements were made by the organizers
for the distribution and display of an
emblem or artificial flower by those attending the demonstration.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
It is obvious that the display in Belfast
on Easter Sunday under such circumstances of any emblem indicating Republican sympathies was calculated
gravely to imperil the peace of the city
and might well have given rise to serious
disturbances.
Instructions were, therefore, issued to
the police that persons wearing these
emblems under circumstances likely to
endanger the peace should be requested
to remove them.
Eight men who refused to do so were
arrested by the police on Easter Sunday
under the provisions of the Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act, and were
subsequently lodged in Belfast Prison.
Their cases were carefully considered in
consultation with the Attorney-General,
and although there is no doubt that they
had been guilty of an offence by acting in
a manner prejudical to the preservation
of the peace and maintenance of order,
for which a prosecution could have been
instituted, the conclusion was finally
arrived at that in view of the serious
warning which had been given by their
arrest and detention, it was unnecessary
to take any further action against them.
Their release was accordingly affected on
the 16th instant.
I have no information as to whether
any of these men have lost their employment in consequence of arrest.

13. Mr. COLLINS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether brick is being
imported from Scotland in connection
with the exterior of the new Belfast
Prison on the Crumlin Road, at a cost
of £9 per thousand with quay charges,
whereas local brick could have been obtained at a price of 60s, and whether he
can explain why preference has been
given to Scotch brick.
I have been asked
Mr. BARBOUR:
to take this question. The question of
the material to be used for the front ard
side elevations of the cottages under
course of construction at Belfast Prison
required serious consideration in view of
the dark mass of stone-walling of the
Prison which forms a background. The
most suitable material to have used was
possibly stone, but this had to be disregarded on account of the high cost involved. The original specification provided for the use of certain facing bricks
which were manufactured in Ulster, but
when the contract was placed, the brick
manufacturers had altered their method
of burning, with the result that the brick
specified could not be obtained. In order
that some degree of harmony with the
stone background should be attained, the
bricks which are at present used were
selected as no locally manufactured
brick of suitable colour was available. I
should
say that the bricks in question are
marketed in Belfast by a local firm of
distributors. The bricks used for the
backs and the return portion of the
cottages are of local manufacture.
The matter was specially brought to
the notice of the Minister, who felt satisfied that it would be a serious mistake to
have a light coloured brick frontage
against the dull stone background.

Local Government (Amendment) Bill.
