Mr. KYLE: The Local Government
(Amendment) Bill, the Second Reading
of which I am now moving, is aimed at
giving effect to that conception of the
franchise to which Mr. Baldwin gave
utterance on March 8th when he was
congratulating the women on attaining
the right to vote at the age of 21. He
said
:-
The franchise does not only mean
franchise, but it means obligation and
opportunity.
It places upon us all the obligation of
taking an active part in the life of our
city, in the affairs of our country. It
confers upon us, or ought to confer upon
us, the opportunity of influencing in the
representative city or county council
the decisions that are there taken. The
reform that this Bill, which I have the
honour to present on behalf of the entire
Opposition, desires to bring about is that
the various city and county councils and
other governing bodies in our area should
be as fully representative of public
opinion in their areas as is humanly
possible, and is drafted to re-establish
the position created by the Imperial
Government in 1919.
The Bill itself is a simple one, and I
think if I put it under three headings
it would put the matter clearly before
the Members of the House. In the first
place the Bill will provide that in any
contested election of members of a local
authority in Northern Ireland each
voter shall have a single transferable vote.
and where two or more members are
elected together the election shall be by
proportional representation. That is
very necessary, as I think has been
demonstrated in the City of Belfast. At
Poor-law Guardians' elections in Belfast
Local Government Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
that in
and some other parts of the Six Counties
some of the wards and areas returned two
or three members. It means
those wards and areas the majority of the
electors being more or less Unionist adherents or Nationalist adherents, as the
case may be, there is no opportunity for
the minority to have representatives.
Take for example the ward of Shankill,
where three guardians are elected. At
the last election that took place there
what are called the official candidates received 3,000 votes, and the Labour candidates received something like 1,800 votes,
or more than one-third of the entire votes
that were cast in that particular ward.
Despite that fact the result is that under
the present system there are no representatives of the minority in that particular area. The same thing obtains in
many other areas. Therefore, it seems to
me, and I think to almost any reasonable person, that it is desirable that if
the franchise means the obligation and
the opportunity of seeing that public
institutions are representative of public
opinion this Bill ought to receive its
Second Reading to-day.
The second point is that the electoral
areas shall be the electoral areas in force
immediately before the commencement of
the Local Government Act (Northern
Ireland), 1922. Thirdly, the rules for
the election of members of a local
authority shall be the rules which were
contained in the Local Elections (P.R.I.)
Order, 1919. This system of the single
transferable vote was introducd, I think,
owing to a very successful experiment in
Sligo in 1919, in which town a very
serious situation had developed, owing, I
may add, to the domination of one particular party in the affairs of the town.
Real faults have been found with the administration of the town. I think it is
notorious that where a city or a country
or a part of a country gets into the hands
of one dominant party the administration
suffers accordingly. Things are done
and acts performed that would not be
possible if there was a painstaking watchful opposition. If there is not an
opposition-for oppositions do not exist in
the ordinary sense of the term in Local
Government bodies-acts are done which
would not be done if the parties were
approximately even in number I think
that cannot be gainsaid.
Have we not an example in our own
City of Belfast? Our administration is
called in question largely, it will be admitted, because of the dominantion exercised by the Unionist party in this city
who have been in unbridled control since
I think
Belfast was granted a council.
it can in truth be said that the best
government can only be had where there
is a watchful, critical and even hypercritical opposition instead of the easygoing criticism and easy-going opposition
we have in this city. There should
be in local bodies a party working for the
public good rather than for party gain.
Therefore, proportional representation
was introduced under the authority of
the Imperial Government, and when the
local elections were held in 1920 all of
us had in Northern Ireland an effective
opportunity of taking our share in public
life.
The facts speak for themselves. Instead
of, as at present, few contests being the
order of the day, every ward in Belfast
and practically over the Six Counties was
contested in 1920. In the City of Belfast,
which is divided into nine wards, there
were contests in every ward, with the
result that the minorities had exactly the
number of members returned to the
Council which their number of votes entitled them to. In Belfast the City
Council consisted of 35 Unionists and 25
others, of whom Labour claimed 12,
Nationalists and Sinn Fein 10 and three
Independents. I am glad to say that one
of the Independents is still a member of
that administrative body and of this
House. Proportional Representation
gave them the opportunity which is the
purpose of the franchise. The minority
representatives were able to sit on the
committees of the Council and to becorne
familiar with the work of the Council
and to take part in criticising what had
been done or was being purposed to be
done by the Council.

The Second Reading of a Bill only

To turn down the principle contained in
this Bill is to give the lie to Mr. Baldwin's exposition of what the franchise
means. We ask for the enactment of a
broad principle that citizens, whether
they are in a majority or in a minority
in any ward in Belfast, or in any other
city or county, should have the right to
send a representative to the local council.
The Bill may require amendment in
respect of details. All I ask for is the
acceptance of the principle, and I would
then hope that the Government will take
such steps as are customary in the Parliaments of civilized countries to give all
that assistance which a Member of Parliament has a right to expect in ensuring
that

expressed in the best possible legal way.

of

Proportional Representation was intended by the Imperial Parliament to
give a voice to minorities. The block
system favoured the large parties and the
organizations with a great deal of money,
but many people believed that there were
interests that could not find expression
under either of the two large political
parties. For that reason an experiment
was tried at Sligo, in, I believe, the year
1919. Sligo borough at that time, to my
own knowledge, had reached a pretty low
level in administrative ability. It had
come practically to the point of bankruptcy.
The result of that election on
Proportional Representation lines gave a
representation to Sinn Fein of seven,
Labour five, Ratepayers eight, and Independents four, a total of 24, so that when
they came to elect a mayor they found
that there were 12 votes on one side and
12 votes on the other side. I think that
we who have some experience of local
administrative affairs find that it is not a
bad thing to have parties pretty evenly
divided in that way. The result of Proportional Representation at Sligo, where
affairs had reached the low standard I
have indicated, was that immediately
things began to look up. In the few
years that followed the rates were reduced, the services were improved, and
the people began to take a more intelligent interest altogether in the affairs of
the borough in consequence of the operation of Proportional Representation. It
is well known that many of the old
Unionist party, who under the block
system could have had no earthly chance of
sitting in the council, had a full representation of eight out of 24.
One need not stress the contrast between
what takes place in the Free State and
what takes place in Northern Ireland.
In the Free State people are satisfied to
give representation to minorities, but in
the North you are not satisfied to give
representation even to majorities. That
is a positive fact. You are not content
unless you possess the control of all offices

a minority. There are 28 unions in the
area known as Northern Ireland. It will
surprise many of you to know that in 14
of these 28 unions there are Nationalist
majorities. You may say that the rate.

upwards of half a dozen different sections

whom are entitled to and would, if in

Proportional Representation was bad, but

was a
thousand times worse. The abolition of
Proportional Representation, as I have
said, was designed to deprive minorities
of reasonable representation, and the

designed to deprive majorities, and substantial majorities, of their rights, and to
put them under the heel of the minority,
who are the satellities of the Government
party.
The gerrymander followed close on
the heels of the abolition of Proportional
Representation in 1922, and both were
evidently part of a preconceived plan.
The result has been, as has been pointed
out by the hon. Member for West. Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), that in all that part of
Ulster which is under the jurisdiction of
this Government the Nationalist party,
notwithstanding their 35 or 34 per cent.
of the population, have control of only
two rural district councils.
Being familiar with Tyrone, I would

the population of Tyrone was 142,000-I

16,000. Of course, the Census was not

Under Proportional Representation,
after the elections held in the year 1920,
the Nationalist body had control of the
majority of Tyrone County Council, and
had a majority on four of the six rural
district councils in the county. That fact
was the reason for the gerrymander, probably the reason for the abolition of Proportional Representation, and certainly
the reason for the gerrymander of Tyrone.
Taking the County Council of Tyrone and
the six rural district councils, at the
election in 1920, there were 78 Nationalist members elected on these seven bodies
as against 61 Unionists. These figures
are approximately in proportion to the
numbers of population and of Local

turned into a minority, and this in a
county where there is a majority of
16,000 Nationalists.

uames and I will mark the ballot paper

""
That example is one that occurred under
my own eyes, and it shows the difficulty
the ordinary citizens, especially the citizens who, perhaps, are not very well
educated, have in recording their votes
correctly under this system of Proportional Representation. And if that be so,
what can be said with regard to the
accuracy of the results which are obtained
as a result of the elections under this system? I say
that some of the results that
have been obtained under Proportional
Representation have really been grotesque,
and do not represent the true view of
the electorate in any way. We know that
it is an expensive system. We know that
it is extremely cumbersome. We know
the confusion that obtains under it. We
know the difficulty that every Member has
in one of these enormous constituencies.
He cannot possibly know more than a
fraction of his constituents, and a very
small fraction of his constituents know
him, even by appearance; and consequently the true state of feeling and
knowledge between the electorate and the
representative has completely disappeared.
People are voting not for personality at
all.
They are voting for shadows, for
someone who, they think, represents the
principle that they adhere to, and in the
result you get no true index of the views
of the electorate as a whole.
Now, there is another blot upon this
system. I do not know whether it has
been referred to. But we all know that
in recent times under this system we
have had very low polls at elections, not
only in this Province but in the Free
State, where Proportional Representation
is still in existence. I have always,
rightly or wrongly-and I believe rightly
-ascribed the lowness of the polls in
these enormous constituencies to the very
thing I have already referred to, namely,
the want of enthusiasm and interest of
the electorate, as a body, in the persons
who are to represent them. It is impossible to get the electorate out to record
their votes when you have a system so
cumbersome as this system of Proportional Representation, and when they are
not really acquainted with the persons on
whose behalf they are recording their
votes.

After Ireland's experience during
the past week, it is certain that the
system of Proportional Representation
has come to stay. We believe that the
early future will see its adoption for
Municipal and Parliamentary elections
throughout the United Kingdom.
The Irish elections, which the
British public and press have followed
with keen interest, establish all the
virtues that were claimed for this
scientific method of feeling the popular
pulse. In the first place the mechanism
has worked without a hitch. In the
next place, the results of the elections
(whether we like them or not) reflect
with an entirely novel fidelity the
strength of the various political and
municipal parties in Ireland.

Wednesday, 25th April, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
RENT RESTRICTION.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister
whether, in view of the volume of
opinion expressed by all parties in Northern Ireland, the Government propose to
introduce legislation continuing the
Rent Restriction Act in respect of all
houses under £52 valuation until such
time as a sufficiency of houses is available
in Northern Ireland.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper (No. 2) in the name of Mr.
Grant:
—
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs
whether the Government of Northern Ireland has decided to accede to the representations put forward by the Ulster
Labour Unionist Association in favour
of postponing from the 1st May,
1928, until the 1st May, 1930, the decontrol of houses between £26 and £52
valuations, and from the 1st May, 1930,
until the 1st May, 1932, the decontrol of
houses of valuations under £26.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I propose to answer
together this question and No. 2 standing in the name of my hon. Friend the
Member for North Belfast.
The Government has carefully reviewed
the whole question of Rent Restriction,
and is satisfied that there is no justification for interferring with the operation
of the Act of 1925 in regard to houses of
valuations between £26 and £52.
In respect of those of lower valuations,
the Government, will ask Parliamentary
sanction early next Session for the introduction of a Bill further postponing the
decontrol of all houses not exceeding £26
valuation, unless by then fully convinced
that an ample number of similar small
dwellings have been erected.
Meanwhile the Government will consider whether the subsidy for the erection
of working-class houses shall be continued
after April, 1929, until such time as it
is assured that sufficient progress has been
made to justify further decontrol without
causing any hardship upon the working
classes.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say whether or not he is prepared to receive representations from
those people who are residing in houses of
a valuation from £26 to £52; and, if
hardship can be proved, will he assure the
House that the matter will be reconsidered by the Government?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government have carefully considered the question from every angle. I, myself, have
received deputations on the subject from
every point of view, and the Government
have arrived at a decision which I think
is a fair and a proper one.
Mr. GRANT: Is the right hon.
Gentleman prepared on behalf of the
Government to give us an assurance that
when restriction ceases to operate in regard to houses of from £26 to £52 valuation, and the tenants find that they are
going to be fleeced by the landlords, the
Government will take some action to prevent exorbitant rents being charged to the
tenants of those houses?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a
hypothetical question, and I could only
give a hypothetical answer to it.
Mr. BEATTIE: May I ask the Minister whether in fairness to this class of
tenant the Government is prepared to set
up a Rent Court, to which in cases of
injustice the tenant or the landlord may
state his case?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I may remind my hon. Friend that the stage of
decontrol that comes into operation on
the 1st May next is only the second of the
stages. The first stage took place when

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The general scope of the Bill
now before the House was explained by
Finance Bill—
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
me last week when moving the Financial
Resolutions on which the Bill is based.
In a Bill of this character, touching, as
it does, on various different questions
affecting the revenue of the Province and
subjects related thereto, it is, perhaps,
more convenient to consider each proposal
separately, and I think it would, thereof hon.
fore, meet with the wishes
Members if I proceed to consider the Bill
clause by clause.
The object of Clause I is to fix the rate
of the duty payable by those wholesale
dealers in spirits who intend to take out
the Special Dealer's Licence authorized by
the Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing
Act which was passed last year.
The circumstances which necessitated
the creation of this special class of licence
were fully explained by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
when he moved the Second Reading of
that Bill in this House on the 1st
November last, but it will not be out of
place for me now to recapitulate briefly
the points which were brought to the
notice of the House on that occasion.
Under the law, as it then existed, a wholesale spirit dealer could not sell spirits to
a retailer at one time in quantities of less
than two gallons of each kind of spirit.
That is to say, he could not make a composite sale of, say, whisky, brandy, and
rum, but was obliged to sell at least two
gallons of each class of liquor, with the
result that in many cases retailers were
obliged to purchase a very much larger
quantity of liquor than their business
actually required. The creation of the
new licence does not in any way affect the
sale of intoxicating liquor by retail, and
I am glad to say that the proposals of the
Government were accepted by all sides of
the House.
As Parliament thus sanctioned the issue
of such licences, it is now necessary to
make provision in a Finance Bill for the
licence duty to be paid by the holders,
and having regard to the existing rates of
duty payable on various comparable
classes of licences, the Government has
come to the decision that an annual duty
of five guineas is in all respects equitable.
Sub-sections (2) and (3) of the Clause
are consequential and provide, respectively, for the repayment of a proportional
part of the duty where business is discontinued and for the form in which licences
are to be issued.
As regards Clause 2, although this is a
very lengthy Clause and appears extremely complicated, the object which it
seeks to achieve is really quite simple. In
accordance with the terms of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923, the licensees of
a number of public-houses have been
obliged to carry out structural alterations
in order to separate that part of their
premises used for the intoxicating liquor
trade from the rest. They have then two
courses open to them in regard to valuation for licence duty purposes, namely,
either to pay on the old valuation of the
whole premises or ask for a re-valuation of
the restricted portion, and at the same
time run the risk of having their poor-law
valuation increased. The effect is that,
rather than run the latter risk, the owner
will continue to pay licence duty on the
premises as a whole. This is not desirable, and therefore the Clause proposes to
give the trader an option of having his
duty assessed as at present, that is to say,
by reference to the entire premises as they
were before the structural alterations were
made, or to have the restricted portion revalued for licence duty purposes but without affecting his poor-law valuation.
Paragraph (a) of Clause 1 gives the
licensee the option to which I have just
referred, and paragraph (b) proceeds to
direct the Commissioner of Valuation, in
the event of the second option being accepted, to carry out the separate valuation of the licensed premises for licensing
purposes according to the principles laid
down in the Valuation Act, 1852. That
is to say, the annual value which would
be placed on the separated portion of the
premises would be the value as ascertained
having regard to present-day values. In
order to encourage applications for such
revision there is a proviso to the effect
that in no case shall the licensed premises
have assigned to them a greater annual
value than that which has hitherto been
assigned to the entire premises. The
paragraph contains provision for the
charging of an appropriate fee; the fee
will be fixed on the same scale as is in
operation for ordinary valuation
assessments.
re-
Before passing on to the next Clause,
I would like to make it clear that the provisions of this Clause in no way affect the
trader's ordinary valuation for rating
purposes. As I have already indicated,
the Clause is designed to remove an existing anomaly, but at the same time it has

Clause 3 deals with the collection of
the Excise Duties in connection with gun

and, as hon. Members will see from this

Hon.
Before proceeding to say more on this
subject, I would like to take this opportunity of paying a high tribute to the
officers of Customs and Excise.
Members will readily understand that on
the transfer of services in 1921 it would
have been almost impossible for our
newly-constituted Departments to have
taken over the whole of the duties which
were transferred, and I refer especially
to those particular services which were
decentralized and necessitated a staff of
trained officers working throughout the
country districts. Accordingly, we found
it desirable to ask-and the Department
of Customs and Excise very readily acceded to our request that they would act
as our agents for the administration of
various services, including, for example,
the Old-age Pensions Service, the administration of the Entertainment Duty,
and the collection of various licence duties.
With the development of our own
Departments, however, I am glad to say
that we have at length reached the position in which we feel that we can properly
take over the administration of several of
these services, and, as hon. Members
know, an Act was passed recently, setting
up new machinery in regard to Old-age
One of the effects of that legispensions.
lation will be a reduction in the number
of Customs and Excise officers operating
in the country districts of Northern Ireland, and it is felt that it would in future
be a matter of very great difficulty indeed
for the remaining officers properly to
supervise the issue of gun licences and
game certificates, since this is a work
which must essentially be carried out by
a considerable staff scattered throughout
our entire area. Accordingly, my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance, has
carefully examined the whole question in
consultation with the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and it has been agreed that, subject to Parliamentary approval, all gun
and game licences will be issued by
constabulary officers acting on behalf of
the Ministry of Finance.
are
It is felt that this change will at once
enable the
the police, who already
brought in touch with a much greater
number of people who must possess firearms permits and certificates, to detect
any attempts on the part of people in
their districts to evade the gun or game
licence duty. I may say that I have received persistent complaints, not only from
individuals, but also from the Game Protection Society, concerning the large
number of persons who make a practice
of shooting game without the necessary
licence. The Government is convinced
that the preservation of game is a considerable potential source of income to
the people of this Province, and it is felt
that it is in the interests of the Province
to strengthen the law, and at the same
time to take such administrative action
as may have the effect of enabling a closer

Clause 4 is designed to give statutory
effect to a concession announced by my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, when making his Budget statement last year. Briefly, the object of the
Clause is to afford relief from Companies
Capital Duty chargeable in each case at
£1 per cent. in connection with reconstruction and amalgamation of companies.
course
It will be readily appreciated, even by
the most casual observer, that industries
which have suffered by recent foreign
competition, or because of other less direct
causes, may wish to strengthen their
position by a consolidation of interests,
that is to say, by amalgamating existing
companies. No doubt, such a
carries with it many results of considerable value, and it not only enables such
companies to reduce heavy overhead
charges, but also ensures that manufactures are continued on the most up-todate lines, and that the disturbing effect
of cut-throat competition amongst individual manufacturers may be minimized.
Under existing laws, however, the full
stamp duties are payable in all such cases
of reconstruction or amalgamation, and it
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour].
has been felt that the burden of these
duties constitutes an undue obstacle which
it is desirable to remove.
This is, in general, the purpose of the
Clause, and, as it deals with a highly
technical matter, I do not think that hon.
Members would desire me to enter into a
detailed explanation of each of the provisions of the Clause, although I should
say that if any Member desires specific
information on any point I will be very
happy to supply him with it. The Clause
is similar to one which was thoroughly
sifted in Great Britain before being embodied in their Finance Act of last year,
and I am informed has worked satisfactorily in its various details.
The object of Clause 5 is, very simply,
to rectify what is evidently an omission in
existing Statutes. It is possible that by
a strict reading of the law as it stands at
present a Letter of Power of Attorney
could be charged with a 10s stamp duty
in respect of each person concerned in
giving the power. There is, however,
considerable doubt on the point, and it
has not up to the present been the practice
of the Ministry of Finance to charge more
than 10s for the stamp duty on a Power
of Attorney, irrespective of the number of
donors or the number of matters covered
by the powers thus granted. In order to
put the question beyond doubt, however,
it is considered desirable specifically to
enact that the fact of more than one person being concerned in the granting of a
power, or of more than one matter being
dealt with, should not attract a liability
to additional stamp duty. No real loss
of duty is involved, as the new Clause will
merely establish beyond doubt the legality
of an existing practice.
Clause 6 is consequential upon the provisions of the Roads Improvement Bill,
which has recently been before this House,
relating to the vesting of land acquired
for road purposes. In order to prevent
delay in the registration of the ownership
of land thus acquired the Roads Improvement Bill provides for the immediate registration of the Vesting Order issued by
the Ministry of Home Affairs prior to the
assessment of compensation to the owner
of the land. Normally, such an Order
can not be registered until the stamp duty
is impressed on it, and this stamp duty,
being an ad valorem duty, cannot be assessed until the compensation is fixed.
To avoid a vicious circle, therefore, Clause
6 declares the Vesting Order exempt from
duty, and provides for the stamps to be
impressed on the receipts issued at a later
date when the compensation has been assessed and paid over. I beg to move.

the development of the industries and

of Northern Ireland.

claim, and I think not without just cause,

Overseas have received the generous

Board of Customs and Excise in the case
of direct trade with foreign countries
and from returns furnished by the
harbour authorities in Northern Ireland
in the case of cross-Channel trade. The
collection of the statistics relative to
Northern Irish railways which, previous
to the 1st April, 1926, was undertaken
by the Imperial Ministry of Transport,
has since that date devolved upon the
Ministry. The Ministry has curtailed
the scope of these statistics to some extent
in order to afford the railway companies
some relief from the expenditure and
labour involved in furnishing returns.
Summaries of these statistics are issued
each month in the local Press.
During the past financial year the
Ministry has participated in
participated in several
exhibitions held under the auspices of the
Empire Marketing Board, and by this
means has succeeded in obtaining, at small
expense, considerable publicity for the
agricultural and manufactured products
of the Province. During the present
financial year the Ministry proposes to
participate in a further series of these
in
exhibitions, approximately twelve
number, which will be held at various
centres in Great Britain.
Examples of other activities in which
the Ministry is directly interested are to
be seen in the proposal to afford further
financial support to the Linen Industry
Publicity Campaign and to the Ulster
Tourist Development Association.
The postal service is, of course, a reserved service, but the Ministry is always
ready to act in a liason capacity for commercial and private users in Northern
Ireland, to lay suggestions and information before the Imperial postal authorities
with a view to effecting alterations designed to improve the postal service in
Northern Ireland.
Hon. Members will remember that the
administration of the fishery services in
Northern Ireland was transferred from
the Imperial Secretary's Department to
the Ministry of Commerce on the 1st
April, 1926. Since that date close attention has been devoted by the Ministry to
the preservation and development of this
valuable asset to the Province. The immediate responsibility for the enforcement
Supply-
Committee
25 APRIL 1928
of the fishery laws is in the hands of four
Boards of Conservators, towards the expenses of three of which Grants-in-Aid
were made during the year 1927-28.
Some months ago, in consequence of the
marked decrease in the catch of eels, a
statutory inquiry was conducted into the
times and methods of eel fishing with a
view to determining what action was required to prevent a further diminution
while permitting of the development of
the eel fisheres to their prudent limit. The
maintenance of healthy stocks of salmon
in our rivers has also received attention,
and the Ministry has assisted towards this
object by contributions to the cost of the
two largest salmon hatcheries in our area.
In the course of the two years during
which the Ministry has been responsible
for the administration of the fisheries
services a survey of the existing fishery
laws has been carried out with a view to
remedying certain defects, and to bring
the law more into conformity with requirements as indicated by the accumulated
experience of the Ministry and its predecessors. The result of this survey' will
come before the House in the form of an
Amending Bill, copies of which are
already in the possession of hon. Members.
The Ministry has also given attention
to sea fisheries and has endeavoured to
assist fishermen by granting loans, repayable over a period of years, for the
purchase of boats, engines, nets and other
equipment. Loans aggregating almost
£2,500 have been issued since April, 1926.
The Ministry has provided considerably
improved accommodation at Ardglass with
a view to the development of the herring
fishery. By the careful inspection of all
pickled herrings submitted by curers for
the official Northern Ireland Crown
Brand, and by a rigorous insistence on a
high standard of quality in order to
qualify for branding, the Ministry has
materially helped to secure for "Northern
Ireland Crowns" a pre-eminent reputation
on the Continental markets-a reputation
which, I am glad to say, has been reflected
in the relatively high price of the Northern Ireland herring. Branding is, of
course, optional, but the value of the
official brand is realized by curers, and increasing advantage is being taken of the
facilities offered by the Ministry in this
respect.
Before leaving the subject of fisheries
I might mention that the fishing rights
in Lough Erne, hitherto owned by the
Crown, were acquired by the Government
of Northern Ireland some months ago.
This transfer of ownership will facilitate
my Ministry in administering the fishery
laws in connection with these waters.
As regards the Power, Transport and
Companies Branch, I am glad to say that
the regular and well-established work of
the Ministry in relation to such matters
as the registration of Companies, Trade
Unions, Friendly and Industrial Provident Societies continues to be carried on
smoothly.
Mr. DEVLIN: Before the right hon.
Gentleman passes away from the question
of fisheries, has he any statement to inake
in regard to the position of the Lough
Neagh fisheries?
Mr. BARBOUR: Not otherwise than
already referred to in regard to the
amending Bill. There was a Report
issued by the inquiry set up as to the eel
fishery in Lough Neagh, and as a result
of that inquiry the amending Bill was
drafted and will be brought before the
House in the course of the next week,
when possibly it would be a more convenient time to deal with that matter.
I should like to refer briefly to the
subject of Industrial Assurance, which
may broadly be described as the insurance of the working classes for small sums
at premiums ranging from 1d to 6d a
week. This work was initiated in the
year 1925 following upon the passing of
the Industrial Assurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1924. The Secretary of the
Ministry acts as Industrial Assurance
Commissioner and exercises judicial
powers in deciding disputes between insured persons and industrial assurance
companies and societies. An indication
of the extent of the work may be gleaned
from the fact that, apart from a large
number of verbal inquiries made and
assistance rendered, no less than 260 disputes were referred to the Commissioner's
office during the year 1927. From the
experience gained I am able to state that
the 1924 Act has conferred real benefit
upon those least able to assert their legal
rights, in providing them with the means
of assistance in relation to the many
questions and problems which arise as to
their rights, and also in providing the
means of adjudication at a low cost. The
report of the Industrial Assurance Commissioner for the year 1927 will be laid
before the House at an early date.
Supply-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
With regard to the development of
electricity, steady progress is being made,
and up to the present time it has not
been necessary to make provision in the
Estimates for public assistance, Hon.
Members will, however, recall the Lisburn Electricity (Confirmation of Agreement) Act, 1927, under which my
Ministry is empowered to grant a loan
of £1,450 so that the main transmission
line, the erection of which from Belfast
to Lisburn is now in contemplation, may
be made suitable for future development
on a larger scale. The Company has recently made an offer of shares to the
public, and the line is likely to be erected
by the autumn of the present year.
During last year generating stations
were established at Lurgan and Armagh,
both being under the control of the respective urban district councils of those
towns. Several other urban districts are
now considering schemes of electricity supply. In the establishment of local generating stations the Electricity Commissioners
have not overlooked the probability that
at a later date the industrial areas of
Northern Ireland may be linked up by
main transmission lines. When that
time comes we in Northern Ireland will
not be faced with the problem of standardizing frequencies, a problem which is
now involving heavy expenditure in the
Central Electricity Board's schemes in
Great Britain. Our problem here, as I
have remarked before, is one of demand
rather than of supply.
It will be within the knowledge of hon.
Members that we have in Northern Ireland two Royal Harbours, Ardglass and
Donaghadee. At Ardglass there has been
in recent years a welcome, though I am
sorry to say fluctuating, revival of the
herring industry which had almost disappeared during the war years. While
the bulk of this industry is still in the
hands of Scottish curers, I am glad to
say that an increasing share is being
obtained by local interests. In order to
foster and encourage the herring fishing
and curing industry, we have carried out
some useful works of improvement at
Ardglass. A section of the sea bed in
the harbour has been reclaimed and converted into curing plots which are now
being surfaced and prepared for occupation this year. A market building has
been opened for the auctioning of fish,
and ten small offices have been provided
in this building for the accommodation
of the fish salesmen and merchants.
These facilities, I am glad to say, have
been much appreciated, and to meet the
demand for additional accommodation I
have arranged to provide this year four
additional offices. The cost will be small
and the rent of £5 per office will give
ample return upon the expenditure
Apart from the Royal Harbours, I need
hardly say that I am keenly interested in
schemes for the improvement of other
harbours on our coasts. I set up a small
Departmental Committee to consider and
report upon the requirements of these
harbours and their report has now been
published.
With regard to other harbours, provision is being made in this year's Estimates for grants in aid of works of improvement in the harbours at Rathlin
Island and Portstewart. Representations
have also been made to my Ministry on
behalf of other harbours, particularly
Ballycastle and Annalong, for which
drawings have been submitted by the
county councils. These proposals will be
considered by the Government in conjunction with the Report of the Departmental Committee.

Hon. Members will recall that during
the past year a Measure consolidating all
statutory provisions relating to quarries
was placed on the Statute Book. The
question of pursuing a policy of consolidation in the matter of Fishery Laws and
Bankruptcy Legislation has been
sidered, but for the time being the
Measures to be brought before you will
deal with Amendments of the existing
law. The task of consolidating either the
Fishery Laws or the Bankruptcy Laws,
while a most desirable one, is of such
colossal dimensions that it must await a
more favourable opportunity.
Turning now to the details of the Estimate the Committee will notice that the

an increase of £30 compared with the
amount voted for the previous year. The
.following alterations have been made in
the staff of the Ministry: One higher
executive and one executive post have
been discontinued, and one acting higher

clerical post created.

Mr. P. O'NEILL: Am I right in
assuming that in discussing this Vote we
can also refer to the matters in the following Vote? I think the Minister in the
statement, he made referred to both.
be
The CHAIRMAN: What can
done is this. This is the first Vote introduced by this particular Ministry, and
the whole policy of the Ministry can,
therefore, be discussed. That is due to
the fact that the Minister's salary is included in this particular Vote, and
though there is no salary in this particular case,
that does not eliminate the
right of Members to criticize. The
Minister's salary is supposed to represent
all the activities of his Department, and
therefore to present a suitable opportunity for a general review of the policy.
When we pass to the next Estimate all
that may be done there is to discuss the
details of the Estimate and not the
policy.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: I hope the activities of the Ministry will not be guaged
by the salary that is paid to the Minister.
The Minister's salary is nil, and we are

that the Ministry engaged with regard to

way or not. I think if we did get the

be so bad in trade or commerce as they

The same would hold good in regard to
the grant in aid of linen research. That

will amount to £1,000 this year. That is

to revive an industry which appears to

the fact stares one in the face that for
many years since the war at any ratethe linen industry is getting worse from
vear to year. For instance, can you
Justify the expenditure of £1,000 which
was incurred across in England in trying
to get protection for the embroidery industry? I do not know whether the
protection which was sought was acquired.
I understood that the greatest opposition.
put up to the proposal was by the repre
sentatives of the British people. I could

industry was introduced you might have
an improvement. I must confess that when

I was astounded at the small wages paid

If it is to be revived or even

of the people that the same wages should
he paid.
Now, with regard to the grant towards
tourist development, I think it is the
duty of the Government to assist tourist
development as much as they can, and in
that respect I believe they are justified.
in giving the amount they do. The fishing industry is a very important one.
It is in the interests of that industry that
the Government should come to their
assistance. There is no doubt about it
that in these coast towns in Down and
Antrim there is a large industry which
has not been properly developed. I do
not think the Government are really in
earnest in endeavouring to develop it.
Committees have been set up and their
reports have been issued, but even with
the very limited scope of that inquiry-I
believe they were curtailed in their
terms of reference they have made
recommendations. I do not think the
Government intend to act upon those recommendations, as the report stated that
at least two of the harbours, Killough and
Ardglass, were capable of development,
particularly Killough. That is a harbour
that can be made very suitable for fishing and for many other commercial
purposes.
It is admitted that it is a question of
money. I should have thought that the
Minister on this Vote would have told u
that the Government had decided to
develop Killough Harbour, and so assist
this fishing industry, which is not getting
the assistance or support that it really
warrants. We know there is a market for
fish in Northern Ireland, that the greater
part of the fish eaten is imported fish.
There is no reason why that should be.
I believe if the Government assisted the
fishermen on the coast of Down and made
proper accommodation for them a wonderful trade would develop there. That
would be of greater assistance to the
people engaged in that particular industry, and it would also be an immense
advantage generally to the people living
in the Six-county area. The Minister of
Commerce has told us that grants amounting to something like £2,000 have been
made to fishermen for nets and other
equipment. That is not a sufficiently
large sum for that purpose. It is really
infinitesimal in a big matter of that sort.
I believe the Ministry can also be
accused of harassing people who got loans.
under the old Fishery Department in
Dublin. These people got loans from
the old Department in Dublin for equipping their boats for fishing purposes
during the war, and in some instances
it was the sureties who had to pay. The
fishermen lost their boats. They were
torpedoed by the German submarines who
were operating in that particular place,
and the men lost their all. When this
Government came in and found those
loans were still outstanding, not only did
they follow these people, but when they
Supply-
Committee
25 APRIL 1928
found they had nothing to pay they followed the sureties and made them pay.
I do not know that they were not legally
right in doing that, but I think in cases
where the money was lost under such circumstances the sureties should not have
been followed for it.
On the whole I think the Ministry can
hardly claim much credit for what they
have done with regard to fishing and the
fishing industry. They have done nothing
with regard to Lough Neagh, but some
of the other Members who are more intinately acquainted with the matter can
ventilate it better than I can. I am sure
that while we all have a very great
respect for the Minister personally, we
think the Ministry has not been the
success it might have been. It may be
that they started operations during an
unfortunate period, a time of trade depression. To some extent that is so, but
even in that case I think they should
have made greater headway in many of
the things they were to do. They should
not have done some of the things they
have done. With regard to linen, if it
is going to be a failure I do not see why
they should spend thousands of pounds
on it. I think they should have
endeavoured to spend more of the money
of the Treasury for the purpose of assisting the fishing industry than they have
done. With these few remarks, I will
leave it to some other Member, if he
thinks fit, to move a reduction in the
Vote.

developed properly, I am convinced that

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
In regard to fisheries, I may say my
Ministry and myself are very greatly interested in the possibilities of the development of the fisheries round about our coast,
but on the other hand we really do have to
take into consideration just exactly whom
we are likely to help in anything we do.
The fishery at Ardglass is carried on by
far the greatest extent by Scottish fishermen who come over here. Unfortunately
it is not a staple industry that gives employment all the year round. These men
follow the course of the herrings round the
coasts of England, Scotland and Ireland,
so that they are only present at Ardglass
for a short period of the year. I am very
sorry that the people of Ardglass, to whom
one would say the development of fishing
would mean more than to any other port
in our Province, have not done more of
themselves to help the fishermen who come
to their port. For instance, the supply
of water is so inadequate there that the
trawlers are only able to get water for
ordinary domestic purposes on board. In
order to fill their boilers they nearly always
have to go to the Isle of Man.
With regard to Killough that, of
course, is a private harbour.
I agree
with everything said in regard to Killough. It has a marvellous position.
Supposing you do develop it what would
you do with it? You say it will make an
admirable port for cross-Channel steamers. No one has ever suggested any line
that would be likely to come to that port.

26 APRIL 1928
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 26th April, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
REPORT OF DR. MCDANIEL, M.D.,
CO. TYRONE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
what steps his Department propose to take
to improve the state of affairs revealed
by the report of Dr. McDaniel, Medical
Officer for the County of Tyrone.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked to
reply to this question.
Action on the report is primarily a
matter for the Regional Education Committees in the county; and these bodies
have already obtained treatment for a
number of children whose parents were
too poor to pay, and where the necessary
treatment could not be given by the
Dispensary Doctors or in the Union
Infirmaries.
Adequate arrangements have not yet
been made for ophthalmic or dental treatment, and I am in correspondence with
the Regional Committees on these
matters.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in that Report it is stated
that some of these complaints are due to
malnutrition, and is his Department
raising the matter with the county
councils to see to the feeding of school
children?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course,
the primary duty falls upon the Regional
Committee, and I have not the slightest
doubt that they will pay due attention to
all recommendations contained in that
Report.
Mr. KYLE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman give the House an assurance
that he on behalf of his Department will
send to the responsible Committees a
request that they should put into operation the matter of the feeding of necessitous school children?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I am not
prepared to dictate to the local councils.
Mr. KYLE: I am not asking you to
dictate to them. 1 am asking you to
send a letter requesting them to do it in
the interests of the children.
TAILORING TRADE IN BELFAST.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of out-workers engaged in the tailoring trade in Belfast; whether it is a fact
that a register of these workers is kept
by his Department; and whether he is
prepared to permit authorized trades
union officials to scrutinize this list, with
a view to assisting employers who do not
adopt the practice of giving out their
work to out-workers to compete with
those who do.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): A list of out-workers is not,
under Statute, required to be kept by
my Department. The onus is, however,
upon employers of out-workers in the
tailoring and certain other trades to do
so and to produce the lists to my inspectors when required.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell us where this list can be
seen? If the list is not kept by his Department, and his inspectors, as he
says, have the right to ask employers to
produce the list of out-workers, where
can the list be seen? Does he mean to
say that no register is kept of the outworkers in this trade?
Mr. ANDREWS: Each firm is responsible to keep a list of its out-workers,
and the list can be seen with the permission of the employer on his premises.
Mr. KYLE: Surely there is some
central registry where the number of outworkers is kept. That is the point I
want to emphasize. I thought the right

EX-SERVICE MEN IN WORK-
HOUSES.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Prime
Minister whether he can state the intentions of the Government with regard
to the large number of ex-Servicemen
who are inmates of various workhouses
in Northern Ireland, and many others
who are on the verge of starvation; and
whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce a Bill to give out-door
relief to these men in order to place them
in the same category as their comrades
in Great Britain.
I have been
Sir DAWSON BATES:
asked to reply to this question.
I am not aware that there is any apex-Servicemen in
preciable number of
the workhouses of Northern Ireland outside Belfast.
In Belfast, as the hon. Member is no
doubt aware, the Guardians have full
powers of granting outdoor relief to ablebodied persons who have need of it.
There is no special legislation in Great
Britain dealing with the conditions on
which ex-Servicemen may obtain outdoor relief, and it would be impossible
for the Government to introduce legislation differentiating as to the conditions
under which various classes of the community could obtain outdoor relief.
Mr. BEATTIE: The Minister is aware
that between 300 and 400 ex-Servicemen
are in the workhouses of Northern Ireland owing to the inattention of the local
authorities in their respective areas in not
applying for permission to bring into
operation Section 13. Owing to the
state of these men they had to be given
indoor relief. I would like to ask the
Minister is the same treatment not to be
meted out to Northern Ireland ex-Servicemen, who went out and fought for King
and country, as is given in Great Britain.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have already
pointed out that the legislation is practically the same as to the conditions under
which outdoor relief is given here and in
Great Britain.
Minister

Vote. The first matter which naturally

that the Vote itself shows a net decrease

it will be seen that the change that has

The Estimate shows evidence on
ing.
its face of several important changes in
Government administration in the current
year, and it so happens that all those administrative changes have arisen in connection with services which have in the
past been financed from the Ministry of
Finance Vote. Accordingly, it is only
proper that the present opportunity should
be taken of commenting upon the financial implications.
The first item that presents itself is
old-age pensions. Hon. Members are
aware that the transfer of the old-age
non-contributory pensions service to the
Ministry of Labour was effected as from
the beginning of the present financial
year, with the result that a large block of
expenditure which appeared under a subhead of last year's Estimate now disappears from this Estimate. The expenditure represented the cost of the Ministry's
agents, the Custom and Excise Authorities, and the Post Office, in administering
the old-age pensions service under an
agency agreement. This change is the
outcome, and indeed I may say, from a
husiness point of view, the only reasonable
outcome that might be expected when the
Ministry of Labour undertook the administration of the contributory pensions
service on the passing of the Widows',
Orphans' and Old Age Contributory Pensions Act, 1925. The administrative savings that will result from the co-ordination
of the two services-the contributory and
the non-contributory old-age pensions-

were referred to by me when the Old Age
Pensions Administraion Act of 1927 was
under consideration earlier in the current

Hon. Members will observe from the

In addition, a sum of £500
has been included for compassionate
gratuities to clerks of committees in hardship cases in accordance with the undertaking given by me at the time the Old
Age Pensions Act of 1927 was under consideration earlier in the Session
The next thing I refer to is the revenue
services. A second important change in
administration is to be found in the
arrangement whereby from the first of
the current month the Ministry of
Finance, assisted by the police authorities,
have undertaken the direct performance
of certain revenue services hitherto administered by the Customs and Excise
authorities under agency agreements,
that is the collection of entertainment
duty and the issue of gun and game
licences. Sub-head M in consequence
shows a considerable saving-something
like £4,000. I am quite confident that
savings will result from these changes,
and that more particularly in respect of
gun and game licences the co-operation of
the police authorities will have a beneficial
effect upon the revenue returns. It is
only fair to draw attention to the fact
that no provision is made for payment to
the Police Vote in respect of the services
thus to be rendered, but my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
will. I am sure, agree with me in saying
that the assumption by the police authorities of these, to them relatively trifling,
duties will not result in any augmentation
of the force. I should, perhaps, in this
connection say that although the police
will now take a more definite share in
this work they always in the past coonerated with the Customs and Excise
authorities in so far as opportunities for
Co-operation arose. The direct interation in matters of entertainment duty
is possible under the existing law, but not
in respect of gun and game licences, and
the necessary provision has been made in
a Bill now before Parliament.
These are the major changes which hon.
Members will observe from a perusal of
the No. 1 Estimate for my Department,
and it is fitting that I should make some
observations, in passing, on the trend of
policy which they indicate. Seven years
ago, when we were first called upon to
undertake the Government of this Province, we had not the staff, nor, if I may
say so, the experience necessary to enable
us to administer several Services which
required almost specialized staffs operating not at headquarters, but over the
whole of the country. It was, therefore,
convenient, indeed, I should say
it
was necessary in the best interests of the
Province, that we should request the Imperial Authorities to continue their administration, and they, for their part,
very readily agreed to facilitate us, as
they have done from first to last.
I do not think that I have on any
previous occasion publicly acknowledged
our indebtedness to the Imperial Authorities for the services they have rendered in
respect of these details of administration.
To this extent, at least, I am afraid that
I have been guilty of a sin of omission, as
it is no reflection on the officers of my Department to say how greatly we would
have been handicapped had we been obliged
suddenly and without due notice to take
over as a going concern services such as,
for instance, the Old Age Pensions
service. Not only have the Imperial
Authorities carried out these various
duties on our behalf, but their work has
throughout been characterized by that
efficiency which we all expect from British
administration.
During the last few years legislation
passed by our Parliament has made it
more and more necessary for the work
involved by a number of other Government activities to be performed locally,
that is to say throughout the country,
and this, in turn, made it increasingly
evident that the time was rapidly approaching when we should ourselves
undertake the responsibility of administering at any rate some of the services
which were being carried on by Imperial
Departments under agency agreements.
We purpose, however, to continue to take

I would like, however, to refer to the staffing of the Works Division, as this is a
subject which generally invites criticism
and more generally, perhaps, criticism
from hon. Members opposite, possibly
from a lack of appreciation of the volume
and the varied nature of their activities.
a
The division falls naturally into two
main sections-the architectural and the
engineering sides-although to a considerable extent these two sub-divisions dovetail into one another in carrying out any
The architects' division, in
special work.
particular, is, of course, responsible for
the care and maintenance of all the Government buildings scattered throughout
our area, in addition to the work which it
is called upon to do in regard to new
works, alterations, and purchases.
The engineering side, on the other
hand, is also called upon in connection
with the work on existing or proposed
buildings; but, in addition, it is responsible for the ordinary maintenance of
royal harbours and, furthermore, has had
heavy demands made upon it during the
last year in connection with advisory and
inspection work concerning other harbours. As hon. Members will know,
the Government have had under careful
consideration for some time various questions affecting harbours, and it has been
necessary for the engineering staff to
make an exhaustive survey of the condition in, I think, practically every harbour
around our coast, in order that provision
may be made for making them serviceable
for the work they were intended to carry
on. This has taken place at practically
every harbour round our coast, involving
an extraordinary amount of work, as can
be well understood.
Other very heavy work has fallen on the
engineering staff as a result of the Government's proposal for the drainage of
the Bann basin and the area round Lough
Erne. In each case it has been necessary
to have detailed surveys carried out, as
the Government could not embark on any
scheme of the magnitude of that involved
in the drainage of the Bann without the
fullest possible technical investigation
having been carried out in advance.
Apart from the important works at Stranmillis, where our large training college
with its various adjuncts is being built in
furtherance of the Government's education policy, many demands have been
made upon the works branch in connection
with the building programmes of local
education authorities, in the building of
new schools and such like all over the
Province, and I am glad to say that the
branch has been able to assist local
authorities to a great extent in erecting
the most suitable type of buildings for
their purposes.
There is also a very extensive prcigramme which the Government have in
operation involving an immense amount
of technical service and advice, that is to
say, the construction and reconstruction
of police barracks over the entire Province. These barracks, as we all recall,
and as has been reported from time to time,
were left to us in a most deplorable condi..
tion. Therefore, it has been necessary, at
vast expense to the taxpayers of Northern
Ireland, not only to build new barracks,
but to recondition many barracks already
existing, which were in the condition I
have described. Exetnsive additions and
alterations have also been found necessary
to the Belfast Prison and to the Malone

Training College. All this has involved
an immense amount of work on the part

But the work of the Department is not

now, I think, been saved from collapse, and it is a great tribute indeed to

The second item I mentioned was Ulster

where, of course, the amount of money is

hring before the people of the country
the advantages from the point of view of
thrift of this very important work. The
entire cost of administration in our case,
including salaries, advertising, cost of
sales by the Post Office, the commission

At our headquarters we gave a retaining fee to Sir Ernest Clark as part-time
Financial Adviser, as he is described.
That has been given up-to my regret in
one sense-at his own request. It is only
Occasionally that I have an opportunity

for the immense services rendered to
Ulster by that distinguished man, to
whom we owe so much.

Mr. POLLOCK: Sir Ernest Clark, I

labour of love, because of his pride in this
little Province of Ulster, which he served

Civil Service establishment he was so
largely responsible. I think it only right
to mention that matter, although it is not
one of very great importance in respect of
our Estimates. His retaining fee was
250 guineas, and that has now ceased.
As regards the Establishment Division

matters; that is, in regard to the matters

With a view to providing more work

The PRIME MINISTER: I would not
have intervened in the debate to-day at

unjust criticism of the salaries of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister, and of

Committee to know that when our new
organization was established, and when
a special Committee of this House was set
up to go into all these matters, the question arose as to whether hon. Members
in this Committee would realize, or could
be got to realize, what had been the
old traditional custom in the Imperial
Parliament, and, in fact, in all Parliaments throughout the world. As I have
said before, I never heard of such criticisms-I may say unfair, nagging, and
discourteous criticisms-as have been
made with regard to the salaries of my
right hon. Friends, being made at any
time in the Imperial House.
Mr. BEATTIE: Because they were
agreed to by both sides of the House.
The PRIME MINISTER: The suggestion was seriously thrown out that if that
old custom was not properly observed in
this new House, steps would have to be
taken, after the decision of the Committee
had been given, to place the salaries upon
the Consolidated Fund. For seven years
now I have hesitated to take a step of
the kind, but if I do not take a step of
of that kind, I am relying upon hon.
Members in this Committee to adopt the
customs of the Imperial Parliament,
where the salaries are placed on the forefront of all the Estimates, for the purpose
of giving hon. Members an opportunity of
criticising the policy generally of the
Government, or of the Department under
review, of knowing whether certain numbers of staff were necessary, and of inquiring generally into the working of the
Department.
It is only right that some understanding on this subject should be reached by
the Committee. I am perfectly frank
when I say that, in my own opinion, it
does not add to the dignity of the Committee, or to the good of the country

hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock), spend their

man dear.

on
the recommendation of that Committee the salaries were accordingly
fixed. That was before there was

when all belonged to the one party. Notwithstanding that they all belonged to the
one party there was considerable controversy in the House with regard to this
matter. Many Members of your own
party objected to these salaries, in fact,

I would not have risen now to intervene but for the, in my opinion, scandalous threat of the Prime Minister. I
do not think Cabinet Ministers are too
well paid at all. I think if a man occupies that position he ought to be well
paid, but just as he is entitled to be well
paid so Members of this House have a
right to say he receives too much if they
like. To take away that power would be
to take out of Parliament the very breath
that gives it life. To threaten to destroy
almost the last remnant of power
minority in opposition here has is less
disastrous to the Opposition than it is to
the permanent existence of this Parliament itself before the people of Ulster.
So far as I am concerned I felt it my
duty to enter that protest.

Three night watchmen, ex-Servicemen,

would like the right hon. Gentleman to

With regard to one particular charge,

Department, £4,561; I find the Parliamentary Counsel, £1,150; I find Parttime Assistant to Parliamentary Counsel,

have heard of the seven plagues of Egypt,

of Northern Ireland. If I may paraphrase a very old poem, I will say
Lawyers to right of them,
Lawyers to left of them,
And the North blundered.
I suppose it is the old case of the seven
lawyers coming in and bringing in seven
other lawyers more wicked than themselves. Wherever you find a lawyer in this

other Estimates, constitutes a scandal.
The people up and down the country in the

Gentleman, the Minister of Finance,

I come to my hon. Friend the Member

at this

which is one of the most comprehensive
and far-reaching ever presented to any

its effects will be very far-reaching not

I would like to thank the Leader of the

fair and perfectly straight-forward

He spoke of the appeals for subscriptions
now so general, and how these appeals
could be checked in the public interest,

in regard to the subscriptions. I suggest
that there is one organization, to which
he referred, that is the Charity Organization Society. If members of the community could realize that this very
important charitable body operates to
examine into the value and soundness of
every application that is made for charitable relief—if, as I say, information were
asked from that body it would, perhaps,
save the pockets of a great many people
who may unfortunately subscribe money
for undesirable objects.
The Charity Commissioners whom he
touched upon deal, of course, with all
questions of public subscriptions that come
under their notice. As a matter of fact
under the Government of Ireland Act I
am the Charity Commissioner. Obviously
I could not undertake such important work
as the determination and distribution of
charities left generally by the bequests of
deceased persons. Therefore, shortly after
the transfer to our authority here I organised a Committee, with the then Lord
Chief Justice, the Right Hon. Denis
Henry, whom, unfortunately, we have
lost, as chairman, and eleven members
representing four religious denominations.
Hon. Members will realise that the great
bulk of these charities come from deceased
persons' assets, and many of these are devoted to church or denominational objects.
Therefore, in order that there should be
no allegation that any particular body was
unfairly treated, I appointed three from
the Catholic Church, three from the Presbyterian Church, three from the Church
of Ireland, and two from the Methodist
Church, the latter being the smallest in
numbers. That body undertakes by
statute through me the allocation of all
matters relating to charity. I think that
should satisfy the hon. Member in regard
to that matter.

probably it would be a better description

this is, because all the Bills that come before this House must pass through his
hands. They must be actually drafted

The consequence is that legal men have to
be brought in from time to time to assist

The Parliamentary Draughtsman, whose

WEARING OF FREE STATE
COLOURS.
4. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is regarded as
an offence against the law to wear the tricolour, the emblem of An Saorstat, in
Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, it is not
an offence against the law in Northern
Ireland to wear or display the colours of
the Irish Free State.
any
At the same time, in the case where
an organization definitely identified with
the Republican movement, or
illegal organization, adopts and openly
displays in the furtherance of, and in
connection with, its activities any emblem
or combination of colours, and where
such display is likely to be prejudicial to
the maintenance of the peace and preservation of order, it is the duty of the
Government to prevent such display,
even where the colours of the emblems so
adopted and displayed happen to coincide with those of a neighbouring State.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
answer, does the right hon. Gentleman
know that practically all countries recognized the tri-colour on the recent flight
of that brave and adventurous Irishman,
Major Fitzmaurice, and that this is the
only assembly I know of that did not even
send a word of congratulation to him?
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise
on this question. That is a question
about the Atlantic flight.
Mr. DEVLIN: Do I understand the
right hon. Gentleman has given orders
that, on mere suspicion, a man can be
arrested for wearing these colours, because they are supposed to be the colours
of an organization of which he may not.
be a member?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. The
position is, that if any individual does
any act which is likely to lead to a breach
of the peace, the Government should,
and will, take action.
Mr. DEVLIN: What proof had the
right hon. Gentleman that these men
were engaged in anything of the kind?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The most
ample proof.
Mr. DEVLIN: What is the proof?
Can the right hon. Gentleman say why
these men were not brought before any
tribunal and tried if they had committed
any offence? I will come into this House
to-morrow wearing one of these badges.
(Laughter.)
SALE OF ILLICIT SPIRIT-
NUMBER OF PROSECUTIONS.
5. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of prosecutions in Northern Ireland in connection with the manufacture
or sale of illicit spirits, also the average
fine imposed, and the number of such
cases in which imprisonment was imposed,
during the three years ending 31st
March, 1926, 1927 and 1928; whether
any conviction has been obtained against
retail-licence holders during the same
periods for these offences, and if there is
any co-operation between the Government
of Northern Ireland and the Free State
Government to prevent the importation
of illicit spirits into their respective
areas.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number of
prosecutions in Northern Ireland in
connection with the manufacture or sale
of illicit spirits during the year ending
31st March, 1926, was 39. The average
fine imposed was £22 5s Od. The number of cases in which imprisonment was
imposed was 7.
During the year ending 31st March,
1927, there were 47 similar prosecutions,
the average fine imposed being £18
14s Od. In 19 cases imprisonment was
imposed.
For the year ending 31st March, 1928,
the number of prosecutions was 18, the
average fine £16 18s Od, and the number
of cases in which imprisonment was imposed was 3.
During the three years previous to the
31st March, 1928, no conviction was obtained against any retail licence holder
for the manufacture or sale of illici'
spirits.
As regards the latter portion of the
question, I may say that in this, as in
other matters, the closest co-operation
exists between the R.U.C. and the Civic
Guard, and it is understood that the
Customs Authorities on both sides of the
Border also act in close co-operation.

MARKETING OF NORTHERN IRE-
LAND PRODUCE.
7. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he can state the
amount of the grant which the Empire
Marketing Board has offered for investigation into the marketing of Northern
Ireland produce; whether he can give the
names of the Committee he proposes to
set up; whether this is supplemental to
the Departmental Committee's report on
transit and marketing; and whether he
intends to take any steps to carry out the
recommendations of this Commission.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Mr. Archdale); The Empire
Marketing Board has made a grant of
£900 per annum for a period of three
years to enable my Ministry to appoint
a Marketing Investigator, with suitable
assistance, to inquire into the conditions of
the marketing of agricultural produce.
The inquiry will in particular be addressed to the complicated methods by
which the produce of the typical small
farmer of Northern Ireland is at present
marketed, and also to the quality, packing, and grading of the agricultural commodities exported through Belfast and
Londonderry, and the conditions of transport of live stock and other produce
shipped to Great Britain. It is not proposed to set up a Committee in connection
with the inquiry and no appointments
have so far been made. The investigations conducted will be additional to
the normal activities of my Department,
and will not be directly related to the
work of the recent Committee on the
Transit, Prices and Marketing of Agricultural Produce, although the report of
that Committee will, doubtless, prove of
value in deciding upon the scheme of inquiry to be pursued.
Action has already been taken with a
view to implement certain of the recommendations of the Departmental Com-

Education Associations Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION
(Mr. Robb): This is a small Bill, and its
purpose is to provide local authorities
with power for the payment of the expenses of education authorities and education committees in subscribing to the
Association of Education Authorities,
and for the payment of members or
officers of this Association in attending
meetings or conferences in conection
1167 Education Associations Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Robb]
therewith. After the constitution of the
education authorities and regional committees an Association of Education
Authorities in Northern was formed, with
the full consent and approbation of the
Government, because they found it very
useful that members of the Association
should have the opportunity of discussing
their problems amongst themselves, and
the Ministry also found it useful that
they should have one body with whom
they could deal when any question arose
between them and the education
authorities.
After the Association had been constituted, the Auditor-General pointed
out that there was, in fact, no statutory
authority for the payment of the subscription of the education authorities to
this Association or of the expenses that
they would incur in attending meetings,
and it is to meet that difficulty that this
Bill has been introduced. That is all
that it does. There is ample precedent
here. The county councils, as such, have
these powers by special Act of Parliament. The rural district councils, as
such, have similar powers, and it is considered advisable that the education
authorities should have the same powers.
These powers are needed by Act of Parliament, and this Bill is introduced in
order to give those powers.
Mr. MCALLISTER: Of whom is this
Association constituted?
Mr. ROBB: The members of the
Association are the education authorities
and the regional education committees.
These committees pay a small subscription
of, I think, two guineas a year for the
general working expenses of the Association. The members come to Belfast, or
some other centre, when any pressing
question for their consideration arises.
The Bill enables the education authorities to pay such expenses as the Ministry
may consider reasonable for the attendance of the officials or members at such
meetings. We have already found it
very useful when questions have arisen,
and we want to deal, not with one or two,
but the regional committees as a whole,
on problems that concern them all.

Fisheries Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
