Mr. BARBOUR: The Bill to which I
now ask the House to give a Second
reading is designed to extend and amend
the provisions of the Fisheries (Ireland)
Acts in their application to Northern
Ireland, and, by more effective regulation, to improve the stocks of fish in
Northern Irish waters, with consequent
benefit both to the wealth of the Province
generally, and to those following the calling of fishermen.
Northern Ireland is fortunate in possessing valuable inland and sea fisheries.
The salmon fisheries of the Rivers Foyle
and Bann have long been famous both as
regards the quality and the quantity of
their fish. The Lough Neagh eel fishery
is generally regarded as the most important of its kind in Europe, while the
stocks of trout and other popular inland
fish either furnish a means of livlihood to
a considerable number of fishermen or attract anglers from many parts of Great
Britain. Our sea fisheries are also valuable, considerable quantities of salmon
being caught annually off our shores, in
addition to the great catches of herring
taken each summer off the County Down
coast.
It is obvious that the conservation of
all these valuable assets constitutes a duty
which no responsible Government would
be justified in neglecting. Certainly, the
history of the Irish fisheries during the
past 80 years bears ample proof that each
successive British Government has turned
its attention in the most earnest fashion
to preserving and developing this national
asset. Only by such action has it been
possible to maintain the stocks of fish in
our rivers and around our coasts, since the
indiscriminate exploitation of any fishery,
however valuable, inevitably leads to
serious depletion and, if indefinitely continued, to practical extinction.
There are in existence some 52 Irish
Fishery Acts, starting with that of the
year 1842.
The last-mentioned Act,
which still forms the main foundation of
our fishery laws, represents a great effort
on the part of the Government of the
day to regulate salmon fishing in Ireland
in such a way as would permit of the
stocks increasing and, at the same time,
allow of the discriminate exploitation of
our salmon fisheries. With growing experience, successive Governments found it
necessary to amend the 1842 Act, always
with a view of conserving and developing
the stock for the benefit of the users and
of those who should follow. As, by the
nature of the case was inevitable, some
of the restrictions imposed by these subsequent amending Acts proved unpopular
amongst fishermen at the time, and agitation for their repeal, or modification in
certain respects, has been a feature in
the history of Irish fishery legislation
even down to the present time.
To any person who applies himself to
the study of the subject, however, the
necessity for maintaining the restrictions
imposed by these various statutes is a
matter in which no reasonable doubt can
be entertained. Some of the restrictions
to which I refer were introduced after the
Fisheries Bill-
Second Reading
1 ΜΔΥ 1928
most exhaustive inquiries, and were imposed as the only practical remedy of a
state of affairs which, if left unchecked,
would ultimately have resulted in the most
serious depletion of our fishery stocks.
For example, the Act of 1863 restricted
the use of bag nets at the mouths or
estuaries of Irish rivers, and in some cases
substituted permission to use only nets of
other types.
I have been approached by representatives of our sea fishermen to promote
legislation designed to undo the effects of
the 1863 Measure, but, in the interests of
all concerned, I have felt myself unable
to entertain such a proposal.
Nothing
can be more mistaken in my view than to
suppose that it will benefit anyone interested in fishing to permit full unfettered
enjoyment of the fisheries without regard
to the conservation of the stocks. The
withdrawal of the 1863 Act restrictions
would inevitably lead to the return of the
serious conditions which the 1863 Act was
specifically designed to remedy, and in a
few years time the Government would be
faced with exactly the same problem as
that with which the Government
faced in 1863.
was
was
A problem of similar character has, in
fact, arisen in the case of our Lough
Neagh eel fishery. Here we have a
fishery offering very great possibilities in
the way of development, but one which
shows a marked decline in the quantities
of mature fish caught each year. The
statutory inquiry held last winter showed,
I think beyond all reasonable doubt, that
this unsatisfactory state of affairs
mainly, if not entirely, due to the
inability of guarding against the capture
of small immature eels by the methods
of fishing at present in use. The cumulative effects of this for a number of years
inevitably showed themselves in a very
striking decrease in the quantities of the
mature eels taken at the weirs at Toome
and Kilrea. Where, as in our own case,
the physical configuration permits the
eels to be captured at a weir, any other
method, however employed, must always
be relatively uneconomic.
Eels enter our rivers as elvers, making
their way, it is believed, from the other
side of the Atlantic. Working their way
up the river they spend from 6 to 8 years
on their feeding grounds which, in the
case of the Bann, are provided by Lough
Neagh. On reaching maturity the eel
ceases feeding, and, according to scientific
opinion migrates to the same waters from
when it originally came. It is apparent,
therefore, that the most economical
method of capture is by means of nets at
the weirs where only the mature-migrating eels will be caught. The great
increase in the use of long lines by the
Lough Neagh fishermen since eels became
such a marketable commodity in England,
about the year 1914, has inevitably prevented great numbers of eels from ever
reaching maturity, as such lines, being
hooked and baited, cannot be made selective in the matter of the weight of eel
which they take.
The inquiry to which I have referred
showed that whereas the average weight
of a mature eel was in the region of 20
ozs. the average weight of a catch of eels
by long line was approximately between
4 and 5 ozs. It can require very little
foresight to foretell the effects of the continuance of the unrestricted use of long
lines throughout the whole of the year,
or as much of it as weather conditions
permit, in the manner practised by the
fishermen.
The Bill has been prepared after consultation between my Ministry and
representatives of fishery interests, and
most of the provisions contained in it
have received the approval, either in
principle or in detail, of those interests.
Whilst the intentions underlying the
various sections of the Bill are, I think,
sufficiently evident from the text of the
Bill itself, I propose, for the convenience
of the House, to take the different parts
of the Bill seriatim and to deal briefly
with the several provisions of each.
to
Part I of the Bill concerns the election
and membership of Boards of Comservators. As hon. Members are doubtless aware, the executive administration
of fishery matters in Northern Ireland is
a large extent entrusted to four
Boards of Conservators consisting of
members elected by the licence-holders in
each of the four districts, together with
a certain number of persons qualified to
act ex-officio. As the law at present
stands, each of these Boards holds office
for a period of three years, at the end of
which a new Board is constituted by way
of election in the manner provided by the
Acts. The restriction of the life of the
Board to a period of three years militates
against continuity of policy, and against
the fulfilment of any extended programme
of development which a Board might be
disposed to undertake.
Fisheries Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
In order to remove this difficulty the
present Bill extends the life of the
several Boards to a period of five years,
the commencing date for the first quinquennial period being fixed as 7th
December, 1930, in order to allow of the
elections under the new arrangement
being held simultaneously in each of the
four districts. The remainder of Part I
of the Bill is designed to remove a minor
difficulty which has arisen out of what
was apparently an oversight in one of the
earlier Acts, viz., the omission of any
provision for the resignation of a member
of a Board who either finds himself incapacited from acting, or is unwilling for
some reason to continue to act, as a Conservator. The Bill, accordingly, provides
for the resignation of a member in such
circumstances, and for the filling of the
vacancy so occasioned by the co-option
of a substitute by the remaining members
of the Board.
Part II of the Bill places certain restrictions on the sale, purchase, capture
and transit of salmon, trout and eels.
The provisions in the existing Acts relating to the illegal capture of salmon and
trout are numerous and stringent, but
their enforcement has been found by experience to be exceedingly difficult where,
as is frequently the case, the fish have
been removed from the place of capture
and cannot be definitely traced to a particular offender. The same difficulty, especially in regard to fish captured during
the close season, has been experienced in
Great Britain, and certain general restrictions upon the possession of salmon and
trout at certain seasons of the year were,
accordingly, enacted by the Imperial
Parliament in 1921. Legislation to the
same end, but on a much more extended
scale, was passed by the Irish Free State
legislature in 1925, the conditions of fisheries in which country are, as hon.
Members will readily understand, almost
identical with those obtaining in Northern
Ireland. Sections 4-9 of the present Bill
follow very closely the provisions embodied in the Irish Free State Measure
to which I have referred.
On one point, however, the present
Measure is more extensive in its application, that is to say, in the case of eels.
Hon. Members may recollect that at the
instance of the Coleraine and Enniskillen
Boards of Conservators I caused a public
inquiry to be held in October last into
the present conditions of eel fishing in
Northern Ireland. The evidence obtained at that inquiry, the Report of
which was made public some time ago,
showed clearly that, if the valuable eel
fisheries of Northern Ireland were to be
preserved and developed in a proper
manner, more effective control of the
capture and possession of eels was essential. Section 10 of the Bill is, accordingly, designed to provide such control.
In passing, it may be well to mention
here that the limitation of the weight of
the eel that may legally be taken in
Northern Irish waters to 8 ounces follows,
in principle, the limitation already existing in the Pollen Fisheries Act of 1891
on the size of pollen that may be captured
in Lough Neagh.

In Part III of the Bill it will be observed that certain alterations have been
made in the rate of licence duty chargeable on different fishing engines.
proposed increase from £1 to £2 in the
rate on single salmon rods has received
the approval of the Ministry's Fisheries
Advisory Committee, a body which may
fairly be regarded as representing all the
principal fishery interests in our
area.
The increase is designed principally to
produce much-needed additional revenue
to the Boards of Conservators and, at a
later date, may also facilitate the making
of some reciprocal arrangements with the
Fishery Authorities in the Irish Free
State whereby licensees in one country
might be allowed certain concessions from
the licence issuing authorities in the other
country during the course of a visit.
Special provision to meet the case of
visiting anglers who desire to fish for only
a short period has been made in Sub-
Section (3) of Section 2, by permitting
Boards of Conservators to issue 14 day
licences at the old rate of £1. No such
provision formerly existed and visiting
anglers were, accordingly, obliged to pay
a full year's licence duty irrespective of
the length of their stay.
The increase of duty on salmon drift
nets from £3 to £6 is based on the recognition of two factors: (1) the great increase in the length of salmon drift nets
habitually used now as compared with
their length when the duty was first imposed, and (2) the catching power of drift
nets as now used being so great as to
render the contribution made by their
users towards the cost of the preservation
of salmon stocks disproportionately small

in comparison with the contributions made

The inquiry into eel fishing called attention to the fact that a net for the
capture of eels was subject to a duty of £3
whilst exactly the same net, if stated to be
intended for the capture of pollen, was
subject to a duty of only £1 10s. Od. It
was obviously impossible to prevent abuses
in such circumstances, and the rate of £3
has, accordingly, been fixed in the Bill to
cover the use of draft nets in the capture
of pollen as well as of trout and eels.
vantage has been taken of this amendment to reduce the statutory maximum
duty on trammel nets to £1, this being the
duty charged in the Coleraine Conservancy
district, in which the majority of trammel net users reside. The fixation in Subsection (2) of Section 2 of the licence duty
for long lines for eels merely establishes
in the Coleraine and other conservancy
districts a duty already operative in the
Enniskillen district.
Section 12 is designed to remove an administrative anomaly. In the Fisheries
Act of 1848 provision was made for the
fixation by Boards of Conservators of a
licence duty on any fishing engine or device
of a kind in respect of which a rate of
duty had not previously been fixed. By
the wording of this Act. however, it was
apparently necessary, before the duty
could be fixed, for the person proposing to
use such an engine or device to make application for the fixation of a duty. Cases
have arisen where the necessary applications were not forthcoming and where,
accordingly, the Board has been precluded from fixing a duty. The present
Bill transfers the power of fixing duties
in such cases to the Ministry of Commerce,
and specifically eliminates the necessity
for any prior application on the part of
the prospective user.
I now pass to Part IV. of the Bill. Representations have from time to time been
made to me by those interested that the
powers of search and seizure at present
conferred upon water bailiffs, etc., are insufficient. Furthermore, the provisions.
included in Part II. of this Bill in regard
to the control of the sale and transit of
salmon, trout and eels, make essential the
extension of the powers of officers charged
with the enforcement of these provisions.
I should like at this stage to emphasize
that, although certain of the provisions
included in the Bill may seem to some
extent onerous or restrictive upon those
engaged in the capture and marketing of
fish, the experience of those concerned elsewhere has shown that they are essentially
practical, and that members of the fishing
industry who loyally co-operate in the
carrying out of the fishery laws, including
the new provisions, derive much more
benefit from any restrictions which may
be imposed than compensates for the extra
trouble to which they may be put. To
offenders against the fishery laws, however, the new provisions are intended to be
prohibitive. Upon such class of persons
hon. Members, I am sure, will not feel
disposed to waste any sympathy.
The provisions in Section 14 are of a
precautionary nature, and are intended to
preclude the appointment or continued employment by a Board of Conservators of
any person or persons either unsuitable or
insufficiently experienced for
for fishery
duties. I need hardly occupy the time of
the House in dealing in detail with
Sections 15, 16 and 18 of the Bill, which
concern purely administrative matters.
These Sections are designed to simplify

It
is believed that the substitution of the

curtails them.
I will deal with the system of election
of Conservators first. This Bill says that
they shall continue in office until the 7th
day of November, 1930. Frankly I
think they should be cancelled altogether
when it comes to that date, and a new
governing body set up to control the fisheries of Ulster. The Conservators are a
most undemocratic body. I wonder does
anyone here know of the manner in which
they are elected. Certain licences carry
so many votes. It is a very simple thing
for any Conservator or body of Conservators to issue as
many salmon rod
licences as they like in order that they
may select their own men, and so send
back their own body by an overwhelming
number of salmon rod licences. It 19
well known that that has been going on
in Northern Ireland for many years, and
it is necessary that some steps should be
taken to have that abuse remedied and
to secure the removal of a body which has
done nothing to remedy the position of
the fishermen, (especially outside fishermen, but only to further the interests of
the combines, which come over here to
draw huge profit out of the people of the

the Minister that a more democratic and

With regard to the question of electing a new member where one has fallen

The most important part of this Bill is
the effort that is made to place one company in complete control of the whole of
the fisheries of Ulster. Take the question
of eels in Lough Neagh. The fishermen,
who are having all the power
authority that they ever had taken from
them, are now to pay £2 for a licence,
which they never had to do before. Is it
fair to penalize men when they were able
to get a living out of this small industry?
At the bidding of a Board of Conservators
or of this great combine which controls
the Ulster fisheries, the Minister of Commerce penalizes them by putting on this
extra tax. These waters have for generations been fished free, and I think it is
most unfair to put a tax on these people
at a time when they are suffering from
acute distress in the carrying on of their
industry. Instead of their being penalized
something should be done to try to ease
the situation. That is what they expected. I understand a Commission sat
and made a report on the subject of the
fisheries. The Commission certainly gave
a decision against the fishermen and in
favour of the large interests.
Then in regard to the abolition of bag
nets and the substitution of draft nets,
draft nets are a most ineffective method
of catching salmon, one which was never
productive and which has died gradually
all round our coasts. The result is that
many who were engaged in it gave it up
and left the district. Round the coastal
towns and in the countryside many
fishermen were employed in bag net
fishing which was really a skilled method
of fishing, and these men have left the
district, and added further to the unemployment in the rural areas. There was
no justification for the removal of these
bag nets. They were removed at the
instance of the large fishing interests in
those days, that is the old landlords.
They managed by the power they had
in the British House of Commons to get
this Act passed. These men never interfered with the fish that were caught
in the open sea as they only went 400
yards from the shore, and the fish had
iniles and miles of open sea.
What about the river nets? What
about the nets that go from one side
to the other so that the salmon cannot
get up? The fish are bound to
get into the big nets of this huge
combine, and SO these nets are
actually implements reducing the number
of salmon coming to our coasts to-day.
The Government should in this Bill have
commenced to curtail the activities of
this particular body, as this deadly
machine is most destructive and will
really ruin the salmon industry in Ulster.
Ulster fishermen have been waiting
anxiously for some Bill, and now that
this Bill has been introduced many of
them who were supporters of the Government this morning will not support them
when the time of electioneering comes
round. I have great pleasure in the
interests of the fishing industry in
Northern Ireland in moving the rejection
of this Bill in its entirety.

and file of our magistrates do not administer the law with the severity with which
the law is intended to be administered.
That is my firm conviction. It has been
one of the weaknesses of our constituțion
that in our Petty Sessions Courts the administration of the law is so weak. I
welcome this Bill, and I hope that a subsequent Bill will be brought in dealing
with game.
As a matter of fact, at the
present moment partridges are nearly extinct in the country, while quail, which
used to be so plentiful forty years ago,
are now totally absent. That is due to
every Dick, Tom and Harry going about
shooting and destroying these birds, and
leaving not a single one to perpetuate its
species. I will vote for the Bill with
great pleasure.
Mr. COLLINS: I want to support the
rejection of this Bill, and to call the

provides that
From and after the commencement
of this section, and save as otherwise
expressly provided in this Part of this
Act, no person shall sell, expose for

salmon, trout, or eels (other than

Have the Government, in preparing this

at all, or had they only in their minds
big establishments, like Sawers, in the
city of Belfast.? This fish trade, all
through the Six Counties, is in the hands
of small men, what might be called oneman businesses, and here the Government
are. first of all, asking them to have a
licence to carry on a business, which is
only for one day in the week in most.
places, and in a certain season two days,
and where it is only an odd time they
handle a salmon at all. First of all, you'
expect them to be licensed, and then you
expect them to keep a register. Are you
going to put the fish shops into the same
position as the public-houses and the
buses, with flying squads of police going
down and inspecting books and the whole

shop? They must keep this register,
stating not only where the fish comes
from, but whom they sell it to. Did
ever anyone hear of such a thing? You
know the type of these men. As a rule,
many of them are not able to write their
names
Then, again, there is another Clause
here I think it is Clause 9—which says
From and after the commencement.
of this section every package containing salmon, trout, or eels in course of
transit in Northern Ireland, shall be

with the words "salmon and trout,'
or the word "salmon" or the word
""
trout. or the word “ eels," as the

thereto the name and address of the

"
Are you thinking of the men who own one
net and one boat. who will be sending
this fish down alone? How can they he
expected to mark, as the Minister of
Commerce expects them to do, every
package containing_salmon, trout, or eels
in this manner? It is quite right that

Sons should do this, but just imagine one
man coming ashore in his boat and rushing for a train or a lorry to get his fish
to market, having to put on all these

These licences hit the poor man. It is
the drift net man, who goes out to sea
at night and takes the risk of laying down
his nets. whose taxation you double to
£6, the man who is crying out for relief,
crying out for bread and you give him a

As regards this question of the magistrates, I think it has come to this, in
connection with all the legislation you are

or gentleman who is a magistrate has any
respect he will send you back your Commission, because you have deprived them
of power under every Act you have

Mr. BARBOUR: I wholeheartedly
support the principle of this Bill, but I
may say at once to hon. Members oppocite that I do not take up an adamant
position at all in the matter, and if any
Amendments are put down which would
meet with their approval, and which
would meet the object which all of us
have in view, I can promise to give them
careful consideration. We all realize that
this is a very valuable natural national asset. We are all greatly concerned about
the welfare of our fishermen, and we are
desirous to provide them with the means
of livelihood, and to make that livelihood
as lucrative as we possibly can. The
promoters of this Bill believe that the
best way of doing that is to ensure that
there is an established supply of fish for
them to catch. That is the aim and
object we have in view.
So far as licences, which have troubled
so many hon. Members on both sides of
the House, are concerned, there again we
must recollect that the Government does
not benefit one penny piece by virtue of
these licences. The money raised by
these licences is a means which is going
to be put into the hands of the Conservators to enforce the law, to protect the
spawning ground of the fish, and to provent poaching. That is the fund to
which licence duties are given.
So far as the drift net fishermen are
concerned, I am sure the Government will
have an open mind, but we must remember that the £3 which they contribute at
present, or the £6 that is suggested under
this Bill, is the only contribution they
make towards the preservation of the
spawning ground. As I say, this is a
matter on which I have an open mind as
to whether £6, or £3, or some intermediate sum, is the appropriate amount.
So far as salmon fishing is concerned, I
did not know that so many poor fishermen took out licences. I know that when
I was interested in salmon fishing I
found the cost ran into figures which
some wealthier men would hesitate to pay.
I thought that, to anyone who could

afford to pay, £1 or £2 would not be very
material. In any case, if the fish were
there, the fisherman would be better able
to pay £2 if he caught his salmon than
£1 if he did not catch his salmon.
As far as eel nets and drift nets are
concerned, great stress has been laid on
the fact that it has been proposed to increase the tax on pollen nets from £1 10s
to £3. Great capital has been made out
of the fact that this is an increase of 100
per cent.
How does that work out? I
think the great probability is that any
fisherman on Lough Neagh is quite as
willing to catch eel as he is to catch
pollen. He has to pay £3 for his old
drift net licence, and in future if he pays
£3 for his cel net he will be able to catch
hoth pollen and eels with it. Therefore,
he will be keeping within the law by the
payment of £3 for what used to cost him
£4 10s.
Mr. LEEKE: Eel and pollen do not
run simultaneously, and in this close season they will clash. Will the one licence
cover all?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes. That will be
£3 instead of £4 10s a year to keep within the law. Then as regards the resident
magistrates, unfortunately, in Northern
Ireland, as, in fact, over Ireland
generally, there is a great deal of sympathy with the poacher. The poacher,
instead of being looked upon as a man
who does a great deal of harm with very
little corresponding benefit to himself, is
looked upon rather as a sporting individual, and when he comes up before a
bench of magistrates it is, to my knowledge, the practice to regard poaching as
a venial offence. The law has recognized
that to such an extent that it has been
found necessary to impose a minimum
penalty. No sooner is that minimum
fine imposed than my right hon. Friend.
the Minister of Home Affairs, and I receive petitions signed by the actual magistrates who imposed that fine, representing the poacher who has been punished
as a most worthy individual who is nearly
always living in distressing circumstances,
and so there is every reason why the
minimum fine should be abrogated and
a moderate sum inserted. We felt it
would be much better to have a resident
magistrate who would not be so subject
to the solicitations of his friends, nor
have personal acquaintance with the

thought that they would be in a position

Turning now to the register that has

I do not think any Member of the House

I am sure we have the sympathy

how and where that fish has been taken.
It seems to me the proposals in the Act
provide the best means of ensuring that.
I can assure hon. Members that apart

I am sure hon. Members knew that Committee was sitting. They had every opportunity of drawing the attention of

It was largely on the findings of that
Committee that this Bill has been
drafted. In addition to that we have

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move, in page 2,
after line 16, to insert "(C) or in respect of
other than elected persons to the committee or authority."
I think this Amendment would go a
long way to meet the criticizms levelled
from these Benches yesterday against the
Bill. The Bill provides that any three
persons who are members of a regional
committee or education committee may be
appointed to attend a conference of associations, and their expenses will be paid
from the county council and public funds.
The purpose of my Amendment is that
none of these persons shall be co-opted
persons on the education authority, but
that they shall be elected persons. There
is a strong feeling in many of these committees, I understand, that people are coopted who have only a passing interest in
educational affairs. We ought to see that
the public should not be asked to pay
the expenses of such persons, who, instead, should seek election to the
authority under which the regional committee or authority sits.
It is for that purpose I move the proviso which has been read out to the Committee. I am sure it will be the sense
of the Committee that it is only right
and proper and fair that those persons
who seek the suffrage of the electors
should be the persons appointed by the
regional committee or education committee to attend these conferences. It is
obvious that such persons are the only
people who have the confidence of the
electors, in a democratic way, anyhow.
The co-opted persons may not have the
confidence of the electors at all.
Therefore, I think it is in the public interests
that when public money is being paid as
expenses it should go to the elected persons I have referred to.

After giving particulars of the
income from the revenue on spirits and
beer he stated:
The interesting feature of this return is the continued decrease in the
use of alcoholic liquors, and I propose
to dwell on that for a moment. If last
year's decrease stood alone I should
be inclined to connect it with the exceptional industrial disturbances, but
reference to past years discloses
a consistent and regular reduction in the use both of spirits
and beer. The trade attributes
this reduction to the heavy duties and
consequent high prices of stimulants,
but whether it arises from this cause or
from a natural change in the drinking
habits of our people must remain a
matter of speculation. The striking
fact, however, remains that the people
of Ulster have consumed less alcohol
during this year, as represented by the
very considerable sum of £270,000 of
duty.
If we translate this reduction in
duty into the cost over the counter, we
find that the total reduction in the expenditure of the people on alcoholic
drinks must have been at least £600,000
last year, and probably more.
In 1914 the consumption in Ulster was
three quarters of a gallon per head of
the population. Last year's return is
one-quarter of a gallon per head of
the population, that is to say, the
people of this Province are consuming
only one-third of the quantities used
in 1914.-(Official Report, vol. 8, col.
1316, 11th, May 1927).

Legitimacy Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): This Bill follows the
Act which came into force in England on 1st January, 1927, under the
title of the Legitimacy Act. As many
Members of this House are no doubt
aware, legitimacy by subsequent marriage
was a thing unknown to English law,
which always refused to accept the principle of legitimation by subsequent marriage, though that principle had been the
law of many civilized and Christian
countries from a very remote period and
had always been the law of Scotland,
where a child born out of wedlock is
legitimated as from the time of the
marriage of its parents. "Other times.
other manners' is a rule which I think
applies to this reform, and in this presumably more enlightened age people are
beginning to realize that though the sins
of the fathers are often visited on the
children to the third and fourth generation there are good and valid reasons why
our law should be reformed so that the
innocent should not suffer for the sins of
the guilty to a greater extent than is
absolutely necessary for the welfare of the
State and the preservation of morals and
virtue. This Bill is a step in that direction. It will to some extent remove the
social stigma attaching to those born out
of wedlock, and it will also remove to
some extent the very practical disabilities
attaching to bastardy in cases to which
the Bill applies.
I think hon. Members will agree that
the word "bastard" is one of the most
Legitimacy Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
cruel words in our language. This is due
to the way in which illegitimates have
been treated socially and legally during
the course of our legal history. It is
commonly used as an expression of contempt which is partly due, as I say, to
the strength of our social conventions and
partly to the legal disabilities which unfortunately follow to the issue. This Bill
on the contrary treats bastardy with compassion, and I think the House need have
little fear that unhallowed births which
are really deplorable will either increase
or decrease as a result of this Measure.
If hon. Members will take up the Bill
they will see that in Clause I children
who are born illegitimate become legitimated by the subsequent marriage of
their parents.
But Sub-clause 2 provides
that:
Nothing in this Act shall operate to
legitimate a person whose father or
mother was married to a third person
when the illegitimate person was born.
That is to say, children born of an adultrous union are not within the scope of
the Bill.
It
Clause 2 provides that persons claiming
that they became legitimate by the subsequent marriage of their parents may
take proceedings under the Legitimacy
Declaration (Ireland) Act, 1868, in the
courts to have that fact established.
is not necessary that these proceedings
should be taken, because legitimation
under the Bill will follow as a matter of
fact, and as a matter of course upon the
marriage of the parents without any declaration, but, of course, there must
always be cases where there will be a
dispute, especially where property and its
devolution depends upon the legitimating of the person claiming, and
consequently the Bill provides that in
those cases they may go to the court for
the purpose of having it determined.
Then in Clause 3 children legitimated
by the Bill are put on the same footing
as if born legitimate, with the exception
which is contained in Sub-clause 2 of
Clause 3 that their seniority in the family
depends upon the date of legitimation,
that is to say, a child born out of wedlock before the Bill is passed becomes
legitimated by the Bill, but he ranks for
seniority after the brothers and sisters
born in wedlock before the Bill, but in
priority to the brothers and sisters born
in wedlock after the Bill becomes law.
This is only to preserve the rights of
the children who are now legitimate as
against those children who are now ille
gitimate, though as regards brothers
and sisters born after the Bill it will
apply to all the family equally, and they
will take their ordinary seniority in the
family. The third Sub-clause of Clause
3 is a saving Clause excluding
legitimated child from taking property
settled with a dignity or title of honour
where the title or honour devolves on
some other person whether a brother or
sister or other person.

will follow as in the case of a legitimate
person. At present, as the House is probably aware, in the case of an illegitimate
child dying intestate the property passes
as bona vacantia to the Crown.

cases where children have been legitimated in Scotland who inherit property
either in Ireland or England. The legiti

macy which flows from the Scottish

That
upon the intestacy of each other.
is following out the Clause I have already
referred to which places them on the same
footing with reference to the property
of each other. Formerly when an illegitimate child died his property, as I said,
vested in the Crown. His mother or
any person dependent on him could only
acquire portion of that property by the
grace of the Crown and had no rights.
Now that has been abolished. If an
illegitimate child dies the property will
go to the mother. If the mother of an
illegitimate child dies her property will
go to the child.
That concludes the provisions of the
Bill with the exception of one or two
small saving Clauses which are really
immaterial. The Schedule to the Bill
provides that in cases where children are
legitimated under the Bill the Registrar-
General of Births and Deaths may, upon
proper evidence being produced to him,
change the original certification of birth
in order to show that the child is legitimate, so that where a child has been
legitimated by subsequent marriage he
will be able to produce a birth certificate
certified by the Registrar-General showing
that his parents were certain persons,
that he is legitimate according to the law
of the land as it will then apply. I think
this is a Bill which very few Members
of this House will take any exception to.
I beg to move.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): I have to move
the Second Reading of this Bill which is
really a lawyers' Bill. The first Clause
is a clause to extend the power of making
leases for schools which is given to trustees
and tenants for life under the Leases for
Schools (Ireland) Act, 1881. By that
Act power was given to these limited
owners to grant leases of land, which was
settled, not exceeding one acre in extent,
for a term up to 900 years at a nominal
rent for the purpose of erecting thereon
a school. Since the Education Act was
passed the titles of a great many schools
have been investigated for the purpose of
having the premises transferred to the
education authority, and it was found
that there were on plots of land schools
already erected which the education
authority were in the process of having
transferred to them, but it was also found
that the owners of the land were limited
owners within the meaning of that Act.
The Government was advised and the
education authorities were advised that
this Leases for Schools Act did not enable
limited owners of that sort to give a
lease or grant to an education authority
of a plot of ground which a school is already on, although it did give the power
to grant a plot of ground for the purpose
of putting a school there. It is to
remedy that defect that the first Clause
is proposed.
•
The second Clause is a different thing.
The Regional Educational Committee at
Armagh are desirous of building enlarged
schools in the city of Armagh, and in the
search for a site there they had great
difficulty in finding one, but eventually
it was suggested that an excellent site
was available upon part of the property
belonging to the Observatory there. The
Observatory has 20 acres of land, and the
governors were perfectly willing to grant
three acres of land to the Armagh
Regional Education Authority for the
purpose of building a school there. When
it was investigated it was found that
under the Act constituting these governors
they had no power to transfer these three
acres to the Education Authority for this
public purpose. Accordingly, Clause 2

handed over to the Government the question of providing accommodation within
reasonable distance of the school for the
principal instruction officer and the subordinate staff has been the subject of
careful examination. It is considered
most desirable that the staff should be
available on the premises at all times to
ensure efficient administration and consequent disciplinary control not only of
the inmates but of the staff as a whole.
The impossibility of obtaining suitable
housing accommodation for the married
staff, in this residential district anywhere
within reasonable distance of the school
has rendered imperative the erection of

grounds, where there is ample space

in but also for the accommodation of

in

Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. HEALY: I have given notice of
a matter I intend to raise on the Adjournment. I raise this matter entirely in the
public interest. On Easter Sunday morning eight men were arrested on the Falls
Road. The Minister of Home Affairs,
questioned on the matter in the House
yesterday, gave no specific reason why these
men were arrested, but indicated in a
general way in his reply that any individual who did any act likely to lead to a
breach of the peace would come within
the ban of the Home Office.
These men,
I understand, were walking peacefully
along a public street. They were not in
possession of any arms, and they were not
doing anything likely to lead to a breach
of the peace. Who, then, is to determine
when a citizen or citizens may safely and
peacefully proceed along the public street,
doing no harm to anyone.
As I understand it, the kernel of the trouble seems
to be that these men were wearing rosettes
or badges of a particular colour. We know
that there is peace in the Six Counties
to-day, peace in Ireland, and indeed peace
in the whole United Kingdom. There is,
therefore, the less reason for this arbitrary
exercise of power on the part of the Home
Office
I do not know whether that extraordinary Act called the Emergency Powers
Act is still on the Statute Book, but I remember that in 1922, when it was enacted,
we had the curious experience of finding
that the areas in the Six Counties that
were the most peaceful were exactly those
areas from which this House decided to
arrest the largest number of people. Places
where there was the most turmoil and
trouble were precisely those from which the
fewest persons were arrested. Who is to
be the judge as to when a person may be
subject to arrest? Is it to be the Home
Office or the learned Attorney-General, or
is it to be any policeman whom one may
meet in the street? It seems to me that if
the action of the Home Office is to be approved by this House any person wearing
a colour that is not acceptable to the
Government may find himself in the
Crumlin Road gaol before evening. There
is an Act on the Statute Book which protects all citizens. That is Magna Charta,
but so far as the people of one political
party in Northern Ireland are concerned
it might as well never have been placed
there. If any man proceeding peacefully
about his business-or, indeed, demonstrating if he so pleases, so long as he does it
in a peaceful way is to be subject to
arrest at the whim of the Home Office or
of a policeman, then I say that liberty
is gone out of the Six Counties altogether.
We on these benches are just as anxious to
preserve the peace of the Six Counties as
any right hon. Gentleman opposite, because we know perfectly well that when
any turmoil occurs it is we have to pay.
""
I have seen the Minister of Home
Affairs rise in his place here on occasions
and boast glibly that he had peace in the
Six Counties now. That is a cheap way
of describing the situation. You can
have peace in a graveyard and nobody
goes about boasting about it. The "Belfast News-Letter,' a Government organ,
to-day asks: "Why are the Nationalists
concerned about the arrest of Republicans? I answer,
because we are interested in preserving the public rights
of the people. You have no right to determine whether I shall be a Republican or whether I shall belong to any other

thrown into prison, and left there.
In this respect, I would like to direct
attention to what prevails in a neighbouring State, the Irish Free State.
There are quite a number of people who
live in the Free State who were

1. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary

AWARDING MERIT MARKS TO
TEACHERS
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education if he will state what precautions are
taken by the Ministry to ensure uniformity in the style and difficulty of
questions set in different schools, for the
purpose of awarding merit marks to
teachers.
Mr. ROBB: In order to secure uniformity in assigning efficiency ratings to
teachers in Public Elementary Schools,
the Ministry requires the concurrence of
a Senior Inspector in the first rating,
and in any alteration of rating proposed
by a Section Inspector. It also provides
for conferences and joint inspections and,
where necessary, for visits by the Chief
Inspector and Senior Chief Inspector.
As the questions set by Inspectors are
varied to suit the detailed syllabus
followed by the teacher and the capacity
of the pupils, it is not desirable that the
style of questions should be uniform.
3. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON
asked the Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry of Education whether, in
assigning merit marks to teachers at
general school inspections, the inspectors
Oral Answers

the school buildings, defects in their upkeep, maintenance of furniture and equipment, or for any defects in the fitness of

Mr. ROBB: The reply to the first and

REGULATION OF SALARIES
OF TEACHERS.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether his Ministry will issue clear
definitions of the Statutory Rules and
Orders regulating salaries of elementary
teachers; whether it is a fact that the
reports furnished by inspectors are occasionally contradictory regarding the
award of merit marks to each teacher
given on the various subjects examined.
Mr. ROBB: The regulations determining the salaries of teachers of Public
Elementary Schools are contained in
Statutory Rules and Orders of Northern
Ireland, 1925, No. 114, and are clearly
defined, although necessarily somewhat
complicated.
The Ministry is not aware that any
contradictory reports have been furnished,
but on rare occasions differences are
observed. If these differences affect the
teacher's rating, steps are taken to determine which estimate is correct.
GRANTING OF DEPENDANTS'
BENEFIT.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that, despite the passing of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, and his public declaration
that the means test has been abolished, a
number of workpeople are being denied
dependants' benefit; whether he can
issue a statement to the effect that
workers having thirty stamps to their
credit during the two years preceding the
date of their claim, or having eight
stamps during the last two years, or
thirty stamps at any time, and are
genuinely seeking work will be granted
unemployment insurance.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The condition known as the
"family income test" has been abolished.
To become entitled to dependants' benefit, a claimant must satisfy the conditions
laid down in the Act of 1928, which have
no relation to the means of the family,
except in so far as the question arises as
to whether a dependant is, in fact, being
maintained by the applicant.
As regards the second part of the
question, an applicant who has thirty
contributions in the two years preceding
the date of his claim, and who is seeking
work will receive benefit if he complies
with the other Statutory conditions and
is free from disqualification. The "30
contributions" condition is, during the
transitional period, waived in the case of
a claimant over 18 years of age who, in
addition to having either 8 contributions
in the preceding two years, or 30 contributions at any time, proves that he is
normally in insurable employment, and
that he has had a reasonable period of
insurable employment during the two
years preceding the date of his claim.

LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been

The Government has already provided
a supply of drinking water at Ardglass
Harbour, and I would draw the attention of the Hon. Member to the fact that
in the Estimates of my Ministry for the
year 1928-29, is included a sum of £600
for the provision of a water supply for
boiler purposes at the harbour.
I have delayed taking action towards
the provision of a supply of boiler water
in view of the fact that for some time
past my Ministry has been in communication with the Rural District Council
and representative residents of Ardglass,
who have been endeavouring to arrange
a comprehensive water scheme for their
town. The position at the moment is,
that the Rural District Council has carried through certain boring operations,
while the taxpayers of Ardglass are considering the extent to which they may be
able to contribute towards the cost of a
scheme undertaken by the local authority.
The hon. Member will readily appreciate
that it would be preferable for the Government to contribute towards the cost of
a comprehensive scheme of water supply
rather than to proceed immediately with
the provision of an independent supply
designed solely to meet the requirements
of fishing vessels using the harbour.

At the end of 1927, Mr.

we cannot express too much gratitude.
He won the esteem and regard, not only

This year the Committee is being asked
to vote for education £29,205 more than
last year, the total amount of the Estimates being £1,895,734. The decrease of
£1,875 in the Vote is due, principally,
to a reorganization of the staff of the

The increase of £31,080 in Vote 2
arises mainly under three Sub-heads. The
the largest increase is in Sub-head F,
under which it has been necessary to provide £25,000 more than last year for
grants to local education authorities under Section 76 of the Education Act.
The Estimates of all the Education Committees for the current financial year
amount to about £271,000, of which about
£250,000 would rank for the grant-in

Judging, however, from the experience of the three preceding years it is
considered unlikely that the total expenditure ranking from the grant will exceed £232,500, in respect of which the
State liability would be about £155,000the figure appearing in the Estmates.
Another large increase in Vote 2 arises

Grant was about 400 more than had been

The returns received from the schools

I may also explain that the decrease

The transfer of schools has proceeded
steadily during the year. there are now
75 transferred schools in Belfast, and 27
in process of transfer, while outside Belfast 107 schools have been transferred,
and 154 are in process of transfer. Thus
423- -over 21 per cent of our 1,948
public elementary schools have either
been transferred or are in course of
transfer.
If the Committee will compare these
figures of transferred schools with those
published a year ago, it will see that very
considerable progress has been made. At
that time the number of schools in which
the transfers were completed was about
90, against 242 to-day, and the number of
four-and-two comunittee schools has increased from 80. to 100. There are,
moreover, some 181 schools at the moment
in process of transfer, and I submit to
the Committee that it is a most encouraging sign to find that negotiations for the
transfer of schools are still proceeding
regularly as a continuous process throughout the Province, and that there is
steady progression in the working-out of
the policy of the Education Act in respect of this important matter.
a
I should remind the Committee that
there is great freedom under the Act in
regard to transfer. Its provisions contemplate the existence side by side of
schools under three different forms of
management, that is to say, the provided
and fully transferred school, under the
complete control of the education authority; the voluntary school, under the socalled four-and-two committee, on which
the education authority has representation; and the voluntary school, under the
individual manager. There is no compulsion as to transfer except that compulsion which arises from the natural
desire, where the circumstances make it
expedient, to secure through transfer
better educational conditions for the
children
We know that, so far, the schools
managed by the Roman Catholic clergy
have not been offered for transfer, and,
whatever their motives may be, there is
no reason why we should quarrel with
them about it. The Act was framed, not
for one portion of the community but for
all, and we are satisfied that it has been,
and will be even in still greater measure
in the future, the means of enormous
improvement in the educational conditions of all classes of children.
In estimating the progress of transfers
we are warranted in omitting from the
total number of schools those which are
under Roman Catholic clerical management as not likely to be offered for
transfer, and we then find that of the
1,200 schools remaining, 242, or 20 per
cent. are transferred, and 180, or 15 per
cent. are in process of transfer, whilst
100, or 8.3 per cent. are under four-andtwo committees--that is to say, about 43
per cent. have abandoned the individual
type of management in favour of one in
which the ratepayers have some element
of representation.
As a considerable number of very large
schools have been transferred, particularly
in the City of Belfast, I shall not be far
wrong if I tell the Committee that probably about 50 per cent. of the children
in our Province omitting for this purpose those taught in schools under Roman
Catholic management are now being.
educated under conditions of popular
local control. Considering that the Act
is in force in the counties only during
three years--and a year longer in the
county boroughs, and that the negotiations for transfer are, as I have pointed
out, proceding in considerable numbers,
I think we may be gratified at the progress
made.
It is pleasing to find that as soon as
schools are transferred the education
authorities at once proceed to effect improvements, and to make better provision.
than has hitherto been possible in many
cases for their heating, cleaning, and
maintenance and for the comfort of the
pupils, and I am convinced that the
example of those well-kept schools will
act as an incentive to those people, who
for whatever reason have not so far
taken kindly to transfer, to imitate their
neighbours. I would urge, on the other
hand, all education authorities to deal
sympathetically with proposals for
transfer, to meet as far as possible the
desire for guarantees and facilities for
Bible instruction and to play a worthy
part in the great revolution in educational administration which is taking
place amongst us without the fact,
perhaps, being fully realized.
Of secondary schools, the High School
for Girls at Enniskillen aud the Academy
at Newtownards have been transferred to
the County Fermanagh and County Down

Education Authorities respectively. It
was not, of course, expected that the

of secondary schools to a very large extent.
Their support of secondary education has

and grants have been made by them to

The education committees are beginning
to realize the necessity for a survey of the
school provision in their areas. Over and
above what has already been done to
provide new schools or remodel old ones it
Is estimated that at least 160 schoolsabout 8 per cent. of our public elementary schools are quite unsuitable,
and will have to be replaced.
In Belfast four new elementary schools
have been completed, and others are being
built or planned. Outside Belfast some
22 new schools are in hand, while 13 new
schools have been, or are being, built
under voluntary management. Many
elementary schools are being extended,
altered and improved in various parts of
the country.
Considerable improvement is noticeable
in the equipment of almost all transferred
schools, and in some of them—especially
in Limavady and Belfast-permanent
school libraries are being built up. Circulating libraries have been established
in Derry City and in Fermanagh and one
is being formed in County Armagh.
New secondary schools are in hand for
Ballymena and Enniskillen. Aid has
been given for extensions to Ballymena
Academy and Lurgan College, and excellent new premises have been provided for
Newtownards Academy by the County
Down Education Committee.
New technical schools are being provided for Cookstown, Omagh, Newcastle,
Portrush, Ballycastle and Coleraine.
Banbridge Technical School has been considerably extended, and in Lurgan it is
proposed to remodel for use as a technical
school some premises which have been
acquired for that purpose.
On the occasion of the debate on the
Education Estimates last year it was suggested that the time had arrived when we
should inquire whether or not we are
getting the best value possible in return
for our great expenditure upon the educational services of the Province.
The hon. and learned Member for
South Belfast (Mr. Black), who first
raised this question, expressed some
doubts as to whether the education given
in the elementary and secondary schools
is as good as that given twenty or thirty
years ago. What the hon. and learned
Member and the other hon. Members
said on this subject has been much in my
mind, and I have been considering
whether or not it is possible to give any
adequate answer to their question.
I fear, however, that it is impossible
for me or indeed for anyone else to
institute a reliable comparison between
the education now given in our schools
and that given in the past. The wellknown tendency to paint a picture of the
days of long ago in glowing colours
renders difficult a fair comparison be
tween the present and the past even if
the conditions were similar. But they
are not similar. It is not only that the
school subjects which are now regarded
as essential are more numerous than a
generation ago, and that in consequence
to most of them only a reduced amount of
time can be given, but our views of the
proper scope of school education have profoundly altered in the last 20 or 30 years.
Formerly the merely literary side of edu
cation received an undue share of attention, and it was not fully recognized, if
recognized at all, that all the child's
faculties, the training of character, of the
hand and eye, of manners and tastes, as
well as attention to physical and hygienic
needs, formed the proper subject matter
of his school life and activities.
narrow curriculum confined to religious
instruction and the three R's is nowhere
considered nowadays as sufficient. Physical training must accompany mental and
intellectual development. The observation and the manual powers must be educated through courses of drawing and
handwork, and the æsthetic taste must be
developed by lessons in singing. It cannot be tolerated that pupils should hear
nothing in school of the essential facts of
the structure and life of the world in
which they live, so that some elementary
notions of nature study-particularly important for rural schools-and physical
science have to be included in the work of
the school-day. All this means more sub-
Α
Ministry of Education 1310
Estimates-
3 MAY 1928
jects, and therefore less attention to
meticulous details of arithmetic and English grammer, with perhaps some falling
off observable in precise knowledge of
spelling and mathematical processes.
This widening of the curriculum is, perhaps, the most remarkable phenomenon in
the modern systems of elementary education found in Great Britain and Western
Europe generally, and in the United
States, and he would indeed sin against
the light who would force upon Ulster
children a narrower course of studies and
a stunted conception of the work and outlook of the school.
To make these observations, however,
is not to admit that even in the essential
subjects there has been any loss of efficiency. The inspectors of the Ministry
are convinced that a vast improvement
has been effected in the past few years in
the power of the average pupil to read
intelligently and to convey to others in
written or spoken language the results of
his reading. And in other subjects,
while there may be a diminution in the
number of facts memorized, there has
been a great advance in the intelligent
appreciation of those facts. The Committee is, no doubt, aware that the
Ministry's inspectors make periodic estimates of the value of the work done in
the schools by individual teachers, and I
am happy to be able to say that the
result of these reports is to show that
never at any previous time were the
teachers of the Province more efficient or
more successful in the discharge of their
duties.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): Hear, hear.
Mr. ROBB: I shall now give the Committee some information in regard to the
qualifications of the teachers. Of approximately 4,500 principal and assistant
teachers in our public elementary schools
3,900-nearly 87 per cent.-have been

and about 600 are untrained-there are in
addition 627 junior assistant mistresses,
the majority of whom are untrained.
About 26 per cent. of the elementary
school teachers are rated as highly
efficient, and 67 per cent. as efficient.
The reports of the Ministry's inspectors
show a distinct improvement in the work
of the elementary schools in all parts of
the Province.
In March, 1928, there were 568 fulltime and 206 part-time teachers in the
secondary schools. Of this number 399
possess university degrees, and 218 have
graduated with honours. The number of
full-time teachers with first and secondclass honour degrees has increased by 54
per cent. in the last five years.
(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Under the secondary teachers' salary
regulations the only teachers in a school
in respect of whom the Ministry reimburses the governing body the amount
of the incremental portion of the salaries
are those who have been appointed to the
authorized staff and who have been
placed, in consequence, upon the salary
scale.
It has not been possible for the Government to accept liability for the award of
increments in respect of the entire previous service of teachers, and the existing
regulations provide that when a secondary
teacher is placed or replaced upon the
salary scale his previous secondary service
while not on the authorized staff of a
school shall be devalued by one-half, and
shall then be calculated for the award
of increments in accordance with the regulations.
.
The Ministry has felt that this regulation in its application to service given
since the operative date of the salary regulations bears unfairly upon secondary
teachers who have not the good fortune
to be placed upon the authorized staffs of
schools, and I am glad to be able to inform the Committee that new regulations
have just been presented to Parliament
under which all full-time secondary
service given in recognized schools in
Northern Ireland, whether on the
authorized staff or not, since 1st August,
1922, shall from the beginning of the
coming school year-1st August nextcount in full for incremental purposes
subject to the other conditions of the regulations, and existing teachers will,
where necessary, be replaced on the scales
as from that date. Preparatory teachers
are to receive a corresponding measure of
recognition for their service.
I have now told the Committee something about our machinery, but the
question put to me last year as to what
we are getting for the money we spend
required, in the answer, an estimate of

the products. I have said something
about our machinery, and now I will
proceed to give an estimate of what we
get out of the machinery. Frankly, I cannot pretend that without an elaborate
investigation, for which there is not the

can be given, but I have made some inquiries and considered some available
criteria, and, for what they are worth, I
give my conclusions.
One of the main objects of all education is to produce good citizens, men and
women of character and initiative and
industry who can do a good day's work
in the community-in agriculture, in industry, in commerce, in the professions,
in literature, scholarship, science or art.
So many of the boys and girls leaving
our elementary schools go into our industries that it seemed to me natural to
make inquiries from employers as to the
calibre and equipment of those whom they
have newly employed. Without pretending that my inquiries were exhaustive,
hardly claiming for them that they were
sufficient, the conclusion I have arrived
at is that the pupils leaving our elementary schools now do not fall behind
those of former days in the amount they
know that they are nimbler of intellect,
but--and I found this a universal complaint they will not work so hard as their
fathers did. By nimbler of intellect I
mean that I got a quite definite opinion
that the modern boy or girl learns new
processes more quickly, and this I can only
attribute to the widening of the curri
culum and the effort now made to develop
their powers of observation and reasoning.
The complaint that they will not work so
hard I heard from nearly every one I
asked, but when I countered this complaint with the query, "was not this a
universal symptom shown by all
ployees," those who made the complaint
as universally answered that it was.
this then I do not think the schools can be
saddled with the blame. The whole
nation does not work so hard-and while
it may be said that the work of schools
should involve a correction of this
tendency, I think we cannot expect the
schools wholly to counteract it, though I
hope they do their best to inculcate industry and condemn the frittering away
of energy in idleness. We can take
em-

comfort in this, however, that in the
markets of the world the products of our

compare as well as they ever did with the

en-
So far as the pupils of our secondary
schools go into business, what I have said
about the pupils of our elementary schools
is also true. Of those who go to universities it is pleasant to note that the best
of them hold their own-perhaps in proportion to their numbers more than hold
their own-in competition with the products of English and Scottish schools for
open scholarships. But of the average,
the conclusion I have come to from what
I have been able to gather is that on the
mathematical side and on the scientific
side the product is as good as it used to
be; that in modern languages it is much
better; but on the classical side there is
a falling off. It is not only that fewer
pupils take classics, but that the standard
reached by the average pupil has fallen.
For this I do not blame the teachers; but
the demands made upon the time of
pupils for teaching in a greater variety of
scientific subjects have been met by reducing the time given to Latin and
Greek, and possibly the natural desire for
easy options has had its influence. For
myself, I regret this, though I am not
sure how best a truer at least truer from
my point of view-balance can be found
nor whether efforts in that direction can
gain the necessary support from a frankly
utilitarian public.
I turn now to school attendance.
School attendance is a little better than
last year, the percentage of average attendance to average number of pupils on
rolls being 83.8. This is, however, entirely due to improvements in Belfast and
Londonderry. Everywhere else there is
a slight drop in the attendance.
Irregular attendance, unless for a
justifiable cause, means waste not only of
the opportunities of the pupils, but waste
of the money of the taxpayer and the
ratepayer, and I earnestly hope that
magistrates at petty sessions will keep
this aspect of the question before them
and see that there is no avoidable evasion
of the Act. It is no kindness to be
lenient in this matter; the children are
bound to suffer, and not only the children
who are irregular in attendance at school,
Estimates-
Ministry of Education

but other children who attend regularly
and work dilengently. Nothing so disorganizes class-work as the presence of
children who, owing to irregularity in
their attendance, are merely a drag upon
their more painstaking and hard-working
fellow pupils.
I now come to the feeding and clothing
of necessitous children, and I am pleased
again to be able to call attention to the
praiseworthy efforts which have been made

hope will readily be followed by other

have provided for expenditure amounting

assistance ot necessitous children.
The feeling in favour of medical inspection is growing, and soon no part of the
Province will be without it. All the committees have made provision of some kind
in their Estimates for this purpose, and
eleven committees have their schemes in
operation.
In the present year there is an increase
of ten per cent. in the number of pupils
attending secondary schools as compared
with the year 1926-27, while that year
showed an increase of 6 per cent. over
the year 1925-26; this is very encouraging.
A part of this increase is no doubt due to
the scholarships granted by the local
education authorities, but the greater part
of it appears to be due to a growing appreciation on the part of the people of the
benefits to be derived from secondry education.
It is gratifying to note also that the
increase is by no means confined to the
lower branches of the school. There 19
during the current school year an increase
of 18 per cent. in the number of pupils
following courses higher than those preparing for the junior certificate. Each
year since the institution of the certificate
examinations there has been an improvement in the percentage of passes in both
the junior and senior examinations. There
has also been a steady increase in the
number of candidates entering for these
examinations, and this year there is a considerable increase in the number of those
about to enter for the senior examination.
Technical instruction has advanced
rapidly in the course of the past year.
There has been a steady increase each year
since the Ministry came into existence, and
in the last school year the number of indidividual students enrolled was well over
23,700. And not only has the number of
students increased, but many new schools
and centres have been opened. Since
1924 fourteen new centres of technical
instruction have been added to those
formerly in existence. The greatest development in this respect has been in
County Down, where, prior to 1914, all
the technical centres were situated on the
fringes of the county.
The technical schools have in many
cases since the recent Act instituted
courses for the training of pharmaceutical
apprentices where they can obtain instruction in botany, chemistry, physics, and
business methods. I am also pleased to be
able to record a great extension in the
number of candidates for the technical
school examinations. This greatly increased entry for the examinations which
has taken place in a couple of years is a
striking testimony to the zeal of the
principals and their staffs.
As a result of negotiations with the
Institute of Chemistry of Great Britain
and Ireland and with the Institution of
Mechanical Engineers the Ministry's Technical School examinations have been recognized as the basis of the award of National
Certificates in chemistry and in mechanical
engineering, and the Ministry is at present
negotiating with the Institute of Naval
Architects and the Worshipful Company
of Shipwrights with a view to securing
similar recognition of those examinations
as the basis of the award of National
Certificates in naval architecture.
The Committee will, I am sure, approve
of the Ministry's policy of awarding
annually trade scholarships to enable

young men engaged in an industry to obtain systematic instruction in the principles of science and art as applied to that

to be very much appreciated both by
apprentices and employers, and 77 were
awarded last year. At a meeting of the
Association of Technical Institutions
which was held in Belfast last June very
great interest was shown in these scholarships, and resolutions were passed drawing
the attention of the Board of Education
in England and of education authorities
in Great Britain generally to the value
and success of the system. After the
congress a considerable number of principals of technical institutions in Great
Britain made further inquiries, and asked
for more detailed particulars of the
scheme.
were
When last year's Estimates
under discussion several hon. Members
appealed for the restoration of the grants
for practical instruction which had formerly been paid by the Ministry to those
committees which in technical schools
under their management gave instruction
to pupils of public elementary schools in
domestic economy and woodwork.
The
Ministry was unable last year to accede to
this request, but since then the whole
question has been further considered,
with the result that I am now able to
inform the Committee that it has been
decided, with the concurrence of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), to lay before Parliament regulations for the payment of
attendance grants for classes of elementary
school pupils in domestic economy and
manual instruction held in technical
schools and centres.
I
Several hon. Members in the debate on
last year's Estimates referred to the curriculum of elementary schools in rural
areas, and expressed themselves as not
quite satisfied that the programme taught
in country schools was entirely suited to
the needs of the farming community.
should like to say that it is the view of the
Ministry that, as a rule, vocational training should not be introduced into the
school course before the pupil has attained
the age of fourteen, or at the very least
thirteen, and that his school life before
that age should be devoted entirely to a
well-balanced general education which will
serve him in after life in any profession
or occupation which he may adopt.
I explained to the Committee last year
that we hoped to develop a new type of
Junior Technical School definitely leading
towards agriculture, but I pointed out at
the same time that for further expansion
we must look for assistance from local
sources. I am now pleased to be able to
tell the Committee that after consultation
with the Ministry of Agriculture a new
type of school suitable for pupils preparing
for an agricultural career has been started
at Lisburn for farmers' sons.
The education and instruction in agriculture afforded by the Ministry of Agriculture and the Committees of Agriculture
in the various counties by means of winter
classes, lectures, and courses at Greenmount Agricultural College and at the
Ulster Dairy School provide practical and
professional training for young men and
women of sixteen years and over; they do
not, however, make provision for that preliminary instruction which is desirable for
pupils between the ages of fourteen and
sixteen-for that this Ministry and the
education authorities are responsibleand it is just here that a school such as the
new Junior Technical School at Lisburn
meets a recognized need. Taking pupils
of about fourteen years of age this school
provides a curriculum which is planned to
give the pupils some understanding of the
principles underlying agriculture, while.
at the same time, continuing their general
education. This is a development which
the Ministry welcomes, and the greatest
credit is due to the Lisburn and Belfast
Regional Committee for its pioneer work
in establishing the school. I am glad to
say that three other places are considering
opening similar schools.
I
The Committee which was appointed by
the Minister in May, 1922, to make
arrangements for the training of teachers
for various grades of schools in Northern
Ireland has during the past year continued
its labours with the same unremitting zeal
which has characterized all its work.
take this opportunity of again expressing
the Ministry's indebtedness to my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, who
is Chairman of that Committee, and to the
individual members, for the self-sacrificing way in which they have devoted their
time and their energy to this very important work. The standard of entrants
at the King's Scholarship Examination is
steadily improving, and there is a corresponding improvement in the output. The
improvement may be attributed largely to
Ministry of Education 1318
Estimates-
3 MAY 1928
the growing appreciation of the generous
scale of salaries offered to public elementary school teachers, and to the policy
of the Training Committee and the
Ministry in encouraging the system of
pupil teachers who receive a course of
