their admission to training colleges.
I am glad to be able to say that the
work of the three recognized training
colleges is proceeding satisfactorily. In
Stranmillis the lecture block is in course
of erection, and will, it is anticipated, be
ready for use next year. The reconditioning of Hampton House for use as a men's
hostel is approaching completion, and it
should be possible to transfer the men
students to the hostel when the college reopens after the summer vacation.
Before I close I should like to mention
that the Ministry's attention has recently
been called to the fact that much misapprehension seems to exist among certain
classes in England and Scotland regarding the political status and industrial and
commercial position of our Province-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and the
Ministry has been considering whether any
steps could usefully be taken to approach
the educational authorities in Great
Britain with a view to having the matter
ventilated through the schools. We have
been in communication with the Board of
Education in England and the Scottish
Education Department, and I am pleased
to say that both these bodies have very
willingly agreed to bring the matter to the
notice of their inspectors. We have also
made representations to publishers of textbooks in general use in the teaching of
geography and history in public elementary and secondary schools across the
Channel, and in every case our views have
been met most cordially and promises made
that in coming editions of those textbooks mistakes and omissions will be
rectified, and the situation of Northern
Ireland set forth in its proper light.
(Hon. Members: Hear. hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: What is meant by that?
Mr. ROBB: In accordance with the
actual facts.
Mr. DEVLIN: What are the actual
facts?
Mr. ROBB: Well now, I would not like
to start to tell the hon. Member that. In
concluding these remarks, which I fear
may have taxed your patience (hon.
Members: No)-I should like to say that
I know no reason why we should be downhearted or despondent as to the success of
our educational policy. Looking back at
the year that has passed I am justified in
saying that there has been a notable advance all along the line, perhaps less in
some directions than we had hoped, but
greater in others than we had dared to
expect. The material conditions in which
our elementary and secondary education.
is carried on, the schoolhouses, their
equipment, and those arrangements that
are necessary for the comfort and wellbeing of the pupils, are everywhere
gradually-in some places rapidly-being
improved. The number of our pupils
completing a full course of elementary
education by taking the leaving certificate
is steadily rising-more scholarships
are being given, and the attendance
at our secondary schools shows a substantial increase. Many new technical
schools are being built and the
facilities provided by our technical
instruction system are being appreciated
and utilized in still greater measure every
year. Our teachers are increasing in efficiency, and their qualifications and training give evidence of a perceptible advance.
The health of the pupils is now receiving
attention in almost all parts of the country
through the setting up of medical school
inspection, and the few areas that have
not yet adopted medical inspection schemes
are now coming into line. We have made
provision for the education of afflicted
children so far as is practicable at the
moment, and suitable instruction and care
are now available for the deaf, and the
dumb, and the blind. We have still to
take up the question of the mentally deficient, and this matter will have our early
and earnest attention. If there be any
misgiving here and there as to the success
of the Act I am confident that, while
plenty remains to be done, enough has
already been accomplished through its
instrumentality to vindicate a thousand
times over the policy which inspired it.
I beg to move.

I want to direct some attention to the

I find from "The Times"
Educational Supplement that the total
cost of elementary school education in
Great Britain is a sum of £32,000,000,

is £320,000 odd, which works out roughly

If we
take the total of £20,000, plus £6,000 for

of inspection in Northern Ireland is about
£2 for every £100 spent on elementary
education. In other words, we are
spending in this inspectorate department
about twice as much as a rich country
like England.
The other day at Newtownards the

We will take a division as set out by the

Looked at in another way, I may say

like I believe it would be good for educational work throughout the countrythe Minister of Education, assisted as I

I will prove before I resume my seat that

I hold that is only fair play.
I have in my hands a circular sent out
by the Ministry of Education, and as it
is a refreshing thing I would like to read
a clause or two of it regarding the heating
of schools.
The Ministry entirely disapproves cf
any expenditure for the equipment,
maintenance or daily upkeep of public
elementary schools being allowed to fall
upon teachers, and its grants are made
to these schools only on the clear understanding that they shall be properly
and fully maintained by the managers.
It is the duty of the latter to make the
necessary arrangements for the lighting
of fires and for the purchase of coal,
firewood, or other fuel for the heating
of the schoolrooms, as well as for the
cleaning of the schoolrooms and premises, and all expenses involved must
be provided by them.
The manager's responsibility does
not, however, preclude his seeking the
reasonable assistance of the teachers
in making arrangements for collecting
contributions from parents or others
for these purposes, and in seeing that
these duties are properly performed by
those employed to carry them out.
In other words, the teacher is not to
be responsible, but to assist the manager
in getting money from the parents.
The work of lighting fires and of
keeping the schoolrooms clean by
daily sweeping and dusting cannot as
a general rule be performed adequately without the regular employment of a charwoman or other hired
person, and in the case of the larger
rural schools and in all schools in cities
and towns the Ministry requires that
these duties shall be carried out in
this way.
But what about the country?
In country schools where the premises are small and not more than two
rooms are in use the trifling work involved in daily sweeping, dusting, and
lighting of fires has hitherto been
easily provided for with the voluntary
assistance of the pupils. The Ministry
does not propose to forbid the practice.
In towns and large rural schools they
are not allowed to do it, but in small
schools the children can be imposed
upon. I think that is unsatisfactory.
Teachers should clearly understand
that while there is no obligation on
them to incur any expense in respect
of these matters, the Ministry requires
them to co-operate loyally with the
school managers in giving effect to the
arrangements that may properly be
made for the comfort of pupils and the
cleanliness and care of the school
premises.

Well, perhaps if the magistrates are given

not consider instructing the teachers to

given at the season when the crops are
being put in and at the season when the
crops are being taken out? That is, such
an extended holiday should not be taken
in the summer time. The teachers who,
I think, have only five days to work in

children of farmers will be available to

is to a farmer. It is a difficult time for
the farmer, and in that way the Minister
would assist them very much.
Then there is medical inspection of
children. That is a very important thing.
I notice that in some county 800 children
were inspected, and 1,000 diseases were
found. (Laughter). I think I am safe
in saying that. It is evident that more
than one disease was found in the same
child. There is no doubt it would be a
serious thing not to have the children
medically inspected, but where is the good
of having an inspection of the children
and letting it stop there? It is not a bit
of use in the wide world unless they are
treated. There is a feeling that it might
not be a prudent thing to place this under
the dispensary doctors. I personally cannot see any other way. There is no use
in one man examining children and the
dispensary doctor atteding to some of
them and private doctors attending to the
others. I think medical inspection
should not be pushed too far until legislation will come in as a result of the
Commission which sat recently on local
government practice. I hope that some
way will be discovered whereby without
overlapping the health of the children
will be carefully attended to. I think the
Ministry might give a lead along that
line.

We hear from time to time criticisms
on various matters concerned with the
machinery for education, the regional
committees, their deeds and alleged misdeeds. Last year I ventured to suggest
that instead of dealing with the machinery
we should get down to the pupil himself,
to see what he is being taught and
how he is being taught. I much
appreciate the course the Parliamentary
Secretary has taken this year in trying
to deal with this matter-in trying to get
into the schools themselves and telling us
what is being taught, how it is being
taught, and giving us an estimate of the
results we are getting for our expenditure.
It is with very great interest that we hear
that the general view he is able to gather
from those with whom he is in touch is
that we are getting good value.
It is a
satisfaction to hear that opinion expressed

The "Christian Union" has been
foremost among the journals which
have demanded an improvement in our

spiritual nature must be developed with
the intellectual.
I will now bring you to what is done
in Canada. Canada is a great model for
the Government in the Six Counties when
it comes to a question of educating our
boys and sending them out as emigrants
to that country. In Canada the school
system is denominational in the four chief
provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Alberta,
and Saskatchewan, and each denomination
that can maintain a separate school for
its children has a separate school. In
these four provinces out of a total of
27,520 schools 21,350 are separate schools
for the different religious denominations.
The Supreme Council of Education in
Quebec and Ontario consists of an equal
number of Catholics and non-Catholics,
each part controlling the schools of its
own colour. In all schools there is an
official called a commissary, which
generally corresponds to our manager.
This system has worked well in Canada,
which is a progressive country containing
nine milions of people.
I will take you now to Europe and I
will refer to the prosperous little Protestant country of Holland. Holland
with a population of seven milions,
mainly Protestant, in 1920 passed a law
putting all private, voluntary, and
church schools on a perfect equality with
the public or Government schools, giving
them equal grants from public moneys,
and the right to appoint their
teachers and select their own text books.

always maintained the principles of religious education from the primary
school to the university. Its denomiown

1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of cases heard before Courts of Referees
in Belfast since April 19th, and the
number of those. who were refused benefits; whether it is by his instructions
that the officials of the Courts of Referees
inform the Court of the overdraft of each

overdrafts are wiped out, this procedure
is regular.
were
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): From 19th April till 5th May
inclusive, 143 appeals against the decision
of the Insurance Officer disallowing
claims to unemployment benefit
heard by the Court of Referees at
Belfast. The Court upheld the Insurance Officer's decision in 130 cases, and
recommended the payment of benefit in
13. All these appeals related to statutory
conditions or disqualifications in force
before the passing of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, 1928.
The Umpire has laid it down that a
claimant's record of employment is a most
important consideration in determining
whether or not he satisfies the statutory
conditions. The statement of contributions paid and benefits received is therefore normally made available to the
Court, as evidence of the claimant's record of employment.
The existence of what has been known
as the overdraft is no longer, in itself, a
bar to entitlement to unemployment
benefit.

He now states they are not a bar to unemployment benefit being granted, and
that the officials of the Court are sup-

Government administration.

not prepared to pledge the Government
at the moment.

Mr. ANDREWS: I have felt some
doubt as to the course which I ought to
follow to-day in introducing the Estimates
of the Labour Ministry. If I were to
deal with our general policy at length, if
I were to enlarge upon the policy in connection with the various branches, if I
were to refer to the many activities of the
Department and to deal with the industrial situation, expressing our fears and
our hopes, I undoubtedly would occupy
a very considerable amount of time and I
might possibly weary hon. Members
opposite.
On this occasion, especially as the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
shakes his head, I am prepared to take
the risk, for I feel that if I adopted the
easier, more modest, and to me more
acceptable, course of simply dealing with
these matters which I feel to be of outstanding importance, I would be sure to
be accused by hon. Members opposite of
having treated them with scant courtesy
and having failed in my duty to give the
Committee the information which hon.
Members have the right to expect.
In dealing with the general policy of
the Department I would like to say at the
very beginning of my remarks that when
our Government was set up one of the
first things that we decided was that as
regards labour matters-those services
which my Department is charged with administering-we would keep in parity with
Great Britain both as regards legislation
and administration. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I may point out that that
policy from which we have never wavered
was decided before hon. Members opposite
came into this House at all.
On several occasions they have pressed
me to a considerable extent to yield in this
direction and in that direction, but if the
Government had been weak enough to
take their advice in connection with this
matter we undoubtedly would have done
irreparable damage to our industrial
classes in Northern Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Our policy was
the outcome of our view that there was no
reason why, because we had accepted a
Parliament of our own to help Great
Britain in her time of difficulty, our industrial classes should suffer as a consequence in their home lives and all those
things which mean so much to them.
We have, therefore, all along never recognized that there were any boundaries
Estimates
Ministry of Labour
8 MAY 1928
within the United Kingdom in connection
with social, industrial, and labour
matters. The result of our policy nas
been that our workers in Northern Ireland
have always felt quite secure in the knowledge that whatever advantages were
given to their fellow-workers in Great
Britain would also be given to them.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
It is not overstating the fact that from
the cradle to the grave these social services
bring assistance to our industrial classes
in almost every period of adversity which
may befall them. In the first place, when
the child appears maternity benefit is
paid. A little later the Ministry of Education comes along with free education,
with feeding for necessitous children, and
with inspection of all the youth of our
country attending school. A little later
if the parent-the bread winner-dies a
widow's pension is given to the mother
and an allowance to the children, and if
both parents die an orphans' pension is
given to those who are left behind.
Again, when the insurance age is reached
if sickness falls upon the insured person
he has the knowledge that he will receive
sickness benefit for a considerable time,
and if the illness is prolonged disablement
benefit until a cure is effected. Then,
again, in the case of unemployment, hon.
Members are aware that very considerable
help is given over prolonged periods.
And, last but not least, when old age
begins to fall upon the faithful worker a
pension is given either on a contributory
or non-contributory basis until the call
comes from the Greatest Ruler of all.
Surely this is a great record, a record of
which any people may feel proud; and it
cannot be denied that no Government in
the world's history has done more than
this, and that no Government, except the
British Government, has done as much.
The PRIME MINISTER:
hear.
Hear;
Mr. ANDREWS: It is interesting at
this stage to consider the financial effect,
or, in other words, the cost of this policy
which I have explained. Hon. Members
will observe in the Estimate that the
State's contribution for 1928-29 will be no
less a sum than £2,663,893 plus £151,752
for administration. To this must be
added the contributions of employers and
employees, namely, £1,355,000, making a
grand total-and a grand total it is--of
over four millions, all of which goes for
the benefit of our industrial classes and
is administered by the Department whica
I have the honour to be the political head.
Sometimes we are told that our Departments are over-staffed. We are told that
the cost of administration is too high.
If this charge can be brought against any
Department-I do not think it can--i
-it
ought to be directed against mine, because
I am responsible for employing almost
half the total staff employed in the
Government Departments. But I do not
believe the Departments are over-staffed,
and one thing I am absolutely certain of
is that the Ministry of Labour is not, and
say here quite frankly that no one can
judge whether a Department is over.
staffed or not unless he has intimate personal knowledge of the work which the
Department is charged with performing.
I
But what is the cost of administration
in the Ministry of Labour? For the year
lying ahead, namely 1928-29-of course, !
refer to the financial year-the cost of the
Department's administration will be 6.6
per cent., or, if the approved societies
expenses are taken into consideration, it
will be 8.9 per cent. I venture to say
that this is a very low figure for dealing
with such important services, especially
having regard to the fact that the payments are made in comparatively small
sums. Now, the work of the Ministry of
Labour can be conveniently divided, I
think, on an occasion like this, into two
heads. First of all, there is the question
of employment in all its aspects, and,
secondly, I propose to deal with the question of insurance.
Dealing with the problems associated
with employment, I would like, in the
first instance, to say that I think it is very
gratifying that Northern Ireland continues to enjoy a reputation second to
none in the land for industrial peace.
That is mainly due to a desire on behalf
of both employers and labour to accomodate with each other, to negotiate with
each other, and to help each other to the
greatest extent that the industry will
permit. Of course, the Ministry of
Labour plays a part, as it is entitled to
do, in this connection, and when my
people I call them by that name
advisedly-hear that trouble is brewing
they immediately get into touch with one
or both parties likely to be affected. We
believe in the old saying that prevention
is better than cure, and, therefore, I am
entitled to say that in far more instances
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
than are generally known through the influence of the Department matters are
adjusted before the public becomes aware
of the fact that there was any danger in
the air.
I think that at this stage I ought to
refer to those problems associated with
Trade Board legislation.
I remember
when Trade Boards were very unpopular. That, I do not think, is so to-day.
I believe it is generally recognized that
in certain industries where there was not
only fierce local competition but also
national and international competition,
what is known as sweating was likely to
result, and therefore Trade Boards were
set up in eighteen of our industries. One
of the complaints against Trade Boards
in the past has been that they tended to
drive trade from the country districts into
the towns and cities. That was recognized
by the Government, and in our Trade
Board Act of 1923 a provision was inserted permitting District Trade Committees to be set up with power to recommend that wages should differentiate between town and country in such a way as
not to bring about the regrettable result
to which I have already referred. Taking
advantage of that provision there has been
established in the boot and shoe repairing
trade a District Committee, which I
understand, has brought about an agreed
result, and in the retail tailoring and
dressmaking trade a committee of the
character which I have indicated is now
being established.
It is particularly gratifying to us all to
know that employment during the past
year was undoubtedly a good deal better
than in the case of its predecessors. In
Northern Ireland approximately a quarter of a million persons are insured under
our Unemployment Insurance Acts.
It
is interesting to know that 139,500 are
men, 89,900 are women, and 19,600 are
juveniles. Again, they are sub-divided
into 68,000 associated with the linen industry in its various branches, 25,000 in
connection with the shipbuilding industry
and engineering in normal times, 30,000
in our distributive trades, 23,000 in our
tailoring trades and making-up trades,
including the shirt and collar trade, which
is identified to such an extent with the
Londonderry area, and 18,000 in our
building trade.
We all of us, I think not unnaturally,
are more inclined to focus our continual
attention upon those who are unemployed
over
rather than upon those who are engaged
in industry. And I think it will interest
the Committee to know that
200,000 of our insured persons that
leaves out, of course, persons employed
in agriculture and domestic service and
other uninsured persons-that
200,000 persons, notwithstanding the
times we have been passing through, have
been continuously employed. That is
after all, reasonably satisfactory.
over
Now, hon. Members may expect, as they
have expected on former occasions, that I
should say something about the prospects.
I am aware of the fact that it is always a
dangerous thing to prophesy, but I have
been particularly careful never to paint
the picture brighter than I felt I was
justified in doing, and I am not going to
do so on this occasion. Of course one cannot approach a proposition of this kind
without realizing what an important part
in our industrial life our staple trade
occupies. The figure I have already cited of
68,000 shows how many of our industrial
workers are engaged in this industry.
Now, as regards our staple trade I have
often heard many people say both in this
House and out of it that it was down and
out. I do not believe that for a moment.
I have had some personal experience of
the linen industry for over 35 years.
has always had its ups and downs
and it has always come through. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) And that it will
do so again I feel absolutely confident.
It
As regards the immediate future I am
somewhat anxious, and I will tell the Committee why. Before the war we were
always dependent to a very large extent
for our raw material, namely flax,
on the supply which came from
Russia. Since the war that unfortunate
country has shipped very little. I
am not altogether surprised, because
after all in that land there is very little
incentive to effort and very little inducement to grow a crop which is a difficult
crop to grow and which is a crop that involves a very great deal of trouble. And
it is not much of an incentive to grow a
crop like that when you know you are
very likely to be deprived of the fruits of
your labour. And therefore we have felt
the backwash of that, and to-day we are
up against somewhat of a shortage of raw
material. Flax is very much above the
normal price, and spinners are naturally
shy about buying under existing conditions. But it is gratifying to feel in this
connection that there are increased sowing
Estimates
Ministry of Labour
8 MAY 1928
in Belgium, in France, and in Holland,
and the brairds are looking well. And
here at home it is estimated that there will
be an increased supply of about 25 per.
cent. So that if the next few months had
passed away I personally feel that there
would be no reason for anxiety.
It is particularly gratifying to know
that our shipbuilding industry is improving throughout the United Kingdom, and
that our principal yard has benefited to its
full share and that its slips are occupied.
It is also gratifying to know that Messrs.
Workman & Clark's yard, which has been
passing through such difficult and trying
times, has now been reformed and that
they are now taking orders, and that it is
reasonable to hope that that yard also will
benefit in the general improvement.
Something was said about artificial silk
the other day in this House, and I should
like briefly to refer to the position as regards this, what I may call, new industry.
With Government assistance a factory was
started at Ballymena which is now producing, I understand, an excellent article
and is giving employment to 600 persons.
I am also glad to know that inquiries are
now taking place with a view to establishing another silk factory in Londonderry.
Other new industries are gradually being
established in our midst and, therefore, as
I think I have already said, we can look
forward to our industrial future not only
with hope but with confidence.
Now in dealing with the question of unemployment we naturally think first of our
disabled ex-Servicemen, and the King's
National Roll Committees continue their
splendid public service in this connection.
All honour to them. At the beginning of
the year 1,570 disabled ex-Servicemen
were unemployed. During the year that
figure was reduced by 500, and I am sure
every hon. Member will be gratified to
know that there are at the present time
4,701 disabled ex-Servicemen working in
enrolled firms. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Hon. Members will naturally desire to
know a little about our relief schemes.
During the year under review 141 schemes
were sanctioned by the Department estimated to cost over £1,000,000, and the
grants sanctioned amounted to £285,000,
and, therefore, I am glad to be able to
inform the Committee that 87 schemes are
at present in hand, the estimated cost of
which will amount to over £1,400,000,
and the work on which will occupy a considerable time before it is completed.
There is another matter that I wish to
take the opportunity of referring to today, because it is part of the policy of the
Government. There is a great deal of
loose thinking and loose talking about our
Richhill Training Centre. At that centre
we have trained and sent to Canada already 178 young men. We have trained
and sent to Australia 72 young men or
250 in all. And there are at the present
time in training 79 for Canada and 12
for Australia, a total of 91.
men
Now, I know quite well that there are
some hon. Members who take the view
that it is not desirable to send, as they
express it, the best blood of Ulster out of
the country. Well, I would like to say
that that is quite mistaken. It is not
the view of the Government that anybody
should be sent from Ulster. What the
policy of the Government is is this-to
bring within the reach of these
young
in our industrial centres the same privilege in this direction which is brought to
young men in Great Britain who, of their
own free will, desire to chance their lot
in another part of the British Empire.
It is a free choice whether they go to
Richhill or not, and the Government,
neither directly nor indirectly, puts the
smallest amount of pressure upon them in
connection with their decision. But may
I point out to the Committee the way that
I view this matter? The Dominion authorities are getting more and more particular as to whom they will accept.
will accept no one now who has not a
knowledge of farming matters and, therefore, if the Government were not to bring
within the reach of these young persons
a knowledge of agriculture they would be
absolutely debarred from exercising the
free choice which I have referred to, and
they would have to remain here in our
cities, employed or unemployed as the
case may be, whether they liked it or not.
They
May I point out in this connection that
the births in Northern Ireland exceed the
deaths each year by no less a number than
7,600, and, therefore, not only have we
some leeway to make up before all our
people who are available for employment
obtain it, but if emigration were to cease
from Northern Ireland vacancies would
have to be found for 7,600 persons each
year in addition.
Now the people of
Northern Ireland have always taken their
part in peopling and fashioning the
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
British Dominions beyond the seas.
Is it
to be held that we are to become so local
and so provincial that our young people
are not to get that opportunity in future?
Now, it is generally recognized that
Ulster men have risen to the very top in
the Dominions. They have helped to
make the Dominions what they are, and,
therefore, as I have already said, the
Government at Richhill is simply bringing
within the reach of these young persons
the opportunity of emigrating in case they
so desire.
The next matter that I wish to refer to
is the problem associated with the Local
Employment Committees. There is an
impression abroad that these are to cease
to function under the Blanesburgh Act.
That is not so. Under the Blanesburgh
Act it will be no longer necessary for
Rota Committees to meet because the
work which the Rota Committees did in
the past is to be transferred under that
Act to Courts of Referees. I have often
heard it stated in this House, and out of
it, that the decisions of Rota Committees
very often were very harsh, and that large
numbers of people quite wrongly were
cut off from benefit. I have always felt
that that was unfair to the Rota Committees, and I must say this to-day that I feel
deeply indebted to those committees, each
and all of them, for the valuable and
difficult services which they have rendered
to Northern Ireland since they came into
being four or five years ago.
During the past year the Rota Committees reviewed 220,500 claims, and they
actually passed 187,800 claims. I am in
a position to inform my hon. Friends that
out of every 100 claims put before the
Rota Committees, taking into consideration the rejections by headquarters, 82
persons received benefit. Surely no one
can say that that was cutting off insured
persons from the "dole," as they call it,
north, south, east and west. I think the
administration of the Act under these
Rota Committees has been very impartial
and very fair, as it ought to be.
In connection with the administration
of unemployment insurance, the charge
is very frequently made, on the other
hand, that large numbers of people get
benefit who ought not to get it at all, and
that a considerable number of them get
it by fraud. That I do not believe to be
true. I do not believe that there are
many cases of fraud, and I can assure the
Committee that the Department takes
care that, when cases of fraud come to
its notice, the persons suspected are
brought to trial. During the past fifteen
months, 323 prosecutions took place, and
of these 288 persons were convicted.
I now want to say a few words in reference to Health Insurance. The number
of people covered by our Health Insurance
Acts is 332,000. The expenditure has
risen compared with the previous year. It
has risen from £654,000 to £783,000. Of
this rise, £33,000 is to be accounted for
by additional benefits; but the expenditure
has risen somewhat during the last few
years, I quite freely admit. In 1925 there
was spent £1 9s 2d per member by the
Approved Societies; in 1926, £1 14s 11d
per member, and in 1927 £2 7s 6d per
member.
I see that one of the Socialist Members
in the British House has been accusing me

against me in this House of harsh administration-
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS -so that it is a

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: They

did not represent the true position of

Mr. KYLE: I protest against such

Again, comparing like with like, as regards salaries only I am asking for
£173,526, whereas the provision for
salaries last year, including the non-contributory old-age pension service, was
£203,334. This year, therefore, I am in

for practically £30,000 less than last

about by the concentration of headquarters offices in one building, and may
I say that not only does that help the
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour

administration generally, but there is an
actual saving which yields about 18 per
cent. on the capital expenditure. Internal reorganization has produced saving
to a considerable extent. The better
state of employment has also caused a

with other services administered by the

some time ago by my right hon. Friend

I am glad to say, likely to be exceeded.
There are only a few other matters

say in this connection that in order to
check certification, which I admit in

A
second referee is now being appointed
with the approval of the Ministry of
Finance. As a matter of fact there is
a grant-in-aid from the approved
societies to bear this additional cost, because of the services rendered to the
approved societies. The object of the
Department is that everybody should get
insurance benefit like every other form of
benefit they are entitled to, but none
should receive benefit if they are not
entitled to it.
If hon. Members will refer to Subhead K they will see that there is a substantial rise of about £11,000 odd. Of
this amount £8,800 is due to the Blanesburgh Act and for the establishment of
the courts of referees in connection therewith, and £3,000 is due to the Old-Age
Pensions Act. If hon. Members will
refer to Sub-head R they will see here a

to administer these great services without administrative expenditure, but, as I
have already shown hon. Members, the

Just before I conclude I would like to
say this, if the Department have inade

have shown and given to the great problems which they have to deal with. It
is only right before I sit down that I
should pay tribute to my hon. Friend

Hear, hear). He and I have worked

this I would say, and then I have done,

The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member
has entirely misconceived the position.
There is no prescriptive right in the Opposition to be called before anybody else.
The practice in debate is, that individual
speeches are as a rule replied to from the
other side. but if no hon. Member gets
up to reply of course I call upon the only
hon. Member who does rise. But to
keep the balance of debate, if an hon.
Member does get up on the other side,
I am in fairness entitled to call him.
That is the universal and recognized rule
of procedure.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Is it
fair that one right hon. Gentleman should
be permitted to make two speeches during the course of a debate, in which some
hon. Members are not permitted to take
part at all!
The CHAIRMAN: The purpose of all

the Minister has been invited to reply

I would like to show the Committee how
reckless the hon. Member for West Belfast
is in the statements which he makes. He
referred to the Widows', Orphans' and
Old Age Contributory Pensions Act, and
he said that we had not put it into operation here for twelve or eighteen months
after they had done so at Westminster.
What are the facts of the case?
Imperial Parliament passed that Measure
on the 7th August, 1925. We here passed
it on the 6th November of the same year.
In other words, we passed it in the soonest
possible time after we knew what the
British Measure contained; and no injustice was done to anyone here, because the
Measure came into operation here on the
4th January, 1926, which was exactly the
same date as it came into operation in
Great Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear,

Mr. ANDREWS: I think the hon.

I understand now is that he suggests the

of the cost, where would be their influence with the local authorities to have
the schemes carried out economically?
Really, no practical suggestions were
made in reference to the solution of this
problem. I take it I am right in saying
that the Government has done everything
humanly possible to relieve the situation,
and we have had, if I may say so, quite a
remarkable success.
When we took over our powers, over
100,000 of our people were unemployed.
That figure has been reduced to somewhere round about 33,000 to-day.
Therefore, I do not think that hon. Members are entitled to say that the Government have not made very considerable
progress. In addition to that, I do maintain that for those for whom work could
not be found we made exactly the same
provision which had been made for their
fellow-workers in Great Britain in similar circumstances. I have not more time,
or I would deal more exhaustively with
the points raised by hon. Members
opposite.
As regards the Whitewell scheme, in
which the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Thomas Henderson) is quite properly interested, all that I will say in
that connection is this: The Guardians
decided that they were not prepared to
continue to pay outdoor relief unless the
Government were prepared in some way
to help in a test scheme. Rather than
have these people deprived altogether of
the means of supporting themselves, the
Government, somewhat reluctantly, agreed
to support, to some little extent, the
scheme, it being clearly understood between the Government representatives
and the representatives of the Guardians
that for the conditions of employment,.or
the wages paid, the Government did not
accept any responsibiliy. That is the
correct position, and it is not necessary,
I think, to deal with it at any greater
length.

Adjournment a matter that has now assumed great importance in relation to
the business of this House. I understand
that, before many Members who are now
present entered the House, certain Standing Orders were passed regulating our
debates, and these Standing Orders provide ten allotted days for the Estimates.
We have seen the character of the discussions that have taken place here, and
those of us who are interested in the
business of this House-the Members who
sit on these benches and the Government,
or some of them, are the only people interested in the business of the Housefeel that we are robbed of those privileges that are common to all Members of
adequately discussing the vital questions
that come before the House of Commons
upon the Estimates. The only healthy
part of our proceedings here are the discussions upon the Estimates. They enable Members to exercise their right of
criticising and analyzing public expenditure and of dealing with the policy of the
various Departments and their methods
of administration.
I do not know what the reason of it
is the Government can, perhaps state it
themselves-but this Parliament differs
from every other Parliament in the world
that I know of in the fact that the
Government Members hardly every speak.
Members on the opposite benches hardly
ever contribute to the debates, and the
result is that all the speeches are confined to Members on this side. That is
an intellectual advantage, but on that
point I do not propose to say anything.

National Health Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'

The
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): When the
Government became responsible for the
administration of National Health Insurance in Northern Ireland it was decided
that there should be no disturbance of
the administrative unity of the scheme
which, from the beginning, had been established on a broad and common basis
for the United Kingdom as a whole.
rights and interests of insured persons in
Northern Ireland are linked up so completely with those of their fellow-members
in Great Britain that it would have been
disastrous if we had taken any step which
would have severed our connection with
the common scheme or attempted to base
our insurance system on any field less wide
than that of the United Kingdom. The
Government accordingly arranged that
the membership of Northern Ireland insured persons in Approved Societies operating here and in Great Britain should
remain unaltered, that our partnership in
the common central funds should con-
1459 Health Insurance Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Gordon]
tinue, and that we should retain our seat
on the National Health Insurance Joint
Committee, which is the central body
charged with co-ordinating administration
throughout the United Kingdom.
Two events have taken place to which I
should now like to refer. First, the several
Acts of Parliament governing the scheme
have been consolidated by an Act passed
at Westminster in 1924 which is the basis
of the law of Northern Ireland as well
as for England, Scotland and Wales.
Secondly, the whole operation of National
Health Insurance has been exhaustively
reviewed by a Royal Commission which
reported to the Imperial Government in
1926. Generally speaking, the Commission reported that the scheme had established its position as a permanent feature
of the social system, and that it should
be continued in the main on its present
basis.
The Commission did, however, make a
number of recommendations affecting the
machinery of the system. At this stage
it has not been found feasible to adopt
two of these recommendations, namely,
the abolition of Insurance Committees
and the partial pooling of the future
surpluses of the approved societies which
administer, the system. But, whilst the
time may not be ripe for these major
structural alterations, there are other
valuable recommendations of the Commission which it is expedient to adopt at
once.
Accordingly, a Bill to amend the Act
of 1924 in order to give effect to those
recommendations has been introduced at

of

1463 Health Insurance Bill—

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Gordon]
The Act has been continued from year
to year and was amended by the Contributory Pensions Act of 1925. The effect
is to continue a person in insurance during
unemployment subject to certain conditions. The first is that he must not have
taken up work which is not of an insurable
nature. The second condition gives the
worker the choice of two alternatives. He
may either show that he has a certain
number of contributions standing to his
credit or that during every period of unemployment he has been available for but
unable to obtain work. If these conditions were fulfilled continuation as an insured person was secured however prolonged the periods of unemployment
might be.
These temporary arrangements have
proved unsatisfactory and difficult to work
in many respects. Confusion has arisen
owing to the different dates of the termination of insurance for the purposes of
Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions, and complications and uncertainties
have arisen with regard to the benefit
rights. Further, persons have been kept
in insurance for protracted periods although they have given up employment
for reasons of their own and paid no contributions for a considerable time.
The Bill proposes to introduce a new
scheme to deal with the case of a person
who is unemployed on lines which have
been agreed with the societies. It is proposed to repeal the Prolongation Actand I want hon. Members opposite to pay particular attention to
this, because I venture to think
they will direct their arguments to
the point I am about to deal withand to substitute for the twelve months
period during which a person remains an
insured person, and the further nine
months period during which he is regarded
as insured for purposes of sanatorium
benefit and pensions, a free period of
about twenty-one months duration on the
average. It will never be less than
eighteen months from the date of a man's
last employment and may last for almost
two years.
It may be that after this free period is
ended the man may still be out of work.
In that case, if before he lost his employment he had been insured for a period
which will be prescribed, and can satisfy
the society that he has been genuinely
seeking work but unable to obtain it, he
will be granted an extension for a further
period of twelve months during which he
will be entitled to benefits at not less than
half rates. After the expiration of this
period he will cease to be an insured person.
and if he subsequently returns to employment he will be required to become a reentrant.
I will now deal with the benefits to
which a person who is continued in insurance under the provisions which I have
outlined may become entitled if ill and
without the proper number of contributions to his credit. Under the ordinary
Health Insurance Code, that man would
be regarded as being in arrears to an
extent varying with the number of stamps
lacking from his cards, and unless he
paid an arrears penalty his rate of
benefit would be reduced or possibly
suspended entirely. During the years of
intense unemployment an arrangement
was made with statutory sanction to
credit genuinely unemployed persons with
a certain number of contributions which
would prevent their rate of benefit falling below one half of the normal amount.
Approved societies were enabled to do this
by grants out of certain Health Insurance
Funds which were made available for the
purposes.
This has been a boon to workers who
have been unemployed for prolonged
periods, but again the arrangement cannot be regarded as entirely satisfactory
as it does not appear to be right that an
unemployed worker genuinely seeking
work should have his benefits reduced by
reason only of the fact that he has been
unable to obtain employment during
limited periods. Under arrangements
which the new Bill proposes, insured persons genuinely looking for insurable work
will not fall into arrears, and, if ill
during the free periods of insurance will
be entitled to the statutory benefits without regard to lack of contributions.
Grants will be made to approved
societies out of the same sources
as hitherto to enable societies to meet
the increased liabilities.
I would like to sum up the effect of
these proposals by saying that a genuinely
unemployed person is to be given a continuous period averaging two and threequarter years before his insurance can be
terminated. For twenty-one months of
1465 Health Insurance Bill-

9 MAY 1928
Second Reading
that period he will be entitled to all
benefits at full rates, and for another.
twelve months he will be entitled to
benefits at not less than half rates. If
he returns to employment before the end
of this period he avoids any break in the
continuity of his insurance both for
Health Insurance and for Contributory
Pensions. The proposals on the whole are
very generous and are to the advantage of
the unemployed worker who is genuinely
seeking work but unable to find it, and
will be much simpler in operation, eliminating much of the work arising out of
the complications of the existing system.
An important concession is proposed in
order to safeguard the pensions position
of insured persons who have grown old in
the industries of the country and because
of advancing years may become genuinely
unemployed after reaching the age of 60.
If they have been ten years in insurance
before ceasing to be employed they will
be kept in insurance for all purposes except sickness and disablement benefit so
long as they remain genuinely unemployed until they reach the age of 65 and
can then qualify for a contributory
pension.
The other proposed alterations of the
machinery of the common scheme fall into
two groups-one dealing with the internal
management of the Societies and the
other dealing with certain extensions of
benefits. In the first group are proposals
regarding the amendment of the rules of
Approved Societies, better control by the
Ministry of their administration, the
amalgamation of branches, the audit of
accounts and the regulation of the disposal of surpluses and such like matters.
The second group is the one to which
I should like to refer in more detail. It
is proposed to bring into full and equitable insurance for the first time a certain
class of people known as deposit contributors. These are people compelled to
pay the usual contributions under the Act
but who have not become members of
Approved Societies and who lodge their
cards with the Post Office. Each of these
persons has his own separate account to
which his contributions are credited, and
he can only draw benefit against the
actual amount standing to his credit.
Once the credit is exhausted he can receive no further benefit no matter how
This has always
long he remains ill.
been a blot on the insurance system, and
we propose to wipe it out.
The persons in this class are composed
of two kinds, those whom a society refuse
to accept as members because of bad
health or for other reasons and those who
refuse or neglect to join a society for
reasons best known to themselves. With
regard to persons who can join a society.
but refuse to do so, we cannot carry compulsion so far as to insist on their joining
a society. But those who would like to
join a society and get the advantage of
insurance but are not able to do so, we
proposé to form into an insurance
group of their own and provide them
with the benefits of insurance at the
ordinary statutory rates. There are
about 1,000 persons of this class of contributor in Northern Ireland, and I feel
that this section of the Act will confer a
great boon upon them.
Besides these people there are persons
who are at present excluded from insurance because they are not technically employed under a contract of service. I
refer to those who are employed under a
contract for the performance of manual
labour such as market-porters, slaughtermen, stonebreakers, tree-fellers and sharefishermen. Generally speaking, there is
a desire on the part of these people for
Health Insurance and now also, of course,
for insurance for Contributory Pensions,
and the Royal Commission was of opinion
that the advantages of insurance should
not be denied them. I think this House
will agree that it is reasonable that they
should not be ruled out on a mere technicality, but that the door should be
opened to permit them to participate in
the advantages of National Health Insurance.
It is also proposed to increase the benefits payable to insured women who cease
work on marriage. At the present
moment they are entitled to sickness
benefit for a limited period, but only at
a reduced rate of 7s 6d a week, and to
a maternity benefit within two years,
which may be reduced if contributions
are in arrears. It is thought that it is
only right that these persons should receive benefit at the full rate and that
there should be no reduction of maternity
benefit for arrears.
Health Insurance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
Again, under the law as it stands today, a person is not entitled to receive
sickness benefit while he is an inmate of
a hospital, and it is entirely within the
discretion of his society whether the benefit otherwise due to the member is paid
to his dependants. It is proposed that in
future the benefit in whole or in part
shall be paid to the dependants. I have
explained and amplified as clearly as
possible the improvements in the common
scheme which it is proposed to introduce
in accordance with the Royal Commission's findings and the wishes of the
Approved Societies, as expressed through
the Consultative Councils here and in
England and Scotland.
I wish to pass now to the domestic
matters which are dealt with in the remaining Clauses of the Bill, to which I
am sure the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. William McMullen) will give
a close and attentive hearing. Clause 2
of the Bill relates to offences and legal
proceedings, and is designed to bring the
provisions of the Health Insurance Code
in this respect into line with those contained in the Unemployment Insurance
Act. It will become an offence for
workers to assist employers in non-compliance in the matter of the payment of
contributions. Machinery will be provided for securing compliance on the part
of companies. The sale or purchase of
used insurance stamps will be punishable
by imprisonment with hard labour. The
period following the date of an offence
within which summary proceedings may
be commenced will be extended from six
months to one year. Contributions due
to the Ministry and amounts of benefit
lost by workers which, under existing
conditions cannot be recovered from employers by civil proceedings in the petty
sessions court, will be recoverable in the
county court.
Clause 3 raises from 2s 4d to 28 8d per
member per annum the amount which
Approved Societies may be required to
pay as the cost of the medical certification
and referee services, and also brings certain provisions of the Northern Ireland
Economy Act into line with the British
Act. Surplus sums in the Stamps Sales
Account are used for two purposes (1) to
assist insured persons who are in arrears
and also, (2) to recoup the Exchequer for
the cost of the provision and sale of insurance stamps. During the passage of the
Economy Bills through the Imperial and
Northern Ireland Parliaments a divergence was introduced in the order of precedence of the claims. In Great Britain
the liquidation of arrears was given the
first claim, the remaining balance, if any,
going to the Exchequer. The Northern
Ireland Economy Act is being altered to
conform to that arrangement.
I know the interest taken by Members
of this House in any scheme of social advancement or social re-organization and
their insistence upon the realization of
things not as they are but as they should
be. I have taken a considerable time to
explain what I consider is an exceedingly
complicated and technical matter in order
that no charge might be levelled against
the Ministry of Labour of introducing a
Bill without offering any explanation regarding the various Clauses. We are all
seeking to achieve the same ideal. Social
insurance is a recognition of those larger
social responsibilities, and in this Bill we
have taken a forward step to remove some
of the defects. We are here to protect
the aged and genuinely unemployed, and
to increase the benefits of those physically
unfit and, therefore, most deserving, the
deposit contributors. This Bill also embraces within our scheme further workmen who desire to make provision for
their wives and families in times of sickness and old age. I commend this Bill
and beg to move its Second Reading.

Mr. HEALY: I have very little fault

This Parliament has been described as a

There was an Insurance Commission
sitting a few years ago, to which the
Parliamentary Secretary has referred,
and one of the recommendations of the
Commission was the pooling of the surpluses of Approved Societies. I think it
an exceedingly great mistake that the
Imperial Parliament could not have legislated on those lines. That would apply
with much greater force to societies on
this side of the Channel than on the other
side, because it is obviously unfair that
two people in the same industry, in
equally good or equally bad health, will
receive different rates of benefit.
In one
case they may receive additional benefits
that are not applicable to the other at all.
There is the other point that there may
be weak societies and strong societiesand we know there are both-and a
strong society is in a much better position
to give its members additional benefits.
At the moment there is one Approved
Society in Northern Ireland that is about
to wind up its affairs and to transfer its
liabilities to another concern. Now the

Society have as much right to get the

Commission had been adopted. It is one

rejected. I agree that it will be of considerable benefit to people who are in irregular employment to have their benefits

Well, I cannot help but feel that this is

therefore think it would be a very wrong

would in effect mean this, that before we

There are certain matters that obviously
Great Britain can more fitly deal with

such as the central fund and international

The only point of very great inportance

and Tyrone (Mr. Healy), who sits opposite me, raised was about the deposit
contributors. I do not think he quite

simply this: At the present time we have
what are known as deposit contributors
Fisheries Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
They are composed of two classes. One
class is those who, for some reason best
known to themselves, could join an approved society but do not do so. That is
their own affair and we do not, therefore,
propose to interfere with them by applying compulsion. There is another class
for whom we have the greatest possible
sympathy, and those are the people who
have been rejected by the approved
societies or by their doctors. It is
those persons-about 1,000 in Northern
Ireland-for whom this Bill is going to
provide and whom it is going to place in
the same position as those who are insured
by approved societies. May I say in conclusion how gratified I am at the reception which this Measure has been
accorded?

This Clause deals with licences for the
sale of fish, and under the Clause as it
stands the individual who requires a
licence must have a certificate from a
Justice of the Peace before the Conservators will grant a licence. I think when
he receives this certificate from a Justice
of the Peace it should be obligatory on
the part of the Conservators to grant the
licence. Where the person engaged in
the business has received a certificate from
a magistrate, I think the licence should
forthwith be issued without the Conservators having the right to refuse especially considering that the Ministry will
have the right to refuse this licence.
The second and third Amendments, as
you see, will be consequential on this
matter, but I think the Ministry should
accept this alteration, as you have ample
power without leaving the right to refuse
the licence in the hands of a third party.
There does not seem to be any reason
why the Conservators should have the
right to refuse a licence when the magistrates have given this certificate, and
when the Ministry have a right to
annul these licences or to refuse to grant
them. It is for that reason that I propose the alteration as it appears upon the
Order Paper, and I think the Minister
should accept this Amendment.

on such premises, and all sales of

received.

behalf by the Ministry of Commerce,

of a rank not lower than sergeant, may

April. It seems they are not to be got

in putting down this Amendment is that
I think it is unreasonable to ask one individual to inform on another. When an

Mr. DEVLIN: I would be glad if the
Attorney-General (Mr. Babington) would
intervene at this stage, to let us know
whether he is prepared, from the legal
standpoint, to justify this Sub-clause.
Like my hon. Friends, I have never

giving information about others when the
law is broken. Here is a case of where,
according to this Sub-clause, every person who obstructs or impedes any person
in the exercise of any of the powers conferred upon him by this Clause commits
an offence. He commits an offence by
obstructing or impeding the law, and he
is legitimately entitled to suffer the
penalty for his own act, but to coerce this
person who has broken the law to include
others and to become a prosecutor of
others is, in my judgment, a grave departure from all our notions of law and
justice in these islands.
Apart altogether from that, I am en.
tirely opposed to coercing people to become informers. This is not like an
ordinary criminal offence, such as
burglary, larceny, or even murder.
These are more or less technical offences,
and to compel any person to give the
name of any other person, and to make
himself unpopular in the community in
which he lives, apart altogether from the
dishonourable action, is in my judgment
a thing that cannot be justified. If I

Supposing, for instance, that fish suspected

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
Members opposite appear to think there
is no precedent for a Clause of this kind,
but I can assure them that that is not so.
The analogy of the liquor traffic that the
hon. Member for West Belfast has given
is no analogy at all, but there is an analogy
which is almost on all fours with the Clause
in this Bill, and that is Rules and Regulations provided by Statute for marine store
dealers. Members of the Committee will
know that there are a large number of
commodities which are dealt in by marine
store dealers, including lead, iron, and
other articles, and they are very commonly
the subject of larceny. The Statute, in
order to facilitate the Crown in pursuing
their inquiries into the larceny of these
articles, has compelled a marine store
dealer to keep books, and he has got to
enter into his book the name and address
of the person from whom he purchases
articles. That is an exact analogy for the
Clause in this Bill. You might say that
any person who has fish in his custody shall
enter in a book the name and address of
the person from whom he purchased it.
Mr. COLLINS: He is already compelled to do that by Clause 7.
All
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL:
that is necessary is for him to give the
name and address verbally when he is
asked for it. It is for the purpose of
enabling the Crown to press a case in
which the Act has been infringed, and
as far as I can see, it does not affect any
principle of law, and there are cases in
which similar restrictions have been put
upon dealers in other commodities. It is
perfectly obvious that where fish is found
in possession of persons who are absolutely reputable, like railway companies,
carriers of various descriptions, etc., it
would be impossible to suggest that they
had come by it illegally, but there is
nothing wrong or contrary to justice in
asking them to disclose the name and address of the person from whom they
obtained the fish. If they give this information to the authorities, as it is their
duty to do as good citizens, then the
authorities can make further inquiries
and see whether the fish were obtained
illegally or not.

NEW CLAUSE (Use of nets, etc., for
capture of fish other than salmon, trout,
or eels).
Notwithstanding anything in this
Act, or in any other enactment to the
contrary, the Ministry of Commerce
may permit the use by the owner of a
several fishery, or by a person or persons authorized in writing by such
owner, of nets or other engines of such
size and description as may be prescribed for the capture of carp, tench,
bream, roach, perch, pike, and other
fresh-water fish, except salmon, trout,
or eels, in any specified fresh-water
river, lake, or pond (or any part
thereof), at any time of the year:
Provided that the said Ministry shall
not authorize the use of any engine of
a type or description the use of which
during the open season for salmon is
prohibited by any enactment or bylaw.

(1) The Ministry of Commerce may,

stocking of that or any other fishery;

scientific purposes, any fish of any
kind specified in the certificate.

whom a certificate is granted under this
section may, subject to the conditions
specified in the certificate, do all or any
of the things which he is authorised by
the certificate to do.

We were told when the Ulster Government took over the fisheries that everybody expected they would deal with them

NEW CLAUSE (Maintenance Orders).
Where an unmarried mother dies in
giving birth to her child, the father or
mother or other relative of the deceased,
or any public authority responsible for
the maintenance of the child, may sue
for a "maintenance order" against the

death.

CATERPILLAR PLAGUE IN
CO. FERMANAGH.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to the caterpillar plague in
County Fermanagh, and, if so, what steps
his Department is taking to counteract the
same.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): My attention has been
directed to what the hon. Member describes as the caterpillar plague in County
Fermanagh. Immediately the visitation
was reported I sent down an inspector of
the Ministry to investigate the matter.
The inspector's report shows that this
caterpillar belongs to a comparatively
rare species of butterfly which frequents
damp waste places where the weeds known
as "Devil's Bit" Scabious is allowed to
flourish. The caterpillar in the natural
state feeds only on this weed and will not
eat grass or cultivated crops. The report
also indicates that the caterpillars were
found only on an isolated area where the
weed mentioned was growing.
My scientific advisers tell me that by
the end of May or beginning of June the
caterpillars will have been transformed
into butterflies. To destroy these caterpillars effectively would necessitate the
use of a poisonous spray which would
later on obviously be dangerous to live
stock grazing on the lands. In the circumstances it is not considered necessary
or desirable to take any steps to deal with
this insect.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
right hon. Gentleman's reply I would like
to ask him whether he is alreday aware
of the fact that there is a market for these
caterpillars in England, and that already
at least one person in Northern Ireland is

CONTRACTS.
2. Mr. KYLE (on behalf of Mr. W.
McMullen) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that the
Kilkeel Board of Guardians do not invite
public tenders for the supply of the
various commodities required by the
Guardians where the value exceeds £10;
and whether he will state what steps he
proposes to take to ensure that all those
desiring to tender shall have an equal
opportunity.
MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): So far as the
Ministry is aware, the Kilkeel Board of
Guardians and the Governors of the
Mourne District Hospital publish advertisements for tenders for supplies over
£10 in value monthly in accordance with
the Regulations; but in regard to a recent
order for coal they appear merely to have
invited quotations from local firms.
for
The Ministry, on a former occasion,
pointed out that advertisements
tenders for the supply of coal should be
published, and the action of the Governors
on this occasion has been referred to the
Local Government Auditor as the lowest
quotation received was not accepted.

Mr. ARCHDALE: While the function of the Ministry is to foster in every
practical way the agricultural industry
as a whole, our policy is to concentrate
on those branches which are of the greatest economic importance. Viewed from
this standpoint live stock and its
products come first. The estimated
value of the total output of agricultural produce from farms in Northern
Ireland during 1925 was:-Live stock,
£5,445,000; milk and dairy produce,
£3,100,000; poultry, eggs and feathers,
£3,370,000; wool, £58,000, making for
live-stock and live-stock products
£11,973,000. The total for farm crops,
including fruit and vegetables, was
£3,300,000, so the Committee will see
that the branch of live-stock and livestock products produced more than all
the farm crops put together. They
make 78.4 per cent., while all farm
crops and fruit and vegetables come only
to 21.6 per cent. The figures stated as
the values of the output for farm crops
do not include the value of the produce
given to live stock on the farms.
In passing I may draw your attention again to the fact that the value of
each of the groups comprised under live
stock (live stock, milk and dairy produce,
poultry, eggs and feathers) +xceeded the
value of the total output of farm crops.
During the present depression certain
branches of live stock have been well
maintained, as far as prices are concerned
compared with pre-war values. I refer
chiefly to pigs, sheep, store cattle, dairy
products, poultry and eggs. If we compare the average increase in value as between the two periods 1911-1913 and
1922-26 of crops we find that in Northern
Ireland live stock and their products sl:ow
a percentage increase of 23 per cent. over
crops. Crops in Northern Ireland show
an increase of 45 per cent. and live stock
and live-stock products show an increase
of 68 per cent. Therefore, there is a
majority-
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Is
this in price or in volume?
Mr. ARCHDALE: In price. That is,
tillage crops 45 per cent. and live-stock
products 68 per cent. It has been proved
over and over again that stock farming
is the real basis of crop farming, and it is
our continual endeavour to foster animal
farming as much as we possibly can.
The successful development of this
branch can be accomplished by increasing
the numbers of breeding stock, by improving quality and by producing animals
that reach maturity at an early age.
Our chief producers of cattle, sheep,
pigs and poultry are the small farmersthe men with holdings of 50 acres and
under. It is an extraordinary thing how
clearly it is proved that farms of 50 acres
and under were the ones that rear more
stock than the big farms in Northern Ireland.
The big farms seem to be given
over to the feeding of older stores and fat
cattle.
Out of 104,000 agricultural holdings in Northern Ireland 89,000 are 50
acres and under. These small farmers,
who are the backbone of our agricultural

Since September last the Ministry, in

The object of introducing these sires is
to improve the quality of our cattle and
sheep and to produce animals that mature
at an early age. Such improvements are
essential if we are to maintain our position on the British market in face of
growing competition. Second- or thirdrate animals can only be sold at inferior
prices and are a dead loss to the producers.

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: What are

Mr. ARCHDALE: An enemy coming

not a twentieth part of the number of
subsidized bulls we have here. We have
far more premium bulls than any other
country. The necessary improvement in
quality and early maturity can only be
brought about by means of superior sires
and by steadily grading up female stock.
So far as beef and mutton are concerned
public taste is changing. Small joints
are now much more in demand than large
ones, and young beef and mutton of high
quality now command much higher prices
than older animals. Early maturing
stock means quicker return and considerable saving in food and thus enables
farmers to keep more breeding stock, that
is, milch cows and ewes.
Milk production is an important section
of the live-stock industry and one which
is capable of great development to the advantage both of producers and consumers.
Improvement can be brought about by
keeping more cows and by selecting
animals with high milk records and by
breeding from these cows and high-class
dairy bulls whose dams and sires also have
high milk records. Farmers who have
dairy stock almost invariably keep pigs
and poultry to consume the separated
milk and buttermilk. Consequently, by
increasing the dairy stock we automatically increase pigs and poultry.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ARCHDALE: Our milk recording work is making satisfactory progress,
although it still falls far short of what is
necessary. In 1921 we had six Societies
with 1,216 cows recorded; in 1928 sixtysix Societies with 13,365 cows recorded.
However, as there are 249,000 cows in the
country there is still much ground to be
made up.
The average yield of each recorded cow approaches 700 gallons per
annum, whereas the average yield of the
cows of the country as a whole is little
more than 400 gallons. Therefore, all
the cows were up to the standard of the
recorded cows we would increase our total
production by seventy million gallons
which, at 6d per gallon, would amount to
£1,750,000-a sum which shows the scope
there is for development.

The variety most extensively grown in
Northern Ireland is "Arran Victory"
(immune), the area planted with this
variety alone being 51,800 acres
roughly one-third of the total potato
area. At first there was a prejudice
against this and other coloured varieties
on the British market, but the Ministry
by propaganda work in Great Britain has
succeeded in popularizing this immune
variety to the great advantage of growers.

Mr. ARCHDALE: One aspect of our
educational schemes may be of interest to
the Members. I refer to the work of the
agricultural overseers. There are now 16
of these officers employed. They are
young men of sound practical knowledge,
who have attended agricultural classes,
but who are less highly qualified than
agricultural instructors. These young
men live and work in the poorest and
most backward districts in the country.
There are, for example, six of them employed in the mountain areas in Counties
Derry and Tyrone, others are at work in
the Glens of County Antrim, in Scuth
Armagh, in the Mourne districts and also
in County Fermanagh. Very good results
are accruing from this development of cur
work, which gives advice on manures,
seeds, feeding of animals, etc., and brings
assistance to the doors of a large number
of industrious small farmers who, in the
past, through force of circumstances, have
had no opportunity of keeping abreast of
modern improvements.
It is certainly the only way of getting
amongst the numerous small farmers in
these parts. These people do not as a
rule read the papers nor do they see the
benefits of our research work, hints and
recommendations. These young fellows
call at the houses, and show the farmers
anything being brought out, and get
them to see the test plots planted in the
various districts. Otherwise the small
farmers have no means of keeping abreast
with modern improvements.
Our research and educational work is
steadily growing and has already borne
fruit which is having a direct influence in
solving agricultural problems, and will, as
it develops, continue, perhaps slowly but
surely, to assist agriculturists in procuring a wider and sounder knowledge so as
to enable them to overcome many of the
difficulties with which they are daily
contending.
