Without going into detail it may
desirable to indicate briefly a few of the
numerous ways in which our research and
experimental work is directly benefiting
the farmer.
Hon. Members will have realized from
my introductory remarks the vital importance of the animal side of our agricultural industry. It is natural, therefore,
that my Ministry should lay great stress
upon the development of our research
work on animal nutrition. It is essential
to realize that this work is closely related
to our live-stock improvement schemes.
Progress in breeding must go hand in
hand with progress in nutrition. Failure
to progress in one direction seriously retards any developments that may be
made in the other.
Our
One of the Ministry's objects in placing
superior bulls throughout the country is
to improve our dairy cows. That is to
say, to make our cows capable of producing 800 or 900 gallons of milk instead of
the general average of 400 gallons.
farmers are breeding such cows and in
increasing numbers every year. The
feeding of 800- or 900-gallon cows is
however, a very different proposition to
the feeding of 400-gallon cows. The cows
are not proportionally greater in size, and
as it is a law of nature that something
cannot be obtained for nothing we have
had to face the problem of how to feed
these cows. My Ministry has developed
a simple system of balanced rations which
enables farmers to feed their cows according to their milk yield. Having tested
out the system we have been rapidly
teaching our farmers how to use and
apply it. The progress that is being
made and the possibilities of this work are
well illustrated by many striking examples of increased yields which have
been brought to our notice.
Another example, which illustrates the
work of our research division, is the development which is taking place in
Northern Ireland in the production of
early-maturing or baby beef. The
first report of our. experimental work
was published in 1925. Now, in
addition to the special annual sales
of baby beef cattle held at the
Belfast markets, there is a steady and
increasing supply of this type of beef
coming on to our local markets every
week. The importance of the work will
be realized from the fact that early-maturing beef or this type is the only beef
which in the English market commands
a price substantially higher than the best
imported beef. Baby beef has the
further important economic advantage of
being a product which our chief foreign
competitors cannot produce. The extent
to which the production of baby beef has
been taken up by our farmers, particularly in County Down, is a most encouraging sign and is evidence that the
farming community is not so backward
in adopting new methods as is frequently
stated,
and
For some time our Chemical
Animal Nutrition Division has been exploring problems connected with the
supply of minerals, that is, lime, phos
phates, etc., in the rations of farm
animals. It is too early to say much
about the work, but it may be of interest
to indicate that there is increasing evidence which shows that many of the problems, such as breeding difficulties, which
arise with highly developed cattle, are
due to inadequate supplies of mineral
salts, particularly in the winter rations.
Some practical results are already beginning to emerge. For example, we know
how to maintain large herds of breeding
sows on farms where little or no milk is
available-milk being the main source of
mineral salts for young animals. Again,
we have evidence that the size of the egg
laid by the hen is determined by the
mineral content of her rations and by altering the mineral content it has been
possible to reduce the number of secondgrade eggs from over 40 per cent. to less
than 10 per cent.
It will be of interest to hon. Members
to know that the Ministry's investigations have thrown considerable light on
the causes of sterility in cattle. Steps
have been taken by the Ministry to demonstrate to the veterinary profession in
Northern Ireland suitable methods of
treatment, and those methods have met
with a most gratifying measure of success.
In co-operation with the Animal
Diseases Research Station in Scotland,
experiments relating to braxy in sheep
were carried out in County Antrim, and
1,150 sheep were vaccinated. The subsequent death rate from braxy amongst
the unvaccinated sheep was 6.25 per
cent. as compared with .22 amongst the
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
10 MAY 1928
vaccinated. The results were regarded
as very satisfactory and vaccination is
now carried out on a large scale by farmers in the Glens districts in County
Antrim.
It is notorious that the consumption
of milk in the British Isles is much less
per capita than in the countries of the
New World and in the Scandanavian
States. The low consumption in Northern Ireland and the British Isles is not
a question of price, but of keeping
qualities. Milk is one of the most difficult products to handle, because of
its poor keeping qualities. As a
consequence, purchases of milk are
reduced to a minimum. This is a
great misfortune in view of the fact
that it is one of the cheapest foodstuffs
on the market, and from a nutritional
point of view the most valuable.
It is
for this reason that we have been exploring the possibilities of producing, under
our conditons, natural raw milk which
will keep sweet for several days. Under
the Sale of Milk Act which came into
operation 1st January last, a beginning has been made in the Production of
Grade A tuberculin-tested milk under
Government licence. The producers are
already taking considerable interest in
this matter, and supplies are coming into Belfast, Portadown, Limavady and
Coleraine, as well as into several of our
hospitals. It is only by placing on the
market a pure supply derived from
healthy cows free from tuberculosis, and
capable of keeping sweet for several days,
that we can hope to expand the liquid
milk trade.
Another important problem which falls
within the survey of this new division is
the very difficult one associated with the
condition of the milk supply to our
creameries. We can only hold our
butter markets if we can succeed in putting on the market a uniform and firstclass article. Scrupulous cleanliness in
the creamery is essential, but it is of little
avail if the milk itself, as it comes from
the farmer, is not a first-class article
from the point of view of cleanliness. I
venture to say that cleanliness in our milk
supply is of far greater importance today than quality. My Ministry proposes to direct its attention to this question. We hope to devise simple and
readily applied means whereby the
creameries will be able to determine the
relative cleanliness of the milk delivered
to them, and we hope thereby that it will
be possible for them to assist in the allimportant work by offering an inducement to the farmers to produce a cleaner
supply.
Owing to attacks of fungus diseases, the
fruit industry in Northern Ireland, particularly apples and gooseberries, has
been in a precarious condition. Research
and experimental work on these crops has
resulted in the discovery of efficient and
cheap measures for controlling diseases
by the adoption of modern spraying
methods, thus enabling fruit growers to
prevent these diseases and to procure a
crop.
Finally, as the Committee will observe,
the Agricultural Services Estimate shows
an increase of £3,000 odd, as compared
with 1927-8. Broadly, this increase is
due to:-
-
(1) An increase of £1,000 in Sub-head
F2, grants to Agricultural Societies;
and
(2) An increase of £2,000 in the three
Forestry Sub-heads, J, J1, and J2.
It will also be noticed that we have a
new division to cope with the dairying
industry, that is the dairy bacteriological
division. Otherwise there are no changes
in the Estimate list. I will endeavour
to answer any questions that may arise
as we go along. I beg to move.

to

I protest with all the vigour at my command against a body capable of such a

My remarks with regard to this Vote

When we met at Stormont I think, if

I would also like to congratulate the

hy letting the farmers know it would be

national life, namely, our industrial conditions and our agricultural conditions
and the only opportunities that Members

Estimates. To-day we were told that

to be taken of other opportunities, but
even those subjects that might be discussed have not been dealt with in a
manner satsfactory to us, and certainly
they have not been dealt with by the

EX-SOLDIERS' COTTAGES IN
LISBELLAW DISTRICT.
2. Colonel WOODS (for Mr. Cooper)
asked the Minister of Finance
whether he is aware that several exsoldiers in Lisbellaw district have applied to him for ex-soldiers' cottages without result; and whether he will ask the
proper authority to reconsider their
applications.
Mr. BARBOUR: I have been asked to
reply.
As the hon. Member is aware, all
matters concerning cottages for ex-Servicemen in Ireland are under the control of
the Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust, which is an Imperial Service, and
consequently questions in respect thereof
should be addressed to the Imperial House
of Commons. As a matter of courtesy,
the Trustees have informed me that when
the present contemplated programme for
the erection of ex-Servicemen's cottages in
Northern Ireland is completed the Trust
will consider whether the funds (if any)
then at their disposal permit of the erection of any additional cottages, in which
event the claims of Lisbellaw for cottages
will not be overlooked.

1927, in which reference is made to the

expense a number of lunatics who are not

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Report of the
Committee of the Belfast Mental Hospital
to which the hon. Member refers has not
yet been received in the Ministry, but I
may say that I have received a resolution
from the Committee on the subject, and

I am aware of the five years' residence

applied in Northern Ireland, would have
in the case of the Belfast Mental Hospital
or any of the other District Lunatic

UNBOUGHT TENANTS-
RESULT OF NEGOTIATIONS.
5. Mr. MARK asked the Prime Minister
whether he is now in a position to announce the result of the negotiations between the British Government and the
Government of Northern Ireland regarding the unbought tenants; and
whether the representations put forward
by the Ulster Farmers' Union have been
embodied in the settlement.
The PRIME MINISTER: Through
the courtesy of the Secretary of State for
the Home Department, with whom I
have been in telegraphic communication,
•I am privileged to give contemporaneously with the answer he is sending to Mr. D. D. Reid's question in the
British House of Commons this afternoon the terms of the agreement which
has been reached by the two Governments.
Briefly, it provides that all tenants
whose holdings have not been dealt with
on or before the Appointed Day (27th
May, 1929) will be placed in the same
financial position as they would be if
their holdings had been dealt with on
that date.
The arrangements to enable this to be
carried out will involve the continued
payment of the present rent till each
holding is finally vested, but a refund of
the difference between the amount of the
annuity ultimately payable to the Government and the current rent from the
27th May, 1929, till the date of vesting
will then be made to the tenants. Furthermore, the term of the land purchase
annunity will run as from 27th May,
1929.
The work of vesting holdings in the
Commission will be continued with all
possible expedition, and the outstanding
cases will be progressively disposed of
within a period of three years from the
date mentioned, by which time with certain possible exceptions which may present special difficulties, the completion
of land purchase in Northern Ireland
will be effected.

ALLOTTED DAYS FOR ESTIMATES.
6. Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL (for Mr.
Devlin) asked the Prime Minister whether
he is prepared to recommend the House
to introduce changes in the Standing
Orders, so as to increase the number of
Allotted Days for the discussion of the
Estimates.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have given
this matter careful consideration and have
compared the practice prevailing at
Westminster with that adopted by this
House.
Allowing for the difference in length of
our Parliamentary day and for the totals
of the respective Estimates, the actual
number of hours allocated for the discussion of our 33 Estimates involving under
£7,000,000 is relatively twelve times as
many as are allocated at Westminster for
the dicussion of 126 Estimates involving
over £400,000,000.
It has to be borne in mind that in comparison with this House there are seventeen times the number of Members in the
British House of Commons.
It will, I think, be generally agreed that
the Committee which drafted our Standing Orders made ample, and indeed
generous, provision for the most exhaustive examination of our Estimates.
I am, therefore, not prepared to adopt
the suggestion of the hon. Member.

8. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: To

May
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:

The PRIME MINISTER:
hand the hon. Member the answer.
I will
The following is the reply:-
The names of Members of this House
to whom invitations have been issued to
have the honour of meeting His Grace the
Governor at lunch at Stormont Castle,
prior to the laying of the foundation stone
of the new Parliament and Administrative Building on the 19th instant are
The Speaker, The Ministers of Finance,
Home Affairs, Labour, Agriculture, and
Commerce, The Chairman of Committees,
The Attorney-General, The Chief Whip,
The Leader of the Opposition, The Leader
of the Nationalist Party and the hon.
Lady Member for Derry.
The names of Senators are -The
Speaker, The Leader of the Senate (Viscount Charlemont), the Marquess of
Londonderry (H.M.L. Co. Down), The
Viscount Massereene and Ferrard
(H.M.L. Co. Antrim), The Viscount
Bangor, Sir Thomas Dixon (H.M.L.
Belfast), The Right Hon. the Lord Mayor
of Belfast and the Mayor of Derry.
One hundred and fifty invitations have
been issued (including ladies). Owing to
accommodation being limited and to the
fact that on a State occasion of this
character it is customary to extend
hospitality to representatives of the
Church, the British Government, the
Forces of the Crown, the Judiciary, H.M.
Lieutenants, Members of the Imperial
Parliament (Lords and Commons), the
Civil Service, Queen's University, distinguished visitors and those immediately
concerned with the actual design and
erection of the building. I regret to say
that it was found impossible to extend the
list.
I may inform the hon. Gentleman, however, that every Member of the Senate and
of the House of Commons will be supplied
with numbered seats for himself and his
wife on the covered stand and will be
invited to tea at the conclusion of the
ceremony.

As the Committee are aware, the
School Sites Act enables limited owners
to make leases of land not exceeding in
extent one acre at a nominal rent for
the purposes of the erection of schools.
The purpose
of Clause 1 of the present
Bill is to extend that power to enable
such limited owners to make leases of
land at a nominal rent on the same terms
where a school is already erected on
the land. It occurred to me it
might be
to extend that
power to enable such limited owners
make leases of land subject to
similar conditions for a playground
attached to the school. A'case came to
my notice where a school itself was held
under a lease and where it was proposed
to take in a little piece of ground adjoining in order to provide a playground
for the school. The actual wording of
the School Sites Act did not cover that
and the actual wording of Clause 1
of this Bill did not cover it. I
thought it would be somewhat of
an improvement, if I may say So,
on the Clause if it were extended
to provide power to make leases of little
pieces of ground for playgrounds as well
as to make leases of ground for the
school itself. It is largely a conveyancing lawyer's Amendment, aud I suggest
to the Committee that it would be an
improvement on the Bill.
Mr. COLLINS: Speaking from the
Opposition Benches I support this

think after the clear description by the

Mr. BLACK: I beg to move in page
1, line 12, at end add as

"The
described in the Leases for

Schools (Ireland) Act, 1881, shall (in
addition to the power of making leases
conferred by that Act or by that Act as

power to

Provided that every lease under the provisions of this sub-section shall reserve
the best rents that can reasonably be
obtained, regard being had to any money
laid out or to be laid out on the premises
leased and generally to the circumstances of the case, and the provisions
of sections five, six and seven of the
Leases for Schools (Ireland) Act, 1881,
shall apply to every such lease.'
This also, I may say, is a conveyancing
lawyer's Amendment. There is just one
slight slip in the Amendment as printed
on the Paper. In the second line of the
proviso the word "rent" should be
inserted instead of "rents." The reason
I venture to suggest this Amendment to
the Committee is because of certain
technical legal difficulties in the way of
limited owners making leases of land for
schools and playgrounds. If limited
owners want to make a long lease-that is
a lease for 99 years--for the purposes of
the erection of a school it is necessary,
unless there is a special power in the
settlement to apply to the Court of
Chancery. If such limited owners want
to make a lease of ground which is not
a lease for building purposes but for a
playground it cannot be done under the
existing law unless there is special power
in the settlement. My Amendment
would give, I think, a convenient power
and not a very widely extended power.
The design of the Amendment is that such
limited owners should be allowed to make
leases for every school or playground.
I have not confined it to one acre.
I recognize that present day ideas are
different to what they were fifty years
ago, and it may be desirable to make
leases for a greater extent than one acre.
I have provided, just as it would be in
the case of a limited owner making a
lease under the Settled Land Acts, that
the lease should reserve the best rent
that can be obtained, so that no damage
would be done to the remainder of the
Settlement. It is further provided that
leases should only be made to the education authorities. I think the Committee will agree that this is not a case in
which any injury could be done to any
owners, especially as the Ministry of
Education have to approve every transaction which it is proposed to carry out.
The whole design of the Clause is a very
limited extension of the existing power
under the Settled Land Act, 1882, which
I think would greatly facilitate the
taking of ground for schools and playgrounds either in the country or cities.
Mr. COLLINS: I support this
Amendment.
Mr. ROBB: The Government accept
the Amendment.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF.
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): This Financial Resolution
arises on Sub-section 3 of Section 1 of the
Bill, a Sub-section which is designed to
give authority for the necessary Exchequer Grant-in-Aid of the expenses of
benefits and administration to be made:
(1) in respect of increased benefits to
certain deposit contributors, and (2) In
respect of benefits to certain additional
classes of insured persons created by the
proposed new law.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Gordon) in his
Second Reading statement has already
touched upon the changes in the law proposed by the Imperial Bill in this connection. Shortly, the changes are
Deposit contributors who by reason of the
state of their health cannot obtain
admission to Approved Societies are
to be included in a special section,
and insured for the normal benefits
of the Act. Additional funds will
be necessary for this purpose, and it
is proposed to obtain them by diverting
certain sums forming part of the Deposit
Contributors' Fund together with the
interest on the balances in the fund,
sources which at present not available for
this purpose.
These sums will in future
be paid into the account of the special
deposit contributors' section, and as they
will enable extra benefits to be paid they
will attract a grant from the Exchequer
in aid of the cost of those benefits and
of the expenses of administration. It is
estimated that the total amount of the
new State grant on account of the special
section of deposit contributors will amount
to approximately £100 per annum.
The Bill further provides that the interest which has accumulated in the
Deposit Contributors' Fund up to 31st
December, 1927-subsequent interest is to
go to the special deposit contributors'
section as explained earlier shall be
credited to the Reserve Suspense Fund,
the main purpose of which is to provide
credits of capital sums in respect of new
entrants into insurance. The actual expenditure of this money on benefits and
expenses of administration will not take
place immediately, but will be spread
over a considerable period in the future.
The relative Exchequer liability, in conformity with the actual expenditure, will
also be spread over a considerable number
of years, and is estimated at approximately
£1,200.
It is estimated that the addition of the
two classes of insured persons to be created
will have the effect of bringing ultimately
into compulsory insurance under Clause
17 of the British Bill about 1,000 additional persons in Northern Ireland, and
the additional Exchequer liability involved is estimated at £280 per annum,
after the expiry of the usual waiting
periods. I beg to move.

those eels which are migrating and consequently have attained full growth, or
at any rate are ready to return to the sea.
It appears these eels are capable of being
kept in boxes in confinement for a comparatively extended period without suffering much detriment, and so it has been the
practice of the owners of these eel wiers
to keep their catches in boxes, in order to
take advantage of the most favourable
market conditions in selling their catch.
But I am informed that these boxes must
he kept in running water. In other
words, owing to the conditions as they
actually exist, the weir proprietor is able
to take advantage of this, but the fishermen, on whose behalf this plea is now put
forward, are unable to take advantage of
it as they have no facilities for keeping
these eel boxes in running water. Now,
the close season for the eels runs from
10th January until the 31st of March,
and in order to allow these eel weir proprietors to take advantage of the market
conditions, although the close season begins on the 10th of January, they are
allowed, with a view to selling these eels,
which presumably have been caught prior
to that date, to keep them in boxes between the 10th of January and the end of
March. In that way, I believe, they are
able to take very good advantage of the
demand existing in the English markets.
Of course, the presumption is that these
eels were caught during the open season
and kept in the way I have described, and
that is giving them ample opportunity for
their legitimate catch during the open
season.
Then in order that there should be a
complete break, and in order to provide
for proper administrative control, this
Bill provides that no one shall be allowed
to have in their possession any eel during
1649.

Mr. LEEKE: I beg to move the rejection of this Bill, because it is of no
advantage to the fishery trade and it
does not protect their interests one way
or another. I think most of the Members of this House will have noticed that
a meeting was held last week of the
fishermen around the coasts of Antrim
and Derry which was attended by represensative men engaged in the fishing industry, and the poorer fishermen were all
there. They passed a resolution, which,
I think, was forwarded to the Minister
of Commerce, asking him to keep this
Bill back until such time as they would
have an opportunity to fully consider the
various Clauses of the Measure so that
they could put forward suggestions for a
Bill which might be of benefit to them
instead of a disadvantage. I do not
know what reply the Minister sent, but
at any rate the fishermen were pretty
strong in their language-and I would
point out that a large percentage of them
were Unionists-and they passed a resolution to the effect that at the next
election not one of them would
support a candidate who was in favour
of that Bill. When the whole of the
people interested are so stronly against
it, I should like to ask the Minister if
he intends to persist in carrying into
effect a Bill which is so hostile to the interests of the fishermen. The only
interests backing this Bill are the river
fishermen, but there is not a single clause
in the whole Bill that is of advantage to
fishermen.
There is one part of the Bill to which
I take strong exception, and that is the
Clause which gives officials the right to
go into any railway station, or wharf,
and seize and examine fish. That is a
very large power to place in the hands
of any official. It will be very harmful
to handle in that way fish that are being
shipped from this country. The officials
should have been told to exercise supervision over the fish at the point at which
they were loaded, and not to take them
out of railway stations, wharves, docks,
or any other place. I agree with the
marking of labels, because I have always
thought that fish from this country did
not get a fair show in the British markets. Only last week I noticed fish
shipped from Coleraine by what are the
largest salmon fishery owners in the
United Kingdom, if not in the world,
and the only fishery owners who are likely
to benefit under the provisions of this
Bill, namely, the Foyle and Bann
Fisheries, and on the top of the boxes
being shipped by these people from Ulster
were the words, clearly branded, “Atlantic Salmon." Another witness of that
was my colleague, the Member for Derry,
who sits on the opposite benches.
think the Government should take some
steps to stop the branding of Ulster fish
in this way by practically the only people
who will reap any benefit from this Bill.
I ask that this Bill should be withdrawn altogether, and that all the fishery
interests concerned should be called together and their views obtained. Then
a Bill could be framed which would be
of some advantage to the fishery industry of Ulster, and which could be passed
with the general consent of the whole

in Ulster. I should also like to draw

I showed then the economic advantages
that would result from the use of bag

nets, and the Member for Tyrone and

Mr. HARBISON: I want to join with

On very broad lines I would oppose the

this House, very often in regard to
Amendments that are proposed, and,
therefore, it may seem rather ungracious
for the Opposition to move and support
the rejection of the Bill on the Motion
for the Third Reading. I do think we
appreciate the way in which the right
hon. Gentleman tried to meet the objections put forward on the Second Reading
and during the Committee stage of this
Bill, and the concessions he has made on
behalf of the Government; but at the
same time I feel that there is no other
course left open to me, even with those
concessions, but to oppose the Third
Reading.
The right hon. Gentleman said that
the object of this Bill was to preserve
our valuable fisheries in Northern Ireland, and to develop them and promote
them. I do not know how this Bill is
going to carry out the object that the
right hon. Gentleman said the Government had in view in introducing it. As
has been pointed out, the Report of the
Royal Commission on salmon fishing in
England and Scotland recommended in
1902 that it was absolutely necessary for
the preservation of the fisheries that netting in narrow waters-that is, in the
rivers should be restricted or prohibited, and that on the other hand,
fishing in the sea was to be
couraged by the
enremoval of
the
prohibition of fixed engines, otherwise
bag nets, on the sea coast outside the
mouths of rivers. I think the House
will admit that sea fishing should be as
unhampered as possible, and that the
place where prohibition is necessary is in
the narrow waters, because with the fixed
engines that these companies are permitted to use in our rivers at present it is
almost impossible for the salmon to escape.
I would urge the right hon. Gentleman
to reconsider the effect of this Bill with
regard to the use of bag nets. In 1863
the rights of these fishermen to use these
nets were taken away, and that drove the
fishermen back to the most primitive
mode of fishing by drift nets, which can
only be carried on under certain conditions. That made it nearly impossible
for those men to earn a living. The right
hon. Gentleman in the Committee stage,
in trying to justify that, said that it
would be a matter of robbing Peter to pay
Paul. But why should the rights of these
fishermen not be restored to them again?
The taking of fish in the open sea, even
with these bag nets, could never affect
the supply of fish the way the taking
of fish in the rivers would do. I hold
that there has been a very good case
made out for these men, that they should
have restored to them the rights that were
taken from them in 1863.
I also wish to protest against Part 3, of
Clause 17.
A court of summary jurisdiction,
when trying any offence under the
Fisheries Acts, or under this Act, shall
be constituted of a resident magistrate.
There is no mistake at all about it, that
the number of prosecutions brought
against farmers for purely technical offences. such as allowing flax water to
run into streams, has had a very bad
effect on the growing of flax in Northern
Ireland. What the hon. Member for
Derry, who sits on the Government
benches (Mr. Mark), has said is quite
true. that numbers of farmers, through
these prosecutions, have entirely given up
the growing of flax, and have not grown
flax for years.
As he said, the putting
of this power into the hands of the resident magistrates may not affect these prosecutions, but that will be the construction put on it by the country people.
Fisheries Bill-
Third Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. G. Henderson]
The present bench of magistrates, knowing the local circumstances and the local
conditions, should be in a better position

who has no knowledge of any of these
things. I do feel that if this placing of
power in the hands of the resident magistrate should result in an increase of fines
in these cases it will have a very deterrent effect on the growing of flax in the
Ulster area.
I do not want to labour this question,
as it has been put before the House by
other hon. Members, but I would ask the

even now, the Government would not be

and the recommendations of these Reports

Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:

Mr. POLLOCK: This is a Measure
which is directed to the promotion of four
different subjects, and I think I had better
outline in advance what these subjects are.
There is, first, the appointment of arbitrators for the valuation of land taken by
public authorities under compulsion.
The second is the appointment of a
Government chemist for the Province.
The third is a more definite method of
auditing the accounts of educational endowments, and the fourth is the appointment of officers in connection with the
probating of small estates. It is anticipated that the effect of the Bill will be not
only to improve administration in some
small particulars, but also to enable some
slight economies to be effected in regard to
some of the services mentioned in the Bill.
Some of these matters have been under
consideration by the Ministry and myself
for a number of years past, but they were
not thought of sufficient importance to
bring before the House individually. The
opportunity was awaited of the introduction of a Bill to cover a number of small
points of the same nature which crop up
from time to time. Such an opportunity
has now occurred.
In the first place the Bill proposes to
make a small change in the method of
appointing official arbitrators to decide
the value of land compulsorily acquired by
local authorities, where agreement has not
been reached between the acquiring authority and the owner in regard to price. Examples of the kind of compulsory acquisition to which I refer are acquisitions
under the Labourers Acts, under private
Acts of Parliament promoted by local
authorities, such as the Belfast Corporation, or the acquisition of land for road
widening purposes under the Bill which
has recently passed through this House.
The existing system of appointment of
arbitrators was set up by the Acquisition
of Land (Assessinent of Compensation)
Act, 1919, under which a panel
of arbitrators was to be selected SO
far as Ireland was concerned by
the Lord Chief Justice, the Master
of the Rolls and the President of
the Surveyors' Institute in Ireland. This,
as you see, was carried into effect about a
year or a year and a half prior to th
transfer of the Parliament to ourselves.
These arbitrators were to hold office for
certain periods, and while holding office
were not to engage in private practice,
Under that Act there was set up for all
Ireland one whole-time official arbitrator,
because clearly there was insufficient work
in Ireland for a regular panel of persons.
When the Government of Northern Ire-

of the Lord Chief Justice and the
President of the Surveyors' Institution in
Ireland, and which removed the proviso
in the original Act which prevented the
members of the panel from engaging in
private practice. As a consequence of
this Act of 1922 certain persons having
knowledge of the value of land, varying in
number from seven to eight, were nominated, and as arbitrations came forward
members of the panel took their turn in
carrying out the work.
I should pehaps here state that the 1919
Act as continued by our own Act made one
important change in respect of these
arbitrations from the arrangement which
existed previously, that is to say, that upon
questions of fact there is no appeal from
the decision of an official arbitrator, but
there is an appeal to the Supreme Court in
case any particular question of law arises
which may prove to be debatable.
From the outset, although the work
itself, so far as I am aware, has been satisfactorily performed by the panel of
arbitrators, one real difficulty has arisen.
That is to say, that the amount of work
which came round to each member of the
panel in rotation has been extremely small.
The panel, therefore, in its negotiations
with the Ministry of Finance, which was
the Department responsible for fixing the
rate of remuneration to be paid, felt that
for occasional work of this character no
other course was open to it but to charge
what it considered to be appropriate fees
for work of a casual nature. These fees
have always, in my opinion, been of that
class which I think in the medical profession are termed euphemistically "good
fees," that is to say, they were very high.
The result has been very unfortunate, because we found ourselves perfectly powerless against the charges that were made.
We could not reduce, nor could
succeed in getting the valuators to reduce
the standard of the fees which they
charged.
we
In consequence, representations have
constantly been made to me for the last
two years by some dozen Rural District
Councils, as well as by the Association of
Rural District Councils, by the Coleraine Chamber of Commerce and by
Members of this House, that some steps
should be taken to relieve local authorities of the initial expenditure involved
in connection with that part of the compensation for land which went in fees
payable to my Ministry designed to
cover the cost of administration.
quite a recent case a local authority
definitely declined to pay the fees
In
which the arbitrator was collecting on
behalf of my Ministry, and a compromise
had to be effected in order to prevent an entire dead-lock. That was
very unsatisfactory. I have, therefore,
after the most careful consideration,
come to the conclusion that the inherent
difficulty, that is to say that of finance,
in the present system could only be overcome by making the amount of work so
great as to make it worth while for the
arbitrators to accept more reasonable
fees in respect of arbitration than the
present which bear so heavily on the local
authorities concerned.
The Bill, therefore, proposes that in
lieu of a panel the Minister of Finance
shall have power to nominate one or
more persons having special knowledge
of the valuation of land in Northern Ireland to act as arbitrators in cases where
land is being compulsorily acquired by
local authorities. By this means I anticipate being able to arrange a more reasonable rate of payment, and at once to reduce
the scale of fees chargeable against local
authorities. The Bill does not propose
to alter the present system where acquisition by anyone but a local authority is
involved. For example, arbitrations in
respect of acquisition by a Government
Department will not come under the provisions of this Bill, because it might be
held to be improper that a Government
Department should nominate an arbitrator where its own interests are involved.
Therefore, that is excluded from the terms
of the Measure. I anticipate, therefore,
that I will have the full support of the
House in the objects we have in view, that
is, to reduce the cost to local authorities
in the case of land compulsorily acquired
for a public purpose. That is the purport
of Clause 1, which I have dealt with at
some considerable length in order that the
House may fully understand the nature of
the change and the interest in which the
change is proposed to be made.
Administrative Provisions Bill-

14 MAY 1928
Second Reading
I come now to Clause No. 2 of the Bill,
and it is à very simple matter.
It proposes to appoint a Government Chemist in
Northern Ireland. The position here has
been somewhat curious in the past, and the
Clause is designed to cover up an omission arising out of the Government of
Ireland Act. Under the Finance Act, 1921,
passed by the Imperial Government on
4th August, 1921, the "principal Government Chemist at the Government Laboratory" (to use the words of the Act) was
made the authority to whom articles of
food or drugs were to be sent for analysis
by Justices or Courts in the case of prosecutions under the sale of Food and
Drugs Acts. This Act was passed after
the Parliament of Northern Ireland came
to function, and there is, therefore, some
doubt as to whether the British Act is
applicable to Northern Ireland, although
it is understood that samples have since
1921 been sent frequently from Northern
Ireland to London by Justices and Courts.
I propose, therefore, that the matter be
placed beyond doubt by taking power to
authorize the Minister of Finance to
appoint a Government Chemist for the
purpose of the Food and Drugs Act, and
for any other statutory function which
may be imposed upon this officer, for example, in connection with samples of lead
paint required to be analyzed under the
Lead Paint (Protection Against Poisoning) Act passed by this House last year.
My present idea is not to appoint a
separate officer for this purpose, but to
arrange for the service to be undertaken
as an agency one on my behalf by the
Government Chemist in London (and I
hope he will be prepared to do so). Thus
this Government would have at its disposal
the services of the most highly trained
chemists to be found in the Kingdom.
Mr. DEVLIN: Free?
Mr. POLLOCK: Well, presumably
there will be some fee in the matter, but
it will not be very material. However,
I think it is better this matter should be
disposed of, and put on a logical and permanent basis, and also on such a basis as
will ensure confidence on the part of those
interested in these matters in which
chemical analysis is required.
The third point with which the Bill
deals affects the audit and the prescription of accounts under the Educational
Endowment (Ireland) Act, 1885. Under
that Act and under the schemes in force
under that Act certain functions were
assigned to the Commissioners of
Charitable Donations and Bequests-and
I need hardly say that the duties which
come under that body in Northern Ireland are now undertaken by the Ministry
of Finance. There are also other certain
duties that were assigned to the Local
Government Board, now the Ministry of
Home Affairs in Northern Ireland. After
consultation between the two Ministries
and the Comptroller and Auditor-General
it has been decided that the machinery of
Government in Northern Ireland would
more appropriately assign the duties of
audit of these Endowments to the Comptroller and Auditor-General, and the prescription of the forms of account kept by
the various Boards of Governors of the
Endowments to the Ministry of Finance.
The auditors of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, whose work is sufficiently heavy,
would thereby be relieved of some duties,
and at the same time the matter is placed
under the control of the real auditing
authority which should undertake the
work. The proposal is, I am sure, one
which will commend itself to the House as
being a logical arrangement.

Accordingly, the Bill proposes to confer

I think this is an equitable Measure.
It does not deprive any section of the

Tuesday, 15th May, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
The question of the letting of these
premises is, in the first instance, one for
the Guardians, and I am sure that they
have no desire to retard the development
of any
new industry, but have endeavoured to carry out their functions in
the interests of those whom they represent.
Oral Answers to Questions.
KILKEEL WORKHOUSE.
1. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. William
McMullen) asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact
that during 1926 Messrs. R. McKee &
Sons, Kilkeel, made an offer to the
Kilkeel Board of Guardians to lease
a portion of the Workhouse, at a
rent of £40 per annum and taxes:
whether this offer was refused, and, if so,
for what reason; whether it is a fact that
the portion of the workhouse in question
has since remained vacant and has fallen
into a state of disrepair; and whether he
can state what valid reason the Guardians
had for refusing this remunerative offer
and retarding the development of a new
industry in the district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In 1927 Messrs.
R. McKee & Sons offered to take certain
portions of the Workhouse premises at
Kilkeel at a rent of £45 and taxes. The
Guardians informed Messrs. McKee's
solicitors that they were prepared to
accept this offer, but excluded from the
letting a field which Messrs. McKee desired
to include, and no further action was
taken by the firm in the matter. It,
therefore, appears that the negotations
were broken off by Messrs. McKee and not
by the Guardians.
The premises have since then remained
vacant, but it is not a fact that they have
fallen into disrepair.

ARREARS OF RENT-ALLEGED
ACTION OF RENT AGENTS.
2. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. William
McMullen) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that some rent
agents in Belfast are attempting to secure
from prospective tenants of houses under
£8 valuation arrears of rent alleged to
have been owing by the previous tenant;
whether he will state if this is legal, and,
if not, what steps he proposes to take to
protect the poor of the city.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware that rent agents are demanding
payment of arrears of rent due by former
tenants as a condition precedent to the
granting of a new tenancy, but if they
are doing so their action is illegal and
contrary to the provisions of Section 8 of
the Increase of Rent and Mortgage
Interest (Restrictions) Act, 1920.
The tenant can recover any such payment under the terms of that Section, and
he has, therefore, full protection at the
present moment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Bill,
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving
the Second Reading of this Bill, which
has for its object the making permanent
of the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act of 1922, I do not desire to say more
than is absolutely necessary as to the
causes which led the Government at that
time to introduce the Measure. Sufficient
to say that we were at that time faced
with an organized campaign of murder
and outrage which had for its primary
object the destruction of the Constitution
of Northern Ireland which has been conferred on the people of Ulster by the
Government of Ireland Act of 1920.
The ordinary law was found quite insufficient to deal with the situation that
had arisen, and I venture to say that if
the principles which were embodied by
us in the Civil Authorities Act of 1922
had been recognized by our predecessors
in the government of Ireland, Ireland
would not hold to-day the unenviable
reputation she does amongst civilized
countries in regard to murders.
The Government of Northern Ireland
realized to the full the futility of depending upon the ordinary law of the land to
meet that situation. The campaign of
intimidation alone prevented the ordinary
law running, and I venture to say the
passing of the Civil Authorities Act, combined with a firm but fair administration
of its provisions, brought about the peace
which, I am glad to say, we are enjoying
to-day.
The introduction of the Civil Authorities Act was in the nature of an experiment, and, for that reason, we deemed it
advisable at that stage not to make it
permanent. We realized at that time
that it might be necessary to pass an Act
of a still more drastic character. Our
experience in regard to the working of
that Act has been most satisfactory, and
we therefore find that, after that experience of its working during the last five
years, we are justified in coming to
Parliament and asking Parliament to
continue it.
con-
Some hon. Members may suggest that
because we are enjoying peace, and have
our full liberty, that now is the time to
relinquish the powers which were
ferred on the Government by that Act.
It is always a pleasant thing to forget the
unpleasant past, but people are foolish
who do not profit by the experience of the
past.
The PRIME MINISTER: Hear,
hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I say here today that while we are living in peace
there are combined forces at work in our
Province and elsewhere that would, on the
slightest relaxation of the law, take full
advantage of the fact to plunge this
Province into a welter of bloodshed
similar to that from which we have only
recently emerged. When I make this
statement, I do so with a full sense of
responsibility.
It would serve no useful purpose to
reveal to the public the full information
which the Government
possess. I propose.
with the liberty of the House, to quote
only a few examples to show the outward
activities of that organization which has
for its avowed object the overthrow of
His Majesty's Government in Northern
Ireland, as by the law established, and
the substitution therefor of an Irish
Republic.
I may be told that this organization
aims at achieving its object by so-called
constitutional means. I must confess
that I find difficulty in understanding how
a process, which has for its object the
overthrow of a Constitution, can be constitutional in its procedure.
There is, however, a section of this
organization and it is the larger section
-which aims at attaining its end-the
establishment of an Irish Republic-by
physical force, and for this purpose,
recruits and maintains what is known as
the "Irish Republican Army." That
title is only too familiar to those who recall the past.
Mr. KYLE: How far past?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend will get an opportunity of putting
his point of view afterwards. I am sure
he will forgive me if I am not to be
diverted by question and answer.

You say you are proud to live under the
English Constitution here. Do you realize what you are going to do by putting
this Act on the Statute Book even for five
years? You are going to suspend that
English Constitution you are talking so
much of. In the twelfth century, six
hundred years ago, there was a tyrannical
King in England known as King John,
and he exercised the same powers against
his subjects in the twelfth century as the
Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act
exercised against my hon. Friend (Mr.
Healy). But the Barons of England were
goaded into insurrection by the tyranny
of this King, and one day they all gathered
in the Cathedral of Bury-St.-Edmunds,
and each swore a solemn oath from the
High Altar that unless he signed a document giving them the rights which
they claimed they would withdraw
their fealty and would rebel against
him.
He prevaricated and refused,
SO the Barons gathered a mighty
army, faced with which King John capitulated, and about the year 1215 he signed
the great Articles of Magna Charta which
you are suspending here to-day.
One of the great movers in that revolutionary movement for that freedom
which you are boasting so much about was
the great Cardinal Langton, and luckily
for the English people to-day there were
no religious differences at that time because no Reformation had come, and the
people could not be divided on side issues.
One of the strongest planks in Magna
Charta is that a man must be tried by his
peers. He cannot be taken away from his
home, as was the Member for Tyrone and

-

moment taken a louder and more penetrating note.

new crisis arose this Bill

authority, or any police constable, or
any member of any of His Majesty's
forces on duty may, where it is
necessary for the purpose of effecting an
arrest in respect of any crime or any
offence against the regulations, exercise

be exercised by a police constable in
effecting arrest in a case where a felony
has been committed.
I want specially to read that because
there is nothing like telling a story one
knows all about. In my town of Newry
there was a nice little boy, eighteen years
of age.
His name was Tommy Carr.
Like many other boys he was excluded
from the Six Counties and lived over the
Border. His mother fell dangerously
ill and was brought to the Mater Hospital, and like a dutiful son he risked all
and came to see his mother.
He was
walking up Hill Street, the main street
of Newry, on a market day, and when
immediately opposite the shop of Messrs.
Lipton a police sergeant saw him and ran
after him. He caught the boy by the
coat and pulled the coat off him, leaving
the coat in his hands, and he then shot
him through the back. The boy died
that night in the Newry Nursing Home.
That is a power this Act gave to a policeman. Because this innocent boy came
into his own town a police sergeant had
the right to shoot him, as he had the same
power of arrest as if the boy had committed a felony. I know myself that no
one regretted that occurrence more than
the sergeant concerned, and if he had not
had that power it never would have happened.
That is one of the legacies we got from
that Act which you now want to put on

O'Hanlon, the well-known chess player,
of Portadown, who was arrested when a
policeman went into his premises and
said he found a piece of paper in his fireplace. They kept him lying in the
Crumlin Road for I do not know how
long. All sorts of suggestions were made
about him, that he was an Intelligence
Officer and so on, and I do not know how
much it cost him to regain his liberty.
These individual cases surely are enough
to chase this Act out of the House, without the big constitutional question to
which I have referred.
Mr. McALLISTER: I rise to oppose
this Bill on various grounds. In the first
place I oppose it because it is a direct
violation of the principle of constitutional
government. As one who has a very deep,
profound and abiding belief in constitutionalism, and who has refused to be provoked from the path of constitutionalism
during all the years that the party opposite
carried on their revolutionary movement,
I protest with all the vigour in my power
against the retention of a Measure such as
this. I do protest against the manner in
which it was introduced, and the highly
provocative speech which the right hon.
Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
made in his endeavour to vindicate his
position and to justify this legislation.
I do not intend to dwell at any length on
some of the matters which have been exhaustively dealt with, but I cannot allow
the introduction of this Measure to pass
without taking exception to the innuendo
which the Minister of Home Affairs endeavoured to make when he suggested that
all the murders and all the illegalities
were committed by one section of the community. I do not intend to deal with
that at any length, but I must say
that I am prepared to put it to the
test, to pledge my party to put it to the
test, and to abide by the result of the publication of the names and addresses of the
various people who were murdered in Northern Ireland, and of the homes and
homesteads that were wrecked, ruined and
burned. I say that if those figures are
published they will vindicate the position
of those whom we represent, and will refute the speech of the right hon. Gentleman in introducing this Measure.
Civil Authorities Bill-
Second Reading
15 MAY 1928
I also object to this Measure because it is
a most reactionary Measure; it is retrograde, and it is a disgrace to any legislative code. It is a libel and a slander upon
the people of Northern Ireland because,
let the party opposite camouflage the position as they like, sidetrack it as they will,
and indulge in special pleading in the most
exhaustive manner, the fact remains that
they have placed upon the brow of the men
of Northern Ireland the brand of inferiority-that they are not to be trusted
with and cannot be given the same freedom as the men of England, of Scotland,
and of other countries; that they cannot
be trusted to differentiate between right
and wrong; that they require special restrictive, repressive and coercive legislation
to make them preserve the laws. On that
ground I also object, and I say that that
principle has been applied, not in this Bill
alone, but that in every Measure that the
Government have introduced they have
shown that they cannot even trust the
Courts to administer their own laws.
They have insisted on imposing minimum
penalties; they have deprived the ordinary
Petty Sessions Courts of their jurisdiction, and by every act of administration,
by every Bill they have introduced, they
have shown their distrust of the working
people, of the common people of Northern
Ireland.
I object to this Bill on other grounds.
I say it is a partisan Bill. It is introduced mainly against one political party.
It will be received by the people whom we
represent not only with suspicion but with
alarm. We know what took place some
years ago, and that the only protection
that the minority in the Six Counties had
was the right of every citizen to be tried
by a properly constituted court. It is a
well-known fact that even in the charge
of murder, when the highest courts of the
lands have gone through the whole form
of trial, when the onus of proof was supposed to be on the Crown, when the prisoner has been defended by the most able
and brilliant counsel, he has been found
guilty of murder and convicted, and after
twenty years it was found that a new inquiry was necessary in order to find out
whether the man was guilty or innocent,
and to vindicate his position.
But what are the powers given under
this Bill? An official in the Home Office
on partial information, second or thirdhand reports, is entitled to confiscate a
man's liberty, to take him from his home,
his employment, and his family. I say
there can be no justification either here
or in any other country for such a state
of affairs, and that that method of legislation cannot be vindicated. As I said, we
look upon this as partizan legislation.
You sit on those benches opposite year
after year, and you proclaim from the
housetops that there must be no coercion
of Northern Ireland; but we say that this
Bill is coercion in its most extreme form
of the minority, the people whom we represent. It is depriving them of their
just right to be tried by their peers, and
subjecting them to be tried by officials of
the Home Office.
course we
The Attorney-General has very fairly
stated that in political matters such as
this none of us is truly impartial, and of
all must accept that view.
There is no one in this House more anxious
for the peace, prosperity and progress of
Northern Ireland than I am, and I say
here deliberately that no Government in
any country had a finer opportunity than
the Government of Northern Ireland had
after the last election of promoting a spirit
of concord and goodwill and of fostering
a spirit of trust and mutual confidence,
but whether deliberately or through want
of knowledge they have taken every opportunity of driving away the confidence of
the people whom we represent.
Bills such as this must naturally raise
grave suspicion and apprehension in the
minds and in the hearts of the minority
in Northern Ireland. I said I did not
intend to dwell at length upon that unpleasant aspect of the question, and upon
the terrible time through which all the
residents in Northern Ireland have passed,
but one remark of the Attorney-General
requires to be answered. He said that it
was not known that Crown forces had
murdered anyone in Northern Ireland. I
say here with deliberation there is not a
man, woman or child in Northern Ireland
that does not know that the McMahon
family were murdered by Crown forces.
There is not a man, woman or child in the
Glens of Antrim who does not know that
the boys in Cushendall were murdered by
Crown forces. I say that in introducing
Measures of this sort Ministers will require
to be more discreet in their language and
in the methods which they employ, because
if they insist on making provocative
speeches they will find a very effective
answer from Members on this side of the
House.

Mr. HARBISON: I rise to support the

I do so for some rather solid reasons.
The first reason is that it is contrary to
human liberty. I listened to the speech

Northern Ireland, and that it was necessary to continue this statute upon the
Statute Book. Immediately the thought
leaped to my mind: What a pity it was
that there was not such a statute upon the
Statute Book in 1914. It would have
have been a most admirable statute to
meet the emergency that had arisen at
that time, and, in my opinion, it is one
of the greatest tragedies in history, a
tragedy not only for England, but for
Ireland, that no such Act as the present
Act, which is about to be continuednot if we can help it was on the Statute Book. Had such an Act been on
the Statute Book in 1914 we would have
been in the position to-day of having a
united Government in Ireland; there
would not have been a British soldier
struck down in Ireland had not the guns
been landed at Larne. I say what a pity
it was that there was no such statute as
this upon the Statute Book at that time.
I am speaking from my own heartfelt
conviction, I am not speaking in any way

man in Ulster at the present time, except perhaps a few Members of the Government, who does not believe that the

Oral Answers to Questions.
CALEDON TELEPHONE SERVICE.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether it is fact that representations have been made by the residents of Caledon, Co. Tyrone, to the Post
Office authorities to have the telephone
installed in that district; whether he can
state the reason why their request has
been ignored; and whether he will use
his influence with the authorities to give
effect to the wishes of the
the people
concerned.
•
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour) From inquiries which I
have caused to be made I learn that the
terms upon which a Telephone Call Office
at Caledon could be provided were communicated to the Dungannon Rural District Council by the Post Office Authorities in the summer of 1925. These terms,
which were based on the assumption that
a Call Office would be installed at Tynan
also, included the provision of a guarantee of £12 10s per annum by the Council.
The matter was considered by the Council
and the offer unanimously rejected, the
Councillor for Caledon stating that there
was no general request for telephone
facilities from the residents in the district.
The matter therefore dropped until last
month, when an inquiry was received by
the Postal Authorities from a Caledon
firm regarding the practicability of installing a Telephone Exchange at Caledon.
in reply to this communication the Post
Office intimated the terms upon which an
Exchange could be provided on the basis
of a minimum of eight subscribers or, failing that minimum, an arrangement under
which the rentals could be specially
assessed. The local firm have acknowledged receipt of these particulars, and
have promised to pursue their inquiries
with a view to ascertaining whether
sufficient subscribers would be forthcoming. In these circumstances the hon.
Member will see that there is no evidence
that the residents in Caledon as a whole
have made representations on the subject
of telephone facilities, and that any communications so far received have been
promptly dealt with by the Postal
Authorities. With regard to the last part
of the question, I would point out for the
information of the hon. Member, that
the Postal Authorities are at all times
prepared to provide telephone facilities
where the other parties interested are
willing to accept the
accept the consequential
financial obligations.

DOG RACING TRACKS.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime
Minister whether it is the intention of the
Government to introduce legislation at an
early date on lines similar to those which
are at present before the Imperial House,
requiring the promoters of existing dogracing tracks, as well as those in contemplation, to receive in the first instance
a licence from the local authority concerned.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is no doubt aware, the Bill at
present before the Imperial Parliament is
not a Government Measure, but was introduced by a Private Member.
It is open to the hon. Member, if he so
desires, and if he considers that the circumstances of dog racing in Northern
Ireland require a measure of local control,
to introduce a similar Bill, but as the
situation is not yet fully developed, even
in Great Britain, I cannot give any undertaking that the Government will automatically follow the lines of British
legislation in this respect, as it is obvious
that before the Government could accept
responsibility for similar legislation, it
would have to be satisfied after detailed
inquiry, and on consideration of representations from responsible authorities,
that the present and future conditions in
regard to dog racing were of such a
character as to justify, if not demand, a
measure of local control.

Mr. DEVLIN: Mr. Moles, before we
proceed to the discussion of the Estimates
on the Paper I desire to call your attention to a ruling you gave in which you
said that on the first of these
Estimates we can only discuss the
general policy of the Ministry involved, and not the details. This is, I
believe, the last of the Allotted Days, and
we have not been allowed to discuss a
single detail in connection with the various
Estimates that have been presented to the
House. I want to know whether the
ruling still continues.
The CHAIRMAN: This is not, to
begin with, the last Allotted Day. The
ninth day will be the last day for Committee proceedings, and the tenth day
will be devoted to Report. My ruling
stands for the simple reason that it is
founded upon
the Rules of Procedure and
the Standing Orders as adopted by this
House.
The invariable procedure is the reason
for it, I think, is obvious, and I have indicated it more than once -that the introduction by the Minister of the first
Estimate is the proper time for the discussion of policy in relation to all the
activities of that Ministry. That practice
is founded upon the fact that in the
first Estimate the Minister's salary is
found, and his salary is supposed to cover
all his activities. I did not rule that
policy only could be covered. What I
did rule was that only upon that occasion
could policy form part of the discussion.
I further ruled that the details of that
particular Estimate were open to discussion at the same period, but that
discussion of the details of the later Estimates could only be taken as and when
those Estimates were presented for consideration. That is the invariable practice founded upon our Rules of Procedure,
as I have indicated.

it means anything, that there are certain
Votes the details of which we cannot dis-

Sir DAWSON BATES: In introducing
this Estimate I think it desirable to remind the Committee that the Ministry of
Home Affairs comprises two self-contained
Departments, one dealing with law and
order, justice, police, prisons and ancillary
matters, and the other with local government administration. I propose
cover as far as possible the operations of
the two Departments, but before reviewing the various activities of the Ministry
I think it well to refer in some detail to
the features of the Estimate which is now
before the Committee dealing with the
staff.
to
As the Committee will see, the Estimate
shows that we are asking for a net sum for
the current financial year of £58,242, as
compared with £60,110 for last year, the
result being a net decrease of £1,868. It
will also be observed that the total staff
employed by or attached to the Ministry
as provided for in the present Estimate
is 150 as against 157 for last year. A
reduction in staff of four clerks and two
temporary inspectors has been found
possible owing to the transfer of the administration of the non-Contributory Old
Age Pension Service from the Ministry of
Home Affairs to the Ministry of Labour
under Section 1 of the Act passed last
A consequential reduction in the
typing staff of two has also been made. A
further reduction of one clerk has been
made in the Accounts Branch of the
Ministry following the disbandment of the
Special Constabulary. On the other hand
we have found it necessary to increase the
Local Government Audit Staff by two
assistant auditors.
Our experience during the last few
years has gone to show that the work of
Local Government Audit has been steadily
increasing in volume and importance, and
that it was nearly impossible for the Local
Government Auditors to keep up-to-date
in their work. This increase is due to a
large extent to the additional statutory
audits imposed by recent legislation, e.g.
-the audit of the accounts of County
Infirmaries and of Regional Education
Committees.
Apart from these changes there are no
other outstanding features in the Estimate
as submitted to the Committee. I might,
however, refer to Sub-head "G"-Special
Inquiries in which it will be seen that
provision has been made for a sum of
£250 to cover the expenses of the Departmental Committee of Inquiry into the
relationship between landlord and tenant
in the case of non-agricultural holdings.
Hon. Members are, no doubt, aware that
there has been in certain localities in
Northern Ireland considerable agitation
and pressure put on the Government to
inquire into the question of the leases in
urban centres, and I accordingly appointed
a Departmental Committee under the
chairmanship of Mr. Megaw to inquire
into the matter.
I propose now to deal at some little
length with the activities of the Home
Office Department of my Ministry, which,
as I have already explained, is concerned with law and order, justice, police,
prisons, etc. In the first place, as the
Committee has, no doubt, observed from
statements made by the various judges
which have appeared from time to time in
the Press, the present condition of affairs
in Northern Ireland in regard to law and
order is on the whole satisfactory. The
number of specially reported cases in 1927
was 1,434 as compared with 1,581 in 1926,
which I think is very satisfactory.
Although there was in some aspects a
noticeable increase in such crimes as
burglary, on the whole the figures I have
quoted show that there has been a decrease in serious crimes.
Ministry of Home Affairs 1758

As I said yesterday, attempts to foment
trouble in our midst by disloyal elements
were apparent, but these activities have
been kept well in hand by the vigilance of
the police, and in consequence of the
wholesome effect of the powers vested in
the Government by the Civil Authorities
Act. In this connection I might also
refer to the great influence for peace
which is exercised by the presence of the
"B" Special Constabulary-a band of devoted men who have in the past rendered
valuable services, and who still for a
nominal retaining fee keep themselves in
training and hold themselves in readiness
to come to the assistance of the Government in the event of any emergency.
As regards the regular police force in
the country, we have endeavoured and
have succeeded in effecting a small but
steady decrease in strength with a corresponding saving to the Exchequer. Steps
have been taken and are being taken with
a view to effecting further economies by
closing up certain barracks in areas where
the responsible police authorities are
satisfied that effective police supervision
can be afforded by police from barracks
in adjoining areas.
As evidence of the economies which
have been and are being effected in connection with police expenditure, I think
it well to quote the following figures:-

Negotations have been entered into
with the War Office for the purchase of
the Military Barracks in Enniskilen,
and, as the Committee is aware, these
premises have been purchased at a reasonable price. It is proposed to utilize these
premises as a depot for the training of
recruits and possibly as a county headquarters and town barracks. This will
enable the Government to dispense with
the present unsatisfactory hutment camp
at Newtownards which hitherto has been
used as a police depot.
I also think it well to point out that
during the past year very considerable
progress has been made in connection with
the disposal of surplus Constabulary
stores. In all cases every effort was made
to advertise the sales as widely as possible
in order to encourage competitive buying.
In some instances where it was not considered advisable to proceed by way of
sale by tender steps were taken to have
the articles sold by public auction. The
articles sold during the past year included
such items as uniforms, £5,000; blankets
and bedding, £3,000; wireless stores,
£800; equipment, £1,950; arms, £3,000,
yielding approximately £16,000.

glad to be able to state that the number

I also think it well to point out that
we have been able by gradual means to
effect a steady reduction in cost of administration. During the financial year
ended 31st March, 1925, the average cost
per prisoner per annum was £112 18s 5d;
the figure for the succeeding year was
£108 17s 4d, while for the year ended
31st March, 1927, the average charge per
prisoner per annum was reduced to
£96 5s 8d.
Mr. DEVLIN: How was that reduction brought about?
Sir DAWSON BATES: By better
administration.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member will have an opportunity of asking any questions afterwards.
