Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Mr. DEVLIN: I am asking you one
now.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It will be
more satisfactory if the hon. Member will
put his questions all together. The only
important item of interest in connection
with our prison administration during the
past year was the escape of four prisoners
from Belfast Prison. As the Committee
is aware, two of these prisoners were
subsequently recaptured and are now in
custody; the remaining two up to the
present have succeeded in evadng recapture. Very full
full and exhaustive
inquiries were made at my direction into
the circumstances under which the
escapes were made, and from an examination of the various reports submitted
to me I am satisfied that no blame could
be attached to any individual officer of
the staff.
At the same time, while the experience
of all Governments is that it is extremely
difficult to make such water-tight arrangements as will rule out all possibility of
escape, it appeared to me from the reports
submitted by the officers that certain improvements both in connection with
administration as well as structural
arrangements could be effected which
would minimize the possibility of escape.
Due and proper steps have been and are
being taken in this respect. It, perhaps,
would not be out of place for me at this
stage to state that the recapture of the
two prisoners referred to reflects considerable credit on the police authorities of
Northern Ireland.
I also think it necessary to point out
that the administration of Belfast Prison
presents exceptional difficulties owing to
the fact that, for reasons of economy, it
has been found necessary to utilize the
Prison not only for ordinary prisoners but
for convicts sentenced to penal servitude.
The latter class are those who are guilty
of serious crimes or who are old offenders.
In regard to their treatment in prison it
is necessary to make certain special
arrangements for the convict prisoners.
They are confined in a separate part of
the institution and receive separate and
distinct treatment. The ordinary prisoners confined for minor offences do not
receive any privileges beyond visits and
letters and being allowed to read newspapers after a period of six months' good
conduct.
On the other hand, a convict confined
for a protracted period receives quite a
number of privileges subject to good conduct. He is allowed, for example
and I hope I am not wearying
the Committee by these details
to have his. own shaving kit
and
knife and fork. At exercise he is allowed
to associate with other convicts, and once
a week he is allowed what is called an
"hour's association" in a room specially
set apart for this purpose. He is also
allowed to receive newspapers, and after
a period of three years he is allowed to
have his meals in association with other
convicts in a specially provided dining
room.
Educational privileges are also provided not only for the local prisoners but
also for the convict prisoners, but it has
been found desirable to keep the classes
-that is the ordinary prisoners and the
convicts quite distinct. Those for the
convicts are held in the afternoons and
those for the local or ordinary prisoners
in the evenings. The convicts as a rule
prove to be a more difficult class to deal
with than the ordinary prisoners. All
that is necessary in the latter case is strict
supervision. but in dealing with the convicts the duties imposed on the prison
staff are much more onerous and exacting.
There is always, as is obvious amongst
this class, a more pronounced tendency to
escape and to give trouble, and the supervision of the convict wing of the prison
imposes a very heavy strain on the prison.
staff.
During the past year no less than 40
lectures were held in the prison, mainly
of an educational character or else dealing with history and travel. In addition
to these lectures 12 concerts were held.
As regards the educational classes, two
are held each week for the ordinary
prisoners and two for convict prisoners,
the subjects taught being mainly history,
geography, arithmetic, drawing, and so
These lectures are held under the
auspices of the "Toc H" Society under
the direction of Mr. W. Armour in cooperation with Mr. Foster, the principal
of the Belfast Academy, and other publicspirited ladies and gentlemen. I cannot
speak too highly of the valuable services
rendered by those who are associated in
this good work.
on.
As I have already pointed out on a previous occasion, the prison at Londonderry
Ministry of Home Affairs 1762
Estimates-
16 MAY 1928
is used merely as a local prison for remand
and short-term prisoners. It has been
suggested on one or two occasions that it
might be possible for us to close this
prison altogether, but this suggestion has
been found on examination to be impracticable, owing to the difficulties in
dealing with cases from the North-West
of the Province, and the expense that
would be entailed in escorting them
to and from Beifast and Londonderry.
I may take this opportunity of mentioning that at the presert time we have
no means of dealing with criminal lunatics
in Northern Ireland. The Committee
will see from the sum put down that we
have to send them to Southern Ireland
where we are charged what we consider
to be the rather extortionate amount of
£192 in respect of each criminal lunatic.
To meet that difficulty we have under con,
sideration a scheme whereby we will provide accommodation for them in Northern Ireland, but hon. Members will
appreciate the difficulties that arise in
setting up such an institution having regard to the smallness of their numbers,
and we are only prepared to establish such
an institution provided we see that it will
mean a saving to the Exchequer.
Turning from the subject of prisons to
that of the Borstal Institution, which has
recently been established at the Malone
Training School, Belfast, I am glad to be
able to say that the establishment of this
institution has had on the whole satisfactory results, the number of Borstal
boys in confinement remaining in the
vicinity of 40. I have had the good
fortune to be able to secure as the Visiting
Committee of that institution a body of
earnest, devoted and hard-working gentlemen, some of whom are Members of this
Committee, and I am glad to take this
opportunity of expressing to them individually and collectively my appreciation
of their valuable services.
One of the most important aspects of the
duties and responsibility of these gentlemen is in connection with the after-life
of the boys, and I think it well to say
that since their appointment they have
shown themselves most active in regard to
the raising of funds with the object of
providing each boy on leaving the institution with a fair chance of earning a living
and leading an honest life. On the whole,
having regard to the character and antecedents of the boys, their conduct has been
satisfactory. One or two escapes, which
are almost inevitable in an institution of
this character, have occurred during the
year, but the cases requiring disciplinary
action at the hands of the Committee
have been comparatively few.
Consequent on representations made to
me by the Committee and my Inspectors
I have, with the approval of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
made arrangements for effecting structural
alterations in the institution which will
have the double object of separating more
completely the Borstal boys from the Reformatory boys, and at the same time
providing more adequate and suitable
accommodation and conveniences for both
classes. It has also been decided to erect
houses to accommodate some of the staff
in order that there may be at all times
a due proportion of the staff living in the
vicinity of the institution.
Turning now to the question of the
administration of justice, as the Committee is aware, the Ministry is responsible
for the local arrangements for the holding
of Petty Sessions Courts, and for the administration of duties by Clerks of Petty
Sessions.
It has been the definite policy of the
Ministry since I have had the privilege
of occupying the post I now do, to endeavour to secure for these posts the most
suitable officers, and with this object
steps have been taken where opportunity
has arisen to amalgamate Petty Sessions
Districts so as to enable larger salaries
to be offered, and to induce a better class
of men to come forward as candidates for
the appointments. This process has been
carried out in 16 cases during the last
few years with satisfactory results.
should say, however, that, before taking
action of this character the Ministry invariably consults the Resident Magistrate
of the district concerned and the police
authorities.

say that there is a movement on foot for
the appointment of Probation Officers in
Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). Up to the present, outside the
City of Belfast the probation system does
not appear to have been widely utilized
or fully appreciated. For the information of hon. Members I may point out
that the appointment of a probation offi-

cer for a Petty Sessions District is in the

to obtain suitable officers in these districts
owing to the limited amount of the fees

I do think, while it is a matter entirely
for themselves, that this Act is not
utilised in the way it might be.
In order to get over this difficulty I
issued an Order recently increasing the
remuneration payable to probation officers
and allowing for a 25 per cent. increase
to officers serving in districts outside
Belfast and Londonderry.
At present
there are only 10 of these officers in
Northern Ireland, six in Belfast, two in

The total number of cases dealt with by

129 occurred in Belfast. I can only
express the hope that the value of the
probation system will be more fully

their districts to do this valuable, though
perhaps not highly paid, work.

Turning now to Local Government
Administration, I perhaps might first
make a reference to the question of
the report of the Commission which
recently sat to consider this matter. The problem is such a big
and very complicated one that I
feel that no step should be taken by the
Government or by Parliament until it is
made clear beyond all doubt that any
change made will be for the better.
Accordingly, I am having every recommendation scrutinized and examined in
the closest possible way by expert officers
with a view to having put clearly before
the Government when the time comes the
results of the various recommendations
both from a financial as well as an administrative point of view.
Under the circumstances I can hold out
no hope of very early legislation on this
important question, and in this respect
I would also like to state that even after
I have, on the advice of my officers,
arrived at any particular conclusions, it
will be necessary for those conclusions to
be examined from a financial point of
view by a special expert Committee,
having regard to the desirability for ensuring that as far as possible the changes
of whatever character they may be will
not impose additional burdens on the
ratepayers.
Hear,
(Hon. Members:
hear).
The whole object of the Commission
was to endeavour to work out what would
be the most economical and efficient
system in regard to the various circumstances, and I propose before making any
suggestion to satisfy myself and this
House when the time comes that as far
as possible no more expensive arrangement is put into operation unless there
are undoubtedly satisfactory reasons for
doing so.
I would like now to deal with the question of Housing, and first of all I think
it well that the Committee should be informed of the undoubted success of the
recent Act passed by the Parliament of
Northern Ireland increasing the subsidy
on the smaller workers' houses from £80
to £100. The best means, I think, of
bringing this home to the Committee is
to quote our records for the last six
months as compared with the corresponding records for the same months in the
previous year.
Taking the last six months, that is up
to April, 1928, I find that no fewer than
2,211 houses were approved for erection
as against 715 for the corresponding six
months to April, 1927. I think those
up
figures justify the action of the Government in increasing the subsidy. Let me
take the total number of houses approved
of under our own Housing Acts since the
first Housing Act was passed in 1924. I
find that the total number of houses
approved of in Northern Ireland during
these four years was as regards builders
no fewer than 9,104 houses and as regards
local authorities 1,343 houses. In other
words, during the last four years as a
result of the Housing Acts of Northern
Ireland we have had 10,447 houses approved, and 7,171 of these houses have
actually been completed.
I will now turn to the provision of
accommodation for labourers in rural

areas under the Labourers Acts. I think
it will interest hon. Members to see what
has been accomplished there. Those hon.
Members who take an interest in the subject are aware that the first Labourers
Act was passed in 1883. I find that
from then up to the time the
Northern Government took over this
administration only 6,118 houses were

On the whole I consider that the

Northern Ireland.

A short time ago we introduced the
Roads Improvement Bill which has not
yet finally passed either the Senate or
this House. That Bill is for the purpose
of facilitating local authorities, for widening corners, narrow roads, and removing
obstructions to view, and make the roads
suitable to modern conditions. I can
only express the earnest hope that this
Measure when passed, coupled with the
Act of 1926, will go a long way towards
decreasing the appalling number of motor
accidents on our public roads. As regards
the question of the licensing and control
of omnibuses which followed the passing
of the Motor Traffic Act, I am glad to be
able to say that this new system has been
put into operation without imposing any
unnecessary hardship or dislocation to the
owners of these vehicles.
I would like to summarize shortly our
operations in regard to this Act as regards omnibuses. The number of omnibuses in respect of which applications for
regular licences have been received (to the
end of April, 1928) is 730. Out of that
number of applications 481 of these
vehicles were found fit as a result of inspection, 85 were refused licences, and in
62 cases the applications were cancelled
at the owners' request. Apparently the
owners realized the vehicles were of such
a hopeless character that they could not
be licensed. Thus 628 of the applications
have been dealt with, leaving 102 vehicles
to be tested, or 14 per cent. of the total.
As hon. Members are aware, it takes the
inspectors time to get round all these
vehicles. Of the 481 fit vehicles satisfactory insurance policies have been produced in respect of 372, and regular, or
what we might call permanent, licences
have been issued. The remaining 109
vehicles are operating on provisional
licences pending the production of satisfactory insurance policies. Adding the
102 vehicles remaining to be tested, the
total number of vehicles operating at the

211.

with, leaving only 132 vehicles to be

The Dairies and Cowsheds Order of
1908 and the Bovine Tuberculosis Order,
1926, ensure a very considerable supervision of the conditions under which milk
and meat are produced and sold, but
several authorities have urged that stricter
measures are necessary, particularly in

matter under consideration. One of the
principal points to be determined is the
most suitable authority to administer any
Order that may be made, and in this connection the recommendations of the Local
Government Commission will be duly
considered.
With regard to the question of Preservatives in Food, by an Order of the
Ministry the use of preservatives and
mineral colouring matter in food has been
prohibited subject to certain exceptions.
The Order in force here, which is similar
to one issued in England and Scotland,
has worked smoothly except in regard to
cream. The prohibition of preservatives
in cream met with strong opposition from
the trade both here and in Great Britain
on the ground that the cream would not
keep long enough to reach the consumers,
and that it would be impossible for the
producer to carry on business.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Hear,
hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The authorities in England and Scotland have refused to modify the Order, but in view of
strong representations made to me by the
dairying interests I decided, after consultation with the Minister of Agriculture,
to postpone its operation till the 1st
January, 1929, so as to give the trade an
opportunity of finding some method of
overcoming the difficulty I have referred
to. It should, however, be pointed out
that medical opinion is strongly against
the use of boric, which is the preservative
mainly used in cream, for the reason that
it is injurious to health, and so far as
the Ministry of Home Affairs is concerned
we cannot undertake to postpone the operation of the Order beyond the date mentioned, 1st January, 1929.

With regard to the policy of the
Government in relation to the police
force, both as to the strength of the Force
and as to its allocation, I was under the
impression that the police force was not
as strong as it appears on this Estimate.
This Estimate gives the figure of 2,916
men.
Within the past few weeks a Police
Bill was passed in this House, and when
it was suggested by my hon. Friend, the
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr
Healy), that 3,000 of a police force was
too large, the Minister of Home Affairs
said that we had not 3,000; we had only
2,500. Indeed, he took the pains to interrupt my hon. Friend to say:-
I have already twice explained to my
hon. Friend that there are not 3,000
men in our Force at the present time.
There are only 2,500 odd. If necessary, we will bring the Force up to
3,000.
When I was advancing arguments against
that Bill, I was under the impression that
the strength of the Force was 2,500, and I
think some Members of the House must
have been deceived as to the strength of
the Force. Even the Prime Minister
himself, in defending the action of the
Government, pointed out that the Force
was a very small one, only 2,500 men. I
expect the Government were working on
some figures, and I cannot understand

Now in regard to the number of accidents on the roads, when this matter was
last discussed I asked for some information
in regard to the times of the day at which
these accidents occurred, whether it was
in the morning, whether it was in the
middle of the day, or whether it was late

know he is very good so far as fulfilling
any undertaking he gives is concerned, and
possibly it escaped his notice on this

We are making what would appear to me
to be most comprehensive provision in regard to all matters except the important
things. We have improved the surfaces of
the roads and quite rightly-we have
widened the roads, we have rounded satisfactorily very dangerous corners, and we
have cleared away hedges where it has not
been possible for a driver to see clearly
round a corner. We seem to have taken
every question into consideration except
the main one.
On a number of occasions before I have
urged on the Committee that some attention should be paid to the number of hours
for which men are employed on these buses
each day. I believe that if I had the
information at my disposal I would be able
to present an unanswerable case for the
limitation of the hours that these men
work per day. I am informed, I do not
know how reliably, that a large number
of these accidents take place when the
drivers are not in a physically fit condition, when their eyesight and physical
capabilities generally have become impaired as a result of the tension during
a very lengthy day. I would ask the
consideration of the Department to this
question. Seeing that the Roads Bill has
not finally passed this House-it is receiving the attention of the Senate at the
moment, I understand-I would ask that
the matter should have the serious consideration of the Department, that they
should take the point I have mentioned
into consideration and see how much importance it carries, and if it carries sufficient importance then the Minister would
be justified in attempting to limit the
hours per day that these drivers, particularly, work.
This would not be any departure from
precedent, because I understand that a
person must be physically fit before the
authorities will give him a certificate. He
will not be given a certificate if he is under
a certain age, so why should the Ministry
not take steps to ensure these men are not
overworked to such an extent as to impair
their fitness, and as a result of their fitness
being impaired run the risk of very
serious accidents occurring on our roads.
We want to minimize the number of accidents taking place on our roads. They are
very considerable at the present time, but
there is no reason why they should not be
substantially reduced, and I am sanguine
that if the right steps are taken a very
satisfactory reduction will be effected.
Finally I want to discuss the question
of Poor Relief. It is possibly an attempt
to anticipate the disclosures that will be
made by the Minister of Finance in regard
to this matter. That is possibly not in
order either, but Belfast has borne a very
heavy burden in regard to outdoor relief.
I understand, although I have not fully
read it up to the moment, that the intention of the Budget introduced recently in
the British Parliament by Mr. Winston
Churchill was to relieve industrial areas
that have been very heavily taxed as a
result of the problem of unemployment
and the large sums that have had to be
disbursed in many of those city areas by

keeping in mind our policy of step by step
with Great Britain, perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Hanna) or his
chief will be able to give us some information as to whether or not their Department propose to depart from the attitude
they have adopted on this question up to
the moment.

Belfast will not be able to compete so
successfully with those cities of Great
Britain which Mr. Churchill proposes to
relieve if our rates for the city are much
higher than they will be across the water.
There will be certain commodities in which

The police set a trap on the road, they

I do think there should be a little give
and take in regard to the administration
of this Act. What we really want to
secure is the safety of the travelling public.
There was a very famous admiral at one
time, and I believe that when he received
an order to retire he put his telescope to
his blind eye and said he could not see it.
I believe that is good history. Now, if a
bus is travelling at a little bit over the

other people, say, into a town to market

if the policeman would happen to have
a blind eye on that occasion and not see

This class of administration has been

anything else knowing the history of the

The result is that we have chaos, disaster,
and disruption all along the line.
The reduction that I have shown could
be made is a small thing in comparison
to what could be brought about by this
Department if they felt inclined to attend
to their duties and see that the administration was properly carried out. They
should do this instead of attaching themselves to the political hustings on every
opportunity. There is another point I
want to bring forward. We had the
Minister asking for barracks for the
R.U.C. all over the Six Counties. There
was a challenge from this side of the
House about the cost of housing the
R.U.C. I made a charge myself that if
the Home Office continued its administration as it was doing the taxpayers were
bound to suffer. By the order of the head
of this Department, in consultation with
his Parliamentary Secretary or his advisers, there have been installed in the
barracks in Northern Ireland electric
lighting plants. There is self-produced
light now in a certain number of the
small barracks throughout Northern Ireland. Every Member will remember that
when I asked the Minister of Home
Affairs a question about it his answer was
not final. I am, however, now in a position
to say I have not the figures with me
because I came unprepared-that this
production plant is costing the taxpayers
of Northern Ireland anything from 100,
to 300 per cent. more than it would have
cost if the light had been received
from the town supply. That is the sort
of administration you have by the head
of a Department who is receiving £1,500
a year. That is not good administration.
No man could defend it. Perhaps the
Parliamentary Secretary will endeavour
to do so. The total cost for depreciation
and renewals and things like that is
taken into the percentage increase I have
set out, because when renewals take place
the plant has got to be removed. It is so
up-to-date and so efficient in reducing the

is a large sum of money asked by the

I do not deny the fact that much has been
done by this Government to solve the
housing problem. It has been done by
every Government. But this Government,
although it is the normal action of all
intelligent Governments in these islands,
regards it as some special virtue on their
part. The money they spend on roads,
on housing, the guarantees they give for
industries they regard all this as some
superhuman scheme of their own.
Nothing of the sort. It is the commonplace amenity of all Governments in relation to these vital matters.
If you have never done it, set yourselves to the question of dealing with
the slums and with preventible poverty.
You have hundreds, even thousands, of
poor people who are not insured, you have
many who are insured and do not get
unemployment insurance, who live in
the big lanes and alleys of our big cities,
who hardly ever breathe fresh air, who
are poisoned with the conditions that
exist in our cities, with their sweating
and other conditions. If you attempted
to solve this problem, then you would
justify yourselves more than in anything
you have done up to now.
My objection to this Government is
that it stands for a fine police, for
picturesque soldiery, for great buildings,
for the creation of impressions upon outsiders, but it never goes to the root of
the things that count. Their action is
more than indefensible. It would be so
easy to solve the problem of slumdom and
poverty, because our area is such a small
and restricted one. It is not like the
problem they have to deal with in a big
country like England or even America.
We have only a small area with a popu
lation of 1,200,000. It would be easy.
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
HOUSE OF COMMONS

if less time was given to politics and
more to reform--it would be easy to
deal with these problems, because not
only have we to deal with them over a
narrow and restricted area, but they are
actually round our very doors. We need
not walk 150 yards until we are able to
find ourselves in these sodden districts
of poverty and slumdom, disease and
crime, because they are all conditions and
factors in the common irritation which
they create in a community.
I, therefore, think that the Government, when all their picturesque parades
are over next week, should settle down
and ask themselves is there a problem of
poverty-preventible poverty; is there a
problem of the slums? Let them examine
into it to find if it is there, and let
them try and find some solution.
You
would then have less to do for prisons,
for lunatic asylums, for tuberculous institutions. You could save it all in giving
life and vitality and character to the debilitated, slum-sodden residents of your
back lanes and alleys. That would be

ended, that if you continue to have men

Having done that, let me state what
are the necessities and requirements in

physique and sufficiently educated to enter
the Force by passing a proper examination.
If they do that there will be no
favouritism and nothing sectarian. What
we want, and what I am thankful to say
we have got, is a police force who introduce their Christian principles into their
lives, so that you could not tell what one
of them is by way of denomination from
the manner in which he arrests a prisoner
or holds on to him. They all do their duty
and that is exactly what we want.

criminal lunatics. We have only got 22

head to keep them. All the Minister

I am perfectly sure that if he
were

The hon. Member opposite always pleads

I would like that as much information as

Take up an Irish history, and you will
find there was an insurrection in 1798,
another in 1847, another in 1867, and
another in 1916. The periods between
all those insurrections were peaceful and
quiet. What brought about peace in
Northern Ireland, as it brought about
peace in Southern Ireland was the "Dump

I want to say that I will never fail to

the "B" Special Constabulary because

Hon. Members asked yesterday why,
if they were the saviours of Ulster, they
were not paid saviour's wages. The "B"
Special Constabulary is a voluntary force.
There is only an allowance made to these
men to pay for boots and other equipment that they could not reasonably be
expected to provide for themselves.
These men have protected the very homes
and property of hon. Gentlemen opposite
when they were not able to stop in their

ceased to be operative once. the causes

operation not only for five years but for
If it is not needed-and some
of the right hon. Gentlemen stated that
they required it in case something that we
cannot foresee would take place why keep
it on the Statute Book? They have not
given us a single reason to show how its
continuance can be justified. In the first
place we were told by the Minister of

in Northern Ireland, it was necessary to

Specials.

Mr. DEVLIN: One of them is part and

place here in Ulster-I cannot get these
people to keep quiet. And then they
will go out. It is customary to show
courtesy to a Member of this Committee
of not carrying on a conversation on the

to sit here and bear the boredom of having to remain in the assembly the least
that ought to be done when Ministers are
in the Committee is to listen to what an
hon. Member has to say. That is all the
more essential since we are dealing with
a Measure that proposes to destroy the

his personal and civic rights, to prevent
public meetings, to arrest private citizens
without charge, to cast them into prison
without stating why they are cast in, and
to keep them there. These proposals
strike at the very root of every fundamental and constitutional principle in
British law, and yet when we come to
consider this Bill Ministers, when they
do choose to come into the House, engage
in conversation instead of listening to the
arguments that are being advanced.
The continuance of the Act upon the

disappeared. Instead of that you keep
them there.
we
What have
here?
Yesterday we discussed an Estimate for
nearly a million for the police force. We
have Royal Ulster Constabulary, we have
Special Constabulary, and we have "B"
Constabulary-three sections of Constabulary to maintain the peace of the Six
Counties. Not only that, but we have in

are tourists, who do not know you as well

and with revolvers in their belts?

Civil Authorities Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
They would come to the conclusion that
the place is in such an abnormal state of
excitement that revolution prevails, and
that it is not safe for decent citizens to
pass through the various districts when a
force of that character is maintained. It
is the frightened feeling of people with a
bad conscience. That is the cause of this.
I say further, that to continue this Bill
is doing infinite mischief to the best interests of the Province. Then we have the
declarations-I quoted one of them
yesterday of the Judges of Assize, who
are in many cases presented with white
gloves symptomatic of the complete freedoom of these districts from crime, and
in every one of those declarations congratulations are extended to the community upon the absolute immunity of
our Northern area above all from abnormal crime, and practically from crime
altogether.
Why, therefore, is this Measure now
on the Statute Book? It is kept there
and brought up here every year for the
purpose of creating irritation, of fostering discontent, of rousing bitter memories of the past, as we saw in the debate
that took place yesterday. Reading the
reports in the Press this morning, one
would have imagined that we
on the
Opposition benches by attacking this
Measure were resurrecting these old,
bitter, and ought-to-be-forgotten things.
There would be no discussion of the character indicated if it had not been for the
Government bringing this Measure along
again to-day. Being an Ulsterman, I
object altogether to letting it go forth
to the people of these islands, and to
people abroad, that
we are such a
criminal community that we require
special provisions of the most extravagant and constitutionally indefensible
character in order to make us behave ourselves.
You
I verily believe that if anything should
arise to disturb our present conditions of
peacefulness, you have ample machinery
at your disposal to deal with anything
like outrage against the welfare or the
peaceful spirit of the Province.
have, as I said, the Royal Ulster Constabulary, for which we pay a million.
You have special constables, the paid
political bodyguard of the right hon.
Gentleman. You have the "B" Specials,
always there, ever faithful, ever sure.
You have not only that, but the whole
powerful forces, naval and military, of
the British Empire to defend you if two
or three people happen to come across the
Border and look crooked at you. These
Gentlemen, these heroic standard-bearers
of Imperial glory, are so sensitive and so
afraid of a few unorganized boys that
they require a multiplicity of military
and semi-military organizations with a
powerful and efficient military machine
and a Special Act of Parliament incorporating as many clauses as would deal
with every crime under the sun. A more
ridiculous or more grotesque position for
a Government with any sense of dignity
to take up, I never knew in all my life.
Therefore, I support the Motion which
has been proposed by my hon. Friend.

The PRIME MINISTER: I will discuss it outside the House, but I do not
think it is in order to go back to that time
and to discuss whether the Ulster people
were rebels or gallant men defending their
liberties. I do not think that would be

the worst day's work that was ever done
in the Imperial House of Commons when
they dropped the Arms Act and cleared
the way for all the agony and trouble aud
disorder that have taken place in Ireland.
Looking back, no one can tell what might
have happened in regard to the peace and
quietude of this country of ours if that
Act had not been taken off the Statute
Book. Are we as responsible Ministers
to do the right thing because it is difficult,
or the wrong thing because it is easy?
One of the arguments used just now
was that it was a stain upon the escutcheon
of Ulster that this Act should be on the
Statute Book at all. It was in order to
remove a little of the stain that my colleagues and I considered it was better to
have this Statute continued for some
time longer rather than to have this sort
of discussion year after year. I would
point out to hon. Members that it does
no good in time of peace which I am
glad to say we are enjoying at presentto raise this question year after year.
You may have four years of absolute
peace, in which case this Act will be
practically shelved. If it is practically
put away, and never taken off the shelf
at all, what harm will it do to anybody?
It has done nothing but secure peace in
our country. Extending the operation of
this Measure for some five years means
that we will not have this annual discussion. It has almost become part of the
law of the land. It has been in operation, I think, for some six years.
Remember that from time to time acts
of a very dangerous character are carried
out in our area which my two right hon.
Friends beside me have to treat under
this Act. If we were to take this Act off
the Statute Book and if there was going
to be a recrudescence of the difficulties we

think of the long-drawn-out, tedious and

a Government again to deal with an outbreak of that kind. Suppose Parliament
is not sitting. Imagine the first shots of

other depredation that might take place.
Suppose those young men in Derry my

it into their heads to start a difficulty such

Parliament together, and going through
the tedium of getting powers again to
deal with an extraordinary situation—and
what might happen in the meantime?
Some hon. Member said that we should
think of the life of even one child in Ulster

in connection with the Home Office
when the Estimate was being considered
yesterday. Is it not far more important

machinery lying to our hand in order that

He brought a claim, as any law-abiding

made to get that man compensated for

The noble Lord has talked about an

I
necessity for this Bill than he did.
think it is evident, so far as the Prime
Minister is concerned that he at least
would have been in favour of making this
a permanent Measure. He complained
that at one stage the British Government
did not keep a permanent Coercion Act on

mistake they ever made was to repeal
the Firearms Act. I am not exactly sure
that when he made that statement he had
the landing of the guns at Larne in his
mind. I suppose that if the Firearms Act
had been in operation at that time those
guns would not have been landed, and
probably a great many that were landed
since would not have been landed.
The troublesome period that ensued
from that time having passed, and peace
having reigned in Ulster now for the last
five or six years I would have thought that
the Government would not have troubled
this House or the outside public with
discussions on a Bill of this character.
You would think that the Government
were living in the hope-I trust I am
wrong that some further troubles similar
to what have already occurred might yet
arise. If that is their hope I trust they
will be disappointed. I honestly believe
that further troubles in this country will
not occur during the lifetime of any of
us here. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We have had peace in Ulster, and indeed
in all Ireland, for quite a number of years
now, and I do not see that we should fling
this red flag at the people.
I am one of those who believe that you
do not get peace by repressive laws.
Peace will come from the good sense and
judgment of the people. I believe that
peace did come to Ireland through the
good sense of the people, not through
force or repressive or coercive laws. I believe it would have been better in the
Government's own interest had they said:
"There is no further necessity for such
an Act as this. If at any time we find
necessity for it we will ask the people for
those additional powers.
When peace
does reign we give the people all the
liberty it is possible in our power to give
them. If we find that liberty being
abused we will want powers to stop that
abuse."
I believe under such circumstances the Government would not at any
time find any trouble in securing those
powers. As I have already said, I do not
think that there will be
further
any
troubles, or an abuse of these powers
again in the lifetime of anyone in this
House. I hope I am right in that
prophecy. I must oppose the passing of
this Clause.

Oral Answers to Questions.
ROAD CONSTRUCTION-CON-
TRACTS FOR MATERIALS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
foreign produced materials are being used
in road construction in five out of the Six
Counties in Northern Ireland, and
whether, in view of the fact that the Road
Fund is being paid by the people of Northern Ireland, he is prepared to circularise the various authorities to the
effect that they should use material produced in Northern Ireland, and thereby
increase employment for local workmen.
it was
of
to
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I would refer the
hon. Member to the reply given by me in
this House to the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) on the
29th March last, in which
pointed out that the Ministry
Home Affairs has already sent
every road authority in Northern Ireland a circular letter indicating that all
contracts for or incidental to road works,
including contracts for materials, are to be
placed preferably in Northern Ireland,
but in any event not outside the United
Kingdom, and that where possible
materials of Northern Ireland or British
manufacture or origin are to be specified.
I am not aware that the road authorities
in Northern Ireland are disregarding the
terms of this circular letter, which was
issued on the 20th July, 1926.
HAIRDRESSING TRADE REGIS-
TRATION.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received representations from employers and employees engaged in the hairdressing
business to the end that a system of
registration should be established in Northern Ireland, and whether the Government is prepared to introduce legislation
to meet the requirements of this business.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received
representation from members of the hairdressing trade advocating the establishment of a system of registration in
Northern Ireland, but I am not in a
position to state that the Government is
prepared to introduce legislation on the
lines suggested.
The hon. Member will doubtless realize
that it would be a dangerous precedent for
the Government to establish by accepting
the responsibility of introducing legislation which would have the effect of
conferring vested interests on a class of
employers and employees for which there
is no justifiable reason.
A reference to the Acts on the Statute
Book dealing with the registration of
members of the various professions will
show that Parliament in the past has
only conferred such privileges in cases
where the activities of the members of
those professions affected the general
health or well-being of the community.
It would be difficult to establish the
principle that hairdressing can be regarded
as a profession affecting either the health
or the well-being of the community, and it
will also be obvious that if the principle
were accepted in connection with this
trade it would be impossible to refuse
similar recognition to other trades of a
similar character.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I would remind the House that
this is the seventh annual Budget of Northern Ireland which I am privileged to
present to the House to-day.
I do not know whether hon. Members
attach any of the traditional significance
to the mystical number. If they do, it
may be that as we have experienced seven
lean years, we may now hope to enter
seven years of peace, prosperity and contentment.
When presenting my Annual Statement of Revenue Expenditure in the past,
I have avoided embellishments, as is befitting when prosaic financial questions
are under discussion.
But in view of the completion of seven
years of Ulster's autonomy, and having
regard to the coincidence of Saturday's
remarkable function, I feel, if I may be
pardoned for a few moments, that I
should indulge in a short retrospect of our
progress during the period of our local
responsibility.
It will be remembered that it was on the
threshold of the year 1921 that the British Parliament decreed that the Six Northern Counties of Ireland should be constituted an autonomous State, with federal
relationship to the Kingdom. This was
a new and startling experiment unprecendented and unknown in British history.
It ran counter to all our preconceived
ideas of the political and economic unity
of these islands, and it was, therefore,
with much misgiving and many doubts
and fears that we undertook the responsibility of conducting the affairs of a selfgoverning State within the ambit of the
Kingdom.
All this, of course, is well-known to the
world. But what is not so well-known,
perhaps, or so fully appreciated is the
initial encouragement and material help
given by the British Government-
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK and especially by
British Departmental Officers, to aid our
faltering footsteps.
Apart from the Statutory obligations
of the Government to provide our public
buildings, we were given the help of
British financial guarantees in respect of
some of our earlier obligations, such as
Ulster Savings Certificates.
And perhaps, most important of all, we
are under great obligation to
Baldwin-
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr.
Mr. POLLOCK- -when, as Chancellor
of the Exchequer, he agreed to the creation of an Arbitration Committee, to
whom the duty was assigned of providing

a formula for the annual adjustment of

And now at the end of seven years of
self-government, some of them anxious
years but all of them years of effort, it is
pertinent to inquire whether we have justified the hopes of those who trusted us,
and believed in us, or belied the vaticinations of those who directly and covertly
worked for our undoing.
My answer to such an inquiry is that
we have internal peace firmly established.
Further, speaking with full knowledge
and authority, I can assure the House
and the country that the financial credit
of Ulster is unassailable.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: Proof of this lies in
the fact that bankers are eager to bid for
our Treasury Bills at rates closely approximating to those of Britain. Again,
under our Loans Guarantee Act, London
issuing houses accept our Government
guarantee on terms that differ only by the
merest fraction from those of the Imperial
guarantee.
But our surest safeguard is the fact
that not only have we paid our way, but
out of our savings have accumulated
Sinking Funds and Reserves, as well as
one-third of our National Revenue, and
I have to express my obligation to Mr.
Churchill for his appreciation of this fact
in his recent Budget Statement.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: Finally, during the
period under review, we have contributed
to the Imperial Services sums amounting
to £22,000,000, and our great ambition
is to be able, with returning trade recovery to contribute in larger measure.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: And now, what relation does the function of Saturday bear
to these results?

Mr. POLLOCK: I now pass on to the
consideration of the results of the financial year which has just ended.
Last year our total revenue from all
sources was £11,024,000, and our expenditure £10,775,000, leaving a balance of
£249,000, showing that we have spent
just about 19s. 6d. out of every £ of our
income and so, by Mr. Micawber's philosophy, should be happy.
There is always something depressing in
holding a post-mortem examination on
the corpse of last year, but there are some
features of the Accounts which deserve
comment.
The first is the remarkable accuracy of
the Estimates which I presented to the
Committee of the House a year ago. Our
Revenue from taxes yielded £8,502,000,
a variation of less than half per
cent. from our expectations, and under
this head I would observe that the receipts from Stamp Duties were exactly
forecasted. Similarly, with one exception, the provision for expenditure proved
to be necessary.
Revenue, 1927-28.
But focussing attention for the moment
on last year's Revenue, I am glad to he
able to repeat the observations I made in
previous years concerning the steady increase in the yield of Motor Taxes.
The
Road Fund needs it all; the more motors
that are put into commission, the more is
my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
pleased, and indeed, I may frankly confess it my own happiness is likely in
future to be measured by the fuel they
use. But we all remember the appallingly
bad condition of our roads a few years
ago, and we should all welcome the enlargement in the receipts from Motor
Taxes, knowing that it enables local
authorities to pursue even more vigorously
their really remarkable work of road construction and improvement.
Death Duties yielded more than we expected. This is a tantalizing source of
revenue, as medical science has not yet
co-operated with us sufficiently to enable
us to attain exactitude. The Chancellor,
in his recent Budget Statement, declared
that death had been his only companion
and friend, by supplying him with the
great and fortuitous increase in the Revenue arising from the demise of so many
wealthy citizens. I am not in a position
to make the same statement in regard to
our returns, but, nevertheless, our figures
show an appreciable increase over the
Estimate.
In speaking of Death Duties, I would
stress a fact relating to investment securities: We are entitled to collect duty
only on those registered here, and so
every man in our Province should-for
the good of his own people make sure,
if he holds any stocks or shares which can
be registered here, that they are registered here. Five per cent. War Loan is an
example, and I believe that £50,000 or
more, which could be spent here for the
benefit of the Province, is lost annually
becaues people will not avail themselves
of the Belfast Register.
Before leaving the subject of Death
Duties I would like to take this opportunity of making a brief reference to life
insurance policies. It has been decided
that the moneys payable under a policy of
insurance taken out by a person domiciled
in Northern Ireland with a company
having his head office in Great Britain are
to be regarded as a British asset. Unless
specific provision is made on the face of
the policy for payment in Northern Ireland, the Death Duties do not accrue to
our Exchequer. As the result of discussion with the Association of Life Insurance Companies, future policies issued
in Northern Ireland will be payable here,
but various complex questions of mortgages and so forth prevent the companies
from initiating any general action so far
as existing policies are concerned, and so
I would appeal to all patriotic persons
holding life insurance policies to
approach the company concerned, with a
view, if possible, of having them endorsed so as to provide that on maturity
they should be paid here. There is quite
a substantial amount of revenue involved.

Hon. Members have become accustomed

When one considers, however, that

Land Purchase Annuities is the only

Expenditure, 1927-28.
The expenditure which has been met
during the past year is not characterized
by any items of exceptional note. It is
satisfactory to be able to say that in
common with the revenue. the expenditure is now becoming more or less stabilized, and this fact is bound to have a
good effect on the industrial position.
But while commenting on this comparative stability of our revenue and expenditure figures, we must not permit
ourselves to be lulled to a state of complacency. We are living in a world of
rapid change. The thoughts, the habits,
the ambitions of to-day, may be regarded
as obsolete or old-fashioned to-morrow,
and thus Governments are compelled,
under the pressure of popular demands,
to adapt themselves to these recurring
movements. Our outlook for the coming
year suggests this commentary.
Hon. Members will see from the figures

for Consolidated Fund Services approximated fairly closely to the Estimate.
The same remark applies also to the
ordinary Transferred Supply Services,

I now come to the question of the Imperial contribution for last year, and it
is perhaps not necessary for me to go into
this subject in any great detail, as I explained it rather fully when introducing
my Budget just twelve months ago.
should point out, however, in case any
hon. Members intend giving me good

the amount of surplus which will ultimately be available in respect of last
year depends entirely on the final determination of the contribution by the
Joint Exchequer Board. I am afraid,
therefore, that I must emphasize the fact
that this balance of £249,000 is provisional. The figure of £1,400,000 which
was decided upon by the Board as the provisional contribution for last year was
based on Estimates and will, of course, be
revised when the Board comes to consider
the actual results of the year. I have
already referred to the fact that happily

Insurance payments was considerably in

so hon. Members will clearly understand

arrived at when the Joint Exchequer
Board has before it not Estimates but

Before proceeding further with my
Statement I would pause for a few
moments to consider a question of some
interest. The inauguration in the Irish
Free State of a new currency system has
not excited very much comment in our
Province, but it has had the direct result
of raising a currency question of no little
importance here, especially in relation to
the ordinary banking operations of the
country.
There are at present six banks operating in Ireland who have the right of
issuing bank notes. Three of them have
their head offices in Ulster and two in
London, the remaining one being domiciled in the Free State, Now, there are
two portions of the note issue of each
bank, namely, "fiduciary issue," against
which no legal tender need be held as

cover, and "excess issue," against which
the bank must hold gold and silver coin
or Treasury notes. The fiduciary issue,
which requires no cover, was determined
by the Irish Bank Act of 1845, allocating
to each bank a fixed amount and totalling
in the agregate £6,354,000 for all the
banks then in Ireland. The reason for
fixing definite amounts was the undesirability of leaving the banks free to issue
as many notes as they wished.
The privilege of these fiduciary or free
note issues has been of material value to
the banks, and has probably facilitated
the opening of branches in many rural
places where the volume of business is not
sufficiently large in the ordinary way to
justify the expense involved in providing
banking facilities. Moreover, the note
issues are very useful to the agricultural
community, which, as is well known,
deals with bank notes rather than with
cheques.
So long as a common currency system
obtained in the whole of Ireland, these
arrangements proceeded in their normal
way, but on the creation of a new currency
system by the Free State powers were
taken by that Government to create a new
fiduciary issue for the banks operating in
the South. This is called the Consolidated Bank Note Issue. The total issue
of all such banks was fixed at £6,000,000,
but notes may not now be issued in excess
of the fiduciary issue except in very special
circumstances. This sum is divided
among the banks roughly according to
the scope of their business in the Free
State. Previous to the Free State
Currency Act of 1927, the total free, or
fiduciary, issue which had been allocated
to all the Irish Banks of Issue amounted
to £6,354,000, and it is clear that we
could not expect the whole of that sum
to become available for banking purposes
in Northern Ireland, by reason of the fact
that a separate fiduciary issue of
£6,000,000 had been created by the Free
State for the use of banks in their area.
The problem which confronted the
British Government was, therefore, to
determine upon an approximate amount
of fiduciary issues for the banks of issue
operating in Ulster, and although the
question of currency remains an Imperial
matter under the Government of Ireland
Act, yet at the request of the banks and,
indeed at the request of the Treasury,
Finance Minister's Statement 1934
The Budget-
21 MAY 1928
my Ministry interested itself with negotations which have extended over a period
of approximately two years and have only
now been concluded.
I am happy to be able to say that
although the difficulties in the way of a
settlement at one time appeared to be
very formidable, yet unanimous agreement has now been reached—(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-between the
British Government and all the Banks of
Issue in Northern Ireland. I am satisfied
that as the result we are now assured of
a sufficient supply of currency to meet
trading requirements, and that the banks
themselves have not suffered any loss as
the result of the readjustment. The
agreement, however, requires statutory
confirmation, and a Bill with that object
in view is now before the Imperial
Parliament.
We have also been obliged to give careful consideration to the question of the
circulation in Northern Ireland of Free
State currency.
As hon. Members will
doubtless be
aware, the Free State
Government has taken every precaution
to ensure that British currency shall not
circulate in the Free State, and indeed the
banks in that area are expressly forbidden
to pay out to the public any_currency
other than their own notes and Free State
legal tender. Similar steps will be taken
here. The necessary statutory authority
is now being sought by the Imperial
Government. Although there is bound to
be a small interchange of British and
Free State currency between individuals
residing near the border, yet the existence
of Free State currency should, I think,
cause no embarrassment in the various
trading centres of our area, especially as
I understand that the banks will be able
to issue notes for the use of bona fide
travellers going across the Border, in the
same way that French and other foreign
notes are issued.
A short time ago I entered upon a discussion with the Treasury in order to see
whether arrangements could not be made
to ensure a more satisfactory circulation of
clean currency notes in Northern Ireland,
but the matter was not pursued to a conclusion, since the impending transfer of
the issue to the Bank of England will, it
is hoped, achieve the result I had in view.

Passing now to the year on which we
have already entered, I will proceed first
of all to give the House an outline of the

Exchequer, and I will then deal with the

The charges which will fall upon the
Consolidated Fund are estimated to total
in all the sum of £821,000, of which
£425,000 represents the payment into the
Road Fund of a corresponding sum which
we expect will be received from Motor
Taxation. This leaves a sum of £396,000,
and in addition to the usual statutory
salaries, which require £4,000, provision
is made in the expenditure from the Consolidated Fund for Sinking Funds and
various other Services.
Referring first to Sinking Funds, I
propose to set apart for this purpose the
sum of £187,000, which will be allocated
to the Land Purchase and Ulster Savings
Certificates Funds. Last year I made a
special allocation of £100,000 to our
Reserve Funds. I think it is sound
finance to continue to make this provision,
and so a similar sum is thus proposed to
be set aside this year. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). It would be impossible to
over-rate the importance of Sinking and
Reserve Funds. I have established two
main classes of Funds; first, for making
provision in respect of debt liabilities, and
second, to maintain diminishing sources
of income, such as the Land Purchase
Annuities, which would in the ordinary
way disappear in course of time. Our
Sinking Fund for the Interest on Ulster
Savings Certificates now stands at over a
quarter of a million pounds, and the Reserve Fund for General Capital Liabilities
at £660,000. What I might term the
"Revenue" Sinking Funds are in an
equally satisfactory condition and total
over £700,000.

for the total amount involved, namely,

I do not propose to make any provision
in the Budget for the expenses of carrying out the Bann Drainage Scheme,
although a sum is included in respect of
preliminary inquiries. As hon. Members
are aware, the proposals of the Government have been in the hands of local
authorities for the past few months,. but I
am not yet in a position to announce their
acceptance of the scheme. The Government itself is fully satisfied that none of
the alternative suggestions which have
been made offer any radical solution of
the problem. We have, moreover, made
a definite offer to the local authorities
concerned-which is universally regarded
as generous and I may at once say that
it must be looked upon as a final offer.
I feel that the local authorities are in the
best position to judge whether their constituents desire the relief from flooding
which the scheme will give, and whether
they think it would be worth the comparatively small contribution required of
them. In short, the fate of the scheme
is now in the hands of the local authorities.
From time to time we hear complaints
that the Bann drainage scheme should be
a national responsibility, and that the
cost should, therefore, fall on the State
Exchequer. Drainage schemes in England are not so regarded. In that part
of the Kingdom the areas benefited pay
at least half the cost. In our case, how-

ever, the State offers to bear three-fourths

and that is that the taxpayers of Belfast,

While on the subject of Entertainment
Tax, I desire to touch on a small matter
in which agriculture is interested
all know, Ireland has long been famed for
its horses, and considerable profit has
accrued to farmers and others directly
engaged in the industry of horse-breeding
as a result of the fine specimens of
thoroughbreads which have and still are
being produced. This is a section of the
agricultural industry which in the past
has received little or no encouragement
from the Government, and I think that
it is desirable that we should, if at all
possible, do something, however small, to
stimulate the industry in view of the
material benefit which it confers on the
Province.
A considerable amount of historical
interest attaches to the beginnings of
horse-racing in the Province. The records
of the Royal Down Corporation are
literally teeming with interest, and show
that in 1685 James II granted a Charter
to a body of public-spirited people who
had voluntarily subscribed to fund
raised to encourage the breeding of horses
by "maintaining a plate to be for ever
run for yearly in the said County (of
Down)."
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: What did
he do five years later on?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Charter enables
the Corporation to hold land direct from
the Crown, and, moreover, authorizes the
Finance Minister's Statement 1942

holding of a special fair for the buying
and selling of horses. Similarly, the
Down Hunts Club was formed by voluntary subscribers and has continued for a
great number of years to carry out comparable work.
But times have changed, and although
the value of the industry continues, public
support tends to wane. To encourage the
responsible authorities, I have decided
that as from the granting of the necessary
statutory powers, exemption from Entertainment Duty will be allowed on horse
races organized by a society or body not
established for profit.
I have had representative deputations
from cinema owners and the Philharmonic Society for the relief of Entertainment Duty on their enterprises, but
whilst sympathizing with their necessities,
I feel that I would not be justified in remitting any further taxes at present, in
view of the uncertainty of the considerable liabilities which appear ahead.

As there is evidently a considerable
degree of general misunderstanding in
regard to the application of the proceeds
of the duty on petrol, it is desirable that
I should take this opportunity of stating
the position occupied by Northern Ireland
vis-a-vis Great Britain.
The petrol duty in great Britain is not,
as seems to be commonly supposed,
specifically appropriated to the scheme for
granting relief from local rates. In the
first place, I apprehend that the revenue
thus raised will be by no means equal to
the burden of the Rating Relief Scheme.
In fact, the revenue from the tax on oils
in Britain is estimated to produce in a full
year about £13,300,000, allowing for the
abandonment of the tax on paraffin, while
the Rating Relief Scheme will cost up to
£30,000,000. That scheme has in Great
Britain been adopted as a part of the
Government's programme for the assistance of agriculture and of the basic industries of the State, and the duty on
petrol merges in the general body of taxation which will meet the general
expenditure of the country.
Pursuing this matter a little further,
hon. Members will recollect that the
Rating Relief Scheme is not intended to
come into operation in Britain until the
autumn of 1929, with the result that the
imposition of the petrol duty this year
provides the Chancellor with a very useful
addition to the surplus which he intends
placing to a Suspensory Fund, presumably
in order to lighten the charge of the
Rating Relief Scheme in its initial years.
I have explained this subject at some
length, because of the fact that I have on
several occasions been asked whether the
revenue which we will derive from the
petrol duty (estimated by the Imperial
Chancellor to amount to £200,000) will
be adequate for the purposes of
Rating Relief Scheme which may be introduced here. If I endeavour to answer
these questions, I find two important
difficulties.

in Great Britain. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
As regards our basic industries, the
burden of rates falls on them with even
greater weight than the rates on farming
land.
The Chancellor gave an example of the
crushing nature of this burden on the
cost of the production of steel and ships.
Let me apply the same reasoning to our
linen trade.
First, the farmer pays his rates to produce flax; the scutcher follows with rates
on his mill; then comes the spinner's
rating on his large buildings, the weaver
on his factory, the bleachers, finishers,
etc., on their works. All this accumulation of charges means that every yard of
linen is charged with rates on at least six
different processes before the final stage
of marketing is reached.
Therefore, it is the Government's view
that the arguments which apply to
British industries apply here with like
•
I expect that many hon. Members are
impatiently awaiting an opportunity of
assailing me with conundrums concerning
the implications of this very important
subject. But it is so intricate and so
many interests are involved that I cannot
do more at the present time than state
the general policy and intentions of the
Government, and this I have already
done.
In order that the subject may receive
the mature and detailed consideration it
requires, I have appointed a small and
efficient inter-departmental committee to
inquire into all its aspects, and I hope,
by the autumn, to be in a position to
deal with it more comprehensively.
I have now finished my Statement of
the present financial position of our State,
and although the future cannot be said
to be free from financial care and grave
responsibilities, I am persuaded that if
we should be blessed with the return of
trade prosperity, we can face these responsibilities, not, perhaps, with a light heart,
but at any rate with confidence borne on
the courage and fortitude which so far
have carried us safely through. I beg to
move. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

I have knowledge of the fact that the
right hon. Gentleman's hands are tied by
Section 32 of the Act which constituted
this Parliament. That Section created a

For the purposes of the financial
provisions of this Act, there shall be
established a Board, to be called the
Joint Exchequer Board, consisting of
two members appointed by the Treasury, one member appointed by the
Treasury of Southern Ireland, one member appointed by the Treasury of
Northern Ireland, and a chairman appointed by His Majesty.
Assuming that Southern Ireland has gone

Exchequer Board the big brother on the
far side of the water has two representatives to our one, so that we may take it
that when the Minister of Finance gets
into a tight corner the two to one will
beat him every time.

again to thank the right hon. Gentleman. I noticed that the hon. Member
who represents the University (Mr.
Johnstone) spoke in terms of high appreciation—and, strange to say, he was supported by the hon. Member for Down
(Mr. Collins) of the action of the Government in increasing the grant to
Queen's University from £36,000 to
£40,000. I am not in a position to

college in Derry. Sometimes people
think that a great many things are done
for Belfast and not for other places, and
while I am not objecting to the increased
grant for Queen's University I think
there ought to have been a grant given
for the College in Derry as well.
The Minister of Finance referred to the
question of the Bann drainage, and he
assured the House that that matter was
now in the hands of the various county
councils of the Six Counties. I presume
be meant to say that if this scheme did
not go on the Government would not be
to blame, but that it would be the fault
of the county councils for not accepting
their share of the responsibility. The
right hon. Gentleman made it clear that
in his Budget he has only made provision
for the preliminary expenses, and I am
sorry that he did not announce that he
had put some money aside for the pur
pose of rendering assistance in connec
tion with the drainage of other rivers as
well as the Bann. In my own constituency we have a river which was taken
away from its natural course.
Mr. POLLOCK: What river is that?
Mr. CRAWFORD: The Glenariffe
river. A hundred years ago the Commissioners of Public Works built a
straight run from this river, but they
neglected it for twenty years, and the
river got silted up. After heavy rains
it gets flooded, and the farmers in the
locality are seriously inconvenienced.

I
[Mr. Crawford]

do hope that in some way, whether out

and if the work is carried out many poor

I gathered that the only relief for
Entertainment Tax that the Government
propose to grant this year is in respect of
horse racing. I think that of all the
people who pay Entertainment Tax those
who attend horse races are the most able
to pay, and I do not think the relief that
the Minister of Finance proposes to give
will help farmers in any way. It may do
so in some way that I do not understand,
but in my opinion it will only encourage
horse racing and tempt people to attend
race meetings, and I do not think that is
a good thing to do. Personally I think
that those who attend these horse races
can afford to pay the Entertainment Tax,
and I would rather have seen the tax on
football matches reduced, because football matches attract young people and
keep them away from other temptations.
We learn from the right hon. Gentleman's speech that the people of Northern
Ireland are spending immense sums of
money on unemployment, education, and
pensions. When we commence to look
into the matter it is very sad to
realise that so many of our young people
are being educated at the expense of the
State, and that they then go abroad to
other countries and leave the old people
at home to be maintained by the State
by means of pensions. I agree with hon.
Members opposite who have said again
and again that it would be a great thing
if this country could devise some means
of keeping our young men at home.
Money spent in that way would be money
wisely spent. I am not saying that the
Government have done nothing in this
respect. They have done a great deal
and I hope they will do even more in the
future. I agree with the Leader of the
Opposition that it would be a good thing
if we could extend our pensions scheme to
widows whose husbands were not contributors to the National Health Insurance Fund.
It is very hard that poor
women, whose husbands die before their
wife reaches the age of 65, cannot get
a pension until they attain that age. I
know cases where it is a downright hardship and where such widows can scarcely
live. I know the difficulty that exists,
but I do sincerely hope that means will
be found to give some little consideration
to widows of this class.
Then I would love to hear the Minister
of Finance announcing that blind persons would be entitled to a pension
before they were fifty years of age. It
is a great handicap to be born blind, and
there are a great many cases personally
known to me where blind persons require
assistance long before they are fifty years
of age.
In conclusion, I should like to say
that I did not find the right hon. Gentleman's speech uninteresting. I enjoyed it
immensely, and as he lifted up the corner
of the screen and allowed us to look into
the mind of the Government I thought
I could see better times coming for the
farmers of this country.

About twelve months ago a lady came
here to Ulster to see an aged relative.
She came on a one-day excursion, and
when she arrived at Belfast from Dublin
she was seized by the police and taken to
the police office and kept there. I went
to the police office and interviewed the
police, and ultimately she was released.
She only intended to come for the one
day. She was to leave that evening.
Did that inspire any resentment?
at all. The incident did not count.
So low had our civic liberty values become that nobody paid the slightest attention to it She committed no offence
whatever. If she did, why did the
Government not arrest her for the
offence? I do not know why the Minister of Home Affairs is amused. What
has tortured the soul of the English Home
Secretary seems to be a source of merriment to our representative of the Home
Office in this country. But that is what
was done in the case of this lady. I object altogether to giving such powers to
any Government, or to allowing the Home
Office, or the police, or any of the agents
of the Government to arrest private
citizens, to put them in prison, and to
keep them there, as was done in this case.
Then we have the case of the wearing
of emblems to which my hon. Friend (Mr.
W. McMullen) referred. I object to any
Government office or any policeman determining what emblems I shall wear. As
a citizen I am perfectly entitled to wear
what I like. If an emblem is provocative
you might as well arrest everyone who
wears an Orange emblem on 12th July,
because it irritates someone who disagrees
with him. A more contemptible thing
for any Government to do I never knew.
If these men who were wearing these
emblems were engaged in any illegal pursuit it was your business to arrest them
and try them for that illegality, but to
allow anyone in the name of smug
officialdom to go out and arrest people for

I was greatly interested in yesterday's
proceedings. It is the first day on which
the Budget has ever been of interest to
anybody or of interest to the House.
The House was always empty. No one
cared, because everyone knew that we
were not dealing with our household expenses in Northern Ireland, because
we have no power over our household expenses. But because certain events took
place which attracted some people to witness our proceedings yesterday the speech
of the right hon. Gentleman was delivered

and who tell us financially what we ought

their spirt of friendship towards themselves in Northern Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I think that that

this 1920 Act was passed and which was

as a responsibility that Ulster was called
upon to bear a contribution to the Imperial Exchequer of £8,000,000 a year.
Now, out of bedlam I do not think it
would be possible to conceive the mentality of any set of reasonable or competent business men, not to speak
politicians, who in view of the circumstances and they have been justified
since agreed to the proposals of the
British Government for this small Northern area of six counties with a population
of one and a quarter millions to give a
contribution to the British Exchequer of
£8,000,000. It was no wonder then that
they were so grateful to these Ministers
who were gathered in the galleries yesterday who relieved them-

I come to another question-the question of widows' pensions. That question
was touched upon yesterday, and I desire
to emphasize it here. Everyone knows
that there has been no more beneficent
Measure passed by Parliament than this
Measure to give pensions to widows and to
orphan children. No doubt the Government hung back for a long time before
they carried it into operation, but by constant and incessant pressure from these
Benches they were ultimately compelled
to place the widows and orphans of this
area in the same position as the widows
and orphans in England. But like all
legislation passed by rather retrograde
politicians, it only solved the problem in
part. No doubt it gives to the widows
of insured persons and to insured women
the advantages of the Act, but why should
not all widows-I mean all necessitous
widows-and children get this pension?
We know what the value of it is. We
have described it before. I would like to
describe it again, although I know this
House does not like sentiment. I would
like to describe it again, because, great and
beneficent as the Old Age Pensions Act
was as a service to humanity, it was not, in
my judgment, comparable to the value of
the Widows' and Orphans' Pensions' Act.
Old people sometimes have the advantage
of having their relatives to maintain them
-and sometimes they are not hard to
maintain-but there is no more tragic
situation than that of the mother of little
children with the bread-winner gone and
with no future before them-a woman
with four or five children, the eldest of
whom is perhaps twelve years of age.

I think he described

is the glorious British policy of equality
of treatment. We have heard of step-bystep, of equal conditions for the people of
Great Britain and Ulster. Well, we
want in relation to the Entertainment
Tax precisely the same conditions as prevail in Great Britain.
I must say that I cannot see why he
continues to keep this tax on cinemas and
theatres, because everybody knows that
the competition among those places is so
great that hardly any of them are able to
make ends meet. That is their business?
It is their business to make ends meet,
and it is your business to let them make
ends meet; but how are they to do it if
you impose a tax of this character upon
them. These picture houses are of tremendous value to the public. I do not
know whether the right hon. Gentleman
ever goes to one of them or not. I used
to be a constant visitor to them for three
years. When I was an absentee from this
House I used to go there twice a week.
Then I came here, not for your entertainment, but for my own. I do not go to
places of entertainment for other people's
entertainment; I go to them for my own.
Very well, then, I have a great appreciation of these institutions, because they are
the poor man's theatre. Poor people can
drop into them and at a small charge they
can get a pleasant two and a half hours.
In this period of trade depression, with
people living in wretched slums, and not
able to make ends meet, it is a great thing
that even the little entertainment they do
get should be got in these picture houses.
The right hon. Gentleman admitted
last year that he had seen the balance
sheets of these cinemas, and I think the
one or two theatres that are in existence
in Belfast are in a similar position. He
had the balance sheets before him, and
he knows that these places do not pay.
I object to the tax for that reason, and I
object to it for another reason. I object
to the incidence of this tax, because it is
a tax upon receipts and not a tax upon
profits. On every ticket that is sold to any
member of the public going into a theatre
or picture house there is a tax. It is the
only tax I know of that is indefensible
from that point of view. If you are going
to maintain a tax upon entertainments or
amusements, whatever you choose to call
them. tax the profits. You will not get
any tax by taxing the profits. Shortly
you will get no tax by taxing them as
you are taxing them, because there are no
profits. and I think that is unfair. I do
not think there exists a condition of things
in any part of the world where a business
concern that is not paying has to pay a
big tribute to the State for carrying on
an unpaying business. There might be

and conditions of service was a stipulation that the engagement might be
terminated by the Department or by the
