Under
Section 59 (1) of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, Mr. McAlonan became an
officer of the Ministry of Agriculture as
from the 1st January, 1922. He continued while in the service of the Ministry
to discharge duties in connection with
the inspection of potatoes. As is well
known, a very substantial and most remunerative trade in the export of potatoes from Northern Ireland is, apart from
Great Britain, carried on with countries
abroad, notably France, the Canary Islands, Malta, and Cyprus, as well as with
the Irish Free State. It is a great deal
the most important of our exports from
this country in the way of agriculture
products, and if we cannot depend upon
the officials whom we have to inspect
them that trade would go to pieces.
Owing to the existence of Black Scab in
certain parts of Northern Ireland, the
admission of potatoes from the area into
the countries named is subject to compliance with very stringent regulations.
The foreign markets are open to the produce on certain conditions only which may
be summarised as follows:-
First, that all exporters shall comply
strictly with the regulations of the importing country.
Second, that the Ministry shall inspect
all potatoes before exportation and
certify them as having been found free
from disease, and,
Third, that the Ministry shall issue
such a certificate for each consignment.
In the issuing of certificates the
Ministry must, of course, depend upon the
honesty of its inspectors, and by honesty
I do not suggest anything in the way of
ordinary dishonesty, but carelessness.
Carelessness in dealing with an individual
consignment, whereby even a small quantity of diseased potatoes was passed for
export would have serious results, as importing countries would lose faith in the
Ministry's inspection service, and the
potato trade of Northern Ireland would
consequently be imperilled, and one of the
most remunerative countries for the
potato trade is the Free State, who are
most particular. Following reports received by the Ministry as to the manner in
which Mr. McAlonan was performing his

on the 15th November, 1926, and I may

having regard to the decision of the Civil
Service Committee, that there was no
other reason actuating the right hon.
Gentleman than a desire to secure a
diminution in the number of Catholics.
in his Department. I am not making
that statement as a Catholic, because, as
the House knows, I am not of that faith.
I am simply trying to interpret the matter
as it would appear to the ordinary man
in the street. If the right hon. Gentleman and the Government are desirous of
convincing the community generally that
theirs is an impartial administration, that
there is no discrimination between
Catholic and Protestant in the Department, I suggest to him even at this late
stage this man should be reinstated.
I do not think it is necessary to
examine this matter further The
Minister has suggested that the Committee could not have thought much
about Mr. McAlonan's claim, because
they only granted him the beggarly
compensation of £65, when he might have
been entitled, as a temporary servant, to
a pension of £65 per annum. What
must they have thought of the Department's case? It may be true to say they
did not give Mr. McAlonan as much as
he could have got, but they gave Mr.
McAlonan the decision, which is much
more than could be said from the Department's point of view, because the decision
was adverse to the Department. The
Government of Northern Ireland have
two representatives on the Committee,
and the British Government, with whom
we are always supposed to be acting in
conjunction, have also a couple of representatives on it. These gentlemen, who,
like Cæsar's wife, are above suspicion,
gave a decision. I am of opinion that the
Civil Service Committee thought once they
gave that decision this man would have
been reinstated by the right hon.
Gentleman in his Department. But he
failed to do that.
The Civil Service Committee says he is
guilty of neither misconduct nor incapacity.
Let us examine it from the point of view of
misconduct. I think the ordinary layman's interpretation would be that if Mr.
McAlonan failed to discharge his duty
from the point of view of securing a sufficient export of these potatoes from
Newry, that would be misconduct. I
do not think the right hon. Gentleman
is very good, so far as definitions are concerned. He tried to deal with the word
"honesty." Whether he was responsible
for the production placed before the
House this afternoon I do not know, but
in my judgment he handled the matter
very badly. It was remarkably hard to
follow, but perhaps it is my knowledge
of English that does not permit me to
follow language of that kind. I apply
an ordinary layman's interpretation to
this. Inasmuch as the Civil Service Committee have stated that this Gentleman
is guilty of neither misconduct nor incapacity, they have clearly vindicated his
character, and any fair and impartial
Departmental chief could only do
thing, and that is completely to reinstate
him and pay him for the time he was
suspended. I suggest that the right hon.
Gentleman, having regard to all the circumstances, if he wants to allay the suspic on aroused in the public mind, or,
one

more important, if he wants to do justice
to a person wronged, has only one
course open, and that is to reinstate the
man.

Mr. LEEKE: Congratulations on his
Budget have been showered upon the
Minister of Finance, but there is one thing
I must say I am very disappointed about,
and that is the question of the Bann
drainage. That has been a burning question--it is a national question, not a local
question-for many years. As long as I
can remember in every election that took
place in County Derry after you stated
your political views on Home Rule the
next thing you put in was "I am in
favour of the Bann drainage." It was
recognized by the then Chief Secretary for
Ireland as a question which should be
dealt with nationally, but the Minister of
Finance here with that cleverness he has
always shown in shoving as much as possible of what should be national taxation
on to local taxation has managed to get
the Bann drainage partly out of the question. He told us he gave 75 per cent.
as against 50 per cent. given in England.
I am not sufficiently versed in what the
English Act covers, but the flooding of the
Bann effects every one of the Six Counties
with the exception of Fermanagh. That
a matter that affects the whole nationfor we are a nation now-should be made
a local charge is to me ridiculous. You
must remember that the agriculturists
have to bear this.

Mr. Gordon.
Mr. POLLOCK: And Belfast.
Mr. LEEKE: You told us about that
yesterday. It is the agriculturists who
will largely have to bear this taxation,
but if it is so that they have to bear such
a big proportion, it must be remembered
that the areas flooded are bearing a
special drainage rate, which amounts to
11d in the £, while the farmers there
lose their crops every year.
Can anyone
look calmly on and see these people, who
have been working in getting in their
crops and investing their capital, losing
their crops and their capital through the
flooding! It has gone on for years. We
were told that when we got our local
Parliament that matter would be dealt
with. We are now over seven years in
being. We have been congratulating
ourselves on grand Budgets yesterday
and to-day, but here is a problem which
affects the welfare of the agricultural
community, and it has not been dealt
with yet. You are trying so to hamper
it with conditions that it is impossible for
local authorities, in the present state of
your finances, to carry it out.
The right hon. Gentleman told us
about how generous the Belfast people
were in paying, without screaming, any
financial losses and how they never made
any protest. It must be remembered
that were it not for the agricultural community of the Six Counties Belfast would
not be here in its present position. It
is dependent on farm products for its
financial position. Equally, Coleraine

The Budget-

[Mr. Leeke]
and Derry make no complaint because
everyone is anxious to see every possible
facility given to the farmers to develop
their industry, because on it depends the
prosperity of industrial areas. Therefore
I cannot see that Belfast can make any
protest against having to pay for what is,
after all, their own interest. I am disappointed in regard to the question of
agricultural rating. The people have
been anxiously looking for a long time to
see what the Northern Government would
do. Protests have been coming from
farmers' unions and resolutions from the
county councils of late asking the Govern-.
ment to adopt in their entirety the proposals in the Churchill Budget.
The Minister of Finance told us yesterday that the suggestions made in the
English Budget were of a provisional
kind, that they were not definite, but he
did give us an assurance that whatever
advantage the English agriculturists
would get the Ulster agriculturists would
not get less. Could he not have made
suggestions provisionally so as to allay the
suspicions of the Ulster farmers? They
are suspicious that the Ulster Government is going to be very slow in adopting
the proposals put forward in the British
Budget. I hope he will be able to give
us something clearer regarding this matter than he has done in his Statement.
He also told us about racing relief. I
do not know how much the Maze and
Down Hunt brought the Exchequer, but
I think it would be a very small sum.
I
would like to see the production of
thoroughbreds a paying proposition in
Northern Ireland. It has never been
that. We do not say they have been a
failure, but as the number has been comparatively small, they have not been a
profitable source of revenue. If the Minister of Finance could abolish the £50 on
the Maze and Down Hunt I would back
him up and give him all the assistance I
could. I would like to ask him
whether this tax will be removed from
small country meetings outside the Maze
and Down Hunt, like, say, Draperstown
or Desertmartin in County Derry. Will
the tax be removed from the poor man's
sports where the people go to what are
called flapper meetings? These are the
only opportunities the agricultural labourers or the farmers get to enjoy a day's
racing. They cannot afford to go to
Liverpool, or Manchester, or such places,
and so I think these small meetings ought
to have freedom from Entertainment Tax.
Of course, in the case of point-to-point
meetings there is no gate and, therefore,
there is no tax.
With regard to the taxation of motors
I want to raise a point. I have raised
this question again and again-in fact I
think the Minister of Finance himself took
the matter up. The Derry hackney motorowners are in a worse position than any
other people in Ulster. They have to pay
double taxation for operating in Northern
Ireland and in the Free State. They do
no trade towards what I may call the
Belfast end of County Derry at all. It
is all through to the Free State, for they
are only five or six miles from the Border.
All their business is done there, and if they
cannot afford to pay the double licence
duty they are unable to run these motors.
I think a special case should be made, and
I would ask the Minister of Finance to
make a special case for the Derry City
hackney owners, who are in a worse position than the hackney owners in any other
part of Ulster. We all know that taxation is high and that roads are not made
in return for the amount paid; but the
roads are improving; at least we are
making an effort to improve them. The
revenue which will arise from petrol could
be, as the hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) suggested, granted to the
farmers towards relief of rates and also
towards the Bann drainage, a question
that is a burning question in five counties.
It is an outstanding question, and I make
a special appeal now that it should be
dealt with effectively.
May I be
I
Mrs. CHICHESTER:
allowed to join in the congratulations
which, as the hon. Member (Mr. Leeke)
who has just sat down says, have been
showered on our Minister of Finance?
would like to deal for a moment with the
question of the relief of agriculture. I
cannot quite understand the particular
point expressed in the last speech to which
we have listened. It is undoubtedly a
fact that very great anticipations have
been aroused throughout Northern Ireland, especially, perhaps, in the rural
districts, as to what would be said by the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) in
his Budget in regard to the relief of rates
as introduced in England. The farmers
throughout the Province have, as we all
The Budget-
General Debate
22 MAY 1928
know, been suffering extreme hardship,
especially in some counties more than in
others, owing to high rates. It is quite
natural, and one could quite understand
that they should be impatient at the
present moment, and that resolutions, as
the last speaker said, have been showering
in upon ordinary Members of this House,
and, I presume, upon the Government.
But I cannot think that these farmers,
and the people generally in the Six
Counties, have really reflected upon the
length of time which the English Chancellor of the Exchequer had to prepare
his plans, the time that has elapsed since
those proposals became known, and the
time which our Minister of Finance has
had to produce his Budget. It is rather
hard to expect him to be able to make
an important announcement such as this
with a few weeks' preparation. After all,
we do know that the farmers in England will have to wait until October, 1929,
in order to experience the relief which
they are expecting. We yesterday had a
pronouncement from the right hon.
Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) which I think
ought to satisfy us all, knowing him as
we know him, and knowing what reliance
can be placed on his promise. We have
the statement made by him that he and
the Government are prepared to see that
the farmers of Northern Ireland will not
be in a worse position than the farmers
in England. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I think that really ought to satisfy us and all reasonable people throughout the Six Counties, and I am quite
certain that the farmers of Northern
Ireland will realize that they have a very,
very definite statement and that their impatience will be satisfied before long.
I cannot quite understand the attitude
of some hou. Members opposite. It is,
as usual-to my mind at ary rate-somewhat inconsistent. The hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. Devlin), and I rather
think the last speaker, said there would
be considerable revenue from the petrol
tax, and he suggested that this should
be used for the purpose of Bann drainage in which the hon. Member (Mr.
Leeke) opposite and I are very keenly
interested. The hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Devlin) also suggested other
purposes to which that petrol tax might
be applied, such as widows' and orphans'
pensions. He seems to think in fact that
the petrol tax is going to be an inexhaustible supply.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: He quite forgets that it is not going to be anything
like adequate for the purpose of the relief
of agricultural rates. Personally, keenly
interested as I am in the drainage of the
Bann, and anxious as I am that it should
be carried out, I certainly think I would
have the whole Province with me if I said
that I thought it would be more necessary
to devote the proceeds of that tax to the
relief of agricultural rates. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). However, touching,
as I am, upon Bann drainage, I would
like to go on and say that I agree with
certain other hon. Members in that I am
very sorry indeed that there is no provision made for this purpose in the Budget
which has been introduced by the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock), and that
consequently another year will be lost,
another year of suffering to the farmers
who are so deeply affected by this terrible
evil.
But I do not agree with other speakers
who have blamed the Government in this
connection What else could the right
hon. Gentleman have done? What other
action could he have taken but the action
which he has taken in this connection? I
think he has very clearly demonstrated
since this matter was first introduced into
this House that he and the Government
are absolutely heart and soul in the
scheme, and are determined, as far as lies
in their power, to give assistance to those
who are menaced by this evil. I think
the offer made by the right hon. Gentleman and the Government was an unprecedented offer and one for which the whole
country ought to be grateful, and one for
which I know those who are actually
sufferers are grateful.
The last speaker said this was a burning
question and a national question, that
generations have asked for it. Generations, we know, have suffered from the
want of a drainage system. The people
affected have used every means in their
power to bring the matter before the
Government here and the Government in
Great Britain, and to make them appreciate their losses. The Government scheme
has been put forward. The Government
offer has been put before the directlyelected representatives of the people in
the local councils. It lies before those
directly-elected representatives at the
present moment. I think I may say that
The Budget-
General Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS

it was received by those representatives
without great enthusiasm. In some cases

My hon. colleague (Mr. Leeke) in the
representation of Derry spoke in very
impassioned terms on this question, and,
of course, he blamed the Government for
not having made provision for this in the
Budget. He also blamed the Government for not giving or offering a sufficient contribution, and said the whole

I would like to ask him why, if he feels so

the rate for this purpose would have been
a flat rate of only about 1d or 1½d-certainly with regard to Derry and Antrim
-when he knows that why was not the

that those representatives may reconsider

have refused to accept the offer.
Before I leave this question, however,

drainproper
age maintenance is carried out, and that

I cannot sit down without saying how

It is
Hon. Members opposite may think that
we receive no benefits for this comparatively small contribution that we make.
They talk about our payments. They say
this money could be better spent in other

to bear our share of the burden?
surely not a benefit which we can discount.
We have the protection of one of the

I hope the day will never come in

Mr. HEALY: In reading the Chancellor's address in the papers to-day
nothing struck me more than the fact that
he was bound hand and foot to another
institution and to another Parliament,
and that the sources of income left to him
were exceedingly narrow. In 1911 the
taxation of the whole of Ireland was just
£11,000,000. In 1928 the taxation of
the Six Counties of Ireland is
exactly the same figure. What has
occurred in the meantime? It is true
that there have been a few social services
introduced meanwhile. But the body of
the people feel that they have got nothing
at all by way of compensation for the continual burdens that have been cast upon
them. The Chancellor of the Exchequer
boasted of the £22,000,000 contribution
that Northern Ireland has paid from the
time of the establishment of this Parliament up to date. But the Imperial contribution fixed at that period was
seven
over
million pounds, almost eight
millions. And Section 23 of the Act of
1920 made it imperative that that should
not be reduced until two years after the
Act was passed.
The Prime Minister speaking on the
Budget a year ago said that although
they paid their Imperial contribution,
which was at £1,400,000, yet they received
back almost £1,000,000. He gave the
figures. We got £868,000, he said, as aid

taking credit for an Imperial contribution
of £1,400,000 the real contribution was
half a million pounds.
Mr. POLLOCK: Are you not glad?
Mr. DEVLIN: Is that a fact?
Mr. HEALY: There is not so much to

Mr. POLLOCK: Hear: hear.
Mr. HEALY: The Member for Down

What in the name of goodness would be

None whatever. And they will not
come.
I would like to ask the Minister of

should when I am on that point alsothe time is pretty short-put another

deficit on the Unemployment Fund?

But the Minister of Finance flatly contradicts himself when, a little while later,
he says he advises those who hold War
Loan and those who hold insurance policies to be sure to get the stipulation inserted that they will only be payable in
Northern Ireland. It strikes me as being

"Love daddy, love mammy, love myself
best of any.
I think if you scratch the
Finance Minister a little bit you will find

There is no use, therefore, pretending

Saxon in the galleries yesterday, and I
can make allowance for that. No doubt
you wished to impress him. There was
a bit of play-acting in that.
The Prime Minister himself, speaking
in May, 1927, said that he could get rid

Well, now, I would suggest to him it
would be an excellent bargain to get rid
of this Imperial contribution even if it is

only half a million pounds. It would do

Mr. HEALY: I recommend him to

mean?
Mr. DEVLIN: Now, Mr. Crawford?
Mr. HEALY: The Free State issue of

I do not see in the Minister's Statement
what the Northern banks were restricted
to.
He said in a general way that they
would issue sufficient to meet trade in the
North. Then he spoke about clean notes.
Many farmers in the North believe that
the policy of deflation started by the
Bank of England in 1920 was the root of
a great deal of the trouble that has fallen
on them from that day to this. The
position they say is like this: A man
bought land at that period at a very high
figure. He probably borrowed the money
out of the bank, and when he went to pay
the money he found he had to pay a great
deal more than he borrowed from the
point of view of values. I will explain
that. At that time a man probably for
ten cattle would realize say £200. To-day
if he were selling those cattle- -an equal
number of cattle he would only realize
about half that amount of money,
so that he would be obliged to sell twice
the quantity of stock, or twice the commodity before he could pay the debt contracted in that period. People say that
the crisis which has fallen upon the farmers and upon the business community is
an entirely artificial one manufactured by
the banks, and that so long as you are
associated with the Bank of England,
which is capable of a policy of that kind,
so long will the community suffer these
reverses.
There is one particular matter to which

attention. He could have reduced the

He might, I suggest, have made it equal

He quoted the figures for Law and
Order as £900,000. That is a very large

He has estimated that the duty on oil

£200,000. The petrol duty, of itself,

you will see that it would equal £2 a head,
so that there is a big deficit, a very wide
gulf to be bridged, between the amount
required for the remission of rates on agricultural lands and buildings and the
amount to be realized from the petrol tax.
You must not forget in this connection
that you collect from the farmers of the
Six Counties £670,000 in land annuities,
which are part of the revenue of this
Parliament. The other day when the
Minister of Finance was speaking of his
generosity towards the farmers, I think
he rather overlooked this point. He
omitted to mention the fact that he was
collecting from the farmers
an amount
three times greater than the amount he
would relieve them of even if he paid the
sum he mentioned.
There are 301 officials in the Department of the right hon. Gentleman, and
they cost £110,316. I would think as an
outsider and I suppose a good many
average persons are outsiders-that 301
officials would be quite sufficient to run
the whole of the Government of Northern
Ireland. Those are not all the officials in
his Department. I find also in his
Department that there are legal charges.
Remuneration of counsel-I suppose that
is the gentleman who drafts the Bills.
Then there is Parliamentary counsel, part
time, and there are various other items
of a similar character. There was recently in the County of Fermanagh a
plague of caterpillars. They swarmed
right over a particular part of the county,
eating the grass and eating the vegetation, but they were not half so destructive
to Northern Ireland as the 301 officials of
the right hon. Gentleman's Department,
and certainly they did not consume nearly
so much grass.
Mr. POLLOCK: If I may, I should
like to reply to the various arguments and
criticizms that have been submitted by
hon. Members, for if I waited any longer
I feel that I might forget some of the
points that have been raised. My hon.
Friend, the Leader of the Opposition,
began his speech more in the nature of an
attack than of criticizm or comment, and
charged me with having produced a
platitudinous Budget. I do not think
that
any statement of revenue and expenditure involving large figures could be
other than platitudinous, unless the
Government submitting it were prepared
to distribute largesse ad libitum over the
whole community. Then I can assure you
it would develop a very material interest.
In the general discussion that has
followed, hon. Members opposite, if I may
say so, did not seem to understand fully
the relationship that a federal State such
as ours bears to the central authority,
and notwithstanding that so many diatribes have been hurled at us because of
our subordination to Great Britain, to the
central authority, we are in no different
position from some of the largest States
of the Empire. We are no different from
the Province of Ontario in relation to the
central authority in Canada. We are no
different from the State of Victoria in
relation to the central authority in
Australia, and so on throughout the
Empire. If my hon. Friends would only
consider the true relationship between a
federal State and a federal Union, perhaps
they would not indulge in so many diatribes against our relationship to the
central authority at Westminster. That
is a general statement with regard to that
matter.
Perhaps I may now deal with some of
the specific matters that have been raised
by hon. Members, and if I may I will
take them backward rather than forward,
because those recently spoken are clearer
in my memory. I will take them also in
relation to speeches rather than persons.
The last speaker (Mr. Healy) has spoken
of the insufficiency of the petrol tax to
effect any improvement in regard to the
relief of rates over the Province of Ulster.
I am fully aware of that, and I am also
quite aware that the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. George Henderson) suggested that £250,000 would be required
for that purpose.
I am seized of the impression, if not the knowledge, that
£250,000 would be quite insufficient for
that purpose.
I do not know exactly the
basis on which the hon. Member arrived
at that conclusion, but I can assure him
that any provisional calculations we have
made show that the sum necessary would
be very much in excess of that figure.
In view of the assurance that I was able
to give in my Budget Statement yesterday,
if hon. Members who ask where is the
money to come from would only trust the
Government having received assurance
that the conditions obtaining in regard to
the relief of rates in Great Britain would
be applied here they would give the
Government the necessary confidence as
the persons who see that the money is
The Budget-
General Debate
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
provided. I think they should be satisfied in the meantime, having regard to the
very crude condition in which the whole
subject is at the present time.
I would like to explain, if I am not
taking up too much time-(hon. Members:
No, no)-that the conditions in Great
Britain are entirely different. There is
no relationship between the conditions on
a farm in England and a farm here, especially in regard to valuation. Valuations in England comprise the land and
buildings; and the houses of the farmers
are valued separately. Here, on the
.contrary, our farm land is valued as one
item, and the farm houses and farm buildings as a second item in the valuation
lists. Thus we have two valuations-the
houses and the farm buildings in the one
case, and the farm lands in the other.
This implies that if we have to carry out
literally the proposal that has been outlined by the Chancellor of the Exchequer
it will be necessary for us to institute a
revaluation of the entire Province, with
a view to discovering the rateable value
of the land and the farm buildings.
The matter, as I say, being in such a
crude state at the present time, it is quite
impossible for me or for any Member of
the Government to give any definite assurances as to the methods that will be necessary in order to carry out the scheme;
but I think that hon. Members on both
sides of the House should be satisfied that
the language I used yesterday covered
a sufficient guarantee that the advantages
which come to the farming community in
Ulster will not be less than those which
obtain in Great Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I think that that
crystallises the whole subject so far as land.
is concerned.
My hon. Friend, the Member for
Derry, as well as another hon. Member,
introduced the question of the Bann, and
as that is a very important subject I make
no excuse for referring to it again. I
stated yesterday that the whole matter
was in the hands of the local authorities.
Drainage has always been regarded as a
local matter. Even when the Imperial
Government spent a sum approximating
£200,000 upon the Bann, the cost was
practically laid upon those who were beneficiaries, and up to the present day they
are paying a rate which means in effect
that they are paying the cost of the relief
that was understood to be given at that
time very insufficient relief, as I quite
freely admit. But our Government, in
reviewing this whole subject, and having
regard to the depressed condition of agriculture generally, came to the conclusion
that they should advance considerably
upon the ordinary and general method of
treating drainage subjects, and consequently they offered what is regarded
generally by everyone who has studied the
subject as a generous national contribution, and if the local authorities who are
responsible for the well-being of the community which they represent do not
regard the question of drainage as of
sufficient importance to impose a mere
fraction by way of a flat rate over the five
counties, then it appears to me that the
subject is not of such a serious character
as has been represented from time to time.
They are the people who should know the
importance of this subject. I am bound
to say that the Government has experienced considerable disappointment at the
luke-warm reception which
the very
generous offer of the Government has
received.
The hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) who dealt with

The rest is made up of various receipts.

As I have said, the five-sixths is not the

this Parliament administer, and which
the people demand-(hon. Members:

of the government of Ulster, it is the cost of

So.
I regret to see that the hon. Member

He mentioned various subjects, but

I think it is hardly competent for the

But there are certain matters that must

burden of every individual care and responsibility, then it would appear to me
we had reached a state such as was never

at any rate came into existence.
My hon. Eriend, the Leader of the

suggests that he would increase the death

other very radical methods of treating

him absolutely in respect of death duties.
1 am bound to admit that in the case of

should pay something towards the State
if it is necessary to raise money for purposes in the interests of the State, but
if you carry that out to the point that
you are withdrawing from the whole industrial system of
of the country the
capital that is required for its development, then I say you are laying a burden
on the country rather than affording any

As regards the Entertainment Tax, one
or two Members have demanded the withdrawal of that tax in its entirety. My
hon. Friend, the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin), who is generally eloquent

hesitation. He described it as a unique
and unnecessary tax, because we are not
in accord with the British Government,
and therefore it should be withdrawn. I
say Entertainment Tax is the most logical
and most defensible of all taxation that
we impose. It is a tax on pure amuse-
It applies in every civilized
country. The principle of Entertainment
Tax exists in every country on earth, that
is civilized countries working under democratic institutions. Therefore, my hon.
Friend need not regard this comparatively
small revenue that we receive from a comparatively small tax imposed on entertainments as being in any sense unique and
peculiar.
ment.

Mr. POLLOCK : I said in regard to

Mr. POLLOCK: I replied to that in

in regard to the Entertainment Tax that
last year when I made a concession upon
the lower tax I was given an assurance.
I have great sympathy with the proprietors
-not because necessarily the Government
has any responsibility for it in their
difficulty and in the changed conditions
that apply. I was assured then that the

thought it was only necessary to apply
some pressure in regard to the tax extending above sixpence up to a shilling.
I suppose if a concession were made in the

upwards should be removed. Therefore,
I do not think that hon. Members who

I am concerned, notwithstanding what
the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) has said,
to vindicate the character of the Joint
Exchequer Board. When the Government of Ireland Act was passed it was
assumed that the two areas would function. One did not. The Board was
appointed on the assumption that such
functioning would take place. When the
South of Ireland elected to withdraw
it became necessary to rearrange the constitution of that Board, and it was then
settled, with our consent, that it should
consist of two persons, one nominated by
the Treasury, one nominated by ourselves,
and a chairman--an independent manmutually agreed upon. That independent
man, Lord Colwyn, has carried out the
functions of the Joint Exchequer Board
in a way that from our point of view is
above criticism. It is a purely independent Board, and further, which is
more important still-it is not as some
hon. Members have suggested acting at its
own sweet will-it dictates authoritatively
what adjustment of our accounts with the
second authority should take place. That
is so determined by a Committee which
was appointed by the British Government
at our request, and known as the Colwyn
Committee. The formula by which that
adjustment is carried out is laid down in
the finding of the Colwyn Committee by
which the Joint Exchequer Board is
bound to be guided, so that it is rather the
law laid down by an independent
authority which guides the Joint Exchequer Board in the matter of adjustment. Let me say frankly that we have
been fairly, honestly and honourably
treated by these English gentlemen.
(Hon Members: Hear, hear). I cannot
say otherwise, because the facts I was
able to relate in my Budget Statement
yesterday bear out clearly the financial
condition in which the State finds itself
at the end of seven years.

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
EX-SERVICEMEN AS TEMPORARY
CLERKS.
1. Mr. P. O'NEILL (on behalf of Mr.
Devlin) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he can state how many disabled
ex-Servicemen are at present serving as
temporary clerks in the various Ministries
under the Northern Government, and
what steps have been taken or are being
taken by the Ministry of Finance to absorb
all these men in permanent posts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): There are at present 72 disabled
ex-Servicemen employed as temporary
clerks in the various Departments in the
Government of Northern Ireland. These
men will have an opportunity of competing
for such permanent clerical vacancies as
are reserved for ex-Servicemen.
PREFERENTIAL
APPOINTMENT
OF EX-SERVICEMEN.
2. Mr. P. O'NEILL (on behalf of Mr.
Devlin) asked the Minister of Finance.
whether it is a fact that a number of ex-
Servicemen are still serving in a temporary capacity since 1921, notwithstanding the guarantee made that all posts must
be filled by ex-Servicemen, preference being given to disabled ex-Servicemen.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is a fact that a
number of ex-Servicemen are still serving
in a temporary capacity, having been
transferred from the Imperial Service to
the Service of the Government of Northern Ireland in the same capacity on the
transfer of Services in the years 1921 and
1922. No guarantee has ever been given
that all Government posts in the Northern
Ireland Service must be filled by ex-Servicemen, because, obviously, any limitation of that nature in respect of the
method of filling public appointments
would be fatal to the present and future
efficiency of the public service. The
Government, however, has always been
fully alive to its responsibilities to ex-Servicemen, and has fulfilled them to the utmost possible extent compatible with efficiency, and, at the outset, all appointments to clerical posts not filled by
officers transferred from the Imperial Service were
reserved for ex-Servicemen.
The more recent arrangements in regard
to recruitment from this class have been
explained in my replies to the hon. Member's previous question.
APPOINTMENT OF BOY CLERKS.
3. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Devlin)
asked the Minister of Finance whether it
is a fact that boy clerks are being brought
into the Civil Service, and are absorbing
all these posts which should be given to
the disabled ex-Servicemen who have been
serving since 1921.
Mr. POLLOCK: For the last four or
five years a system of open competition
into the Northern Ireland Civil Service
for youths between the ages of 17 and 19
has been in operation. As indicated,
however, in my reply to the previous
question of the hon. Member, a proportion of clerical vacancies has always been
and is still being reserved for ex-Service
temporary clerks, both disabled and not
disabled.
TRANSFERRED EX-SERVICEMEN.
4. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Devlin)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he can state what steps the Ministry of
Finance have taken in respect of five ex-
Servicemen (one of whom was badly
disabled) to safeguard these men who
transferred to a Government Department
under the jurisdiction of the Imperial
Government in November, 1925; and
whether these men are on loan to this
Department or actually transferred to
the Imperial Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: I regret that from the
particulars supplied. I am unable to
identify with precision the five cases to
which the hon. Member refers, but I am
aware that in the year 1925 several ex-
Servicemen who had previously been employed as temporary clerks in Northern
Ireland Departments obtained similar
work in Imperial Departments in Belfast,
a number of them on the direct recommendation of my Ministry.
No question arose as to the loan or transfer of
these men to the Imperial Departments,
because they were, in any event, due for
retrenchment in the several Ministries
in which they were serving, their appointments in those Departments having been
of a purely temporary character.

CLASS VI.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
First Resolution read a Second time.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move a reduction of £1,000. I want to do so as a
protest against the action of the
Ministry of Agriculture in making
a grant of £1,300 to
£1,300 to the Ulster
Farmers' Union. In my opinion this
is a case of subsidizing that particular organization to an extent that is not
warranted. This organization consists
of farmers who are well able to maintain
their own trade union without the assistance of the Government. I cannot see
at all that these farmers should be in the
position to take £1,300 of public money
to enable them to maintain their organization in the country. I do not think there
is in the world another country where a
grant similar to this is made to an
organization which exists specifically for
the purpose of benefiting one particular
class of the community. It is just the
same thing as if the trade union I have
the honour to belong to made application
to the Government, holding meetings as
we do for educational purposes, for a
grant of £1,300 to enable it to carry on
its activities. Apparently this Farmers'
Union, despite their activities, have not
been able to convince the farmers of
Northern Ireland of the necessity of cooperation to that extent which, in my
opinion, is necessary to enable the farmers
to get decent prices for their produce.
Nor do they see to it that the agricultural labourers, who are employed on the
farms, are paid a reasonable wage for the
work they do. I think that until the
Farmers' Union or the Ministry of Agriculture they are synonymous—are able
to convince the farmers in Northern Ireland of the necessity of co-operation, particularly as regards the purchase of seed,
the use of machinery, and co-operative
marketing, no grant should be made to
this organization.
I want also to take the opportunity
afforded me on the Report stage to complain about the lines that the Ministry of
Agriculture seem to be going on in regard to agricultural research. Further,
I want to mention what I think is very
necessary in the interests of one of our
staple industries--I refer to the linen
trade. I suggest that the Government
should take a number of acres of land as
an experimental farm to grow flax. The
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
23 MAY 1928
Ministry could in conjunction with the
Ministry of Commerce set up a central retting plant with the new machinery that is
now available for scutching purposes. I
think if they did so it would probably
mean a fixed price for the farmer for a
period of five
say
It would further
years.
mean that the flax would be bought on
the field by the Government and so save
the farmers any further trouble as far as
the retting and scutching of flax are concerned. I am strengthened in that view
by the Report of the Departmental Committee on the transit, prices, and marketing of agricultural produce which was set
up by the Ministry. Paragraph 45 on
page 17 says:-
We are particularly interested to receive evidence regarding a contemplated
revolution in the manner of dealing
with the flax crop. In brief, the proposed scheme, which is at present under
trial, would substitute a direct sale by
the farmer to the spinner of his flax
un-retted and in the field for the existing system under which the flax must
be retted and scutched before purchase
by the spinner.
The only difference in the suggestion
I am making and the suggestion of the
Departmental Committee is that instead
of the spinner coming in it should be the
Government that should purchase the
flax on the field and that the Ministry in
conjunction with the Ministry of Commerce should establish a station for retting and scutching the flax. This would
enable spinners to get flax even of a better quality than they can get at present.
I think the Ministry of Agriculture have
been very negligent in their duties in
regard to this particular matter which
concerns one of the staple industries of
Northern Ireland. It is worthy of comment also that this Committee I have already referred to on page 7 of this Report refers to the enormous transport
charges which our farmers are compelled
to pay. It says:-
-
Apples in barrels are carried from
New York, Boston, Nova Scotia, etc.,
to any port in the United Kingdom for
3s 9d per barrel; while apples in barrels from many stations in the County
Armagh cost 4s 5d per barrel to London.
That is a thing that the Ministry of Agriculture could very well take up with the
carrying companies to the end that our
farmers may be put on an equal footing
with the farmers in any other part of
the world. Take eggs. They say:-
Eggs from Enniskillen to Liverpool
cost 65s per ton, whereas eggs from
Hamburg to Liverpool cost 50s per ton.
I think those figures are enough to warrant criticizm of the right hon. Gentleman who has control of the Ministry of
Agriculture. I think more important
than either of the matters I have mentioned is the matter of marketing. Every
party in the State has been investigating
the question of the marketing of produce.
They have all said this question is one of
the most important if not the most important. This Committee was, I think,
primarily set up to bring about, if possible,
some adjustment of the prices paid by the
consumers and the prices received by the
producer, but apparently very little if
anything has been done in that respect.
It seems to me as an ordinary observer
that the question of the prices received by
the cultivator for his produce is probably
the most important factor in determining
whether the industry is prosperous or the
reverse. I think that the farmers cannot
be held primarily responsible for this, for
it seems to me that the farmers' chief concern is and ought to be with the actual
work on the farm itself, and that after
that all the facilities possible to be
afforded should be afforded by any Government that take any interest in the
affairs of the country.
It is to be borne in mind that the farmers and agricultural labourers represent
60 per cent. of the entire working population of Northern Ireland. It is, I
think, something well worth the consideration of the Government. The party to
which I have the honour to belong issued
a Report in which it states that co-operation, transport facilities and stabilization
of prices are the three things that could
be tackled by any Government that were
really in earnest on this particular subject.
There are other reforms which will probably take a longer time and which if carried into effect would be of tremendous
importance, but if these three things were
attempted and brought into being in
Northern Ireland it would enable this
basic industry to be in a more prosperous
condition than it is to-day. It is for that
reason I draw the attenton of the House
to what I would call the lack of intelligent
Ministry of Agriculture 2100
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
direction of the Ministry of Agriculture,
in this particular connection, particularly bearing in mind the fact that
the subsidy of £1,300 to the Farmers'
Union was to carry out this important
work and it was not done. These are
the three things I wanted to mention in
regard to agriculture, and I have no doubt
that the Minister should have something
to say as to why the Report of his Committee has not been put into force as far
as it is possible for the Ministry to do.
There is another matter I want to mention and that is with regard to the amount
of relief the farmers are getting in agricultural rates. It seems to me that there
should be some line drawn between those
farmers who are really producing foodstuffs and those who have their land in
grass. I am strengthened in that view
by the report of the Irish Labour Party
on Labour and Agriculture in which they
state and most people will agree with
it-
The farmer who tills his land and improves his holding ought to be recognized by the State as worthy of more
generous consideration than the farmer
who leaves his land in grass; and the
sparsely populated areas of rich land
ought to be made to bear a share of
the undue burden now borne by the
thickly populated areas of poor land.
In regard to thickly populated areas, it
is interesting to note that in Northern
Ireland we have a higher percentage of
small farmers than they have in any
other country. In Northern Ireland in
1924 eighty-six per cent of the holdings
were under fifty acres; Irish Free State,
78.5 per cent; England and Wales, 65.5
per cent.; and Scotland, 66.3 per cent.
It will be seen that the small holders are
greater in number in Northern Ireland
than they are in any other country. It
seems to me to add weight to the opinion
I have expressed that the Department of
Agriculture should be more easily accessible to the small farmers of our Province.
It should not be through the agency of
the Farmers' Union, which is more or
less a political organization, and exists
to bolster up the Government in any
action they may think fit to take, however wrong that action. It is through
the Department itself that these small
holdings should be assisted. I think


additional assistance also should be given
to the agricultural labourers who should
be paid a living wage. The wages paid
in Northern Ireland, in regard to farm
labourers, are nothing short of disgraceful.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: Hear, hear.
Mr. KYLE: A great many of the
farms in Northern Ireland, of course,
are worked by the people who own the
farms. One has nothing to say in regard to that, but where farmers employ
men there ought to be a wage laid down
and paid by the farmers that will enable the farm labourers to live in more
decency and comfort than it is possible
for them to do under the miserable wages
they are paid to-day. I attempted, two
years ago to get this House to realize its
responsibility to the argicultural labourers
by introducing a Measure to establish
wages boards to the end that the agricultural labourer might be paid a living
wage for his work. The Government have
not up to the present seen fit, despite these
inadequate wages, to do anything in that
line. I want to criticize as strongly as I
possibly can the action of the Government
in regard to these three important things
that I have mentioned, namely, transport,
marketing and that other point with regard to the establishment of an experimental farm for the growing of flax, so
that the farmer may be saved the trouble
he now has with regard to the retting and
scutching of flax.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am sorry to interrupt, but may I say that so far as the
question of wages is concerned it would
not be in order to develop that on this
Estimate, because the payment of wages is
not dircetly a Government matter except
in so far as they may legislate to make a
minimum wage applicable? That is a
matter for legislation, and legislation cannot be discussed on the Estimates.
Mr. KYLE: I was just referring to it
by way of example to show how the
Government neglect the interests of the
agricultural labourers in that connection.
In regard to the point I mentioned a
moment or two ago, namely, co-operative
marketing, it is very interesting to note
that one-fifth of the whole of the agricultural produce sold by farmers in the
United States is handled through cooperative channels.
In Canada about 70
Ministry of Agriculture 2102

per cent. of the wheat production is
handled by the farmers' co-operative
pools, in Russia and Siberia the bulk of
flax and other products is sold through cooperative channels. We used to get 75

I want to suggest that if co-operative

and enable higher wages to be paid to the
agricultural labourer. I have pleasure in
moving the reduction of this Estimate by
£1,000.
Mr. MARK: I gladly avail myself of
the opportunity of speaking generally on
the very important subject of agriculture
and Government agricultural policy. It
is admitted that agriculture has passed,
and is passing, through a very depressing
time. This depression is world wide. The
farmers of the United States are as hard
hit as those of Great Britain. Germany
and the British Dominions overseas are
making similar complaints, but, notwithstanding this those who are able to study
the situation and who take an unselfish
and unprejudiced view must admit that,
on the whole, great progress has been
made towards the development of the
agricultural industry in Northern Ireland. Whether we take the Horse Breeding Act; the Live Stock Act or the Eggs
Act, in each and all of these we find enshrined a policy and a principle which,
when they have fully fructified, will assist
very materially in placing Northern Ireland in the forefront of countries which
are, with foresight, developing their agriculture. In promoting these Measures,
some of which, as I stated in the House
last week, might be described as revolutionary, it was inevitable that imperfections would arise in their administration, but I have to admit from personal
experience that where such cases
were
brought to the notice of the Ministry
every effort was made to mitigate any
temporary injustice. The Live Stock
Breeding Act has undoubtedly brought
about a marked improvement in the
class and quality of cattle produced in
Northern Ireland; and so far as the Eggs
Act is concerned, even those who were
opposed to this Measure in the first instance are now compelled to admit that
it has re-established our important egg industry in the Cross-Channel markets,
where, before the passing of the Act, this
trade was almost threatened with extinction.
In connection with both these Measures
it will stand to the credit of the Government that they have shown themselves in
many respects to be pioneers in promoting
agricultural legislation, and have displayed a vision which, as I have said, must
ultimately, to a very great extent, promote the prosperity of the farming community in Northern Ireland. Notwitha
standing that I think I can claim, in all
modesty, to have as an extensive and
practical experience of actual farming as
any Member of this House. It has been
stated that I, and the organization of
which I have the honour to be President
this year, have been always too subservient
to Government policy. It would be impossible to conceive a more unfair statement. It is true that, generally speaking,
the Farmers' Union have supported
Government policy, but only when, after
consideration and investigation, we have
decided that the Measure or Measures
were in the best interests of agriculture.
We have not hesitated, as occasion arose,
both to criticize and oppose, and as
result of our representations we have, on
not a few occasions, succeeded in securing
amendments of policy which we felt to be
essential. If we have not, like others
who lay claim to a deeper knowledge of
the farmers' interests and more practical
sympathy with their welfare, been bellowing from public platforms, like Bulls of
Bashan, it does not follow that in our own
way we have not been able to accomplish
much more by conference and negotiations
than by breathing out fire and slaughter,
although, as I have already said, we have
not hesitated-nor shall we hesitatewhen occasion
arises,
strongly to
oppose any Measure or policy which we
think inimical to the best interests of the
farmers.
.

from one cause and another.
May I also say that it is to me a matter
of great regret that the flax-producing

for the Clyde was re-shipped and sent to
New York, showing that the market and
the prices there are better than can be
secured in this country. However, it
will mean a scarcity of meat, and I think
the policy of our Government in fostering
Cow-testing Associations will materially
increase the number of young stock, while
the Live Stock Breeding Act and the
licensing of only the best bulls will mean
that we will be producing only the best
cattle for stores and beef. From this
point of view I think we in Northern Ireland are going to share in a brighter
future so far as cattle raising in concerned.
It has been estimated that Great
Britain has been getting 50 per cent. of
her beef supplies from abroad, but
countries which formerly sent all their
beef exports to us are now sending part
of them to the Continent and the United
States. This means that Great Britain
must produce more beef and rely on Ireland to send more beef and stores than
formerly. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
In this connection, as I have said, I have
to commend the policy of the Minister
of Agriculture in fostering the improvement of all classes of live stock, including
poultry. The encouragement of Cow-testing Associations will materially increase
the number of young stock, and the Live
Stock Breeding Act and licensing of
only the best bulls will bring about early
maturity in our cattle and the best
quality of meat that can be produced.
It is gratifying to know that since 1925
the number of cows and in-calf heifers has
increased by 20,770; breeding ewes by
over 48,000, and breeding pigs by almost
14,000, whilst poultry have increased by
1,164,000.
Apart from the question of developing
our agricultural production along the
most modern lines, I must say I would
like to see legislation introduced at an
early date for the compulsory inspection
and grading of all our farm produce for
export, because I think that the one thing
more than any other which is affecting
the Ulster farmer to-day is the keen,
scientific and skilfully organized competition which he has now to meet, not only
from foreign countries, but from our
friends in the Colonies of the Empire. It
will no longer do for farmers to expect
that their customers will take produce of
any character marketed in any sort
of way. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
We have at our door the best markets in
the world, situated as we are within a few
hours of some of the largest consuming
centres; we have the best farmers that can
be found, and we have as good land as
any other country and on the whole as
good a climate, and we can supply
articles of the highest quality, but we require the application of the most modern
methods of grading and standardisation.
I am glad to learn from the Budget
Statement of the Minister of Finance that
the farmers of Northern Ireland will
receive equivalent relief in the matter of
local rates to that proposed by the Imperial Chancellor of the Exchequer in his
recent Budget speech.
There is a further way which would
materially assist the farmers, and this
is by securing substantial reductions in
the cost of transport of farm produce.
The contrast in the cost of transport overseas and our local charges-from actual
figures submitted to the Agricultural
Prices Committee is astounding, and I
was indeed gratified to see that some time
ago the Prime Minister and other
members of the Cabinet called into consultation the representatives of the
various steamship and railway companies, with a view to securing reductions
in these charges which are much too
heavy at the present time, and which act
in some cases almost to the point of prohibition in our competition in the cross-
Channel markets with foreign and Colonial
producers.
In this connection I should like to bring
to the notice of the Minister of Finance
a matter which arises in regard to the
cost of transit. The Imperial Chancellor
of the Exchequer, when dealing with this
matter in his Budget speech, announced
that certain moneys would be given to the
railway companies in order that they
might be able to reduce the cost of transport of agricultural produce. That undoubtedly will assist the British farmer
very substantially, but we, further removed as we are from the British market,
are not only affected by railway transit
but also by Cross-Channel steamboat transit, and I would like to ask the Minister if
he could get this reduction made to apply
to all through rates on agricultural produce. It may be that the finances at his
command would not be sufficient to cover

all agricultural produce, but he should

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE

If
he would be good enough to go out to

answer to nearly all his queries to me.
We show there every sort of means of improving produce, improving cattle, improving flax, and the various means of
putting more money into the farmers'
pockets, and so helping the agricultural
labourers to get what they deserve in the

He objects to the Farmers' Union
particularly, but then another objection of his is that we have so many
small farmers, which really is the reason

We have found the Ulster Farmers'
Union one of the finest educational bodies
in the whole of the country. When our
agricultural instructor or our fowl instructor wants to give a lecture the
Farmers' Union is approached with a view
to getting a number of young men together to hear what the instructor has to
tell. We know well in this country that
unless matters are brought to the immediate notice of the farmers they do not
get the benefit of the facilities provided
for them, although we publish many
pamphlets for their assistance and guidance.
The hon. Member wished us to take
farms in order that we might grow flax to
help the linen trade, and I suppose he
wants the Government to buy the flax from
the farmers at a fixed price. For many
years past, both under the old Department and under my Ministry, experiments
have been carried on all over the country
in order to show the farmers the flax that
suited them best. At Stormont we have
brought out new breeds of flax, as good as
the J.W.S., of which we have all heard
so much. These new varieties are being
grown in every part of the country, so
that the farmers can see what is best for
their land. I am afraid that the Government will not be able to start retting and
scutching machines all over the country.
A central retting and scutching machine
would be of no service to the farmers, as
there would be too much carriage on the
product. Some time ago a company was
established in County Down with a new
system of retting and scutching, and that
company ended in dire disaster-they lost
all their money.
With regard to shipping charges, we
have had many meetings with the companies on that subject since the Committee made their report, and we are also
in communication with them at the present time with the object of getting them
to reduce their charges. My hon. Friend
must remember, however, that there are
about six handlings of goods between
Armagh and England, whereas from New
York to England there are only two, one
at either end. The number of handlings
adds enormously to the charges.
Companies themselves state that the Agriculture Committee in their report seem to
have got hold of one or two exceptional
cases, and that the charges are not nearly
so high as the Committee said.

is, however, very difficult to establish a

and he made certain allegations which he
would have very great difficulty in
establishing. I desire to direct my remarks this afternoon to rebutting those,
in my judgment, indefensible remarks
that fell from the hon. and learned
Gentleman. The first mis-statement of
which the hon. and learned Gentleman
was guilty was that he alleged I said that
both he and the head of the Department
were incompetent persons. I deny having
made use of such an observation, and if
the hon. and learned Gentleman will take
the trouble to peruse "Hansard" he will
discover that my remarks were that this
was the worst managed Department, in
my judgment, in the whole of the Government. I said that opinions might differ

the chief of the Department and the
Parliamentary Secretary were responsible
for that state of affairs. They may, of
course, argue that that is tantamount to
saying they are incompetent persons. I

single out the Parliamentary Secretary for
special tribute. It would be very difficult,
therefore, for the hon. and learned Gentleman to say that I described him as an
incompetent person.
I am not concerned with the personal
aspect of this matter. I am more concerned about subjects on which I shall
offer criticism. It is with these things I

doing so I want to call the attention of
the Minister to the fact that certain constituents of mine petitioned him recently
in regard to their dwelling-houses in
Rutherglen Street in North Belfast.
These houses were built of material sold
to some contractor in Belfast, which was
got from houses pulled down in May
Street. The Ministry of Home Affairs, I
understand, gave a subsidy to
the
builder of those houses. The petitioners
say:
Having been in possession for some
time we have found that the houses
have been built about 75 per cent.
from very old material, and the remainder from very poor material.
This old material was taken from old
houses in May Street which were built
over one hundred years ago, and includes bricks, doors, windows, joists.
rafters, et cetera.
This comes under the administration of
the Ministry of Home Affairs in their
giving a grant to builders who build
houses with rotten material and are now
charging tenants exorbitant prices for
their houses. The Ministry of Home
Affairs are responsible through their inspectors, who passed this material as
being fit to build houses for people to live
in. I think it is quite right that they
should be indicted for this disgusting
and disgraceful trasaction.
Mr. HANNA: Will the hon. Gentleman tell me where these houses are?
Mr. KYLE: Certainly. If the Parlianentary Secretary consults his Department he will find three people who reside
in 32, 34 and 36 Rutherglen Street
petitioned them in regard to getting redress for the particular grievance I have
mentioned. These people were charged
£425 for these houses which the Government subsidized to the tune, I think, of
£120 per house. These petitioners want
relief from the Ministry and they hold
the Ministry, as I do, responsible for the

The
There is another matter I want to mention in connection with the Ministry of
Home Affairs. I want to draw public
attention to the fact that in Northern
Ireland it costs £126 14s to keep a
prisoner in jail for twelve months.
Minister of Labour in the Northern
Government thinks £46 16s is enough to
keep an unemployed man. I do not want
to suggest that all the unemployed would
be better in jail, but that at least would
cost the Government more money.
Certainly, they would be better fed and
better housed than a great many of them
are to-day. It is true to say that the
Government of Northern Ireland believe
in keeping prisoners who have committed
an offence against the law in a better condition than those men who have done so
much in the creation of the huge ships
we are never done boasting about, and the
magnificent linen we prate so much
about, and who carry on the industries,
generally speaking, of Northern Ireland.
While those men are being starved the
Government apparently stand by and are
not prepared to take action.
Another matter I want to draw attention to is the exorbitant legal charges.
If hon. Members will turn to page 68 of
the Estimates they will see legal charges
which are, I think, indefensible. The
Attorney-General for Northern Ireland
gets £2,500 a year; the legal adviser
(part-time) gets £50 a month or £600 a
year; the Chief Crown Solicitor £1,405 a
year, the Assistant Chief Crown Solicitor
£1,096 a year, the Crown Solicitor for
Londonderry, Armagh and Tyrone sums
varying from £540 to £330. In addition
to all these legal officers, despite the fact
that the Parliamentary Secretary himself
is a very competent lawyer, there are fees
for additional counsel amounting to
£2,650. I cannot understand why we
should pay the Attorney-General to conduct prosecutions at the instance of the

FINES ON BOOKMAKERS.
1. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the number of bookmakers who were fined
during the year 1927 in the City of
Belfast; the amount of such fines, and in
what way such sums accruing were
utilized.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply to this question.
During the year 1927 there were 612
prosecutions under the Betting Houses
Act, 1853, for offences in the City of
Belfast. The total fines imposed amounted
to £3,526, of which, in accordance with
Section 9 of the above-mentioned Act,
one-half was paid to the Belfast Corporation, and one-half to the informers. In
all cases the informers were the police, and
the proportion of the fines awarded to
them was credited to the R.U.C. Reward
Fund, in accordance with Section 4 (5)
of the Constabulary Act (Northern Ireland), 1922.
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I would like
to ask the right hon. Gentleman as to
whether the police are under instructions
to visit bookmakers in Belfast periodically
for the purpose of enforcing those fines.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The general
instructions to the police are to enforce
the law.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman say whether or not the amount
of money allocated to the fund for the
officers themselves is used by the officers
for the benefit of the officers or by the
right hon. Gentleman for other purposes?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It goes into
the Reward Furd which is used for the
benefit of the men serving.
Would the
Mr. W. McMULLEN :
right hon. Gentleman say what is the law
on the subject?
Sir DAWSON BATES: On what
subject?
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: The
question of bookmakers.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Ask the
Attorney-General.
CASE OF MR. PATRICK THORN-
BURY.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
present whereabouts of Mr. Patrick
Thornbury, against whom an Exclusion
Order is at present in existence; whether
he is at present in Northern Ireland; and,
if so, what steps the Minister proposes to
take in the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am informed
that on Monday last, the 21st inst.,
Patrick Thornbury, a school teacher,
against whom an Exclusion Order is now
in operation, was arrested in Dublin and
remanded on a charge of being in possession of a considerable quantity of ammunition. It is an interesting coincidence
that at the time of his arrest he was the
subject matter of discussion in this House.
Mr.
KYLE: Was the right hon.
Gentleman in consultation with the
Ministry of Home Affairs in Dublin to get
this information?

MOURNE DISTRICT HOSPITAL
CONTRACTS.
3. Mr. W. MCMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it
is a fact that Mr. Robert Forsythe, who
is Chairman of the Kilkeel Rural District
Council and a Governor of Mourne District Hospital, supplies the above-mentioned hospital with potatoes; and if he
will state whether other merchants have
any opportunity to tender; and, if not
what steps he proposes to take to ensure
equality of opportunity to all merchants
who desire to tender.
The following question also stood on the
Order Paper:
5. Mr. MCMULLEN: To ask the
Minister of Home Affairs whether Mr. E.
McGonigle, Chairman of Kilkeel Board
of Guardians and Chief Governor of the
new hospital, supplies the hospital in
question with beef and bacon without
tenders being invited, and if he would
state whether such procedure is regular,
and if not what steps he proposes to take
to regularize the question of tendering.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the hon.
Member's permission I will answer this
question and question No. 5 standing in
his name together.
No official information has as yet been
received as to the specific transaction referred to, but in any event the Ministry
has no jurisdiction to interfere in a matter
of this character.
or
Under the Regulations governing
the administration of Workhouses and
District Hospitals, the Guardians
Governors as the case may be are required
to advertize for tenders for supplies where
the requirements are estimated to exceed
ten pounds per month, and if the
Guardians neglect without the express
sanction of the Ministry to follow the prescribed procedure, their action is likely to
be reviewed and questioned by the Local
Government Auditor, and any ratepayer
in the district is entitled to appear before
the auditor and to object to any payments being made in respect of such
contracts.
With regard to the suggestion that
members of the Board of Guardians or
Board of Governors have entered into contracts with the Guardians or Governors,
as the case may be, I desire to state that
under the Application of Enactments
Order, 1898, any member of a local
authority who so interests himself in any
bargain or contract with the local author-
'ity of wihch he is a member becomes thereby disqualified, and if he acts or votes
when so disqualified he is liable on summary coviction to a penalty not exceeding
£20.
It is no part of the duty of the
Ministry of Home Affairs to take any
action in regard to initiating the appropriate legal preceedings, but it is open to
any interested person to do so.
At the same time the matter is being
investigated by the Ministry, and the
papers will be referred to the Local
Government Auditor for such action as he
may deem fit in regard to the method of
accepting tenders and entering into contracts.

Summer Adjournment
24 MAY 1928
RENTS OF COTTAGES IN BALLY-
MENA RURAL DISTRICT.
4. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that at a meeting of the Ballymena
Rural District Council, held on the 12th
instant, it was decided to increase the
rents of the cottages under the control of
the Council by 50 per cent.; and whether
it is a fact that the existing rents cover
all charges against the cottages; and, if
so, what steps he proposes to take to prevent the occupiers being rack-rented.
Sir DAWSON BATES: At a recent
meeting of the Ballymena Rural District
Council, a Resolution was passed increasing the rents of existing cottages in the
rural district by varying amounts. This
Resolution which must receive the sanction of the Ministry before becoming
operative, is at present under the consideration of my Department.
It is not a fact that the existing rents
cover all charges against the cottages, and
there is at present a deficit on the account.
All applications for sanction to inincreases of rents under the Labourers
Acts are carefully scrutinized by the
Ministry, and increases are only allowed
where the existing rents are low and cast
an undue burden upon the rates. The
present application will receive the same
careful scrutiny, and the hon. Member
may rest assured that no increase which
cannot be fully justified will be sanctioned.
Summer Adjournment of the House.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House, at its rising this day,
do adjourn until 12 noon on Monday, 4th
of June, and that after the report of Royal
Assent to Acts agreed to by both Houses,
Mr. Speaker do adjourn the House without Question put, until Tuesday, the 9th
October, provided always that in the
event of any Bill being returned from the
Senate with Amendments, Mr. Speaker
may give notice that the House shall meet
at such earlier date as he may consider
necessary, and thereupon the House shall
meet at the time stated in such notice,
and shall transact its business as if it had
been duly adjourned to that date, and at
its rising shall adjourn until 12 noon on
Monday, the 4th of June, and further
provided that if it appears to the satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation
with the Government, that the public
interest requires that the House should
meet at any earlier time during the adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give notice
that he is so satisfied, and thereupon the
House shall meet at the time stated in
such notice, and shall transact its business
as if it had been duly adjourned to that
date.
Mr. KYLE: I want to move the deletion of the words "without Question put"

that the Government should have the right

probably the intention of the Government in this respect is to prevent discussion on any subject that might arise

opportunity of discussion on such an important matter as that or any other important matter, that might arise.
fore, I beg to move the deletion of the
words" without Question put."

Mr. KYLE: There are some questions
I want to raise on the Appropriation Bill,
the first of which is in connection with the
administration of the Department of
the right hon. Gentleman the Minister
of Labour in regard to the fact that
his Department are not paying sufficient attention to claims for national
health insurance and unemployment insurance. I refer to an employer of labour
who was working on the erection of some
buildings which were put up by the
Government, or for the Government, and
owing to the fact that he did not stamp
the cards of four men there was the chance
of these men being denied their benefit.
One of the men wrote to the Minister of
Labour asking what they were prepared
to do about the matter, and the Ministry
of Labour replied on 17th January in the
following terms:-
I am directed by the Ministry of
Labour to refer to previous correspondence and to the visit to you of an
inspector of this Department relative to
the recovery of arrears of insurance contributions in respect of your employment by the employer whom I have
mentioned.
In connection with this matter, I am
to express regret that the circumstances of the case are such that the Department does not feel justified in
instituting legal proceedings for the recovery of the arrears in question.
am, however, to direct your attention
I
to Section 98 of the National Health
Insurance Act, 1924, and Section 24 of
the Unemployment Insurance Act,
1920, which provide that where an employee has been deprived of any
benefit by reason of his employer's
failure to pay the requisite contributions at the proper time, he is entitled to recover from the employer
summarily, as a civil debt, a sum equal
to the amount of benefit so lost.
It is not that the men themselves were
refused benefit, but that the right hon.
Gentleman's Department are permitting
people to break the law in regard to the
stamping of unemployment and national
health insurance cards. Also, this employer has still to pay some money in the
form of wages to these men. I want to
protest bitterly against this employer being permitted to work on these buildings
under the ægis of this or the British
Government, and I want to indict the
right hon. Gentleman's Department for
not seeing that the cards of these men are
stamped. If this or any other employer
does not stamp employees' cards he should
be made amenable to the law.
Another matter in connection with the
same Department is the question of
plasterers in Belfast city who have an
agreement with the individual employers
to be paid at the rate of 1s 9d an hour
while they are engaged at their work.
Immediately any of these men become discharged from their employment and go to
seek employment insurance benefit they
are asked to take up work at 1s 8d an
hour, and when they refuse they are
denied unemployment insurance benefit. I
want to say the Government are acting
in this matter as a strike-breaking agency,
and are deliberately allying themselves
with the employers who are desirous of
reducing the working people's wages.
