I want to deal now with a more important matter than either of those two
matters I have mentioned, and that is the
administration of the courts of referees in
the Northern area. There is a form that
has been issued by the Department called
U.I. 82a. And one of the qualifications
under the heading of ""Transitional provisions" is so worded that the court of
referees in nine cases out of ten turns
down the applicant for unemployment
insurance benefit. Paragraph
reads:-
(c)
(c) He has during the two years immediately preceding the date of the
application for benefit been employed
in an insurable employment to such
an extent as was reasonable, having
regard to all the circumstances of his
case, and in particular to the opportunities for obtaining suitable
ployment during that period.
em-
We thought when the right hon. Gentleman said in his speech on the Unemployment Insurance Bill not very long ago that
if a man had eight stamps during the last
two years or thirty stamps at any time he
would be entitled to unemployment insurance benefit. However, under this paragraph of the regulations which I have
read out, nine out of every ten applicants
for unemployment insurance benefit cannot fulfil the first statutory condition,
with the result that a great many
people are being denied unemployment insurance benefit, and the impression, which I agree with, is getting abroad
that the Ministry of Labour is administering this Act in a cruel and heartless
manner so far as these people who are
claiming this unemployment insurance
benefit are concerned.
A friend of mine the other day had a
case of a man who had ten stamps during
the last two years, and had 400 stamps
prior to that. Everybody knows the state
of industry so far as shipbuilding and
engineering are concerned. Everybody
knows that it has been exceedingly difficult
to get work during the last three or four
years owing to the lack of orders, the
speeding up of man power in the place,
and the installation of modern machines
to take the place of man power.
I am
sure our friend the "Lobby Correspondent" will say we are desirous of scrapping
machinery and going back to hand labour
because we say that one of the reasons
opportunities for employment were
limited during 1926, 1927, and 1928
was the installation of modern machines
to take the place of man power.
I will give an example of what is
happening in Harland and Wolff's. A
"Bonn" blending machine has been introduced into the plumbing department. It
is operated by one plumber and his helper
and is doing the work of twenty men.
In addition to that, up-to-date machinery is being installed in every department,
and it is exceedingly difficult for a man
to get work, particularly during a period
of industrial depression such as we have
been enduring. It is very hard for craftsmen and labourers to get employment. I
give the instance of that machine, and I
know that hon. Members on this side of
the House and on that side will give instances of other machines which have been
introduced and which make it difficult for
working people to obtain employment.
As a matter of fact, in normal times
Harland & Wolff's employ 300 plumbers.
To-day they are employing 60. There
are 730 trade union plumbers in this district and the trade union register shows
that 300 are unemployed. Within the
past six months 40 plumbers were sent to
Southampton, and 20 joiners have also
been sent there.
During the last two years many unemployed shipyard workers went voluntarily
to Ergland and Scotland to work, but
unfortunately they have been paid off and
are coming back to Belfast. Within the
past two months the joiners' trade union
have had as many as 1,000 men unemployed out of a total membership of 3,000.
Therefore, I think it is true to say that
SO far as craftsmen and labourers are
concerned it is extremely difficult to prove
that they have been genuinely seeking
work when the Ministry puts in this
Clause in regard to their being employed
during a period of time that was reasonable. If trade had been normal all these
men would have been employed.
addition to the facts I have already given,
no fewer than three firms in the engineering trade have shut down altogether in
Belfast. They are Messrs. Travers & Co.,
Springfield Road; Messrs. Taylor & Co.,
Townsend Street, and Messrs Mayne
& Co., Matier Street. In consequence,
men employed for years in the engineering
trade have been idle for the last two years

and six months and are now denied unemployment insurance benefit despite the fact

In addition to the firms I have mentioned and I could mention many others
-Gallaher's tobacco factory and Murray's
tobacco factory are working short time.
They have been doing so for two years and

In the textile trade the Belfast Ropeworks
are working short time in many of their departments, while Gunning Campbell's

factory have been closed down entirely for
two years.
Outside Belfast spinning mills
have been closed down for two years past
in Newry, Cookstown, Coalisland and elsewhere. In view of those facts I think it
is a perfectly fair thing to get up and indict the Minister of Labour for heartless
administration. These people cannot find
employment, and as they are not employed
for a reasonable period they are thereby
disqualified.
It has been extremely difficult for the
worker to get benefit from the courts of
referees set up under the new Act, in fact,
it was difficult at all times. I have stated
in this House, and the right hon. Gentleman has borne it out by figures he gave
me in answer to a question I put recently, that practically nine out of ten of
the cases before the courts of referees are
turned down owing to this particular
factor, "not genuinely seeking work." It
is impossible to get evidence from employers that will convince a court of
referees. Employers in Belfast and outside Belfast are very loath to give a certificate to people at the mill gate or the
workshop gate looking for work. I think
anyone in this House who has worked on
the Queen's Island will agree that they
do not give chits or lines to certify that
people are looking for work, and then because these men have not got this evidence they are turned down. I have
myself represented a man at a court of
referees, and he has stated that for a year
he has been at the shipyard gates every
morning the shipyard was open. He had
never been able to get employed despite
that fact. He was turned down, and
others were turned down in similar circumstances. I think we are justified in
this kind is
saying administration of
something against which we should protest as vehemently as possible.

About two years ago I myself asked a

Affairs to lay on the Table of the House

and in the report of that meeting it is

made against Mrs. Whan were bogus
charges.
Now, if that is right and if that does
appear in the report--and apparently
these legal gentlemen have had the

it was
a secret document. District-Inspector Allen stated in his report that the
evidence on which this lady was convicted
was bogus evidence, and that the Belfast
Detective Office had not given to the case
the care, attention, and thorough investigation which it demanded. But that
was not all. When the lady was before
a judge and jury on a charge of assault
and robbery the Belfast Detective Office
had evidence-and this is the serious part
of our charge against the Ministry of
Home Affairs-which, had they disclosed
it, would have had an altogether different
effect on the proceedings.
I want to submit to the House that

of the Ministry of Home Affairs if

right hon. Gentleman to state whether it
is true or not in the interests of law and

House. It is also stated that this District-Inspector Allen asked the Home
Office-or his superiors who really are
the people in the Home Office to take
a certain course of action, and, despite
the fact that this District-Inspector who
was put on to prove this woman's guilt,

into it believing the woman was guilty, but
owing to the evidence which he had collected he submttted a report in which

of action was not followed. That being
the case it is surely the obvious thing now
for the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) and his Department to come
forward and say that their Detective
Office made a mistake for which they are
responsible in this House, that is if they
do the right and proper thing by this
woman, who has been so cruelly wronged

that report of the District-Inspector.
Further than that, not only did this

the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) refused. on the Attorney-General's behalf, not very long ago to reconmend that a King's Pardon should be
granted to this woman, which is the lawyer's way of getting out of a difficulty.
I think this case shows that the right
hon. Gentleman's Department in some
respects needs considerable overhaul.

Now since that time some proceedings
have taken place in the Summons Court. I
do not want to discuss this afternoon the
merits either of Mrs. Whan's or the Walker's case, but I want to point out in fairness to those on this side of the House
that we did interest ourselves in this case.
We thought the woman was wrongfully

candidly here and now that I refuse to
be a party to any proceeding that is going
to make political capital out of the Whan
case. It has been going from one side

our hands at one time and we did ail we

of those legal people said about them

that it has gone from our hands to their
hands they probably will be telling them

it to be clearly understood that we pushed

I challenge the right hon. Gentleman
on that subject, because if I am not right
I want the right hon. Gentleman to institute proceedings against Mr. Reid,

which, had they disclosed it, would have
had an entirely different effect on the
proceedings.
If that means anything at all, it means
that the Detective Office was in possession of certain information which they
held back, and that the holding back of
that evidence was calculated to defeat
the ends of justice. In point of fact it
goes further. It accuses the officers of

Office, and levelled against the Detective

either to disclose District-Inspector

In this case there were two parties. There
was a lady called Mrs. Whan, and there
were a gentleman and lady called Mr.
and Mrs. Walker. In April, 1922, Mrs.
Walker brought a private prosecution
against Mrs. Whan, alleging that Mrs.
Whan had attempted to murder her by
sending poisoned chocolates to her. The
Crown had no part in that prosecution.
It was brought by Mrs. Walker as a private prosecution, which she was entitled
to do, and informations were refused by
the justices after hearing the evidence
of the Walkers.
The next step in the case was in May,
1922, when Mrs. Walker again brought a
private prosecution against Mrs. Whan
charging her with assault, and on that
occasion again the Crown had nothing
to say to the prosecution. It was brought
by Mrs. Walker in her private capacity.
The evidence was gone into fully on both
sides in the petty sessions court in Belfast, and Mrs. Whan was convicted on
the evidence of the Walkers, and she was
sentenced to two months' imprisonment by
the justices, which term she duly served.
I want to point out to the House in connection with that particular prosecution
that being brought as a summary prosecution at petty sessions it was open to
Mrs. Whan and her advisers, who were,
I understand, the two gentlemen whose
names have been mentioned in the House,
namely, Mr. Waters, the solicitor, and
Mr. Reid, barrister-it was open to them
to have appealed that case and taken it
before the Recorder, but they did not
do that. There was no appeal and Mrs.
Whan duly served her two months' sentence.
In August, 1922, after the sentence
had been served, Mrs. Walker complained
to the police that she had been assaulted
and robbed of certain articles of jewellery
by Mrs. Whan, and the police, as it was
their duty to do, asked Mrs. Walker
would she swear an information, because
without an information it was impossible
for them to proceed. The information
was duly sworn and Mrs. Whan was arrested by the police, and on the evidence
of the Walkers again she was returned
for trial to the City Commission. It is
in respect of the period between her being returned for trial on this charge and
the date of the City Commission that she
was in custody. She was in custody
from the 15th August, 1922, until January, 1923, and the reason she was in
custody during that period was that although the justices who returned her for
trial offered her bail she refused to give
bail and voluntarily remained in prison
or rather in custody during that period of
six months.
The depositions in that case based on
the evidence of the Walkers were submitted to the Attorney-General who
directed a prosecution by the Crown.
This was the first and last case in which
any proceedings were taken against Mrs.
Whan on the authority of the Attorney-
General. The case went on.
It was
tried before the Lord Chief Justice and
a jury of the City of Belfast in January,
1923. Mrs. Whan was defended by a
solicitor and counsel, and the jury after
a careful trial found her guilty and she
was sentenced to six months' imprisonment, not to be put into operation providing she gave an undertaking not to
interfere with the Walkers in future.
She refused to give that undertaking in
the first instance, but on the next day
she gave an undertaking and was let out,
giving bail to be of good behaviour,
so in fact she served no sentence in respect of that conviction by a jury of the
City of Belfast.

I have most carefully read the records
of these proceedings and I can find no
evidence whatever of any impropriety in
the conduct of this case. It turned, of
course, entirely upon the credibility of
witnesses. The Walkers, on the one hand,
swore that this assault had taken place;
Mrs. Whan, on the other hand, alleged
that it had not taken place, and she produced witnesses to prove an alibi.
was not believed by the jury, and everyone, I think, in this House knows perfectly well that the Attorney-General or
counsel who represented the Crown are
not and cannot be called upon to form any
personal opinion as to whether persons
who are charged and tried are guilty or
not guilty. It is entirely a matter for
the jury before whom prisoners come. In
this particular case the verdict was given
against Mrs. Whan. So far as this case
itself is concerned I can find in the record
absolutely nothing to suggest that the case
was not perfectly and fairly represented,
that Mrs. Whan was not adequately defended, and it was entirely a matter for
the jury to make up their minds as to
which of the two parties were telling the
truth with reference to this assault.

This speech was not delivered in the vehement manner in which I am accustomed
to deliver my utterances, but in the cool.
deliberate, and determined manner in

this House. This oration was most interesting, not so much for what it contained, as for the absence of what it
might have contained. As I listened to
the hon. Member reciting with such lucid
detail the operations of the Department.
presided over by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale), I could not help but
think that it was a kind of casket in which

Farmers' Union for his continued

much more interesting if it had contained

that organization had done with the
money which they had received last year
from the Ministry of Agriculture, and

what new developments they intended to
promote during the present year, in consideration of the increased subsidy which
the Ministry have decided to give them.
His constituents will, like my own, I venture to say, think that even the wellcompiled oration which was delivered here
yesterday is very poor value for the
Government subsidy which the Ulster
Farmers' Union has received.
I would like to say that I was quite interested in the reply which the Minister

Now I may be told, as I have been told
before, that the Ulster Farmers' Union
and the Ulster Farmers' Produce Company are two separate and distinct organizations, in fact that they have no dealings at all one with the other. I must
confess that it is very difficult for me to
believe such an assertion. An examination of the personnel of these two organzations will, I think, convince anyone who
wishes to know the truth of the matter
that, although trading under different
names, they still are under the same
management and still are one and the
same concern. In the Ulster Farmers'
Produce Company there are six directors.
One of these directors is the President of
the Ulster Farmers' Union. Four other
directors are vice-presidents of the Ulster
Farmers' Union. The sixth director is a
county representative on the directorate
of the Ulster Farmers' Union, and then
the Secretary of the Ulster Farmers' Produce Company, Mr. Thomas McDowell, is
none other personage than the secretary
of the Ulster Farmers' Produce Company.

I have just had handed to me a copy of
the balance sheet of the Ulster Farmers'
Produce Society for the year ended 31st
December, 1927. I may say that there
was some difficulty in getting this balance
sheet. I had a Votice on the Paper on
Monday. I called at the Ministry of
Commerce at 11 o'clock on Wednesday of
this week. The return had not then been
lodged. The Minister of Commerce, in
reply to my question that afternoon, said
that the return had been lodged, and he
informed me later that it was only lodged
at one o'clock yesterday. Referring to
the balance sheet of 1927, I can only say
that it is no improvement on the balance
sheet of 1926. The loss during the year
amounted to £2,282 7s 10d.
I am quite prepared to admit that the
loss for the year ended 31st December,
1927, was not so much as in the previous
year, but neither the directors nor the
management are to blame for that, because the turnover for the year just closed
was only something like 25 per cent. of
the turnover for the year 1926. If a sum
in proportion would give us the correct
figures, it should be something like this:
if on a turnover of some £68,000 the Ulster Farmers' Produce Company lost
£5,000 odd, how much should they lose on
a turnover of £17,000? I have figured
it out, and I find that if they had kept up
to the high standard which they had set
in the previous year they would have lost
only £1,300 to the 31st December, 1927.
But evidently they were not satisfied with
the amount of money that they had lost
in the previous year. They wanted to go
one better, and this year we find that on a
turnover of £17,000 their actual loss is
£2,282 7s 10d, more by almost 100 per
cent. on their turnover than the loss for
the year ended 31st December, 1926.
As I said before this company continued to trade for a short time under the
name of the Ulster Farmers' Produce
Company, and although launched, as the
directors said, on sound business lines,
the results obtained, judging from any
standpoint, but particularly from the
standpoint of the shareholders, were not
very satisfactory, for I find that in their
first year's trading, although their turnover was something like £260.000, the
net profit on the year's trading was only
£29 18s 1d. I think everyone in the
House will 'admit that that is a very small
percentage, and that very few members of
any corporation would be satisfied with
that percentage of profit on the turnover.

The Leader of the Opposition made

in connection with both unemployment

This year already we have had 155 prosecutions against employers; fines and
costs have been awarded to the extent of
£375, and arrears have been paid to the

The taking of these prosecutions is not
as simple as it appears. You have got
to be reasonably sure that you have
evidence to support the contention of the
Department that what is tantamount to
a crime has taken place. Then, again,
there are various other matters that one
has got to consider before a prosecution.
is embarked upon. The hon. Member referred to a case in which an empiɔyer--

far worse than that of the insured person.
This employer only got work at intervals. He had been evicted from his
house, and it was found that he was actually living in one room, with his wife
and five children, and that he had nothing
to pay with. The only thing we could
have done would have been to take
a prosecution against him, and he would.
have been put in prison, which would
have left his wife and five children in a

actually an applicant for out-door relief.
Hon. Members frequently talk about
sympathetic administration, and it was
really out of sympathy for this man that
action was not taken, and also because it
obviously would have been fruitless to
do so. If a fine had been inflicted, if
costs had been awarded, if he had been
told that he must pay up certain arrears,
nothing would have been obtained, for the
man had nothing to give. The Department felt that the wiser course-the more
reasonable course- to take was to get as
much as possible from the man from time
to time towards paying the arrears when
he was able to obtain a small contract.
In that way, over a number of years, the
Department was able to collect £8 from
this man, and later on it may be possible to collect more, if he happens to get
further contracts.
The arrears that have been collected
are credited to certain of his employees,
and again I maintain that a very reasonable course is taken. We do not apportion the arrears over all those who have
been his workers in the past. What we
do is, we credit the contributions to those
who require them most, in order to qualify
them for benefit. That is a sympathetic
way of dealing with the matter.

The hon. Member made a pretty lengthy
reference to the matter of labour-saving
machinery. I do not know exactly where
he stands in that matter. Obviously the
employers of Northern Ireland must adopt
modern methods of production, otherwise
the cost of production in Northern Ireland
would be much higher than the cost of
production of similar commodities
throughout the world. Therefore, I maintain, that in order that employment may
be given to our people here, it is absolutely
necessary that our cost of production
should be in harmony with the cost of production in other countries. None of us
want to see wages cut in order to produce
that result, but still the result has got
to be attained, and my opinion, for what it
is worth, is that, short of cutting wages,
it can only be attained by adopting
modern methods of production. Take, as
an example, the question of hand looms.
The hand loom industry was of very substantial importance in Northern Ireland
some years ago. Well, the mechanical loom
came along and trade was changed from
one class of loom to the other. Supposing
the employers had been so short-sighted as
not to adopt the power loom, I think the
linen trade would have about left Northern Ireland altogether by this time.
Undoubtedly, the modern loom would
have been started in other places, and the
result is that the whole trade would have
followed the loom.
I do not think there is any other matter the hoń. Member referred to that I

not carried out in a sympathetic and impartial way; in fact, the charge very often
brought against me is that it is too sympathetic. However, I put the one charge

we do say is that the Ministry of Labour
and the Northern Government should administer the law and that the workpeople employed by any employer, big
or small, should be paid what they are
entitled to, and neither more nor less.
That is all I am asking for.
Mr. ANDREWS: The worker, as I
have already said, has not been deprived
of anything.
Mr. KYLE: He has been deprived of
his wages.
Mr. ANDREWS: He is actually getting benefit at the present time.
Whether he was deprived of wages by his
employer when acting properly I do not
know, but it is not my duty to see that
employers pay the employee his wages.
The employee must see to that himself.
If I were to accept the responsibility of
seeing that every employer in Northern
Ireland acted as he should in paying
wages to every employee I do not know
where my responsibility would end. Parliament, thank goodness, has never placed
that responsibility on me.
May I say this, that I do think the
hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) is taking a very
unsympathetic view of this case. I have
already told him of the sad circumstances
under which this man and his wife and
children are living in a single room. I may
further say that one of the inspectors
who went to collect the arrears found the
wife and children living in such terrible
privations that the inspector, out of his
own generosity and in response to the
dictates of his heart, actually put his
hand in his pocket and gave the woman
something to keep herself and her
children.
As regards the matter which has been
raised by the hon. Member (Mr. W.
McMullen), I do not fully understand all
the circumstances about the case. I did
not know that the hon. Member was going
to raise it, but I understand that while
my inspectors were making certain inquiries to see whether the man had been
entitled to obtain unemployment benefit
or not they discovered certain other matters which, in the discharge of their responsible duties, they were bound to
report. It was considered by another
Department that this evidence ought to
be disclosed for a different purpose.
Those are the facts, and I do not think
anything irregular has been done. If
no crime has been committed no harm

CLAUSE 2 (Prevention of obstruction
to view at corners).
(1) Where a local authority are of
opinion that it is necessary, for the prevention of danger arising from obstruction to the view of persons using a road
maintainable by the authority, to impose
restrictions with respect to any land at
or near any corner or bend or road junction in such road, the local authority
may serve a notice-
(a) upon the owner or occupier of the
land directing him to alter the height
or character of any wall (not being
a wall forming part of the structure
of a permanent edifice), fence or hedge
thereon so as to cause it to conform
with any requirements specified in the
notice; or
(b) upon every owner, occupier and
lessee of the land restraining them,
either absolutely or subject to such
conditions as may be specified in the
notice, from permitting any building,
wall, fence or hedge to be erected or
planted on the land:
Provided that-
(i) there shall be annexed to any notice
served under this section a plan showing the land to which the notice relates; and
*
*
*
*
*
(3) If any person upon whom notice
has been ser ved under this section objects to comply with any requirement of
the notice, or objects to any restriction
imposed thereby, he may, within twentyone days after the receipt of the notice,
send his objection in writing, stating the
grounds thereof, to the authority by
whom the notice was served, and thereupon the question whether the notice
shall be withdrawn as respects any requirement or restriction objected to shall
be determined, if the parties so agree, by
a single arbitrator appointed by them,
or, in default of such agreement as
aforesaid, shall be determined by the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
*
If any question arises whether compensation is payable under this provision, the question shall be decided by
the county court having jurisdiction
where the land is situate, and a county
court shall have jurisdiction to deal with
any such question, notwithstanding
that, by reason of the amount of claim
or otherwise, the case would not, but for
this provision, be within the jurisdiction
of a county court.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Game Preservation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I do not think
that it is necessary
to offer any
excuse for the introduction of the
present Measure, which has, for its object the better preservation of game. If
the present poaching and shooting out-ofseason is allowed to continue at its present
rate, it is only a question of time until
game will become practically extinct in
Northern Ireland.
: 220
Game Preservation Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The intensity of poaching appears to
be due to a variety of reasons, and it is
a fact that large numbers of the general
public look with a comparatively lenient
eye on poaching offences. Undoubtedly
the unpopularity of the old Landlord
system, and the general impression that
Game Rights were the property of the
leisured and wealthy classes alone contributed much to bring this unsatisfactory condition of affairs about. Much
water, however, has flowed under the
bridges since the first Game Act was
introduced, and it is a fact that while
in the old days Game Rights only vested
in a comparative few, Game Rights to-day
belong to very many thousands.
This is due to a variety of circumstances, but principally to the operations
of the Land Purchase Acts. Under the
old Acts, the voluntary purchase Acts, in
many cases the Game Rights passed to the
purchasing tenants, and under the recent
Land Act of 1925, under which we hope
the balance of all agricultural tenancies
will before long, become vested in the
occupying tenant, it is expressly provided
that, in the absence of a voluntary agreement between the landlord and the
tenant, the rights pass to the Land Commission who can make whatever arrangements they think right, either with the
landlord or the occupying tenants.
Therefore, instead of, as I said before,
this being a matter that only interests a
few landlords, it is of vital interest to
the purchasing tenants. Looking at it
from that point of view when we were
considering the form of the Bill, I set up
a small Committee to advise me in regard
to these matters. I had the advantage of
the presence on that Committee of Mr.
Jackson, the President of the Farmers'
Union, who is in a position to speak from
the tenants' point of view. I might say
here that I appreciate greatly the help
which I received from this Committee,
whose practical knowledge of the subject.
and of the rather complicated code of
Game Laws was of great assistance to
me.
One may look with a certain amount of
leniency on the poacher who may have an
odd shot at game when it does not belong
to him, but I think no one can have any
patience with the individuals who, for
the sake of gain, shoot out of season, and
sell birds at a large profit to themselves.
The damage done by poachers is not by
any means confined to the destruction of
game. I have received from time to time
numerous complaints from farmers concerning the damage done by poachers to
their fences when trespassing on their
lands.
We read in the papers every
Twelfth that birds that were supposed to be shot early in the
Highlands were conveyed by aeroplane
in order to supply the tables in
some of the big restaurants in London,
but we do not hear of the enormous
number of birds that are shot in Northern
Ireland days before the 12th and sent
surreptitiously over to be used on the
night of the 12th August, and, therefore,
as I said before, unless something is done
to tighten up the Game Laws, game will
become extinct in Northern Ireland.
I do not think it necessary to dwell on
what must be obvious to every hon.
Member, and that is, the value of game
as a national asset.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: You have
only to go to Scotland and see the numbers of visitors and amount of employment that follows through the preservation of game, to realise that in no
sense can Game be regarded as a matter
of purely private interest.
Coming now to the Clauses of the Bill.
I think the first Clause is perhaps the
most important one, and requires some
explanation. The Constabulary Act of
1836 definitely provides that the Constabulary should not be used in any way
whatever for the purpose of enforcing
the game rights. It is doubtful why such
a prohibition was inserted in the Act,
and I think it was felt by the powers
that be in those days that if such a
power was not definitely taken away
from the police that it would be the subject of much abuse at the hands of the
game owners who were in those days
the landlords in Ireland, and who would
seek to use their influence to utilise the
police as gamekeepers. However, whatever the cause may have been it, would
be out of place now to continue this prohibition if we are to do anything to
preserve the game as a National asset in
Northern Ireland, and while we propose
to remove this limitation, we have inserted a proviso to ensure that we do
Game Preservation Bill-
Second Reading.
9 OCTOBER 1928

not in any way intend to turn the police
into gamekeepers, or relieve those who
have Game Rights of their own responsibility of protecting their rights. But
what we do propose to do is to give the
police wider powers in the ordinary
course of their duty to ensure that the
Game Laws are enforced.
May I give an example of what I
mean? If a Constable sees
an individual shooting out of season, it would be
his duty to enter those lands and take
the necessary steps to see that the individual was dealt with by law.
Dealing now with Clause 2, may
I point out that at the present time the
law enables the constable to enter private
land if he actually sees a person carrying a gun and demand the gun licence.
At the same time he has no power to
demand to see the game licence. If the
gun licence which the constable is entitled to demand is not forthcoming, and
if the individual does not give his name,
the constable has power to arrest him.
Under Clause 2, we propose to extend
this power to enable the constable to demand the game licence, and it also enables the constable to search the bag, or
motor car, or, generally, the premises in
which the individual may be. Hitherto,
the right to demand the game licence was
confined to the Excise Authorities, but
this is quite impracticable now, and the
result is, to a very large extent, the Revenue is defrauded by individuals
shooting without game licences.
Coming now to Clause 3 this provides
that a Register shall be kept by every
licenced game keeper. As the law now
stands, every game dealer must have a
licence, and he is only supposed to buy
game from those who have the legal
right to shoot, but it has often been said
that without receivers there would be no
thieves, and the same remark might
readily be applied in regard to poaching,
but unfortunately at the present time
there are certain dealers who deal extensively with those who acquire game
that has been illegally shot. This
Clause simply provides for the keeping
of a Register which must be open to the
police authorities for inspection from
time to time. It will, in no sense, impose a burden on the honest, game
dealer. In order to ensure that the
power given by this Clause will be exercised discreetly and not unnecessarily,
the power can only be exercised by an
officer of not less than the rank of sergeant.
Coming to Clause 4, while dealers
have had to have a licence for the keeping of game, game under the old Act
for that purpose did not include woodcock and snipe. This Clause will have
the effect of bringing these two classes
of birds under the law for the purpose
of registration.
With regard to Clause 5, as I have already indicated, it is a known fact that
a great many birds are shot in Northern
Ireland out of season and sold at high
prices in England. With a view of trying to stop this practice, this Clause provides that all boxes and packages containing game shall be so labelled with
the address of the consignor.
Coming now to Clause 6, the constable,
under the law as it now stands, can only
search a person if that individual is on a
highway, a street, or public place, and if
he has good reason to believe that he is
coming from land where he has been unlawfully in search of game. In the event
of a refusal on the part of the individual
to give his name, he has only the right to
summon the individual. I think hon.
Members will appreciate how useless these
particular powers are, as an individual,
the moment he saw the constable, could
step into an adjoining field, and the
constable would be powerless. The effect,
briefly, of Clause 6 is to extend these
powers which the police have at the
present time to practically any places,
but I think it right to point out that no
power of arrest is given under this
Clause.

Sir EDWARD
ARCHDALE: As
my hon. Friend (Mr. George Henderson) has just said, the growing
of potatoes is one of our Northern
Ireland specialities. The trade is an
exceedingly valuable one. Moreover
the potato is our chief tillage crop and
upon it our system of crop rotation depends. The total area grown in Northern
Ireland in 1928 exceeds the area under
potatoes in Scotland by 10,500 acres and
the average quantity of potatoes exported
from Northern Ireland is about 200,000
tons per annum. We are able to pro-

duce as good potatoes as any country in
the world but if top price on the British market is to be obtained marketing
methods must be improved.
Complaints have been made to our Department and to all the merchants by
cross-Channel buyers that the potatoes
they get are not properly graded, and
they cannot depend when they buy
potatoes on getting what they bought.
We have been strongly of opinion here
in Northern Ireland, before this Parliament began, that there should be some
measure brought in to enable us to regulate the grading of potatoes for export.
But by a Clause in the 1920 Act we were
prevented from doing that. During the
last session of Parliament the Government
have been pressing the Imperial Government to bring in some Measure in the
Imperial Parliament which would allow
us to regulate traffic in potatoes or anything else we export to England, and by
a Miscellaneous Provisions Bill which only
passed a short time ago in the Imperial
Parliament-the last Bill that was passed
in this session-we have been enabled to
bring in this Bill which regulates export.
The Committee presided over a short
time ago by the hon. Member for Derry
(Mr. Mark) on the marketing of agricultural produce made a very strong
pronouncement which I would like to
read:
"We received conclusive evidence that
Northern Ireland at present stands in
the gravest danger of losing its chief
outlet for its important potato industry. In many of the large British
consuming areas, buyers are evincing
the strongest disinclination to take
Northern Ireland potatoes. These
buyers complain, and the justice of
their complaint is beyond question, of
inferior selection and dressing; of the
mixing of varieties of dissimilar keeping, cooking and table qualities; of the
incorrect description of consignments;
of waste through the use of improper
bags; of shortage of weight; and of
other undesirable features. Unfortunately these shortcomings on the part of
our own consignments are accentuated
by the condition in which certain of our
foreign competitors place their inspected
potatoes on the British market.
foreign markets with which Northern
Ireland formely conducted an important export trade in seed potatoes, the
In
same unsatisfactory position is disclosed,
and certain of those markets are now
being increasingly supplied from other
sources with seed of guaranteed purity
and quality. We are emphatically of
the opinion that the taking of legislative action to restore confidence in our
potato exports is a matter of urgency."
I may say, too, that the Ulster Farmers'
Union and the Agricultural Committee in
almost every county in Northern Ireland
are in favour of such legislation.
Standardization of agricultural produce
has the same advantages as in any other
line of production. It enables the importer to order without inspection, because he knows he can rely on receiving
an article of uniform excellence. He can,
therefore, afford to pay a higher price.
In the case of ungraded produce the
British distributor has to make due allowance for wastage, re-handling and disorganization of business. All these costs
must ultimately be borne by the Irish producer. These facts have been recognized
by British Dominions and foreign
countries with the result that the vast
bulk of agricultural produce from abroad
is now graded before being placed on the
British market.
The Marketing of Eggs Act passed by
this House in 1924 has led to improved
quality and grading and as a result our
eggs now hold a commanding position on
the British market. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). Moreover all progressive
producers and merchants are now so convinced that this legislation has been to
their advantage that breaches of the Eggs
Act are quite uncommon. The conditions
laid down have proved satisfactory and
the confidence engendered by the supply
of uniformly high-class consignments has
led to enhanced prices and increased demands. Furthermore, the result has been
a substantial increase in our poultry population. We hope for similar results from
the Potato Marketing Bill now submitted,
that is increased demand and increased
prices.
We know for a fact that Irish seed
potatoes are better than any other seed
potatoes. By every trial in England and
every trial in this country, Irish seed
potatoes are better than Scottish seed
potatoes and the Scottish seed potato
trade in England is being rather disturbed
because they are not taking such good care
as they should take. Many English seed
2267 Marketing of Potatoes Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Archdale]
merchants have told us that now is our
time to get on with our seed potato trade
and many of our North of Ireland progressive farmers are going in for the seed
potato trade with England which we hope
by this means to make much more secure
and to get higher prices because
people can depend on the consignment.
the
The chief features of the measure are:
(1). All merchants exporting potatoes
to Great Britain must be licensed and in
the first instance every person applying
for a license will obtain one-its continuance depending on compliance with the
Regulations. The fee of £1 will be
charged for each licence.
(2). Potatoes exported to Great Britain,
must, with certain minor exceptions, be
accompanied by a certificate of an inspector that they are of the prescribed
standard of quality and have been graded
and packed in a proper manner.
In
order to help to cover the cost of administering the Act a fee of 6d per ton will
be charged for all potatoes inspected.
(3). It is also proposed to grant permits for potatoes coming within certain
categories, such as lots grown by the exporters, lots sent for experimental demonstration, or similar purposes, and lots
of less than, say, one ton. Licences will
not be required in these cases but consignments may be inspected.
(4). Where, for the purpose of issuing
a permit, inspection of a consignment is
necessary fees at the rate of 6d per ton
will be charged but for the permit itself
no fee will be charged.
The Bill provides that at present its
provisions shall not apply to potatoes sent
to the Irish Free State but later on an
arrangement can be made to have such
exports inspected if considered desirable.
At the Border there is considerable trade
done in potatoes and it would not do if
we did anything to stop that at present
until the Bill gets into working order.
The intention is that the Act shall
come into force on the first day of February next-the period intervening between
the passage of the measure and its coming
into operation being devoted to the
training of the necessary staff and the
education of the farmer and the merchant
in the provisions of the Act.
We have been written to over and over
again by almost every agricultural district urging this grading and we have had
meetings with the leading potato_exporters, and although I honestly say they are
not in agreement still the majority of
them are in favour of the Bill. They
all say something is necessary. I do not
know that there is anything further I
can say about the Bill. I can go into
the various clauses or not according to
the wish of the House.
Motion made and Question "That the
debate be now adjourned," put, and
agreed to.-(Mr. George Henderson).

Hon. Members will recollect that

in the United States of America.
contribution was made on the basis of a

As hon. Members are aware, the organisation of the advertising campaign is
carried out by a Committee in New York,
composed largely of the local representatives of Northern Ireland firms. I have
had the advantage of personal contact
with this Committee during my visits to
the United States and I am glad to be
able to tell the Committee that their
meetings are animated by keenness and
harmony which are reflected in the undoubted vigour with which the campaign
has been, and is being, waged.
In order to interest traders in linen
damask a trade magazine entitled "The
Linen Guildsman" has been published
each month since October, 1926, some
3,000 copies being circulated each month
to the buying departments of retail establishments throughout the length and
breadth of the United States, while advertising in trade journals has also been
undertaken. Lecturers have been appointed to visit all the leading cities and
to give public demonstrations of the
merits and artistic qualities of linen as an
article of universal household use. The
wireless has been pressed into the service
of linen by the Committee, and, coincident
with the lectures and broadcast talks,
special displays of linen are arranged in
the different localities.
A large number of advertisements have
been inserted in American newspapers
and magazines with a view to reaching
the actual consumer. From October 1st,
1927, to January 1st, 1928, no less than
350 articles appeared in American newspapers and magazines, covering a circulation of over 25 million readers.
The success of this publicity campaign
has encouraged the linen industry to extend its scope, and it has been decided to
advertise not only damasks but other
linens as well and, further, to extend the
campaign to the home market and to the
Dominions. Although the United States
is still the most important individual overseas market, the British Empire is becoming year by year a larger consumer of
linen goods. In 1913 the United States
bought 47.6% of
47.6% of the total United

behalf of some particular section of the

in the world-that is to say, if we are to

There is another reason why I have a
very strenuous objection to the voting of
these sums of money. The hon. Member
for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin) has stated
that we on this side have always rendered
any assistance in our power so far as the
linen trade is concerned. I think no
Member on the Government side of the
Committee can disagree with that statement. I do want to impress upon the
Government another reason why Irish
linen is not as popular in the American
markets as it used to be. It is because
there is a growing consciousness amongst
the American people that the work people
who produce this linen in the mills and
factories of the North of Ireland are underpaid, are miserably paid, are the worst
paid workers in textiles in the United
Kingdom or in Great Britain and Ireland.
They are worse paid than wool workers,
they are worse paid than worsted workers,
they are worse paid than cotton workers,
they are worse paid than jute workers.
We produce the finest material in the
world in the form of Irish linen, and yet
we are the worst paid set of workers. I
want to submit to the right hon. Gentleman that perhaps this has something to
do with the unpopularity of Irish linen.
No American, no Englishman, and for
that matter no Irishman worthy of the
name, desires to use material that is
produced by sweated labour, produced by
people who do not get sufficient wages to
enable them to live decently. I suggest
to the right hon. Gentleman that the
minds of the Government might be applied to that particular end of the linen
trade. I think the last sum of money
that is asked for here is probably even

the linen industry he got down to the hard

in Northern Ireland. So far as 99.9
of the people of the United States
are concerned they do not care two raps

not through politics but owing to an

reasons.
with the exception of Czecko-Slovakia
they have all suffered in the same way as

have injured us. I think it is unfair to

whole cause of the trouble is due to political
We have not the monopoly now
that we had 50 years ago. We are competing now with the whole world. We

With regard to the Lough Swilly Railway I am sure if the hon. Member for
West Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen) below

thoroughly he would raise no objections.
That railway is serving a very large portion of a very large county with a terminus
in the City of Derry. If it was closed
up it would do an enormous amount of
harm and cause a great deal of suffering
to those least able to bear it. I for one
never advocate subsidies if it can be helped
at all, but I think this is one exceptional
case where a subsidy ought to be given. I
agree with the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. W. McMullen) that the Government should go into the thing carefully
and see whether the money is being well
spent, that is to say, whether it is worth
spending money on and whether other
means could be provided of carrying on
the traffic without a subsidy. The Government is doing the right thing in giving
the subsidy, and I hope the Committee
will pass it.

GOVERNMENT HOSPITALITY.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £400 be granted to His Majesty as a
grant in aid of the Government Hospitality Fund, in the year ending 31st
March, 1929."
Mr. POLLOCK: In the month of April
last I submitted to the Committee a small
Vote on account of Government Hospitality for £400. That original estimate
was based upon ordinary calculations as
to the amount that would likely be required to entertain distinguished visitors
during the year upon which we were then
entering. But, as hon. Members will, I
am sure, realise, an estimate of this kind
differs very materially from those of our
ordinary services. In the latter case, that
is in respect of our usual services, hon.
Members will recall the wonderful harmony that exists between the estimate and
the actual working out of the amount. But
in this matter, which lay in my hands, I
confess I made a miscalculation.
I was
anxious, naturally, to limit the Vote as
low as I thought I legitimately could. I
had an idea that £400 and the comparatively small balance that was carried over
would have been sufficient to entertain
distinguished visitors as they might appear
during the year.
There were, however, several rather exceptional events which I feel it is
necessary to mention to the Committee in order that hon. Members
may realise why I am appearing here to-

Oral Answers to Questions.
INSPECTION OF POTATOES-
REVENUE.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
total amount collected by his Department
during the season 1927-1928 for the
inspection of potatoes in stores, and
whether, as this amount indirectly comes
out of the pocket of the producers, he will
consider the advisability of abandoning
the said charge.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): The
total amount received in respect of the
inspection of potatoes for export during
the year ended 31st August, 1928, was
£2,277 158 Od.
It is not proposed to abandon this
charge which has been in force for a
number of years without causing any
hardship.
PRICES OF FLOUR, MEAT, AND
BACON.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
fact that whilst a considerable reduction
in the price of flour has taken place
during the past six months, no proportionate reduction has taken place in the
price of bread; whether he is aware of the
fact that flour is being retailed in the City
of Belfast at a much higher price than in
most rural districts which have higher
freight charges to pay; whether he is
also aware of the fact that meat and
bacon are being sold throughout the City
of Belfast and many other places at prices
out of all proportion to what is being
paid to the farmers for their cattle and
pigs; and whether in view of all these
facts he will seriously consider the
advisability of setting up a Food Council
for Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am informed that the
current price of bread in Belfast is 91d
per quartern loaf, as compared with 9d
in Glasgow, where, as the hon. Members
will be aware, the price of bread is
regulated by a sliding scale based upon
the current price of flour. At the same
time I am informed that the consumer
in Belfast is allowed a discount which has
recently been increased to 1/2d in the £.
There would appear, accordingly, to be
an approximate parity between the Belfast and Glasgow rates. The current
price of bread in Dublin is 10d and in
Cork 10d to 11d per quartern loaf and no
discount is allowed.
I am, nevertheless, aware that, as
stated by the hon. Member, there has
been a considerable reduction in the price
of flour during recent months, and I am
glad to have been given this opportunity
of expressing the hope in this House that
the master bakers of the city may find it
possible to accord to the consumer further
relief in the price of bread at an early
date.
With regard to the comparative price
of flour in the city of Belfast and country
districts, no representations have hitherto been made to me on this subject, and
the hon. Member will appreciate that a
proper investigation of this matter would
take a considerable time.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Similarly with regard to the prices of
meat and bacon, the hon. Member will
have gathered from the reports issued to
the Press from time to time of the proceedings of the Food Council that this is
a matter of the greatest complexity upon
which no arbitrary pronouncement can be
made. The hon. Member will recall that
in the report on the transit, prices and
marketing of agricultural produce presented to Parliament by the Committee
over which my hon. Friend the Member
for Derry (Mr. Mark) so ably presided, a
similar conclusion was reached with regard to the great intricacy of questions
affecting retail prices. As I informed the
hon. Member in my reply to his question
on the 24th November last, my Department is keeping in close touch with the
proceedings of the Food Council in Great
Britain. That Council, as the hon. Member will be aware, has at present no statutory powers, but should steps be taken
in Great Britain to create a statutory
body, and should representations on the
subject of food prices be made to the
Government by organised bodies of public
opinion, the Government will be prepared
to consider, in the light of such representations, the advisability of taking
similar steps in Northern Ireland.

linen.
Mr. BARBOUR: I am aware of the
relative rates of wages operative in the
linen, cotton and woollen industries, but
I would remind the hon. Member that the
rates of wages at present ruling in the
linen trade were, for the most part, fixed
under agreements made through the
medium of collective bargaining between
representatives of employers and workers,
agreements in the promotion of which the
hon. Member has always taken an active
and helpful part.
In reply to the latter part of the question I would inform the hon. Member that
there is no ground upon which the Government would conceive itself justified in
withholding at this stage assistance towards the linen advertising campaign.
On the contrary, it is the opinion of the
Government that in helping to stimulate
the demand for Ulster linen the Government is taking the most effective steps
possible in the interests of all connected
with the trade.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman state whether it is the intention of the Government that the wages
paid the linen workers should compare
favourably with the wages paid in the
woollen and worsted trades?
Mr. BARBOUR: If I be in order
in answering a question of this kind I
think it must be obvious to hon. Members
of this House that the rate of wages paid
in one industry does not necessarily react
on the rate of wages paid in another industry. In the linen industry we have
to take into consideration the rates of
wages paid in other countries in producing
the article concerned. It might be well
for the hon. Member to know that the
rates of wages paid in the linen trade in
the North of Ireland are, I think, with
the exception of only the United States,
higher than in any other country. I may
quote one or two instances to reassure him
on that point. The most striking differences are in the cases of skilled artisans.

4. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether the Government intends
taking immediate steps to provide suitable
school accommodation in Northern Ireland for all mentally deficient children in
this area; and whether the Government is
aware of the fact that a child in Omagh
who is mentally deficient is being deprived
of an education owing to the fact that
there is not a school even in Southern Ireland under Protestant management where
a child such as this could be sent.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): As stated in my
reply to similar questions on the same
subject from the hon. Member on the 24th
April last, the duty of providing school
accommodation for mentally defective
children does not rest upon the Ministry
of Education, but upon the local education authorities.
The Ministry is aware of the lack of
suitable provision for the education of
mentally defective children of the Protestant denominations in Northern Ireland. The question of making such
provision is still under consideration and
the preliminary inquiries to which I referred in my previous replies have not
yet been completed.
Returns of the numbers of mentally
defective children in their respective areas
have been received from the majority of
the education authorities but, owing to
the fact that medical inspection schemes.
are not yet fully in operation in all areas,
some authorities have not yet been able to
furnish the necessary information. It is
hoped, however, that sufficient information will be available in a short time to
enable the Ministry to give further attention to the matter. The solution of the
problem of educating such children is
bound up with the proposals contained in
the recent Report of the Departmental
Commission on Local Government Administration.
With regard to the second part of the
hon. Member's question, the only case in
Omagh which has come under the notice
of the Ministry is that of a mentally defective boy of a Protestant denomination
who has been certified as educatable.
Although there is no certified school available to which Protestant mentally defective children can be sent, this boy is not
being deprived of education as the
Regional Committee has, with the Ministry's approval, made such temporary
arrangements for his instruction as are
possible in the circumstances.

ROSTREVOR HOTEL LICENCE-
MR. PATRICK MORGAN.
13. Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether it
is a fact that Mr. Patrick Morgan, proprietor of the Central Hotel, Rostrevor,
whose premises are structurally adapted
for use, and are bona fide used as an
hotel, having eleven bedrooms, has been
notified by the local sergeant of police
that he must cease supplying teas and
dinners on Sundays, and, if the above
facts are correct, will he state the authority of the police force for depriving Mr.
Morgan of his means of livelihood.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In the course
of prosecutions against the proprietor of
the premises referred to for permitting the
consumption of intoxicating liquor during
prohibited hours and for opening during
prohibited hours, the defence was made
that the premises were structurally
adapted for use and were bona fide used
as an hotel.
The Court did not accept this defence
and decided that the premises were not
an hotel. It was open to the defendant
to challenge this decision on appeal, but
he did not do so. Following on this decision, the police warned the proprietor
that no teas or dinners should be supplied
to the public save during ordinary opening hours.
I consider that the police acted most
properly in advising the proprietor of
these premises as to his liability in this
respect.

Sir DAWSON BATES: No orders

any way with the Union men speaking to

As regards the hon. Member's reference to incidents which took place on the

of Gawn Street and Newtownards Road
close to the Imperial Bus Company's premises. As a crowd collected, and caused

duty, and I see no reason to adopt the

This
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
is a Bill with the object of raising the
standard of reliability of our potato exports from Northern Ireland. I think
that with that object there will be general
agreement from all parts of the House.
This is not at all a political question. It
is entirely a question of trade and commerce and it is one where we can all
irrespective of any political question emphatically get our legs under the table and
discuss what is best in the interests of this
very important branch of agricultural industry. The right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Agriculture, in introducing
the Bill, rightly stressed the importance of
our potato crop. It is the centre round
which all our tillage farming revolves.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: . If we
can enlarge and expand the area under
potatoes we must of necessity encourage
and expand tillage farming in every direction. Therefore there is no branch of our

effective way of encouraging production of
anything is to ensure that it may be
sold at a price which will show some
profit to the producer. That is really the
acid test of any plan put forward in this
House for the encouragement of industry.
Will it in the opinion of this House have
any chance of increasing the price the producer gets for his potatoes?
While we are all agreed that it is necessary to do something to raise the standard
of our potato exports and also to give them
more reliability I doubt if there will be

not emanate to any appreciable extent
from the growers, and I am forced back to
the conclusion that this Bill is mainly a
bureaucratic and Departmental Bill. The
right hon. Gentleman in introducing the
Bill laid stress on the report of the Committee on the Marketing of Agricultural
Produce, and he quoted from that report.
The report stated as follows:
"We received conclusive evidence
that Northern Ireland at present stands
in the gravest danger of losing its chief
outlet for its important potato industry.
In many of the large British consuming
areas buyers are evincing the strongest
disinclination to take Northern Ireland
potatoes."
I think the most moderate remark I can
make on that, is that it is grossly exaggerated. Because if that were true we would
be dealing with a branch of agricultural
industry that is declining. We are not;
we are dealing with a branch of our agricultural industry that is expanding and
growing. The figures the right hon.
Gentleman himself put before the House
give proof of that. He was able to tell
the House with satisfaction that this year
we were growing 10,500 acres more than
Scotland even. Therefore potato growing
in Northern Ireland is not a declining
branch of agricultural industry. I am
glad to say it. Now I want to say further
that I have some admiration for the heads
of our export trade in Northern Ireland
because they have extended this trade by
business initiative and ability under rather
difficult circumstances. When one market
has been closed, as unfortunately they
have been, they have with keen business
ability sought other markets for an outlet
for agricultural produce.

You really cannot run the Northern
Ireland export trade on a cast-iron system. You cannot just run the trade so
that so much is sent out every day and
examined and a certificate got for them.
As I understand it this trade comes in

say 5,000 tons to be delivered on a certain

object to the Bill because it is bureaucratic. It is following the bad precedent

I do not claim that sometimes there is

The largest exporter in Ulster

I say, therefore, that the proportion must

Of course there is this difficulty
about making a hard and fast standard
for potatoes in Northern Ireland. We
have a great diversity of soil. On the
farm that I had at Randalstown for a
great number of years, I could have got
potatoes out of red soil at one end of a
field, and out of black soil at the other
end. I understand that some of our
agricultural competitors on the Continent have not that difficulty to contend
with, because they can get hundreds and
thousands of acres of almost the same
texture. But there is a great diversity
of land in Northern Ireland; there is a
great diversity to be found even on one
farm.
Then there is another factor: This is
largely a country of small holdings. Even
if you had general inspection to-morrow,
I do not believe you would eliminate all
complaints so far as the export trade is
concerned, because when a shipper exports potatoes, the market on the other
side may turn against the importer, and
he may have to keep those potatoes lying
for two or three weeks on a wharf or at a
station. Even if the potatoes were inspected before they left Northern Ireland it is possible that when they reached
the man that the importer would sell
them to they would be in an unsatisfactory condition. So, even with general
inspection, you are not going to eliminate entirely causes of complaint, because
you are dealing with what is, to some extent, a perishable article, and with an
article which fluctuates a great deal in
price, with the result that the buyer has
to store the potatoes before he can market them.

potato industry is of paramount importance to Northern Ireland, and while we
hear from the Opposition that we on the
Government side are not, in unity on this
Bill I say that the Members on the Opposition side did not agree in their arguments.
The first question I ask myself about this
Bill is, is it going to do anything to enable the farmers to get better prices for
their produce? If it is going to help the
farmers to get a fairer proportion of the
amount the consumers are paying then I
am for the Bill heart and soul. I recognise that to-day in Northern Ireland
potatoes are being sold by farmers at
about £2 per ton, and in this city of
Belfast potatoes are being sold retail to
consumers at 8d a stone or 5/4 a cwt.
It is not at all fair that the man who
has the most trouble in growing the potatoes should have only 2/- when the people
who are going to consume the produce
have to pay 5/4. If this Bill will do
something to get the farmer better and
fairer prices for his produce I will be
entirely in favour of it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I would like to say I am
altogether in favour of the inspection of
potatoes and of the licensing of potato
merchants. The inspection of potatoes
is absolutely necessary, and if we are to
put our potatoes on the market in the
condition in which the consumer wishes
to get them we must have them inspected
and we must have them going forth from
. Northern Ireland bearing the hall mark
of genuineness. Unfortunately, a great
deal of harm has been done to our potato
trade by farmers who put their stuff on
the market in a condition that did not
obtain for it the best possible price. That
also did a great deal of harm to the potato
trade in general.
I would like to say in reply to what
the hon. Member for Down (Mr. P.
O'Neill) has stated that the inspection of
potatoes has done a great deal of good.
I live in an area where potato inspection
is already in force and I am in entire
agreement with it. I hold that inspection has done a great deal to improve the
potato industry. I am confirmed in my
opinion by the fact that at the meeting
of the County Committee of Agriculture
at Omagh a short time ago farmers proposed and seconded a resolution asking
the Government to enforce inspection all
over. Therefore, it is not fair to say
that the inspection of the potato crop has
proved a failure. It has been a great success. I hold that if the Government instead of putting this very drastic Measure into operation would only enlarge the
present system of potato inspection everything that is necessary would be done.
I would also like to say that I believe
in the licensing of potato exporters and
that only men who know their business
and are prepared to do justice not only
to the consumers but also to the producers should be licensed. A great deal
of harm has been done to the potato industry in Northern Ireland by people who
know nothing whatever about the business dabbling in it. I think the worst
offenders have been the Ulster Farmers'
Produce Company who dabbled in the
potato trade to the detriment of the
whole industry and who, according to
their balance sheet, have lost more than
all the potato merchants of Northern
Ireland put together. I hope that when
he comes to issue the licences the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Agriculture, will see to it that such people as the
Ulster Farmers' Produce Company will
not be licensed to export potatoes, and
that only men who know something about
the business and are prepared to do it in
an honourable way and without any financial aid from the Government will be allowed to carry on the potato trade from
Northern Ireland.
We have lost a great many of our
potato markets. Hon. Members have
heard that the United States of America
have closed down their market against us.
That is not, the fault of the Northern
Government, who have done what they
could to keep the market open. As the
hon. Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke)
said, it was the farmers of the West of
America who wanted to protect their own
produce who brought pressure to bear on
the Government and got them to close
the ports against the import of our Irish
potatoes.

LOCAL OPTION.
PROPOSED APPOINTMENT OF
ROYAL COMMISSION.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move:
"That in the opinion of this House a
Royal Commission should be appointed to
inquire into and report on the working of
the Local Option Acts in operation in
Scotland and other methods for the control
of the manufacture and sale of intoxicating liquor."
I am proposing the Resolution on the
Paper to-day because I think it is
necessary to clear up the present unsatisfactory state of public opinion on
this apparently important subject. This
confusion has been caused to some very
considerable extent by the unprecedented
action of the Prime Minister in his speech
at Newry some months ago, when he endeavoured to define what action Parliament should take on this particular question. To release the forces, which are
now contending together on this subject,
for higher and more righteous work, if I
may use that word, I think if all the
energy that is being expended on this
particular campaign, or as the Minister of
Finance called it "this raging, tearing
campaign," was spent in trying to get
work for the workless, or if that is too
much to expect, in trying to get free
school books and free meals for hungry
children, it would be ever so much a better
cause than the cause of either of the two
contending parties at the present time.
This Resolution asks for a Royal Commission. I hope when this Resolution has
been carried in the House that the various
protagonists will be put on this Royal
Commission as well as a number of impartial persons, so that due consideration
may be given to the opinions of what I
conceive to be a very considerable number
of people in Northern Ireland who are not
very much concerned about the campaign
that is causing so much commotion in the
minds of many supporters of the Government as well as the supporters of many
other Members of this House. I say we
should have a number of impartial persons
on this Commission to temper the oratory
of both these particular factions before a
decision is arrived at. I hope also that
the Prime Minister will make it perfectly
clear to the House that when this Royal
Commission reports he-if he is Prime
Minister at the time-will give effect to
the findings of that Commission.
The issues on this question cut across
all parties in the State. I think there is
no gainsaying that. I belong to a Party
that is not very formidable in the North
of Ireland. It is perhaps more formidable in Great Britain. We find that this
issue cuts across the Party I have the
honour to be a member of, and one can
gather from the Press how much the
Party opposite is divided on
this particular subject. Therefore, I think it is
all the more necessary to have a Royal
Commission appointed to go into this
question very thoroughly. I said the issue
cuts across all parties in the House, and
therefore I think it is more eminently
suited for solution by the appointment of
a Royal Commission. At any rate
Governments in other countries have
thought fit to appoint Commissions and to
make inquiries, and as a matter of fact
to make considerable experiments.
doubt hon. Members on the other side
who have been in America will give us
illustrations of the experiments that have
been attempted and tried in that country.

think that is consistent with my attitude

one keeps one's eyes open in Belfast city

-or local veto as I call it has been in
Scotland. When the first polls were
taken in Scotland in 1920 there were 584
areas polled, and I find that for no change
there were 706.727 votes cast. for limitations 19,400, and for no licences 453,278,
showing a majority against prohibition of
234.049. Without wearying the House
by going seriatim through the figures I
have before me I may say that only on
one occasion-that was in 1924. when
there were only three elections held. and

till the present time was there a majority
for prohibition in these districts amounting to 440 people. I ask you if Northern
Ireland is to be thrown into the throes of
