between 6 a.m. and 10 p.m. I may say
that this was the pill mixed with the jam
of the 1920 Act. The 1920 Act on the
whole was a good Act and was an Act
that was passed as a result of the
Washington Convention of 1919. Therefore I think I am on safe ground in saying that the rest of the Act, the good
part of it, is permanent. The British
Parliament when passing this Act decided that owing to the emergency nature of
that particular Section of the 1920 Act
it was desirable that, it should be of a
temporary nature and it was passed for
a period of five years. That five years
has long since expired and yet we are
proposing to-day to carry on Section 2
of the 1920 Act which empowers employers to employ women
and young
persons between sixteen and eighteen on
the two shift system from 6 a.m. till
10 p.m.
I think it is rather ridiculous
to argue that the pressure that led to the
insertion of that Section still exists.
I think it is fairly obvious that there
is no emergency so far as the employment
of women and young persons are concerned to justify the Northern Government coming along and asking for the
continuance of this Act which empowers
those people to be employed from 6 a.m.
to 10 p.m. on a two shift system. It wil!
be remembered that 1920 was a boom
year, but 1928 sees us perhaps at the
bottom of the depression. Therefore, in
my opinion there can be no excuse for
retaining this Section of the 1920 Act on
the Statute Book. I think the Committee
would be well advised to consider why
this Section is bad from the social point
of view.
In the first place, the early shift, the
6 a. m. start, reintroduces the system of
getting up in the middle of the night to
go to work, the bad old system of the
pre-breakfast start. All industrial research fatigue work has proved that this
is a mistake both from the point of view
of the health of the worker engaged and
also from that of the industry itself, because in the various reports issued by the
Ministry of Reconstruction in connection
with the health of munition workers
statistics were given proving that before
breakfast was the worst time of the day
from the point of view of accidents in
2397 Expiring Laws Bill-
17 OCTOBER 1928

Committee
industry, that it causes inefficiency, and
that it causes broken time. Those of us
who worked under that particular system
of the early start know quite well that it
was a common thing for workpeople in
the shipyards and in the mills and factories to lose a considerable amount of
time by sleeping in in the morning.
That dislocated to some extent the work
in the firm and it promoted inefficiency
to the extent that the employers were
perhaps not so hostile to the reduction
of hours as they would have been had
work been carried on in the early morning as efficiently as from half-past eight
or nine o'clock in the day. The fact that
this is a bad system is proved by nearly
all industrial firms dropping the 6 a.m.
start. I do not suppose there are more
than a few hundred industrial workers in
Northern Ireland who have got to start at
6 a.m. That, I think, demonstrates that
the social conscience of the community
has decided against the 6 a.m. start. That
being the case, I want the Committee to
consider that as the first reason why they
should agree that Section 2 of the Act of
1920 should be dropped.
In the second place, the shift ending at
10 p.m. is very late for young persons of
16, 17 and 18 years of age who need a
great deal more sleep than many of them
can get. I think from the parents' point
of view it is a mistake to agree to maintain this particular system, having regard
to the fact that many of the workers have
considerable distances to go to and from
their work. This keeps them out to later
hours than many people like to see their
children of 16, 17, and 18 kept out to at
night. Surely we in 1928 want to do
everything to encourage people to make
themselves better citizens, and constantly
being out on late shifts makes it impossible for these young persons to attend
night classes or to adopt any other means
of improving either their education or
themselves generally.
Then, in the third place, the three shift.
system makes for constant changing of
one's method of living. Anyone who has
any experience or if he has met and talked
with operatives who work the three shift
system know that their health suffers in
consequence of the changing meal hours.
It seems to me all this is deleterious to the
health of the workman. At the present
time those who are so concerned about the
rate of maternal mortality are laying
stress on the fact that the heavy death
rate among mothers may be due to unhealthy occupations when girls or young
women, and one notices with a great deal
of pride the action of the highest lady in
our State and the interest that she and
many others are taking in this all-important question of maternal mortality.
I want to suggest that to give power
to employers to employ young girls between sixteen and eighteen on this two
shift system is to do something that will
not hinder unhealthy conditions because
everybody agrees that the years I have
mentioned are tremendously important
in the lives not only of young men but
of young women. Therefore, we should
not do anything which would injure the
health of the future mothers of the race,
especially when, as I say, there is no
emergency, and I think it is agreed there
is no emergency at the present, time which
calls for this legislation. I believe I have
said enough to justify my moving that
this Section 2 of the Act of 1920 be relegated to the limbo of forgotten things.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The hon. Member has put his
views before the Committee very clearly
from his standpoint, but there are a few
aspects of the position which I think he
has omitted to consider. I take it we are
all agreed that what we want is to get
as much work for our people as possible,
and one way to bring about that desir-.
able result is to encourage employers to
extend their businesses and to establish
new businesses in our midst. If we as a
Government, or if I as the head of my
Department, were to put impediments in
the way of employers carrying on their
work or if we fettered them unduly it
would have a very discouraging effect.
As a matter of fact, this power which I
possess is enjoyed by the Home Secretary
in Great Britain, and it is also enjoyed
in the United States of America and is
exercised there as well as in European
countries.
I should point out quite fairly at
this stage that in Northern Ireland permission has only been given on two
occasions. In one instance it was in
connection with a firm of bleachers who
found themselves short of a particular
class of plant. This was holding up their
work unduly, and they had not the building ready to enable them to put the new
Expiring Laws Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Mr. Andrews]
plant in. They immediately proceeded
to erect a building and to order
machinery. During the time that this
work of construction was being carried
on they asked for this permission, and
I readily granted it, because I felt that it
would create employment for some people
in connection with that firm who otherwise would not get it. As a matter of
fact, that hope of mine has proved to be
justified.
In the other case, permission was
granted in the case of the "Sunsheen"
artificial silk factory, which we all rejoice
to see has been started in our midst.
The manufacture of artificial silk is exceptional in some ways. It is more
chemical than mechanical, and it is allimportant that the acid which is used in
the spinning department should be as
quickly as possible removed from fibre,
otherwise it would have an injurious
effect. The reeling process is the one
which follows the spinning, and the yarn
must be reeled before it is washed and
dried. This firm asked permission in
order that they might have this injurious
acid removed from the fibre after it was
spun. They pointed out to me that if
they were permitted to adopt this course
it would enable them to employ a very
considerable number of additional
workers.
They have done so. There are over
450 workers in that concern at the present time. I felt it was up to me, and
I feel so still, to encourage that firm to
extend its premises and give still more
employment. I may say that, the position
of the workers is very carefully safeguarded. I have not the power to grant
this concession unless on an application
from the employers and with the consent
also of the majority of the workers. In
each of the two cases where I have given
this consent I sent one of our inspectors
down to ascertain if what was said to me
was absolutely correct and also if the
majority of the workers were willing that
the two shifts should be adopted. The
inspector on his visits found out that the
workers were desirous of it. I visited
the "Sunsheen " factory myself and was
very much interested in the process.
I
discovered how necessary it was that the
chemicals should be removed from the
fibre as soon as possible.
I feel I can assure hon. Members that
there is no likelihood of this power which
I possess being abused in any way. On
the contrary I really think it would be
very much against the interests of our
industrial community, both workers and
employers, if on occasions and for temporary periods I was prevented from
giving this concession which I personally
feel to be necessary. Having stated
exactly what the position is and how
seldom the power is exercised and how
carefully the interests of the workers are
safeguarded, I hope that the hon. Member who put down this Amendment will
not feel it necessary to press it to a
division.
Mr. WM. MCMULLEN: I want to take
this opportunity of suggesting to the
Government that in viewing this problem
they are taking a wrong perspective altogether. Unless my information is wrong
the 1920 Act embodied a feature of wartime industrial activity. I share the view
of the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle) that the
Government are following a reactionary
policy so far as this question is concerned.
As the Minister of Labour and the Prime
Minister must know the whole trend of
industrial legislation during the course of
the last century was for the purpose of
curtailing the hours of employment of
youthful male and female employees. It
appears to me that this Act of Parliament
is altogether reactionary from that point
of view, inasmuch as it gives people the
right to make application to the Minister
of Labour for the purpose of employing
these young people in the direction suggested by my hon. Friend (Mr. Kyle).
1928.
There is an aspect of this matter that
makes it all the more important to differentiate between the year 1920 and the year
As the hon. Member has pointed
out the year 1920 was a boom year. Unfortunately and regrettably 1928 is a
slump year, and we have unprecedented
unemployment. In view of that circumstance and in view of the fact that our
present industrial situation is entirely
different to 1920 one would imagine that
the Government would have new and fresh
views so far as this problem is concerned.
There is one feature of industry in Belfast
and in many parts of the Province. Young
boys and girls are employed possibly from
the age of 14 or 16 years until 18 years
or when the Trade Board may operate,
and the whole tendency of employers at
the present time is to squeeze out those
older children and bring in a fresh batch
at the age of 14 or 16 years, when it is
Expiring Laws Bill-
Committee
17 OCTOBER 1928
possible to pay them the lowest wage.
From an economic point of view apart
from the social and moral effects of this
the Government should certainly take this
whole question into consideration.
Scientific analyses have been made on
the other side with regard to this problem
of unemployment in relation to the employment of juveniles, and it has been
pointed out that it would be an economic
proposition from the point of view of the
State to take all the youth and aged out
of industry and give the fit male and
female workers-relatively young-an opportunity of carrying on. In that respect
the saving on unemployment benefit would
be tremendous and would more than compensate for what is paid out in old age
pensions. In regard to this question one
would imagine that the Government would
have some fresh views on the subject, but
I discover that the Government have no
such thing. They want us to re-enact the
1920 position when things were altogether
different. We have had an argument put
forward as to Sunsheen, Ltd., Ballymena.
I have had information conveyed to me
during the past week that the conditions
are not ideal so far as Sunsheen is concerned. I have not had first hand information, but I believe my information
is reliable, and if it is it would go to show
that these people are not working under
ideal conditions as has been suggested by
the Minister of Labour.
I think it is a great mistake on the
part of the Government to allow this to
be re-enacted. In view of the statement
made by the Minister of Labour it would
be fair to ask the Government whether the
extension of business or the starting of
new businesses would justify in the
exploitation of these young people. No
one is more keen to see old businesses extended and new businesses started than I
and my colleagues, but we do not want
that to be done at the expense of the
health, time and sweat possibly of these
young people. If businesses are going to
be extended I hope so far as Belfast and
Northern Ireland are concerned it is not
going to be done by the sweat and at the
expense of the health of the young people.
Let all businesses be extended in a reasonable way.
I think the Government, and
particularly the Ministry of Labour,
should suggest to the employers that it is
not in the interests of the State that so
many juveniles should be employed in industry at the present time. That is done
at the expense of the older male and
|
female workers. I share the view of my
Colleague (Mr. Kyle) that the Government are taking a reactionary step in this
matter, and the Committee would be justified in supporting the Amendment to delete this from the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill. .

of

the Statute Book.

ATTORNEY-GENERAL
(Mr.
The
Babington): The Government consider

Book. As the hon. Member (Mr. Kyle)

or
At the same time there is no doubt

another occur.
So far as the various

should be repealed, and the Government
consider that there is no reason why

the present year.

Poor Relief Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Poor Relief Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second time.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of
this Bill is to remedy the defects in, and
to improve the machinery of, the existing
law in regard to the granting by Boards
of Guardians in Northern Ireland of what
is known as special Outdoor Relief in cases
where exceptional distress prevails in any
particular area. In order to understand
what the existing difficulties are, and how
this Bill will operate, I think it desirable
that I should explain in detail the law in
regard to the general question of Poor
Relief, and particularly the question of
Outdoor Relief.
Most hon. Members are aware that the
fundamental Act on which our present
system of Poor Relief is based is the Poor
Relief Act of 1838. The underlying
principle of that Act was that Poor Relief
should be afforded in the Workhouse, and
that Outdoor Relief should only be
granted under the most exceptional circumstances, which I propose to explain
later.
Following the passing of the 1838 Act,
Ireland was divided into Unions in which
workhouses were established. Hon.
Members will realise that at the time the
Act was possed, the social conditions of
the people in Ireland were very different
from those which exist to-day. Destitution was rife, and the standard of living,
particularly in regard to the working
classes, was far below that which exists today. Pestilence and famine were of
common occurrence, and, accordingly,
carrying out their policy, the Government
of the day felt constrained to build a great
chain of institutions known as workhouses,
in which hundreds of people could be accommodated under circumstances which
would not be tolerated to-day.
It was intended by the Authorities in
those days that the conditions under which
Poor Relief was given in workhouses
should not be made of too attractive a
character, and, as a natural consequence
of the carrying out of this policy, the Act
also prescribed, within very narrow limits,
the conditions under which Outdoor Relief
should be given.
Now I might point out shortly the conditions under which Outdoor Relief could
be granted, as distinct from Indoor Relief.
First of all it only applied to destitute
poor persons permanently disabled from
labour by reason of old age, infirmity, or
bodily or mental defect. I am speaking
now of outdoor relief. Another qualification was that of destitute persons being
disabled from labour by reason of severe
sickness or serious accident whereby their
families were deprived of the means of obtaining subsistence. A third condition
made it applicable to destitute widows,
having two or more legitimate children
dependent upon them. But in addition
to this, no person in occupation of more
than one quarter of an acre could receive
Outdoor Relief.
These were the limitations under the
Act of 1838 and subsequent amending
enactments under which Outdoor Relief
could be given, and hon. Members will
appreciate how very narrow these limitations are. I do not propose to say anything as to whether those conditions were
appropriate in those days, but I do say
this, that these conditions are not suitable
to modern ideas or standards. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
To diverge rather from the main question-I refer to workhouses-it might be
interesting to the House to know that in
Northern Ireland there were formerly 27
workhouses. This number I am glad to
say has been reduced to 15 and the process of reduction is still proceeding, and
personally I am in great hopes that progress will be made along these lines and
that workhouses as we know them will
soon be a thing of the past and that
county homes as recommended by the
Poor-Law Commission will take their
place.
However, coming back to the main
point, I come to the Act of 1898, which
was the first Act to extend the benefit of
out-door relief. At the time when the
1898 Act was passed, it is perfectly obvious, the framers of that Measure felt
as we do to-day that the time had come
when the terms on which Outdoor Relief should be granted should be made
more elastic, and accordingly, in that
Act the Section known as Section 13 with
which I think hon. Members are familiar,
was inserted. This enabled Boards of
Guardians, under certain conditions, in
Poor Relief Bill-
Second Reading
17 OCTOBER 1928
cases of exceptional distress to grant outdoor relief to able-bodied persons with
the approval of the Local Government
Board, and here we have, for the first
time under the Poor Law Code, the recognition of the principle that under
modern industrial conditions, provision
must be made for the hard-working industrious worker, who, through no fault
of his own, finds himself and his family
at the point of destitution, and for whom
the workhouse would be most inappropriate relief.
At the same time, I do not think the
framers of that Act had before their
minds the conditions which prevail to-day.
It is probable that those legislators had
more in their minds the conditions which
prevailed in some of the outlying
districts of Ireland where, owing to the
failure of the crop or other causes, waves
of destitution were continually occurring.
At all events, whatever was the cause of
the insertion of this Section, it has, since
that date, been utilised from time to time
by Boards of Guardians, and by the old
Local Government Board for the purpose
of relieving the exceptional distress which
prevailed from time to time in the poor
parts of Ireland.
the
Following the establishment of
Government of Northern Ireland, it was
found that as in other industrial centres
in the United Kingdom, a state of affairs
had arisen out of the industrial depression which cailed for special measures of
relief. The Belfast Board of Guardians
found themselves faced with a serious
situation and, finally, in December, 1923,
they represented the facts to the Home
Office in Belfast, and an Order was issued
authorizing them to grant Outdoor Relief to able-bodied persons.
It might be convenient to hon. Members if I was to explain the machinery
under which the Application for the
Order is made, because I think Hon.
Members will agree with me that the
method prescribed by the Act is of a most
cumbersome character. Section 13 of the
Act of 1898 provides that where a Board
of Guardians is satisfied that exceptional
distress prevails, they may apply through
the County Council or the County
Borough Council according to the situation. Hon. Members will appreciate that
boards of guardians are not rating authorities, but county councils and county
borough councils are. The machinery
provided, therefore, was that application
should be made through the local rating
authority. Then having applied to the
local rating authority the application had
to come before the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I think hon. Members will see
afterwards one of the defects where there
is a conflict of interest between the board
of guardians and the rating authority.
The Act expressly limits the operation
of the Order to a period of two months,
and accordingly, if, at the end of that
period, the Guardians still find the same
conditions of destitution prevailing, they
have again to apply for a further Order,
and the application has again to go before
the County Council or the County Borough
Council concerned, and again the Ministry
of Home Affairs has to make a new Order,
and the new Order can in no case be made
for period longer than two months.
Therefore, I think all hon. Members will
agree with me that this machinery is
entirely out of date.
Apart altogether from the Act of 1898
where an Order is made under the Clause
in question half the cost is to be borne by
the union and the other half is to be borne
as a county-at-large charge by either the
county council or the county borough
council. Hon. Members will realise that
this particular aspect of the question
operates adversely against destitute ablebodied persons in particular localities
where the county council refuse to endorse
the action of the board of guardians, because, after all, the guardians have a local.
knowledge which the county council cannot have and they have also a sense of responsibility which I am glad to think
boards of guardians in Northern Ireland
are prepared to shoulder.
The effect of this Clause is, that if the
county council refuses to acquiesce in the
application made by the board of guardians, the matter can go no further. I know
of one or two cases in Northern Ireland
where boards of guardians have applied to
the local rating authority to put the Section into operation, and have met with a
refusal. Therefore the application could
go no further. To deal with these particular cases these boards applied to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and, ultimately, as a temporary expedient, we
were enabled to do something to
help those unfortunate inviduals. Hon.
Members will, therefore, I think, agree
with me that the machinery, as pro-
Poor Relief Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
vided by the law as it now stands, is both
unnecessarily cumbersome and to a large
extent ineffective.
The present Bill proposes to repeal the
Section in question, and to substitute what
I may describe as a straightforward and
simple procedure, and it is proposed that
where the Ministry of Home Affairs is
satisfied that in any area exceptional distress prevails, the Ministry will be enabled, under the Bill, to make a simple
order authorizing the guardians for any
period of one month, or two months, or six
months, as the case may be, to administer
outdoor relief to able-bodied persons who
are destitute through no fault of their
own, and who are obviously not fit subjects
for relief inside the workhouse.
It may
be asked by hon. Members on what
grounds the Ministry of Home Affairs may
consider itself satisfied that such a condition of affairs exists, but a glance at the
Bill will show that it is open to any board
of guardians to make representations to
this effect.
My experience of boards of guardians in
Northern Ireland is that representations
made by them should not be lightly turned
down, but, independent altogether of
that, I might explain that the inspectors
of the Ministry are in the closest possible
touch with the social conditions which prevail throughout Northern Ireland. It is
their constant duty to keep themselves
closely informed, through the relieving
officers, and other machinery, of the state
of affairs in every area, but, in addition to
this-I think my hon. Friends below the
gangway will appreciate this-most valuable information could be and is obtained
from time to time from the Ministry of
Labour through the various unemployment committees, which are only too well
aware of the condition of affairs that
exists.
Therefore, I suggest to this House,
that this Bill will afford machinery that
is both elastic and more in accordance
with modern requirements, and once an
order is issued, it will empower the
guardians, with their own local knowledge, and their sense of responsibility
to the ratepayers, to consider the various
claims which may be made to them, and
to deal with them in not alone a practical but a sympathetic manner.
For some time past the situation in
Belfast has been the subject of constant
correspondence and discussions between
the Belfast Board of Guardians and the
Ministry of Home Affairs. The Guardians
have undoubtedly realised the seriousness
of the situation, and I find from the returns which I have received that the
numbers of persons who received special
outdoor relief increased from 65 at the
end of 1924 to 5,629 in September 1927.
Recently, however, the Guardians, acting no doubt as they considered proper in
the interests of the ratepayers, have endeavoured to relieve themselves of this
responsibility. They have pointed out
that the Government should assume financial responsibility for the class of persons
who were claiming special outdoor relief.
The Guardians have been informed over
and over again that the Government has
assumed, in regard to the workers of our
community, an enormous financial burden, and that it would be impossible for
the Government to accept further liability.
May I refer to the increase of the benefits under the Acts passed by this House?
There have been the Old Age Pensions
Acts, the Contributory Pensions Act, the
Widows' and Orphans' Act, and th
various Amendments in regard to the
Unemployment Insurance Acts. The
Government have made it clear that once
a man or woman has ceased to be entitled to unemployment benefit or other
State benefit, and that man or woman, as
the case may be, is in a state of destitution, it becomes the duty of the Guardians at that stage to assume responsibility for the necessary assistance to be
afforded to that individual. The
Guardians have admitted that they are
prepared to assume that responsibility,
but only in the form that the individual
should enter the workhouse.
I do suggest to this House that that contention
under modern conditions cannot be accepted by any responsible Government.

of mine, and the principle which I have

1. Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL asked
the Minister of Finance whether it is

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Perhaps the hon. Member will
kindly repeat his question on Tuesday
next, as at the moment I am not in a

AGRICULTURAL CREDITS.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether he has seen any particulars of the Agricultural Mortgage
Corporation to help British farmers with
long-term loans which the Imperial Government set up by their Agricultural
Credits Act of 1928, which gives a free
preliminary grant of £750,000 as well as
promising £10,000 a year towards administrative costs; and whether he will give
similar credit facilities to the farmers of
Northern Ireland, who are as badly circumstanced as the farmers in England
and Wales.
Mr. POLLOCK : I am aware of the
provisions made in the British Agricultural Credits Act of this year for setting
up a Mortgage Corporation, including the
provision of an interest-free loan (not,
as the hon. Member states, a grant) of
an amount not exceeding £750,000, together with a grant of £10,000 a year
towards administrative costs but limited
to a period of 10 years. At the time the
Bill was going through the British House
I consulted with my right hon. Friend
the Minister of Agriculture, but in view
of the complete dissimilarity of the position in Northern Ireland we came to the
conclusion that there was no need for a
similar experiment in Northern Ireland.
I would remind the hon. Member that
one of the main provisions of the British
Act is the granting of facilities for longterm loans to enable farmers to purchase
their holdings. Provision for this has
long been made by the British Government in Northern Ireland through the intermediary of the Land Purchase Code,
the cost of which to the State and incidentally now to the Northern Ireland Exchequer is far in excess of the cost of the
new scheme to the British Exchequer.
In regard to credit facilities for shorter
terms, I would remind the hon. Member
that through the medium of the Government Loans Fund, facilities are already
provided and availed of for loans for such
purposes as equipment of poultry farm
purchase of thoroughbred stock, the more
expensive types of machinery and the
like.
Mr. HEALY: Will the right hon.
Gentleman say whether if representations
are made to him from the farmers. who
are mostly concerned he will introduce
legislation along the lines of the British
Agricultural Credits Act.
I cannot
Mr. POLLOCK: No, Sir.
give any such undertaking on behalf of
the Government for the reason I have
mentioned. The dissimilarity between
the creditors in Great Britain and in
Northern Ireland makes it quite obvious
that the arrangements contemplated
there are not applicable here.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Rent and Mortgage Interest (Restrictions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): The Bill
which I have the honour of presenting
2461 Rent Restrictions Bill-

18 OCTOBER 1928
Second Reading
to this House is very short. The object,
of it is apparent on the face of the Bill,
and in these circumstances it will be unnecessary for me to trouble the House
with any detailed explanation. The
position at the moment is that, under the
Rent and Mortgage Restriction Act of
1925, dwellinghouses of which the rateable valuation does not exceed £26 will
become decontrolled on the 1st May,
1930, and in these circumstances, it is
necessary for the Government, to consider very carefully as to whether the
enforcement of this Act will inflict undue
It
hardship on any particular class.
is also the duty of the Government not
to wait until the last moment before
giving a decision. It is only equitable
that if, in our judgment, the circumstances are such as to warrant the continuance of control for a further period,
that early intimation should be given to
all parties concerned.
The Government has given this matter
for some time past very grave consideration, and in reply to a question which I
think was put to me by my hon. Friend
the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) in April of last year, I then
stated in respect of houses of the valuation I have mentioned that the Government was prepared to ask for Parliamentary sanction at an early date for the
introduction of a Bill further postponing
the decontrol of these houses unless by
that time we were fully satisfied that an
ample number of small dwellings had
been erected. That was the attitude and
the policy of the Government at that
time.
I desire to emphasise what must be apparent to most hon. Members that the
system of control of rents can culy be regarded as a temporary expedient, and can
only be justified on the ground that the
shortage of houses has been brought about
by a national emergency. Until the outbreak of war in 1914, houses in Northern
Ireland were both abundant and cheap,
and it is often said that the citizens of
Belfast were better housed and more
cheaply housed than those of any place in
the United Kingdom. If, however, the
supply of houses is to equal the demand,
it is necessary that there should be a constant and a steady stream of building to
take the place of houses that are worn
out, and to meet an increasing population.
The restriction in the building of houses
during the war, and the subsequent inflation of the price of building materials
brought about an acute shortage, with the
result that the price of houses to be sold
and the rents of houses which were let increased by leaps and bounds.
To meet these circumstances, various
Rent Restriction Acts were passed, but
these Acts are only a palliative, and not
a remedy, and should be removed so soon
as it is possible without inflicting an undue hardship on any portion of the community. That is the policy of the
Government. The only remedy for the
present condition of affairs is obviously to
provide a sufficient number of houses in
order that the ordinary economic laws can
again operate. This I propose to refer to
later.
Dealing with the present object of this
Bill, that is, to extend the period of decontrol in regard to the houses which are
at present under control, namely, houses
of a valuation of £26 and under, may I
tell the House that in Belfast alone there
are approximately 79,000 houses of this
category, and, therefore, I think hon.
Members will fully appreciate the extent
and importance of the problem that we
have got to face. This class of house is
inhabited for the most part by a portion
of the community who are least able to
provide houses for themselves, and who
are people of very moderate means, principally the artisan and labouring classes,
who certainly, in these difficult times
through which we are passing, deserve the
greatest consideration from the community.
Had the Government been convinced
that in 1930 the supply of houses then
existing would be sufficient to meet
the demands of the people, they
would not have hesitated to carry out the
policy laid down in the 1925 Acts. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) As I have already stated, it is, in the opinion of the
Government, against the public interest
that control should be continued for one
moment longer than is absolutely necessary.
The Government, after surveying the
whole situation, have come to the conclusion that in spite of the increasing
number of houses which have been, and
are being, built, with the aid of the subsidy which the Government is affording,
the supply of houses of the valuation
---
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
which I have mentioned will be inadequate to meet the demands at 1st May,
1930. Therefore, the Government propose to implement the undertaking which
I gave to this House in April last, and
propose, under this Bill, to extend the
period of control which would otherwise
terminate on 1st May, 1930, to 1st May,
1933. If the Government was simply to
continue rent control, and take no steps
to see that a sufficient number of houses
are being built, they would be failing in
their duty. From the time that, the
Government took office, they have never
lost sight of this question. Our State
subsidy scheme has worked, and is working, most satisfactorily, and the success
of our policy may be gauged from the
fact that under these schemes 15,000
houses have been approved.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Hon. Members will recollect that, in the first instance, subsidies were given for houses
with a minimum of 600 superficial feet
and a maximum of 950 superficial feet,
but the practical result of our experience
was that builders concentrated more on
the larger type of houses-houses which
were, owing to their cost, beyond the
means of the ordinary working man. Accordingly, under our last Housing Act, we
limited the subsidy-at that time £80—
to houses between a minimum of 500 and
a maximum of 650 superficial feet, instead of the old maximum of 950
superficial feet. In addition, we increased the subsidy by the sum of £20,
thus bringing it up to £100. I think I
am correct in saying that the policy of
the Government in this direction has been
more than fully justified. It might be
of interest to the House to know that we
are approving of plans for houses of the
type I have mentioned at the rate of 400
to 500 a month. When I give those
figures I should mention that they represent an average and that there are
sometimes no fewer than 600 houses built
per month. One sees the improvement
when one contrasts these figures with
those of 1926, when the average ran between 100 and 150 per month.
But even if the present satisfactory progress is continued, there will still be, in
May, 1930, an insufficiency of the type
of house to which this Bill is directed,
and, therefore, in all the circumstances,
the Government is satisfied that the control should not be taken off until May,
1933. The Government proposed to continue their policy of fostering the erection
of houses of the type I have mentioned,
and I hope when 1933 comes the necessity
for further control will have passed away,
but, if, on the other hand, the situation
is not sufficiently improved by that time,
it will be the duty of the Government
of that day to consider whether or not
it may be necessary to come before this
House to ask for a further extension. I
have endeavoured in these few words to
explain why the Government ask this
House to approve of this Bill. I beg to
move.

difficult to get the sanitary authority to

so far as this Bill is concerned. The
burden of everyone's complaint who has
spoken from these benches has been that
the Government do not propose to reimpose control on houses between £8
valuation and £26. I think there is a
distinct grievance there because anyone
with any knowledge of the housing problem in Belfast or the Six Counties
realises the enormous increase of rent
that has taken place when the house has
become vacant. I think the fetish of
supply and
and demand operates in the
Government's mind to a very considerable extent. Whether they follow it out
sufficiently fully or not I am in some
doubt, because I would be inclined to
think that if the supply of houses met
the demand there would not be these
extraordinary increases in rents that
have taken place
The right hon. Gentleman, in introducing this Measure this afternoon, gave
certain figures in regard to the number
of houses below £26 valuation. But it
was not made transparently clear to me
whether these were between £8 and £96
or from the lowest right up to £26. We
were not given any information as to
what the demand for these houses was.
Now I am of opinion that the demand
exceeds the supply so far as these houses
are concerned, and why the Government
should relax control under these circumstances is what I cannot understand. I
know a house which the people were
bound to leave under legislation that was
Rent Restrictions Bill-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading

[Mr. W. McMullen]
passed by this Government where the
house can be claimed by the single house
owner. That house was below £26 valuation and the people were paying approximately £30 per annum in rent. They
were able to secure the house next door
that had become vacant. The landlord
let this house to these people but they
were compelled to pay £1 a week rent.
That meant approximately an increase of
£22 a year.
I wonder if the Government
attempt to justify that state of affairs or
whether they argue that the supply of
houses meets the demand. As I understand the law of economics if these equilibrate an enormous increase of rent should
not take place under the law of supply
and demand. But where an increase of
rent of the character described does take
place I think it proves conclusively that
the supply of houses does not meet the
demand. Therefore, according to their
own argument the Government are not
justified in taking off control.
The principal point I want to ask is
this. Sometime ago the Government
would only give a subsidy on houses of a
superficial area of 650 feet. Apart from
the new houses that are being built I
understand houses of this character are
invariably below £8 valuation. Would
the Government bear this point in mind?
They are giving encouragement to build
houses below £8. Of course I quite
agree with extending control so far as
these houses are concerned. But in the
present policy the Government are pursuing they are taking no steps to meet the
housing shortage between £8 and £26
valuation. That appears to me to be a
hopelessly inconsistent policy. If the
Government would extend the subsidy to
houses of 750 superficial feet or even 950,
even if you did not extend control, the
situation would be eased so far as houses
of £8 to £26 are concerned. But unless
the Government are prepared to extend
the subsidy to that type of house it
simply means the present situation is
going to be continuous and to become
worse between £8 and £26, and some of
these houses will become uninhabitable.
Therefore competition will become keener
and the landlords will hold the tenants up
to ransom and the people who desire to
occupy houses between £8 and £26 valuation will be fleeced more than they are
fleeced at the present time.
Therefore I am at a loss to understand
the attitude taken up by the Government, and I want to deprecate it, in
common with those who have spoken from
these benches, having regard to the fact
that the subsidy is restricted to houses of
650 superficial feet and that no attempt
is made to reimpose control so far as these
houses between £8 and £26 are concerned. I would like the Parliamentary
Secretary to address himself to this point
as to whether there is a sufficiency of
houses for these people who want to occupy
them, and if not whether the Government
would not be justified in extending the
subsidy to these houses or in the alternative in reimposing control, thereby preventing people from being exploited in
the reckless and shameless fashion that is
being done at the present time.
I would like finally to reinforce the
point made by the hon. Member for
North Belfast, who sits behind me, in
regard to the point that a number of people
who desire to occupy better dwellings are
forced into kitchen houses much against
their will. I believe there are many
types of people in Belfast at the present
time who desire to occupy houses between
£8 and £26 valuation, but cannot owing
to the fact that none or very few of this
type of houses are being built at the present time. According to the figures given
by the Departmental Chief something like
450 houses per month are being built,
but they are houses of the lower valuation, and therefore people are compelled
to occupy houses of a lower valuation than
they desire. Judged from all these
points of view the Government are certainly not pursuing a satisfactory policy,
and I would like the Parliamentary
Secretary or his Chief to consider the
points that have been submitted, and
when we come to the Committee Stage of
the Bill some attempt may be made to
improve this Bill which admittedly goes
a small way to meet the present situation,
but in the judgment of the people who
occupy these benches it is not of sufficient force to give protection to that desirable section of the community who
Occupy houses between £8 and £26
valuation.
Mr. BLACK: I regret the Government have had so easy a passage with
this Bill in one sense. My reason for
regret is because of the paucity of detailed information given by the Minister
in moving the Second Reading. To a
great extent the Bill denotes a remarkable change of policy in the Government.
The houses proposed to be covered by the
Rent Restrictions Bill-
18 OCTOBER 1928
Second Reading
Bill are houses of very different typeshouses from the smallest house up to
houses of a valuation of £26. Now a
house of the valuation of £8 is very
different from a house of £26 valuationvery different in type and very different
in the income of the occupier and in his
circumstances. But a house of a valuation of £25 is very little different from
a house of a valuation of £27. It seems
a most remarkable thing on the face of
it that a man who is occupying a house
of a valuation of £25 or £26 should continue to be protected against an increase
of rent, while the man who occupies a
house of £27 or £28 valuation is no
longer protected, and, as we have seen
in actual practice in Belfast during the
last three months, has been compelled to
pay a huge increase over and above the
rent which was fixed on that house by
the control provisions of the Increase of
Rent Act.
The effect of that is this, that amongst
many people who are in houses of £27,
£28 and £30 valuation there is a
great feeling of hardship, and not only
that but there is a general feeling of
actual hardship. There is a feeling of
resentment that a man in the same terrace or the next terrace, whose valuation
has been fixed perhaps at a distance of
year or two from the first man-that by
that sheer accident of bringing about a
difference of a few pounds valuation one
man should only have to pay the forty
per cent. increase in rent, while the other
man is compelled to pay 100 or 140 per
cent. increase in rent.
You may say that there is bound to be
a line drawn. No doubt there is, but the
line has been drawn just in the middle
of the ordinary middle class population
in the city of Belfast. The result is that
instead of separating two different types
of people, the well-off people and those
who work hard and save, and live very
frugally, you have drawn it across the
middle of the people. Why fix the £26
line? The only reason that I can guess
for the fixing of the £26 is that it was in
the first Act, the Act of 1925, which was
produced hurriedly, passed hurriedly, and
as everyone knows was clumsily drawn
and hurried through. Surely because it
was fixed at £26 there is no reason why
the Government should not review the
whole situation and consider at what
rent the different lines and different
periods of decontrol should be fixed.
In some subsequent Acts control was
extended to higher valuations up to £78.
A man who can afford to live in a house
valued at £78 does not need great protection. But when you come down to the
smaller houses, in and about £30, you
are dealing there with a good middleclass of Ulsterman. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) It is a great hardship on a
man being compelled to pay a huge increase of rent, double his pre-war rent,
and his next door neighbour, by a sheer
accident of valuation, gets off with a
much lower rent. I think in introducing
this Bill the Minister ought to have given
some statistics justifying the continuance
of control on the £22 to £26 valuation,
and justifying the removal of control on
the £26 to £30, and showing why the
line was retained there.
There were one or two suggestions made
by the Opposition which I do not think
will be within the scope of the Bill or be
of assistance, but one suggestion was.
made and that was in regard to houses
from £8 to £22 valuation, when a
vacancy occurs the control should be continued. One knows why the £8 to £22
provision was included in the 1925 Act.
The reason is that the original design of
the Increase of Rent Acts was not to
stereotype the rent upon all houses. The
original design was to protect the sitting
occupier. The idea was that you were
protecting the man in the possession of a
house at a fair rent, but when that house
fell vacant there was no man to protect
and there was no reason to stereotype the
rent on the house. I am afraid that the
Government will, through the policy
which they have carried out in the last
year, be faced with a considerable and
not ill-founded demand for some such
amendment as has been suggested by the
Opposition. What you have got now to
consider is that a large number of people
are not voluntarily leaving houses, but
are being forcibly dispossessed of houses
slightly above the £26 mark because they
are unable to pay the rents demanded.
You are having now, and are going to
have still more in the future a bigger influx of people demanding accommodation
at rents lower than the rents they were
compelled to pay on de-control houses.
Of course, at the present stage we cannot
do other than support the Bill, but on the
general policy the Government ought to
take a wider and larger view. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. HANNA: I would like, if I may,
to try to bring the House back to a consideration of what the question is that has
got to be answered now; and it is a very
simple one. At a time of national crisis
it was found necessary to pass these rent
restriction laws, which were purely expediency laws. It never was intended
that they should be kept permanently on
the Statute Book. Indeed, it has been
the oft-reiterated policy of the Government that at the earliest possible moment,
consistent, of course. with the performance of their duty to the people to
avoid hardship, they would come back
to normal conditions. I think that policy
is almost universally accepted in every
part of this House, except possibly on the
Front Bench below the gangway. In the
opinion of hon. Members below the gangway this is an electioneering dodge. A
number of years ago an hon. Member
opposite moved an Amendment to continue this for fifteen years from the
period at which he was then speaking.
Mr. BEATTIE: Until 1940.
Mr. HANNA: Yes, to 1940. The hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant)
also claims that this represents his policy,
and the hon. Member for South Belfast
(Mr. Black) wound up by saying that it
would be impossible to resist the passing
of this Measure which has for its objects
this, and this only, that it makes no
change in the law as it stands at the
moment in relation to landlord and
tenant in respect of dwelling-houses.
The only thing it does is to secure that
until May, 1933, none of the evil consequences that we would hate to see falling on the working classes who live in
humble homes could possibly happen.
There could not be any cavil or dispute
with that in any part of the House. I
am perfectly sure that all Members of the
House will join unanimously in trying to
secure for these people the very fullest
protection the law can afford.

Mr. BEATTIE: What the hon. Member for North Belfast was complaining
about, and what we complain about, is

Mr. HANNA: The hon. Member for

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I said

Mr. HANNA: That is the language of

It is impossible to build palaces, and

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: The argument I advanced a moment or two ago
with regard to this Clause has been
greatly strengthened by the vote which
has just taken place. This Clause, as we
know, relates to the granting of licences.
The Ministry have power to revoke or
suspend these licences because of the noncompliance of the holder with the prescribed conditions, or for any other reason
that the Ministry may deem sufficient.
The Committee will easily see that the
powers given to the Ministry here are
very great and could be very easily abused
without any redress for the holder of
the licence. I suggest that there should
be some court of appeal, other than the
Ministry, to which, if a licence has been
revoked or suspended, the licence holder
could go. There are only the two parties
to the matter, namely the potato factor
and the Ministry. Say some dispute
arises in regard to a licence, whether it
has been abused in some way or not, the
Ministry have the sole right to say they
will refuse to renew this licence. That
is a power that should not be extended
to the Ministry under these conditions.
The potato merchant himself should have
some rights as well as the Ministry. He
may have very good reasons and a very
good answer to the complaints made and
the reasons given by the Ministry for suspending or revoking the licence. If the
Minister himself would give an assurance
that he will have some court of appeal,
some independent tribunal other than
those who take the licence away, to which
the merchant could go it would meet the
case. In all matters of this sort there is
a court of appeal for an individual who
has been penalised. There is no doubt
that it would be a serious penalty to a
man, who had been engaged in the potato
trade possibly for years and whose only
means of livlihood it was, if, because of
some irregularity in connection with this
licence, the Ministry saw fit to suspend
:
or revoke the licence and put him out of
trade altogether without any appeal. I
think the suggestion is a reasonable one,
and the Minister, before the Bill finally
goes through the House, should give some
assurance that there will be a court of
appeal in cases of this sort.

I am sure the Minister of Agriculture
is and will be anxious that as many
people as possible should hold these
licences, because by doing so he would
increase that competition which is
essential. At the same time the right
hon. Gentleman must admit, no matter
how anxious he may be to avoid it, that
all these schemes and all these Acts are
carried out by Government officials-and
of course the Minister is responsible for
the acts of those officials-and very often
these men, through not having any outside experience, deal very harshly with
the people who are trading under these
schemes. The very fact of a man
committing a small offence, perhaps through
no fault of his own but through carelessness on the part of his servant, should
not deprive him of the licence and the
right to carry on the business which he
has been pursuing for years. Questions
of that kind should be subject to review,
and the only way they could be reviewed
impartially would be by having some
committee or some court of appeal by
which the matter might be fully and imimpartially considered. I fully endorse
what my colleague has said on the subject.
Question put, "That the Clause stand
part of the Bill."
The Committee divided: Ayes, 23;
Noes, 7.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I want
to point out that if this Clause is passed
as it stands it will to some extent hamper
the free movement of potatoes in Northern Ireland. As the Clause stands, no
potatoes can be moved for export without
a certificate from the inspector. A possible way out would be to examine the
potatoes at the port of embarkation. Up
to that point a certificate would not be
needed for movement in the Province. I
know that may seem hard on the exporters in inland districts, but they are in
favour of it, even in Ballymena.
The reason they gave is this and I
think it is an important point at the
present time not more than 30 per cent.
of the potato exports go through the
stores. They are put on rail direct from
the farms. They say if you compel us
to pass the potatoes through our stores
for the purposes of inspection, it will impose a heavy burden upon us. While this
other system on paper seems to be ideal.
I am afraid that in the working out it
will not prove so efficient or effective as
is thought. If you examine potatoes at
Ballymena, for example, and grant a
certificate, there may come a sudden frost,
as sometimes happens in our climate,
and it may have a serious effect upon the
consignment. If the potatoes were
examined at the boat, it would to some
extent prevent that trouble. I do feel
that what this Bill should aim at is the
minimum of interference with business
people compatible with the principles of
the Bill.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Hear,
hear.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I fear
that if you pass this Clause as it stands
you restrict the free movement of potatoes
over the Province. That is to say, a certificate would have to be granted before
they could be moved. You cannot have
an inspector standing at every man's store.
If you are going to inspect the potatoes
at the stores, what is the estimate of the
Ministry as to the number of inspectors
that will be required? If a man at Ballymena, Coagh, or any other point, wanted
to put 200 or 300 tons on rail on a certain
day, he would have to wait until he could
have the consignment inspected before he
could arrange with a carrier for conveyance, because the carrier could not legally
do the work without a certificate. I think
that is a point the Government would do
well to consider, because, as I have said
before, what we should aim at is raising
the standards of our exports with the least
possible interference with legitimate business and legitimate trade.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: We are

I am

CLAUSE 9.-(Offences, prosecutions
and application of sums.)
(1) Any person who sends, or attempts
to send, potatoes out of Northern Ireland in contravention of any provision of
this Act or rule made thereunder, or in
breach of any condition of a licence, certificate of an inspector, or permit granted
or issued to such person under this Act,
shall be liable on conviction for the first
offence to a fine of five pounds, or any
greater sum not exceeding ten pounds,
and for the second offence to a fine of ten
pounds or any greater sum not exceeding
twenty pounds, and for the third or any
subsequent offence to a fine of twenty
pounds or any greater sum not exceeding
fifty pounds.

Tuesday, 23rd October, 1928.

Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Local Bills.-Standing Orders.
PART VIII.
JOINT COMMITTEES ON BILLS.
108.-(Hour of meeting, &c., of Committees on opposed Bills).
Every Joint Committee on opposed
Bills shall meet not later than eleven
o'clock every morning, and shall sit
till four, and shall not meet at a later
hour nor adjourn at an earlier hour
without leave of both Houses or without reporting to both Houses the cause
of such later meeting or earlier adjournment. No Committee shall adjourn over any day except Saturday,
Sunday, Christmas Day, and Good
Friday, without leave of both Houses,
or without reporting to both Houses
the cause of such adjournment, but
should a Committee meet on a
Saturday the sitting is to be in conformity with this Order.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles): I beg to move,
"That Standing Orders relative to Local
Bills be amended as follows:-
:-
Order No. 108, line 6, after the word
"except" ("except Saturday") to insert
the word "Friday." And after the word
"Sunday" ("Saturday, Sunday") to insert the word "Monday."
The object of this Amendment may be
stated very shortly to the House. It will
allow a Committee to adjourn from
Thursday until the following Tuesday, if
it thinks fit. That is, to confine its
sittings to days on which the House is
sitting.
Question: "That those words be there
inserted," put, and agreed to.

P.E. SCHOOL, ROLL No. 10809.
1. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN
(for Mr. Beattie) asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether public elementary
school, Roll No. 10809, has been transferred to the Local Regional Educational
Committee or has been offered to that
Committee; whether an advertisement,
signed by the Secretary of that Committee, appeared in the local newspaper
inviting applications for the office of
temporary principal of the said school;
whether the said Committee were unaware that such an advertisement was to
be inserted, and gave no authority for the
same; whether the said Secretary intimated that he would not consider
applications from teachers who had not
received their diplomas; whether he
appoints teachers and has the right to
commit to the waste paper basket whatever applications he pleases; who
authorized him to decide that the
principal of this school was to be a
temporary principal; who authorized him
to decide that a teacher who has not yet
received his or her diploma is ineligible;
whether, as students who have passed
their examinations and completed their
training courses cannot receive their
diplomas until they have taught at least
two years satisfactorily, applications for
appointments from them are not to be
considered; and whether he will state how
they are to obtain their diplomas.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): An arrangement for the transfer of this school to
the education authority was entered into
by the school trustees, the manager and
the education authority early last year
and approved by the Ministry. Owing
to unexpected difficulties, however, the
conveyance of the school buildings has
not yet been completed and pending the
completion of this conveyance the Regional Education Committee has carried
on the management of the school.
The Ministry has no information in regard to the steps taken by the Regional
Education Committee to appoint a new
principal in the school, nor is it aware
to what extent the Secretary has been
authorized to act in the manner stated in
the question.
It may, however, point out that,
according to the Ministry's regulations,
a teacher who has not obtained his training diploma is not eligible for recognition
as principal of a school such as the school
referred to in which the average attendance is about 50 pupils.
Teachers have adequate opportunities
of obtaining their diplomas as assistants
or as principals of small schools.
KING'S SCHOLARS.
2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he will state how many King's
Scholars completed their course of training and passed satisfactorily in July,
1927, and in July, 1928, respectively;
how many of the former and how many
of the latter respectively have been appointed to teacherships in Northern Ireland; how many in each case have
migrated to Great Britain; how many in
each case have migrated to the British
Dominions and other countries; how
many in each case have gone to other
employments in Northern Ireland; how
many in each case are unemployed; and
whether he will take steps to ensure that
the supply of trained teachers will be
only equal to the demand.
Mr. ROBB: 177 teachers successfully
completed their training in 1927, and of
this number 162 have secured employment in Public Elementary Schools in
Northern Ireland, 8 are continuing their
studies at the university for a degree, and
7 have not yet secured appointments.
154 teachers successfully completed
their training in 1928. Up to the
present the appointments of 58 of these
teachers have been approved by the Ministry, and it is anticipated that employment will be available for the remainder
before the termination of the present
training session.
The Ministry has no information that
any teachers trained in 1927 or 1928 have
gone to Great Britain or the British
Dominions or have taken up other employment, with the exception of one
woman teacher who, it is understood, is
entering upon missionary work abroad.

I can assure the hon. Member that it

CLASS.
a
3. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether an unemployed, though qualified, teacher was candidate for the
teachership of a boys' evening class for
unemployed juveniles under the control
of the Education Committee of Londonderry City; whether a principal of a day.
public elementary school, enjoying a
salary of £600 per annum,
was appointed; and what steps he proposed to
take, if any, to ease the unemployment
situation by abolishing cases of pluralism.
Mr. ROBB: The Ministry is aware
that the principal teacher of a day public
elementary school has been appointed
teacher of a boys' evening class for unemployed juveniles under the control of
the Education Committee of the city of
Londonderry. It appears from their
minutes that the Committee had under
consideration the appointment of another
teacher whose name is not on the list of
teachers serving in a permanent capacity
in a public elementary school.
Teachers of evening elementary schools
are appointed by the school managers,
and the Ministry does not interfere with
their discretion in the selection of qualified teachers. It is, therefore, open to
a manager to select the candidate who
appears to be best qualified for the work.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I may say that it would not be
in the interest of the pupils attending
evening schools to prohibit the employment in this part-time work of experienced teachers serving in day schools.

EX-SERVICE CIVIL SERVANTS.
5. Major SHILLINGTON (for Mr.
Lloyd Campbell) asked the Minister of
Finance whether it is the intention of the
Government to institute a "P" Class of
ex-Servicemen in the Civil Service in
Northern Ireland, in order to follow
along the same lines as Great Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: Last year in discussion
with the British Legion, I undertook to
review from time to time the position of
the ex-Service Temporary Clerks serving
in the Civil Service with a view to ascertaining whether further steps could be
taken to absorb a larger number in our
permanent establishment. In pursuance
of this undertaking, consultations have
taken place with the Civil Service Representative Council in Northern Irelandwhich is recognised by the Government
as the appropriate body for consultation
in connection with such matters and investigation has been made into the present and prospective requirements of our
Departments. As a result, I am satisfied that justification exists for providing
definite established and pensionable posts
for seventy-five of those ex-Service Temporary Clerks who have not up to now
secured places in the established clerical
grade. This is the utmost extension of
our permanent establishment which can be
contemplated without incurring an undue
risk of redundancy later on.
As regards those ex-Service Temporary
Clerks who are unsuccessful in obtaining
admission to the established Class, I
should like to assure the House that when
retrenchments become necessary, these
men will, in the matter of notice, and
compassionate gratuities where payable,
be treated as generously as their comrades
in Great Britain.

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE
CERTIFICATES.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Kyle) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware of the practice of dispensary doctors in Belfast of
compelling poor patients to attend their
own private houses to issue certificates for
National Health Insurance purposes, and
charging these patients one shilling for
them; and whether he will issue instructions to the Belfast Poor Law Guardians
that dispensary doctors are not to charge
a fee for the issuing of these certificates.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The matter referred to in the hon. Member's question
is one over which I have very little
control.
It is no part of the duty of a dispensary
medical officer as such, to issue certificates to dispensary patients for National
Health Insurance purposes. If a certificate is required it is a personal matter
between the doctor and the patient, so
far as the administration of the Poor
Relief Acts is concerned.
I should, however, add that if a dispensary medical officer were to exact any
substantial fee for such a certificate, I
should regard it as a colourable device
to obtain payment for his medical services from a dispensary patient, and take
action accordingly.
It was brought to the notice of the
Ministry some time ago that fees were
being charged by some medical officers for
the issue of certificates in maternity
cases, and it was thought desirable to
issue a circular to boards of guardians
stating that while the Ministry could not
prevent a nominal fee being charged it
could not countenance anything beyond
this.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would
the right hon. Gentleman give an undertaking to inquire into the allegation contained in this question and find out
whether there is any substance in it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend will give me any facts I will certainly inquire into them.
HOUSING ACT (NORTHERN IRE-
LAND-SUPERFICIAL AREA.
7. Mr.
THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he will consider the advisability
of extending the housing subsidy to embrace houses from 650 superficial feet to
750 superficial feet, and thus enable
families to enjoy more convenience and
comfort.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is probably aware, a Bill is being
presented to the House, continuing the
present subsidy arrangements for a further year, that is up to the 1st April,
1930.
The hon. Member may remember when
the Housing Act was passed last year reducing the floor area from 950 to 650
superficial feet for subsidy houses, it was
clearly explained to Parliament and
accepted by Parliament that the main object of the reduction was to stimulate the
provision of houses for the poorer classes
of workers at rents which they would be
generally able to pay. If any departure
were made from that policy as suggested
by the hon. Member, the beneficial results
of it would be defeated.
The success of this policy has been remarkable as may be gauged from the fact
that under the new arrangements, new
houses are being approved at the rate of
from 400-500 a month, whereas under
the old arrangement, where a subsidy was
given to larger houses, the numbers submitted for approval did not usually exceed 130 a month.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I quite
admit that the Ministry have been responsible for quite a large number of houses

people, but there is a great demand for
houses of 950 feet at the present time-

to take any steps to keep in line with the

couraged the appointment of fully
trained and qualified midwives in the
various districts throughout Northern

PORK CURING-NEW PROCESS.
12. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has seen the
statement of the President of the Armour
Packing Company of America, that owing
to the abundance of the corn crop and the
discovery of a new process in the curing
of pig meat for long distance exportation,
the American shippers have perfected
plans for capturing the British trade, and
if he has considered what the effect will
be upon the farmers of Northern Ireland,
and what action he proposes to take.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have seen the
statement referred to. As the hon. Member for Fermanagh is aware, the bacon
trade is a fluctuating trade and there is
no doubt that a bumper harvest in the
U.S.A. would probably be reflected in increased exports of bacon to the British
markets. At the same time the chief
factors in capturing a market are quality
and price and my Ministry will not relax
any efforts to focus the attention of Northern Ireland producers on these points.
In
any event it remains to be seen whether
the new process referred to will have the
effect claimed for it.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Poor Relief Bill.

CLAUSE 1 (Powers of Ministry of
Home Affairs and Guardians as to exceptional distress).
Mr. WM. McMULLEN: There is
one portion of this Clause I desire to
speak against, and it will be found on
page 2, Sub-section 3. This is in connection with the area of charge so far as
outdoor relief is concerned. I am of
opinion that the charge should not be
localised at all, and that the financial
responsibilities in regard to relief disbursed in Belfast should be borne by the
entire area of Northern Ireland. The
Committee will remember that when this
Bill was being given a Second reading I
directed attention to this aspect of the
matter, and I then gave reasons why in
my opinion the charge should not fall
directly upon the ratepayers of Belfast,
but that on the contrary it should be
borne by the entire taxpayers of Northern
Ireland.
I suppose I will not be permitted to
anticipate the legislation that is likely to
be introduced in this Parliament during
the present Session, but if the derating
proposals, which I understand are to be
introduced by the Minister of Finance,
are similar to the proposals to be introduced in the British Parliament, I believe
it is the intention in cases of this kind
that the charge should be borne by a large
and not by a local area at all. In view
of this circumstance and in view also of
the fact that Belfast is not responsible
for the degree of unemployment that
exists I am of opinion that the ratepayers of Belfast should not be saddled
with this responsibility.
I should point out that Belfast like
every other industrial centre is suffering
as a result of the world war. Forces were
let loose which have been responsible for
an increase in the National Debt from
seven hundred millions as it stood in 1914
until I think the figure at the moment
is approximately seven thousand five
hundred millions. In other words, the
National Debt has increased by about ten
times since 1914. And the war has been
directly responsible for that.
In my
judgment that factor together with the
hurried deflation policy followed by the
British Government is responsible in a
large measure for the industrial situation
that we are experiencing in Belfast at the
present time.
Having regard to the fact that the
Belfast citizens were not responsible for
the policy that has brought about this
unfortunate situation and that the Board
of Guardians may be expected to disburse
outdoor relief to a considerable number
of people as they were doing before
they took their recent action to discontinue the payment of outdoor relief, I
am of opinion that it would be a more
equitable burden if the charge were distributed over the entire area rather than
being put on the ratepayers of Belfast.
I am going to oppose this Clause, and I
hope, though the right hon. Gentleman
will not agree to its deletion, he will make
some alteration in it.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: On the
Second reading of the Bill I raised a
similar question to that raised by the hon.
Member. My idea, however, was from
what might be considered a different
point of view. I said that under the Bill
the Ministry have the right to fix the area

No doubt, under the Bill the county
councils, who are the rating authorities,
have the right to levy some portion of
this charge as a county-at-large charge,
but I think it would be found that the
county councils are not inclined to make
county-at-large charges where these
charges can be placed over a smaller area.
Members of county councils are jealous in
guarding the districts they represent and
consequently are not in favour of charges
being put on those districts if it can be
avoided. I think in very few instances,
if any at all, will the county councils
make a county-at-large charge for these
cases of exceptional distress. If they do
E not the charges will come on the districts
where exceptional distress occurs and
which are least capable of bearing the
burden. A better plan would be that
the Government should make some contribution towards this fund and show an
earnest of their appreciation of the disttress in any particular district. The
Government, I suggest, should pay at
least half of the cost, and let the area
in which distress occurs and in which the
payments were made provide the other
half. It is for these reasons I am not in
agreement with the Clause as it is, and I
would like to hear a statement from the
Minister as to the area which will be
fixed.

I had occasion to draw the Parliamentary Secretary's attention to a very important matter in connection with poor-law
relief administration, and that is the
question of advertising the applicant's
name on the hoardings throughout the
City. If the Minister of Home Affairs
should happen to be reduced in circumstances in the near future and should
apply for poor relief the right hon.
Gentleman's name would be on the
hoardings of the City of Belfast. It is
to avoid anything of that nature that I
draw the attention of the Committee to
this very important matter. You can
realize the feelings of anyone irrespective
of whether he is a Minister or not on
going along the street and seeing the
neighbours reading his name on a poster
saying that he was applying for poorlaw relief. I think this is an opportune
time to have this injustice that is being
perpetrated on the citizens of Belfast
abolished. I would suggest that the
Minister should introduce a Clause into
the Bill stopping that from taking place.
It is an abomination.
There is another thing. I think the
Minister should introduce a Clause to
prevent anyone who has made an application for poor-law relief from being exploited. The present law enables anyone
giving out this relief to exploit the
applicants to the detriment of people who
are trying to get a living wage. The
right hon. Gentleman has heard discussed in this House the exploiting of the
men at Whitewel! who were applicants for
poor-law relief. I think it is absolutely
essential that the right hon. Gentleman
should put a stop to that. A man is
asked to work four days at hard manual
labour before he receives 15s in coupons.
It is deplorable that that should exist in
Northern Ireland. I do not care who the
body is dealing out this relief, to ask
respectable citizens to do any such thing
is tantamount to slavery. I would
appeal to the right hon. Gentleman when
the Bill is in Committee to introduce a
Clause to debar bodies from exploiting
men in this way and from putting the
names of applicants on the hoardings.

I have already been going into this

hon. Friend to get rid of this unfair
thing on poor individuals. The law was
passed something like 40 or 50 years ago

these individuals who unfortunately had
to apply for relief. I am going into the
whole question to see whether it needs
legislation to alter it or whether it can be
done by regulation. If it requires legislation I propose to introduce an alteration in this Bill on the Report Stage.

My Motion is put down with a specific
object. It is to the effect that this
House views with grave concern the unchallenged statements made on the public
platform in Belfast and Dromore, County
Down, and widely reported in the Press
in Northern Ireland, that District Inspector Allen, in July, 1924, accused
Head Constable Slacke of the Belfast
Detective Department, of concealing evidence at the trial of Mrs.. Whan in January, 1923, which in the interests of Justice
Head Constable Slacke should have
closed, and which if disclosed in his
-District Inspector Allen's-opinion
would have resulted in Mrs. Whan being
acquitted of the charges then preferred
against her, and considers it to be the
imperative duty of the Government, in
fairness to Head Constable Slacke, to set
up an impartial tribunal, which will inspire confidence, to investigate whether the
said statements are true, or false; and if
found to be false such proceedings be
forthwith instituted against those persons
who have made, and are still making,
the said false statements as will vindicate
Head Constable Slacke and the honour
and integrity of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, and at the same time remove
the settled conviction in the public mind
that, owing to the reprehensible conduct
of responsible servants of the Crown, Mrs.
Whan has been cruelly victimised by a
serious miscarriage of justice.
District Inspector Allen satisfied himself that Mrs. Whan's convictions were
obtained on perjured evidence. He reported to his superiors in July, 1924, that
Head Constable Slacke concealed evidence favourable to Mrs. Whan at her
trial in January, 1923. District Inspector Allen asked permission to take proceedings at once against the Walkers for
criminal conspiracy; failing that permission he asked to be allowed to hand over
to Mr. Watters, solicitor, his report, to
enable Mr. Watters to obtain the evidence
to institute civil proceedings against the
Walkers.
