In the debate in Parliament in May,
1928, the Attorney-General began his
narrative from April, 1922. He skipped
the important fact that although the prosecutions only began in April, 1922, the
Detective Department and Head-Constable Slacke had charge of the case from
October, 1921. In May, 1928, the
Attorney-General said it was obvious to
any person with any knowledge of the
law that no public charge lies against any
Department of the Crown for the suppression of D.I. Allen's Report of July,
1924. Mrs. Whan's legal advisers never
suggested any action lies against the
Crown for the suppression of the document. They said that any Government
that would suppress such a document
should not be entrusted with administeran
ing the King's justice. Here was
admission that it was suppressed. Oscar
Slater's friends never suggested any
action lay against the Crown, nor did Miss
Savidge's friends. But the King's
Ministers in London, when it was brought
home to them that an injustice had been
done, put that injustice right.

[The Attorney-General]
ceedings themselves. This Motion which
is now under discussion has attacked the
question from a different point of view,
and no doubt, as the last speaker (Mr.
William McMullen) has made perfectly
plain, this is an attempt to raise the
question of the guilt or innocence of Mrs.
Whan and to suggest that there is evidence that there was a miscarriage of
justice, and that steps should be taken to
have that miscarriage righted.
I do resent one suggestion, and that is
that this matter has been treated by the
Government in a cynical fashion. Speaking for myself, I can say that I have
given this case from the time it
first came under my observation the most
careful attention I could possibly give it,
and I do not think there is any avenue
that could have been explored for the
purpose of arriving at a definite conclusion which I did not investigate personally. I interviewed the various members
of the police force who had charge of this
case. I had to set the statements of the
one side against the statements of the
other side, that is, the statements made
on behalf of Mrs. Whan against the statements made on behalf of Mrs. Walker.
and I had to come to a conclusion upon
them.
I came to the best conclusion I
possibly could, and the opinion I came to,
as stated by the last speaker, was after
some additional information had been
supplied by District Inspector Allen that
it was a case that should be investigated.
As I said when the matter was before
the House in May last, so far as I could
see from a careful examination of the record of the proceedings before the Lord
Chief Justice when Mrs. Whan was
found guilty, and of the other proceedings
against her by the Walkers there was
nothing to cast any doubt upon the propriety of the convictions against her. It
was only when the suggestion was raised
that the evidence against her was perjured evidence and that that could be
established, not by anything that took
place in the court, but by some outside
evidence, I came to the conclusion that
the matter must necessarily be tried.
Accordingly, as the last speaker has
stated, I directed proceedings to be
brought against the Walkers before the
magistrates based upon the evidence of
District Inspector Allen-that was the
evidence he had submitted in his report
-together with further evidence which
he had procured between the time the
matter had been before my predecessor
and the time it came before me.
As I said before, and as I say again,
the only doubt that could be thrown upon
the propriety of the convictions that took
place in this case as against Mrs. Whan
was the suggestion that the evidence
against her was evidence that was perjured. Accordingly, the Walkers were
put upon their trial before a most competent resident magistrate. After hearing all the evidence, including that of
Mr. Allen and of all the persons who had
any information to give on behalf of Mrs.
Whan, informations were refused. They
were refused, as has been stated, on two
grounds. They were refused, first of all,
on the ground that there was no evidence
of conspiracy, but a further charge was
also presented to the resident magistrate
by my direction, namely, that of attempting to pervert the course of justice, and
even upon that the resident magistrate,
upon all the evidence which he had listened to with supreme patience for over
six days, said that in his opinion there
was no evidence upon which he could
fairly send the Walkers for trial before
a jury.
There the matter stands. It stands
where it stood in May last, and anybody
who knows anything about the administration of justice will know it is impossible for me to put the matter any further
than it stood then. Now, the charge
comes up in a different form. The
Motion that is set down here is a Motion
inviting the Government to set up a committee to inquire into certain statements
which have been made in public in connection with this case, and which reflect
upon the honour of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. The House will appreciate
that a great many statements have been
made in this case, some of them made, I
am sure, with the knowledge that they
were not true, and some of them made
by persons who are fully convinced that
the statements they have made are true,
but I take leave to doubt the satisfactory
nature of their information. So far as
this suggested committee is concerned it
would be idle, having regard to all the
loose statements, and talk, and gossip,
and the statements that have been attributed to District-Inspector Allen or to
Head Constable Slacke or to any of the

NEWRY CANAL.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Captain Dixon).
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: There is
a question, of which I have given the
Prime Minister private notice, to which I
wish to draw the attention of the House and
in which I want if possible to enlist the
sympathy of the Government. It is a
matter of very great importance to the
town of Newry. Most hon. Members,
Adjournment-
Newry Canal
23 OCTOBER 1928
I am sure, will have seen by the Press
what has occurred there within the last
day or two. The culvert under the
canal, which runs from the town of Newry
to the sea, has given way with the result that the canal is now absolutely dry,
and I am afraid will remain so for a
considerable time because not only of the
expense but of the engineering difficulty
in restoring the canal to its former
position.
Why I mention the matter here is:
This canal is run by the Newry Port and
Harbour Trust, a public trust run in the
interests not only of the town of Newry
but of the locality. The harbour of
Newry serves a large area not only of
County Down but County Armagh and
County Tyrone and some of the other
counties, including Fermanagh I believe.
The revenue of the Trust has hardly been
sufficient to cover the expenses. Indeed,
the rates of the town have to bear a proportion of whatever loss is incurred in
connection with it. The Trust is not at
present in a position to go to the expense,
nor do I think it would be fair to ask
this Trust to go to the expense that will
be required in order to put this Canal in
working order again. I suggest that this
is an instance of where the Government
might and should come in with assistance.
The House knows that already the Government have given considerable assistance
to other districts.
Mr. POLLOCK: And to Newry also.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: And to
Newry also. But this is a particular case
of where an unforeseen amount of damage
has arisen, and I believe in this instance
the port of Newry is as well entitled to
assistance as were, say, the people of
Derry who got quite a considerable amount
of money by way of a grant. I believe
the Government in this instance should
step in and say this is a port they have
the right to preserve, because if this port
is not restored to its former position
naturally much of our imports would be
diverted in other directions, probably
not even in Northern Ireland. In order
to preserve these imports I believe the
Government should now step in and say
"We are in sympathy with this, and in
order to show our sympathy we are prepared to make a substantial grant in
order to repair this damage which has
been done.' I would like if the Prime
""
Minister would state here to-day that
the Government are prepared to consider
what I have mentioned.
Mr DAVISON: I would like to support the claim which has been made on
behalf of Newry and to ask the Government to do what they can to help Newry
under the circumstances. No town in
Northern Ireland has suffered more in its
trade by reason of the division of the
country than Newry. It is just like
Derry. A large portion of its trade was
cut off owing to the separation, and the
Newry people cannot now afford to suffer
in their trade as they will suffer if the
canal is not put into proper order. The
Government found it necessary to help
Derry with regard to the bridge, and it
would surely only be a fair thing that
they should do the same in regard to the
port of Newry. The repair of the canal.
will involve very considerable expense and
would seriously cripple the town of Newry
and the Harbour Trust. If the money
can be found for doing it I would
earnestly press upon the Government the
necessity for considering the claims of
Newry.
Mr. COLLINS: I would like to support the remarks of the two hon. Members who have spoken before me. This
is a real calamity that has happened not
only to Newry but to a very large portion
of the Six Counties. I would like to impress upon the Government what a calamity it is by reading a few figures of the
imports which I took from particulars I
got prior to the Boundary Commission.
In the year 1924 the coal imported
through Newry amounted to 172,000
tons-3,000 tons a week. That goes by
lighter to supply Portadown and other
places over the Six Counties. It also imported 280,074 tons of maize, 4,595 tons
of grain products and feeding stuffs, 6,867
tons of flour, and 2,241 tons of cement.
These did not include general cargoes by
the Dundalk & Newry Steampacket Co.,
which send two boats into the town, because they paid a capitation allowance
to the Harbour Trust and the particulars
are never reported. You see the effect
of that on the whole area. Farmers will
suffer from the cost on feeding stuffs, and
millowners will suffer from competition.
Worst of all if the port is held up for
some time most of the traffic
diverted through other ports.

reason I ask the Government to give assistance to Newry and give it speedily.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I can assure hon.
Gentlemen who spoke from both sides of
the House that the Government is quite
alive to the importance of Newry as a
port. Their appreciation of that was
already shown in 1924 when the Government made a grant of £2,500 to assist
the Newry Port and Harbour authorities
in the renovation of the lock gates. It
is quite correct, as stated by hon. Members, that the port is run by the Newry
Port and Harbour authorities who have
the right to levy certain dues on imports
into the port. If they are not sufficient
to cover working expenses a claim is made
on the rates in order to enable the work
to be carried out. In 1921 the call on
the rates was £452, and in the year 1927
the call on the rates was £905. This
disaster, as it has been called, is of such
recent occurrence that the Government
has not been able to form any opinion
on it, neither has any report reached it
as to the extent of it or the probable cost
of repair; but I may say that instructions
have already been given to our engineer
to go down and make an investigation
of the extent of the damage, the time
required to make the repairs and the cost
of the repairs. It would not be proper
at the moment to say exactly what can
be done or what the Government is prepared to do, but I can assure hon. Members that the Government will take the
matter into consideration with the
greatest sympathy.

Loans Guarantee [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922
to 1928, by increasing from ten million
five hundred thousand pounds to eleven
million five hundred thousand pounds
the limit on the aggregate capital amount
of the Loans, the principal or interest of
which may be guaranteed by the Ministry
of Finance under the Loans Guarantee
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922; and by
extending to the thirty-first day of March,
nineteen hundred and thirty the period
within which guarantees may be given
thereunder; and to charge on the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland any
moneys required for fulfilling any such
guarantees."-Governor's Recommendation signified-(Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY of
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Mr. Barbour): The policy recommended by this resolution is the extension of the operation of the Loans
Guarantee machinery for a furthur period
of one year and the increasing by a sum
of one million pounds of the statutory
maximum within which guarantees may
be given by the Ministry of Finance.
Unless extended by furthur legislation
the Loans Guarantee Acts will automatically come to an end on 31st March
next, and although it has been the
Government's intention to leave the question of extending legislation in abeyance
nutil next spring, the activities of the
Ministry in this conection during the last
few months have so reduced the cash
margin within the existing statutory
maximum of ten million five hundred
thousand pounds laid down by the Act of
1927, that the Government has decided to
seek furthur powers at the present
juncture.
The position at the present time is that
guarantees have been issued or are about
to issue aggregating a sum of £9,680,657,
leaving a margin of approximately seven
hundred thousand pounds for further
undertakings. It is proposed to increase
this existing margin by a further one
million pounds, thus giving the Ministry
power to issue new guarantees aggregating
one million seven hundred thousand
pounds. The actual outstanding liability
of the State in respect of the guarantees
which have been issued is £8,632,530.
It is encouraging to know that very important orders have been secured in the
course of last year by our Belfast shipyards without recourse being had to these
Government facilities; yet hon. Members
Loans Guarantee¬
Committee.

in view of the benefits which continue to

the Government consider its continuance
fully justified. I beg to move.

That brings in a very important

rent restrictions. In the days when rent
restriction was working under the 1915
Act rents did bear some relation to the
wages that the ordinary operatives in the

built, the rent of which varies from 9s 6d
to 22s 6d a week, I think the proportion
that the tenant is asked to pay in rent is
something that very few of the workers,
even the skilled operative, can afford to
pay. Take the skilled worker in the
Belfast shipyards who is earning round
about 52s to 60s a week, I think it is too
much that one-sixth of that person's income should be devoted to the payment of
rent. Again, take the wages of the
ordinary female textile worker who is
earning from 21s to 25s a week, surely to
ask her to pay 10s a week in rent is something that no Committee could agree to.
Therefore, I suggest that the Amendment

administer the law, not to make laws or
to dictate policy. It is for Parliament
here to dictate policy, and when this Bill
is introduced here, if the Committee
think it proper--I think it proper of
course that the Rent Act should be continued for a period then let it be continued, but let Parliament decide. And
when the time stipulated by this Bill has
elapsed, or has nearly elapsed and we are
coming on to 1933, the persons to decide
in 1931 or 1932 whether the Rent Acts
are to be continued or not are not the
judges. The proper persons to decide
are
the elected representatives of the
people. It is only democratic to retain
the matter under the control of Parliament and of the elected representatives of
the people, instead of delegating the
matter to judges, whose business is not
to make legislation but to administer
legislation.

Queen's University of Belfast Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY of
the MINISTRY of FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The Bill, the Second Reading of
which I am now privileged to move, makes
provision for the payment of additional
grants to the Queen's University of Belfast; secondly, it gives Parliamentary
approval to the arrangement already
entered into between the Queen's University authorities and the Ministry of
Agriculture whereby the expenses of the
Agricultural Faculty of the University
are defrayed by the State: and thirdly,
it contains a Clause empowering the Governing Body of the University to borrow
money. I propose to refer to the three
Clauses of the Bill in some detail.
Under Clause 1, which will require to
form the subject of a Financial Resolution, it is proposed to increase the existing annual Parliamentary grant to the
University by a sum of £4,000 per annum.
The present annual Parliamentary grant,
which is contained in the Estimates for
Educational Services-it is mentioned on
page 115 of the Estimates-amounts to
£36,000 per annum and is made up of
£10,000 which was formerly paid out of
the Church Temporalities Fund a fund
which no longer exists, having been
merged in the Exchequer £18,000
which was the original grant under the
Irish Universities Act, 1908, to which
must be added the sum of £8,000 conferred by the Government of Ireland Act,
1920. The present proposed addition of
£4,000 will bring the total State assistance to the University to a figure of
£40,000 per annum.
In putting forward this proposal I may
state that the Minister has very carefully
considered the present circumstances of
the University and has satisfied himself
that this additional grant is fully justified
having regard to the changes in economic
conditions, the normal growth of the
University, particularly since the Government of Northern Ireland was established, and the needs of the University.
The Government are further satisfied that
had the University remained subject to
the University Grants Committee, upon
whose recommendations Government
grants are made to the British Universities, the Queen's University might have
expected to receive supplementary annual
assistance from State sources of at least
the equivalent of the grant of £4,000 now
proposed. It will be noted that this increased grant is to date from 1st October
of the present year, so that a sum of
£2.000 will be payable in the current
financial year. If this Bill meets with the
approval of the House, a supplementary
Estimate will be introduced in due course
to enable the payment of this sum to be
made in the present financial year.
Clause 2 deals with the new Agricultural Faculty, the necessary accommodation for which has been recently provided
-partly at the expense of the State and
partly out of the resources of the University--for the teaching of applied agricultural sciences in connection with the Agri-
2641 Queen's University Bill-
£642
24 OCTOBER 1928
Second Reading.
cultural Faculty of the University and for
the agricultural research and experimental work of the Ministry of Agriculture
and of the University. The running expenses of this Faculty have been voted
from year to year in recoupment to the
University authorities, and if hon. Members will refer to page 125 of the Estimates they will see therein set out the
estimated payments for the current year.
It has been felt, however, that now that
the Faculty has been moved to its permanent home, which was declared open
by His Grace the Governor during the
summer of this year, a continuing liability of this kind should be set upon a
more definite statutory basis than the
annual Estimates and the Appropriation
Act. Consequently Clause 2 of the Bill
provides for the desired record being
placed on the Statute Book. The detailed
expenditure will, of course, continue to be
shown in the annual Estimates.
No reference is made in Sub-section (b)
of this Clause to the professors and
lecturers of this Faculty. These gentlemen are, in fact, the chiefs and their
assistants in the Ministry's Research Division, on whom the University for academic purposes conferred the titles of
professors and lecturers, but without any
salary payment from University funds,
that is to say the professorial and lecturing work of the Faculty is performed by
civil servants whose salaries are already
borne in their primary capacity as such
on the estimates of the Ministry of Agriculture.
It will be noted that, in addition to the
payment of the subordinate staff and of
the general maintenance costs, provision
is made for an increase in the amount of
the Capital Construction Grant from the
sum of £34,500, which was laid down in
sub-section (1) of section 13 of the Government Loans and Exchequer Provisions
Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, to a sum
not exceeding £35,500, that is to say an
increase in the maximum grant of £1,000.
It is not expected that the full amount of
£1,000 will be required in connection with
this capital work, but it is known that
supplementary works and fittings will
make some further limited provision
necessary. I would remind hon. Members that this expenditure finally comes
out of the Capital Fund No. 2, which was
provided by the the Imperial Exchequer
to enable counterparts of certain buildings
situated in Dublin to be erected
Northern Ireland.
in
Clause 3 of the Bill has been framed
so as to meet the express wishes of the
Governing Body of the University that
they may be given the power to borrow
money for certain capital purposes, which
are enumerated under four heads in the
Clause itself. The present buildings have
been provided in the main from State
funds supplied to the University before
1908 or under the Universities Act of that
year, but modern requirements in the
matter of laboratories and so forth render
it, necessary that further construction
shall take place at no distant date, and
it is to ease the burden of the resultant
expenditure that this borrowing power is
being given. I beg to move.

25 OCTOBER 1928

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th October, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMONEY MODEL SCHOOL-
WAGES OF JANITORS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
amount of money spent for the year ended
31st March last in wages of janitors in
the Ballymoney Model School; the number of other transferred schools in the
North Antrim region; the number of
which have janitors, and the money expended on their wages; and the arrangements made for lighting fires and cleaning school rooms where no janitors are
retained.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb.): The wages of the
janitor in Ballymoney Model School
amount to £68 18 0 per annum.
There
are 11 other transferred schools in the
area of the North Antrim Regional Education Committee. The Ministry has no
information in regard to the wages paid
to janitors of any other transferred school
in the area, with the exception of Bushmills, the janitor of which receives 25/-
per week.
The only schools in which the Ministry
does not require the employment of hired
help to discharge the duties of lighting
the fires and daily cleansing of the school
premises are small country schools with
not more than two rooms. In these
schools, provided that there is no objection on the part of the parents, the
Ministry does not interfere with the practice which has been hitherto in force of
arranging for the carrying out of the
trifling work involved in the lighting of
fires and the daily sweeping and dusting
of the rooms by the voluntary assistance
of the pupils.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the hon. and
learned Gentleman make arrangements
whereby the pupils in the small schools
would not be charged with this upkeep?
I think he should see that this is carried
out in the smaller schools.
Mr. ROBB: If there is any objection
on the part of parents they can make it
to the education authority.
Mr. BEATTIE: Surely the hon. and
learned Gentleman is aware that the
parents will not make any objection to
the small contribution, although they
are unable to bear it. It is the poorer
class of children that go to the small
schools.
NEWRY TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION
-TEACHING OF IRISH.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he has seen the resolution passed by the Newry Teachers'

fees to mothers for signing the certificates

IMPORTATION OF FOREIGN
LINEN.
14. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Commerce whether
it is a fact that large consignments of
foreign linen goods are being imported
into Northern Ireland and are being sold
as Irish linen, and, if so, what steps he
proposes to take to safeguard real Irish
linen.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am aware that considerable quantities of foreign linen
goods are unfortunately imported into
Northern Ireland and it is possible that
buyers of linen goods may occasionally
purchase such goods under the impression
that they are Irish linens. A remedy
for such abuse is, however, provided by
the provisions of the Merchandise Marks
Act, 1926, whereby application may be
made to a Standing Committee of the
Board of Trade for an Order in Council
requiring the compulsory marking of
imported linens at the time of sale, or
exposure for sale, with an indication of
origin. My Ministry has called the
attention of the Associations connected
with the linen trade to this remedy, but
the latter hold the view that a more
satisfactory solution of the difficulty
would be for Irish merchants to mark
their products "Irish linen."
In many
instances this is being done at the present
time.
I am glad that the hon. Member has
drawn attention to this matter and trust
that his reference to it may lead the
public to insist in their purchases of linen
on being supplied with the manufactures
of our own people.
Mr THOMAS HENDERSON: Does
the right hon. Gentleman not think his
Department should have a registered
trade mark, and also that it should prosecute anyone guilty of such an offence,
because that is one of the things that has
helped to ruin Irish linen?
Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.
Gentleman know there is a distinctive
Irish trade mark which would leave the
buying public in no doubt as to whether
it was Irish linen or not, namely,
Deanta i-nEireann-that is Irish.

an interpreter in. (Laughter).

Mr. CRAWFORD: I feel profoundly
disappointed at the interpretation put

like to make a special appeal to him. I
think it would be quite within the bounds
of the Bill to interpret it in such a way
as to meet the case or cases which are
so strongly before my mind at the present
time. I know one particular case of two
old women who have a small farm of between four and five acres. They have
lived in the house since they were born,
and their fathers and grandfathers lived
there before them. Evil times have come
upon them, they have got badly behind
so far as finance is concerned, and this
small farm is mortgaged to the extent
of £20. A strong breeze has blown down
one end of the house and they have been
compelled to bring their beds into the
kitchen. I spoke to them recently and
they said they thought there was nothing
but the workhouse for them. None of
their name and connection had ever been
there before, and they both said they
would rather be carried to the graveyard
than have to go to the workhouse. Simply
because they have this piece of land they
cannot get outdoor relief.
poor
Now when I go back to these

and that it should not be interpreted to
mean that everybody in the district must
be in a state of poverty and distress. I do
hope that this matter will receive the attention of the right hon. Gentleman, and
that he will give me a sympathetic answer
on a subject on which I feel very strongly.

25 OCTOBER 1928
Any officer or constable of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary (in this Act
referred to as an "officer or constable')
may enforce the Acts relating to the
laws for the preservation of game, notwithstanding anything in section fifteen
of the Constabulary (Ireland) Act,
1836, as it applies to the said Constabulary:
Provided that no officer or constable
shall enter upon any lands for the sole
purpose of enforcing the game rights
of any owner or occupier of such lands,
or of any person to whom such owner
or occupier may have granted the
game rights over such lands.
Mr. COOPER: I beg to move in Clause
1, line 12, to omit the word "sole" ("for
the sole purpose"). The section reads:
"Provided that no officer or constable
shall enter upon any lands for the sole
purpose of enforcing the game rights of
any owner or occupier of such lands, or
of any person to whom such owner or
occupier may have granted the game
rights over such lands.'
""
Now this Section may lead to very remarkable results. I may say that I am
not in any way opposed to the preservation of game. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In fact I am one of those who
would like to see game preserved. But in
the constituency which I represent the
game rights are reserved on practically
every holding in the county to the landlord. I would like to give an instance to
show you what my objection is. I happen
to own two pieces of land. One is in a
townland called Relagh, and the landlord,
Lord Enniskillen, has the game rights. I
own another piece of land of which
Colonel Archdale has the game rights reserved. Both these lands are excellent
shooting lands. There are numbers of
pheasants, woodcock, snipe and so forth.
Neither landlord ever interferes with my
shooting nor does either landlord ever put
his foot on the lands nor does he in any
way try to preserve the game. I am not
able, because the game rights are vested in
another, to preserve the game myself. The
result is that instead of these reservations
preserving the game they have the opposite effect and the lands are open to every
poacher in the country. If either of these
gentlemen wished to come and shoot the
lands he would be heartily welcome. He
would be welcomed on the adjoining lands
belonging to his tenants.
They never
shoot them, and if this Section is allowed
to remain as it is any policeman could go
upon either of these lands for the purpose
of enforcing the game rights of the owner,
who does not wish him to do it, who never
looks after his game, and never looks after
his game rights. Therefore I beg to move
that the word "sole" should be left out.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Perhaps before
formally replying to my hon. Friend I
might explain to the Committee that the
Government have decided to pursue a certain course in regard to this Measure. As
I explained on the Second Reading this
is a Bill from which we looked for
tremendous benefit-
The CHAIRMAN: It would be better
for the right hon. Gentleman not to go
into the purpose of the Bill. If I permit
him to do so I must permit other hon.
Members to do so.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I propose for
certain reasons to leave it to the Committee-to take the Whips off with regard to
these various amendments, and with your
permission may I shortly state my reasons
for doing so?
The CHAIRMAN: Yes; but it must
not become the subject matter of debate.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government from the very first, as I explained
on the Second Reading, felt that this
Measure would confer a great benefit particularly on the agricultural community.
I referred particularly to the farming
community. That being so the Government came to the conclusion that this being
essentially a non-political Measure there
was no reason why the Whips should not
be taken off. I hope the Committee will
now try, instead of asking for amendments
which will have the effect of making the
Bill useless to everybody, to consider each
amendment on its merits and combine together to bring about a good Bill. I think
everybody in this House will agree with
me that if we can bring about a condition
of affairs where we will have game preserved much good will result to the community as a whole. With regard to the
amendment which has been moved by my
hon. Friend, personally I see no objection.
The only thing I do say is this that in debating the passing or rejection of these
amendments hon. Members will give due
weight to the purpose of the Bill.

Mr. DAVISON: I beg to move in
page 1, line 14, leave out from "person"
("of any person to whom") to the end of
line 15, and insert "in whom the game
rights over such lands are vested."
This Clause generally extends to police
officers and constables the power of enforcing the game laws, but the proviso, to
which I am now moving an Amendment,
limits those powers. The intention of it
is to forbid the police entering upon lands
for the sole purpose of enforcing game
rights. There is an enumeration there of
the persons interested in game rights, and
it is intended to be, I think, an exhaustive
enumeration, but the police could enter
lands for the purpose of challenging the
game rights of any persons who are not
subject to the proviso. The enumeration
at present in the Clause is:
No officer or constable shall enter upon
any lands for the sole purpose of enforcing the game rights of any owner
or occupier of such lands, or of any
person to whom such owner or occupier
may have granted the game rights over
such lands.
That would exclude landlords who had
reserved the game rights to themselves.
I now move the Amendment for the purpose of including these and forbidding a
constable entering lands for the purpose
of enforcing such game rights. I move to
strike out:
"to whom such owner or occupier may
have granted the game rights over such
lands"
and in place of that to insert:
"in whom the game rights over such
lands are vested."
These words would be wide enough to
cover all
persons who are interested in the
game rights of any lands, and so carry
out what I believe is the intention of the
proviso.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government feel that this is an Amendment
that should be accepted as it clarifies the
the Clause and will improve it.
Mr. McHUGH: This Amendment

is conveyed to him. There are very few
owners or occupiers of land have any deed
of the kind at the present moment. The
whole thing is in abeyance. What the
hon. and learned Gentleman has suggested would prevent the owner of any
farm shooting upon it until he satisfied

policy of the law up to the present stage,

be freed from the expense entailed upon

Mr. McHUGH: And yet the hon.
Member tries to make an impression on
the Committee that in a few years' time
this will come to be a very valuable asset

I am afraid many hon. Members present
will have passed away by then. Certain
statements have been made with reference
to the destruction of game. I have a
thorough knowledge of the game in my
locality. Game are plentiful there, and
I say that most of the destruction is due
to the wet season. No Member has made
that point yet. I have seen dozens of
young birds dead owing to the wet season
and not owing to the poachers as has been
repeatedly stated here. What the tenant
farmers object to and what we object to
is that a policeman should be turned into
a gamekeeper. If these gentlemen are so
anxious to enjoy sporting rights in Northern Ireland the very least that should be
expected is that they pay for it and not
ask the State to pay for it.
So far as I am concerned I may say I
am as anxious as any other person to
preserve game. On many occasions I have
pointed out to gentlemen where game
were on my land, and I even went to the
very place and showed them the game.
To me it was a pleasure to see those people
shooting game. We are opposed to
poachers. The great difficulty is that
friction will arise between the tenants and
the police force. A policeman has the
right of entry to any man's farm to demand his licence, and so forth. That is
bound to create friction. I could give
one instance where the agent got into a
dispute with the tenants with regard to
the shooting of a hare, and what was the
result? It was a place much frequented
by game. The tenants entered into a
combine owing to the hostile attitude of
the agent and they destroyed all the
game. That can be done by any tenant
if he is aroused; he can destroy eggs, and
no policeman can prevent that.
I say
that the powers the policemen are to get
should be confined. The farmers should
be allowed the same liberty as the British
Government gave them in Ireland prior to
the law being handed over to the present
Government. I certainly do object to
armed policemen coming into my farm
and telling me what I am to do and what
I am not to do.

happen regarding the other case. As I
read the Bill it gives the magistrate full
discretion to fine from as low an amount

does prevent a magistrate from being

to make the fine £20, or £25, or £30,

even of a second offence-when he might

2721 Game Preservation Bill

25 OCTOBER 1928
Adjournment.
Amendment agreed to.
NEW CLAUSE (Close season for
woodcock and snipe.)
No person shall, on any pretence
whatsoever, kill or destroy any woodcock or snipe, between the fifteenth
day of February and the twelfth day
of August in any year, or wilfully
destroy the eggs or nest of any woodcock; and any person offending against
this section shall be liable to the same
penalty as is imposed by an Act passed
by the Irish Parliament in the session
held in the twenty-seventh year of the
reign of His Majesty King George the
Third, chapter thirty-five, intituled,
An Act for the Preservation of the
Game, upon persons offending against
that Act. The provisions of the Wild
Birds Protection Acts, 1880 to 1908,
shall cease to apply with respect to
woodcock and snipe or the eggs of
woodcock and snipe.
Brought up, and read a First time.
Major SHILLINGTON: I beg to
move, "That the Clause be now read a
Second time." As this matter stands at
present the close season varies in different
counties in Northern Ireland. The present close season begins on the 1st March
and it ends on the 1st September in
some counties, and on the 1st October in
others. It is proposed in this New Clause
that the close season for woodcock and
snipe shall begin on the 15th February
and end on the 12th August. I think
hon. Members will realize that it will be
an advantage to have uniformity in regard to the close season. I do not know
whether any changes will be necessary
owing to the Amendments already accepted in connection with snipe, but I
hope that the Government will agree to
accept this Clause, and, if it has to be
modified, to make the necessary alterations between now and the Report Stage.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government are prepared to accept this New
Clause. It may need some modification,
but we accept the principle of it, and we
can make any change that may be necessary on the Report Stage.

Clause read a Second time, and added
to the Bill.

That state of affairs does not justify this

are difficulties in the way, but the difficulties could be quite simply surmounted.
Given goodwill on the part of the Minister

I listened to what has been said to-day
both at Question time and now, and the
whole question resolves itself into this
that just so soon as the Irish Free State
fall into line, not alone with Northern Ireland but with Great Britain's system in
connection with benefits and in connection
with contributions, just so soon will my
right hon Friend be able to enter into a
system of reciprocity with them and not
till then. And as matters stand to-day I
understand from him that he could not
have dealt with that case in any other
way under the law as it stands to-day.
Therefore the charges made against him
of having departed in any way from
what is the proper practice are unsupported. The same practice would have
been carried out if this case had occurred
on the other side of the Channel. We
are under an obligation to carry out these
statutes in the same way in which they
are carried out in Britain. That is the
policy of the Government here to-day and
the policy my right hon. Friend will
carry out.
Mr. KYLE: On a point of Order.
The noble Lord states that it is his policy

out where in Great Britain there is a

the Minister of Labour, in these Acts of

CONDITION OF THE SHORE ROAD.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his attention has been drawn to
the dangerous and unsanitary condition of
the Shore Road, outside the city
boundary and, if so, whether he is prepared to take action to remedy these evils.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No complaints
have reached the Ministry with regard to
the condition of the Shore Road outside
the City Boundary. I have, however,
made inquiries, and find that there has
been some temporary flooding due to the
bursting of a culvert under the road, and
that some sewers have been obstructed by
the debris carried into them by the overflow.
I understand that the culvert has been
repaired by the County Council, and that
the Sanitary Authority concerned is
having the sewers cleaned out. This
action on the part of the local authorities
should remedy any nuisance that may have
been temporarily caused.
FORTNIGHTLY PAY FOR R.U.C.
5. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he will consider the advisability
of paying the members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary fortnightly instead
of, as at present, monthly, and thus
remedying a grievance which exists among
a large number of men in the Force who
are married and have families.
Sir DAWSON BATES: An alteration
such as that suggested by the hon. Member would cause a very heavy increase in
the work involved in the payment of
salaries, etc., and corresponding additional expenses. I do not think that we
would be justified in adopting the proposal
unless there were very substantial grounds
in favour of it, or unless the existing
system constituted a substantial grievance
to the members of the Police Force.
The system is similar to that adopted in
the Royal Irish Constabulary, and I have
no reason to believe that there is any real
grievance among the members of the
Force.

PAY DAY.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked

aware that the pay-day for a large
number of recipients of Unemployed Insurance benefit has been changed from
Friday to Tuesday; whether this means

in view of the hardship caused, he will

Fridays, or failing this, to have payment
made up to Saturday where payment is
made on a Tuesday.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers
30 OCTOBER 1928
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In order to avoid congestion,
it was found necessary to distribute the
payment of unemployment insurance
benefit over three days in the week-
Tuesday, Thursday and Friday—instead
of the normal arrangement to pay on
Friday for the week ending on Wednesday.
As the claimant receives his benefit in
weekly periods, any hardship which may
be involved by the temporary re-arrangement of the pay days only occurs in connection with the first payment.
I regret that at present it would not
be practicable to pay all benefit on
Fridays nor to arrange for the Tuesday
payments to be made up to Saturday as
suggested, but I can assure the hon. Member that I am anxious to revert to the
normal arrangement as soon as, through
a fall in unemployment, it can be done.
without causing congestion.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I propose to
reply to this question.
On the 31st March, 1926, there was a
cash balance of £525,000 to the credit of
the Road Fund which was temporarily invested, but it must be borne in mind that
this sum includes the collection for the
first quarter of the calendar year, which
is, of course, the most fruitful collection
period. The amount collected during the
quarter did not come to credit of the
fund until the last day of the quarter,
and out of this balance the grants, during
the next financial year, had to be to a
large extent financed.
It must also be remembered that, as
against the balance to credit of the fund
at the end of any year there are considerable liabilities in respect of grants which
cannot be ascertained until the expenditure of the Local Authorities has been
made up after the close of the year.

£40.000
The principal argument in favour of an
increase was the fact that if our pre-transfer conditions had obtained the University
would automatically have been a very considerable beneficiary under a provision
that was made by the Imperial Parliament for additional grants to universities
in Great Britain. It is a fact that so far
as State grants are concerned we do not
occupy a creditable position in regard to
Our University. English universities
such as Birmingham, Manchester, Bristol,
Aberystwith and others have not only very
considerable State grants-on about the
same basis that we give to our own University-but these grants are supplemented by very large subsidies from the
local municipal authorities in the different
localities I have mentioned. Here in Northern Ireland we have not risen to anything like that standard, I am sorry to say.
I do not know whether it is our insular
position or whether it is that the local
authorities have not realised the advantages of higher education, but whatever
the cause may be it is a mere pittance
that is offered by the local authorities to
our University with the result that it is
not unnatural that they should endeavour to fall back on the State for sufficient
support to carry on their requirements.
The object of this additional sum is largely
to provide for residential arrangements
-the calls of residence in regard to the
university. That is so far as the first
feature of this is concerned.
The second is the transfer-I can use no
other word; a grant does not exactly describe it of a sum of £36,000 to the University for the purpose of providing a
building for agricultural research. This
money is provided by the Imperial

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of
this Bill is to extend the time for the
operation of Section 1 of the Housing
Act of 1927, and if this House passes the
measure, it will mean that subsidies will
be continued in respect of the houses coming within the Act up to 31st March, 1930.
In dealing with this matter, I think it
might be of interest to this House to state
briefly the various Acts that have been
passed dealing with the Housing problem,
particularly those relating to the question
of "subsidy," and I think hon. Members,
when they look at the results which
followed the passing of these various
measures, will realise that the policy
which this Government has adopted regarding the principle of subsidy is one
which has been fully justified by the
results.
The first attempt which appears to have
been made by the British Government to
deal with the acute shortage of houses in
Ireland following the War was the Act of
1919, under which power was given to
urban authorities to erect houses, the
Government providing £1 5s Od in respect
of every £1 of rent collected by the
authority. The Act lapsed in 1922, and
the figures I have, go to show that during
the 3 years in which the Act was in operation, only 502 houses were provided. Of
these, 459 were built in Belfast, most of
them being entirely unsuitable to the resources of the working man.
I might remind the House that the
Government, some years ago, commuted
the huge liability that they were under in
respect of the Belfast houses by a lump
sum payment of no less than £220,000.
A later Act was passed in 1919, and
this Act, for the first time, introduced
the principle of paying a subsidy to a
private builder, but the great defect of
this Act was was that it provided for a
maximum of 1,400 superficial feet, and
builders concentrated on this type, and
I think that hon. Members opposite will
agree that a house of that description
could not possibly come within the resources of the working man. This Act
was also a failure, as I find that only
533 houses were built under it within
a period of 3 years.
Now I come to the first of the subsidy
Acts passed by the Parliament of Northern Ireland, that is, the Act of 1923.
The Act, the scope of which was limited
to urban areas, provided that a subsidy
should be given of £60 for each house
built in urban areas, whether by the
urban authorities or by private owners,
Housing Bill—
Second Reading
30 OCTOBER 1928
The
and limited the house to an area of between 600 and 950 superficial feet.
Act also allowed the urban authorities to
supplement the grants by grants not exceeding £40, or if they preferred they
could give loans of £100 free of interest
for 25 years. That Act operated up to
1st April, 1925. As a result of the working of this Act, I find that at the date
when it lapsed, no fewer than 2,530
houses had been approved, and 850
actually built.
The next Act was the Act of 1925 which
extended the scope of the Act to rural
districts. The old Act had applied only
to urban districts. It also increased the
Government subsidy to £80 where a house
was completed within six months, and it
further provided that local authorities
could, if they so desired, exempt houses
from rates for a period of 10 years. There
is no doubt that this Act appears to have
still further encouraged the building of
houses because during the financial year
1926, 3,119 houses were approved of which
no fewer than 2,262 houses were comipleted.
Then we come to the last Act, the Act
passed in 1927. This Act, as hon. Members are aware, reduced the size of the
house to a maximum of 650 superficial
feet. Hon. Members are aware of the
reasons which actuated the Government
in taking this course, reasons which are
fully justified as the following figures will
show.
I find that for the year ended 31st
March, 1928, no fewer than 3,599 houses
were approved of, of which 2,092 were
completed, while, for the last seven
months, I find there is a still furthur increase in the number approved-the number being 3,692, as compared with 3,599
for twelve months.
Mr. BEATTIE: How many houses
were finished?
Sir DAWSON BATES: For the seven
months the number finished was 1185.
With regard to the necessity for more
houses, and for the continuance of the assistance which is at present being given,
I do not think it is necessary for me to
labour the point to this House at length.
This House has recently approved of a
Bill which has for its object the retention
of the Rent Restriction Acts for a furthur
period on the smaller types of houses. The
justification for that step was that the
supply of houses available and suitable
had not overtaken the demand. The only
way to meet the acute shortage which still
exists is to facilitate building operations,
especially by private builders. I do not
attempt to disguise from the House that
these housing subsidies constitute a heavy
financial burden on the State, but, after
all, this question goes to the root of the
health, well-being and prosperity of the
community.
It
I am glad to think that the local
authorities are fully alive to the necessity
of having houses erected in districts, and
I am glad to think that no less than 20
urban districts and 16 rural districts are
supplementing the facilities afforded by
the Government to provide houses.
may be said that the Government are providing large profits for builders, but I
would point out that the subsidy is payable to any person or groups of persons
who build a house or houses which comply

would further suggest if there are these
huge profits to be made by these builders.
that perhaps philanthropic individuals or

could do a great deal towards improving

I believe
that, if they did this, they would have a

if he inserted a Clause in this Bill that

should be used.
There are some great firms in the City

window sashes to compete with foreign
firms. Foreign countries are exploiting their workers, but we in this part
of the Empire are most anxious to see
our workers getting a fair living wage.
At the present time some of them are receiving no wages at all. The Minister
of Labour's pigeon holes are flooded with

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Ex-Service Men (Government Posts).
Colonel WOODS: I beg to move:
"That in the opinion of this House the
offer of the Government, announced by
the Minister of Finance on Tuesday,
23rd instant, to allot 75 permanent established posts to be filled by ex-Service
temporary clerks at present employed
in various Government departments in
Northern Ireland is not considered a
sufficiently generous recognition of the
claims of the ex-Service men concerned;
and further, that this House is of the
opinion that, apart from any wastage
in the established service which may
in
due course be filled from the ranks of
the remaining ex-Service temporaries,
after the 75 posts referred to have been
filled, a permanent non-pensionable
class-equivalent to that which exists
under the Guinness agreement in the
Imperial Service-should be formed
from those ex-Service men still remaining in the temporary service."
The
I am sure the House will forgive me if
I have to refer more than occasionally to
my notes as they deal with the past history of this question. It is with very
mixed feelings that I rise to propose, and
ask the House to accept, the Motion which
appears upon the Order Paper.
very genuine pleasure which I derive at all
times from any little service which I might
be able to render to ex-Service men
tinged on this occasion with no small

could and should have been settled by the

settled long ago.
is
The question of the resettlement of
these ex-Service men in the Civil Service
is not a new one, it is not a problem that
has only arisen within the past few
months. It has been with us since
the inception of our Civil Service
and as time elapses it becomes more
acute. The whole question should have
been faced by the Northern Government
in 1925, when the British Government
faced it and made a great and honest
effort to dispose of it by giving over 16,000
ex-Service temporary clerks security of
tenure in the Imperial Civil Service. In
view of all the oft-repeated declarations
that our Northern Government intended
so far as possible to keep step by step with
Great Britain it is hard to understand
why the Minister of Finance and the
Government allowed Northern Ireland to
get out of step in dealing with this question in 1925, and has allowed Northern
Ireland to remain stupidly out of step
ever since. Our Civil Service may be only
a recruit when compared to many of the
other Services throughout the worldespecially the British Service-but since
we are content, and I think rightly so, to
march to the Imperial tune, surely in this
matter now before the House we have been
marching out of step too long. I am inclined to think, and not without some
cause, that the fault rests to no small extent with some of the officers of our
Service who have been, and still are, deliberately content with the present state
of affairs and who consider themselves
superior to following the British example.
In this respect I can only say that since
we were so proud to ask these 250 ex-
Service men-whose fate is merged in the
Motion before the House-to go step by
step with Great Britain and the British
Empire from 1914 to 1918 when it was a
question of sacrifice and suffering in order
to achieve the security of the Empire, and
this part of the Empire, we should not be
so base or ungrateful as to stand apart
now from the splendid precedent of Great
Britain in giving these men- -themselves
and their dependants some measure of
security that is easily within our power to
offer.
I do not accuse the Government of a
want of sympathy with the ambitions of
the ex-Service men affected by this Motion
but, at the same time, I cannot agree that
there has been any feverish anxiety shown
to come to grips with the problem, and, of
course, the true test as to the Government's attitude towards the ex-Service
men for whom I plead to-day will be found
in the way in which the members of the
Government respond to the Motion before
the House to-day. Let us examine the
position. There are at the present
moment about 250, or perhaps 270, temporary ex-Service Civil Servants employed
by the Government of Northern Ireland.
They are, for the greater part, men who
served in His Majesty's fighting forces
during the great war and very many
them are seriously disabled-physically

disabled, I mean- -as a result of their war
service. They are, indeed, all disabled,

the fact that the last fourteen years, the
most vital part of their lives have been
given in war and peace, in the case of very
many of them, to the service of the State.
Many of these temporary Civil servants
were only boys when war broke out, some
of them, indeed, under the normal recruiting age. Yet they went into the
ranks of the army or joined up in the
navy and did not hesitate for a single
instant to reckon the cost.
The cost has been a heavy one. They
returned from the war and entered the
temporary service of the State-in some
Imperial Government Department probably or within a year or two after the
Armistice found temporary employment
under the Northern Government. When
our own administration was formed,
and for
some time afterwards, a
good number of Imperial Civil Service
temporaries cast in their lot with the
Northern Government, hoping that under
a home administration they would have a
greater opportunity for security. Many
of these men are still serving in a temporary capacity.
In the short time at my disposal since
the Motion before the House was tabled
I have been able to obtain-without a
great deal of assistance from responsible
Government Departments some statistics
which perhaps will serve a more useful
purpose than any speech that might be
made in favour of the Motion to-day.
I have been furnished with the figures relating to the Headquarter Offices of the
Ministry which employs the majority of
these temporary ex-Servicemen, I refer to
the Ministry of Labour, and I have also
obtained particulars regarding three other
Departments in the City in which a small
number of the temporaries are employed.
In the Ministry of Labour (Ormeau
Avenue and Corporation Street), the
Ministry of Agriculture the Ministry of
Finance, the Ministry of Commerce, and
the Ministry of Home Affairs and engaged
on work relating to the Law Courts and
the Land Commission, there are at least
171 ex-service temporaries employed
locally-that is in the Belfast offices of
these different Ministries or Departments.
Of these 171
125 men have over 2 years' service,
119 have over three years' service,
101 have over 4 years' service,
86 have over 5 years' service, and so on.
There are about 60 men, I believe, employed in the Ministry of Labour outoffices such as Newry, Portadown, Ballycastle and the other outlying towns.
These 60 men are for the most part men
who helped to open those offices after the
war and have been employed in the same
district ever since. Their length of service should compare very favourably with
any other offices or Department of Government administration and it is not unreasonable to assume that these men can
boast of a longer period of government
service temporary of course than the
bulk of their colleagues in the Belfast
Offices of the Ministry of Labour. I tried
to obtain the exact figures as to the length
of service of the men in the out-offices of
this Ministry, but in the short time in my
disposal, have not yet succeeded.
Taking the Belfast figures as a basis,
however, we arrive at what after all must
be a fairly accurate conclusion. Twothirds of the Belfast temporaries-119—
have over three years' service, and we
can assume that a similar proportion of
the country office temporaries have at
least the same period of service—that is,
40 of the men. The House can safely
conclude, therefore that there are at least
180 temporary ex-Service civil servants
-probably nearer 200-with over three
years' service. If the Minister is prepared to refute these figures I hope he
will give us the official statistics, but my
inquiries convince me that the information
I have given is fairly accurate. In face
of these facts and figures I think the
House will agree that it is high time we
turned our promises to practical account
so far as these men are concerned, and I
say emphatically that the Government's
offer of 75 posts does not meet the position
at all and cannot in any sense of the word
be regarded as a solution of the problem.

the demand put forward was that a "P"
class should be formed in the Northern

which has existed in the Imperial Civil
Service since 1925. That demand was made
the subject of a communication addressed

ex-
Had the men concerned-the
Service temporary clerks-asked for 75
established posts at the outset, the
gentlemen who guide the official activities
of the Department over which the Minister
of Finance so ably presides would undoubtedly have convinced the Minister
that such a demand was impossible and
would probably have replied to it in the
spirit of their letter of the 18th Sept.,
which I have already quoted. But now
that we know the actual position, that 75
permanent established places can be
found-or made if you like-for the ex-
Service temporaries, we are better able
to face it.
Since the inception of the Northern
Civil Service open examinations for boys
and girls have been held each year, but
not until 1927 was there a limited competition for the ex-Service temporaries.
The boys and girls have had a pretty fair
monopoly up to now, and the 75 places
now offered to the ex-Servicemen should
belong by right to those men and should
not be regarded as something in the
nature of a big concession on the part of
the Government. The 75 posts are accepted in part-settlement, but there must be
something more. There must be a permanent non-pensionable class formed
from those men who do not get selected
for permanent pensionable appointment.
In other words a "P" class should also be
formed in Northern Ireland.
The Minister will probably argue that
75 permanent posts is the extreme limit
to which the Government could go without undue risks to the continuity of the
service. Assuming that such is the case,
it is not an answer to the request for a
"P" class. The formation of such a
class does not imply that the work upon
which the men of the class would be engaged should be permanent work. Here
is how Colonel Guiuness, the late Financial
Secretary to the British Treasury, who
was responsible for the introduction of
this class in Great Britain, explained this
aspect:-

.
The men appointed to the "P"
class are to be given permanency not
in permanent posts, but in a permanency of occupation on a succession
of temporary jobs.
The number of these temporary jobs may
diminish-I know that is one of the
official side's arguments-but, on the
other hand, it is an entirely one-sided
view. The British Government at the
moment are trying to anticipate the
additions to staff that may be necessary
as a result of fresh legislation and new
social services in the future, and they are
doing this as part of their great attempt
to give permanency of employment to their
remaining ex-Service temporaries.
Let
our own Minister of Finance remember
that, while trade and employment may
improve, with a consequent reduction of
the staffs in the Ministry of Labour,
fresh legislation such as the de-rating
scheme, the Marketing of Potatoes Bill,
the Representation of the People Bill,
and other electoral measures may very
well call for additional or transferred temporary or semi-permanent
staffs. There is no question of creating
more permanent posts than the service
can reasonably be expected to bear. It
can reasonably be expected to bear 75
established posts, so you have offered
that number, but it must also be remembered that the great majority of
your two hundred and fifty ex-Servicemen have been engaged for years now in
a succession of temporary jobs in the
Civil Service, and I submit that the time
has come to give these men permanency
of occupation in their work in the same
way as their colleagues in Great Britain
have been given permanency.
There is,
in my opinion, no genuine reason for turning down such a demand. The men
have an unanswerable case.

to the Civil Service Representative Council of Northern Ireland, which, after all,
is only the equivalent or the nearest equivalent we have in Northern Ireland to the
National Whitley Council? The British
Treasury did not go to the Whitley Council for the very simple reason that the
ex-Servicemen affected were not represented as ex-Servicemen on that Council.
The British Government conducted
direct negotiations with the Association
that represented the interests of the men
-the same association as represents the
men in Northern Ireland to-day-an
Association which, by the very experience
it gained in dealing with this problem in

should have been invited to confer with
our own Government on the question. I
refer to the Association of ex-Service
Civil Servants. In defending this method
of direct negotiation the then Financial
Secretary to the British Treasury said, in

This was the only organisation to
whom I could go. It was no good
going to the National Whitley Council,

Service Civil Servants, as such.
The National Whitley Council is
organised on a basis of grades and it
does not recognise such interests as the
ex-Service Civil Servants. We are told
that what we have done is against the
principles of Whitleyism. The system
of collective negotiation in the Civil

Service does not prevent-and never

Let us compare this result with the results achieved by the British Government
in 1925. The Northern Government now
offers pensionable posts to three-tenths of

250-and goes no further. The British

and gave permanent established posts to
almost two-fifths of the temporaries-or

Two of these examinations took place in

Well, the British Government have

Open recruitment to the British Civil
Service has I am informed reliably been
indefinitely suspended. A Treasury
order has been issued that no further

Secretary to the Treasury is at present

in the permanent service.
I think the House will agree that this
is an example which should inspire our
own Government to greater things than
the mere offer of 75 posts which was made
on Tuesday last, and I think the sooner
our Minister of Finance takes the situation into his own hands- -as the Financial Secretary to the British Treasury
did in 1925-instead of being led by the
Departmental chiefs in a matter which,

he House.
It may be contended, of course, that
our Financial arrangements with the
British Government would not permit a
"P" class to be set up in Northern Ireland, that the Colwyn Report imposes a
restriction. Personally, I cannot see
the force of such an argument, because
the creation of a "P" class does not in-

volve any financial change whatever.
The pay of this class would be the same

I am authorised to say that the Association of ex-Service Civil Servants representing the ex-Service Civil Servants in both
the British and Northern Ireland
Services, is prepared at any time, should

One strange argument I have heard advanced from time to time is that the ex-
Servicemen in Great Britain were conscripts-men who had to serve and for
that reason there is bound to be a greater
proportion of ex-Servicemen in the
British Civil Service than in our own.
This is a line of argument I have no desire to follow, but this much I will say:
That it is all the more reason why the ex-
Servicemen in our Northern Civil Service,
who were all volunteers, should get equal
or perhaps more generous treatment than
those in the British Civil Service. I hope
the House appreciates the importance of
that point. In the war-days we used to
hear it said-and Members of this House
who used to appear on recruiting platforms will remember the saying-" One
volunteer is worth ten conscripts." Well,
when it comes to a question of measuring
the relative value of service afterwards
we should not forget that principle.
One more point in passing. I have
heard it hinted that the Association of
Ex-Service Civil Servants does not represent the men affected. That in itself
would be no argument against the
principle of recognition that is bound up
with the men's claim. But in order that
there may be no doubt about the matter,
I want promptly and emphatically to repudiate such a suggestion. I have been
in contact with a good many ex-Service
movements, but I can conscientiously state
that I have not yet been identified with
one in which the men were so earnestly
and enthusiastically united. I have here
the register of the North Ireland Branch
of
of the Association of Ex-Service Civil

own Registrar
Friendly Societies-by whom a certificate

Should there still be any doubt on this

But that is not all. Here is a petition
-in course of preparation and which I
hope it will not be necessary ultimately

Surely that should dispose of any doubts
as to the question of representative
capacity or the wishes of the men concerned. In conclusion I would appeal to
the Minister of Finance, to the Government and to the House to accept the
Motion now submitted. The 75 posts
make no happy appeal to the great body
of temporary Civil Servants. They still
retain that spirit of loyalty and brotherhood towards one another that found its
birth in the hectic days of war, and they
all recognise that while 75 might attain
security they also realise that the other
175 or 195-the big majority-would be

and formed a "P" class from the remaining temporaries.
The issue is clear. It is not-and cannot be made a party one. I have shown
that it is not a good economic proposition
to cast these men-who for the most part
are married and with families-into the
ranks of the unemployed. They and
their dependants suffered enough anxiety
and sacrifices during the terrible war
years without adding to that anxiety
and extracting more sacrifices now.

Government is in a position-no matter
what technical objections may be quoted

gave and suffered without murmur or

for the good name of our young State,

If the Government is not prepared to

I can guess what the feelings of the

In addition and this is a most important factor in the matter-we have made

going to place men in that position. It is

That is the position I take up in regard to
the "P" class. They would be looked
down upon as a Brahmin looks down upon

HOUSE OF COMMONS
2815 Ex-Servicemen in Civil Service
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 31st October, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
EX-SERVICE MEN IN THE CIVIL
SERVICE.
Major SHILLINGTON (by Private
Notice) asked the Prime Minister whether
in view of yesterday's proceedings he is in
a position to make any statement regarding the Government's intentions.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I have been in consultation
with my right hon. friend the Minister
of Finance and am convinced that the
Cabinet's proposals regarding the staffing
of the Civil Service as outlined by him
yesterday afternoon secured more advantageous terms to ex-Servicemen as a class,
than would be the case were the British
Govenment method to be adopted, and
further, that the introduction of a new
class of any description between permanent and temporary clerks would not be
conducive to the smooth working of our
Civil Service as a whole.
As, however, a difference of opinion appears to exist regarding the figures upon
which this conclusion is arrived at he is
having a memorandum prepared setting
forth the actual circumstances in full detail, which will be embodied in a White
Paper and circulated to hon. Members,
and if as the result of this meticulous reexamination any new salient facts should
be revealed he will be pleased sympathetically to consider the possibility of absorbing a larger number of ex-Service men
into the permanent ranks of the pensionable Civil Service.
I think it right to sound a note of
warning that false hopes should not be
raised by this statement, but the House
ay be assured that every member of the
Government is as fully alive to their in-
Representation of People Bill 2816
debtedness and obligations to the ex-Service men of Ulster as are those who yesterday had an opportunity of voicing their
views in the matter.

Major SHILLINGTON: I thank the
noble Lord for that statement.
Mr. BEATTIE. I would like to ask
the Prime Minister if he is prepared to
take all the ex-Service men out of the
workhouses in Northern Ireland and make
some provision for maintaining them outside those dark and dismal holes.
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise
out of the reply.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Representation of the People Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question Proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'
The MINISTER OF HOME AF.
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): Hon Members will appreciate that this Bill only
deals with the franchise of our local Parliament, and the franchise for local
government elections in Northern Ireland. The main object of it is to confer
upon the women of Northern Ireland the
same rights which have been excerised
hitherto by men; in other words, to assimilate the franchise for men and women.
Hon. Members are aware that recently a
similar Act was passed by the Imperial Parliament dealing with the elections to that
Parliament, but of course hon. Members
will appreciate that the Imperial Act did
not in any way deal with elections either
to our own Parliament or for local authorities.
As this is a somewhat complicated
matter I hope hon. Members will not
think I am dealing with the question at
too great length, but it is desirable that
I should deal in some detail with
the qualifications for men and women for
our own parliamentary and local government elections. May I explain what are
the qualifications for men in regard to
our own Parliament, that is, the qualifi
2817 Representation of People Bill- 31 OCTOBER 1928
Second Reading

Mr. SPEAKER: The Minister must,
of course, be allowed to explain the Bill.
Mr. BEATTIE: That is all I asked
for. I asked for an explanation as to
why three years is in the Bill.
cations that exist to-day? First of all,
the individual must be twenty-one years
of age and not subject to any disability
such as being a lunatic, an alien, or, say,
a Peer of the Realm. He must also have
what is known as a residence qualification;
or, if he has not that, he must qualify as
regards a business qualification. I should
explain that a "residence" qualification
means that the individual must be ordinarily resident in Northern Ireland for a
period of six months before the qualifying
date; while a "business premises" qualification implies that the individual must
be in occupation for a similar period of

Coming now to the existing qualifications for women for our local Parliamentary franchise, those which exist at present
are as follow:-A woman must be 30
years of age and upwards and not subject to the legal disability I have referred
to, and she must be the occupier or the
tenant of a dwelling-house for a period of
six months before the qualifying date; or
she must be 30 years of age and be the
occupier, as owner or tenant, of the lands
or premises other than a dwelling-house
of a valuation of at least £5, for a period
of six months before the qualifying date.

the local government register, and with
whom she resides. Those are the three
qualifications that exist at the present
time to enable a woman to vote for our
own local Parliament.
The new conditions which will be imposed on women will be of a much simpler
kind, because we propose that they will
be precisely those I have already indicated
as regards the men. In addition, a woman
will be entitled by virtue of being married
to have a vote in respect of her husband's
business premises qualification. In other
words, we give a man a vote by virtue of
his wife's qualification, and we give a wife
a vote by reason of the husband's qualification.

Oral Answers to Questions.
PAYMENT OF UNEMPLOYMENT
INSURANCE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that in a
decision of the umpire regarding_unemployment insurance to workers in Messrs.
William Ewart & Son, Crumlin Road,
who made a claim to benefit inside ten
weeks from their previous claim, that he
has decided against them, and in so doing
has broken the law, which states that if a
worker claims inside ten weeks from a
previous claim that worker is entitled to
a repeat claim without a waiting period;
and what action he proposes to take to
see that these workers get their just claim.
:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) The umpire is appointed by
His Grace the Governor and is not in any
way subject to my control in interpreting
the law relating to unemployment insurance.
It would obviously be improper
for me to presume either to criticize or
defend his judgment.
I would point out, however, that, in
putting this question, the hon. Member
appears to be under a misapprehension.
While it is true that unemployed workers
who have drawn benefit may receive
further benefit within ten weeks without
a fresh waiting period, it is necessary for
them to establish that they satisfy the
statutory conditions. It was the nonfulfilment of one of these conditions which
led to the disallowance of the claims referred to in the question.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman tell the House what that other
disallowance was ?
Mr. ANDREWS: G.S.W.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that
these workpeople were only out from 24th
September to the 1st October, when they
resumed work, and were employed by
Messrs. William Ewart & Son, could the
right hon. Gentleman state how he can
tell the House that these people were disallowed benefit on the ground of not
genuinely seeking work?
Mr. ANDREWS: I did not tell the
House that these people were rightly or
wrongly disallowed this payment. What
I did tell the House was that the duty
rested upon the umpire, who is quite
independent.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the unsatisfactory reply of the right hon. Gentleman
I will take the opportunity of raising this
question on the Adjournment.
INSTRUCTIONS TO LABOUR
EXCHANGE MANAGERS.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Labour whether he has seen a report of a
meeting held in Charlemont, County
Armagh, at which Organiser Getgood, of
the Workers' Union, is stated to have
said he was convinced that secret instructions were being issued to labour exchange
managers in Northern Ireland, with a
view to depriving claimants of the unemployment insurance benefit to which they
were legally entitled, and whether there
is any foundation for this statement.
Oral Answers
Housing Bill
1 NOVEMBER 1928
Mr. ANDREWS: My attention has
been drawn to the statement. There is
not the slightest foundation for the suggestion and I am surprised that a responsible officer of a trade union, if he is correctly reported, should spread such an
inaccurate report.
Mr. KYLE: Is it not a fact that all
instructions sent to the managers of exchanges are marked "Private and confidential"? And is it not a fact that the
Ministry from time to time bring the
managers of the various exchanges in different parts of the country to headquarters and place before them the disallowances imposed by the various branch
officers?
Mr. ANDREWS: That really is not
involved in the question. What I was
asked was if I had circulated instructions
with the object of illegally depriving persons of benefit.

Mr. BEATTIE: On the last day when

Home Secretary said that the welfare of
