a healthy community, one that will be
able to stand the test when the testing
time comes, and that will be classified as
Al instead of C3.
The subsidy is being granted for houses
of from 550 superficial feet to 650 superficial feet. I am not going to say that
perhaps in certain circumstances that
superficial area would not be quite sufficient, but on the law of the average numbers in the families of the industrial
classes, which I give as five, I do not
think it could be contended by the
Government that the accommodation and
breathing space required for a family of
five people could be got in a house of
650 superficial feet. I have heard it said
that
anyone who wants to make a good investment should invest in the building of
subsidy houses of 650 superficial feet. To
my own knowledge that investment, I regret to say, has been carried out, and it
is stated that it has been a profit-making
business for some individuals recently.
I am in favour of the subsidy being continued. I am in favour, and I think the
Government are also inclined to favour, of
the subsidy being made the means of pro-

viding houses that will meet the needs
and requirements of the people and which
also will provide an economic rent. Rent
is a matter that should be given serious
consideration by the Government. There
is no mention of it in the Bill. Now, I
understand that a house of 650 superficial feet can be built at approximately
£265. That gives a large room below and
two bedrooms and a small box room
above. It is impossible to put a bed in
the small room in one of these houses of
650 superficial feet. I am sure the Minister has followed the correspondence on
the subject in the Press, and has read
a letter from "Preplexed" setting out the

in the rooms of
houses of the superficial area I am speaking about.
a
We are all inclined to say that laboursaving appliances should be put into the
home, that the housewife should be protected from the laborious work she had
to do in the past, and that more up-todate hygienic conditions should be introduced so that dust cannot collect and
rooms can be kept perfectly pure during
the day and night. That is really an
utter impossibility in the case of
house of 650 superficial feet. Dust
will gather on any little furnishings
in the room, and it is impossible
for the housewife to remove pieces of
furniture in the room without injuring
herself. I had all this in mind before
this gentleman I refer to wrote in the
Press. When you get a bed of 6ft. by
4ft. in a room of 8ft. by 6ft. it reminds
me of the statement made by a Labour
Member in the British House of Commons
that in the mornings his wife had to stand
on the landing until he put on his
trousers. The same condition of affairs
applies to the house of 650 superficial
feet. You are not allocating for sleeping
accommodation the space that is necessary
to meet the needs and requirements of the
medical authorities. My opinion as an
ordinary layman is that a room of 8ft. by
6ft. is not sufficient for two persons.
Then you have what you call mixed
families. The working classes, where
mixed families exist, have great difficulty
owing to their economic position in providing homes owing to the amount of
rent that is asked for three-roomed, fourroomed or five-roomed houses. I think
the Minister himself could very well have
added another 100 feet to the superficial
area set out. It would just meet the
same requirements that he is endeavouring to fulfil at the moment. It may be
contended that this would increase the
cost. I know it will increase the number
of bricks and quantity of mortar, which
will cost money.
The actual cost would
be increased from £50 to £100, but remember that we are giving the subsidy
in order to get houses built and let at
an economic rent. What should be done
is that the amount of the subsidy should
be taken away from the total cost of the
house, and the rent fixed on the amount
that is left. In other words, if a house
costs £400 the rent would be based on
£260. The rent on a £260 house would
work out at pre-war rates. I want to
say-and I did not make it clear to the
House before-that the relation of rent
to wages should be only one-eighth.
In pre-war days my people lived in a
house which was rented at 5/- a week.
We had two bedrooms front and back,
two attics and a return. To-day you
could not get that house at a less rent
than £1 a week. I say that subsidy
houses can be built to-day with equal
accommodation for a little more money
on the total cost and they can also be let
at a more economic rent than the present
houses with a 650 superficial feet area,
because the builders to-day-and I say
this fearlessly are taking the £140 as a
clear profit. A case came under my
notice not long ago where the valuer refused to take into his calculations the
£140 subsidy on the value of the house,
and he deducted that amount. The
Corporation was asked for a loan on the
total value of the house, but the valuer
refused to take into his calculations the
subsidy and he valued the house at £140
less than the contractor was willing to
accept for that house.
That proves conclusively the builders are taking into
account the £140 as profit over and
above the actual value of the house.
The Minister, I think, could strike a
rent on the net price of the house, that is
£260. That house should be let at anything from 7/6 to 8/- per week. That
house with 100 superficial more feet
would give a certain amount of comfort
and provide good, healthy conditions for
the inhabitants.

buys a pair of boots, puts them on and

they could not find a house anywhere, a
self-respecting man who is anxious to have
a clean home for his wife and family, do
you think he will complain if he is removed from a two-roomed dwelling,
crowded out, with others all round, without any amenities, to a place like that?
Do you think he will complain if the new
boot is too tight on his foot? I think he
will be grateful for the efforts that have
been made on his behalf.
Take another type of house, with a
parlour-kitchen and three bedrooms and
a large scullery which is really a kitchen.
The parlour kitchen is 12ft. 2 in. by 11ft.
1 in., and the best bedroom is 14ft. by
12ft. 2 in. Then we have a further type
with a kitchen-scullery, a large kitchen
or living room 11ft, by 11ft., with two
large bedrooms, and a smaller room which
could also in emergency be used as a bedroom.
The very best that skill and ingenuity
can do to secure the best results from the
Housing Bill
Game Preservation Bi

money and resources available has been 1
done, and the interest that has been
manifested in this matter on all sides of
the House will only encourage my right
hon. Friend and his colleagues in the
Cabinet, and those of us who have the
honour and privilege of serving in any
capacity in connection with the matter,
to do the best we can, both now and in
the future, to try to get rid of the difficulties that exist by reason of the overcrowding that is taking place.
Let me say this to the House before I
sit down. If you attempt to impose conditions on the builders of these houses
they immediately retire and they cease to
build. We have found, as a result of our
experience in dealing with all these other
Acts, that it is far better in the meantime to allow the work to go on expeditiously and quickly and so have houses,
than to impose conditions, even though
they were well and kindly meant, that
would have the effect of retarding the
building of those houses.
The statement has been made during
the course of the debate that we are doing
nothing in connection with the slums. Ĭ
do not propose to say more than this in
regard to that matter. There is no Member of the Government who does not share
the very keenest desire that has been expressed by any Member, no matter where
he sits, to try to do something to get rid
of our slums, but would it not be a cruel
thing to attempt at this time to do anything of a very practical nature? I will
point out why. The first thing you would
have to do would be to turn the people
out of the slums at a time when there are
no other homes for them. That would be
cruel; it would be impossible to do that
at this time. We can all live in hope
that when houses have been provided, and
when we come back to more or less normal
times and the more houses are put up
the sooner we will get back-it will be
possible to deal with this other matter in
such a way as appears proper and wise to
the government of the day.
In answer to the hon. Member for
Antrim, who spoke last (Mr. George
Henderson), I have to say that I am inclined to agree with him that the
Labourers' Cottage code is the only way
by which he can reasonably hope, at this
time, anyhow, to get houses for the
labouring classes in our rural districts. In
regard to the other point that he raised,
I am informed-I am not very familiar
with it just at the moment myself—there
is existing machinery for advancing money
to small farmers for the construction of
homes. I will be very glad to obtain
further information for the hon. Gentleman, and also for myself, and for all who
are interested in regard to that rather
important matter.
I feel confident that the House is quite
ready to give us the Second Reading of
this Bill, and I think it will be rewarded
at the end of another year when it sees
thousands more of these comfortable homes
available for our very deserving workingclass people.

CLAUSE 7 (Close season for snipe and
woodcock).
No person shall, on any pretence
whatsoever, kill or destroy any woodcock or snipe, between the fifteenth day
of February and the twelfth day of
August in any year, or wilfully destroy
the eggs or nest of any woodcock; and
any person offending against this section shall be liable to the same penalty
as is imposed by an Act passed by the
Irish Parliament in the session held in
the twenty-seventh year of the reign of
His Majesty King George the Third,
chapter thirty-five, intituled, An Act
for the Preservation of the Game, upon
persons offending against that Act.
The provisions of the Wild Birds Protection Acts, 1880 to 1908, shall cease
to apply with respect to woodcock and
snipe or the eggs of woodcock and snipe.

ledge whatever can see clearly that the

this is here attributed to the poacher

Why? As a justification for this very.
much-amended Bill. Any excuse what

years, and yet there is no voice raised by

you are passing year by year, and so taking away from them the freedom handed
down to them by the British Government about your attachment to which you

Mr. MCALLISTER: I rise to oppose

are reactionary, retrograde, non-progressive, and entirely out of keeping with a
Parliament of this period. It cannot be
suggested that I have any selfish interest
in intervening in this debate.
As a
matter of fact I never fired a shot of any

every shape and form and for every purpose. Therefore, I say I can have no
self-interest in the part I have taken in
regard to this Bill.
The hon. and learned Gentleman (Mr.

it would have been well if people had not
known where guns were to be found. I
cordially agree with him, but his interpretation of the position and mine are
quite different, for he thinks that in a

and that the other should be defenceless,

be pursued in the ordinary constitutional
course.
I object to the extension of the authority of the police. It has been the safeguard of the citizen up to the present that
a policeman, with or without suspicion, of

do so.

I am also opposed to this Measure because there is no demand for it. It is an
unpopular Measure. Anybody who has
read the Press since the Bill was brought
to the notice of the people of Northern
Ireland must have seen that it is highly
unpopular, that it has no support, and is,
as I suggest, class legislation of a most
apparent character. There has been no
demand made by the farmers for it. Not
a single farming body or a single farmer
I have seen has supported it either in the
Press, on the public platform, or in any
other way.
I also take great exception to the penalties embodied in the Bill. I am as much
in favour of promoting and increasing
game in the country as any man in the
House, so much so that I suggest to the
Government that the only method of
doing it efficiently and successfully, and
of testing the real value of game preservation in Northern Ireland, is as has
been done in Canada and various other
countries to have a close season for two
years with, perhaps, a few open days in
each season by special authority from
some body set up by this Bill. That is
the only practical way from an economic
point of view of testing the value of game
preservation in Northern Ireland.
I am opposed as strongly as I possibly
can be to the shocking fines that are embodied in this Bill. Think for a moment
that if a farmer, perhaps on his own
land, goes out and shoots a hare he is
liable to a fine of £25 for the second offence and £10 for the first offence. And
suppose he is charged under three counts,
he is liable to a fine of £30 for the first
offence, and for the second offence to a
fine of £75, all for shooting one hare.
Any person associated with the law or
any ordinary person taking a reasonable
view of legislation which embodies punitive measures such as that will agree that
it cannot be defended in this House or

Mr. KYLE: I gave notice to the Minister of Labour that in view of the unsatisfactory reply that I received regarding
the workers in Ewart's Mill, on the Crumlin Road, that have been denied
employment insurance, I would raise the
question on the Motion for the Adjournment. When I put down the question, I
was under the impression that the decision
against these workpeople was given in
connection with the fact that their claim
was made inside ten weeks from the previous period of unemployment. The
Regulation of the Ministry states:-
Any two such continuous periods of
three or more days are treated as continuous with one another if they are
separated by not more than ten weeks.
These workpeople were employed on the
21st of July, after the holidays, and were
put out again on the 24th September.
They resumed work on the 1st of October.
When they were put out of their employment, they signed at the Employment
Exchange, and I understand that the firm
gave notice to the Employment Exchange
that these people were out of employment
for that week.
This is one of the largest mills in
Belfast, employing a very considerable
number of workpeople. I suppose there
are 500 or 600 people involved. The
Minister stated, in answer to a supplementary question, that they were refused
benefit, not because they were more than
ten weeks employed, but because they
were not genuinely seeking work. A more
monstrous decision has never been arrived
at by any responsible Minister.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is not my decision.
Mr. KYLE: The Minister says it was
not his decision. Whose decision was it?
Am I to take it that it was the Umpire's
decision? Then I want to hold that the
Umpire was wrong, and I submit that
argument to any Member of this House.
I do not care on what side he sits. These
people were not in employment more than
ten weeks from their previous unemployment when they became unemployed
again, and the law distinctly states that
they are entitled, without a further waiting period, to unemployment insurance
benefit.
In view of the fact that this firm was
only off from the 24th September to the 1st
of October, how could the Minister of
Labour or the Umpire for Northern Ireland say that these 500 or 600 people
could all find employment, that they could
even look for employment, that they could
Unemployment Payment,

HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Kyle]
go to the firm and demand their unemployment insurance cards and their National
Health Insurance cards and lodge them at
the Employment Exchange to satisfy the

Then, if they had done so, the Ministry
of Labour could rightfully have said that
they left their work of their own accord,
without any reason for doing so, and

because these people did not lift
their Unemployment
Insurance and
National Health Insurance cards and lodge
them at the Exchange, the Ministry say
they are not genuinely seeking work. How
can a person be genuinely seeking work
when the firm holds his cards, and how
can it be said that he is not genuinely seeking work when as a matter of fact he is
only suspended by the firm for a week?
The position is positively monstrous, and
nobody but the Minister of Labour of
Northern Ireland could defend such an
action, that is to say, if he proposes to
defend such an indefensible action.
I want to say that these people, who,
in the main, are constituents of mine,
should not be denied what after all is
their just claim. It is a perfectly legal
claim that they have made to the Ministry.
I would like to hear from the right hon.
Gentleman how he can say that these
people are not genuinely seeking employment when in the first instance their cards
are held by the firm. In the second instance, if they had lifted their cards and
gone to the Exchange, it would have taken
the Exchange about three days to have
registered their claims, and it would have
taken some little time further to grant
them their cards at the end of the next
three days when they were starting work
again. How he can defend an action of
that character, I do not know. It is to
get justice done to these people in Messrs.
William Ewart & Son's employment that
I am raising this question. I want to
give the right hon. Gentleman an opportunity, if possible, to get out of the difficult position that his Department or he
himself has created.
The other matter I want to raise concerns the Ministry of Home Affairs, and
I have given private notice to the Parliamentary Secretary of my intention. I am
not sure that he will be able to answer me.
I want to draw the attention of the
Government to the fact that there are unlicensed drivers and unlicensed conductors
in charge of the Belfast Omnibus Company's buses in Belfast to-day. I understand that the Ministry of Home Affairs
have been made aware of the fact that
unlicensed motor drivers and unlicensed
conductors are in charge of the B.O.C.
buses to-day in the city of Belfast. I
want to ask the right hon. Gentleman if
he will put a stop to that undesirable state
of affairs.
I have been informed that the Ministry
have been made aware of these facts, and
that they have refused to take any action
because, forsooth, there is a trade dispute
between the B.O.C. and their work people,
owing to the dismissal-the wrongful dismissal of one man who refused to work
another shift after doing nineteen hours
in one day. I hold, and I think any
sensible person will hold, that if this man
had taken that additional run he would
have been imperilling the lives of the
people whom he would have been driving.
In view of these circumstances, the
Minister of Home Affairs should not permit the B.O.C. or any other company or
individual to break the law laid down by
statute.
These are all very important matters,
and in reference to the first one I raised
I would like to hear the Minister of
Labour say in this House that he is prepared in view of the new facts to have this
matter re-considered by the umpire so
that these people might get the benefit
they are entitled to.

It is quite true to say that workers are
required to have two waiting
periods during a period of ten weeks.
That is perfectly true, but it was not
because of that that these workers were
denied benefit; they were turned down
because they were not held to be genuinely
seeking work. Does the hon. Member
suggest that workers who are not
genuinely seeking work should get benefit
whether the period of unemployment is
short or long? If that principle was to
be admitted then the result obviously
would be that all the conditions for the
receipt of benefit might be abolished and
all tests might be abolished. Then the
benefit would be paid to all comers.
That would be disastrous. It would
place the fund in bankruptcy, it would
put us so much out of step with Great
Britain in regard to our re-insurance
agreement that there would be disastrous
results, and it would be most demoralizing to our people. The hon. Member has
stated quite clearly that I decided that
these people were not genuinely seeking
employment. I decided nothing of the
kind, and I said in answer to his question
it would be quite improper of me to presume to criticize the umpire's decision
just as it would be improper for the Minister of Home Affairs to criticize the decision of a judge of the High Court.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DANCE HALLS IN EAST BELFAST.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of licensed dance halls in East
Belfast and the number of unlicensed
ones; and what supervision is exercised
over the unlicensed halls in order to see
that the Public Health Act of 1890 is
not violated.
The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): There are
four premises in East Belfast licensed
under the Public Health Acts for music
and dancing.
According to reports received from the
police two cases have come under notice
where premises not so licensed have been
used for public dancing.
PAYMENT OF PETTY SESSIONS
CLERKS' SALARIES.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if it
is a fact that Petty Sessions Clerks have
to make monthly returns of their financial
accounts to his Department, and when
they have £10 and upwards on hands to
lodge it to the credit of the Ministry; and
whether, if this is so, the Minister will
consider paying Petty Sessions Clerks'
salaries monthly instead of quarterly, as
at present.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a
fact that the Petty Sessions Clerks make
monthly returns of their financial
accounts. Their financial accounts are
rendered quarterly to the Ministry of
Home Affairs, but at the same time they
are required to inform us monthly as to
the sums they have on hands, and if these
sums amount to £10 or upwards to lodge
the sum to the credit of the Ministry.
As regards the latter part of the
question, I have not received any representations from the Petty Sessions Clerks
in regard to the suggestion that their
salaries should be paid monthly, and in
these circumstances, and as the suggested
change would involve considerable extra
work and consequential expense, I do not
consider that it would be justifiable to
adopt the suggestion made by the hon.
Member.

also examined, in conjunction with my

Credits adopted in the Irish Free State
in the year 1927, but I am satisfied that
the
for which it was devised are
purposes
served equally well, and at an equal or

there can be no question of the convenience of our system as compared with

the first place the minimum rate is 6 per

FLOODING IN COUNTY
FERMANAGH.
5. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has yet received a
petition signed by over 90 tenants residing along the River Sillies, at Boho, Co.
Fermanagh, claiming exemption from the
current half-year's rent owing to the
recent flooding, as a resuit of which most
of the crops in the low-lying lands have
been ruined, and what action he proposes
to take in view of the gravity of the
position.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have received a
copy of the petition to which the hon.
Member refers, and I regret that I am
unable to grant the exemption from the
current half-year's annuity which the
petitioners request.
Proposals have been made from time
to time involving a general or partial
postponement of, or relief from, payment
of annuities due under the Land Purchase
Acts, one such proposal being made as
recently as the 18th of last month by the
hon. Member himself, and I have on each
occasion had to indicate to this House
that such proposals are impracticable.
I might add that technical investigations into the question of Lough Erne
flooding are now in an advanced stage,

and the preparation of a Drainage
Scheme affecting the catchment area will
be put in hand as soon as possible.
Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.
Gentleman not know that any scheme

these people along the low-lying borders
of Lough Erne? Is the right hon.

and is he prepared to do anything in a

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. POLLOCK: I am aware that there
has been great hardship in that part of
the country from time to time because

two years.
But it appears from the investigations, that have been made that it
is flooding in the Lower Lough Ernethe rise of the Lough-that banks the
water in the Sillies river and therefore
causes this flooding, loss, and inconvenience. But if they yielded to the prayer
of the petition-which, by the way, is

Mr. HEALY: Does the right hon.

parts of the country, and is he not prepared to give special and exceptional

absolutely covered by floods?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do know all about
this, because the Sillies river case is one
which has been before the Government
for the last two years. The difficulty is how

Ministry is informed that the amount of

Question again proposed, "That the
words proposed to be left out stand part

Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: This
Bill is remarkable both for its inclusions
and its omissions. I would like to say in
the first place that it would ill become.
anyone who occupies these Benches to
oppose that portion of the Bill which proposes to enfranchise women. I should
point out that when the Labour Party
was formed in 1900, one of the first resolutions passed that was 28 years ago—
was that women should have the vote at
21 years of age. Therefore, 28 years
afterwards it is not likely that anyone
who claims to represent labour would
oppose that portion of the Bill which proposes to equalize the franchise.
I want to protest most vehemently
against that portion of the Bill which proposes to reintroduce plural voting. This,
in my opinion, is one of the most reactionary Clauses ever introduced into
any Bill, and shows what the intention
of the Government in regard to enfranchisement really is, because whatever
advantage has been given by the one
hand has been taken away by the other.
One rather fancies the Minister of Home
Affairs in the role of a person who with
one hand is extending the franchise and
has got a dagger in the other hand behind
his back prepared to stab a democratic
body. That is how the whole situation.
appears to me.
I would like to ascertain what justificacation there is in a Bill that proposes to
deal with the parliamentary franchise for
the introduction of matters relating to
local government. I know very well
from my knowledge of these matters and
from reading the activities of the Imperial
Parliament that the party represented by
the right hon. Gentleman who introduced
this Bill never were in favour of the
principle at all. If I desired I could deal
with the whole of the Bills introduced in
the Imperial Parliament so far as this
matter is concerned, and I could show
conclusively that not only the Unionist
Party but the Liberal Party have blocked
every attempt to enfranchise
from as far back as 1906 to the present
day.
women

front on the part of the Government? It
was explained a short time ago by one of
the Chamberlains, I think, it was Mr.
Neville Chamberlain. Mr. Neville
Chamberlain was speaking in some part
of Britain a few weeks ago, and he made

Mr. T. W. McMULLAN:
Members opposite seem to be under the

A company

more than one vote for his company. A

one
This concession of one vote to one individual is simply recognizing a principle
that has been in the British Constitution
for, I think, 160 or 170 years, namely,
that taxation and representation should
go together. It was not in 1832 that this
principle was first established. The
American colonists quarrelled with England because they did not get representation though they were taxed, and the result of that quarrel was that we lost the
American colonies. I think our British
people had the lesson very well rubbed
into them that where the individual was
taxed he had the right to have a vote as
to the disposal of the money that was
taken from him.
I think we in the business community
should be very grateful to the Government. I personally feel grateful to them
for having recognized that an injustice
has been imposed upon the business community for so long and that that injustice
is at last to be removed. Those who for
so long have paid a very large proportion
of rates in our city should have something
to say as to how the representatives who
are to spend those rates should be chosen..
I have great pleasure in supporting this
Bill in all its Clauses. I feel that as far
as the young woman of twenty-one is concerned she is probably more capable of
exercising the vote than the young man of
twenty-one, because as a general rule our
young women develop more quickly than
our young men. I am glad that we are
recognizing the principle that women
should have an equal right with men in
selecting Members of Parliament and
representatives of local institutions.

Measure. What do we find? We find

franchise to all ladies of full age, and
yet the next moment it undermines and
destroys that right.
Let us contrast the action of Northern Ireland with that of the Free State.
It is most remarkable, in many respects.
There is a special Clause in this Bill that
is before the House to the effect that no
person of full age shall be entitled to vote
in Northern Ireland unless he or she has
been resident here for three years. That
is a remarkable Clause. It is put in for
the sole purpose of preventing many citizens of the country from exercising the
franchise, people who contribute to the
upkeep of the country, and who are the
bone and sinew of the country. It is not
the man with the big purse, or with money
lying in he bank, that contributes most to
the upkeep and development of the
country.

Northern Ireland. I myself keep servants. I had just one from Northern
Ireland. He was born in Northern Ireland, and remained in Northern Ireland
until I asked him to come over into my

"Every person, without distinction of

Mr. HANNA: I will not pursue this
matter of the Free State to any great
length. What they do or what they do

qualification for citizenship in the Free
State at all. They must know that there

We are doing nobody an injustice in
regard to this matter. Will any person
deny that we have a right to protect ourselves from an influx of people if we
think there is an influx coming undesired
by us? We have that right and we are
going to exercise it, and that is just what
the Bill amounts to.
Let me come to one other suggestion in
connection with the matter of personation. Did ever you see SO many
hon. Gentlemen standing in white sheets
before in your life? All want personation put an end to. I am just as anxious
to have an end put to personation as any
hon. Member in this House. But to
suggest it on this thing shows either a
want of appreciation of the rules of our
House or something else that I cannot
give expression to. How could we put
into this Bill matter that is to alter the
criminal law? Because personation is a
criminal offence. How could we on this
Bill, a perfectly civil Bill, do something
to affect a criminal offence? I will cooperate with any Members of this House
and help them to get rid of personation.
I do not mind their dissociating themselves from personation. Nobody would
be deceived by that. What I do object
to is that the name of any right hon.
Gentleman or hon. Gentleman should be

think the hon. Member who spoke and

Minister of Home Affairs' name certainly
spoke with very bad taste.

not very tasteful to you.

land), 1927, by enabling the Ministry of

6 NOVEMBER 1928
Home Affairs to make grants under
Section one of the Housing Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, being grants chargeable
upon the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland or the growing produce thereof,
in respect of the construction of houses
completed before the first day of April,
one thousand nine hundred and thirty,
and being of the type and dimensions set

--(Governor's recommendation signified.
-Mr. Pollock).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): My right hon. Friend (Sir
Dawson Bates) in moving the Second
Reading of the Housing Bill, indicated
the very considerable increase in the
numbers of houses which are being built
with the aid of the State subsidy,
especially since, under the Housing Act
of last year, the amount of the subsidy
in respect of the smaller type of house
(namely, of less than 650 superficial feet)
was increased to £100 for houses completed within six months, the subsidy on
the larger type being discontinued.
As the object of the Resolution now before the Committee is to secure authority
for the continuance of these grants for a
further year,
I think the Committee may
wish to know what the cost of the grants
has been up to date, and to have some
indication of the probable expenditure
during the year covered by this Resolution.
In the period from the passing of the
Housing Act of 1923 up to the 31st March
last the total payments by the Government in respect of housing grants were as
follows:-By private builders, 5,184
houses built; £382,840 grants paid;
by Local Authorities, 1,157 houses built;
£76,320 grants paid; or a total payment
by the Government of £459,160 in respect
of 6,341 houses.
.
In the six months ended 30th September last a total sum of £157,180 was paid,
that is to say, more than one-third of
the total amount paid in the five years up
to the 31st March, 1928. This amount
was almost wholly in respect of the
smaller type of house. It is estimated
that in the full year up to the 31st March
next a total sum of no less than £323,000
will have been paid, representing grants
for 3,350 additional houses.
I think that these figures are sufficient
to show that under the scheme which is
now in operation and for the continuance
of which the Government seeks the approval of the Committee, we are rapidly
moving towards a solution of the difficulties caused by the shortage of houses
which can be let at a rent within the
means of the average working man.
It is, of course, difficult to forecast with
any close degree of accuracy what the cost
of the scheme will be in the year beginning on the 1st April, next, but in the
light of the figures I have already given
it seems possible that as many as 4,000
additional houses qualifying for the grant
will be built during the year, the grants
for which would amount to £400,000. By
the year 1930 therefore this Government
will have spent not less than one million
pounds on housing subsidies, a record
which shows the Government's care and
forethought for the needs of the working
classes of the community. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to speak on this

I understand that the right hon.

built on the Donegall Road, I think, as

representing the workers, the inspector
was satisfied that the work was not being
done in a proper fashion, and that the

was bound to fall off within a very short

think that the right hon. Gentleman
should give us some assurance in the first
place that there are specifications, and,
in the second place, that the specifications
are fulfilled by the building contractor.

everyday life of Parliament, for the convenient and better discussion of all these

Sir DAWSON BATES: In respect to
the two points raised by my hon. Friend
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle)
last night and which you, Mr. Moles,
ruled out of order on the Financial Resolution, I would just like to draw the attention of my hon. Friend to the system
which is adopted in regard to the payment
of subsidies. First of all, the plans must
be drawn up and inspected by the local
authority and passed by them. They have
also to be submitted to the Ministry and
passed by them, and the building operations afterwards must all comply with
the specifications laid down. If my hon.
Friend wishes I will be only too glad to
give him the specification from which he
will see that the utmost care is taken to
ensure that the bricks, timber and other
material used in the building are of a suitable quality. In addition to that, during
the progress of the building the house is
liable to be inspected by the local authority just like any other house and also by
our inspector. Before a subsidy can be
granted the house has to pass an official
inspection, not alone by the surveyor of
the local authority but by the inspector
of the Ministry. It does not follow that.
because a house is built the subsidy is
given.
I have before me the figures which show
that in at least 32 cases no subsidy was
given on the ground that the house was
imperfectly built, and in hundreds of
other cases the builders were informed that
having regard to the way in which the
houses had been built no subsidy would be
paid unless the defects were remedied. If
I may quote an example, that applies particularly to the houses in connection with
the scandal over the housing question in
the Belfast Corporation. No subsidy was
given in connection with those houses until
the defects complained of had been
remedied. From time to time we have
found it better to alter the specification.
For example, in regard to timber some
time ago we altered the specification to
meet the very case that arose then, and we
have specified that in future the timber
used in those houses should be a class of
timber certainly not of that quality that
we heard so much about. Then there was
the case my hon. Friend referred to.
There we had the Board of Works engineers on to those houses to see whether
or not they complied with the conditions
laid down.
In regard to the question of town
planning, I quite admit there is necessity
to extend the powers of the local authorities. My hon. Friend knows that in
England the local authority is also the
planning authority. The great object of
town planning is to try to avoid undue
congestion in towns and big areas. We
have been in consultation-I only mention this to show the matter is not overlooked by the Government-with the
Municipal Association which is the association connected with all the municipal
authorities. We have been in touch with
them and also with the Belfast Corporation. At the present time we are actually
awaiting suggestions from them. When
we do produce a Measure we want to try
to produce one that will meet the situation. I think those are the few points I
desired to mention.

that a class of house was being built that
was utterly useless for the purposes of the
working man; in other words, it was so
expensive that he could not possibly live
in it. And these same local authorities
represented to the Government that there
was only one solution to this housing
problem, and that was to provide houses
at a rent that the working man could pay.
In response to those representations the
Government considered the whole matter,
and, in order that a great impetus might
be given to house building, the Government agreed to increase the subsidy from
£80 to £100 on the assumption that if
these smaller houses were built-kitchen
houses as they are known and have been
known for a generation-there would be
such a momentum given to building that
in a few years it would .automatically
bring the housing crisis to an end; in
other words, that when the larger number of houses were built then the natural
laws of supply and demand would bring
the rents of houses down to a rate that
the working man could pay.
That is the position the Government
and all the authorities have aimed at
That is what the British Government are
aiming at in Britain, and that is what the
Government are aiming at here, namely.
to bring down the rents of houses so that

Beattie). This subsidy is an attempt to

Mr. DEVLIN: Convenient, yes.
What is the fact? That a working man,
if he is to be what you all desire him to
be, a stable and conservative member of
society, must have something to make him
conservative and something to make him
contented, and how can you have a contented citizen living in a house of the

Beattie) has described, a class of house
which you are encouraging not only local
councils but private exploiters to build.
These houses are, in my judgment, simply
places in which people are permitted to
sleep at night. I understand from my
hon. Friend-I have no personal experience that they sleep under certain
physical limitations. A house ought to
be more than that. The hon. Member
has stated that a man's house-whether
he be rich or poor--ought to be his castle.
The best of people's lives are spent in
their houses. Their characters are formed
in their home. Their moral life is largely
moulded on their home life, and if you
are going to cabin and confine a man who
has to engage in laborious toil to a home
where there is no place to sit down, where
there is no place for him to associate with
his wife and children under felicitous
domestic circumstances then you turn him
into a resentful propagandist against

Therefore I will not give my sanction in

which creates a house such as that described to-day in this Committee. The
Minister of Finance says the Government
are going to create more of these houses
than will subsequently be wanted. No
matter how many you create you will not
solve the housing problem, but you will
lay deeper and deeper the roots of popular
discontent amongst the mass of the people.
In my judgment, when the Government
was considering this question of subsidies,
they ought to have given some consideration to the question of rents. You
allow these people to get the subsidy, and
to charge any rent they please, and I
understand from the figures quoted in this
House that the amount spent upon the
building of these houses by the private
builder, with the substantial subsidy
given by the State and the local councils,
would enable these houses to be let at a
far lower rent than they are let at now.
If you agree to the proposal of my hon.
Friend, the Member for East Belfast (Mr.
Beattie), to extend the number of superficial feet by another hundred, that will
enable you, in my judgment, to get comparatively decent houses, not houses that
I would regard as adequate, but comparatively decent houses at the rents that they
charge for the houses which he has described. For that reason I think it would
have been worth the while of the Government to have given more thought to this
question, to have agreed to this proposal of
another hundred superficial feet, and
when they were giving these subsidies or
grants to have come to terms with the
builders as to the rents to be charged.
I do not think that the wages paid at
present are very much larger than the
wages paid before the war. I think, for
instance, if you take the shipyard workers, you will find that their wages are
no higher than they were before the war.
Mr. BEATTIE: They are lower.

instances they are lower. If the wages are
lower, the rents are higher. I remember

sort of house could not be got now for
ten shillings a week, although the wages
are either the same or lower. Therefore, I
say that the whole method by which this
housing problem has been approached by
the Government has been an unsatisfactory
method. In England, which is the model

I come to another question. I am altogether opposed to the policy which has
been established by the Government that
if houses are built either by councils or
private builders, the subsidy is given
without any question. This whole housing
question ought to have been dealt with side
by side with the question of town planning
as was pointed out yesterday by the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle). I
spoke a moment ago of the workingman,
the father of a family, coming home, and
the conditions under which he lives in
one of those small houses. But what
about the children? My hon. Friend has
said that the children are never inside
because there is no room for them there.
The only living accommodation is the
kitchen; the mother is engaged in the
kitchen doing the domestic work, and
the children are driven out to the streets.
A very simple, but very obvious, proposal was made some time ago and I say
all honour to the very distinguished citizen of Belfast from whom the proposal
emanated, namely the Town Clerk, Sir
Robert Meyer. I had better take one
area in order more effectively to impress
upon the Members of this House the idea
that I want to express. You start at the
Queen's Bridge and go to the Newtownards Road area. There you will see,
I forget how many, hundreds of streets,
with thousands of small houses. They
are narrow streets, no doubt, and the
houses are small, but in each of those
Housing Bill-
Committee

houses there are living a father and
mother and perhaps five or six children.
Those children go to school, and when
they come home from school the house
is too small to allow for any of the amenities and the joys and the simple pleasures
in which rich and poor children alike
engage. What is done? They are cast
out upon the paved centres of those
streets.
One of the suggestions Sir Robert
Meyer made-I do not know whether it
was ever faced or argued in the City
Council-was that those streets ought to
be asphalted or macadamized, that all
traffic ought to be stopped in those streets
after four o'clock in the afternoon, and
that the centres of the streets should be
given over to the children for playgrounds. That would not cause any inconvenience, because I do not see what
necessity there is for vehicular traffic in
those streets after four o'clock in the
afternoon. The vehicles are merely distributing parcels, and those could be distributed earlier in the day. If you cannot give them green fields, because you
have never had a decent town planning
scheme by which playgrounds could be
created for the children, if you cannot
allow them to stay in their homes because
this system of small houses which you
are stereotyping prevents them from remaining in their homes, if you cannot
give them an opportunity for enjoyment
in any other way, then the only course
is what I describe, to make those streets
as far as possible sufficiently attractive
and joyful-if it is possible to be joyful
under such circumstances for them to
play on the streets. The right hon.

Government thought it better to withdraw all subsidies and endeavour to get

Motion made, and Question proposed:
AMENDMENT OF LAW.
1. That it is expedient to amend the
law relating to Stamp Duty and a Duty
of Excise.
STAMP DUTY ON BANKERS'
LICENCES.
II. That as from the twenty-fifth day
of March, nineteen hundred and twentynine, there shall be charged in respect of
every licence to be taken out annually by
a banker under an Act of the present
Session a Stamp Duty of thirty pounds.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): It would, perhaps, be convenient if the two Resolutions on the
Order Paper-one being the usual general
Resolution and the other a specific
Resolution covering the grant of a new
duty-were to be dealt with in the same
speech. In moving their adoption I am
constrained to think that my task will be
an easy one inasmuch as the Bill to be
introduced upon them is not likely to be
regarded as contentious, its subject matter being only minor in character.
The main proposal, which is the subject
of the second Resolution, is the creation
of a banker's licence as such to replace
the present licence which is a licence to
issue unstamped promissory notes, or, as
we more familiarly term them, bank notes.
A bank will in future pay a licence duty
for the privilege of carrying on the business of banking instead of paying for the
privilege of issuing unstamped documents.
Under the old arrangement two banks
operating in Northern Ireland, which
are non-note issuing banks, and a third
bank, which was specifically exempted
under old Imperial legislation, escaped
payment of licence duty in Northern Ireland in any form, and it is now proposed
to correct these anomalies by substituting
a new form of licence duty which will
place all banks on a par. The rate of
duty proposed, namely, £30 for each
licence with a maximum of £120, is the
same as the present duty.
Bankers' Licences
Committee
7 NOVEMBER 1928
A second amendment of the law
relating to Stamp Duty in its relation to
the business of banking, and which is independent of the licence duty provision
to which I have just referred, is covered
by the general Resolution which appears
first on the Order Paper. It relates to
the payment of composition duty on unstamped bills of exchange and bank post
bills which, I may say for the information
of hon. Members, are the technical terms
for bank documents passing between
the several offices in connection with
"Clearing House" activities. It is
rather in the nature of a re-enactment
than an amendment, being designed to
replace a couple of scattered sections of
existing Acts. It leaves undisturbed the
present arrangement with regard to composition duty on these bills of exchange
and bank post bills, the double taxation
relief arrangements between Northern
Ireland and the Irish Free State making
it more convenient that each bank should
continue to compound and pay according
to the location of its head office in Ireland; that is to say, the Irish Free State
Exchequer will receive composition duty
on such documents in the case of banks
whose Irish head offices are located in the
Irish Free State, while the duty will
accrue to the Northern Ireland Exchequer
in the case of banks whose head offices are
situate in Northern Ireland. Although
the provisions of the Bill will be found to
be somewhat technical, hon. Members
will doubtless be satisfied at this stage
with my assurance that they have already
been brought to the notice of the banks
concerned and they have raised no objection to them.
The general Resolution also refers to
an amendment of the law relating to a
duty of Excise, the duty in question being
Entertainments Duty. It is now proposed
to give effect to the undertaking given by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) in the course of
his Budget statement, namely, that as
from the 1st day of June last an entertainment consisting solely of one or more
horse-races will be exempt from the duty.
It is also proposed to include provisions
of a minor character designed to clear up
some points of doubt or alleviate cases of
hardship that have arisen under the administration of the present law relating
to Entertainments Duty.

Oral Answers to Questions.
RETIREMENT AND RESIGNATION
OF TEACHERS.
3. Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL asked
the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education whether he can
state the number of circuits with their
sub-divisions into which Northern Ireland is divided for the purpose of
elementary education, and can he give a
return for the past three years showing
for each circuit and its sub-divisions the
following particulars: (1) The number
of teachers who retired with less than 40
years' service; (2) the number of teachers
who resigned through ill-health; (3) the
number of teachers who died while in the
actual service of the Ministry.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The number
of circuits into which elementary schools
in Northern Ireland are divided for inspection purposes is four, and the number
of sub-divisions is thirteen.
The particulars in the return sought in
the latter portion of the question are not
available in the form in which they are
asked for, and their preparation in this
form would cause such an interruption of
work that the Ministry thinks that the
time and labour involved would be entirely disproportionate to any educational
usefulness of the return when obtained.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: May I ask the hon.
Gentleman as this is a matter of considerable importance, not alone to the teachers
but to many people sympathetically
engaged in educational work, is an hon.
Member not entitled to information when
he asks for it?
Mr. ROBB: If the hon. Member will
put down a Motion asking for this return and if the House, after having been
informed of the cost of the answer,
sanctions it, the Ministry will readily
undertake the work of preparing it.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: In view of the
answer given is it necessary for an hon.
Member to put down a specific Motion
when he asks for a specific answer to a
specific question, which should be within
the reach of the Ministry of the hon.
Gentleman?
Mr.
SPEAKER: The proper course,
and really the one that should have been
taken where a question asks for statistics,
is to put down a Motion for an unopposed
return, and, assuming, that is, that the
Government agree to give the information, that Motion could be put down any
day before Questions as an unopposed
Motion and taken formally and passed.
If it was opposed, of course, I do not
know quite when he would get an opportunity of moving it. Unopposed Motions
asking for statistics of this kind are
generally granted by the Government,
and the proper way is to put down the
Motion on the Paper before Questions.
Mr. O'NEILL: Surely to ask for a
return of the number of teachers who
have retired in a certain district in
Northern Ireland does not involve such a
huge amount of labour that the Ministry
could not give it when a Member asks a
question?
Mr. ROBB: I do not know whether
this is the proper time for me to say that
this would involve one Department investigating 755 cases. When they had
investigated these, each five would have
to be segregated into one of three categories, and each category would have to
be sub-divided into thirteen divisions.
I am informed by the officials of my
Department-part of the information is
in our Department-that the least estimate of time which it would take our
Department to compile this return is the
time of 33 men for two days. After we
had finished with it, it would then have to
go to the Department of Finance, who would
have to go through the same performance,
and what time it would take them I do
not know. Whether the return is worth
that is a matter for the House.
Ministry has no objection to give this
information, but if the information is not
available without excessive trouble and
cost, it is for the House to say.

England and Scotland. Further employment for secondary teachers could only

8. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON asked

to suffer
children of Portadown have

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend, the Prime
Minister, to reply to this question.
My attention has been drawn to a report in the Press of a Meeting of the
Portadown Urban District Council held
on the 5th inst., at which statements were
made that there was considerable destitution in the town.
I also understand that the Urban District Council have decided to call a special
meeting to consider what steps should be
taken to relieve the distress referred to
In this connection 1 think it well to
state that the Urban District Council
have on hands at the moment a very com
prehensive sewerage scheme which will
involve an expenditure of over £70,000.
The Ministry of Home Affairs has sanctioned a loan amounting to nearly
£47,000 in connection with the scheme,
and it is understood that the Ministry of
Labour has undertaken to make substantial grants in respect of the scheme out
of the Unemployment Relief Fund.
It is hoped that the work which this
scheme will involve will go far towards
relieving the situation.
I should also add that the relief of destitution in any particular area is a matter for the consideration of the Board of
Guardians concerned, and the Ministry
has already taken steps to draw the at
tention of the Lurgan Board of Guardians
to the situation referred to, and to request them to have immediate inquiries
made by their Relieving Officers with a

necessary or desirable to relieve cases of
destitution which may be reported.
At the same time, the Ministry has
directed its Poor Law Inspector to make
independent investigations with a view to
seeing whether the circumstances are such
as to warrant action being taken under
the Bill which has recently been passed
through this House dealing with special
Outdoor Relief.

KILKEEL AND NEWRY-SUBSIDY
HOUSES.
11. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. William
McMullen) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that builders
and contractors in the Kilkeel and Newry
district are using seashore gravel and
sand in the erection of subsidy houses;
whether this is a contravention of the
specifications issued by his Department;
and, if so, what action he proposes to take
in the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that seashore gravel and sand is used in
making mortar in Kilkeel and elsewhere,
and its use for this purpose is not a contravention of the Ministry's specification.
I am informed that most architects
prefer this sand to inferior pit sand, and
that the shore sand obtained at Kilkeel
is particularly good, being sharp and free
from loam.
It would be contrary to the Ministry's
rules, however, to use this sand in the
making of concrete as the sand used for
this purpose must be free from salt.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister whether he is aware that
seashore sand has a certain effect on the
bricks going into the building, whether
he is aware that the face of the brick is
destroyed by this class of sand being used,
and does he approve of sand being used
as described by my hon. Colleague?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course
this is a very technical matter, and,
therefore, I must be guided by my
technical officers. I understand that this
sand is quite useful and quite good for
the purpose of making mortar, but not
for the purpose of making cement. If
the sand is to be used for concrete it can
be washed and made suitable in that way.

12. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of

the housing schemes at present in operation; whether he is satisfied that builders
Oral Answers.

receiving the subsidy are carrying out the
work in a proper manner, and can he
state whether it is a fact that subsidies
are given to builders of houses without
specifications being produced.
Sir DAWSON BATES: An Inspector
of the Ministry accompanied by two representatives of the Plasterers' Association visited a number of houses which
were complained of, and found that in
some cases cracks have developed in the
skimming or final coat of plaster. In one
case only had these defects developed to
any extent.
This cracking is caused by the final
coat being applied before the second coat
was sufficiently dry, and the defect would
only become apparent after there had
been fires in the houses for some time. If
the houses were left unoccupied for some
time after completion, and the plaster
work allowed to dry out naturally, it is
unlikely that cracks would develop.
In all cases the defects have been or are
being remedied by the contractor.
I am satisfied that so far as can be
ascertained from inspection, builders receiving the subsidies are carrying out the
work in a proper manner.
No subsidy is paid on any house until
the inspectors of the Ministry are satisfied
that it complies with the specification
laid down in the Ministry's Rules.

Mr. BEATTIE: I regret that this House
is now coming to its final decision on a question of this kind without thoroughly going
into the merits of the case as it stands
to-day. I am about to reply to the Prime
Minister's speech of yesterday. We are
told that the subsidy is being granted
with the object of providing houses for
the very poor. Houses must be provided
for all classes of people who desire them,
and the requirements of all classes in the
community are not alike. The subsidy is
being used not to provide homes for the
homeless but is being used at present to
provide profits for the profiteers.
Mr. KYLE:
Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: That being so I cannot allow this Third Reading to go through
unchallenged. I do not mean unchallenged in the Lobby but unchallenged on
the floor of the House. We are told by
the Prime Minister that we must have a
small house so as to be able to let it at
an economic rent to the people. I want
to say that if the cramped housing conditions of the industrial classes are not going
to have the serious consideration of this
House then I leave the industrial classes
to deal with the Government at their next
opportunity. Some hon. Members on
the last occasion said they were not afraid.
Some hon. Members have gone from this
House just because of their adamant attitude regarding the desires of the people
of Northern Ireland. The people clamoured for certain legislation. That legislation was not brought in, and the people
told them they would endeavour to put
an Opposition into this House so that
their needs and requirements might receive attention. Hence my reason for
being here to-day.
I
I have been told repeatedly by the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Home Affairs (Mr. Hanna) that he does
not agree that a house of 650 superficial
feet is a suitable home for all classes.
agree that it may be suitable for a certain class of family, the small family for
instance, but when you come to families
of five, and then extend to eight, and then
go a step further and extend to ten,
surely it is not the intention of the
Government to cram such families into the
accommodation provided for a family of
two. It seems clear to me that that is
the object and the intention. I claim
again that by directing the subsidy in a
proper direction we can have larger homes
at an economic rent. Allowing £240 as
the price of a house of 700 superficial feet,
and fixing the price of a house of 750
superficial feet at £260 I claim that the
rent should not at the present time reach
anything more than 7/6 to 8/6 per week.
We have 650 superficial feet houses being
built on the Seaview site and the cost is
8/7.
We were told on the Second Reading
that the plans for anything between 400
and 500 houses were being passed
every month. That would bring us up to
anything between 3,000 and 4,000 homes.
I am not aware that anything of that kind
is contemplated for the future at all. I
understand that the Corporation have
something like 253 of the same class ready
for being attended to. I think there are
somewhere about 367 previously built,
but if that is the case it took twelve
months to build the number of houses I
have stated, and I understand that the
terms of the contract are that the contractor is to have those 253 houses completed in twelve months.
Now we leave that type of house.
People are rushing for it and the reason
they are rushing for it is because a small
corner of your own is better that the big
healthy room belonging to a tenant who
wishes to charge an exorbitant rent.
That is not the opinion of the Government
at all. The opinion of the Government
is that anything is good enough for the
working classes, but when they select a

is good enough for you should also be good
enough for the class I represent, and I
am not prepared to stand by and allow

wisdom 650 superficial feet is quite

When I heard the Minister of Commerce

this House and to have that bank estab-

the occasion for our Housing Acts, and

Following the War there was a great

of the
state of those who were absolutely helpless
and unable to find homes for themselves.
Let me trace the history of the question
in order to show exactly what happened.
What happened? The 950 superficial
feet house was built and the subsidy was
given. I regret to have to say that I do
not believe that at this present day five
per cent. of those houses which were built
under the Government subsidy are occupied by the class of people they were intended for at the time they were built.

made alterations. After the most careful
inquiry, after being advised by our experts and after having consulted builders
and architects and people outside we came
to the conclusion that if we were to build
a house of 650 superficial feet it might
be done at a rent, not an economic rent,

whom we set out to benefit could reasonably be expected to rise to.

ask hon. Members opposite to appreciate

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: There

of the kitchen. That is the state of affairs

there must be a space for a bath in some

is there any possibility of any of these

The proper

As I have said before, I believe this is a

get them.
Take the case of the room of 15

a sideboard in the living room. That

The fireplace takes another four feet because in a working-class house there is
usually a nice fender. The table would

and then you have also the space for the

hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) went

Iwould be astounded. I have seen the

Representation of the People Bill.
Considered in Committee.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Assimilation of parliamentary franchise of men and women.)
For the purpose of providing that the
parliamentary franchise in respect of
elections of members to serve in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland shall
be the same for men and women, subsections (1) and (2) of section four of
the Representation of the People Act,
1918 (in this Act referred to as "the
principal Act") shall be repealed in
their application to such elections, and
the following sections shall be substituted for sections one and two of that
Act in their application as aforesaid:
*
*
*
*
*
*
*
(Section to be substituted for the said
section two.)
"A person shall be entitled to be
registered as a parliamentary elector
for a university constituency if he or
she is of full age and not subject to any
legal incapacity, and has received a
degree (other than an honorary degree)
at the university which forms the
constituency."

A POINT OF ORDER.
Mr. DEVLIN: On a point of Order.
We have been discussing to-day the ques
tion of the representation of graduates of
the University. In the Act that established this Parliament it was declared that
the method of election for this Parliament
should be that of Proportional Representation and that that should continue for,
I think, a period of three years, and that
if after that time this Parliament so decided, a method of election other than
Proportional Representation might be
adopted by this House. There was no
reference to the right of this Government
to change the franchise other than the
method of representation, namely, the
method of Proportional Representation,
and I put it to you that this debate and
this Bill are out of order, that the Government have no right whatever to introduce
these matters, and that the only power
they have under the Act of 1920 is the
power to change from Proportional Representation to another method of electoral
selection.
Mr.

General has, I think, to give his decision
that they are within the powers of this
Parliament.
It is not for me to express an opinion
as to whether or not any particular Bill
is within the powers of this Parliament.
So far as I know there is nothing in this
Franchise Bill that is outside the powers
of this Parliament, but that is a matter
for the Law Officers of the Crown to

Mr. DEVLIN: Is it the Law Officers
of the Crown, who are the agents and

the Law Officers of the Crown in Great
Britain?
Mr. SPEAKER: Subject to what the

8 NOVEMBER 1928


The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I
should explain that there is a double safeguard against anything such as the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) fears occurring. Not
only has my right hon. and learned
Friend, the Attorney-General, to certify
that our Acts, whatever they may be, fall
within the ambit of the powers given to
us under the Act of 1920, but all the
Acts are submitted to the Home Office on
the other side, and there the Secretary
of State, if at any time he considers we
are exceeding our powers in any Bill we
introduce, has power of withholding the
Assent to it, and in that case, of course,
we would not be able to proceed with the
Measure. So that there is a double check.
Not only has my right hon. and learned
Friend, the Attorney-General, to give
his certificate, but also the British
Government, through the Law Officers on
the other side, have a right to object if
they see anything in our proposed legislation that is ultra vires.
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I suggest that
it would be well, as a matter of convention, that these Bills should be sent over
to whoever is the authority on the
other side to declare whether we are within our legal powers before they are discussed in this House?
The PRIME MINISTER: They are
sent over.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did they sanction this?
The PRIME MINISTER: Certainly.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will write to Joynson-
Hicks. (Laughter).

STABLES AS HUMAN DWELLINGS
IN ENNISKILLEN DISTRICT.
1. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether his attention has
been directed to the report of Dr.
M'Cloy, medical inspector in his Department, of his recent inspection of Enniskillen Urban District, in which Dr.
McCloy referred to certain stables, now
occupied as human dwellings, and
recommended the Council to promote
at once a housing scheme suitable
for the working classes; and whether
he will cause a public inquiry to
be held into the failure of the Council
to provide adequate housing accommodation for the workers of the district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The report to
which the hon. Member refers was
furnished by one of the medical inspectors
to my Department, which communicated
the contents to the Enniskillen Urban
District Council, and urged the Council
to take steps to remedy the housing
conditions in the town.
The Council, which has recently completed a scheme of 28 houses, had the
Ministry's letter before them at their
meeting on the 5th instant, and have
referred it to the Improvement Committee
for consideration.
I have no reason to suppose that the
Council will ignore the matter, and I do
not consider that an inquiry would serve
any useful purpose at present.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the Enniskillen Urban

discharged on redundancy from Government Departments is reckoned for the
purpose of determining starting pay, increments and sick leave facilities on the
re-allocation of such clerks to temporary

in Treasury Memorandum E. 3797, dated
12th November, 1923); and, if such temporary civilian service has not previously
been so reckoned, does the Minister propose retrospectively to revise the existing
regulations on the lines indicated in the
Treasury Memorandum already quoted.
Mr. POLLOCK: The answer to the first
part of the hon. Member's question is in
the affirmative, save that as regards temporary staff whose present term of reemployment commenced earlier than the
1st June, 1927, previous service ceased to
be reckonable where the break in employment lasted for over three months instead

adopted in full.
The second part of the question arises
in respect only of those clerks affected by
the foregoing qualification.

2. Mr. T. HENDERSON asked the

aware that omnibus drivers and conductors, employees of firms plying for hire
in Northern Ireland, are working 106
hours weekly; and will he state whether it
is the intention of the Government to
introduce legislation in order to put an
end to the exploiting of these workers,
and thus help to reduce unemployment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to answer this question. If
on occasions omnibus drivers and conductors are working the hours indicated
by the hon. Member, I am inclined to
think that the circumstances are exceptional. I hope the hon. Member will
agree that, for the present at any rate,
the matter may reasonably be left with
the responsible Trade Union leaders.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Failing
the Trades Union leaders taking action
will the right hon. Gentleman, as representing the Minister of Home Affairs, take
action to put a stop to this slavery, and
so reduce the number of unemployed on

Mr. ANDREWS: Whenever such a
question arises as suggested by my hon.
Friend, the Government will consider the
matter.

union?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am not aware of
the fact that these men have not an
effective trade union.
Mr. DEVLIN: An effective trade
union?
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes.

not have the same rights and privileges as

support it?

before.
CLOSING OF MONKSTOWN MILL.
5. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he can
state if it is a fact that Monkstown mill
and factory have been closed for the past
fourteen years, causing considerable hardship in that district, and whether he will
state if his Department has made any
effort to re-open the factory.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I am sorry that the factory to
which the hon. Member refers was closed
down some years prior to the establishment of the Parliament of Northern Ireland. It is also unfortunately the case
that many active concerns are unable at
the present time to maintain full-time
production.
In regard to the latter part of the question, I think the hon. Member will appreciate that, while my Ministry is ready
at all times to take steps towards assisting
an industry as a whole or towards attracting new industries to the locality, it cannot carry its efforts to the point of reopening a particular mill or factory which
has been closed down on account of trading
difficulties of one kind or another.

It becomes much worse when the fact is

Whatever might be said in favour of a

anything can be said in defence of a

In my opinion there is no justification

principle contained in the Bill. I would

According to the discussion that took
place on this matter on the last day I see
that the whole thing appeared to centre
round the degree of skill acquired by a
doctor. I do not think any of us have a

the medical profession towards the poor
of our city and all other cities.
I want to make it perfectly clear that

Clause ordered to stand part of the
Bill.
CLAUSE 2
(Assimilation of local
government franchise of men and women):
(1) For the purpose of providing
that the local government franchise in
Northern Ireland shall be the same
for men and women, sub-section (3)
of section four of the principal Act
shall be repealed in its application to
the said franchise, and the following
section shall be substituted for section
three of that Act in its application as
aforesaid:-
-
"A person shall be entitled to be
registered as a local government
elector for a local government electoral area if he or she is of full age
and not subject to any legal incapacity, and-
(a) is on the last day of the
qualifying period occupying in
that area, as owner or tenant, any
land or premises (not being a
dwelling-house) of a yearly value
of not less than five pounds, or a
dwelling-house; and
(b) has during the whole of the
qualifying period So occupied,
either in that area or, if that area
is not an administrative county or
a county borough, in any administrative county or county borough
in which the area is wholly or
partly situate, any land or premises (not being a dwelling-house)
of such yearly value as aforesaid,
or a dwelling-house; or
*
*
*
*
*
*
*
(ii) for the purposes of this section
the word tenant' shall include a
person who occupies a room or
rooms as a lodger only where the
room or rooms is or are let to that
person in an unfurnished state;
and
(iii) for the purpose of paragraph
(c) of this section, a naval or military voter who is registered in
respect of a residence qualification
which he or she would have had but
for his or her service shall be
deemed to be resident in accordance
with that qualification."
(2) The Local Government (Franchise) Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
is hereby repealed.

also forgot to tell us that at the last

Sidney Webb, had written a book, that in
that book were 42 positive remedies for
unemployment, and that during the

into operation so that this land of ours
would be a land flowing with milk and

What was the result? When one of
the Clydeside Socialists got up in the
House of Commons and asked Mr. Tom
Shaw when they were going to stop fooling
with their own party and the people of
this country and when they were going to
submit the positive remedies for unemployment the reply, as is well known, was,
"You cannot take rabbits out of a hat."
We knew before Mr. Tom Shaw was
Minister of Labour that the Socialist
Party were very clever in doing conjuring
tricks. We would have thought that
some of those positive remedies would have
been introduced and the people of this

Ireland need not fear to go before the

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The number of appointments made to the staff of Belfast
Prison during the past twelve months is
11. Of these 6 had previous military service, and of the remaining five, two were
appointed on the grounds of special qualifications; the remaining three, although
possessing no previous military, police or
prison service were, after careful investigation of the qualifications of the available candidates, considered most suitable
for the positions.
One of the officers appointed for special
clerical duties was, prior to his appointment, employed in a linen firm, but it was
understood that his employment with the
firm concerned was about to terminate at
the time he was selected for appointment
in the Prison Service.
Colonel WOODS: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if he can possibly be justified in appointing a man who was still
in the employment of a Belfast linen firm
to the Prison Service when there are so
many ex-Servicemen available to fill the
position.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If the man is
more suitable I consider I am amply justified. In regard to the suggestion that
I do not give preference to ex-Servicemen,
I would point out that out of 33 appointments made since 1921, 25 were given to
ex-Servicemen.
