Sir DAWSON BATES: I am; and I
may say I am extremely glad to have this
opportunity of making a full statement on
this matter, as it will, I hope, be the means
of removing a great deal of misapprehension which has arisen, partly as a result of
an imperfect knowledge of the arrangements actually arrived at and the reasons
which led to these arrangements, and
partly, I regret to say, as the result of
deliberate misrepresentation of the facts
by those who are personally interested.
The matter is of such importance that I
am sure I will be forgiven if I take the
time of the House at some length.
up
I would, first of all, ask the House to
consider carefully the problems with which
the Government is faced, and to appreciate
them fully. I think it is necessary to ask
the House to allow me to show the attitude
that all Governments have had to take up
for generations past in regard to the
traffic problem.
It has long been an established principle
that there was a duty imposed on the State
to ensure that passenger traffic, whether it
is by road, rail or sea, is properly conducted. It has always been recognised
that where a privilege has been conferred
on companies or individuals of carrying
passengers for hire it is the bounden duty
of the State to see that such obligations
are imposed on the bodies or persons enjoying these privileges; first of all, to provide for the safety of the public and, at
the same time, to give the public reasonable facilities at reasonable fares.
It cannot be disputed that the tendency
is for transport that is left to itself to
become practically a monopoly, and if you
have that tendency it is absolutely
essential that the State should interfere
to protect the public. And therefore we
have to consider what should be the principles which should guide the State in
interfering in the case of road passenger
traffic.
I suggest that the first essential is that
this traffic should be conducted with due regard to the safety of the ordinary users of
the road. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I further suggest that it must also be conducted with due regard to the safety of
the passengers; and third, that it must be
conducted with due regard to the convenience of the travelling public. That is
to say, that the public are entitled to be
provided with reasonable facilities at
reasonable fares.
I can mention several other factors, but
there is one factor that must not be lost
sight of, and that is, that due regard must
be paid to the wear and tear of our roads,
which, at the present time, is a matter of
concern, not alone to the Government, but
to the various local authorities.
I have said that these principles have
Even
been recognised for many years.
the old stage coach was not free from regulation, and when we come to the days of
the railways, the Parliaments of those
days, realising the added danger to the
travelling public by this form of transport, imposed restrictions solely in the
interests of the travelling and the general
public. If hon. Members will take the
trouble of reading the history of any of
the great English railways they will see
that there was much resentment felt at
the restrictions which were then imposed
on the railways, as it was felt that these
restrictions were imposed, not in the interests of the general public, but in the
interests of other competing transport
systems, such as canals. So far as railways are concerned these restrictions, instead of being lessened, have been increased from year to year in view of the
increasing dangers following
increased speeds at which passengers were
carried.
on
the
But the State took a further step. In
return for the concessions given to the
railways they imposed conditions as to
the maximum fares and minimum services, and the result to-day is that every
railway must provide for the benefit of
the public a certain number of trains
every day and at certain fares-fares
which they could not increase without the
authority of the State.

What was said of the railway restrictions by the superficial critic in those days
is very similar to what is being said by
the ill-informed critic of our proposals
to-day, but looking back everyone can
appreciate that the restrictions and obligations imposed were both reasonable and
necessary.
Coming now to tramways, we find a
similar state of affairs. We find that
where Parliament has given an exclusive
right to a tramway undertaking to work
a service within a certain area, that it has,
in return for that, imposed on the undertaking heavy obligations compelling the

tramways to carry workmen at cheaper
fares, and compelling them also to provide
convenient services on all sections of the
roads in that area whether they were paying routes or the reverse.
We come now to the ordinary hackney
vehicle. From time immemorial the
local authority had the right to license and
limit the number of hackney vehicles plying in any particular area, and also to
provide for the fares that these vehicles,
which are limited in number, should
charge to the public, and that they were
constructed and maintained in a suitable
manner.
This Parliament itself has dealt with
this matter. In 1926, as hon. Members
are aware, the Motor Traffic Act was
passed. That Act required that all public service vehicles must comply with the
conditions which were designed to secure
that the vehicles were of proper construction, and that the drivers were physically
fit, and were otherwise qualified to drive
the machine, and, above all, that the
owners would be in a position to meet all
legal claims for compensation for injury
caused by their vehicles. It also subjected the drivers of road passenger vehicles, in common with other forms of motor
transport, to very heavy penalties for
breaches of the law which would
danger the lives of either their passengers
or the general public. Parliament again.
showed its concern in the problem of road
transport when it passed the Roads Improvement Act, which had for its object
the making of the roads more safe for
motor users and for the public.
en-
While these Measures have proved most
useful, motor transport has increased with
such rapidity that they cannot be regarded as, in any sense, a final solution
of the problem. The House might be interested to know that the number of public service motor vehicles of the omnibus
type has more than doubled in four years.
No one in this House can contemplate
with equanimity that last year, in this
small Province of ours, with a population
of 1 million, there were no fewer than
1,436 accidents, involving injury to no
fewer than 1,530 persons and the death
of 102, while up to October of this year,
a period of only seven months, there were
no fewer than 1,217 accidents, involving
injury to 1,320 people and the death of
93.
When I quote these figures, I do not
wish to place the responsibility for these
accidents on the buses. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). That responsibility must be
shared, not alone by them, but by other
motor users, and even by pedestrains. I
only quote these figures to get the House
to realise the seriousness of the problem,
and the heavy responsibility which lies
upon my shoulders-a responsibility which
I am entitled to ask the House to share
with me. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The question of the traffic problem in
Belfast has been prominently before the
public for some time, and it is perhaps
well that I should refer to it first, but I
would ask the House not to lose sight of
the fact that it is really only part of a
larger problem. It is examined at very
considerable length in the report of the
inspectors whom I appointed to hold an
inquiry into the application for confirmation of by-laws submitted for approval
by the Belfast Corporation. The matter
is dealt with at very considerable length,
both on general principles and with particular regard to the situation in Belfast
itself. This report and the correspondence following upon it are now in the
hands of hon. Members.
I cannot hope in the time at my disposal to go into the matter at the same
length to-day, but I propose to endeavour
to give the House a summary of the situa
tion that presented itself to me. May I
first of all point out that by the Belfast
Tramway Acts the Imperial Parliament
conferred on the Corporation what was,
in practice, the exclusive right to road
transport within the city, and under that
authority the Corporation, on behalf of
the citizens, invested very large sums of
money, and acting upon that authority
the Corporation constructed the present
tramway system. But Parliament also
conferred on the Corporation the means
of preserving their exclusive right by enabling them to endorse conditions on
licences issued by them, without which no
omnibus could ply in the city.
In 1926 this Parliament realised that
the time had come when, in place of each
local authority in Northern Ireland having the power to issue licences with or
without examination, there should be a
centralised system for the purpose of ensuring better inspection of the vehicles
and uniformity in regard to the terms in
which they were issued, and if no other

This Section enables local authorities to

hire in the city without restriction.
The Act was passed in November,
1926, and in order to give ample opportunity to every local authority, such as
the Belfast Corporation, to frame the
by-laws to give effect to the powers that
were conferred on them of regulating the
traffic, we did not bring the Act into
operation until the 1st July, 1927, which,
in effect, gave ample opportunity to any
local authority to frame and present their
by-laws for confirmation.
Unfortunately, the Belfast Corporation were dilatory in the matter and did not present
any by-laws for confirmation until nearly
a year afterwards.
But, owing to the procedure which is
prescribed by Act of Parliament, before
the by-laws can be confirmed, involving
the holding of a public inquiry, it would
have been impossible for the Ministry to
have given a decision on the by-laws until
a very short time ago. In the meantime
the omnibus proprietors seized the opportunity in the early part of June last to
put services into the streets of Belfast,
and entered into an intensive competition
with the tramway undertaking.
The evidence at the inquiry was conclusive. It showed first that unrestricted
competition by motor omnibuses must result in the closing down of the Tramway
undertaking with disastrous results from
a financial point of view to the city, and
heavy financial burdens on the ratepayers. It showed secondly that it produced great congestion of the traffic, and
consequent danger to the public. It
further showed that this unrestricted
competition must in the end place the
public at the mercy of the ordinary omnibus proprietors who, unlike the tramway
undertaking, are not under any obligation as regards either the fares to be
charged or the services to be provided.
sums
Under the Acts, the Belfast Tramway
undertaking has to pay rates
on its
permanent way, which forms part of the
city streets. It has to make and maintain this permanent way out of its earnings. It has to pay substantial
every year to the general funds of the
Corporation by way of rent, and it must,
above all, maintain convenient services for
the public whether those routes are paying or not, and if there are losses in any
one particular route they must be borne
out of profits on the more thickly populated routes.
It is also bound to carry workmen during
certain hours at half the ordinary fare, a
traffic which naturally results in a loss
which has to be borne out of the general
profits of the undertaking. It has been
estimated that whereas the tax payable
by an omnibus amounts to approximately
£2 per seat per annum, the obligations
cast on the tramway undertaking are
equivalent to at least £4 a seat. It must
be obvious to every Member of this House
that, with the advent of unrestricted and
uncontrolled motor omnibus competition,
a state of chaos was produced in the city
of Belfast which was dangerous to the
safety of the public.
The central streets of Belfast at the
present time cannot be crossed by the
ordinary pedestrian without considerable
danger to life or limb, and therefore I
think hon. Members will agree with me
that no one could contemplate a continuance of that condition of affairs. The
position was sufficiently bad in this respect
at the date of the inquiry, which was
commenced on the 27th August last, but
within a day or two afterwards it was
stated that negotiations for a settlement
were proceeding during the inquiry involving a payment of a sum of money to
those omnibus proprietors who were plying in Belfast.
The effect of this was that omnibus
proprietors either purchased new vehicles,
or brought their vehicles in from the
country, to ply in the streets of Belfast
with a view of sharing in the spoil, and
eight new services were placed on the
streets within a few days. Some of these
services were not ordinary omnibuses.
Some of them were chars-a-bancs which had
been used during the summer, and which,
for the time being, had been converted
into improvised omnibuses of a wholly
unsuitable character. I do not think
anyone can suggest that any of these vchi-

cles so placed on the streets of Belfast
were placed there with any desire that
they should remain there permanently,
or that they should fulfil a public need.
The object of their being placed there was
only too obvious. I do not quarrel with
the desire on the part of these proprietors
to obtain employment for their vehicles,
but I will lend no assistance, nor give
any countenance, to what I believe was
the real motive of such operators, which
was to obtain a share of the £30,000 which
would have come from the pockets of the
Belfast ratepayers. In return for what?
In return for the sale of an artificial and
a so-called vested interest.
The position was sufficiently bad from
a traffic point of view in August, but it
is infinitely worse now, and, as I said before, no one in this House can sit by and
see the situation continue. May I point
out that in Great Britain it is the invariable practice of Parliament to protect municipal transport undertakings,
and in no town of any size in Great Britain
is unrestricted competition allowed?
The position, therefore, in Belfast may
be summed up very shortly:-
(1) The traffic was reduced to a condition of chaos, constituting a menace to
the safety of the public;
(2) The municipal undertaking was
being driven into a state of bankruptcy;
(3) The omnibuses were carrying on a
cut-throat competition, not alone with the
tramway undertaking, but with each
other, and confining their energies to the
profitable streets in the city of Belfast,
leaving the trams the privilege of looking
after the non-paying routes and sparsely
populated areas.
It is unquestionable that, as a result of
this omnibus competition, the public were,
for the moment, being carried at cheaper
rates than hitherto. They were getting
greatly improved facilities, but I am satisfied that this advantage was entirely of a
temporary character and could not possibly be maintained without driving both
forms of transport into bankruptcy. But
there was a further development of the
situation which was bound to arise at a
very early date. Indeed, steps had already been taken in that direction.
The Corporation of Belfast were not
likely to stand idly by and see their undertaking wiped out of existence without
using to the full the powers which they
had, and I have no hesitation in saying
that in the absence of any interference by
the Government they would be fully justified in taking the course they proposed in
the interest of the ratepayers.
Under the Acts the Corporation have
power to run buses within the city, and
had actually ordered the first instalment of
a fleet of buses to put on the streets to fight
the existing omnibus competition. We
would then have had the spectacle of competition between private omnibuses and
the tramways, and between the Corporation omnibuses and the private omnibuses.
Whatever might have happened to the
larger private operators who were running
on the streets of Belfast, there can be no
question but that the small proprietor
would have gone to the wall, but in any
event such traffic war would have produced
not a traffic system but a traffic shambles.
I would like the House to visualise the
position which would have arisen if the
tramways were driven off the streets and
the Corporation did not enter on omnibus
traffic. The public would then have been
left at the mercy of the omnibus proprietors
who would then have been free to exact
what fares they pleased without restriction. There would have been no control
as to the services which these vehicles
would render. They would not have been
compelled to serve unprofitable routes, but
probably would have confined themselves
to the routes which paid them best.
The first essential of a city service is
that it should be of a comprehensive character, that is, that every part of the city
should be provided with adequate means
of transport, whether the routes are profitable or not, and this, I suggest, can obviously be done only where the traffic is controlled by one authority who can frame a
comprehensive scheme for co-ordinating
traffic in the area. The service must be
of a regular character, and I further suggest that there is no scope in the city traffic
for the vehicle which perambulates the
streets at irregular intervals, such as the
peak hour, seeking chance passengers, and
there are a large number of these vehicles
on the streets of Belfast to-day.
The system of transport for a large city
must be looked at as a whole, so that,
without charging unreasonable fares, the
profits made on the more thickly populated
routes can be used to meet the losses incurred in supplying adequate means of

restricted competition on such routes as

competitors were absolutely regardless of

unand dangerous driving was prevalent. We
had buses starting at the same time, racing

where arrangements were entered into by

that the vehicles were more carefully

But, while I make this admission, in
other respects I regard these private arrangements as a menace to the travelling
public unless they are strictly controlled.
There is serious risk, indeed in the
course of time almost a certainty, that the
interests of the travelling public will be
a

being the case, I think it is the duty of

what would then amount to a vested interest, and have the right to exploit these

Where there is no agreement between
the owners, the large operator has a
tremendous advantage over his small competitor, who must, eventually, be driven
off the road if the competition is unrestricted, and I would ask hon. Members to bear
this point particularly in mind, having regard to a matter which I shall have to
refer to later. As I have already pointed
out, unrestricted competition may mean
low fares temporarily. These fares mean
loss to the operators, and what is invariably lost sight of by the public is, that this
loss must invariably sooner or later be
paid for by the public themselves.
To sum up then, the position of the
country is as follows: On the one hand
we have either unrestricted competition,
congestion of the roads and reckless driving, with consequent danger to the travelling and the general public, or on the other
hand we have the other evil, competition
restricted by private arrangement amounting to nothing less than unrestricted
monopolies.
In trying to find a solution to this
problem, what have we got to aim at? In
both town and country what we want is
regular services, running a sufficient
number of vehicles to meet the legitimate
needs of the travelling public, running regularly at scheduled times and at reasonable fares from and to suitable points. I

believe in this way and in this way only

It is absolutely no use having a frequent service at cut rates for a short time,
and then when one of the operators has

So far as we are concerned, we do not care
whether the operator is large or small so
long as he runs an adequate and satisfactory service.
There is one aspect of the matter that I
would just like to refer to in passing. It
has been demonstrated, if demonstration
was needed, that in a city such as Belfast,
while the tramway undertaking remains
an essential part of the transport system,
omnibuses are also essential in order to
give a service such as the public of Belfast are entitled to demand. This fact
has been realised for many years in all the
large cities of Great Britain, and I would
be no party to depriving the citizens of
Belfast of a service of omnibuses co-ordinated with the tramway service. There
are routes and portions of routes where
the tramway is the best method of transport. On the other hand there are routes
and portions of routes where the omnibus
is the best method of transport, and what
we must get is a composite system which
will meet the needs of each area in the
best possible way. As the House is
aware, the Belfast Corporation is taking
over 50 buses from the private operators,
and I have no doubt that if, in the opinion
of their most experienced manager, who
has been responsible for providing one of
the most efficient city transport systems
in England where buses are co-ordinated
with the tramway system, he finds that
further omnibuses are necessary, the Corporation will make further provision.
This is, perhaps, a somewhat bald

the existing facilities provided by all
forms of transport, including railways, and
thirdly, the ability of the applicant to
provide an adequate and satisfactory
service.

As regards the new services created in
the country since the 27th August last,
they will be allowed to continue provided
the need for such services is shown. I
would like to emphasise that the limitation of licences on any particular route is
Bus-Tramway Agreement. 3238
Traffic Regulations-

only to remain in force if, and so long
only as the Ministry is satisfied that an
adequate and satisfactory service is being
provided. Every omnibus proprietor will
have to satisfy the Ministry that he is
providing a service which is meeting the
reasonable needs of the public, and that
he is charging reasonable fares.
It has been suggested that there is free
competition at the moment, but this is
far from being the real state of affairs.
It is common knowledge that the two
largest operators in Northern Ireland,
after conducting a traffic war for some
time, have entered into private arrangements strictly limiting, if not abolishing,
competition between them.
It
It has also been suggested that the
agreement which has been arrived at has
been made exclusively in the interest of
the large operator, and that the interests
of the small operator have been sacrificed.
This is one of the grossest pieces of misrepresentation which I have ever heard.
is-may I say y?-a deliberate falsehood
spread by interested persons in order to
rope in a number of small operators who
may not be in a position to ascertain the
facts, and to obtain their support in
order that the selfish interests of these
particular persons may be served.
What are the facts? Hitherto the
small operator has been largely at the
mercy of the large omnibus proprietors.
Where this unfortunate man has built up
by his industry a business in the country
and has served the needs of a small area
•
regularly for some years, the large
operator, casting covetous eyes on this
territory, proceeds to swamp the route
with vehicles at cut fares until his unfortunate competitor is driven into bankruptcy. That power is now taken away
by the terms which the Ministry insisted
should be included in the agreement. On
the one hand, the small operator providing
a genuine service will be protected so long
as he continues to supply a service
which is adequate and satisfactory and
meets the public needs. On the other
hand, and this is a great benefit which
accrues to the large operator, where he has
established a proper service on a route
and is serving the public well, he will, in
his turn, be protected against a form of
blackmail which has become prevalent.
namely, men of straw setting up a service
at uneconomic rates in competition, not
with the object of establishing a permanent service, but of making it worth
while to the large operator to buy them off.
Such competition is not in the public interest, because the cost of it is ultimately
borne by the public itself.
It has been said that we are limiting the
number of licences, and it has been said
I am creating monopolies. This I
emphatically deny. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I am doing away with
monopolies. (Hon.
Members: Hear,
hear.) What I am doing is taking control, not in the interests of any class of
operator, but in the interests of the
public. As I have already pointed out,
in many cases there is already a virtual
monopoly, and on the remaining routes
I have no doubt that if matters were left
to take their course there would very
shortly be an uncontrolled monopoly.
The Government came to the conclusion
that if there is to be limitation of competition, as undoubtedly there is, and will
be, it is far better that it should be
subject to a State control which will only
be exercised in the interests of the public.
The Government, therefore, have agreed
to the principles of the arrangement proposed, because they think that the
arrangement is in the public interest.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
arrangement can in its essentials be carried out at once by the exercise of the
powers given to the Ministry of Home
Affairs under the Motor Traffic Act of
1926, but in order that they may be
carried out in their entirety it will be
necessary for the Government to propose
legislation to Parliament, and I intend
to introduce the necessary legislation in
the next Session.
In the course of the preparation of the
necessary measure to be introduced into
this House I propose before finally submitting the Bill to the House to consultas I have always done in the past- -all interests concerned, including omnibus
owners, railways and the Roads' Advisory
Committee, which, as hon. Members are
aware, is a statutory body representing
the various transport interests, including
local authorities.
It has been suggested that we have sold
the roads of Northern Ireland to two of
the largest operators. I cannot conceive
how any intelligent person who reads even
the portion of the correspondence between
the parties, which was published in the
Bus-Tramway Agreement. 3240
Traffic Regulations-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
Press, could honestly make such a suggestion. As I have pointed out already,
this agreement applies to every operator
in Northern Ireland, whether large or
small. They will operate on the roads
subject to a control which is infinitely
more strict than has been in existence
hitherto. The public will have a protection that they never had before. I say
that the allegation was not made bonafide. I have not sold the roads.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN:
said you did?
Who
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am regaining
control of the roads and saving them for
the public, and that is the policy of the
Government. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). There is another thing I wish to
emphasise, and that is, that we have
made it very clear that there is going to be
no saleable interests in bus licences. Under no circumstances will we allow that.
We are not going to permit the publichouse situation to arise again. We have
laid it down in the clearest terms that
if there is any change of ownership, the
licence must be surrendered to the Ministry, and the Ministry will be at full
liberty to reissue it to any person they
deem fit: Such a provision is absolutely
inconsistent with monopoly, and shows
more clearly than anything else the utter
absurdity of the suggestions which have
been made.
May I again point out to the House
that the limitation of licences has been
found necessary in every part of Great
Britain, a power which is exercised every
day by all local authorities who are the
licensing authority outside London. London, however, has been cited as the great
example of the benefits of free competition, but those who use such an argument
lose sight of the fact that with the unlimited issue of licences, the situation in
London had become so intolerable that
the Imperial Parliament found it
necessary to pass the London Traffic Act
of 1924, giving powers to limit the issue
of licences and to co-ordinate the traffic.
I do not suggest that the scale of traffic
in Northern Ireland is comparable to
London, but we can at least learn this from
London, that every year that the problem
is left undealt with adds to the difficulties. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
traffic of London, owing to the vested
interests which had grown up under unrestricted competition, has now become
so great as to render the traffic problem of
London the despair of Commission after
Commission.

As is evidenced by the Motion which
was placed on the Paper yesterday by my
hon. Friend the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle), there is some natural concern as to the fate of the employees of
the various companies who are operating
City traffic, and in order to reassure those
who may be doubtful on this point, I
would refer them to the condition which
we insisted being put in the agreement
under which the Corporation would recruit the drivers and conductors which
they require from amongst the employees
of the private operators who were carrying on city traffic.
Just one word in conclusion. I have
heard and read a great deal of destructive criticism of this agreement. I have
not yet seen one constructive suggestion
as to an alternative method of dealing
with the problem. Are we to allow the
matter to drift into the position which
it has got into in Great Britain and
other countries? May I refer to a leading article which appeared in the "Irish
Times" which points out that we have
set an example to London and Dublin
in our determined attempt to solve the
traffic problem. Now, I suggest, is the
proper time, not a few years hence when
the difficulties will have enormously increased. As I have already said, it is
a problem of the greatest difficulty and
I have given it the most careful consideration, and I am satisfied that the
solution I have proposed is not only the
true one, but the only one.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that
it is only within the last hour or hour
and a half that Members have had the
White Paper in their hands, I think
we are indebted to the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs, for
the lengthy explanation that he has given
of this matter. I am sure we all hope
that we will set an example to London
and Dublin in regard to the method of
traffic control. However, I think there
is room for grave doubt as to the capability of the right hon. Gentleman or
his Government to set an example to
anybody in the control of anything anywhere.

will undoubtedly charge whatever fares

Government. But in this matter we are
really carrying out a common traffic
system for the whole of Ulster, and,
therefore, we think it would be better for
us to tackle this problem as a whole and
let the public, the bus owners, and all
others know at an early stage where they
will actually stand in future, rather than
to go on drifting for some years when
there would be very great difficulty indeed in catching up with what we are able
to do to-day; and in the meantime we
would, I am afraid, be looking at more
and more accidents, and more and more
deaths taking place without us as a
Parliament having taken the steps to
avoid them. So far my right hon. Friend
(Sir Dawson Bates) has thoroughly vindicated himself in having taken the steps
he did in connection with this agreement.
Mr. DEVLIN: I am very glad to be
able to join with the noble Lord the

Mr. DEVLIN: Neither do I think this

the House into his 'confidence.
with this question in all its complexities.

thought it was essential for the information of hon. Members that such a document should be issued.
I cannot pat the Government on the
back, as the Prime Minister has patted
himself and his colleagues on the back,
because of the wonderful wisdom they
have displayed in coming forward at this
stage to deal with this problem and to
bring about a solution. It is not their

them. We never would have had this

and the complications that have arisen
from the lack of vision shown by the Corporation in not handling this question at
an earlier stage, just as the same lack of
vision has been shown by the railways in
not seeing the necessity for supplementing
the railway traffic by bus traffic, which
anyone with eyes in his head could see
was obviously to be one of the great traffic
factors of the future. That is what
brought this question up, not the prevention of accidents; it was not in order
to avoid those fatalities, a list of which
has been read by the Minister of Home
Affairs to-day. These were not the
reasons at all. If the Government twelve
months ago had taken up this question
and had dealt with it in the comprehensive way in which they have dealt with it
to-day then they would have been entitled to the tribute they now pay to
their own belated efforts.
However, I do not want to be too controversial on this subject. I just want to
say a word or two on the general question.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. George
Henderson), to whose admirable speech I
listened with great attention, though I disagree with most of it-in fact the speeches
I admire most are the speeches with which
I disagree delivered an impeachment of
the Government for daring to give a
monoply to the city authority.
I am
opposed to monoplies, but not to public
monoplies. What is this monoply? It is
the property of the public State; it
belongs to the State; to the citizens
and the people of the State. They
can control it for good or for ill. If they
elect a bad Corporation they pay the price.
If they elect a good Corporation they get
the reward. If there is any justification
at all for the ownership of public utilities
by public authorities surely it is the ownership of our vehicular transport that so
touches every branch of life, civic and
otherwise.
Therefore, I say that, in so far as the
Government give a full and complete
monoply in the control of all that makes
for the traffic of our city and of all the
conveniences incidental to it, I am fully
in accord with them. You must have a
public authority of some sort. The Corporation is the public authority for the
moment. Some people do not like it.
Some people want commissioners. If the
commissioners are appointed they are the
public authority. Whoever may be in
charge of the civic administration of the
community is the public authority. I
myself have never joined in any attack on
the Corporation, past or present. I think
they are entitled to a good deal of the
criticism-though perhaps they are not
entitled to all of it-that has been levelled
at them, but this I do say: They are the
elected representatives of the people, and
as a democrat I stand for the defence of
the elected representatives of the people.
As I say, if the people are so lacking in
wisdom or in the genuine political instinct
as not to select proper persons to defend
their interests then the people must suffer
for it. That is all I have to say in
regard to that point.
In the second place, I am very glad of
the arrangements that have been made
with regard to private buses within the
city area. There is no doubt-and the
strange thing is that I am now standing
with the white sheet of the penitent round
me-I was a tremendous believer in bringing in these buses. I believed the more
competition there was the better it would
be for the citizens. I myself, although
I was told that no citizen of Belfast
should travel on these buses, and that if
you supported the buses you would destroy the tramway which was civic and
corporate property, went on the buses.
But what has been my experience?
When these buses got into the city they
did not give the accommodation or the
convenience to the people that they had
promised to give.
Let me give a case in point. I live at
Glengormley. A bus takes me there more
quickly than the tram, and I do not get
seasick on a bus as I would on many of

It

Every one of our modern evils-economical and industrial-is due to the fact that

hear.
Mr. DEVLIN -in London, or in

The second point is this.

Again, I say to the Prime Minister that

I just want to say this before I sit down.
The hon. Member for Antrim has said

I sat as

think it would be a grave injustice-I

SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
HOME AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I
would like to give expression to the
thanks my right hon. Friend and myself
feel to every Member of the House for the
manner in which they have approached
this matter, and for the frank way in
which they acknowledged and emphasized
the parts of this contract that they
thought were for good in the hope that
this big problem that has given us all so
much anxiety and care should be solved.
Every hon. Member in the House must be
perfectly satisfied with what we have done
in regard to the City of Belfast. The
trams in Belfast were owned by the ratepayers of Belfast and they were being
utilized in the manner in which they
were and to the extent to which they
were, solely in the interests of the ratepayers of Belfast.
The buses that came in came in to be
used and were used solely in the interests
of the man who owned them. He operated
where there was money to be made, and
he never went near the parts of the City
where he was not going to make money.
I do not blame him. If I had been a
bus owner I do not know that I would
have acted differently. That was the
fact. And their activities were carried
on to such an extent that having passed
to the state of being a nuisance they came
to be a menace. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) And then it was necessary that
steps should be taken. As has been
pointed out and proved, it was necessary
to deal with this problem because we
'could see, and every hon. Member in the
House could see, that the same state of
affairs would exist on those remunerative
routes in the country.
Now I want to emphasize for a moment
the point that has been made by the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)-
indeed by quite a number of hon. Members. That was in regard to the alarm
in the country about the small bus owner.
That was got up as a deliberate fama by a
number of interested people. They
formed an association about a week ago
Bus-Tramway Agreement. 3274
14 NOVEMBER 1928
Traffic Regulations-
Mr. W. MCMULLEN: A week ago?
Mr. HANNA: I think it was a week
ago, and a gentleman called Hurst moved
a resolution:-
"That we, representing some 70
Ulster bus owners and others interested
in road transport, protest emphatically
against a Government Departmen,
supposed to act in the interets of all,
assisting certain bus owners to secure a
monopoly of country services.
consider the action of the Home Office
illegal, unconstitutional, and unprecedented in any free country, and we
ask for and rely on the support of the
Ulster public in whatever steps may be
necessary to annul this action and prevent such monopoly."
In speaking to the resolution the gentleman stated that the Ministry of Home
Affairs is solely responsible and unless you
are going to fight without kid gloves you
are going to lose. If ever any man required to wear gloves to cover the dirt on
his hands it was this man.
We are prepared to take off the gloves at any time.
Within a week or so before it that gentleman sought to be appointed agent for one
of the bus proprietors who, it was thought,
would acquire something in the nature of
a monopoly, and he wanted to sell his
buses at a certain price with a 5 per cent
commission. And then he was to head a
deputation of bus owners to us in the
Home Office yesterday. There is the
beginning of this terrible fama. He
would collect the small bus owners and
sell their buses at a commission and then
tell us that they are a Passengers' Protection Society. No matter how foolish
the right hon. Gentleman and myself look
we know what is going on, and when
people take off gloves to fight us—we do
not want to fight-
Mr. HEALY: But by jingo if you do!
Mr. HANNA-but we are going to
stand up and answer.
What is the exact
position in regard to these people in the
country? There is no suggestion of taking
the buses off the streets of Belfast and
putting them on the roads in the counties.
There is no such bargain as that at all.
Those people who were supplying a service
of buses on the 27th of August in the rural
areas are to be allowed to continue the
services that they gave. And they were
pioneers in going out there and establishing services of their kind, and in my view
they are entitled to some little consideration in that regard. They had bought
their buses; they had established their
services, and it would be very wrong to put
them on exactly the same level as the
gentlemen of the Road Passengers' Protection Association. How could you do
that? How could you stand at the Treasury Box and justify any such attitude?
What do we do? We say to them-not
that you will have a monopoly-no such
thing. They are to have no monopoly.
They cannot sell or barter the licence they
have got.
The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
G. Henderson) said why not give
them some sort of goodwill, but just
before that he told us that these big
corporations would not obey us.
If you
give them a saleable interest, what will
happen? The strong man will come in
again, and he will buy up the small ones
if we give a saleable interest, and then
you will have a monopoly. But what have
we?
We have this arrangement made in
the country, and the man who has a service and has his buses there will be allowed
to continue. Not only that, but if a
further service is required on that road
and he can rise to it and give a satisfactory,
safe and adequate service then he is to
have a chance of doing it.
But if he cannot then another person will be licensed
to go out if he has got proper buses.
We are not in any shape or form interfering with the rights or privileges of the
rural districts as they exist at the moment.
We do nothing to disturb them. It would
be impossible to do as the hon. Member
suggests to give these rural authorities
licensing power, and I will tell you why.
You would have no uniformity in regard
to this matter at all; you would
have one rural district council allowing licences to a certain number of
buses, and you would have another that
would take an altogether different view
on account of the difference in the condition of the roads or some matter of that
sort. If any rural or other authority is
satisfied that a suitable and adequate service of buses is not being offered in their
district they can, just in the same way as
any single individual may do, come and
make representations to us, so that something could be done as far as lies within
our power to see that they would have a
proper service.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
We
The hon. Member for West Belfast suggested that in relation to what took place
in the city of Belfast, Home Affairs might
have acted more than a year ago.
had acted, but the statutory obligation
imposed on Belfast Corporation was a
matter that only they themselves could
fulfil. They did not produce the by-laws. I
think it was a great pity that the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) was taken away from the Corporation. I understand that if he had
remained there he would have had the bylaws presented in good time, and all this
thing would have been avoided.
The word monopoly has been mentioned.
I cannot understand its use in regard to
this matter. The word monopoly suggests
having power, complete control. There
is nothing of the kind here. If you have
a monopoly of something it is something
you can sell. There is nothing here that
anybody can sell or keep except on the
strictest of strict conditions. How anybody who appreciates the meaning of
English words, and particularly the word
monopoly, can suggest that there is anything in the nature of monopoly here is a
matter that gives me a wonderful amount
of concern. On the whole there has been
nothing but praise and support of the
action taken by the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates).
There is one other thing I want to say.
I have been in very close association, as
hon. Members know, with the Minister of
Home Affairs in regard to this matter,
and I would like to take this opportunity
of paying my tribute to the single purpose
and honesty with which he approached
this difficult matter and carried it out.
If ever there was a situation where there
was no shadow of leaning on one side or
another here is a case. There was no
leaning towards the railway companies,
or towards the big bus owners as against
the small bus owners, or towards the
small bus owners as against the big ones.
The one matter that was kept in the
forefront by the right hon. Gentlemanand I had the honour to help him with
the assistance of the very able staff we
have at the Home Office-was the safety
and convenience of the public, and because we have kept that so closely
before us and followed it so rigidly
practically for the first time in this House
there has been unanimous approval of the
action taken by the Minister of Home
Affairs in connection with this matter.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

Thursday, 15th November, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
THE GOVERNMENT'S DERATING
PROPOSALS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether, in view of the importance of his derating proposals, as outlined in his speech to a Unionist association,
he is prepared to seek the opinion of the
various local authorities on his scheme of
derating, and to issue his scheme to
Members of the House as a White Paper;
and whether he considers it desirable to
inform his own party meetings of proposals of which he keeps the general
public in ignorance.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): A Bill dealing with the
machinery which will be required in connection with the derating of certain
hereditaments will be presented in the
House this afternoon. I hope that it
will be possible to take the Second Reading next week, when a full statement will
be made in regard to the proposals to
which the Bill relates.
The Derating Scheme itself will form
the subject of further legislation, and
the hon. Member may rest assured that
the local authorities will be consulted
during the preparation of the Measure.
Mr. KYLE: In view of the fact that
a White Paper was issued in June last
explaining the derating proposals adumbrated in the British House of Commons.
to enable these authorities and other interested people to make full inquiry into
those proposals, would the right hon.,
Gentleman not expedite the matter of
issuing a White Paper explaining the derating proposals? He says this Bill
merely explains the machinery for his
derating proposals. What I want issued
is a White Paper explaining how it is.
going to affect the local councils in the
Six Counties.
Mr. POLLOCK: The matter will be
expedited as much as possible under the
circumstances, but I would remind the
hon. Member that the character of the
Measure in the Imperial Parliament is
a totally different matter from that which
governs our proceedings here, but that
later on when the implications and all
the details of our proposals are worked
out between the local authorities and ourselves, then it will be time enough to issue
a White Paper explanatory of the entire
subject. As the ultimate Measure will
not become operative until the month of
October next year there can be no particular reason for any unnecessary hurry
in the matter.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
whether the right hon. Gentleman thinks
it desirable to inform party meetings
of the proposals of which he keeps this
House in ignorance.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think it necessary either to offer any explanation
or defence of my action in that matter.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If I did
I would remind the hon. Member that
when I opened my Budget in the month.
of May last I entered into this matter
at very considerable length, and my
action on the date referred to by hon.
Members was merely a reiteration and
amplification of what I said then.

DEATH OF MRS. A. CASSIDY,
BELFAST.
4. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
order an inquiry into all the circumstances
governing the death of Mrs. A. Cassidy,
of 52 Sultan Street, who died in childbirth
on the 28th October last.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As promised by me
on the 8th instant, I have made inquiries
into this matter, and I find that the
woman in question was not a Dispensary
patient, but was attended as a private
patient by a doctor and midwife.
In these circumstances I have no jurisdiction to make formal inquiry, but, on
the other hand, under the provisions of
the Midwives (Ireland) Act, 1918, the
Belfast Corporation acts as the supervising
authority over midwives, and any question
as to the treatment of the patient by the
midwife concerned should be dealt with
by the Corporation.
At the same time I have received a report on the matter from the Public Health
Department of the Belfast Corporation,
from which it appears that that Department has been fully alive to the circumstances of the woman's confinement, and
subsequent death, and that it is not considered that there was any neglect or incompetence on the part of the midwife
who attended on the patient.
It is also understood that the cause of
death in this case was really kidney
disease.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman whether he
is aware that this lady suffered for five
hours and a half from hæmorrhage, and
during that time it was not possible to
get proper medical skill and attention.
Having regard to that unsatisfactory state
of affairs does he not think it is a duty

Mr. W. MCMULLEN: I would like

MATERNITY MORTALITY IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has seen a report in the Press to the effect that the
Minister of Health in Great Britain proposes to have an inquiry into every case
of maternal mortality in childbirth in
Great Britain; and whether he is prepared to follow this example in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member appears to be under a misapprehension as to the action being taken by
the Minister of Health in Great Britain
in this matter, as I understand that the
proposal in Great Britain is to obtain
reports in such cases from the Local
Medical Officers of Health, in order to
obtain statistics and medical information
as to the cause of death in each case.
In this connection I would refer the
hon. Member to the reply given to him by
me on the 23rd ultimo, to the effect that
the Ministry of Home Affairs is taking
all steps within its power to collect and
collate information regarding maternal
mortality and the causes of death.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that a special committee was
appointed in Great Britain to make inquiries into all deaths arising out of
maternity cases, and Sir George Newman
is chairman of that committee, and is he
prepared to set up a similar committee in
Northern Ireland in view of the fact that
deaths from this cause are higher in
Northern Ireland than in the Free State
or in Great Britain ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As a committee has been appointed by the Minister
of Health in England for the purpose of
collecting this particular information I
might inform the hon. Member that the
Ministry of Home Affairs before the
setting up of the English Committee had
already taken steps to collect and collate
the information.

Sir DAWSON BATES: That is the

Mr. W. MCMULLEN: Would the right
hon. Gentleman be prepared to disclose
the information he was able to collate?
So far as we know the rate is exceptionally
high in Northern Ireland, and I would
like to inquire whether the information
collected would not warrant some action
being taken by the right hon. Gentleman.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am afraid that does
not arise out of the original question.
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I ask whether,

take steps on the basis of that
information?

RAILWAY AMALGAMATION.
7. Mr. KYLE asked the Prime Minister whether he will give effect to the
promise made at Belleek in 1923, and subsequent statements in the House, on the
question of unification or amalgamation
of railways in Northern Ireland.
The PRIME MINISTER: I would
refer the hon. Member to
a very full
reply given him by the Minister of Commerce (Mr. Barbour), to a similar
question on the 8th November last, and
in addition would point out that the substance of my remarks at Belleek was an
expression of hope that ultimately transport charges might be made more easy
for farmers.
I am happy to say that this pressing
problem will be satisfactorily solved in a
different manner. As will be seen by the
Order Paper my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance has given notice of
the presentation of a Bill paving the way
for relief to the farming community, by
a grant from the Exchequer, to ensure,
among other matters, a reduction of
freightage and transport charges on certain agricultural and other staple products by rail, canal and sea, beginning
on the first of next month.
Mr. KYLE: Does that reply mean
that the Prime Minister is not prepared
to carry out the statement he made at
Belleek, namely, that it was desirable
that the railways of Northern Ireland
should be amalgamated?
The PRIME MINISTER: I have
answered that question by referring my
hon. Friend to the reply given by the
Minister of Commerce.
Mr. KYLE: That was last year's
reply.
The PRIME MINISTER: The position is exactly the same now as it was
then.
Mr. HEALY: Nothing has been done.

CLAUSE 2 (Assimilation of local
government franchise of men and
women).
(1) For the purpose of providing that
the local government franchise in Northern Ireland shall be the same for men
and women, sub-section (3) of section
four of the princpal Act shall be repealed in its application to the said
franchise, and the following section
shall be substituted for section three of
that Act in its application as aforesaid:
"A person shall be entitled to be registered as a local government elector
for a local government electoral area if
he or she is of full age and not subject
to any legal incapacity, and—
*
(a) is on the last day of the qualifying period occupying in that area,
as owner or tenant, any land or premises (not being a dwelling-house) of
a yearly value of not less than five
pounds, or a dwelling house; and
(b) has during the whole of the
qualifying period so occupied, either
in that area or, if that area is not
an administrative county or a county
borough, in any adminstrative county
or county borough in which the area
is wholly or partly situate, any land
or premises (not being a dwellinghouse) of such yearly value as aforesaid, or a dwelling-house; or
*
*
*
*
*
*
(ii) for the purposes of this section
the word 'tenant' shall include a person who occupies a room or rooms as
a lodger only where the room or rooms
is or are let to that person in an unfurnished state; and
(iii) for the purpose of paragraph
(c) of this section, a naval or military
voter who is registered in respect of a
residence qualification which he or
she would have had but for his or her
service shall be deemed to be resident
in accordance with that qualification."
(2) The Local Government (Franchise) Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, is
hereby repealed.

I mentioned on the Second Reading of
this Bill that there is a great number of
houses in the various towns that have a
valuation of £3, £4, £5, £6, and £7 10s.
The father and the mother of a household
take one of these houses. This Amendment does not aim in any way at the
tenant of the house; the tenant of the
house will still have a vote as formerly,
and if the tenant is married his wife will
have a vote as formerly. Unfortunately
the practice has sprung up of, say, two
sons of the father and of the tenant
coming to the Revision Court and saying
that they are sub-tenants of rooms
that house under their father. They will
come and say that they own the furniture
in the room, that they cook their own
meals in their own room, and that the
room is their house. As soon
as those
two sons have been disposed of, probably
two daughters will get up, and they will
claim to be joint tenants of another house
which is another room in the same house.
They will come in and say that they own
the furniture in their own rooms, and
that they cook their meals in their own
rooms. The Amendment that I am proposing does not in any way disentitle the
tenant of the house or his wife, no matter
what the valuation may be, to get a vote;
it only aims at preventing the local
government franchise being extended
sometimes to ten or twelve persons in
these small houses who are only members
of the family, and who really are only
lodgers in that house.

Mr. HANNA: The fundamental

that a bona fide inhabitant should be entitled to exercise the franchise, irrespective of whether he lives in a house of

home in our area. It is perfectly true

the evidence given in relation
matter by those who claim the vote. If
they can prove to the satisfaction of
the revising barrister that they have
in deed an inhabitant interest in the
house then their names will go on the
list. The machinery I recognize has
been altered to some little extent. All we
can hope is that by a fair and unbiassed
administration of the law as few abuses
as possible will exist in this regard, but
it will be impossible-and I am sure the
hon. Member will recognise this-when
there is very great congestion, when there
is very great shortage of houses, and
when people are compelled to live for the

inclined to live in-it will be impossible
in all the circumstances of the case and
having regard to the fundamental principle and policy I have indicated for the
Government to accept the Amendment.

After listening very carefully to the

This Amendment deals with another class
of case altogether. It is well known that
where a man in the country dies leaving
a farm of land, even if he makes a will
and the will is not proved the next-of-kin
in possession can come in and claim the
vote. I will show you exactly how that
works out. We will say a man owns a
farm and he dies leaving his son and two
daughters or two sons and two daughters.
He leaves the farm by his will to one of
his sons, and that son then becomes the
owner of the farm. No probate of the
will is taken out and the two daughters
come to the next revision sessions and
they claim local government votes as
owners and occupiers of that farm.
Mr. McHUGH: What age are they?
Mr. COOPER:
Aged 21 and
years upwards. The result of that is that two
persons are registered as local government
electors for that farm although they have
no interest whatever either in law or
equity in the farm. The same thing
happens where a man dies without a will
at all and where no administration is taken
out, because in that case the same two
daughters come and claim to be owners and
occupiers of he farm. They say no administration has been taken out, and
therefore both are registered as local
government electors. Those people were
given votes by a decision of the Court of
Appeal in Dublin some years ago. The
decision was that where a will had not
been proved or letters of administration
had not been taken out these people were
the next-of-kin in possession. It led to

other. They are asked if probate of the
will has been taken out and they say no.
They are asked if letters of administration

is very well known that letters of administration or probate have been taken out in

CLAUSE 3 (Local Government Franchise (Companies) ).
The principal Act as amended by
this Act shall, in its application to the
local government franchise in Northern
Ireland, have effect as if the following
section were inserted therein after section three:-
*
"4.-(1) Where any company has,
during the whole of the twelve months
ending on the last day of the qualifying period, occupied as owner or
tenant any land or premises of the
yearly value of not less than ten
pounds in a local government electoral
area in Northern Ireland, and is rated
for the relief of the poor in respect of
such land or premises, then, subject
to the provisions of this section, such
company may make a claim to have
such person as is specified in the claim.
registered as a local government elector in respect of the said land or
premises, and the said person shall be
entitled to be registered accordingly.
Such occupation of land or premises
by a company as complies with the
requirements aforesaid is hereinafter
referred to as a company qualification.'
"(2) Where a company qualification is derived from land or premises
of a yearly value greater than ten
pounds, a claim under this section
may be made by the company for the
registration of each one of several
persons, not exceeding in any case six,
and, subject as aforesaid, each such
person shall be entitled to be registered; provided that the yearly value
of the land or premises from which
the company qualification is derived
is not less than the amount produced
by multiplying ten pounds by the
number of persons in respect of whom
the claim is made.

Mr. KYLE: This is a Clause that has
met with much criticism from this
side of the House and also much opposition amongst democratic organisations outside. I understand the attitude of
supporters of many of the Members of
the Cabinet in desiring to see the vote
given to representatives of bricks and
mortar and the representatives of money.
That is one of the reasons why I want to
see this Clause deleted from the Bill. I
think it is an iniquitous proposal and unparalleled in modern times to give companies votes. It is a very popular thing
to say why should a company that has a
3315 Representation of People Bill- 15 NOVEMBER 1928

[Mr. Kyle]
certain stake in the city of Belfast or the
Six Counties not be entitled to representation on the local governing body because
they own property. There is a certain
amount of sympathy attached to that particular expression. I think a good deal
of it is misguided. Nobody here desires
to see any person denied a vote for local
government purposes, but we do not want
to see that person receiving a vote simply
because he or she is wealthier than other
people in the city of Belfast. That is the
sole purpose of our objection to this
Clause.
I want the right hon. Gentleman to
treat this matter as seriously as he possibly
can, and try if he can to give instances
of where a similar Clause has been
introduced in any Bill that has been
passed in recent years by any legislature in the whole world. The whole
tendency of modern times is to say "One
man, one vote." That was an election
cry for many years, and was, I think. accepted even by members of the Conservative party, but the present Unionist administration in Northern Ireland is
trying to be more Tory than the Tories
themselves. In becoming so I think they
are giving us a weapon to beat them with.
It is quite true they may gain some local
government seats by reason of companies
getting six votes each, but surely it is not
seriously suggested that that is going to
mean cleaner or better local government.
Business men have been running Belfast
for quite a number of years-ever since
I took any interest in politics at all. It
has been alleged business men who have
been running our local affairs. They
have made such an unholy mess of it that
there has been an agitation in the country
for Commissioners. As a matter of fact
the Government themselves have had to
step in and make an arrangement with
the bus owners, for instance, to regulate
the transport traffic in the city. These
business men were not able to do it themselves. If we give them six votes in addition to the one they have, is it going to
make local government any more efficient?
If there was any hope of that it would
certainly modify the very considerable
objections we have to the proposal.
We on this side desire efficient local
government. In the administration of
the Act a tremendous lot depends on
whether the people are comfortably
housed and properly looked after. It is
not, I think, a fact that these business
men, who are being cajoled into supporting the Unionist party, have been very
efficient administrators. They have been
a laughing stock. Look at Belfast. I
am not so certain that even the County
Councils-many admirable members of
which I see in the House-are so efficiently administered, or that they are going
to make themselves more efficient by
giving companies votes. We would have
more sympathy in this matter if it could
be proved it was going to mean greater
and better administration. Apart from
that it is surely too late in the day for
the Government to set up this new fancy
franchise. In these modern times the
day of fancy franchise should be over.
It is true that we have got a fancy franchise for the Belfast Harbour Board, but
that was enacted a great many years ago.
No Government passing legislation for
Great Britain and for this country has
up to the present ever proposed to pass
an Act of Parliament that would lay
down, simply because some people are
wealthier than other people, they should
have more votes than ordinary citizens.
No person, whether he calls himself a
Tory or Socialist, could advocate a more
admirable or fairer principle than that
of one man one vote. These votes should
have the same value. People who have six
votes are wealthy men. That is a state
of affairs that I do not think this Committee should agree to for one moment.
The Amendment which the right hon.
Gentleman moved himself, and which
was accepted, limits to some extent the
possibility of a number of companies in
the same premises having quite a lot of
votes. Take premises in Belfast valued
at £500 or £600, and there are many
such. Before this Amendment was put
in it would have meant that no fewer
than ten companies could have six votes.
That is so absurd a thing nobody could
defend it. While the right hon. Gentleman has limited the. Clause to some extent it does not take away the iniquity
of the proposal to give votes to inanimate
objects. The inanimate objects are
limited companies with no bodies to kick
and no souls to save.
The representatives of these inanimate
bodies will have votes. The argument
was used here that as certain private companies have provided facilities for sport

THE DERRY MILK SUPPLY.
2. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether his attention has been drawn to
the proceedings of the Public Health
Committee of the Derry Corporation,
in which it is stated that under
the existing law there is great diffi
culty in securing convictions against
offenders; and, if so, whether the Government will amend the law in that respect,
in order to secure to the public a pure
supply of milk.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to answer this question. I am
aware that a number of cases against milk
vendors in Londonderry City have been
dismissed by the magistrates on the
ground that the milk was sold as it came
from the cow. Under the existing law,
the milk falls below the prescribed standard, the onus of showing that it has not
been tampered with rests upon the vendor,
and if he is able to satisfy the magistrates
on this point he is entitled to have the
case against him dismissed.
if
The question of the sufficiency of the
evidence is a matter for the magistrates,
and the Ministry has no function in this
respect.
I may add, however, that the law relating to the milk standards has been the
subject of discussion for a considerable
time by those concerned in the production
of milk, and by the experts of the local
authorities concerned, both as regards the
agricultural point of view and the point
of view of the consumer, and I am following the discussions carefully with a view
to taking whatever action may appear
most suitable.
48,747 cwt.

The Ministry understands that the
houses to which the hon. Member refers
have in the past suffered on occasions
through flooding after heavy rains
mainly owing to the inability of the
existing drainage system to cope at all
times with the heavy flow of storm
water.

and the Antrim County Council, and the
Belfast Rural District Council, and it
is understood that each of these
bodies is already making arrangements
which will obviate the possibility of flooding in the future.

Gentleman any idea of the danger it is to

a very serious accident happened there
quite recently and a death occurred. A
horse fell over an enbankment of ten
or fifteen feet and there is likely to be
loss of life in the near future.
Mr. HANNA: The matter is engaging the attention of the authorities whose
function it is to attend to it.

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The ob
ject of this Bill is to provide that wher
cattle, sheep and swine shipped through
Northern Ireland ports are slaughtered
3389 Slaughtered Animals Bill-

20 OCTOBER, 1928
Second Reading.
in British landing places on account of
foot-and-mouth disease compensation will
be available. The Bill provides that a
small levy per head will be made
on animals exported and these contributions will form an insurance fund out
of which compensation will be payable
in the circumstances mentioned.
The intention is that the administration of the Act should be in the hands
of trustees appointed by the trade interests concerned, and the scheme will be
self-supporting, no expenditure from
public funds being involved.
The Bill had had a generally favourable reception and the only complaint is
that it does not go far enough. It has
been suggested that its scope should be
widened so as to cover losses due to detention in lairages. In order to appreciate fully the problem to be dealt with
it seems desirable to set out the existing
position in regard to slaughter and compensation.
At present, when animals are
slaughtered in Ireland by official order
on account of foot-and-mouth disease, the
appropriate Irish Government is responsible for compensation. Similarly, when
animals are slaughtered in Great Britain, otherwise than in a landing stage,
the British Government is liable. Prior
to the passing of the Importation of
Animals Act, 1922, by the Imperial Parliament, the British Government was
liable, even when animals were slaughtered
in landing places. By that Act, however, the British Government relieved
itself of this liability, and it is this landing place gap that now remains to be
bridged. This unsatisfactory position
has been frequently stressed by the cattle
trade. A number of animals have already been slaughtered in British lairages
and the owners have received no compensation, but this Bill gives the power to
pay, even in these retrospective cases.
This retrospective clause must not be lost
sight of when considering the proposal to
extend the scope of the Measure. Losses
due to slaughter are definitely known and
can be checked. Clearly, however, it
would, after a lapse of time, be difficult,
if not impossible, to verify claims in respect of vague losses due to detention.
It is, therefore, clear that even if the demand for an extension of the measure as
proposed were admitted it could not, for
the reasons stated, be made retrospective.
a
However, the fundamental objection to
widening the scope of the Bill is that such
course must involve higher insurance
fees at Northern Ireland ports than at
Free State ports. In this connection it
may be remarked that a scheme similar
to the one embodied in this Bill, and with
corresponding contributions, has already
been put into operation in the Irish Free
State.
It is essential that nothing should be
done which might have the effect of
jeopardising the trade of our ports, and
it seems obvious that higher insurance
contributions might have such an effect.
I am not, therefore, prepared, on the information at present before me, to recommend any scheme involving higher contributions than those embodied in this
Bill.
Experience of the actual working of
the Measure will, doubtless, suggest ways
in which it can be improved, and if a
reasonable case can be made out to have
risks, other than slaughter, included
without at the same time jeopardising
trade through Northern Ireland ports the
question of extension can be reconsidered
at a future date.
Difficulties arising out of the wording
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
have heretofore prevented this matter
being dealt with in a satisfactory way in
this Parliament. Any doubts as to our
powers have, however, now been removed by the Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act recently passed
by the Imperial Parliament, so that the
way is clear to deal with the matter.
The sum of money we propose is very
small, 2d for cattle, d for sheep, and
a penny for pigs. The matter will be
worked by the parties concerned and no
money at all will be paid by the Government. I beg to move.

The principal factors in causation
were the critical periods. The main
potent contributing factor was prolonged mental stress due to the continued and exceptional industrial
depression. Number of patients admitted to Purdysburn Mental Hospital
from 1st January to date, 438, double
for 1925.
Of course, it inevitably follows that if a
decent working man is taken off the
unemployment list he is worried to death
as to what will happen to him and his
wife and children. This worry goes on
from day to day and becomes a continuous
part of his life. Is it any wonder that
there is an increase in mental disorders,
and in the state of things described by
Dr. Graham?
I know a man who came to me the
other day. He is engaged in the insurance business, and I took this statement
from him. He says:
I am twenty years at this work and
I can honestly say that I never saw
anything approaching the appalling
poverty now existing in Belfast. Every
time I call at most of the houses I miss
some article of furniture, presumably
pawned or sold, and I see a serious
difference in the health of the husband
and wife and especially the young
people. They are more starved looking,
more listless, with less hope. Most of
them had the unemployment benefit
which was stopped, then they got a few
coupons from the Board of Guardians,
and now they are living or rather dying
of slow starvation.
That is the opinion of an experienced
insurance agent, who by the nature of
his occupation gathers perhaps more
accurate information as to the conditions
of the people than any other person.
But we do not have to go to insurance
agents. We know there is not a day we

through unemployment. We will pass
from insurance agents to the larger and
more impartial authorities. From Derry,
Portadown, Lurgan and other places we

exists.

rive at some solution by which this

That is the situation we are in. Destitution and poverty are rampant in Northern Ireland at the present time. Our
Ministry of Labour are turning large numbers of people off unemployment benefit.
Those people are not able to turn to the
Poor-law Guardians in Belfast or in other

This Section, in my opinion, is a deliberate, a disreputable and a dishonest
attempt on the part of the Government
to create votes of this nature. There is
no mistaking those adjectives. I say deliberate, disreputable, and dishonest. I
will be told, of course, that the Opposition
can take advantage of this Section as well
as the Government, but that is no answer
to my argument. A man who has robbed
a bank of £500, and who has been caught
in the act by a passer-by, might as well
say to the passer-by, "Say nothing about
it, and I will give you half the spoil."
That would be tantamount to the Government telling us that we can take advantage
of this fraud that can be perpetrated
under this Section.
We will be told, doubtless, that one-man
companies will not be formed for the purpose of creating these bogus votes, but the
Government, as I say, deliberately leave
the door open to the creation of these
bogus votes, and if they did not want
votes created in this way they would have
put a limit on the capital of the company
and on the number of shareholders in the
company. It is similar to the case of a
man going on holiday for a month, and
deliberately leaving a £10 note on his
dressing-table just to see whether his servant will take it or not. The servant is
probably honest, and when he sees the
note at first it is no temptation to him,
but he knows it is there, and the temptation grows every day until eventually
he takes the note. There are such companies already on the register in the city,
and they will be bound to ask for the six
votes to which they will be entitled under
this Section, if it is passed as it stands.
Further, companies of a similar nature will
undoubtedly be formed for the purpose of
getting these votes for their members and
officers.
I come to the real reason why this

The argument has been so overwhelming that no further words from me should
be necessary. I cannot see that it ought

[Mr. Kyle]
When we had business men introduced
into the British Parliament during the
war there was not a single one of them
who was a success in his Department.
It is quite true that Lord Rhondda, who
ran the food supply of the nation before
Johnny Clynes took it on, did it fairly
well, but that was outside his particular
business and Lord Rhondda was an exceptionally clever man. But we have no
exceptionally clever business men in Northern Ireland. There may have been one
or two other little Departments which
were fairly successfully administered by
business men but they were nearly always
with brilliant exceptions like the late
Lord Pirrie, who ran the department of
merchant shipping-with brilliant exceptions like these business men have proved
their absolute incapacity for government,
and also for business, as the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) suggests. I think that it has
been proved by the state of employment
that they cannot run their businesses.
They have to appeal for State aid, for
loans guarantees to bolster up their
private businesses. If they cannot run
their own businesses how on earth do they
hope to be able to run a municipality,
where common sense is required, or a
local government area where a great deal
of acumen is needed, and even above
common sense and acumen a sound heart
and some little judgment?
Therefore, I appeal to the representatives of the legal profession on
the Government side to get up, apart
from the Minister of Home Affairs
and his able assistant, and give us
some reason for the introduction of
this vicious principle of plural voting.
We thought we had got rid of this
plural vote idea. We thought that in the
year 1928, and approaching 1929, no
Government would have been so reactionary as to make this proposal. We had
reckoned without the Northern Government. We had reckoned without the
representatives-of what? What do they
represent? Echo answers "What?"
We
had reckoned without the Northern Government. No other Government anywhere
has made such a monstrous proposal. It

of the Committee are in favour of this

any demand for this Clause. Tell us the
name of any local Unionist association
that wanted this, or even if that reactionary body, the Unionist Labour Association, wanted it.
