HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee

[Mr. Miller]
Local Government Act was passed, without changing the electoral divisions. The
result was that 100 voters in one district
have as much power as 1,800 in another.
Then Proportional Representation came
in, I think the year 1918; that was when
the real gerrymandering took place. The
Government in Dublin Castle at that time
was in the hands of a nominal Chief
Secretary, but the real Chief Secretary
was a gentleman well known to everybody.
The Local Government Board sent down
proposals for grouping the electoral
divisions, in order to form constituencies
for the system of Proportional Representation. Those proposals were put before
the various boards-the county councils
and the district councils-and they were
approved of by both. They went back to
Dublin Castle, and we all wondered why
they were not sent out in the form of an
Order. That went on until within a
fortnight of the election, and then these
provisions were sprung on us suddenly.
In the meantime, someone had gone in by
the back door and had changed them
slightly, but in such a way that they
turned Unionist divisions into Nationalist,
divisions. Then when the election took
place it was found that for the first time
in history the Nationalists had got
command.

who is an Irishman with six months' residence can have a vote. It does not make
any odds whether he comes from Belfast,
Derry, Coleraine, or even Portadown. If
he is an Irishman with six months' residence he has a vote. Under this Bill you
can have a vote if you come from Manchester, or Glasgow, or Liverpool, but
you cannot have a vote if you have lived
in Dublin, or Monaghan, or Cork. You
deserted three counties when you carried
the Act of 1920. In Monaghan and
Cavan and in parts of Donegal there are
a very large number of Orangemen and
Protestants. You left them in the lurch,
but these men hold their celebrations on
12th July. They are equally loyal to the
glorious, pious and immortal memory, and
they are more consistent in their loyalty
than you are. The Orangemen in
Monaghan are the best Orangemen in Ireland, and the Orangemen of Fermanagh
are better Orangemen still. In fact, the
farther they are away from the contamination of Belfast the purer they are in their
devotion to the finer feelings.
These Orangemen are to be branded as
aliens. Brother Knight of Monaghan is
to be branded with De Valera. (Laughter.) They are to be branded as aliens.
Having driven them into the Free State,
having deserted them and left them
in the Free State to the tender
mercies of their abiding and enduring enemies, you now say: "If you
want to come back to loyal Ulster, to the
bosom of your family; if you want to
come back here and enjoy the glories of
the Belfast atmosphere, you will have to
come and live here for three years before
you can enjoy that citizenship." That is
the proposal which is contained in the Bill
before the House to-day. England would
not do that with these people, but you do
it. You not only desert them but you
disfranchise them. You prevent them from
coming back here to their own city to enjoy its privileges. Take another case, the
case of the Canadian emigrants whom you
train at Richhill. Supposing they go to
Canada and find out at the end of three
or four years that Canada is no place for
them.

is to withdraw this Clause, and I suggest
to the Prime Minister and to the Parliamentary Secretary the advisability of
adopting that course. I have no doubt
that the Chairman is correct, but according to my deduction from the ruling of
the Chairman there does not appear to
my mind to be very much reason why this
Clause should be incorporated in the Bill.
Therefore, I suggest that for the purpose
of dealing with this matter expeditiously,
the Prime Minister and the Parliamentary
Secretary should now agree to the withdrawal of this Clause, and let us proceed
to examine the Clauses that are more controversial than this one.
This does not appear to me to be a
very controversial Clause at all. I thought
at first it was a highly controversial
Clause, but I understand now that it is
not controversial, and that we are not
permitted to examine the Schedule,
which appears to me to have a fairly
direct bearing so far as Clause 5 is concerned. Although we are precluded from
discussing this in the very careful and
close fashion in which we desire to discuss
it, I think there is sufficient justification
for the Government to reconsider their
whole attitude towards this Clause 5. I
seriously suggest, therefore, to the Prime
Minister and to the Parliamentary
Secretary that they should see the wisdom of the suggestion I am making and
agree to the withdrawal of this Clause.
I should point out that Clause 5 appears
to be perfectly superfluous, if it is confirming, as I believe, those matters that
we have discussed very fully-matters
that we have already decided. It is
simply a duplication of effort, and it would
appear to be redundant. From that point
of view, and understanding from the previous discussion in Parliament this afternoon that the Government have a
strong objection to superfluous words and
redundant sentences, we think this
strengthens the case for the withdrawal of
the Clause, so that we could proceed in
the time at our disposal to a close and
careful examination of the remaining
Clauses in the Bill to ensure that they
are not more pernicious in character than
this Clause 5.
I know that a very large number of
citizens of Belfast, and of other parts of
Northern Ireland with whom I have come
in contact, have a very deep objection to
this Clause. They hold the same opinion
in regard to Clause 5 that I hold, that the
Government should withdraw it. I have
been told more than once-in fact, I have
been told on a score of occasionsthat among other Clauses in this Bill the
Government have no mandate for this
Clause at all. Therefore, they hold, as
I do, that it would be better to withdraw
it than to cause resentment amongst the
people who, up to the present, have been
supporters of the Government. I am informed that unless the Government withdraw Clause 5 they are likely, primarily
or ultimately, to alienate the sympathy
of their supporters and to lose their votes
at the next election. We should rather
welcome the inclusion of this Clause for
that reason, if it were not for the very
objectionable features in it. I am not
influenced to a very marked extent by
the views that are held by Government
supporters. Rather am I influenced by
the number of people who object to this
Clause on principle, and it is on principle
that I now offer my objection to this
Clause.
I hope that the Members of the Committee will not allow this Clause to pass
through as quickly as the Parliamentary
Secretary suggests, because it is not quite
as simple and as innocuous as we are led
to believe it is. I think that behind these
somewhat confused lines there are many
sinister motives lurking. In view of the
short explanation given by the Parliamen-

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 22nd November, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS-
INSPECTION SYSTEM.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he is aware that all
the unions of public elementary school
teachers functioning in Northern Ireland
have expressed the utmost dissatisfaction
with the present system of inspection;
whether some inspectors consult managers
regarding the rating which they should
give instead of passing an impartial judgment on the work done by the teachers,
and that before visiting a school for the
first time some inspectors invite local persons to state their opinion regarding the
teachers; whether facts regarding the
schools which they learned as inspectors
and which are supposed to be treated as
confidential are divulged to outsiders;
whether inspectors adversely report upon
teachers within a few years of retiring on
full pension with a view to inducing them
to resign, and also on teachers of schools
with declining averages with a view to
having them removed and grants withdrawn from their schools, and refrain
from giving teachers a higher rating than
their predecessors did; and whether he
will consider the propriety of holding a
searching inquiry into inspection methods
generally.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Dissatisfaction with the present system of inspection
of public elementary schools has been expressed in varying degrees by some of the
teachers' unions in Northern Ireland, but
it is by no means the case that these
opinions have been expressed by all the
unions or in emphatic terms. I would
remind the hon. Member that only three
of the five elementary teachers who were
members of the Lynn Committee joined
in a reservation expressing dissatisfaction
with the system.
The Ministry does not believe that there
is any foundation for the allegations contained in the remaining part of the question, and action of the kind suggested, if
such took place, would meet with strong
disapproval. The hon. Member will find
on reference to the table on page 58 of
the Ministry's Annual Report for 1927-
28 that the number of teachers rated as
"highly efficient" and "efficient" respectively shows a well-marked progressive increase since 1922, while the number of
those not so rated has decreased from 14.9
to 5.8 per cent.
It is not proposed to hold an inquiry
as suggested in the question.
SMALL SCHOOLS-PRINCIPAL-
SHIPS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parlia
mentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry has
decided that teachers, after they leave
the training college, and before they
receive their diplomas, are ineligible for
principalships save those of one-teacher
schools with an average attendance below
thirty; whether he is aware that it is
more difficult to conduct such schools and
to bring them up to and keep them in a
state of efficiency than schools with
larger attendances and staffs of teachers;
whether the same efficiency is expected in
these small schools as in schools with
much larger attendances and full staffs;
and whether he is aware that for this
reason many young teachers of skill and
zeal are deprived of their diplomas.
Mr. ROBB: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative:
the Ministry does not encourage ex
students of the training colleges who are
necessarily without actual experience of
school work, except such as may be
obtained during the training course, to
take up positions as principals, and these
posts are open to such persons only in
very small schools with an attendance of
less than thirty pupils.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
22 NOVEMBER 1928
The Ministry is aware that there are
special difficulties in conducting small
schools, but these circumstances are
taken into account by the inspectors so
far as is reasonable when estimating the
value of the teachers' work, and the
Ministry has no reason to believe that on
account of them any young teachers of
skill and experience are deprived of their
diplomas. At the same time the Ministry would be glad if all candidates for
teaching posts would take up assistant-
11 ships on first leaving the training college,
but it is feared that to prohibit their
employment as principals of small

schools would make it difficult for the
managers of such schools to find teachers
for them.
MINISTRY OF EDUCATION—
REGULATIONS AND STATUTORY
ORDERS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry of
Education has issued in book form its
Regulations and Statutory Orders, and, if
not, whether it proposes to do so; and
how may those who are not teachers, but
zinterested in education, obtain copies of
the circular not on sale.
Mr. ROBB: The Ministry has not
issued its Regulations or Statutory Rules
and Orders in book form and does not
propose to do so as it is much less expensive to the majority of purchasers to
obtain separately those regulations in
which they are interested. Copies of the
Ministry's circulars are sent to all
school managers and governing bodies
concerned. Applications from other persons interested in education for copies of
particular circulars may be made to the
Ministry.
DIPLOMAS-RECOGNITION OF
TEACHERS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state how many
teachers in the triennium ended the 31st
March, 1928, have been dismissed on
account of not having received their
diplomas; how many have voluntarily resigned for the same reason; and whether
h3 is aware that some inspectors adversely
report upon young teachers with a view
of having their diplomas withheld.
Mr ROBB: Within the period
mentioned by the hon. Member recognition has been withdrawn from two
teachers on account of failure to obtain
their diplomas. In ten other cases recognition in a particular position has
been withdrawn, but the persons concerned have been allowed to seek appointments in a less responsible capacity.
The Ministry is not aware that any
teacher has resigned voluntarily on
account of not having received his diploma.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
FUND.
6. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of Finance whether the actuarial
investigation into the pension fund for
secondary school teachers, promised for
this year, has been held, and, if so, with
what result; and whether any revision of
the pension scheme is to be made in consequence.
7. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of Finance whether any portion of the
money paid by secondary school teachers
and schools towards the pension fund is
absorbed by the pension fund for primary
school teachers, and, if so, in what
proportion.
8. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of Finance whether any of the moneys
contributed by secondary schools and
teachers are invested in interest bearing
securities, and, if so, whether the increment is likely to be sufficent to provide
better pensions in the future, when larger
numbers of secondary teachers qualify
for pension.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As Questions 6, 7, and 8 are
concerned with the same subject, perhaps
my hon. Friend (Mr. Johnstone), will
pardon me if I deal with them all in a
single answer.
By Section 1 of the Teachers' Superannuation Act, 1926, all teachers' superannuation funds were amalgamated under
the name of the Teachers' Superannuation Fund, and all income and expenditure
in respect of secondary teachers is incorporated in the transactions on this
fund.
The Government actuary, who is conducting the actuarial investigation of the
Teachers' Superannuation Fund, has indicated that he is nearing the completion
of his work, and it is hoped that his report will be received before the end of
this calendar year. The report of this
investigation will in due course be laid
before the House, but until then it would
be premature to make any statement in
regard to any one class of teacher. Each
class will, of course, be treated separately
according to Sub-section (3) of Section 2
of the Teachers' Superannuation Act.
SUPERVISION OF PRIVATE
SLAUGHTER HOUSES.
9. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of
private slaughter houses in Northern Ire
land, and whether the Government are
taking any steps to have those places put
under official supervision in order to protect the health of the citizens of Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to the
latest return available there are 178
private slaughter houses in Northern Ireland. All of these, which are situated in
County Boroughs and Urban Districts, are
registered and subject to regulation
and inspection by the local Sanitary
Authority.
Some rural district councils have
acquired similar powers of regulation and
inspection of slaughter houses in their
respective areas, and with regard to those
other rural district councils where the
power does not exist the Ministry is at
present considering whether any, and, if
so, what steps should be taken to extend
the principle of inspection and regulation
generally, but the hon. Member must appreciate that it would be inappropriate
without careful consideration of the circumstances which obtain in these various
areas to apply rigid uniform rules, having
regard to the fact that in the rural areas
ia Northern Ireland a considerable number
of animals are slaughtered for the dead
meat trade in farm buildings which could
not be otherwise regarded as slaughter
houses.
Certain recommendations, however, in
this regard have been made by the Local
Government Commission, and these recommendations are being carefully
followed up.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I
wonder is the Minister aware that there
are a good many instances of where tubercular cattle are killed in these private
slaughter-houses and sold to the citizens
for human consumption. I am delighted
that the Minister has taken action, but
would the right hon. Gentleman tell me
if any other people have drawn his attention to this very serious matter?

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Finance (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
It
Mr. POLLOCK: The details of this
small Measure were given, in fact, by my
hon. Friend who usually sits beside me on
the Money Resolution which was submitted to the Committee last week.
is concerned especially with small matters
in regard to our arrangement with the
business of banks and entertainment duty.
In fact it is divided into two parts, one
relating as I have said to the business of
bankers, and the other to some comparatively unimportant changes and relief
in respect of the entertainment duty.
In respect of banking business, hitherto
the banker has paid licence duty for the
privilege of issuing unstamped notes.
But since 1828, exactly 100 years ago,
when the first imposition of a licence duty
was made in the Imperial Parliament, the
Bank of Ireland was exempt from the payment of any licence duty. I suppose that
was largely because it was the official
Government bank and it had close relations with Government matters. In
addition to that there are two banks at
present operating in Northern Ireland
that were not in existence at that time.
They did not issue any notes, and so escaped any payment, although they paid a
special duty in lieu of licence duty to
cover unstamped notes.
Finance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
It is now proposed in this small Measure to alter the system by relating the
licence to the business of banks so that
all banks operating in Northern Ireland
will require to be licensed and placed on
the same basis. The first Clause of the
Measure provides for the payment of
stamp duty to the amount of £30 for a
branch and a maximum of £120, that is
a bank operating with four branches.
Clauses 1 and 2 make provision for these
matters and also that the licence will remain in force for one year and will be
renewed in the ordinary way from year
to year.
In the carrying out of this system it is provided that three licences are
issued for the three principal offices and
all the remaining branches are named in
the fourth licence so that the maximum
of £120, being four thirties, will be provided for.
Then the old Act of 1828, to which I
have referred, laid down certain conditions in respect of banks taking out
licences to issue unstamped notes. At
that time security by bond was required,
but the question of the continuity of this
matter is of no great importance. These
conditions are still continued in the case
of note-issuing banks, and the new licence
will be recognised as a licence granted
under the Act of 1828. The special
exemption from the payment of licence
duty which the Bank of Ireland has enjoyed is now withdrawn, and the Bank
of Ireland will be in the same position as
all other banks operating in Northern
Ireland.
Up to the present, note-issuing banks
have been obliged to give bonds for the
proper performance of the conditions
imposed on them. The Ministry of
Finance should be able to dispense with
this security if it sees fit.
Of course, I
think it is not necessary in the case of
banks of such standing as are operating
in Northern Ireland and no bonds are
to be required. Therefore, that part of
the conditions of the Act of 1828 may be
withdrawn. The remaining two Subsections deal with fines and definitions,
and are of no importance.
When we come to Clause 3 we find that
this Clause deals with duty on Bills
of Exchange and bank post bills,
which, as those who are familiar
with banks know, are issued in large
numbers every day. The clause
repeals two Sections of the provisions
impler form.
and re-enacts them

The idea is to get rid of the present anomaly of the Scottish Act, and

of which only one Clause, it seems,

now
The present position in regard to composition duty and double taxation relief
will remain undisturbed. In effect
these are the particulars of this small
Measure which simply concerns the rearrangement of the conditions under
which our relations with the banks operating in Northern Ireland are carried on.
They are not of such great importance
from the point of view of any material
financial relations that are involved as to
give us any concern.
in-
I come now to the question of entertainments duty. Hon. Members will, I
have no doubt, recall that in my Budget
speech I made reference to the proposal
of the Government that relief should be
given to the two horse-racing associations
that exist in Northern Ireland.
I explained at considerable length at that
time that it was not because of
any
terest the Government had in horse-racing
per se that this would be done, but that
we were concerned to assist the farmers,
notably the farmers in the Counties of
Antrim and Down, in breeding thoroughbred horses for hunting and racing. The
Government fully realize that that would
redound, at any rate to some extent, to
the improvement of the stock in the
country and at the same time induce
larger financial returns to the farmers who
were encouraging the breeding of this
class of horses.
This Finance Measure confirms the
arrangement that was outlined in my
Budget speech, and will be found in
Clause 4. There is also another small
matter which is really a matter of definition. Under the existing arrangement
the exemption from entertainments duty
is confined to games or sports which are
played or contested, that is to say, displays are ruled out. Paragraph (a) in
Clause 5 extends the concession to gymnastic and athletic displays. It is intended that boy scouts, girl guides, and
institutions of that class which are presumably established in the public interests shall benefit.
22 NOVEMBER 1928

would facilitate to a large degree the pay..
ments of small amounts by agriculturists.
The 1927 Act deals with indoor and
outdoor sports, and some doubt may arise
in respect of the interpretation of the
Act as regards boxing. Paragraph (b)
of Clause 5 declared it to be a sport ordinarily contested indoors. The effect is that
exemption can only be granted if there
is no prize money or remuneration. It
is essential to make exemption contingent
upon a limitation in expenses. If the
expenses of any charitable entertainment
exceed 30 per cent. and are within the
ambit of taxation then Clause 6 is
intended to relieve those charitable
institutions where hardships may exist
due to the intervention of boisterous
weather or that may tend to reduce the
attendance beyond the calculations that
were originally made in regard to the tax
upon them. We think that relief should
be given when mishaps of that kind
occur. In fact, this Clause will grant
exemption to all charitable entertainments where the expenses are under £10.
As I have said, the matters are of a
trivial and unimportant character, but
they are necessary in order in some cases
to clarify the position in regard to banking and to clear up the position in regard
to entertainments tax.

Mr. POLLOCK: I can answer that
question, too. It appears that interest in
horse-racing had died down so much that
the attendances at these races and the
entrance fees were not sufficient to pay
the expenses.
We found that the burden
of the tax largely interfered with the
possibility of these races continuing to
take place, and it was in order that these
races might be continued, and that these
testing grounds for horses might be continued, that relief was given. It is not
a very large amount, but the object was
to enable those responsible to carry on
enterprises that otherwise would have
been discontinued.
The only other question was raised
by the hon. and gallant Member for
Armagh (Major Shillington), who is
interested in boxing. The object of this
little reference to boxing in the Measure,
which I have submitted, is to let the
House understand that boxing, unless
remuneration or prize money is given to
the contestants, would be relieved from
any charge. Otherwise it comes within
the ambit of the tax. I think these were
all the points that were raised in connection with this small Measure, and I hope
the House will see that it is necessary to
pass it for the purpose and convenience
of financial matters.

Sir EDWARD
ARCHDALE:
The
object of this Bill is to provide that when
cattle, sheep, and swine shipped through
Northern Ireland ports are slaughtered
in British landing-places on account of
foot-and-mouth disease compensation will
be available. The Bill provides that a
small levy per head will be made on
animals exported and these contributions
will form an Insurance fund out of which
compensation will be payable in the
circumstances mentioned.
The intention is that the administration of the Act should be in the hands of
trustees appointed by the trade interests
concerned, and the scheme will be selfsupporting, no expenditure from public
funds being involved.
The Bill has had a generally favourable reception, and the only complaint is
that it does not go far enough. It has
been suggested that its scope should be
widened so as to cover losses due to
detention in lairages. In order to appreciate fully the problem to be dealt with
it seems desirable to set out the existing
position in regard to slaughter and compensation.
At present when animals are slaugh
tered in Ireland by official order on
account of foot-and-mouth disease the
appropriate Irish Government is responsible for compensation. Similarly when
animals are slaughtered in Great Britain,
otherwise than in a landing place, the
British Government is liable. Prior to
the passing of the Importation of Animals
Act, 1922, by the Imperial Parliament,
the British Government was liable, even
when animals were slaughtered in landing
places. By that Act, however, the
British Government relieved itself of this
liability and it is this landing place gap
that now remains to be bridged.
unsatisfactory position has been frequently
stressed by the cattle trade. A number
of animals have already been slaughtered
in British lairages and the owners have
received no compensation, but this Bill
gives the power to pay, even in these
retrospective cases.
This
3789 Slaughtered Animals Bill-- 22 NOVEMBER 1928

Second Reading
This retrospective Clause must not be
lost sight of when considering the proposal
to extend the scope of the Measure.
Losses due to slaughter are definitely
known and can be checked. Clearly,
however, it would, after a lapse of time,
be difficult, if not impossible, to verify
claims in respect of vague losses due to
detention. It is therefore clear that,
even if the demand for an extension of
the Measure as proposed were admitted,
it could not, for the reasons stated, be
made retrospective.
However, the fundamental objection to
widening the scope of the Bill is that such
a
course must involve higher insurance
fees at Northern Ireland ports than at
Free State ports. In this connection it
may be remarked that a scheme similar
to the one embodied in this Bill, and with
corresponding contributions, has already
been put into operation in the Irish Free
State. It is essential that nothing
should be done which might have the
effect of prejudicing the trade of our ports
and it seems obvious that higher insurance contributions might have such an
effect. I am not, therefore, prepared, on
the information at present before me, to
recommend any scheme involving higher
contributions than those embodied in this
Bill.
Experience of the actual working of the
Measure will, doubtless, suggest ways in
which it can be improved, and if a reasonable case can be made out to have risks,
other than slaughter, included without at
the same time jeopardising trade through
Northern Ireland ports the question
of extension can be re-considered at a
future date.
Difficulties arising out of the wording
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
have heretofore prevented this matter
being dealt with in a satisfactory way in
this Parliament. Any doubts as to our
powers have, however, now been removed
by the Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous
Provisions) Act recently passed by the
Imperial Parliament, so that the way is
clear to deal with the matter.

The present Bill takes us a long step
further. In many of the large consuming
centres in Great Britain the transfer of
foreign eggs to Irish cases before exposure
for sale has become almost a trade practice,
and the mixing of foreign and home eggs
is more or less openly done. Detection is

No
of our eggs suffers in consequence.
single factor has been so detrimental to
the Home poultry industry as the sale of
imported eggs as home produced. After
the lapse of a few months any such substitution will become a difficult matter
indeed.
Under the Merchandise Marks Act, 1926,
provision is made for the marking, in
certain cases, of imported produce, and it
has been agreed to prescribe that all imported eggs shall, at the time of landing
in the United Kingdom of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland be individually
marked with an indication of the country
of origin. This arrangement was
reached subject to the proviso that preserved eggs, whatever their origin, and
home-produced cold-stored eggs, are also
marked to indicate that they have been
submitted to such process. The Bill is
thus part of the machinery for ensuring
that any egg, other than a home-produced
fresh egg, must bear a mark which will
let the consumer know the sort of egg he
is buying. In the whole matter we have
been in the closest touch with the appropriate Imperial Departments, and the
present Bill follows very closely on the
lines of the special provisions as to eggs
contained in the Agricultural Produce
(Grading and Marking) Act, 1928, which
received the Royal Assent on the 3rd
August.
Briefly summarised, the effect of the
Bill is to amend the Marketing of Eggs
Acts (Northern Ireland), 1924 and 1926,
in the following respects:-(a) to bring
the basis for the registration of premises used for the preservation of eggs in
Northern Ireland into accord with that
established for Great Britain by the Agricultural Produce (Grading and Marking)
Act, 1928; this is achieved by a slight
modification including premises used for
the chemical storage of eggs amongst
those that must be registered with the
Ministry; (b) to make it unlawful to
cause British eggs which have been kept
in cold storage or chemical storage to be
removed from such premises, unless the
eggs have been marked in such manner
as the Ministry may prescribe-such provisions to remain operative so long as an
Order of His Majesty in Council under
the Merchandise Marks Act of 1926, is in
force prohibiting the sale in the United
Kingdom of unmarked impor* eggs; and
(c) to make it an offence to sell or expose
for sale preserved eggs, irrespective of the
country of origin, unless each egg is
marked as prescribed by the Ministry.
The marking of all cold-stored eggs produced in Great Britain and Northern
Ireland and the marking of all imported
eggs will, I confidently anticipate, give
a substantial impetus to the Ulster trade
in new-laid and fresh eggs, since they,
with like classes in Great Britain, will be
the only unmarked eggs on the market.

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The

If we

the difficulty now is to produce a hen that

Northern Ireland, but the mark will be
sufficiently large to let people see it. It
is because we did not want to lose many
millions of foreign eggs that go into cold
storage that we decided to mark them
going out instead of going in.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill which
I now have the honour to ask the House
to give a Second Reading to is one which
I think will commend itself to hon. Members. It is designed to remove certain
inconveniences which local authorities are
put to before they can promote a private
Bill in Parliament. Under the Borough
Funds (Ireland) Act, 1888, certain local
authorities can use their funds for promoting a Bill in Parliament, but the Act,
in the interests of the electors, prescribed
certain procedure for the purpose of ascertaining the wishes of the electors so as to
ensure that any Bill that was promoted
in Parliament had the goodwill of the
electors. I desire, first of all, to impress
on hon. Members that this Bill does not
propose in any way to interfere with the
principle contained in the Act of 1888.
The local authority will still be under the
control of the electors as regards the desirability of putting forward a Bill, and
that principle, I suggest, is an excellent
one and one which should be preserved.
At the same time the experience of years
past has shown that there are several defects in the machinery for giving effect to
this principle, and it is desirable that these
defects should be removed.
I propose to deal very shortly with what
these defects are. Under Section 7 of the
Borough Funds Act, 1888, when a local
authority desires to promote a Bill in Parliament and it has passed the necessary
resolution to that effect it must call a
meeting of local government electors in
order to obtain their approval of the proposed Measure. At this meeting a resolution is put in favour of the promotion
of the Bill. That resolution must be put
in favour of the Bill as a whole, and it
cannot be put in favour of different parts
of the Bill, such as Part 1, Part 2, or
Part 3. The Bill must be submitted to
the meeting as a whole, and if the resolution is defeated the Bill is killed, and
nothing further can be done. If, on the
other hand, the promoters of the Bill succeed in carrying the resolution approving
of the Bill it is still open for any five
electors present at the meeting to demand
a plebiscite of the electors, and this
plebiscite must be taken.
Notice taken, that ten Members were

House counted, and ten Members being
present;
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I was

whole or against it. I might point out
that this is a one-sided agreement, because
while a local authority might be defeated

In recent times we have had a very striking illustration showing the inconvenience
which may result from what I might
describe as a rather antiquated procedure.
Hon. Members will remember that last
year the Belfast Corporation took steps
to promote an omnibus Bill containing a
highly controversial provision in regard
to the Corporation running buses outside
their own area. But the Bill also dealt
with several very useful and desirable
matters. For example, it proposed to incorporate power to hand over certain land
for the purpose of building a hospital.
But the vote was taken at the meeting
called by the Belfast Corporation and the
vote at that meeting was unfavourable
to the Bill. Five electors present
then demanded a plebiscite. While the
only contentious matter in the Bill was
the question of the buses at the same time
the electors at that plebiscite had to decide
whether or not they approved of the Bill
as a whole. They were in the position
that they had either to lose some part
they desired or to swallow a part they did
not desire.
In Bangor also an omnibus Bill
was promoted in 1926. It contained
amongst other things a Clause under

baths. There were several other very
useful provisions, but there was a very
strong feeling as to whether or not the
inhabitants of Bangor needed baths and
when a plebiscite was taken the Bill was
thrown out. I might point out that a

Bill was
passed called the Borough Funds Act,
1903, which amended the procedure, and
we propose to adopt in this Bill similar
procedure. Now the Bill provides that
at the meeting called by the local authority the Measure which the local authority
intends to promote may be voted on in
parts or in Clauses instead of the Bill
being put to the electors as a whole, and
we also propose it will be open either to
the local authority or to the electors within a period of seven days to demand a
plebiscite, but in order to save the electors
expense it is provided that if the electors.
wish a plebiscite the requisition shall be
signed by at least 100 electors or onetwentieth of the electors whichever is
smaller. Then there is another objection.
As the law now stands it is not necessary
for the local authority to print the Bill
before submitting it for the approval of
the electors. The result is that at these
meetings called the only information the
electors have is a statement put forward
by the local authority which might be a
biassed statement and even inaccurate.
At all events it puts the electors in a very
difficult position in thoroughly understanding what they are asked to vote
about. In this Bill we propose that the
Bill must be printed before the meeting
is called and that a copy will be available
for anyone who desires it.
Then there is another difficulty. There
is some doubt at the present time whether
in the event of the local authority being
beaten on the question whether or not
they should promote a Bill, they have
the right to pay for the expenses of promoting the Bill up to the time it was
rejected by the electors. We propose to
remedy this difficulty. There is another
point which I am sure will appeal to my
hon. Friend from Antrim.
At the present time county councils and county
boroughs have the right to use the funds
of the local authority to oppose any Bill
which they think may adversely affect the
electors. There is no power in urban
councils to oppose any Measure. As a result they are very seriously affected in
having no locus standi to use the funds
of the ratepayers to oppose a Bill which,
if it passed, might adversely affect the
ratepayers. I might point out at the
same time that we propose to safeguard
the electors to this extent that before
urban councils will be in a position to
spend the ratepayers' money in opposing
any Bill they must obtain the sanction of
the Ministry of Home Affars. These are
the main points of the Bill, and I beg to
move.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): For some time past it has been
apparent that many of the industries of
the Kingdom had reached a condition of
depression which promised to become
chronic unless some steps were taken to
reach the root of the disease. The causes
of the trouble were not difficult of diagnosis, but the remedy was not so obvious.
The great basic industries of the country,
such as agriculture, coal, textiles and the
important steel trade were all affected by
a multiplicity of adverse conditions both
internal and external. The trade situation had reached the point that foreign
competitors, favoured by labour conditions of lower wages, longer hours and
the depreciation of international exchanges, where able to outbid us in most
of the markets of the world where British
goods were formerly dominant.
To add
to the acuteness of the position, the home
market, by reason of the traditional freetrade policy of the country, was invaded
to such a serious extent that many industries were threatened with extinction.
Many statesmen and eminent economists
favoured a policy of limited protection of
those industries which had to face the full
blast of foreign competition, but the acute
differences of political opinion which prevailed on this great question paralyzed
the defensive powers of the country
and left us open and unarmed against invasion. Without attemping to analyze
here how far a protective policy might
prove the salvation of the economic life
of the country, I may say it was obvious
to all who had studied the situation that
3825 Rating and Valuation Bill-
Rating and Valuation Bill- 3826
26 NOVEMBER 1928
active measures must be taken to assist industry in meeting its many difficulties and
so to remove the dreadful load of unemployment which was the natural corollary of these conditions and which
threatened to gain a stranglehold on the
entire country.
It was not unnatural, therefore, and
hardly caused any surprise, that the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in submitting the
Financial Budget of the Kingdom, announced that the Government had determined to ask Parliament to adopt a farreaching scheme by which the heavy burden of rating should in great part be
removed from the productive industries
of the country; that agricultural land and
buildings, which were probably the
greatest sufferers by foreign competition,
should be entirely relieved from the payment of all rates; and that the contraction
of the sources of revenue of the local
authorities resulting from such a policy
should be made good from the national
purse. All this is, of course, common
knowledge, and I need not enlarge upon
it further than to state that as the Province under our control is being affected
by trade depression identical with that
existing in Great Britain, our Government had no hesitation in deciding to ask
Parliament to follow the British lead in
respect of this important matter.
In view of this decision, I established
a small Departmental Technical Com-
1mittee to investigate the problem in so far
i as it affected our Northern area. Whilst
our general policy was expected naturally
to follow the British lead, the local conditions in Ulster differed so materially
from those existing in Britain that it was
necessary that the working of the measure
of relief should be closely investigated so
that the matter might be dealt with in a
way suitable to conditions obtaining in the
Province. Following this investigation,
we are now able, in the Measure which I
am submitting to the House, to offer a first
instalment of the legislation which will be
necessary to give effect to the proposed
relief.
Before proceeding to consider the Bill,
I should like to express a sense of obligation to Members on all sides of the
House for the consideration they have
shown in not pressing me for details of
this far-reaching scheme of rating reform
during the time I was engaged in making

the many inquiries necessary for its preparation.
This Measure is intended to provide
machinery to put the stheme into operation, and as a preliminary I must amplify
the outline which I gave in my Budget
statement.
It is proposed to give relief from rates;
Firstly, to agricultural land and buildings;
Secondly, to productive industry; and
Lastly, in respect of freight-transport.
Of course, the relief will entail a deficiency in the budgets of local authorities.
This will be made good by the Exchequer,
so that the ratepayers who do not get
relief will incur no additional burden by
the relief being given to farmers and industrialists in their own districts. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The present Bill
does not deal with these payments from
the Exchequer to local authorities or the
method and principles on which they will
be assessed; that will be the subject matter
of a separate Measure to be introduced in
the spring. In order that every aspect
of this question may receive the fullest
consideration I have set up a small Inter-
Departmental Committee to investigate
the subject very carefully and to consult
local authorities on the many points of
detail which are bound to arise out of a
comprehensive scheme of this character.
I come first to agriculture. The rating
of agricultural land has engaged the attention of successive Governments for the
last generation. At first the relief was
very small; it has been gradually increased, until at the present day our State
is annually contributing over a quarter of
a million, which amounts roughly to onethird of the rates chargeable on agricultural land.
The idea of partial derating for agriculture is thus not new, but the step
which is now being taken represents not
only finality, but a remarkable advance
on anything. which had previously been
thought of. The additional relief is estimated at £457,000.
In addition to land we propose to go
a step further, and farm offices will be ex-

empted. Here we are at a disadvantage,

valued and relief given on that result.
The total relief under this head is estimated at £55,000. Taking land and
buildings together, Ulster agriculturists
will thus directly benefit to the extent of
£512,000 per annum.
I must pause here in order to make certain that the scope of the scheme in its
relation to agriculture is beyond any possibility of doubt. The exemption will
apply to all rates, whether county-atlarge, union, or district rates, exclusive of
malicious injury rates, drainage rates,
and water rates in so far as water rates
represent a distinct payment for water
used on farms.
There have been may debates in the
House on the subject of agriculture, and
the many forms in which the State has
assisted the industry have frequently been
expounded. But the complete derating
of land and farm buildings constitutes
a boon which must a few years ago have
been beyond the expectations of any
farmer. I think that the whole farming
community will realise the generosity of
these proposals. This is not a "gesture"
to agriculture; it is practical help, and I
feel sure that not even the benefits of the
Land Purchase Acts are comparable to the
relief which will result from these proposals.
And now I turn to the Bill to show
how this scheme will actually be applied

In other words, we propose to apply as
from 1st October, 1929, complete derating
to all agricultural land which the
partial relief now applies, and, in addition, to land used for agricultural purposes and situated in county boroughs or
urban districts, but we exclude land used

of agricultural buildings in paragraph (b)

I do not think that any more detailed
explanation of these two Clauses is required. In short, they provide the machinery for the derating of agricultural
land and buildings and provide for the
necessary alteration of the valuation lists.
I now pass to the consideration of the
relief to be given to productive industry,
and I must preface my remarks with the
observation that while in Great Britain
this section of their scheme is the most important-from the point of view of finance
at any rate conditions in Northern Ireland are such that industrial relief takes
second place to agriculture.
This is to be expected, since we
primarily an agricultural community and
the result is therefore natural. The fact
that industry will receive in the aggregate
about one-quarter of the total relief given
to agriculture in no way indicates a failure
on the part of the Government to recog
nise the difficulties which beset the manufacturers of our Province. We are doing
exactly the same for our industries as is
being done for British manufacturers in
their scheme, and, in addition, we are able
to apply the relief in the most beneficial
way.

We propose to give industrial hereditaments relief to the extent of 75 per cent.
of all rates, whether county-at-large,
union, or district rates, but excluding
malicious injury rates. Water rates,
where they are in the nature of a general
public charge, will be included in the relief, but charges which are made in respect
of definite consumption of water, that is
to say, meter charges or special rates, will
not be included. The 25 per cent. which
is remaining is considered to be a fair
contribution by the industrial concerns to
actual benefits derived from local health
services and so forth.
I estimate that the total relief to industry will be £120,000 a year. In comparison with turnover, for instance, the
figure assumes very small proportions, and
I do not pretend that this direct relief
will work any startling transformation in
the condition of trade. The fact remains
that we are largely relieving industry of
a charge which, to say the least, was not
created on a scientific basis and which,
moreover, never had any relation to industry's taxable capacity. Rates in industrial areas move in a vicious circle;
bad trade brings with it unemployment,
and thus creates charges which fall partly
on the very factories which, because of
the condition of affairs, are literally
y struggling for existence.
The relief which it is proposed to give
will therefore serve to place rating on a
sounder basis. It may not mean very
much to individual manufacturers, but it
may, however small, make just the difference to a factory on the point of closing
down or to the placing of an important
order or contract. The first step, however, is to determine what are industrial
hereditaments for the purposes of this
relief, and Clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill are
designed to achieve this object.
Hon. Members will at once notice that
the relief is confined to productive industry-in fact that is its essence. We
must concentrate our energies on assisting
the factories and mills of the Province.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
hear). Any
other method would merely dissipate our
resources. Because, so far as industrial

of all prosperity, and assistance to them
is passed on to distributors, retailers and
ultimately to the general public.
this reason, dwelling-houses, retail shops,

I come now to the consideration of the
third head of the Scheme, that is to say,
freight-transport relief, and I am faced
with the task of explaining a very involved
and difficult subject. The question of
freights has long been a bone of contention; committees have investigated it;
there have been long conferences with the
carrying companies; but we have always
been faced with incontrovertible economic
facts, although I am bound to say railway
companies have invariably been willing to
meet our representations to the best of
their ability.
We propose to follow the British scheme
in relieving railways, docks and canals of
75 per cent. of their rates, in the same
way as we are relieving productive industry; but we do not propose to allow the
Companies, or Boards concerned to retain
this relief in their own pockets. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) The relief thus
given, which will amount to about
£40,000, must be passed on by them in
the shape of rebates on freight charges in
the case of certain selected commodities,
because the money is not great enough
to go over the whole range of articles.

Before proceeding to examine the relevant clauses of the Bill, I would like to
deal in greater detail with the actual
operation of this part of the derating
scheme. In order to make the relief as
effective as possible, it has been decided
that the funds thus available shall, as far
as the Railway Companies are concerned,
be paid into a pool to be held by the Ministry of Finance. This is necessary, because otherwise one Company having a
smaller share of the selected traffics would
be in a position to give abnormally high
rebates as compared to another. My Department will then, on the basis of freight
returns rendered by the Companies, determine a percentage rebate to be allowed
off the charges on the various commodities
in question. The rebates will actually be
made by the Companies when making
their freight charges and they will draw
The
on the pool to recoup themselves.
amount of the rebate is likely to be in
the region of 10 per cent. of the normal
charge.
The same procedure will be followed in
regard to Dock and Harbour dues, so far
as these smaller Harbours which come
into the Schemes are concerned. Although the present Bill does not embrace
these details, I may perhaps be allowed to
state what commodities will benefit.
The Government has laid down as the
main principle to be followed that the
relief shall be directed to reduce freights
on those commodities which form the
basis of agriculture and industry in the
Province.
We have also had to look at those industries which are suffering most from
trade depression. Further, it is very important to bear in mind the fact that the
total sum available-about £40,000-is
comparatively small, and therefore if it is
to be of any real assistance, the list must
be kept as short as possible. This argument needs no elaboration, since it must
be obvious that if every class of goods
dealt with by the railways and docks were
admitted to a share in the relief, the
actual amount payable in respect of any
one item would be of no avail whatever.
After careful consideration it has been
decided that the relief will be applied to
the following traffics, so far as the railways and canals are concerned :-
Industrial coal (excluding coal to be
used by public utility undertakings)
terminating in Northern Ireland.
That is to say, gasworks and electric undertakings will not come under this

It will thus be seen that this freighttransport relief will constitute a further
measure of assistance to the basic industries. In itself it may not be of great
significance but, taken with the relief to
be given to industrial hereditaments, it
should afford useful aid.
Clauses 6 and 7 of the Bill provide for
the distinction in the Valuation Lists of
Freight-Transport Hereditaments in respect of which relief will be given. These
provisions are of a very technical character
and are mainly concerned with definitions.
There are, however, one or two matters
to which reference is desirable.
It will be noted that relief will only be
given to those railways having at least
two stations in Northern Ireland. In
calculating the rebates on through traffic
from Northern Ireland to the Free State,
the basis will be the freight from the
point of origin to the Station in Northern
Ireland nearest the border. Consequently, as a matter of working convenience, we must rule out railways such
as the County Donegal Joint Committee
which have only one station in our area.
Secondly, light railways may qualify for
the relief, so that the Clogher Valley Railway, for example, will be included. The
farmers and others using that railway will
benefit accordingly, although the cost of
running the system is already borne to a

The
considerable extent by the State.
relief of the rates on agricultural land and
buildings will add materially to the State's
assistance in respect of the railway, but
notwithstanding this, I have decided to
allow freight-transport relief to extend to
this concern.
Turning now to harbours, I must point
out certain limitations. Under Clause 6
relief will not be given in respect of docks
or harbours of the following classes:-
(1) belonging to local authorities;
(2) or of a valuation under £20;
(3) or used mainly for merchandise belonging to or intended for the
owners or lessees of the dock.
I think these exceptions are almost selfexplanatory. In the first place, the rating
of its own harbour by a local authority is
without statutory support and is, in effect,
a matter of book-keeping. As regards the
valuation qualification, it would be impossible, in practice, to pass on relief through
the dues charged at the smallest harbours,
and lastly, I think we are wise in ruling
out, as has been done in Great Britain,
harbours owned by persons or companies
and used by them mainly for their own
businesses.
The present Bill will not operate until
1st October, 1929; an earlier date is impossible administratively and financially.
But in order to assist industry, even partially, forthwith I propose in the course
of the next few days to lay before the
House a Paper giving details of the freighttransport side of the scheme, including
docks and canals, which it is proposed to
operate from 1st December next, to be
financed in advance of the statutory Derating Scheme by means of a direct Vote
of this House to be taken before Christmas.
The scheme will follow in its scope
the outline which I have given this afternoon, but which cannot operate as a permanent arrangement until the Local
Government financial legislation in the
Spring empowers the local authorities to
put the entire Derating Scheme into operation.
I have endeavoured to offer the House,
in outline, the first legislative instalment
of this great comprehensive and farreaching scheme of rating reform. Whilst,
as I have said before, it may not introduce an industrial millennium, still I have
no doubt it will help to give a new outlook
on life to many of its beneficiaries and perhaps encourage some to greater effort and
enterprise. This is the spirit in which we
enter upon it, and we can only hope and
pray that the result may justify the effort.
I beg to move.

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: With regard to this Clause there have been
various complaints by the cattle trade on
this part of the Bill that we have not remodelled the Bill and made it open to
a man to obtain compensation for letention across the water. It would be impossible for us to remodel the Clause as
it stands at present and make it possible
that these men should obtain compensation, for not only is it impossible to find
out accurately how much would be due for
compensation for the last three years, but
the Bill as it stands will make compensation payable retrospectively for
slaughter. Therefore, we can hardly introduce in this Bill a retrospective Clause
for the payment of compensation for detention. Apart from that, we find that
the dealers in the North West Association
are willing to take the Bill as it stands,
and the dealers in the Free State have
already got a Bill of the same sort.
What I would ask those who are dissatisfied to do is this, to wait a short time

have this Bill working for a little time,

Bill to cover this matter that is now under discussion. We are quite willing to

for a joint Bill to be brought in to amend
this one, so that compensation for Jetention will be payable in the future.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): I beg to move in page 3, lines
27 and 28, to leave out the words "having
his head office in Northern Ireland."
In moving the Amendment which stands
in the name of my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock), it is necessary that I
should explain what is, I am afraid, a
very technical matter. The words which
it is now proposed to omit were inserted
in the original draft Clause as it was intended at the time the Clause was framed
to continue as regards Bills of Exchange
and Bank Post Bills, the present informal arrangement whereby the Northern
Ireland Exchequer collected the composition duty on Bills made or drawn by the
three Northern Ireland Banks, irrespective of the area in which the Bills were
drawn, and conversely the remaining
Banks paid the full composition duty to
the Irish Free State Exchequer.
After further examination of the problem, however, it seems likely that the
Banks will experience no difficulty in arranging for such Bills to be segregated as
between the two areas, and, as the new
currency conditions have made it necessary to discontinue this informal basis of
apportioning the composition duty on
ordinary Bank notes between the two Exchequers, it is thought only logical to
arrange if it can be conveniently done
for the segregation of duty in the minor
case of Bills of Exchange and Bank Post
Bills. As hon. Members will be aware
the Clause is permissive, but as it stands
at the moment it would preclude the
Ministry of Finance from agreeing with
the Irish Free State Revenue authorities
to any revision in the system. Any
action on the lines I have suggested would
only be taken after consultation with the
Banks and the Free State Revenue Commission. I may add that the duty involved is trifling in comparison with the
composition duty payable on ordinary
Bank notes.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

PORT OF BELFAST-SHIPPING
FACILITIES FOR CATTLE AND
SHEEP.
1.
Mr. GEORGE
HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Agriculture whether
his attention has been drawn to statements in the Press that our cattle and
sheep trade from the Port of Belfast is
being seriously hampered and endangered
by want of sufficient shipping facilities for
prompt dispatch, and what steps he proposes to take to secure the necessary
facilities.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): My attention
has been drawn to the statements in the
Press, to which the hon. Member refers.
This question of the facilities for the shipment of live stock from Belfast is at
present being investigated by my Ministry, and I hope, in due course, to let the
hon. Member know the result. I may say
that so far as our inquiries have gone they
indicate that the difficulty is the shipment
of sheep and lambs on Monday night.
NORTHERN IRELAND CIVIL
SERVICE.
EMPLOYMENT OF EX-SERVICE-
MEN.
2. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
when it is the intention of the Government to issue a White Paper dealing with
the question of the employment of ex-
Servicemen in the Northern Ireland Civil
Service.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): A White Paper dealing with
the employment of temporary ex-Servicemen will be circulated to Members to-day.
In it the 75 additional permanent posts
which I have already announced have been
included.
In addition, I have pleasure in announcing that, after further discussion with my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour,
whose Department is principally concerned, as a further evidence of the
Government's anxiety to deal generously
in this matter, an additional 25 temporary
ex-Service clerks will shortly be given
permanent and pensionable status, making
a total of 100 instead of the 75 first proposed.
Colonel WOODS: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he thinks this
is the last concession he can give to these
ex-Service temporary civil servants?
Mr. POLLOCK: At the present time
I should say the answer is in the affirmative, that is to say, while it would be impossible for me or anyone standing at this
Table to enter into any obligation in regard to the future, the Government at
present think they have gone to the very
limit of safety in the action they have
taken and in the spirit of generosity they
have displayed towards the ex-Servicemen.
Colonel WOODS: Then may I take it
there is hope of an improvement in the
future?
Mr. POLLOCK:
happen in this world.
Anything may

HOUSE OF COMMONS

SELECTION OF ADDITIONAL
APPOINTMENTS.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the method
to be adopted in the selection of the additional appointments of ex-Servicemen to
the permanent ranks of the Civil Service.
Mr. POLLOCK: The Civil Service
Commission has decided to select the men
to fill the 100 permanent clerical posts to
which I have referred in my previous
reply by means of a Selection Board comprised of higher officials of the Departments concerned, who themselves will all
be ex-Servicemen. This Board will have
before them reports furnished by the immediate superiors of each of the ex-
Servicemen who come before them.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if he has consulted the
Association of Ex-Service Temporary Civi!
Servants? If not, can he give any valid
reason why that was not done as it was
done in the Imperial Service?
Mr. POLLOCK: No. I can only repeat what I have just said, namely, that
this matter will be carried out and completed by those who are ex-Service men,
and, therefore, in my judgment it is not
necessary that any other tribunal should
be consulted.
Colonel WOODS: Does the right hon.
Gentleman consider that the Imperial
Service were misguided when they consulted, and consulted alone, the Association of Ex-Service Temporary Civil Servants; is he not aware that they have been
in correspondence with the Government
on this particular subject; and is it not
right that they should be recognized and
consulted regarding a subject of which
they have expert knowledge?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Imperial Government is necessarily a law to itself. So far
as our own local arrangements are concerned I am quite satisfied that we have
taken every possible step to obtain the
views of the ex-Servicemen.
Colonel WOODS: Will there be nobody
on this Committee that is to be set up
representing the actual men concerned
and not the higher officials of the Departments? It is the men themselves who are
to be considered and not the higher
officials.
Mr. POLLOCK: In a selection where
efficiency is necessary one of the features
of the investigation or examination, it is
perfectly obvious, is that those officials
who have had relation with those temporary servants must necessarily have a larger
experience of their fitness than others.
NORTHERN IRELAND LAND ACT,

4. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Prime Minister whether the Government have been consulted about, and have
approved of, the provisions of the amending Bill to the 1925 Northern Ireland
Land Act, which has been introduced in
the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
take this question.
The answer to the hon. Member's question is in the affirmative. He will recollect that in reply to the hon. Member
for Derry, the Prime Minister announced
in this House on the 14th May last the
terms of an agreement which had been
reached between this Government and the
Imperial Government in regard to tennants whose holdings will not have been
dealt with on or before the 27th May of
next year.
The Amending Bill which has
now been introduced in the Imperial
Parliament is designed to give effect to
that arrangement.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask the Minister
if anything can be put into this Bill to
provide for the cases of fee farm grantees
and leases renewable for ever?
Mr. SPEAKER: What can be put in a
Bill in the Imperial Parliament is not
a question for this House.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I would
like to ask the right hon. Gentleman if
he remembers giving a promise to the
hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
regarding the point raised by another
hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
that he would advise the Imperial
Government so that this matter might be
dealt with in the Amending Bill? I
would like, further, to ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he is aware that there is an
urgent demand and necessity for further
Amendments to this 1925 Act and if he
will give time for this House to discuss
this Measure so that these Amendments
may be suggested to the Government?

as possible the Bill also made provision
that as from the 1st December following,
that is in a few days, relief should be
given in respect of freight arrangements
with railways, canals and also docks and
harbours. It must be quite clear if this
relief is to be given by the Government
to railways and docks that the necessary
money must be provided to carry out the
cperation. If hon. Members will consult
the sheet that no doubt is in their hands
they will have a full explanation of the
machinery by which this money will be
distributed. The amount is £10,000 that
I am asking the Committee to agree to.
It is estimated that this sum will be approximately sufficient to carry out the
scheme as from the 1st December until the
end of the financial year, that is the 31st
March. I explained the full details of
this Measure so recently as Monday that
everything that is implied in the Measure
and also in this vote must be within the
memory of hon. Members. Therefore, with the particulars that are given
as a footnote on the sheet and with the
information that I also provided hon.
Members with on Monday, I think I need
not prosecute this matter any further. T
beg to move.

CLASS II.
No. 11.
THIEPVAL WAR MEMORIAL.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding £6,755 be granted to His Majesty for
the service of the year ending on the 31st
March, 1929, for expenditure in connection with the maintenance of the Thiepval War Memorial."
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates.
HOUSE OF COMMONS

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): I am glad to have the opportunity of presenting this Supplementary
Estimate to the Committee. The object
the Estimate, which requires no
apology, is, as explained on the paper
itself, to establish a Fund to provide in
perpetuity for the maintenance of the
Thiepval Memorial,
This memorial, it is hardly necessary
to say, was erected some years ago on the
Somme battlefield and is a tribute in
particular to the men of the Ulster
Division who fought there in 1916, but it
may also be regarded as a monument
erected by Ulster to the memory of all
those of her sons who fought in the Great
War. I dare say some hon. Members
present may have actually visited this
Memorial, but for those who have not
had that privilege I may read the inscription that stands on it:
This Tower is dedicated to the Glory
of God, in grateful memory of the
officers, non-commissioned officers and
men of the 36th (Ulster) Division, and
of the sons of Ulster in other forces who
laid down their lives in the Great War,
and of all their comrades-in-arms who,
by Divine grace, were spared to testify
to their glorious deeds.
Hon. Members are, of course, aware
that this Memorial stands on the site of
the famous advance of the Ulster Division
on the 1st July, 1916. The Memorial
was erected by means of public subscription and it is considered only right and
proper that the maintenance of the
Memorial should, as in the case. of the
Memorials erected in France by Newfoundland, Canada and Australia, be a
charge upon the Government of the
people by whom the Memorial was
erected.
Accordingly, the Committee is asked to
vote a sum sufficient in the first place to
recoup to the Patriotic Fund the costs of
maintenance for the last seven years, and
in the second place to provide a capital
sum which, when invested in trustee
securities, will yield a yearly income suflicient for the payment of the caretaker's
wages and other expenses incidental to the
upkeep of the Memorial and its surroundings. I may mention that the Patriotic
Fund, which it is now proposed to recoup
for its expenses in looking after the
Memorial for the last seven years, was
raised mainly for the purpose of assisting
ex-Service men belonging to the Ulster
Division and their dependants. Part of
the Vote will thus go to make good to that
Fund expenditure incurred from it on an
object which, though allied, is not perhaps
strictly within the original scheme of the
Fund, and thereby a sum of £1,255 will
be released and made available for the
original purpose, namely, the relief of
distress among these ex-Service men.
It has not yet been possible to estimate
the exact annual sum required to carry
out the work, but while it is not expected
to exceed a sum of £250 per annum, it
is possible that a capital sum producing
a lesser amount may be sufficient, and the
wording of the Estimate provides for this
contingency.
The note refers to a small balance of
£231 remaining over from the original
building account. There are one or two
alterations needed at the present moment
in connection with the Memorial which
may absorb about £100 or £150 of this
money, and the balance will be retained
by the Ministry of Finance and will be
available at any time in the event of any
unusual item of expenditure arising on
upkeep.
Some reference should perhaps be made
as regards the body upon which the responsibility for the proper care of the
memorial will rest, and hon. Members
will observe from the descriptive matter
on the Estimate itself that the Minister of
Finance, the Secretary or an Assistant
Secretary of the Ministry, and a representative of the trustees of the Patriotic
Fund will form a Committee for this purpose.
I beg to move.
I

grant for the Ulster War Memorial.
am entirely in favour of the Government

this war memorial. In the first place we
have the Minister of Finance (Mr.
Pollock). I certainly do not take any
exception to the present Minister of
Finance nor to his successors, provided
that they be Ulstermen and people who

Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding three thousand, five hundred pounds,
be granted to His Majesty for the service of the year ending on the 31st
March, 1929, to defray the expenses of the
Ministry of Commerce in respect of Harbours (1 Geo. IV, c. 113; 39 and 40
Vic., c. 236), Railway, Fishery and Commercial Services, including certain Grants
in Aid (16 Geo. V, c. 4 (N.I.), and payments under Section 6 of 13 and 14 Geo.

9; 52 and 53 Vic., c. 66; and s. 10 of 13
and 14 Geo. V, c. 31."
Mr. BARBOUR: The Supplementary
Estimate now before the Committee will
require only a very brief explanation.
Hon. Members will remember that partly
as a result of the exceptional storm on the
night of Friday, 19th October last, a
fault developed in the bottom of the
Newry Canal at the point where it passes
over the small river carrying the sewage
of the West Ward of the town of Newry.
The result of this damage is that the
waters of the Canal pass unchecked into
the river and ultimately to the sea, thus
rendering navigation impossible. In view
of the urgency of the matter I received
a deputation from the Newry Port and
Harbour Trust on the 29th ultimo, when
the financial condition of the Trust and
proposals for the repair of the damage,
based on expert advice, were placed be-
Supply-
Supplementary Estimates.
28 NOVEMBER 1928
fore me. I was satisfied from the particulars furnished that the Trust was not
in a position to raise further moneys as
its assets were already fully mortgaged,
and that if the Government were to withhold its assistance shipping facilities to
the town of Newry would cease.
In view of all the circumstances, it was
eventually decided that the Government
should make an out-an-out grant towards
the cost of the necessary repairs of 50 per
cent. of the total expenditure thereon up
to a maximum amount of £3,500, conditional upon the Urban District Council
of Newry undertaking to accept liability
for the provision of the balance of the
expenditure necessary for the completion
of the remedial works; the Government
to advance the necessary moneys to the
Newry Urban District Council, such
moneys to be repayable, with interest, at
the current rate for Government loans
over a period of 30 years. The Urban
District Council of Newry has signified its
agreement to these conditions. The
amount, namely £3,500, for the provision
of which the sanction of the Committee
is now sought, represents the Government's contribution to the expenditure
involved in these remedial works.
to move.

shown to their constituents in their very
great difficulty.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg
to move in page 3, line 27, leave out

This Clause is really giving effect to the
last part of Clause 2; that is, it proposes
to derate what is defined in Clause 2 as
agricultural buildings. I would like to
congratulate the right hon. Gentleman
on the manner in which he has approached this question, namely, that there
should be an automatic adjustment with
regard to the valuation of these hereditaments, because at the present time, as the
Committee have been informed and
as most hon. Members are well aware,
the dwelling house and agricultural
buildings on farms are valued together.
There is not a separate valuation as between the dwelling house and the agricultural buildings. The right hon.
Gentleman, I think, at first thought it
would be necessary in this case to have a
revaluation of the two hereditaments.
However, he has adopted the suggestion that instead of a revaluation, which
would be expensive and cause a good deal
of delay, there should be an automatic
adjustment of these hereditaments.
The Amendment standing in my
name proposes that the automatic adjustment should be on a fifty-fifty basis.
Fifty per cent. of the valuation now on
the total buildings should be credited as
on the agricultural houses and fifty per
cent on the dwelling house. The effect
of that would be that fifty per cent. of the
present valuation on agricultural buildings
would be derated. Of course. the right
hon. Gentleman will no doubt say that
anybody who feels aggrieved has the
right to appeal against this one-third.
At the same time I think the Committee
should be concerned, in the first instance,
to have this apportionment as fair as possible. I do not think the State would
lose anything if this Amendment standing in my name were passed. Really,
the apportionment would, if anything, be
=in favour of the State as against the
farmer, because if we take the average
farm over the Six County area you will
find, I think, that the agricultural build-
#ings are really much more extensive than
the dwelling house. In a great many instances these dwelling houses are very unpretentious buildings, and with regard to
the agricultural buildings the tenants
have been compelled in recent years in a
good many cases by Act of Parliament to
improve them. Under the Dairies and
Cowsheds Order they have been compelled, in some cases, to improve the
agricultural buildings so as to comply
with the requirements of the law. They
have also been compelled, from the
economic standpoint, to erect haysheds
and piggeries on more modern lines than
what used to prevail.
I think the Amendment I put forward
would provide for a fairer proportionment of the values. While we still retain the right for any man who feels
aggrieved to appeal, yet I think this
Committee would be striking a fair apportionment. It may be said that in
asking for this we are very ungenerous,
but the proposal in this Bill is to derate
entirely agricultural land and what is described as agricultural buildings. I think
instead of one-third being the proportion
for agricultural buildings it should be
one-half. I do not wish to detain the

this Amendment the Committee will be

in asking for this we are asking for something that is outlandish. In England the

farm buildings under their Bill entirely
derated, and I do hold that if we want to
derate entirely what are defined in this
Bill as farm buildings we will not be
going anything too far in derating onehalf of the entire valuation of the buildings on agricultural holdings.
