Mr. POLLOCK: Perhaps I had better
take the different features of this Clause
in their order before I come to the definite question which my hon. and gallant
Friend (Colonel Woods) has propounded.
This Clause is mainly concerned with the
definition of what does and what does not
come under the designation of industrial
hereditaments. It will be seen by reference to the first part of the Clause
that there are certain matters set out.
TELLER FOR THE NOES-
Mr. George Henderson.
The expression "industrial hereditament"
means any property occupied or used as
a mine, quarry, or mineral railway, or,
subject to the later provisions of the
Clause, as a factory or workshop. Then
the Clause goes on to outline those classes
of property which do not come under the
designation of industrial hereditament,
and if my hon. and gallant Friend
(Colonel Woods) will look at the Clause
he will see that they include anything
used for
(a) the purposes of a dwelling-house;
(b) the purposes of a retail shop;
(c) the purposes of distributive wholesale business;
(d) purposes of storage;
(e) the purposes of a public supply
undertaking;
(f) any other purposes, whether or
not similar to any of the foregoing
which are not those of a factory or
workshop.
The point raised by the hon. and
gallant Member has been disposed of by
much wiser heads than his or mine. The
British Government in dealing with this
far-reaching Measure, and having, I suppose, like
ourselves, certain sums of
money to dispose of in helping industry
and agriculture, were compelled to exclude everything that could not be regarded as coming under the heading
"Productive." Just as the land produces
crops, factories produce goods, and anything outside these two features of desscription was ruled out. Therefore, a
stable, which is outside a factory, or even
other buildings that are not physically
connected with and used purely for the

purpose of manufacture do not come within the ambit of this scheme. In sub-
Clause (2) it is stated that
"For the purposes of this Act any
place used by the occupier for the housing or maintenance of his road vehicles
or as stables shall, notwithstanding that
it is situate within the close, curtilage
or precincts"
that is presumably within the walls of the
factory-
"forming a factory or workshop and
used in connection therewith, be
deemed not to form part of the factory
or workshop, but save as aforesaid, the
expressions "factory" and "workshop"
have respectively the same meanings as
in the Factory and Workshop Acts,
1901 to 1920."
As I say, wiser heads than mine have
settled the principle on which this is
based and it would be very improper for
us to depart from the British basis, because in the claims we will make as a
charge upon our revenue for the expenditure involved in this great Measure we
must be able to justify ourselves. That
is the really important point about our
position. We must justify everything
we do, and certainly we could not justify
the inclusion of garages, stables, and

of the factory, which we would have to
do if we adopted the suggestion of the
hon. and gallant Member (Colonel
Woods).
But then under sub-Clause (3) the hon.

mine, quarry, mineral railway, factory,
or workshop, then, for the purposes of
determining whether the several hereditaments are industrial hereditaments
they shall be treated as if they formed

In that case they would come under the

If we continue the Clause which we are

The descriptions set out in this Bill are
so clear there should be no misapprehension at all as to the character of the
buildings that are to receive relief.

in order to come under this relief, must
be used by outside merchants or shippers.
Finally, in sub-clause (c), there is a provision that dock offices must be separately
valued; they will not be deemed as part
of a hereditament that will benefit under
this Measure.

there need be no ambiguity in regard to
that. Sub-section 2 of the Clause sets out
that where one part is used for one purpose, and another part is used for a second
purpose, the proportions of the net annual
value of the hereditament attributable to
the occupation and user for the several
transport purposes shall be distinguished.
The third sub-section indicates that those
features of a railway undertaking or a canal
undertaking that are not part and parcel
of the machinery of the railway or the
canal must be excluded; that is to say, the
ordinary railway hotel in a railway station,
or a dwelling-house for any of the servants,
or a place of public refreshment in connection with railways or canals must be excluded from the purview of the Measure.
In the matter of valuation, the Commissioner will have to take account of all those
things. The paragraphs below make provision for what I have just said:
"Provided that

other place primarily occupied and
used for warehousing merchandise
not in the course of being transported, shall be deemed to be occupied and used for transport purposes.

SHEEP WORRYING NEAR
DONAGHADEE.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether it
is a fact that a dog belonging to Mr.
Roland De Lacherois or Miss Annie De
Lacherois, of Ballywilliam, Donaghadee,
was unlicensed in 1927; why no prosecution was undertaken when the attention of the police was drawn to the
matter: whether he is aware that on two
occasions this dog has been caught
worrying sheep; why it is still allowed to
run uncontrolled after sunset; and why
no prosecution has been undertaken.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I understand from
inquiry that the dog referred to by the
hon. Member was duly licensed in Newtownards by its former owner for the
year 1927. It would appear that Mr. De
Lacherois omitted to obtain a transfer of
the licence when the dog came into his
possession. As the police were unaware
of this fact, no proceedings were instituted. Mr. De Lacherois has taken out
a licence for 1928.
Referring to the latter part of the hon.
Member's question, I understand that
the dog is stated to have chased sheep on
two occasions. As regards the first, civil
proceedings are still pending. As regards the second, the police supplied the
owner of the sheep with the names of
the owners of the dogs involved, but he
declined to proceed in the matter. The
police have summoned the owners of the
dogs to show cause why the dogs should
not be destroyed or kept under proper
control, and the case will be for hearing
on the 8th instant.
I may add that the police have never
found the dog in question wandering
uncontrolled after sunset.

A Question of Procedure.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I wish
to ask your ruling on a matter of which
I have already given notice. During the
discussion on the agreement concluded between the Belfast Corporation and the bus
companies I raised the point that any
legislation that would be necessary to
carry out this agreement should take the
form of a private Bill or Bills rather than
a public Bill. I should be obliged, therefore, if you would let us have your views
upon this point.
Mr. SPEAKER: The question raised
by the hon. Member is receiving, and will
continue to receive, my careful consideration, with the assistance of the advice of
the Speaker's Counsel and Examiner of
Petitions for Local Bills.
It is impossible for me to give any
definite ruling at this stage, and I shall
have to wait until I see the Bill which is
to be introduced. I may say, however,
that the general rule governing private
Bill legislation is that Bills for the particular interest or benefit of any person
or persons are treated as private Bills
whether they be for the interest of an
individual, of a public company or corporation, or of a parish, city, county, or
other locality. The procedure on such
Bills is, of course, entirely different to the
procedure on public bills, and all interests.
opposed to the object of a private Bill
are given an opportunity of appearing before the Committee of Members of both
Houses which examines the Bill, and of
being heard themselves or by their
counsel.
I will not say more now than that it
seems to me there may be some aspects of
the proposed legislation which might
come within the scope of a private Bill
or within that of a "hybrid" Bill-that
is, a Bill partly public and partly private.
I may add that there are a number of
precedents of Bills being ordered to be
withdrawn as public Bills and re-introduced as private Bills and vice versa.

Mr. SPEAKER: With regard to
Standing Order No. 9-about an adjournment on a definite matter of urgent public
importance the hon. Member, I am
afraid, has quite misconceived that.
It
does not apply to a matter of this kind at
all. It is intended where any question of
public importance arises outside the House
-a question of public policy-then before
the Orders of the Day are entered upon,
any Member rising in his place may claim
to move the adjournment of the House,
in order to discuss this definite matter of
urgent public importance. As a matter of
fact it has never been made use of in this
House, but it is of very common occurrence in the Imperial Parliament.
Notice must be given before the Orders
of the Day are entered upon, and then if
the Speaker allows it and if ten Members
support it, it comes on for discussion at
half-past Four o'clock. It is simply a
means of allowing Members time to discuss some urgent definite matter that
arises a matter of public policy-when
they would not otherwise have a chance.
It is clearly and obviously never intended
to apply to such a state of affairs as happened last Thursday week. I am perfectly
clear on that. I am afraid that there is
certainly no appeal to any higher tribunal.
Parliament must conduct its affairs in its
own way, and it has given authority to
the Speaker, or in his absence the Deputy-

not perceive. That is the sole matter I

I
put the Question in the first instance, and

heard me or not I do not know. There

Division having been so vehemently challenged in the first instance, I assumed a
challenge in the second case. I thereupon
asked a Teller for the Ayes, and received
intimation from the Government Chief
Whip (Captain Dixon) that he was going
to act as Teller for the Ayes. I asked
not once but twice for a Teller for the

Gentleman will agree with me in that.
That being the position, as it presented
itself to me in the Chair-and there were
hon. Gentlemen on both sides sitting a
great deal nearer the Chair than my hon.
Friend (Mr. Kyle) who I am sure can
bear witness that what I say is the truth
--there being, therefore, no Teller for the
Noes I treated it, as the Rules of Procedure require, as an unchallenged Division and declared that the Ayes have it.

make. It was not my business to discuss

My hon. Friend asked a question and
I only appreciated it when my attention

Any grant in aid of relief that is already in existence will certainly not be
withheld.
My mind, of course, was directed to what

already in existence as to agricultural land

land. I think it right, lest my reply if
commonly read or known might have given
rise to some misapprehension, that my
hon. Friend should direct his attention to
paragraph (b) of Sub-section 2 of Clause 2
of the Bill:
Agricultural land which is situate
within the boundary of an urban district, and used as farm land, market
gardens, nursery grounds, orchards or
allotments, or as a plantation or a wood,
or for the growth of saleable underwood,
and is not land which is part of an ornamental park, garden or pleasure ground,
nor land used mainly or exclusively for
purposes of sport or recreation.
One very important matter in connection with this Measure is that it should as
far as is possible come in line with the
British Measure. If we expand the character or volume of our relief it would obviously prejudice our case very materially
when we presented our accounts for adjustment. It is not, nor can it be, defensible for us to give relief in any greater
measure than is contemplated in the
British Measure. I am not now going to
argue the merits or demerits of this particular part because it will be discussed fully
when the ultimate Measure is presented to
this House during next Session, when it
can be more fully entered into, but I think
I may venture so far as to say that it does
not seem appropriate that land which is
designed entirely and purely for sporting
purposes should be placed in the same
category as agricultural land.

Mr. KYLE: I want to say a word cr

Bill. I see it is the intention of the
Government to supplement certain funds
that were subscribed by certain gentlemen to erect a war memorial. It seems
to me that this £1,255 which is going to

up an illegality which apparently has
taken place. I understand that this
Patriotic Fund was subscribed to help ex-
Servicemen and their dependants, and it
was used for the purpose of erecting or
helping to erect a memorial. If right
hon. Gentlemen had been at the back of
the City Hall opposite the offices of the
Minister of Finance last week they would
have seen a tremendous queue of ex-
Servicemen or their dependants waiting
for assistance from charitable sources.
Now we are going to vote £1,255 to reimburse the Patriotic Fund for doing
something with their money which they
were not entitled to do. In other words,
to cover up an illegality the Government
are prepared to compel the ex-Servicemen
of Belfast to pay in taxation to keep up
a war memorial.
It would be far more to the point if the
Government would keep ex-Servicemen in
the way they were led to believe they
would be kept when the war commenced
and shortly after the war was over. The
statement was then made that a grateful
country would reward them, that a grateful country would never forget them.
There are thousands of ex-Servicemen
roaming the streets of Belfast and in the
Six Counties and the Government quietly
say they have nothing to do with it, that
it is a matter for the British Government.
Therefore these men starve or go to the
workhouse or do whatever they jolly well
please, so far as the Government of Northern Ireland is concerned.
I think it is nothing short of a
monstrous proposal that the Government

feel that this plan is a very roundabout

question. I submit that the suggestion
I have put to the House is a simpler and
much less expensive way. In making

1925 Act. The first point I would like

the Bill. I think this House will agree

of this question it should include all bona
fide agricultural and pasture holdings.
Section 20 of the Act of 1925 definitely
excludes certain holdings from the operations of this Act. It excludes certain
types of leases, fee farm grants, leases for
lives, leases renewable for ever, and leases
of which there is more than 60 years to
ru. If these holdings are bona fide
agricultural holdings why should they be
excluded? I was not aware myself that
there were as many of these cases over
Ulster as there are, but I have letters
nearly every week from people saying
they are excluded under this Section 20
although they are bona fide agricultural
tenants. The same mistake seems to have
been made in the Act of 1881, although
it was a very much larger mistake.
The leaseholders were left out of the
benefits of the fair rent courts, and it was

leaseholders were allowed into the fair
rent courts. I hold that this new
Amending Bill should include all these

Minister is a sort of Samson. When these

into. I am amazed that such a thing

I have

The bus business is not in a satisfactory
condition. The hon. Member has referred
to some facts. I can quote him a case
where a person can travel 36 miles for twopence. All I can say is that people who
think they can continue to travel for ever
at a fare that is below cost price are living
in a fool's paradise. To suggest for one
moment, as my hon. Friend has done, that
I am taking away any of the powers of the
road authorities is entirely wrong. The
powers of the road authorities are going to
remain exactly the same.
They have
power, as my hon. Friend knows, to close
third-class roads. I think he is one of
those that advocate that power should be
given to them under the Roads Act to close
first- and second-class roads also. That is
a proposition that the Government could
not accede to.
In regard to the conditions under which
these licences are going to be issued, the
arrangement that has been made in regard
to the country was not contingent on what
we did in regard to Belfast. They are
absolutely separate and distinct problems.

dealing with the Belfast traffic, I felt that
that was a suitable time to deal with the
problem in the country.
After all, my
hon. Friend must realize that Belfast has

and to ensure that in the future the

many schools at present have temporary
principals and in how many it has been

Mr. ROBB: There are at present nineteen schools under principals temporarily recognized and fourteen under
locum tenens principals. Those under
locum tenens teachers are generally
schools in which the manager will appoint
a fully qualified teacher as soon as he can
obtain one.
As a rule the temporary principals are
persons appointed to schools which are
about to be superseded by new schools,
etc., and in which the Ministry has not
considered it equitable to confer permanent recognition on the teacher, as such

place at the Table): I have to acquaint
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, where His Grace
the Governor, on behalf of His Majesty
the King, delivered in his speech to both
Houses of Parliament as follows:-
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I congratulate you upon the result
of your labours during the session now
concluded.
I feel that widespread satisfaction will
be occasioned by the extension of the
Franchise to women of 21 years of age.
I am glad that the powers of Local
Authorities in connection with the widening and improving of our road systems
have been extended. Every step in this
direction safeguards users of our highways
by minimising the risk of accident.
The decision of my Government to
postpone till 1933 decontrol of rents of
the smaller type of dwellings and to
continue the housing subsidy for a
further year causes me profound gratification, as I feel that if the present rate
of building is maintained one at least of
the many difficulties facing the working
classes will be rapidly overcome.
The necessary preliminaries in connection with the drainage of Lough Neagh
and the River Bann have been initiated.
I earnestly hope that when the scheme
is completed relief from flooding so long
looked forward to and so urgently required will be amply afforded.
It is satisfactory to note the passage of
further legislation remedying difficulties
and removing anomalies in the laws
dealing with the sale and consumption
of intoxicating liquors; and that in
particular steps have been taken, with
beneficial results, enabling a stricter
control to be exercised over the sale and
consumption of noxious beverages.
A National Health Insurance Measure
has passed into law which will extend
the usefulness and simplify the machinery of that scheme, and an Unemployment Insurance Act has been passed
placing on a simpler and more equitable
basis the conditions governing the distribution of benefit to unemployed workers.
The administrative changes in connection
with the Non-Contributory Old Age
Pensions were smoothly and satisfactorily
effected.
I am glad to observe that during the
present year there has been a welcome
increase of activity in the shipbuilding
industry with consequent additional employment. The operation of the Loans
Guarantee Acts has been a very important
contributory factor in this improvement.
The limit within which guarantees may
be issued has been extended from ten and
a half million pounds to eleven and a half
million pounds.
I note that additional support to the
Linen Publicity Campaign has been
afforded, but I regret that owing mainly
to international causes, this trade is still
in a depressed condition.
ment.
My Government has continued its policy
of subsidising schemes beneficial to the
community which are promoted by public
bodies for the purpose of giving employ-
During the present year grants
amounting to two hundred and fifty-four
thousand pounds have facilitated the initiation of one hundred such schemes on
which the expenditure on wages alone
will, it is estimated, amount to three
hundred and forty-one thousand pounds.
The placing upon the Statute Book of
the first of the measures designed to give
effect to the Government's proposals for
de-rating of Agriculture and productive
industry is a very satisfactory feature of
your labours. The operation of the provisions relating to freight and other transport charges will provide a measure of
immediate relief.
Legislation has been passed to regulate
the sale of fish and to secure the better
preservation of the inland fisheries. This
Act comes into full operation at the
beginning of next year, and it is hoped
that the benefits which are expected to
accrue therefrom will manifest themselves
within the coming season.
It is gratifying to observe the success
that has attended legislation already
passed in the interests of the egg industry.
This augurs well for the third Marketing
of Eggs Act that has so recently been
added to the Statute Book to advance
yet further the interests of that most
important branch of agricultural activity.
Regard has also been paid to the potato
trade, and you have satisfied progressive
agriculturists by passing the Marketing
of Potatoes Act, kindred in principle ani
purpose to the enactments relating to the
marketing of eggs.
Proclamation.
End of Session.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
I am glad that it has been found
possible to make provision for additional
financial assistance to meet the needs of
Queen's University. I trust this will be
of value in furthering the educational
requirements of the community.
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank you for the provision of
supplies for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I note with great satisfaction that
good order generally prevails throughout
Northern Ireland and that there has been
a diminution of serious crime.
A gratifying feature of the industrial
life of Northern Ireland is its continued
immunity, save in very rare instances,
from trade disputes, and the maintenance
of harmonious relations between
ployers and employed.
em-
It is my earnest prayer that the blessing
of Almighty God may rest upon all your
past and coming labours.
After which the Proclamation proroguing Parliament was read as followeth :
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall in His Majesty's name
summon, prorogue and
the
dissolve
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern Ireland should be prorogued to the twentysixth day of February, One Thousand
Nine Hundred and Twenty-nine:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT ED-
WARD, DUKE OF ABERCORN,
KNIGHT OF THE MOST NOBLE
ORDER OF THE GARTER, KNIGHT
OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS OR-
DER OF ST. PATRICK, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation
do publish and declare His Majesty's
Pleasure that the said Parliament be, as
from the reading of this Proclamation in
the Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the twenty-sixth day
of February, One Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-nine.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
twenty-sixth day of February, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twentynine, assemble and be holden for the despatch of divers urgent and important
affairs, and the Senators and Members of
the House of Commons of Northern
Ireland are hereby required to give their
attendance accordingly.
Given at the Council Chamber, Belfast,
the seventeeth day of December, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twentyeight.
Signed by his own hand.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday, 6th March, 1928), of the Second
Parliament of Northern Ireland, in the
Nineteenth year of the Reign of His
Majesty King George the Fifth.

COUNTY INFIRMARIES
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether any attempi is being
made, in view of the report of the Vice-
Regal Commission, to establish the County
Infirmaries in the Northern area on a more
effective basis, and to make provision, as in
other County establishments, for pensions
for the surgical staff, nurses, and other
officials?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson' Bates): I am fully alive to the importance of the question raised by the hon.
Member, and I have under consideration
the question to what extent the ratepayers
might be asked to join in contributing the
funds necessary to provide pensions for the
Officials of these Institutions.
I hope to be able to introduce a Bill making provision for this purpose at the earliest
possible moment.

(Mr. McKeown): the question, I presume, refers to the Committee, which, under

ur

Poor Law Valuations.
STATEMENT BY MINISTER OF
FINANCE.
3. Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH asked
the Minister of Finance whether he is aware
that manufacturers and merchants who
have made additions or improvements to
their property, have been mulcted in
enormous increases in their Poor Law
Valuations, which are altogether out of proportion to the relative Poor Law Valuations
of other premises in the same vicinity; and
whether it is the fact that this method of
penalizing improvements is seriously retarding the development of the Province, and
that many overdue improvements have been
deferred in consequence. Whether the Government will give this matter its earnest
attention, so that all properties, the valuations of which have been increased during
the period of high cost in building construction, be revised. Whether regard should not
be paid solely to the commercial value of
the improvement, and that in all other
respects new buildings, messuages and
premises under revision should be valued in
like proportion to the values of similar
premises within the same area, which have
not been so revised. Whether, if a shed be
attached to a private dwelling-house, such
a slight addition should be an occasion for
the revision of the valuation of the entire
house and garden, and whether Poor Law
Valuations are not often greatly increased
owing to the circumstance of the erection
of such trivial structures. Whether new
private dwelling-houses are not valued at
a much higher rate than similar houses in
the same locality built before the
Whether this method of valuation is not
unfair; and is not the occupier of a new
house sufficiently penalised by the present
high cost of building construction, whilst
this course seriously retards the erection of
private dwelling-houses and the general
development of the City?
war.
Poor Law Valuations.
Poor Law Valuations.
8 MAY 1923
The
(Mr.
MINISTER OF FINANCE
Pollock): This is a very long and comprehensive question, and I must ask the indulgence
of the House if I have to make an equally
long, and, I hope, equally comprehensive,
reply.
The point raised by my hon. Friend is one
which is by no means new, and to which I
have given very considerable thought and
attention since the time when the functions
previously exercised by the Commissioner of
Valuation for Ireland were, as regards the
Northern area, transferred to the jurisdiction
of the Northern Government.
As hon. Members are aware, the Valuation
Law under which the annual revisions are
carried through is, to say the least of it,
in a very unsatisfactory state-(hon. Members: "Hear, hear ")-and in practice gives
rise to all manner of anomalies.
It may not be out of place if I survey here
briefly the history of the present system of
valuation. The basic statute upon which
valuations are founded is an Act of 1852, following upon the passing of which a general
valuation of the whole of Ireland was instituted. The Act of 1852 contemplated periodical general revaluations, but since the date
of the completion of what is known as the
"Griffith Valuation," carried through in the
period, 1852-1866, no general valuation of property in Northern Ireland has taken place,
though as regards the County Borough of
Belfast a general revaluation was carried
through in 1906.
Each year, following on the provisions of
the 1852 Act, as amended by subsequent legislation, a patchwork revision of existing valuations is carried through in respect of buildings
which have been included in the revision
lists, by the local authority concerned. In
this connection I would like to make clear
that the valuation officers of the Ministry of
Finance have no power whatever to carry
through revaluations except in the cases submitted for revaluation by local authorities.
A practice has arisen amongst local authorities of including in the revision lists only new
properties or those which have undergone
certain alterations. I am advised, however,
that there is no reason in law why the revision
lists prepared by the local authorities should
be restricted to cases where alterations have
taken place in the structure. Local authorities may in their discretion include, in the
revision lists, any buildings, the valuaton of
which they consider requires amendment,
The inadequacy of the existing valuation law
coupled with the practice of including in
valuation lists all cases where alterations or
improvements have been effected has given
rise to the inequities and anomalies in valuations to which the hon. Member has called
attention.
When the valuation department is notified
by the local authority that a certain property
is to be revalued, it is for the officers of that
department to estimate the net annual value
of the property, which in the words of the
1852 Statute is to be based upon 'the rent
for which one year with another the same
might in its actual state be reasonably expected to let from year to year." In effect, the
valuation is based on the estimated net rental
value, and the annual value referred to in
the Statute has been interpreted by judicial
decision to mean the net rental of the property at the time the valuation is fixed. There
is an exception to this rule in the case of new
dwelling-houses, the pre-war annual value of
which is estimated at a sum not exceeding
£78. Under the Rent Restriction Acts, such
houses are assessed on a pre-war valuation
basis, but apart from this exception, it happens that with the inflated rents obtaining
at the present time, property-owners whose
buildings are listed for revision find themselves faced with assessments which, from a
taxation standpoint, compare very unfavourably with the valuations of buildings in the
same neighbourhood which have not been included in the revision list.
This anomaly, as I have mentioned, is by
no means a new problem. Bills, which had
as their object the improvement of the valuation system, were introduced into the Imperial
House of Commons in 1866, 1873 and in 1877,
but none of the three measures met with any
success. The Royal Commission on Local
Taxation in 1902 and the Royal Commission
on Income Tax in 1920 made specific reference
to the anomalies existing in the methods of
valuation in Ireland. On general lines the
one clear method of arriving at equitable
valuations would be to have a complete revaluation of all property throughout Northern
Ireland, but as hon. Members will readily
appreciate, such a proposal would involve
financial, economic and political considerations of far-reaching effect. In order, however, to endeavour to eliminate the inequalities of the existing system, I propose to set
up at an early date a small committee to
advise upon the revision of the existing
Valuation Law.
Mr. LYNN: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask the Finance Minister whether he
is not aware that the real cause of complaint
at the present time is that the valuations
are not made on the rental value, but on the
costs of building, which are abnormal?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not fully aware of
that, because the valuers are regulated
strictly by the Statute, and while I do not
suppose that other considerations do not
enter into their calculations, such
as the
cubing of the building and such like, the
condition of the valuation is set out very
clearly in the Statute.

But I am fully aware that in the valuations

variations in the valuations, and each of

Mr. LYNN: Would my right hon. Friend

Mr. POLLOCK: I should not be surprised.
Mr. LYNN: Seeing the very great importance of this point, from every aspect of the
case, would my right hon. Friend consider

Mr. McGUFFIN: In connection with the

Committee, which is specifically appointed
to do a specific work, and whose credit is

it does.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: Arising

that a certain formula will have to be

affairs, so that premises re-valued will be
on the same basis exactly as adjoining premises
Mr. POLLOCK: To give a definite assurance that certain measures will be adopted
is, I think, at the moment premature, and,
in the absence of expert knowledge, expert
information, and general evidence from the
community, I do not believe that I would
be justified in entering into any undertaking.
But, certainly, I give this assurance-that
the Government will be guided by the recommendations of any practical Committee
that issues its report.
Mr. LYNN: Will the Prime
Minister
answer the question-Will he give a day for
the discussion of the subject, or a day on
which the debate can take place on the
motion for the adjournment?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir JAMES
CRAIG): Of course my hon. Friend (Mr.
Lynn) knows that we are always most
anxious to allow time for the discussion of
any important matter; but I think perhaps
he might defer asking for a day, not only
until my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) has
established the Committee to which he has
referred, but also until the Government here
have had some opportunity of considering
the result of what is taking place on the
same subject at Westminster, where the
question is as acute as it is here.
BROADCASTING STATION IN ULSTER.
4. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether, in view of the increasing
desire for the establishment of a Broadcasting Station in the Six County Area, he is now
in a position to make a statement with
respect to the matter?
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): The establishment of a Broadcasting Station in the Six County Area is a
matter which, under the agreement entered
into by His Majesty's Postmaster-General,
can only be undertaken by the British
Broadcasting Company. So far, the Northern
Government have not been approached by
the Company in regard to the establishment
of such a station; but I may inform the hon.
Member that, if and when, a formal application is made by the Company, the Northern
Government will raise no objection, provided
that certain essential conditions are complied
with.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
does that imply that he is prepared to offer
a subsidy on a British Broadcasting Station
being established in the Northern Area; or
may I ask him if he would change the course
of procedure and approach the Company
rather than that they should approach the
Ministry?
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: Arising out of
that answer, I would like to ask the right
hon. Gentleman if, before he takes any steps
in this matter, he will consult a committee,
or, at least, persons representing both professional and amateur wireless operators in
the Northern Area?
Mr. ARCHDALE: In answer to the hon.
Member (Mr. McGuffin), it is imperative on
the Broadcasting Company to apply to the
Northern Government. We do not apply to
them, or give them a subsidy. With regard
to what my hon. Friend (Mr. Lloyd Campbell) says, I am certain when they do apply
every interest concerned will be consulted.

The CHAIRMAN: Perhaps hon. Members
would give consideration to the convenience
of the Ministry when they hand in manuscript amendments at the Table, and also
hand to the hon. Gentleman in charge of the

to be handed to me now, and I think copies

CLAUSE 7 (Definition of elementary education and public elementary school, etc.)
For the purposes of this Act, the expression "elementary education" means an
education based upon instruction in the
reading and writing of the English language and in arithmetic, provided for pupils
who are in general of an age below fourteen
years, and the expression "public elementary
school" means a school or department of a
school in respect of which grants are paid
out of moneys provided by Parliament, and
in which elementary education is the principal part of the education provided.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): I beg to move,
"In Clause 7, page 13, line 14, after the
second 'education' ('means an education')
insert 'both literary and moral.'"
The provisions of the Bill in regard to elementary education have been criticised on the
ground that they mention specifically the
purely literary side of the education and the
purely denominational side of religious education, being silent upon the general moral
instruction which is a necessary part of
education. It was, as the Minister has explained, never intended to negative moral
instruction. Rather, it was assumed that
the education authorities would provide for
it without looking for specific authority from
the text of the Bill.
It appears, however,
that it is necessary to give such specific
authority, and accordingly it is suggested
that the elementary education should be
expressly required to be both literary and
moral. These words being taken from
Chapter I. of the Rules and Regulations of
the Commissioners of National Education in
Ireland, it is presumed that they stood the
test of time, and they will make it clear
that no change in the existing system is
contemplated. I beg to move.
Mr. LYNN: I would like to ask my hon.
Friend what he really means by moral ininstruction? After all, the teaching of Confucius or Buddha is moral instruction, and
some of the French atheists impart very
fine moral instruction. Does he mean by
moral instruction, religious instruction?
Mr. McKEOWN: With regard to the point
raised by my hon. Friend, moral instruction,
I think, can be taught in every classroom of
the school. Moral instruction is a thing that
might run through the daily work of
the school. It does not refer to religious instruction, which will be dealt with at a later
stage.
Amendment agreed to.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move,
"In Clause 7, page 13, line 16, after
' arithmetic' (and in arithmetic ') insert
' and the elementary principles of domestic
economy.""
I am putting this amendment down, because
I notice that the marginal note to the Clause
says:-
"Definition of elementary education and
public elementary school, etc."
by
Well, I cannot accept that definition as to
include only the teaching of reading, writing
and arithmetic. It seems to me that the
teaching of domestic economy-and
domestic economy I mean the teaching of
elementary cooking and sewing-is an absolutely fundamental part of education. It
fits girls to become good wives and mothers,
and to be able to look after their homes. I
do hope that the Ministry will see fit to treat
this subject as a really important one, and
that comfortable accommodation for the
teaching of domestic economy, where that
accommodation does not already exist, will
be provided.
Education Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: In supporting
this amendment, I agree with what the hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) says,
that one of the great things required in any
system of education to-day is not merely the
well-known three R's. The three R's are
very useful, but after all what has to be
recognised is the state in which many of the
houses and slums are. I think a great
deal can be done both for the male child
as well as the female child in that way.
The hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) has alluded to the teaching of
elementary cooking and sewing. She has
referred mainly to the teaching of girls,
but she has not mentioned the teaching of
boys in that subject. The boy has also
something to learn in domestic economy,
namely, the general keeping together and
general looking after of a house. This means
a duty to a very large extent. It is mainly,
however, on account of the girl that 1 am
supporting the amendment. I do think that
a very large amount of comfort and happiness would be brought into many a home if
only girls had learned in their early daysto use what is perhaps a vulgar expression,
but which bears a solemn truth-"to feed
the beast." I speak as one of the beasts.
There is no doubt whatever that when a
man comes home tired from his day's work
and finds a comfortable well-kept home, a
well-cooked meal, and a well-looked-after
shirt he is much happier, and his health,
too, is much better.
Mr. LYNN: I congratulate the hon
Member (Mr. Lloyd Campbell), who has just
spoken, on the fact that he is evidently a
very good specimen of the value of domestic
economy. But while I am absolutely in
sympathy with the amendment moved by the
hon. Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester), 1
think there are many other things that
might be put in at the same time. Domestic
economy of course, is an essential thing, but
I would suggest that there is such a thing as
political economy. because we have reached
a stage when people are saying that you can
get something for nothing and can get things
without producing them, and nonsense of that
sort. It is absolutely necessary that these
things should be taught as well. The trouble
is to get a definition of what elementary
education really is. I am quite sure,
whether the Ministry accept the amendment
or not, it will in its regulations see to it that
domestic economy is taught in the schools. I
agree with every word the hon. Member for
Derry (Mrs. Chichester) has said on the subject, but there are so many important
matters that ought to be taught that I do not
know that it is really possible to define them
all in a Bill.
Captain MULHOLLAND: I think the
object of the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) is merely to draw attention to the
practical importance of the principles of
domestic economy. If that were not so I
should agree with the hon. Member for West
Belfast (Mr. Lynn), who says that other subbe
for
jects might
introduced-civics,
instance. When I read this clause carefully,
however, I saw that it is education based
upon instruction in reading, writing and
arithmetic. I presume these subjects are
simply the basic principles on which education is founded.
Mr. DONALD: I would not wish to encourage domestic economy being taught in
our elementary schools at all, for the simple
reason that I would welcome and advocate
a separate building for that purpose. I hope
that in dealing with this matter the Government will recognise that we should have a
separate structure like other centres for the
teaching of these subjects. For that reason,
I am not much enamoured of the amendment.
Mr. McKEOWN: I am sure all hon. Members will agree with what has been stated by
those who proposed this amendment; but, as
my hon. Friend the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn) has pointed out, let everything
be in its proper place. The basic subjects are
undoubtedly reading, writing, and arithmetic. These are mentioned in the Clause,
and run through the whole elementary school
course. There are, of course, other subjects,
such as drawing, manual instruction, and
domestic economy, which find places at suitable stages in the elementary school course.
This has always been the case, and always
will be so, but, short of the full syllabus,
which could not be incorporated in the Bill,
it would not be possible to give a full statement of everything that might or ought to be
taught in an elementary school. I am sorry
I am obliged to resist the amendment.
Amendment by leave withdrawn.

before me when I expressed a wish that the
Report of the Departmental Committee on
curricula should be issued before this Bill
came to the Committee Stage. The reason
I did so was because I notice that in Secondary and University education the curriculum
has increased in difficulty-and very materially-within the last thirty years, while in
the primary school it has practically
remained fixed. The way I look at it is that
we are wanting to have a higher class of
teacher, with higher intellectual and educational status, and yet we do not propose to
allocate to him a more important or a higher
scale of duty. It appears to me as if we
were calling upon the teacher to be educated
to a high degree for no particular purpose.
I submit that, in so far as primary education is concerned, the scholars were better
done for fifty years ago. It seems a sweeping
statement to make, but I allege that it is true.
When education was less under control, there
was a far freer and broader basis of education given. At the time to which I refer it
was quite a common thing for a schoolmaster, who did not make any pretentions at
all to what is called University education or
distinction, to teach subjects that are
regarded as outside the scope of the present
curriculum of the primary schools. Let me
instance what I mean. It was quite a common thing then for a boy leaving school to
know a considerable amount about Euclid
and algebra, and more particularly about
geometry and mensuration. These are
subjects that if they are taught in the
schools now must be regarded as extras.
Why should they be regarded as extras? I am
inclined to believe that we are restricting the
efforts of the child too much, as if it was not
competent for the child until it had reached
a certain age to comprehend the principles
involved in these particular subjects I have
mentioned. If it is the intention, as I presume it is the intention, of the Ministry of
Education to lead out the faculties of the
child you cannot begin too soon, and by
merely drumming into its memory a certain
amount of facts and data, which it is supposed to retain but seldom does retain, without any particular advantage you are not conducing, I believe, to the education of the
child.
I present the case from a more practical
point of view. In many instances the children at school to-day will not have the advantages of a secondary education. These boys
will go into their respective workshops, and
will suffer from limitations in knowledge in
matters about which they should know a good
deal. Take, for instance, a boy going to the
trade of carpentering who knows nothing
about mensuration or geometry. He is very
considerably handicapped for the want of
knowledge of these subjects. It would be
equally true, though not perhaps within the
scope of the amendment, in reference to what
we call the elementary principles of mechanics. Knowledge of these is at present denied
to the children and they have no other opportunity in the world of acquiring the knowledge. You have teachers very well qualified
to teach those subjects, and I cannot for the
life of me see why a child must wait until it
is entering the secondary stage in order that
these subjects may be inculcated. For my
part I am inclined to think that it does not
matter at what stage a child is initiated into
these subjects provided the necessary instruction is given. I have known what it is to
pass through the workshops. I have known
men of excellent manual skill fearfully restricted for want of knowledge of these principles. Yet you tell me you are going to
equip a child for life by sending him out without this knowledge. I want you to furnish
the child to the limit of his ability, and it is
just as much in the elementary schools as in
the secondary schools that you have differentiation in ability. You have children restricted in their progress by reason of having
to wait for those who are slower or of smaller
receptive capacity. I think that should not
be. I think it should be within the province
of the principal, if he thinks right, to segregate the scholars according to ability, and
within the prescribed hours these subjects
should be taught as ordinary and not as
special or extra subjects. At the moment
they are special subjects and there is a
capitation grant paid in respect of them.
That is not the way in which we hope this
Ministry is going to conduct primary education in the future. I would, therefore,
suggest that it is all-important that at the
present time the Ministry should outline--
and very definitely, too-what is really meant
by elementary education, or by what is set
forth in the Clause here as "elementary
education." Elementary education, as the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn)
has suggested, may mean anything unless you
define it. It may include anything, but I
am not going to ask you to include within it
certain things to my mind practically negligible. What I am inviting you to do is to
include things that are of paramount importance for the children who may never reach
the secondary school. It is all-important for
their future interests, and I, therefore, invite
the Minister of Education to say whether
subjects such as algebra, Euclid, ensuration and geometry will come within the term
of "arithmetic." I cannot at the moment see
how they can, though I see no reason why a
child learning arithmetic should not learn
algebra----

should be a strict hand kept on expenditure.
In the case of really necessitous children I
do think the local authorities ought to come
to their aid and provide books, but, believe
me, if you are going to provide them for the
whole of the school children in Belfast they
will not cost what they are costing to-day,
but ten times more, because there will be
no necessity for economy. It will be said,
These are the education authorities books.
Why need we preserve them or care for
them?" I think a strong case has been made
out for the adoption of this amendment, and
I hope the Ministry will meet it.

CLAUSE 9 (Necessity for Schools).
If at any time it is determined by the
Ministry that the continuance of a provided
school or of a public elementary school
transferred to an education authority is not
necessary, no grants out of moneys provided
by Parliament shall be payable by the
Ministry to or in respect of such school, and
steps shall be taken by the education
authority for discontinuing any such school
within such time as the Ministry may
direct and for providing for the education
of the children in attendance thereat by
such other means as may be approved by
the Ministry:
Provided always that in the case of a
school transferred to the education
authority the terms and conditions on which
the transfer has been effected shall be duly
complied with.

Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move.
"That the position of the unmarried mother

Unmarried Mothers.

8 MAY 1923
This is in accordance with notice and in
accordance with the practice - although I
believe that this is the first occasion on which
the right has been exercised-that a private
Member may put down notice for a particular
day in the week and have discussed any
matter that he thinks sufficiently urgent to
demand attention. That is what I have done
in order to bring before the House this very
important question of illigitimacy, or the
lack of provision for the unmarried mother
in the Six Counties. It has been long before
the public. The late Mr. Barrie had charge
of a Bill which was brought forward by the
Ulster Members for presentation in the
Imperial Parliament with the object of
having this serious state of affairs remedied.
An Amending Bill to the Act that is at present in force in England, was introduced in
the British House of Commons during the
war.
The Ulster Members took a very keen
interest in the question, and spoke very
strongly with the object of having the Bill
extended to Ireland. The Member for East
Belfast (Captain Dixon), our capable Whip,
made a very eloquent speech on that
occasion, and the Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Lynn), and I think also the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin), spoke on the
subject, urging that an Amending Bill should
not only be passed for England but extended
to Ireland so as to give protection to the
people who were affected in Ireland by this
question.
I myself have pressed this matter. I have
attended public meetings, three of them in
Belfast one of them presided over by her
Grace the Duchess of Abercorn, another presided over by Lady Craig, and a third presided over by Sir Robert Kennedy-some of
them in the City Hall of Belfast-drawing
attention to this important matter, and urging that steps should be taken to have some
protection provided for our girls in Ulster.
I also introduced a deputation to the
Minister of Home Affairs, a deputation representing all the social institutions that exist
in Ulster, to press this matter upon him. I
had had resolutions sent to me from labour
associations, from the executive committee of
the Protestant Teachers' Association, andthe most striking one of all-from the
United Council of the Protestant Churches
of Ireland which met recently at Belfast and
passed a resolution on this important subject.
All these resolutions have been without
effect-practically without effect. Any efforts
that these people have been making, and that
I have been making, have been simply
ploughing the sand. The matter is in the
hands of the Ministry of Home Affairs, and
it seems to me that the Ministry in respect
of this measure, and indeed of all measures
that affect social reform, are a law unto themselves, and they pay little attention to anyone. In any event we have now been more
than two years in office in this House and
nothing has been done. Two years have been
wasted, and I would like to ask the House to
look at the other side of the picture, and I
think when I describe it, they will agree
with me that it is an extraordinary thing that
something has not been done, and that the
case demands urgent action.
I got from the Ministry of Finance the
figures for illegitimacy in the Six Counties in
1922. Belfast had 394 illegitimate children
born in 1922, and in the other portions of
Ulster-that is, in the Six Counties-there
were 854. That makes a total of 1,248 in the
area that this Parliament is responsible for,
and if you double that, you have 2,496probably there will be something more than
that-representing the two years that we
have been in office. When you look at the
fact that the Ministry of Home Affairs had it
within their power to remedy this condition of
affairs, you naturally ask what they have
done for these 2,496 mothers and for the
2,496 children. I may say here that last
Session a Bill was introduced into this
House applying to this area of Northern Ireland no fewer than half-a-dozen little Bills
that were extended simply by means of a
clause, and the whole thing was run through
without any discussion and without any
expense. When that measure was going
through the House, I got up here and I
begged that the Minister of Home Affairs
would add the Bastardy Act to those halfdozen Bills. It could have been done by a
stroke of the pen, and something could have
been done for those 2,496 mothers and a
similar number of children. I do not know
if the Home Office and the officials who administer it look any deeper than the surface,
and ever ask themselves what has become of
those mothers and what has become of those
helpless children? I know that they have
medical men engaged upon their staff. I do
not think they consult them very often. I
know that there are medical Merabers in this
House, and I know from experience that--
while I may tender advice it is very rarely
taken. But I can lift a little portion of the
curtain, and tell this House what has befallen
some of those children. I have here a report of the Malone Reformatory Home for
1921 and 1922. There were 112 births in that
Home during 1922. Of those cases, there were
14 very serious and requiring very great care
on the part of the doctors who attended them.
Two of the mothers died, and four of the
Unmarried Mothers.
Unmarried Mothers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
[Dr. Morrison]
children were stillborn. There are six deaths
-two of mothers and four of babies-in the
112 children that were attended in that
Home. I do not think that in any place to
which these poor women could have been
taken they could have received better
attention than they received in that Home,
and I ask the House to consider seriously the
position of the others who were less fortunate,
and the mortality amongst them and
amongst their innocent children?
I may
mention in passing that for their attendance
there are five doctors there giving their services free, doing work which they consider
a duty and also a privilege, work that is
voluntarily taken upon themselves by the
doctors in Belfast, and which I think, when
a final estimate of values is being made, will
be pronounced by the Supreme Judge to be
worthy of the encomium of "Inasmuch
as
Now, I ask, what is being done for these
children? The Ministry of Home Affairs is
dealing, and dealing effectively I think, with
criminals in our city and in the Six County
area. I was complimenting the Minister not
more than ten days ago, when the Estimates
were being discussed, and I told him that
there were other portions of his Department
on which I could not speak so favourably.
I say that, while he is effectively dealing
with criminals, the policy he has adopted at
the Home Office with regard to these infants
and to this question is breeding children who
will be criminals.
My opinion is that a woman is the highest
and the most perfect form of created being.
We raise our hats to them, we give them our
seats in the trams and in the trains, and we
open doors for them. I submit-and I think
it cannot be denied in this House-that for
two years the Home Minister has been forcing open a door, and through that door he
has pushed 2,496 victims with their children
either to their graves or to the brothels that
exist in Belfast. In doing that, he has in
my opinion made himself responsible for a
gross act of injustice. He is in my opinion refusing help to the victim, while at the same
time he is protecting the criminal and setting
a premium upon crime. This Bastardy Act
is a simple measure which has been in force
in England for 50 years. It enables the
mother of an illegitimate child to summon
the father before the magistrates, and if she
can produce it is not a case of her own
statement alone-confirmatory evidence that
satisfies the magistrates, a decree is given or
a maintenance order is issued by the magistrates making the person liable for the support
of the child. This Amending Bill, which was
introduced in the English House of
Commons, and passed the Second reading by
an enormous majority, is an extension of that
Act. No one has found fault with the Act
as it was worked in England, but after the
passage of fifty years it has been found better
to add something else to it with the object
of remedying some of the defects that press
upon the poor mother, and sometimes upon
the child. I should be quite satisfied if we
followed the English example, and took this
Bill which has passed the Second reading.
This Amending Bill, I may assure you has
been before the Imperial House for five or
six years, and time was never found for its
passage until now. I will be satisfied if the
House adopt that measure, but if they
cannot do that, let them bring in a short
Bill making provision for the extension of
the Bastardy Act to this country.
As a man who knows the conditions that
prevail in the country, and who has been
told about the conditions in Belfast, I can
tell you that if the House passes this Bill, or
indeed if we had had it for the last fifty
years. this dirty, discreditable picture would
be wholly different. Countless lives would
have been saved-the lives of young, fresh
women, and the lives of helpless infants. It
is an appalling thing to think that of the 112
young women who were confined in the
Malone Home 36 were under 20 years of age,
and one was under the age of 15. That is the
state of things that exists in Belfast to-day.
That is the state of things that exists all
over rural Ulster to-day. I think it is a
terrible pity that through the stupidity-I
cannot call it anything else but the unthinkable stupidity-of the Home Office, we had
not this Bill extended to Ulster two years
ago.
It would have saved at least half the
number of deaths that have occurred during
these two years. That is my opinion as a
medical man. The persons in rural Ulster today who are guilty of these actions and who
seduce innocent, helpless, possibly emotional
girls, are irresponsible boys and lads who
have no sense of morality and no sense of
justice. You canot inflict a penalty on them,
because they have no real estate. If you get
a decree against them in the Quarter
Sessions Court you are not able to recover
anything.
As a matter of fact, no legal proceedings
are taken now in regard to putting any
penalty on these fellows. If you took the
trouble you would get nothing for your decree. If a man has real estate and is the
possessor of any land or any house property
or anything like that, he is particularly careful that he does not transgress in this way,
and the result is that these are not the men

are
responsible for begetting illegitimate children.
If you could put a penalty on those other
irresponsible members of the community and
make them pay 5s a week for the support of
the child, it would, in my opinion, reduce
this terrible picture by at least one-half.
The bulk of the domestic servants in this great
city come from the country. They
brought in and exposed to all these dangers.
I think that the Members from Belfast should
aid us from the country and should help the
people who protest against this thing and do
their best to have this awful condition of
affairs and this terrible injustice remedied.
I appeal to the Members who represent the
farming community in this House. They are
returned to this House by the votes of
labourers whose daughters come to earn their
living in Belfast. I think these men who
have voted for Members of Parliament have
a right to look for help and protection from
them in this matter. I appeal to the Labour
Members in Belfast and in this House. These
people are sent here to represent the workers
and the children of the workers, and to represent in a special way the helpless and unprovided for. I look to both these sections
to help us in this matter.
If this House is desirous of helping, all I
ask hon. Members to do is to pass this resolution, which is down on the Order Paper,
stating that action should be taken without
delay to protect the young people in our
community from the evils that surround
them in this special crisis. That is all I ask
you to do.
I am sure if you take up that
position the Home Office will be bound to
take action. I can also assure you that if
you do that you will take a great step in
advance to protect our girls, to diminish
suffering, to reduce the deaths that are taking
place in our midst, and to do something that
will effectively make this community of ours
what we would all like to see it a sweet,
clean, healthy community, where not only
the beasts and birds are protected, but where
all members of the human family are equally
afforded the protection they have a right to
expect in a civilised community. I beg to
move.

Ireland. I have not pressed this question before, because I understood that the Ministry
of Home Affairs, or the Government, were
waiting for the English Bill which is under

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO

:
Mrs. CHICHESTER: However, I do think
that the time has come when we must press
this matter, and urge the Ministry to reconsider the decision they have come to, or at
any rate to consider sympathetically what we
are now putting before them. I cannot
believe that they have realised how much

Acts of 1872 and 1873 justice, or at any rate.
the element of justice, is done to the illegiti-
Imate child and its mother in England, but
a very different state of affairs exists in Ireland, and it is almost impossible to believe
that we are not in the dark ages.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I do not think I am
speaking too strongly when I say that the
present condition of affairs here cries aloud
to man and the God of man for a remedy. I
am not making an appeal or a plea here for
justice or for pity on behalf of the women,
although there is much that I might say,
which might be said by others, on the subject, but I am one of those who believe that
what we SOW we must reap.
It is the
mother who reaps in shame, sorrow. anguish
and suffering. and it is in the nature of
things for the father to pass on. But surely
we can expect, we can demand, that the
financial responsibility is to a certain extent
borne by the man. We cannot allow him to
escape. It is only elementary justice that
when parenthood can be proved, and of course
absolutely proved, the man must be made
to contribute to the support of his child. As
I said before, it is not for the woman I am
making an appeal; it is for the child. It is
the innocent child who suffers in these cases.
In that connection, if I may be allowed to
quote them, there are some words here which
have been inserted in a document printed by
the National Society for the Prevention of
Cruelty to Children. The words so adequately express the present situation of the
child that I do not think I could put it as
well, and certainly no better:
"And even a greater wrong is being
done to children born under the triple
disadvantage of shame, cloud, and
physical risk. Many are doomed from
birth, others struggle for an enfeebled
existence, and a certain proportion become
national encumbrances."
Unmarried Mothers.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mrs. Chichester]
They are left to starve in some cases.
There is no alternative for them but to be
brought up as workhouse children, and yet
our care and our need is for a healthy, virile
race. What a contradiction! It has always
been said that the sins of the father must be
visited upon the children. Man has carried
out that law, because forgetting whom it is
going to punish, he carried it out unthinkingly and unfeelingly throughout the generations. I appeal to the Government to bring
in a Bill, or at any rate bring us into conformity with the English Bill, as soon as
possible. I know how busy they have been,
and I know, especially under the conditions
from which we have suffered in the North of
Ireland, how impossible it has been to carry
through all the legislation which is absolutely necessary. They have been delayed
for nearly two years on account of those conditions, and
as the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) has said, I wonder
how many innocent children have suffered for
that delay.
I ask the Government to bring us into
conformity with the English Bill, and then,
perhaps, when further reforms are carried
out across the water, they may take another
step forward and bring us again into conformity with the existing laws in England,
but I must say that I wish it was
possible for the Government to go still
further and bring in a Bill of their own, for
there are many other injustices which call
for remedy. There is the injustice done to
the illegitimate child whose parents subsequently marry, and who is left branded and
alone, although, perhaps, its brothers and
sisters enjoy all the privileges which should
be his. I am not going to labour that point.
There is only one other remark which I
should like to make. I wonder if it is fully
realised that the fact that these Acts do not
apply to Ireland has an effect not only upon
the mother of an illegitimate child but also
upon a deserted wife in Ireland. As I
understand it, a deserted wife under present
conditions, owing to the fact that these Acts
do not apply to Ireland, cannot summon her
husband for desertion, because there is a
clause to the effect that the payment of any
sum so ordered-that is ordered by the
Court to be paid by the husband for her
maintenance-shall be enforceable and enforced against the husband in the same
manner as the payment of money is enforced
under an order of affiliation. There is no
affiliation in Ireland, and so the deserted wife
has no remedy. I support the hon. Member
for the University (Dr. Morrison) in his
appeal to the Government, though I cannot
quite support him in all he has said in indictment of the Government, and I do hope they
will accede to our request and bring in this
Bill at the earliest opportunity.
severe.

(Dr Morrison), and so very ably and so very

must dissociate myself from some of the

I think he was just a little bit unnecessarily
At the same time I can quite understand his feelings in regard to a matter of
this character. I think we are dealing with a
subject that appeals to the sympathies of the
House as a whole, and that I am perfectly
certain must have the sympathy, support, and

complained of is that the Minister of Home

British House of Commons constitute another
question, and I think a good many of the matters contained in it would naturally require the
careful consideration of the Government. I
think this House would at all times seek in
this matter to help those who really cannot
help themselves. The position I have always
taken up on matters of this kind is that there
cannot be one separate law for the man and
another separate law for the woman. The man
in these cases ought to be not only prepared
but compelled to bear the responsibility. I
do not say the Government is going to bring
about a moral reformation in connection with
this matter by an Act of Parliament, but I
do say they can bring in something that will
act as a deterrent, and that will at the same
time bring home the responsibility to one party
in connection with these things. The right
to support ought to be secured where it is
possible to secure it, and undoubtedly the
Government have an opportunity of bringing
in a measure--shall I call it?-of social reform,
something that will appeal to the sympathy
and secure the support of the House as a
whole. I do not wish to labour the matter
any further. I feel I am speaking to a House

have been left out of sight? So far as the
Ministry of Home Affairs is concerned I know
the officials and the men in charge of things
were kept busy from day to day in dealing
with the absolutely essential matters then
before them. So far as the other speakers
are concerned I am absolutely in sympathy
with what they have said, and with every
word of it; but to charge the Government
for not introducing legislative measures, and
to suggest that it is maladministration on
their part to continue the present system is,
I think, bardly warranted by the state of
affairs.
The Ministry of Home Affairs, and the
Government as a whole, recognise that the
law in Ireland is very unsatisfactory. It
has been unsatisfactory for over fifty years,
as the hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) has said, but if during those fifty
years there has been no attempt made to
reform the law, could it have been accomplished within the two years during which this
Government has been in office? The matter
is one that cannot be dealt with hurriedly.
It is one that requires a considerable amount
of investigation, I do not say in regard to
the making of a father of an illegitimate
child responsible for its upkeep, but in
regard to the other question with which it
is so much allied. Legitimisation in the case
of the subsequent marriage of the parents is
one that is not very easily dealt with, seeing
that the rights of property are involved, and
it is one that is giving difficulty on the other
side. The Government are waiting until they
find what is being done there, until they see
if both the matters alluded to cannot be dealt
with in one measure.
The hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) in his indictment commenced by
stating the number of cases of illegitimate
children in Belfast and Ultser. I happen to
have before me the return of the Belfast
Board of Guardians. They have a single
mother's history sheet for their lying-in hospital. Lest there might be any misconception from the figures, which the hon. Member so proudly, shall I say, displayed, I would
like to refer to that return, and I think the
House will perhaps see what is a truer aspect.
of the question of illegitimacy than that with
which the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) has
furnished us. In February, 1921, there was
a list of seventy-one such cases submitted,
not one of which belonged to Belfast during
the preceding nine months. The cases came
from, among other places, Dublin, Cavan,
Clones, Glasgow, Dundalk, Meath, Southport,
Roscommon, Kildare, Hereford, and
Greenock. According to the figures given by
the hon. Member for the University all these
would be categorised as cases of illegitimacy
arising in Ulster and in Belfast. I have
taken the precaution of trying to avert that
impression, because when my hon. Friend
(Dr. Morrison) is stating a case I think he is
occasionally inclined to overstate it, and in
his desire to get rid of what he regards, and
rightly so. as a grievance he got lost somewhat to his sense of proportion.
ever

greatest sympathy, and their desire is that

Why should the Ministry of Home Affairs,

absolutely easy. If it is so absolutely easy,
why does he not bring in a private measure,
and then it can pass through the House?
There certainly will be no opposition on the
part of the Government if such a measure is

large charge.

of the Bill in this House and its introduction in the Senate public aufhorities and
those interested in this very difficult subject
-the management of roads in the counties
have made certain representations, and those

Counties as a whole, were so important from

I fear there has been a certain amount of
misunderstanding on the part of some of the
rural district councils in regard to the attitude of the Government in connection with
the proposals under the Bill for the future
management of these roads. It has been suggested that we desire to cast a reflection on
rural district councils. That is not so; but
I think it will be perfectly obvious to hon.
Members who have had experience of county
council and rural district council management that if there is to be any general improvement in the management of the roads,
there must be purely controlling bodies, and
more uniformity in regard to their management. Another objection put forward on behalf of certain rural district councils is that
this new arrangement will impose a great
burden upon the rural districts. I must say
that, having gone into this matter very carefully, I cannot agree with that point of view.
I believe that in many cases it will not alone
be more economical in the general cost of the
roads, but more economical to the ratepayers.
I would remind hon. Members that Class 1
and 2 roads only constitute something like 15
per cent, or 20 per cent. of the total roads in
the county.
The other amendment which has been inserted in the Bill by the Senate gives power
to local authorities to close any road during
reconstruction or repair, and I am sure hon.
Members will agree that in a narrow road it
is practically impossible to make a good job
of repairing it unless it is possible to close
that road entirely to traffic during the period
of reconstruction. I beg to move.

Sir DAWSON BATES: Yes, except to the

Except in so far as they are represented on

roads and I think that will tend to lower

they are little more than lanes-and I do
think those could be safely left to the Rural
District Councils. The County Surveyor is
really a servant of the County Council. He
prepares his estimates, and goes to the Rural
District Councils with those estimates, and
asks for a certain sum. In some cases the
Rural District Councils are generous and
liberal-minded, but in other cases his estimates are cut down, as in my own case, by
one-half. The County Surveyor goes back to
his County Council. He has to abide, and
the County Council has to abide, by the decision of the Rural District Council, and the
result is that the roads in certain counties are
in the deplorable condition that they are in
at the present time, and a disgrace, if I may
say so, to the whole community. I do hope it
will be possible to make this a uniform matter, that the House will agree with the Senate's

Criminal Evidence Bill.
Order for consideration of Senate's Amendments read.
Mr. MEGAW: I beg to move: "That the
House do now consider the amendments of
the Senate."
I wish just to give a few words of explanation to the House as to the nature of the
amendments that were introduced in the
Senate. This Bill we are dealing with introduces the principle that has been adopted
in England for so many years of allowing a
prisoner to give evidence on his own behalf.
That was introduced in 1898 by the British
Government. It was necessary under the
Schedule of the English Act to have certain
enactments still kept in force. The principle
of the English Act was to make a prisoner a
voluntary witness, 'but not a compellable
witness, but there was a class of case in
which it was found necessary that the
prisoner's wife who was also precluded from
giving evidence, should be enabled to give
751 Criminal Evidence Bill--

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Senate's Amendments.
[Mr. Megaw.]
evidence too. Those were included in the
Schedule as in the Schedule to the English
Act. In the meantime a number of other
enactments of the same class had arisen that
enabled in Ireland a prisoner's wife to give
evidence and to make her a compellable witness against him, so that it becomes necessary for us if these new enactments are to
be kept in force to include them in the
Schedule. The first lot of amendments here
are to include those Acts in the First
Schedule so as to enable a prisoner's wife
to be a compellable witness against him.
They deal chiefly with offences that relate
to troubles between a husband and wife.
Besides that there is a Second Schedule that
requires some amendment in regard to Acts
that have become no longer necessary by
reason of this Bill of ours being put into law.
In the Second Schedule are included others
that have become necessary. The effect of
the amendments introduced by the Senate is
that they are really drafting amendments so
as to keep the records right-we shall have
still in force those enactments that enable
a prisoner's wife to be compellable to give
evidence against him, and they enable us also
to repeal Acts that are no longer necessary.
With one exception those are the only
matters dealt with in the amendments of
the Senate. The other is one dealing with
the date on which the Act comes into operation. As originally drafted the date was
two months after the passing of the Act.
Well, for administrative reasons it is thought
necessary and better to have a definite date.
As the Assizes go out on the 1st July it has
been thought better to put the 30th June
as the date on which the Act comes into
operation. This will give ample time for
all persons interested to have made themselves acquainted with the provisions of the
Act. I beg to move.
Question put and agreed to.
