CLAUSE 11 (Nursery Schools).
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I do not propose to
move any amendment to this Clause. I had a
conversation with the Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. McKeown) yesterday, and
there is one point in connection with the
Clause which I wish to bring up. This Clause
provides that Nursery Schools and special
classes may be provided for
"children over two and under five years of
age, or such later age as may be approved
by the Ministry, whose attendance at such
a school is necessary or desirable for their
healthy physical and mental development.”
It is within the knowledge of this committee
that an open-air school is being carried on
at the present time at Graymount in .onnection with the tuberculosis scheme. That is a
most admirable thing, and the probability is
that other schools of the same kind for
children who are what we might call delicate
or disposed to bad health should be established. I would like to know whether this
clause would cover the case of schools of that
type, and whether the Ministry contemplates
the establishment of such schools under this
clause. It is a point in connection with which
I think power should be taken by the Ministry, because these children are not afflicted
children in the technical sense of the word.
An afflicted child is either mentally deficient,
blind or deaf or dumb. These children have
all their faculties, but their state of health
makes it essential that they should be put
under more hygienic conditions. I want to
know whether the Ministry consider that this
Clause would cover schools for tubercular
children, and, if not, will it be amended in
the Report stage to cover such cases?
Mr. McKEOWN: The point raised by the
hon. Member (Mr. Johnstone) is an important one, because very useful work is done
in the schools to which he refers. We believe
that these schools are covered by this Clause,
but we will make sure before we reach the
Report stage.

The deletion of Sub-section 7 is consequen.
tial on the amendments made in Committee

CLAUSE 15 (Duties of education authorities
in relation to voluntary schools).
15.-(1) It shall be the duty of the education authority to consider the needs of
any public elementary school within the
education area which is not a provided
school or a transferred school but which
complies with the requirements of the
Ministry in relation to public elementary
schools (in this Act referred to as a "voluntary school").
(2) If the managers or body controlling
a voluntary school-
(a) satisfy the education authority
that the school will be carried on for
some stated period, not being less than
eighteen months, as a public elementary
school, free of any charge to the education authority over and above the
contribution hereinafter provided for;
and
(b) submit to the education authority
estimates of-
(i) any proposed expenditure on the
lighting, heating and cleansing of the
school premises and grounds;
(ii) such proposed expenditure on
equipment, repairs, renewals, and
general upkeep as should ordinarily
be met from year to year,
it shall be the duty of the education
authority, if they have approved of the
estimates, to contribute a sum equal to
one-half of the expenditure within such
estimates:
Provided that if any demand is made
by the managers or body controlling a
voluntary school for a contribution towards any expenditure within such estimates, other than expenditure on the
lighting, heating, and cleansing of the
school premises and grounds, the education authority shall not make a contribution in accordance with such demand unless a school committee is
appointed for the school, in accordance
with a scheme framed under this Act, to
consist of not more than two representatives of the education committee, and
not more than four representatives of
the managers or trustees, and to have
power to associate with themselves, in an
advisory capacity, representatives of the
parents of children attending the school
and representatives of the school
teachers.
(3) Any question which may arise as
to any contribution under the preceding
sub-section shall be referred to the
Ministry, whose decision shall be final.

The Minister of Education and the education authorities have had due notice of
this amendment because it is on the paper,
I admit it opens up a very big question but if
is not quite so big as the question involved
in the amendment rejected a few moments
ago, or the one in the last amendment which
the Minister promised to consider. The
latter amendment cuts across the whole Bill,
and this amendment only partially cuts
across the Bill. I think it would be wise to
allow a little cutting across the Bill on the
lines I have indicated, because I regard this
as a very important and a very serious
question. I hold here a resolution passed by
the Synod of Ballymena and Coleraine, which
represents probably one hundred Presbyterian churches, to the effect that schools
erected on church ground at great sacrifice by
the people who wish to continue their
present system of government should be
allowed, in lieu of rent, such a sum as would
enable them to keep these schools in repair
without making a profit on them. That
touches the question of voluntary schools,
which in my opinion, is the kernel
of this whole question, and with it is intimately allied the question of religious
teaching. The section of this House which
is associated with me do not want religion
divorced from education, because in that
case, to my mind, education would be like
rain falling on sand-useless for growth or
development. I understand some arrangement has been made satisfactory to the
Churches, and that the religious question has
been settled, but whether that is so or not
I do not know. I would like an assurance
on that point. The Government are introducing a great measure of reform, and I
would ask that they should not link it up
with a coercion Act. I submit it is a
coercion Act if you introduce a Clause penalising a voluntary school by denying it, for
COLscience sake, if it is forced into a particular position, a claim that it could legitimately make against the State. I think we
should have a system of education that would
attract unto itself all these voluntary schools.
I would like you to look at the position as
it presents itself to me. I am closely identi
fied with two voluntary schools. Of one
I am the patron or sole trustee and also
manager, and I have associated with me a
committee, and an educational authority as
referee in case of dispute. Nothing can be
fairer or broader than that. We appoint the
teacher and we have paid every single penny
necessary for the building and upkeep of that
school and the only money that has been paid
by the State is the salary of the teacher. In
connection with another school, for the building of which I was primarily responsible, we
spent £1,000 and it could not be built now
for less than £1,500. It is on church premises, and it is a voluntary school in connection
with the church. To force us under the
management of an authority that may be
animated by feelings hostile to
unfair, and I do not think this
House should be asked to sanction
any such thing. If we, the people who own
a voluntary school, have made sacrifices in
building and maintaining the school, I think
we should not be placed in a worse position
than districts which have never spent a
penny or done anything for education
Therefore I think a concession might be
made to the owners of voluntary schools by
allowing them to continue their present
system of management and give them 50 per
cent. of the cost of cleansing, lighting, and
heating, and at the same time give them a
right that will preclude any question of
profit. What right has an education authous is

rity to claim free of rent the school of the

It is most unreasonable, and it opens up a far
bigger question when you come to deal with
the Roman Catholic Church. The Roman
Catholic Church has this serious claim to
make upon us as a moderate and broadminded House. They are impeded and
handicapped by a conscience clause which is
an Article of their faith that they must
control education. The one thing we want in
Ulster and the one thing most necessary for
the welfare and prosperity of Ulster is that
we should avoid religious dissension, and
there is no way in which religious dissension
is more likely to arise than through this question of voluntary schools and the control of
these voluntary schools. The Roman Catholic
Church has 700 schools in our area, and if we
get into conflict with them it will be a bad
thing for us. Religious controversy is the
very last thing that we should encourage, and
we should sacrifice everything except principle
in order to avoid it. I think this concession
which I suggest will meet many of the Protestant Churches and Protestant people who
at great sacrifice have built schools of their
own and kept them going, and it will meet
the Roman Catholics in a reasonable spirit
and may have some influence in softening
prejudices and strife and the hatred that religious controversy engenders. In this clause
you are opening a door to a very dangerous
condition of things and it is a conflict that
every wise man should desire to avoid.
can do it if you make this concession without
the sacrifice of principle. I speak not as a
Presbyterian but as a man who is animated
by friendly considerations towards all the
Churches. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We
have heard on a thousand platforms how
broad and fair and liberty-loving we are. Here
is an opportunity without any sacrifice of
principle to prove it for the men who built
the voluntary schools and the Roman Catholics who are loyal in our community. It was
pointed out here that when an attempt was
made to lead these people into an act of
rebellion against the constituted authority in

per cent. proved themselves in spite of great

think we should meet that spirit with the

reject this amendment, but to consider it

in regard to the character of the proposal that
my hon. Friend (Dr. Morrison) has made. I
am sure this House and the country generally
want to do what is fair and just and reasonable, and those of us who have been taking a
special interest in education have tried not
only to be fair but to meet the prejudice of
our Roman Catholic fellow-countrymen.
agree with my hon. Friend that we want to
damp dissension down rather than encourage it. How is this amendment of
his going to help us to get what,
after all, is the one thing we should
keep before our mind, a unified and highlyefficient system of education? If you are
going to give half the lighting, half the heating and half the cleansing and pay the rent
why should anybody come into the unified
system at all? I think you would not get 5
per cent. of the schools under those conditions.
While anxious to see that no injustice is done
to the people who made these sacrifices, I
think my hon. Friend should ask himself
supposing he refused to allow his school to
be used any longer for educational purposes.
what would happen to the people in his
district?
Dr. MORRISON: They would have to
build another school?
Mr. LYNN: They would have to build
another school, and out of whose pocket will

Mr. LYNN: I do not know what you call

It is just like the establishment of football

fund. I do not know how many I have contributed to myself that I have never seen.
I think the point is whether the State is

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
The hon. Member for the University (Dr.
Morrison) has raised a very important discussion, and my hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn) has
given the reply which, I think, is the only
reply that can be given. I must say at once
it would be quite impossible for the Government to accept the amendment which my
hon. Friend has proposed. He suggested
that the amendment which was proposed by
the hon. Member behind him (Mr. Miller)
cut right across the Bill, and that his
amendment cut partially across the Bill.
That is quite right. It is necessary in the
policy which we have before us to adhere to
Clause 15 which, I think, is one of the most
important Clauses in the Bill. The hon.
Member made a very eloquent and very
courageous speech, and he put forward a
point which is in all our minds. We all owe
a great debt of gratitude to the Churches for
the part which they have played in the promotion of education, and I think that this
is a debt which the community will never be
able to repay. It is only in very recent
years that the community have assumed
the responsibility of educating the children,
and the community have been fortunate in
that the ground was fertilized by the great
Churches which expended all their efforts in
educating the young. Those are benefits
which we are reaping now, and for which
those various Churches are entitled to the
fullest gratitude of the community. But in
the system of education which I am endeavouring to set up in the Six Counties, we
have to consider great principles. After all,
I am a representative of the people, and the
suggestion which I am making in the Bill
is that the schools should be transferred to
the people to be controlled under a democratic system. For that purpose I am hoping
that the Churches will find it possible to
transfer their schools to the local authorities.
As to those owners of schools who do not
desire to transfer, it is necessary for them
to incur and maintain certain responsibilities, and I cannot help feeling that in
the suggestion which the hon. Gentleman
(Dr. Morrison) is making, he is really
asking us to destroy the whole principle
which we have in our minds, in the Bill.
The question of transfer is one which is
very plainly put down in the Bill and it is
quite impossible for me, as I am sure hon.
Members will understand, to undertake to
accept any transfer which is so hedged about
by restrictions and so trammelled by arrangements that it would not under any circumstances be a transfer at all. I must have a
genuine transfer or no transfer.
Members: Hear, hear.) I feel sure hon. Members will realise that what we are virtually
saying is that if a school is placed under
(Hon.
a
local authority, which means it comes
under democratic control, we then are entitled to spend public money in maintaining
that school. On the other hand, those who
are interested in schools-and I need hardly
say I am willing and anxious to pay a tribute to them for the interest which they
gave in the schools-if they desire to maintain the further interest that is entailed
after transfer. it is necessary for them to
undergo certain obligations, and that is really
what the Bill amounts to. The hon. Member speaks of the duty of the Ministry of
attracting schools. That is quite true. We
want to attract schools-at a certain price.
It is quite impossible for us to undertake in
the name of the community to pay a price-
I am not speaking of the actual transfer
money-I mean to pay a price which would
mean allowing jurisdiction and latitude to the
managers of schools which, we hope, they will
transfer to the local authority. It is for these
reasons the Government cannot under any circumstances accept the amendment which the
hon. Member has moved. Clause 15 explains,
as far as we are able in legal phraseology to
explain, the utmost limit to which we are
prepared to go, and I cannot help feeling that
that clause is entirely in consonance with the
wishes of the majority of the people of this
Province. I, therefore, regret very much that
I am unable to accept the amendment which
the hon. Member has proposed.
Dr. MORRISON: The rules governing this
Committee allow me to say a word or two in
reply. I am not in agreement with the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) in his
attitude on this question. I would ask the
House to remember that when this important
Committee over which he presided sat it was
very early in our history as a self-governing
community and the friction which had arisen
over the settlement of Parliamentary autho
rity for Northern Ireland had not died down
and we were denied on that Committee advice
from the reasonable section of the Roman
Catholic community who are joining with us
and who are as anxious as we are to avoid
friction. We have never heard and the Com
mittee has never heard the views of the Roman
Catholic Church. I think that Church was
unwise in not putting them before the Committee. Be that as it may, we do not know
the Roman Catholic standpoint, but the posi
tion is that they are debarred by conscience
sake from taking part in any secular system
or semi-secular system or any system that excludes them from the control of education:
They would at the same time be taxed for the
upkeep of these other schools to which
they cannot allow their children to go. 1
submit that the working out of this treatment
of voluntary schools is penalising people for
conscience sake. I may be wrong, but that
is how I work it out. While I am willing to
Education Bill-
9 MAY 1923
Committee.
stand by my party and defend them in everything that is legitimate and straight, I cannot
go out on any public platform and say that to
compel Roman Catholics to violate their cousciences, to apply this Education Act of ours
to compel them to contribute to the national
system of education and to voluntary schools
that are transferred when they cannot trans
fer their own, to compel them to pay rates
for the support and upkeep of those same
voluntary schools, is a system that I can
defend in public, and I regret exceedingly
the attitude this House has taken up.
As I told you there are 700 Roman Catholic
schools in this area. You can ignore the
Protestant schools, and you can ignore the
Presbyterian schools, though we probably feel
quite as strongly as Roman Catholics in this
matter. But you cannot ignore the minority
and you must face this question of the 700
schools. If these people do not transfer their
schools, and if you have to build schools for
one-third of the population of this province
it would be a tax on the National Exchequer
of £700,000. After you have built them you
are then faced with this impossible situation
that the head of the Roman Catholic Church
may issue an edict to say that those people
cannot go into these schools, and they will
not go into them. It is a deplorable position.
Religious controversy impedes progress and
impedes harmony in any State, and if this
thing cannot be done without a sacrifice of
principle, it should be avoided. I can say
nothing further. I have put my views before
you. I would like to defer to every religious
community. I do not care a rap what any
man's religion is so long as he is loyal and
law-abiding. I cannot go with the Government in this matter. I make this statement
and this protest, and I warn the House it is
taking a course that it will live to regret.
Mr. LYNN: I think it would be a great
pity if the hon. Member's statement were
allowed to go out unchallenged. The hon.
Member, if I may say say so, is more loyal
than the King and more Papistical than the
Vatican. We live and learn. I always
thought that conscience was not a matter that
was bounded by geography. I should have
thought that if the conscience of a Scotch
Roman Catholic allowed him to accept conditions that are not nearly so good as the
conditions contained in this Bill it would
have allowed him to accept the conditions
laid down here. My hon. Friend has referred
to the fact that the Roman Catholic Church
gave us no help on the Committee over which
I presided. That is quite true. May I say
this for his information that as far as I have
been able to gather from people who can
speak with a great deal of authority for the
Roman Catholic Church, they are not only
satisfied but highly delighted, and a great
many were surprised, that we had gone so
far in the way of meeting them.
I know a good deal of propaganda can be
made out of the speech of my hon. Friend.
The idea will go out that we are here trying
to penalise Roman Catholics because of the
views they hold. I have nothing but the
highest respect for men who hold views and
are prepared to make sacrifices for them, but
I really cannot see where we have damaged
or done anything unfair or unjust to Roman
Catholics. I must say personally, and I think
1 speak for most Members of the House, that
I have had only one object in view right
through this whole controversy, and that was
to try how to get the best system of edu
cation. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I think we have met the Roman Catholic
Church in a fairer, and really in a broader
way than they have been met in England or
Scotland. I know the bulk of Roman Catholic people feel that we are dealing fairly with
them. Indeed, the only criticism I have
heard from Roman Catholics is that we have
been much too generous to the prejudice of
the heads of their own Church, and they
would have much preferred if we had taken
the line of forcing them to come in. I do
deprecate the statement that the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) has made. I know it is
done from a conscientious point of view, but
I think it ought to go out from this House
that we are not trying to penalise Roman
Catholics, Presbyterians, Methodists, Episcopalians, or any other persuasion, but only
trying to get the best system of education we
can with the least possible injury to even
prejudices, because it is prejudice we have
to deal with in any section of the community.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
I join with the hon. Member (Mr. Lynn) in
expressing regret at the speech from the hon.
Member for the University (Dr. Morrison).
That propaganda will be made out of his
speech, of course, is obvious. I am very glad
at what my hon. Friend (Mr. Lynn) has
said. My endeavour all through has been to
maintain the even scales of justice. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I cannot help feeling that in the steps we have taken we have
accomplished that object. The hon. Member
(Dr. Morrison) alluded to the fact that the
Roman Catholics in Northern Ireland did
not take advantage of the invitation which
I pressed on them, an invitation which I
think received the support of every rightminded man in the province. I regret that
they could not see their way to accept that
invitation, but I do feel-I think it is tho
opinion of the majority-that in the deliberations of the Committee a strict impartiality was practised. Every single thing
was done to enable a system of education
to be established that would do no injustice

I may be

mentary schools by the Act. We do not

that would refer to schools that were not considered directly under the management of the

would be the case in transferred or provided

CLAUSE 19 (Power to aid Higher
Education):
It shall be the duty of the education
authority to take such steps (whether by
the provision of schools or otherwise) as
seem to them desirable, subject to the provisions of this Act and the scheme approved
by the Ministry, to supply or aid the supply
of higher education and to promote the
general co-ordination of all forms of
education.
Mr. McKEOWN: I beg to move in Clause
19, page 19, line 34, after the word "schools"
to insert the words "or by contributing towards the provision, equipment, alteration,
enlargement or reconstruction of a school."
The object of this amendment is to meet the
views of those who consider that this Bill is
not sufficiently definite as to the assistance
that may be given to higher education. Reference has been made to this on more than one
occasion, and this amendment is simply to put
it more definitely than it was in the Bill. The
clause as it stands is drawn very widely, but
the amendment makes it clear that under
it the full assistance is given.
Mr. DUFF: I am sorry to have to get up
so often, but we have been more or less put
on our honour to look after the increasing
duties that are being placed upon the education authorities, and when we find amendments amplifying the duties that have
already been drawn up in the Bill being
moved we find ourselves in rather a difficult
position. Again this Clause in the Bill is
practically the same as the corresponding
Clause in the English Education Act, and yet
we find it necessary to suit local conditions
that that Clause should be amplified. I just
wish to ask the Ministry to give us as light a
burden to bear as possible.
The MARQUESS OF LONDONDERRY:
I think, perhaps, my hon. Friend (Mr. Duff)
is unduly apprehensive. I feel sure that he
will agree that in the interests of education
every possible latitude should be given to
these authorities. We certainly feel that the
authorities will act very wisely and very judiciously, and I am sure that the authority
which the hon. Member represents will be
able to carry out these duties with efficiency
and with wisdom. Therefore, I do not feel
that he need be apprehensive about these
powers and the suggestions that are made
to the authorities with reference to education.
Mr. LYNN: Surely there cannot be any
objection to allowing the local education
authority the power of equipping, altering,
enlarging, or reconstructing a school. For
example in some districts it might be possible
to save the ratepayers a very large sum of
money. Surely the hon. Member (Mr. Duff)
would not deprive the local authority, of
which he is a distinguished member, of the
privilege and right of using these powers if
necessary.
Mr. DUFF: That is just the very point.
We have a very keen standard of duty, and
when the word "duty" is put into the Bill
we are assuming that it is going to be a
duty and not the exercise of a power.
The CHAIRMAN: I think, if the hon.
Member will allow me, I may call his attention to the words in line 35 ("as seem to
them desirable.")
Mr. DUFF: I am very pleased that you
have drawn attention to those words, because
it is not that we wish to appear in the
slightest degree over-suspicious, but a duty
is a duty, and a duty is something different
from a power. If we are to understand that
the words inserted in the Bill-"It shall be
the duty of the education authority"-are not
going to have a very wide or a very general
application, then we are perfectly satisfied,
but up till the present we are assuming that
when those words are put into a Bill they
make it obligatory on the part of the education authority to carry them out. If that is
so, then we are going to be made to take on
very heavy financial burdens, but if we are to
understand that these words are not mandatory or obligatory then, of course, we are perfectly satisfied, because we think the more
generously and broadly this Education Bill is
framed the better. But behind our minds we
have this fear that when it is said to be a
duty it is a duty to carry it out.
Mr. LYNN: I am sorry to intervene again,
but I remember that three or four years ago,
when largely at the instigation of the Belfast
Corporation I took part-as you, Mr. Moles
did-in commending a Bill to the considertion of the Imperial Parliament, the complaint then made was that they were not
allowed this privilege. Now that we are offering them that privilege they are suggesting
that we are really offering them too much. I
do not think my hon. Friend (Mr. Duff) is as
reasonable in this instance as he usually is.
Mr. DUFF: I am sorry that the hon. Member for West Belfast (Mr. Lynn) thought it
necessary to say that. It is our conception of
the word "duty" that I am dealing with, and
we must make it perfectly clear. If by
making it perfectly clear we are to take the
disclaimers that are being expressed in the
Hansard of to-day then we are satisfied.

Urban Committees, in their own interest
and in the interest of the co-ordination of
public education throughout the Province,
will gladly hand over to them the administration of technical instruction in the
urban districts without misgiving and
without regret.
Hon. Members will see from that that it
is the aim of the Ministry that these Committees should come under the local education
authority, and that, as has been pointed out
over and over again, tends to co-ordination.
We are pleased to hear the remarks of the
hon. Member for the University (Mr.
Johnstone), and I am sure the Ministry will
not lose sight of them.
Mr. LYNN: I should say that my hon.
Friend the Member for the University has
been quite consistent all along, because in
the Education Committee he did object, but
we are dealing, not with an ideal, but with
what is practicable at the moment. I quite
agree that the ideal would be to get one
Education Committee for all branches of
education; but you have got certain factors
to bear in mind. You have these Technical
Committees in operation, and it is much
better to merge them into the general system
than to try to coerce them. I think that in
the long run the provision made in the Bill
will carry us to the end of our journey more
quickly than by taking a short cut, and foreing these Committees in at the beginning.
We do not want any unnecessary friction at
the commencement. We want to bring these
people with us, and get their help and experience, but in the meantime I think it will
be found better to let the Bill pass.

Mr. McKEOWN: I beg to move this
amendment. In the Bill as it stands it was
believed that full effect had been given to
the recommendations of the Lynn Committee so far as legislative effect could be
given to these recommendations, and it was
also believed that the system hitherto in
operation in the National Schools had been

fears have been expressed that the wording

which, while non-catechetical, might include

impart it in every school within their parish

proved persons. I beg to move.

the great ideal of religion. A great authority
has said:
Where the first lessons of life are
hindered by no hard heart and uncongenial
culture you will have in the child the development of a heavenly reverence for all
aspects of religion, but when you begin to
question that belief, there is exactly where
the influence is going to fail.
If it were possible even for the Churches to
come to an agreement with regard to what
they would preach, then I see a modified
reason why religious education should be
conducted in the school. But what have we?
We have actually a confession of failure at
the outset in the fact that you are taking
different classrooms, to be taught different
forms of belief, all under the one great name

towards religion.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I am very sorry indeed
that such a serious discussion has to be initiated in such an attenuated House. I thought
that the matter was sufficiently serious to
warrant the attendance of nearly every Member. Nothing has been so much discussed in
the public Press for a long time as the attitude of the Ministry to religious education
and the duty of the Churches in respect of it.
I would have thought that on an occasion of
this sort we would have had a strong muster
of our Members in order to see what would
eventually take place regarding Part 5 of the
Bill. In a certain sense I regard the success
of the Bill as to a large extent dependent upon
the result of our discussion on this Clause.
If we are going to retain religious teaching
in the schools I am not disposed to believe
it will produce very successful results. We
have had it on trial for a long time, and I
think a splendid opportunity has been afforded
the Ministry, if they thought it right to embrace it, of giving us a chance of seeing
schools conducted upon a strictly secular basis.
I think that is the rift within the lute. We
would have had splendid music, but under
the circumstances it may become mute. One
runs a great risk in opposing this Clause, because he is regarded as Godless or irreligious
or inimical to Church influence or Church
authority. All those things I resent so far as
I am concerned. I am speaking from the
basis of conviction when I say that while I
am just as much interested in the promotion
of religious knowledge amongst children as
perhaps any clergyman who represents any
particular denomination, I am at the same
time inclined to believe you could find a more
congenial atmosphere for the propagation of
spiritual life in the children than in what is
called the national school. I cannot imagine,
if your object is to foster religion in a child
and not merely dogmatical teaching, that the
atmosphere of a national school is the proper
one in which to do it. I imagine that religion
in the proper acceptation of the term is not
dependent upon what one believes. It rather
depends upon what one is. And how is a child
to be fashioned in character if not by influence and example? Example is a far more
potent force in the cultivation of religion
than the mere dogmatical teaching that is
provided, as suggested, in catechetical instruction in schools. Children are not naturally
irreligious. They would grow up in religion
if they had the opportunity.
What I say, and what I insist upon, is
that it is the environment we have got to do
with. Take the children of the better class.
They are sent to schools. There is no solicitude with regard to how their religious wellbeing is going to be looked after, because they
live in a congenial atmosphere at home. They
know they will not have to depend on school
influence or school authority to raise in them
You have Trinitarians, Unitarians, Predestinarians, and you have the advocates of
Free Will, and many others that may be
represented in the religious teaching in the
schools, and in order that these views may be
promulgated and inculcated in the children,
you have to segregate the children and take
them into different rooms, so that they may
not interfere with one another, and then
when they come out of the classrooms they
are brought in to receive instruction where
there is no difference at all. What I maintain is that if the Churches can settle their
own differences there would be very little
difficulty in respect of the teaching of
religious education in the school. Dean Inge
had said, and said very forcibly, that "there
is a most outstanding divergence amongst
the Churches with regard to doctrine, but
that the Saints never contradict each other."
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). In my opinion
it amounts to this, that if we are set upon
inculcating in children piety and genuine
religion we will not introduce a difference
between the denominations. It is only when
the question of doctrine is introduced that
these difficulties arise.
The clergy at the present time are very
jealous over this matter in order that the
rights of the children may be preserved, and
in order that religion may be inculcated in
them. I wonder do the clergy attach to it as
high importance and as great sacredness as
I do? The way I look at the matter is this.
The clergy have been set apart and ordained
for this specific duty because of some particular quality which we will call in this
case spirituality, and I maintain that where
duty is recognised in a minister of religion
he cannot delegate it to a secular authority
to discharge. I regret very much indeed that
religious education is provided for in the Bill
at all. because if it were founded on a secular
basis we would be free from all that acrimony
that exists at the present time, and free, also,

Clause 26 refers to religious education in
provided or transferred schools. It has been
settled by an arrangement with the various
Churches, but those who made the arrangement seem to have forgotten all about
Clause 27. From what I could see yesterday
when talking this matter over it seems that
they completely forgot about voluntary
schools and what was to take place in
voluntary schools. Clause 27 provides for
religious education in voluntary schools. 1
am told that in the City of Belfast at the
present time in many Roman Catholic
schools the majority of the children, on account of the pressure, are Protestants, and
yet no Protestant clergyman would have any
right under this Bill as far as I can see to
go in and teach at any time in these schools.
In the same way in Presbyterian schools in
which there may be a large percentage of
Methodist or Church of Ireland pupils the
clergyman of either the Methodist or Church
of Ireland persuasion would have no right of
entry and no right of teaching, so that a
great many could get no catechetical education by their own Minister. I think that is
a blot on the Bill, and it is probably a
matter that was forgotten by the heads of
the Churches when they met the other day.
I think it would be only fair to give the
clergy the liberty of entering and of teaching
their own children. I beg to move,

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 6th March, 1928.
VOLUME IX.
The Fourth Session of the Second
Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet 6th March, 1928, in the
Eighteenth year of the Reign of King
George V, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.P.)
in person.
The House met at Ten minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.)
in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.), was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report to
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate to hear His
Grace's Speech on behalf of the
Crown, to both Houses of Parliament;
of which I have for greater accuracy
obtained a copy. The Speech is as
follows:
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I am much gratified by the knowledge
that industrial peace continues to prevail throughout Northern Ireland.
Trade disputes wherever they have
occurred have proved gravely detrimental to national progress and
prosperity.
The unemployment position this year
has improved considerably as compared
with the corresponding period of 1927,
and I hope that even greater
improvement will develop during the
remainder of the
and as time
proceeds.
year,
I am pleased to observe that under
those provisions of the Contributory
Pensions Act which came into operation
on the Second of January last 8,900
persons who have attained the age of

years have received Old Age

Pensions, increasing the total number of
men, women and children, enjoying
the benefits of Pensions, contributory
and non-contributory, to 78,000.
In view of the success which has
attended the operations of the Loans
Guarantee Acts, my Government propose to extend for a further period the
power of giving facilities to industry.
A Measure will be submitted modifying in certain respects the financial
provisions of the Constabulary Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922, and amending the provisions of that Act dealing
with the contributions payable by local
authorities for additional Police forces
stationed in their respective areas.
Proposals will also be laid before you
regarding the registration of Nursing
and Maternity Homes and for the
better regulation of street trading in
our towns.
It was found impracticable last
Session to consider proposals relative to
the improvement of roads by local
authorities and the acquisition of land
for road purposes. A Bill dealing with
these matters will be submitted forthwith for your consideration.
Other Measures will be laid before
you dealing with:-
Unemployment Insurance.
National Health Insurance.
The adoption of children.
Legitimacy.
The storage and transport of
Petroleum.
Superannuation and other Trust
Funds.
The amendment of the law relating
to Fisheries.
The amendment of the law relating
to Bankruptcy.
and the amendment of the existing
Game Laws.

The results which have attended the

Linen Industry in the United States
during the past two years have been

extension to a wider market. You will
accordingly be asked to vote an

The Estimates for the Public Services
will be laid before you in due course.

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
6 MARCH 1928
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to Your Grace for the Speech which
Your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."
I would like to thank the Government
for allowing me to move this Address. 1
have one special reason for this and that
is that it gives me the opportunity, however inadequate my words may be, of letting those who sent me to this House to
represent them know that I am fulfilling
the trust imposed upon me, and which I
willingly accepted, of loyally supporting
our present Prime Minister and Government.
Everyone will, I am sure, welcome the
fact that the revised old-age pensions
scheme is now in work, and the numbers
show how far-reaching are the benefits.
It is very gratifying to learn that the
Government have decided to extend the
working of the Loans Guarantee Act, because I am satisfied that the facilities
accorded by that Act have contributed
very largely towards providing employment, and I hope that as a result of their
taking their courage in their hands, and
continuing it, they will reap the benefit
of seeing much less unemployment in the
future.
We see in the newspapers that Workman, Clark & Co. have been bought up.
We can only hope that whoever may now
become responsible for the working of the
firm will soon get orders for ships, and,
if necessary, avail themselves of the
Loans Guarantee Act, so that, ere long,
the yards will again be in full swing, and
so provide a still greater amount of
employment.

It is satisfactory to learn that what one
might almost have called the strained
relations" existing between the local
authorities and the Government on the
question of the charges for additional
police have, as we hope, now been satisfactorily settled.

In dealing with the acquisition of land
for road purposes, I can't think that the
local authorities have had any large number of cases where the owner of land has
taken up the position of trying to "salt"
the local authority. I don't think that
is a trait in the character of the people of
Northern Ireland. At the same time
there are sure to be some such cases, and
it is only fair to the community at large
that where land is required for the general
good and safety that the authority should
have power to acquire it, and, at the
same time, be compelled to pay a fair and
just price for it. The improvement of
the roads has become a very serious prohlem, but, unfortunately, it is by no
means a simple one. All sorts of interests have to be considered. It is a
problem which has only come into existence in its present acute form within the
last few years, and, like all new problems,
the correct solution will only be arrived
at as the result of experience.
In bringing in a Bill to amend the
laws on bankruptcy, the Government is,
2t least, bringing forward a Measure
which has long been needed, and which
will be of very valuable service to the
commercial community if it is, as I am
sure it will be, a Bill to do away with
some of the blatant absurdities which
exist at present. For example, a person
may get through his bankruptcy with the
payment of 6d in the £, and he can set
up the next day in his wife's name, or
in an assumed name, without any penalty.
That is simply putting a premium on
the dishonest trader and a heavy handicap on the honest trader who is trying
to carry on his business in a fair manner.
Also the delays which were entailed were
quite unnecessary.
We have heard of
thelaw's delays," and certainly the
Bankruptcy laws were by no means
behindhand in showing the truth of that
saying.
I see that the Government proposes to
deal with the laws relating to Fisheries

Debate on the Address
[Mr. Lloyd Campbell]
and Game. Doubtless some people will
say that the preservation of game, etc.,
is merely pandering to the rich. Such is
by no means the case. Fish and game
are two very valuable assets to a community from a financial point of view,
provided these assets are properly utilized.
In the past there has been no proper
control, and what little control existed
has been very poorly exercised. If the
laws were good and were properly enforced the money which would accrue
from the pursuit and sale of game, etc.,
in Northern Ireland would be a very
welcome asset indeed to the Chancellor
of the Exchequer, and would also bring
a large amount of money into the pockets
of all those concerned, either rectly or
indirectly, in what would with t doubt
become a very fair-sized and valuable
business. As things are to-day, the
amount of money lost through want of
proper control is large, but if proper laws
and control were instituted and carried
out, then I am satisfied that the financial
benefit would be indeed great.
The Wild Fowl, Game and Fish Preservation Society, two years ago, distributed in small lots amongst farmers over
5,000 pheasant eggs, and the result has
proved in many places quite satisfactory.
During the past year I understand that
the Ministry of Commerce have taken
considerable interest in the exhibitions
arranged by the Empire Marketing
Board. During the last year I believe
they took part in some eight displays, and
I can only hope that during the present
year that number will be doubled or
trebled. One of the first essentials for
getting a market for one's goods is to get
into touch with the consumer, and
already, through these exhibitions, the
products of Northern Ireland have been
brought directly home to the consumer.
I
What man would not prefer to wear a
suit of clothes which was made from
Empire-grown wool and manufactured
throughout within the Empire rather
than go to some foreign country which
often heavily taxes our imports?
believe that if the Empire had a ring
fence round it and no internal barriers,
that it could be self-consuming and selfproducing to its full capacity. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) That may be an
ideal view, but at any rate it is a worthy
ideal, and one well worth aiming at.
These exhibitions fulfil a twofold purpose. Firstly, they bring home to many
people the fact that we all-Northern
Ireland, Australia, Canada, and all the
other units are members of one great
Commonwealth-the British Empire.
Secondly, these exhibitions show us that it
is to our mutual benefit to buy from those
who buy from us. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The housewife learns that she can
buy Empire products, such as flour,
raisins, meat and many other things
cheaper and better than if she bought
those articles outside the Empire.
Some people seem to think that the
grant which has been given to the
publicity campaign for the linen industry
has been in the nature of a subsidy. Such
is by no means the case. By far the
largest industry-by that I mean the industry that affects, directly or indirectly,
the largest number of persons in North
Ireland, is the linen industry. If it could
be brought back to its former state it
would mean a very much larger circulation of money in the Province, and that
in its turn would mean that the butcher,
the baker, the candlestick maker-not
forgetting agriculture-would benefit very
largely by the revival of the linen trade.
In the past two years the Government
has contributed 10s. for every £1 which
has been subscribed by the trade, and the
propaganda has proved so successful, although confined to one country, viz., the
U.S.A., that the trade feel justified in
wanting to spread the gospel of "Use
Irish Linen" further afield, and try to
make an equal success in other countries.
I am glad the Government have seen it
in this light, and that they express their
willingness to carry on a grant for a
further period.
I am not a pessimist, far from it.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) At the
same time I do not believe in undue
optimism. Optimism if carried to excess,
like anything else, becomes a danger, but
if properly handled is a very great tonic.
I believe that trade is reviving, slowly
perhaps, but surely. One of the chief
factors that are helping on that general
revival is the feeling of mutual trust and
confidence, which is every day becoming
stronger, between all those engaged in
industry; the realization that each and
every one of us is dependent on his neighbour; that we must all work for the comnion good, whatever our task may be.

Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.

He was speaking at a men's

our Social Reform measures will

Mr. KYLE: Capitalist.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL:
"I confess that I sometimes regard

If we in Northern Ireland bear that in

Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I beg to move.
We may appear at times to have conflicting interests, but we realize that the
interests of the classes we represent are in
reality identical, and that the success or
failure of one is bound up in the success
or failure of the other. If the farmer
prospers the town benefits; if the farmer
fails the town suffers. If manufactures
and trades flourish the farmer has better
markets for his produce, but if they are
depressed the farmer's markets are bad
and his prices suffer. As my hon. Friend
has just told the House, we are beginning
to realize this interdependence of one with
another, farmer and townsman, employer
and employed. We are not going to
succeed in re-establishing our trade by
industrial strife or by accentuating
sectional differences in the community.

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Davison]
The Government cannot possibly engage upon any task of greater importance
to the community at large. The farmers
are the backbone of Ulster. If we allow
them to go down or be driven out of the
country by stress of circumstances we can
never make good the loss. No success in
any other sphere of labour or commerce
would compensate Ulster for the loss of
her farmers. At present agriculture is
facing a crisis, and there appears no sign
of immediate improvement. The prices
of farm produce of all kinds have gone
down and down, but the prices of all that
the farmer has to buy have kept up.
He
buys cattle at the beginning of the season,
feeds them and cares for them, and at the
end of the season he is offered less than
he paid for them. It is the same with
almost everything else. The fruit crop,
which used to be the mainstay of many a
County Armagh farmer, has ceased to be
profitable.
Over and above this great inducements
are offered to the young men of the farming class to emigrate. We must see that
there are inducements for them to stay
here and work the farms of Ulster. The
first step is to realize the serious state of
affairs we have got so far. The Government, as we read in the King's Speech,
are alive to the present depressed conditions. The next thing is to take steps
to improve these conditions. We are
promised this. In its consideration of
the necessary steps the Government ought
to have the support of every Member of
this House regardless of what constituency
he represents, whether urban or rural,
and regardless of what his politics may
be. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
to the marketing of his produce and help
him to secure the most profitable markets.
It may encourage co-operation among
farmers so that both in buying and
selling he may be in a stronger position.
Above all it may see that all possible
economies are effected both in central and
local government, so that the burden of
taxation may be lessened and life eased
not only for the farmer but for all who
have to contribute.
This ought to be above party. I know
the Government are in earnest to do all in
their power for the farming community.
The farmer does not want charity or
doles. Anything that we could do or
have the money to do in that way would

The keynote of the King's Speech is

peace. No big contentious Measures are

I often think that Acts of Parliament are

are to the individual. Sometimes they
may be necessary, but the fewer taken the
better. The habit in the case of either
is fatal. All the same, Acts of Parliament are sometime necessary, and I congratulate the Government upon the moderation of their programme in general and
upon the objects of those Measures
which they propose to introduce.

They were designed for horse vehicles,
and are not fit for our fast motor traffic.

wanted by our road authorities if the
necessary alterations and improvements

are
no longer for merely local

Davison), I can only say that he fulfilled

a distinguished member of the Northern
Bar.
I think, if I am right, this is the

The Leader of the Opposition, as far

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address

to the Speech delivered to-day, because
there does not seem to him to be enough
matter in it to irritate him sufficiently
so that he can tear it about during the
Session. It is purposely so. I have said
before, and I state here to-day, that what
Ulster requires, and what I think Great
Britain-indeed the whole world-requires is that there should be as little
contentious legislation as possible introduced, because we want, if we can, to
settle down to real work and progress.
Therefore if there is nothing of outstanding brilliancy or importance in the
Gracious Speech of to-day, at all events
it will ensure that we will be able to give
the most careful consideration to such
Measures as are mentioned, and I hope
we will be able to carry through a very
profitable Session.

public money, and how necessary it was

TEE ON NORTHERN HARBOURS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has yet received
the Report of the Inter-Departmental
Committee on Northern Harbours, and
when it may be expected to be made
public; whether he is aware of the growing feeling of dissatisfaction amongst the
traders of Killough at the delay in having
the harbour attended to.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
The Report is at present in the hands of
the printers, and I hope to be able to
make it available to the House within the
next few days. With regard to the last
part of the question, the hon. Member
will find that the case put forward in
favour of the development of Killough
Harbour for fishery purposes is fully dealt.
with in the Report.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: Might I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if he is aware that
this question of Killough Harbour has
been under consideration now for almost
two years, and will he tell the House the
cause of the delay in regard to this harbour.
Mr. BARBOUR: I think the hon
Member will find, when he receives the
Report, that the question of the development of Killough Harbour had to be considered in its relation to the interests and
advantages offered by other ports round
our coastal area.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen a

That Council had before it a motion

that I believed no basis to a Pensions Act

and orphans' portion of this Act has
been in operation for a period of two

seen much to confirm my view, because I

dozens of people have been denied pensions

move as an Amendment to the Address
at the end to add the words:-
___________
But humbly regret that no mention

and holders of building leases, in order
to secure for those tenants a measure
of fair rent, fixity of tenure, compensation for improvement and goodwill in
cases of disturbance.
The subject of this Amendment is not
new to the House. It has been discussed
here very exhaustively. As a matter of
fact, my first recollection of a debate
here is that it was on this particular
subject. A very strong case was made out
on behalf of certain leaseholders in Northern Ireland whose leases are about to
expire. In cases such as these landlords
have refused to renew the leases except
at sums altogether out of proportion to
what they should be. When the case of
these leaseholders was put before this
House it was strongly supported not alone
by the proposer, the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. McAllister), but by different
Members on the other side.
Such an impression was made by the
arguments used that the Prime Minister
undertook, when the suggestion was
made to him that the British House of
Commons was considering this particular
subject, that if the British Government
introduced legislation on the subject he
would consider the advisability of having
that legislation made applicable to
Northern Ireland. An appeal was also
made at that time that a Commission or
Committee might be set up to inquire
into this matter. The Government were
not then inclined to set up a Committee,
at least, when that debate took place
they did not promise to set up a Committee.
had received a Second Reading in the
Imperial House of Commons and that a
Committee was considering it there, and
was he prepared to give this House an
assurance that he would introduce a Bill
being considered by the Imperial House
of Commons.
From a question which the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle)
asked in October last I am afraid the
Government do not intend to do anything
in this matter. My hon. Friend asked
the Minister of Home Affairs if he is
aware that a Landlord and Tenant Bill
The right hon. Gentleman replied:
are
No. I think the conditions of
tenure in Northern Ireland
entirely different from those in

2015).

I am afraid of is that he may introduce
no Bill at all.
Mr. KYLE: Hear, hear.
Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL: I am
afraid that the idea of the Government
at that time was to shelve this subject because they put up the Attorney-General
to tell of the difficulties of dealing with
this matter, and to point out that the
law of contract was so sacrosanct that it
could not be broken. Contracts that
were harsh and unconscionable have been
broken. I believe many of these contracts between landlord and tenant are
harsh and unconscionable, and that they
should be broken without any hesitation
on the part of the Government or of
anyone who has the power to break them.
Nothing in my judgment has given more
trouble and annoyance to owners of
property and leaseholders than insecurity,
and I think it is a crying scandal that the
Government do not set up some machinery
to deal with this matter.
It should not be a difficult thing for the
Government to fix what is a fair and just
rent for a tenant to pay. I do not see
why they should have any difficulty in
doing that because they are not asked to
do anything unreasonable. None of the
tenants that I know wish to have anything
they are not entitled to. If a leaseholder or tenant acquires a house or a plot
of land from a landlord and pays him a
fair yearly rent for it, at the expiration
181 Debate on the Address-

8 MARCH 1928
Leasehold Tenure
of the lease no individual should be

confiscate the property. Some persons

no
In the same way a tenant of a house
should not be disturbed or put out of the
house, whether it be a business house or
a private house, simply because the landlord thinks he can squeeze a higher rent
or a fine in connection with it. Therefore, I think it is up to the Government
to give us a promise that at the expiration
of the labours of this Committee-and I
hope it will not be much longer at workthey will introduce a Bill that will prevent
this robbing of the people and put an end
to this confiscation of property. The
reason this Amendment is put down is
that many of us are of the opinion the
Government are not in earnest in this
matter, that they simply want to pass it
over, and that they are not prepared to
do the work any Government in such
circumstances should do, that is, to give
protection to the people.
The Government took a long time to
set up this Committee, and if they take
a similar length of time to consider its
findings I can quite understand that by
the time a Bill is introduced there will be
a new Government here. The Government should immediately introduce a Bill
that will prevent any man confiscating
property or fining the tenant in an
amount by way of extra rent, or by some
of the other methods of extraction these
individuals seem to have. I hope that
during the discussion to-day the Minister
of Home Affairs will promise to do so.
I beg to move.

guarantee £6 10s 0d per ton for saved,

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): My attention has been
directed to an advertisement inviting
Northern Ireland farmers to grow
300,000 acres of flax. The advertisement
states that a certain firm is prepared to
I think it right to point out that on a
moderate estimate the guarantee mentioned might involve a sum of over three

PRICE OF LIME.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether his attention has been drawn to the disadvantage which farmers are subject to, owing
to the prohibitive price of lime, and
whether he will consider the introduction
of some scheme that would reduce the
price of this mineral, which is so much
required by the farming community.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am aware of the
fact that the price of lime has considerably increased since 1914, due largely
to the increased cost of labour and the
increased price of coal.
Lime is undoubtedly of benefit when
applied to land which is being cultivated,
especially land of a stiff clay character
and peaty land; but practically all the
experiments carried out for the last ten
years throughout Great Britain and
Ireland indicate that when lime is applied
to grass land it has little or no effect,
and that much better results can be procured from the application of phosphatic
manures, such as basic slag, superphosphate, mineral phosphates, etc.
I am prepared to consider applications
from owners of lime quarries for loans to
enable them to procure grinding
machinery so that lime could be applied
to land without having to be burnt in a
lime kiln.

Oral Answers
13 MARCH 1928
BELFAST ELECTRICAL SUB-
STATION.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he has seen the proposal of the Belfast Corporation to buy
a piece of land for the erection of an
electrical sub-station; whether he can
state the price that it is proposed to pay
for this property, who is the owner of it,
and whether he is satisfied that the Belfast citizens are not being overcharged.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am aware of the proposal to which the hon. Member refers.
I should explain, however, that the matter is one which lies primarily within the
discretion of the Electricity Commissioners for Northern Ireland, who have
power to grant, or to withhold, sanction
for a loan to cover the expenditure involved. I am informed that in the present case the Electricity Commissioners,
after satisfying themselves as to the
merits of the proposal, have granted the
loan sanction for £1,000 for the purchase
of the site from the trustees of the late
W. W. Kennedy.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman prepared to make representations to
the Electricity Commissioners, in view of
the fact that it has been estimated that
the value of the land, or at least the
price given, is going to be £8,500 an acre.
Is he prepared to make representations to
the Electricity Commissioners to have a
further investigation before they authorise this absolutely inordinate price to be
expended on land for this purpose.
Mr. KYLE: Do I gather that the
right hon. Gentleman states that he is
prepared to accept responsibility on behalf of the Government for the purchase
of this land at this inordinate price?
Mr. BARBOUR: No. So far as the
papers which I have gone through reveal,
the ordinary procedure in this connection
has been gone through by the regular
authority. The selection of the land, in
the first instance, is a matter for the Belfast Corporation, and thereafter it is submitted to the Electricity Commissioners,
who are a semi-independent body, and
they review it in the light of the suitability of the site itself, the purpose intended, and, naturally, in the case of
electricity, in relation to the load which
exists in the neighbourhood which will be
supplied from that station. Having regard to all the circumstances I have not
seen anything of an irregular character,
or any matter that would call for my
intervention, if indeed, it would be appropriate for me to intervene in the
matter.
Mr. SPEAKER: I understand from
the Minister that it is a matter over which
the Government has no control. Again,
I must remind the hon. Member that he
must not get into the habit of criticising
the action of other elected bodies, whether
the Belfast Corporation or the Board of
Guardians, when the responsibility is
theirs.
Mr. KYLE: I have no desire to criticise other elected bodies, except that we.
as a Parliament, are responsible to some
extent, or have been held responsible, for
the activities of some of the local authorities, and particularly the Belfast Corporation. I was only wanting, if I
could, to see whether or not the Government were prepared to be responsible for
the purchase of this land.
Mr. SPEAKER: That would raise a
very large question. If the Government
became responsible for the deeds and misdeeds of local authorities who are elected
bodies we should be in an impossible
position, and I gather that the Electricity
Commissioners are also not responsible to
the Government.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is quite open to
the ratepayers, if they think fit, to call
for an inquiry into this matter.

Firstly, the object of the Pensions Increase Acts was to alleviate hardships in
the case of persons drawing small prewar pensions; the Acts apply not only to
teachers, but to all other types of public
servants; the time and means barrier is
an essential feature, which could not with
any propriety be removed.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.

seriatim :

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend, who is
prevented from attending the House, to
reply to this question.
It is undoubtedly difficult to adjust
Trade Board Rates of Wages to the conditions under which retail trades are carried
on in country districts. Trade Boards, as
the hon. Lady knows, have been set up to
prevent what are known as "sweated"
rates of wages, and but for these Boards
very low wages might be paid in some
districts. On the other hand, if the
wages fixed by the Boards are uneconomic,
employers may be faced with the competition of the self-employed person or the
cheap factory-made article, and may be
unable to continue to give employment at
all. It is between these difficulties that
the Boards, in determining the rates, have
to strike a proper balance.

Before dealing with the provisions of

When dealing with the Traffic Bill of

During the year 1927, there were no

in endeavouring to enforce the observance of the law, the number of fatal

authorities has decreased. Again and

vehicles on roads which are constructed
with such a surface that they are not
fit for these vehicles to go on at a high
speed. I am advised on the highest
authority that the wear and tear on a
road due to a particular vehicle increases
in the ratio of the square of the speed,
in other words the damage done to a road
by a heavy motor vehicle travelling at
20 miles an hour is four times the
damage which would be done by the same
vehicle at 10 miles an hour. Similarly
the damage done by the same vehicle at
30 miles an hour would be nine times
greater than the damage done at 10 miles
an hour.

As I have already indicated, the
Measure which is now before the House
is more to ensure that the roads will be
safer for the use of motor traffic. None
of our roads were built for the purpose
of carrying motor traffic, and the result
of that in many cases is that they are
positively dangerous when so used.
In 1921 we had 11,700 motor vehicles
licensed in Northern Ireland, while for
1926 the number was increased to no
less a sum than 30,000, while for 1927
that number was increased to no less a
figure than 31,400. In other words, out
of a population of 1,254,000 we have one
vehicle for every 40 inhabitants, as contrasted with England where there is one
vehicle to every 22. But what has made
it all the more necessary that further
steps should be taken to make the roads
safer for motor traffic has been the
enormous increase in the bus traffic. In
1924 we had only 346 motor omnibuses
licensed in Northern Ireland, and in the
corresponding month of 1927 the number
had increased to 719. For some time
past it has been felt that the powers

Clause 4 enables the local authorities
to prescribe a building line. At the
present time the Corporation in Belfast
and certain other urban authorities have
powers under their local Acts to prescribe
building lines, but local authorities in
general have not, and it has been found
that some provision of this character is
urgently required, not merely in urban
districts, but in areas under the jurisdiction of road authorities in rural areas.
Of recent years extensive building operations have been undertaken in many
areas, not under the control of urban
authorities, and these developments have
rendered the powers which we now seek
urgently necessary. We do not propose

any part of a road maintainable by them,

they must then consider any objection
received by interested parties.
If an interested party is able to prove

he will be entitled to recover compensation
from the local authority. Such compensation will be fixed by the official
arbitrator under the Acquisition of Land

no claimant will be able to recover compensation in respect of anything done by
him after the date of the service of the

building line.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In regard to the questions that
have been submitted here to me by hon.
Members opposite, there is very little
analogy between the conditions under
which farmers can secure money and those
in regard to large industrialists. The
arrangements for advances to farmers are
very much simpler, if I may say so, than
those which are governed by the Loans
Guarantee Acts. If the conditions which
the Loans Guarantee Acts provide for were
asked from farmers I do not suppose there
are two per cent. in the country that would
take advantage of them. In the first
place the guarantees in connection with
shipbuilding, which is the industry that
has been mainly referred to in the discussion by hon. Members opposite, require
security of the most ample kind-not only
the standing of the concerns which ask for
the loans, but also the charging of that
property with the liability attaching to
the advance. It is quite obvious that
farmers would be in no position to furnish
guarantees of the character I am referring to.
I repeat that farmers can secure it by
a very simple method. All they have to
do is to put forward their request.
The
Ministry, over which my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr.
Archdale) presides, examines the application, and if the application is a reasonable
one the procedure is very simple after
that, and the money is advanced by banks,
who are guaranteed by the Government,
and at a rate of interest, of course, very
much less than anything comtemplated in
connection with the Loans Guarantee Acts.
It seems to be an impression in the minds
of hon. Members opposite that the operation of this Act really is only intended to
apply to shipowning and shipbuilding.
That is quite a misapprehension. There
is no one or no company which desires to
expend capital money on the establishment of an industry that does not come
under the ambit or umbrella of the Loans
Guarantee Acts providing all the conditions are satisfactory. It should be made
clear to hon. Members that the Government cannot and will not risk the money
of the taxpayers unless the security is of
such a character that there is no possible
chance of the advance being loaded on the
Government. That is really the principal
factor which the small and very capable
business committee looking after this
matter must have regard to in discussing
the guarantees under these Acts.

the proposed system which really is in

There is one other matter that I would

no case has the road authority been empowered to enter upon lands against the

The hon. Gentleman who shares with

Therefore, in the case of the taking of a

What is the next stage? The next
stage is the amount of compensation.
That is to be fixed by an arbitrator-an
official arbitrator-and if the person from
whom any land is taken is dissatisfied he
goes straight to the county court. I
cannot conceive of a more simple procedure than that. The hon. and learned
Gentleman says,
"Let him go to the
judge of assize." His Majesty's Judges
of Assize go out on circuit twice a year,
and all the time you will be waiting to get
a strip of land, to take off a corner, or
make some improvement of that kind.
You have got to wait until either July
or March for the coming of the judge of
assize, and learned counsel will have to
be engaged before the judge of assize can
determine whether or not we will take
off a piece of land, or how much money
is to be paid for taking off some corner.
That would be ridiculous and would
defeat the whole object of this Bill.
Where the county only want to take land,
as they took it before for other purposes,
all the law that is in existence up to now
is still available for them, but for the purposes of this Act, the Government propose
to set up this perfectly simple machinery
that will act quickly, that will perform
its functions in the time it should do, and
that will secure payment to any person
who is injured by it. I cannot conceive
any more simple procedure than the procedure that has been indicated here.

that there was to be an endowment fund

interim grant was to be made by Parliament each year of such amount as, with
the interest payable on sums already
accumulated in the Endowment Fund,
would give an income of £3,000 a year
for its upkeep. This was originally proposed to be done in five years at £12,000
a year, but at the request of the Ministry
of Finance we have this year increased the
grant so as to make it up to the £60,000
at the earliest possible date. It is found
that it would be much more to the interest
of the Ministry of Finance to complete
the sum of £60,000 instead of waiting for
five years. It is now proposed to add
£12,000 this year so as to hasten the
completion of the Endowment Fund.

As regards the replacement of livestock, it will be within the recollection
of hon. Members that, owing to the great

1,600 loans to the total amount of

1925 for three years. The Ministry have
been able, with the assistance of the
Ministry of Finance, to make it easier for
the farmers to pay off these loans by
spreading the period of repayment over
five years instead of over three as originally provided. We have ample evidence
that the livestock replacement loans have
been of the greatest value to the small
farmers in many districts who were so unfortunate as to lose animals through
disease due to recent inclement seasons.
The amount next before us is for the
forestry unemployment relief scheme..

is hoped that during the coming year

Members: Hear, hear). With this end

this next year.

15 MARCH 1928
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 15th March, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. Speaker in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
CONTRIBUTORY
PENSIONS ACT.
1.
Mr.
WILLIAM MCMULLEN
asked the Minister of Labour whether it
is a fact that a number of employers have
taken advantage of the ten shillings per
week which is paid to old-age pensioners
under the Widows', Orphans' and Old
Age Contributory Pensions Act, to
reduce the wages of their employees, and
whether he would state if the Government will introduce an Amending Act to
put an end to this practice.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Cases in which the facts were
similar to those mentioned by the hon.
Member have been reported to me, but I
think they are of rare occurrence, and
I am glad to be able to say that in
certain instances where retrenchments
had taken place or where wages had been
reduced the matter has been rectified.
I made, as I think the hon. Member
knows, a very definite public statement,
when the matter was first brought to my
notice, to the effect that I felt that employers ought only to take into consideration efficiency, and that they should not
take advantage of the Contributory
Pensions Act in order either to reduce
wages or discharge their employees.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would
the right hon. Gentleman be prepared
to promote an Amending Bill to penalize
employers who are guilty of this practice
of reducing men's wages on the ground
that they are receiving pensions?
On the other hand, I feel that legislation to fix the wages to be paid to such
persons and to make it compulsory for
employers to employ them, or to compel
them to work for certain employers would,
for very obvious reasons, prove to be ineffective and the Government does not,
therefore, propose to promote such legisiation.
Mr. ANDREWS: No, Sir. I would
imagine the hon. Member knows, from
his knowledge of industrial relations, that
such a scheme would not be workable in
practice.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Is the
right hon. Gentleman aware that a
number of cases of this kind have occurred
since he made the speech referred to, and
under those circumstances is he prepared
to make another speech importuning employers not to take advantage of men in
this way?
Mr. ANDREWS: I think the answer
I have given to the question will be sufficient for the purpose.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
I would refer the hon. Member to the
reply given by me on the 18th October
iast to a similar question by the hon.
Member for North Belfast.
As the hon. Member may be aware, the
Imperial Act, experience of the working
of which we are awaiting, has been in
operation for a period of less than three
months.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Prime
Minister say if it is the practice of this
Government to wait until experience has
been gained of the working of the Imperial Act before introducing a Bill on
similar lines in this House?
Mr. BARBOUR: Not necessarily,
but I think that in this case there is
occasion for it.
