Mr. BARBOUR: The nature of this
expenditure is given in an explanatory
way under the various headings, but for
the information of hon. Members I will
elaborate a little on that. The net
amount of £2,255 for this Estimate is
made up of the items of expenditure
shown under Section II, which are not
recoverable from any particular Ministry,
namely, an initial outlay incurred on the
survey of the Lough and River Erne with
a view to deciding whether any improved
drainage scheme is necessary or possible
in that area, and an expenditure in carrying out certain borings in the bed of the
River Bann in order to enable the figures
of expenditure of the drainage scheme already outlined for that district to be
more accurately tested, and a sum of
£105 for the purchase from the Imperial
Commissioners of Crown lands of their
rights in the shooting, fishing and
accreted lands of Lough Erne.
It was
considered by both Governments to be
more satisfactory that these rights should
be taken over by our local Government.
As regards Departmental services provided under Section III the sum of
£3,526-which is, of course, offset by a
corresponding credit from Departments
--is made up as follows:
Under Sub-head K a sum of £1,200
is required to meet expenditure already
incurred by the installation of a new
central heating system at Stormont
Castle. The old heating system was installed about 30 years ago and had become
antiquated, necessitating a heavy expenditure on maintenance and extravagant
fuel consumption.

The PRIME MINISTER: When the
Act of 1920 was first introduced-it is no
secret to-day-there was a Clause in the
original draft that Northern Ireland and
Southern Ireland were to be allocated the
sum of one million sterling in order to
provide themselves with Parliament
Houses and administrative buildings, and
whatever premises were necessary to set
them off upon their new lives. When the
matter had been gone into for some time,
I pointed out to the British Cabinet of the
day that owing to the high cost of building
at that time it would place Northern Ireland in a very serious financial position to
have to provide these buildings as compared with the position in which Southern
Ireland was at the time with its buildings
complete and fit for Government offices,
and for carrying on administration in
every direction. Owing to that we here
in Northern Ireland would be placed in a
very prejudicial position.
In consequence of those representations His Majesty's Government of the
day altered that Clause in the Act of 1920,
and undertook to put Northern Ireland
in full possession of a House of Parliament and the necessary administrative
buildings, to be equipped properly without any charge to the taxpayers of
Northern Ireland. I think I have made
that perfectly clear. I am only a passing

PRESERVATIVES IN CREAM.
1. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he is
aware that the recent Order of the Imperial Government prohibiting the use of
preservatives in cream has killed the import of cream from Northern Ireland to
England and Scotland; and whether he
will make representations to the Ministry
of Health to have this Order revoked.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to reply to this question.
I understand that the recent Order
made by the Ministry of Health, Whitehall, on the subject of preservatives in
cream has undoubtedly adversely affected
the export of preserved cream from
Northern Ireland to Great Britain
At the same time I should explain to
the hon. Member that the Order referred
to was made by the Minister of Health
after the most careful consideration of
specific recommendations made to him
by a Committee of experts appointed to
consider the question of the injurious
effect on public health of certain preservatives in food.
The Minister of Health was SO
concerned at the representations and recommendations made
made by this
by this expert

Committee that he has steadfastly re
fused, in spite of repeated applications,
to consider the question of revoking or

of Home Affairs, as the Minister of
Health for Northern Ireland, concurs in
the principles which actuated the Minister
of Health regarding the dangers to
public health from preservatives in

HIGHER RATES FOR DUTY ON
MOTOR LORRIES AND CARS.
being made in advance and involving no
cost for collection.
2. Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Finance whether the higher
rates charged for duty on motor lorries
and cars, when the duty is paid quarterly
instead of yearly, is not a discouragement
to the occasional user and also a penalty
on the poorer owner; and whether he
would reconsider this matter and issue
quarterly licences at the same rate as that
paid for annual licences, these payments
Mr. HANNA: I have been asked to
reply to this question.
The higher rates of duty charged for
quarterly licences in respect of motor
vehicles are not a discouragement to the
occasional user of such vehicles. On the
contrary, it has been found that the privilege of being able to obtain such licences
even at such higher rate is
very much
appreciated, particularly as it enables
owners who desire to do so to put their
cars out of use during the winter quarter.
The granting of quarterly licences
entails a considerable amount of extra
work and expense on the licensing
authorities, and it is for this reason that
the small extra charge of one-tenth the
amount of duty is made.
This extra charge is only half that
made for quarterly licences prior to 1st
January, 1925, when an extra 20 per
cent. was charged for the privilege.
The reduction from 20 per cent. to 10
per cent. so increased the popularity of
quarterly licences that it is obvious that
were the surcharge to be still further reduced, no annual licences would be taken
out, and considerable unnecessary additional work would devolve on licensing
authorities, necessitating substantially increased staffs.

FORESTRY SCHEME-NUMBER OF
WORKERS EMPLOYED.
6.
Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. W.
McMullen) asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he can state the number
of workers employed in the Forestry
Scheme under his Department, and the
rates of wages paid.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): By reason of a sad bereavement in the family of my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr.
Archdale) I am empowered to take this
question. The number of labourers employed on the Ministry's forestry operations is 83, and their wages range from
24s per week to 359 per week according
to district--the rate paid being based on
the current local wage for agricultural
labourers. There are also eight foremen
and assistant foremen employed at wages
ranging from 33s to 55s per week.
In certain cases workmen are provided
with cottages free of rent. I may say
that all men on 24s a week have free
cottages.
Seventeen boys are also employed at
wages of from 15s to 23s per week
according to age. These boys are chiefly
engaged on work connected with the
Ministry's forestry nurseries.

Mr. KYLE: I beg to move a reduction
of £1,000 in this Vote on Account, in
order to call attention to the state of the
administration in the Ministry of Labour.
I have given notice of this to the right
hon. Gentleman's private secretary. The
first matter I want to deal with is the
question of the Courts of Referees.
Courts of Referees are set up under Act
of Parliament, and the chairmen of them
are appointed by the Ministry of Labour.
They are supposed to be persons independent of the Ministry or of the Government. What I want to suggest is that in
G
Supply-

Vote on Account
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
future these appointments ought to be
made by the Crown and not by the
Ministry, because we have had an answer
from the Minister of Labour to-day, in
which he states that his Department has
issued instructions to the Courts of
Referees that they are to be a channel of
communication for giving instructions to
these appeals officers.
I want to submit to this Committee
that the Ministry of Labour has no right
under the Act of Parliament to issue
instructions to the Courts of Referees.
The Courts of Referees being statutory
bodies the Ministry has no right to interfere with their working or to prejudice
their decisions in any way. What happens
at the present moment is that when a man
or woman makes a claim to benefit at the
local Employment Exchange the Exchange officials put a series of questions,
with which they are no doubt provided
by the Department, quite legitimate
questions, asking the persons where they
have been looking for work, and if they
have been genuinely seeking employment.
To the average man with ordinary
intelligence those questions present no
difficulty, but a very great number of
people when they appear before Government officials seem to lose their heads.
They cannot answer the questions in a
straightforward manner, with the result
that when their claims are submitted to
the Court of Referees they are prejudiced
by the answers given to the questions submitted by the Exchange officials. In
other words the Exchange officials set a
trap for the unemployed persons, and the
applicants when they appear before the
Court of Referees fall into the trap set for
them. The result is that the Minister
can then declare that so many more people
have ceased to be unemployed.
If a worker is sick that renders him incapable of performing his work efficiently,
and all his employer has got to do is to
write on the Form the Ministry sends him
that the person was guilty of misconduct
and the application for benefit is treated
accordingly by the Court of Referees.
The employer who signs this Form is not
expected to attend the Court of Referees
to allow either the applicant or the
applicant's representative to ask him.
questions regarding the manner in which
the worker performed his work. In fact,
it is stated specifically in this Form that
the information which the employer gives
will be treated confidentially. I protest
against this method of denying people
unemployment insurance benefit, because
I hold it is unfair. It is entirely against.
all the traditions of fair play which I
always fondly assumed were in operation
in this country as well as in Great Britain.
Further, I want to know by what right
the Minister of Labour has defined what
is not defined in the Act of Parliament.
He says in this Form, issued under the
heading "Ministry of Labour," that one
of the disqualifications for an insured
contributor is misconduct. He goes on to
define what misconduct is. He has no
right to do so; that should be determined
by the Court of Referees. The Minister
defines misconduct as including breaches
of discipline, and conduct inconsistent
with conditions of service, or rendering a
worker incapable of performing his work
efficiently.
I may say I never received such shocks
as I have during the past year or two.
Being a member of this Committee I
realize how the working people are liable
to suffer loss of benefit which they have
paid for through the wiles of Governments
who see a circular of this character filled
in. That these Forms should be a means
of disqualifying a person from benefit is
something that no fair-minded person can
defend, particularly in view of the fact
that the employer's word is accepted in
99 cases out of 100, and the workman who
is examined by the Court of Referees does
not count for a snap of the fingers.
The workman appears before the chairman of the Court of Referees and before
the representative of the employers and
the representative of the workers and is
quizzed right, left and centre as to how
he left his employment.
He is put
through the third degree before the Court.
yet the employer has nothing to do but
write anything he likes, and that reply
by the employer is treated as confidential
and used to the detriment of the workman.
Again, I say that is surely a state of
affairs that no right-minded person could
defend. The employer, if he gets evidence against a workman and writes that
evidence on this U.I.85 Form should,
equally with the workman, be summoned
to attend the Court of Referees before an
applicant is disqualified.

Mr. GYLE: I was very much surprised
indeed when I heard the Prime Minister
suggest that the Leader of the Opposition,
instead of criticizing the Estimates and
moving a reduction of £1,000, should
rather have congratulated the Government on the fact that the Estimate was
less than last year by a sum of £298,000.
I would have been in agreement with the
Prime Minister, but when you come to
examine the figures and to look down the
various items you find that there is no
real saving of £298,000 in the strict sense
of the term. My Friend, the Member
for Antrim (Mr. George Henderson),
pointed out that for Unemployment Insurance we are estimating for £300,000
as against a total estimate for last year
of £1,260,000. That £300,000 is for
three months, and if you multiply it by
four, as you do in most other cases, you
will find that this suggested saving absolutely disappears altogether. Therefore,
instead of saving £298,000, we are going
on in practically the same old sweet way.
If anyone tells me that this £298,000
has really been saved out of Unemployment Insurance, then I say the Minister
of Finance is making a very grave
mistake. We certainly find that
a considerable number of people
have been turned off the Unemployment Insurance Register, but we who
go among the working classes, and know
something about working-class conditions,
realize that the people are not so very
much better off than they were this time
last year.
It may be that some more
people have been taken into employment
in the shipyards, but, unfortunately,
there has not been that absorption of
labour that we all hoped for. Last week
I was at a meeting of unemployed and I
felt very serious about the whole matter
of unemployment in this city. It is becoming a grave scandal. To-day I saw
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. T.
Henderson) hand to the Prime Minister
a letter that came from an ex-Serviceman,
who is in the workhouse with his three
children. That is the sort of thing we
come across over and over again. We
find that people are being taken off the
Unemployment Register and driven into
the workhouse.
are walking the streets of Belfast unable
to obtain employment, and they are refused unemployment benefit on the
ground that they are not genuinely seeking work.
We have people coming to
our doors and we have letters asking us
for God's sake to try to get work for these
people, and we cannot do it. I am afraid
that this supposed saving of £298,000 in
Unemployment Insurance will prove to
be a myth. I hope it will not prove to be
a myth, and that people will really get
employment; but if things go on as they

found for them in some way, and instead

put to one side for the purpose of finding
work in some way for the people.
Mr. POLLOCK: One man.

hundreds of men. Thousands of people
Mr. ANDREWS: In what way?

Unemployment Insurance Bill-
Second Reading
justification is two-fold. In the first
place, this is a most important Measure
affecting not only our insured persons, but
also their employers and the general taxpayers to a very substantial extent; and,
in the second place, it is a somewhat complicated Measure.
Lord Carson in the House of Lords described it as a Measure of great difficulty
due to the fact that it referred to so many
previous Acts. I must say at this stage
that I feel personally very grateful to
our Parliamentary draftsman for the pains
he has taken and the skill he has displayed in effecting a considerable amount
of consolidation work in connection with
this Measure, which will make my task
much lighter to-day. Of course, all the
provisions of the Act, of which this is
in effect the counterpart, have been preserved; at the same time he has, by means
of the consolidation he has carried out,
removed the necessity of having so many
references in the Bill to earlier Measures.
The study of the evolution of unemployment insurance is a very interesting
one, because it shows how narrow and
small beginnings can lead to greater
things through an aroused social conscience prompted by all the best instincts
of the human heart. The genesis of unemployment insurance is to be found in
the action of the friendly societies
and the trade unions-all honour to them
-dating as far back as 1905. At that time
122 Friendly Societies, with a membership
of 75,000, paid benefit or allowances to
unemployed members and also gave experses allowances to those members who
were unemployed and who sought employment at places considerably distant
from their home. In the same year 81
trade unions did what was tantamount to
the same thing. They gave benefits on
the average ranging from 10s to 12s to
to unemployed members for short periods.
It is interesting to remember that they
also introduced waiting periods and gaps
of considerable length.

It was not until 1911 that the State

In 1916 this Measure was extended to

In 1919 benefit was raised to 11s. for
adults and 5s. 6d. for boys and girls.
Again in 1920 a new Measure was introduced, which is one of great importance
and has been looked upon as the principal
Act ever since. It covered all employees
employed in manual work and those whose

In all eleven million workers were covered

The Imperial Minister of Labour came
to the conclusion that unemployment insurance legislation had got into a very unsatisfactory condition. One temporary
Measure after another, as I have tried
to show, was added to the Statute Book
without, perhaps, a great deal of regard

Moreover, it was felt that two forms of

from both sides of the House will agree
with that view. I certainly do. Standard benefit was received as a right, and
extended benefit was purely discretionary.

are men greatly respected not only in

considered this problem for about two
years, and they received evidence from
employers' associations and trade unions,
from local authorities, and, in fact, from
everybody who was willing to give evidence which would help to solve
very difficult problem. The Committee
brought in a unanimous report during
last year, and I think it should be remembered that it was unanimous, notwithstanding that the interests represented
on the Committee were of very various
kinds.
a
The chief findings of the Committee,
briefly stated, are as follows: That a compulsory contributory scheme is necessary;
that there should be only one form of
benefit; that there should be a single
form of procedure for the adjudication of
claims by the insurance officer, the Courts
of Referees, and the umpire; that the
arbitrary restrictions imposed by the onein-six rule and the 26-weeks rule should
be removed, and instead of that claims
should be examined every 13 weeks; that
the scheme should be wide in its scope;
and that contracting-out should not be
permitted. Certain changes were also
suggested as regards rates of benefit, as
regards contributions and dependants'
allowances and the classes of dependants.
which should be included. And with
that preliminary statement I now come
to the present Bill.
The counterpart of this Measure was
introduced at Westminster in August
last, and it was based, in practically every
particular, upon the report of the Blanesburgh Committee, with the exception of
its financial provisions, to which I will
refer later. The Bill was passed in Great
Britain last autumn, and it will come into
operation upon the 19th of next
month. It is
necessary that we
should keep our scheme on parallel
lines with the British one
account of our reinsurance agreement
with Great Britain, which has been such
a tremendous advantage (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-to our working people
in Northern Ireland-it has actually
brought to our Unemployment Fund no
less a sum that £3,000,000, contributed
in part by the British Treasury and in
part by my right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance. When I speak of keeping on parallel lines with Great Britain
I have behind me a considerable weight of
authority, because I feel, whatever hon.
Members opposite may at times say, the
vast majority of our people in Northern
Ireland desire that we should do so.
And

This Bill requires that all persons engaged in manual work and those whose
salaries are under £250 a year, except
agricultural workers and domestic servents, should be insured. The contributions remain as at present-8d from the
employer, 7d from the worker, and 6d
from the State. I am only giving the
weekly contributions payable by men as an
example. The total contributions it will
be seen therefore amount to 21d. Now,
this is the departure from the Blanesburgh
Committee's report to which I have referred. The Blanesburgh Committee suggested that the contributions should be
equal as between the employer, the worker,
and the State and that 5d should be contributed by each, making a total of 15d.
But having regard to the fact that the
British fund is overdrawn at the present
time to the extent of over £22,000,000—
our suspense debt is even heavier in proportion-it was felt that the contributions
suggested by the report would not be
sufficient to restore solvency to the fund
by a repayment of the debt. Now, a
great deal was made of this departure at
Westminster, due to the fact that it was
considered that the State was not contributing its fair share.
Well, whatever grounds there may have
been for that complaint in Great Britain.
there are no such grounds here, and for
this reason. When we take into account
the ordinary statutory contribution from
the State and the equalization payment
from the Imperial Treasury, and also the
equalization payment from our own
Treasury, we find that instead of the State
contributing one-third of the total amount
the State will actually be contributing

circumstances, and therefore we ought to
accept it.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr.
Kyle) used what, to my mind, was a

that the Six County area is a noneconomic unit, and then he went on to
point out that the relative number of

Wednesday, 21st March, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
WALKER v. WHAN CASE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is prepared to
issue, as a White Paper, the report presented by Mr. T. J. Allen on the Walker
versus Whan case.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am not prepared
to publish the report presented by the
officer referred to in this particular case.
The case has already been fully dealt
with by the competent courts, and it
would not be in the public interest to reopen it.
Mr. KYLE: In the view of the fact
that the information contained in District-
Inspector Allen's report was before a local
court, and is, therefore, not a secret
document, will the right hon. Gentleman
not satisfy the country by publishing the
report as a White Paper?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, Sir; I am
not prepared to publish any report that
the Government may receive from one of
their Constabulary officers.

of in kind.
decided to adhere to their previous
decisions to pay outdoor relief in kind.

of Guardians at its meeting yesterday
As the Guardians came to this decision

EQUAL FRANCHISE BILL.

Minister whether it is the intention of

enfranchised under the Equal Franchise

General Election, and whether it is intended to amend the electoral laws

Britain.
SO
Sir DAWSON BATES: My right hon.
Friend the Prime Minister has asked me
to reply to this question.
It is the intention of the Government
that the next General Election for the
Parliament of Northern Ireland will be
held on the extended franchise prescribed
by the Bill referred to by the hon.
Member.
On the other hand, the Government do
not consider that there is any necessity.
to have two franchise qualifying periods
and two Registers, as they have in Great
Britain, on account of the additional
heavy expense involved.

that the average income in Ireland as a

I think myself that probably the Members of the Government would be glad if
they could in any way shed the effects of

Prime Minister told the House that these
salaries were fixed by a Committee that

salaries were fixed there has been a considerable reduction in wages. There has
been a great depression in the agricultural industry, there has been a great depression in all our industries, and there
has been a tremendous amount of unemployment. Therefore, I say that the circumstances under which those salaries
were fixed are totally different from the
circumstances prevailing in our area today. I think that in itself would constitute a reason why a committee should be
appointed to take into consideration the

Major SHILLINGTON: This Amendment is more or less a Vote of Censure
upon the Committee appointed to consider this question of salaries when our
Parliament was first set up in 1921, and
as I was a member of that Committee I
fear I would not be doing my duty if I
did not say a few words. That Committee had lengthened sittings. It made
inquiries from a great number of different sources and interviewed representatives of different Colonial Governments,
and after careful deliberation it came to
the conclusion that the salaries they recommended were salaries that this area
of ours could afford to pay its Prime
Minister and the principal heads of the
Department.

The hon. Member for Down (Mr. P.
O'Neill) spoke of the limitation of the
Government guarantee to a term of two
years when the Money Resolution came
on. I said something in reply, pointing
that the construction of such large ships
are built in our principal yard required almost two years at any rate,
and that, therefore, a guarantee limited
to two years would be of no earthly use
to any shipowner, because in the majority
of cases the shipbuilder only received his
money from the shipowner at the end of
the construction of the ship. Therefore,
you will see how perfectly absurd it would
be to place limits such as the hon. Member had in mind. It would have no
value to them, and could have no efficacy
if such limits were imposed. As a matter
of fact, insurance companies, who advance
the major portion of the money in these
cases, are perfectly satisfied to continue
the security to a term of 10 or 12 years.
Of course, repayment is made from year
to year, as the shipowner is able from the
earnings of the ship to repay.
a
As to results, no one can decry them.
We have succeeded by the operation of
this Measure in keeping our principal
shipyard fully employed. We have been
able to assist in the introduction of a new
industry, a textile industry, in Northern
Ireland. We have advanced money for
other purposes, electric light work,
weaving factory, and such like. All these
things, of course, have been directed to
the one purpose to which I have referred,
that is, the creation of employment. I
think the Government can congratulate
itself to this extent, that it has succeeded
in providing employment for a very large
number of men that would otherwise have
been walking the streets. It has been
one of the most useful Acts, and one of
the simplest, and, to some extent, one of
the least troublesome that the Government has passed during the seven years
of its existence. At any rate I, myself,
feel that the small committee which was

Oral Answers to Questions.
STANDARD OF MARKING IN
GEOGRAPHY.
1. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
why a difference was made in the standard
of marking between boys' and girls'
answers in geography at the June, 1927,
certificate examination; if it was made in
any subject other than geography; if it
was made with the sanction of the
Ministry, and, if so, on which of the
official "Regulations for the Secondary
School Certificate Examinations" the
Ministry's sanction was based.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The following paragraph appears in the report of
the examiner in geography:-
"When the teaching of the subject is
not on a high level, it usually happens
that the girls do worse than the boys.
This is decidedly the case in geography
in many cases, and though the examiner
deliberately marked girls very easily,
the proportion of failures among them
is very high. In the senior examination, 66 out of 98 boys, but only 21 out
of 82 girls passed."
The Ministry knows of no difference in
the standard of marking between boys and
girls in other subjects. The standards to
be adopted in marking the answers of
candidates are left to the discretion of the
examiners, and no specific instructions on
this subject are issued by the Ministry,
but the examiners are informed that the
papers are to be so set as to be suitable for
the average student reasonably well
taught, and that they should be marked
accordingly.
JUNIOR CERTIFICATE EXAMINA-
TION. NEW REGULATION
2. Mr. GYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether candidates at the junior certificate examination, in June, 1928, who
pass in both history and geography, will
he debarred by a new Regulation from
counting both subjects towards passing
the examination as a whole; if this Regulation will be enforced against senior
candidates; and if it is the considered
policy of the Ministry of Education that
both history and geography should not be
taught in the junior classes of secondary
schools.
Mr. ROBB: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
There are separate regulations for the
Junior and Senior Certificate Examinations, and, therefore, the conditions for
passing the junior examination do not
apply to the senior examination. In reply
to the last part of the question, the
Ministry's policy is set forth in a circular
which was issued to the schools in September last, and which is in the following
terms:-
"The attention of heads of schools is
drawn to Regulation 20 of the Regulations for the Secondary School Certificate Examinations (1928). Under
former regulations history and geography formed a composite subject

and the Ministry hopes that the great
majority of candidates will take both

shall be in addition to the provision made
by the aforesaid Resolution."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): It will be within the recollection of hon. Members that a Resolution
Payment of Senators

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Payment of Senators
[Mr. Pollock]
was passed by this House on the 18th
March, 1924, to the effect that arrangements should be made for the payment to
members of the Senate at a rate of two
guineas per diem in respect of their expenses for attendance at meetings or
Select Committees of the Senate or Joint
Committees of both Houses, with the
maximum limit for each Senator of 80
guineas a year. When moving the Resolution at the time I expressed the opinion
that as the principle of payment of
Members of this House had been
cepted it could only be considered equitable that a similar principle should be
extended to the case of Senators. The
reason for basing the payment in their
case on attendance instead of adopting
the scheme applicable in this House of
paying an annual amount was that the
number of days on which the Senate sits
varies very much.
ac-
It has now been found that the arrangement does not meet the necessities of
every case, and this Resolution proposes
that, in addition to the payments made
in pursuance of the existing Resolution,
there should be paid an annual flat amount
of £100 to such Senators as make a signed
declaration to the effect that owing to insufficiency of means the normal scale of
payment for attendances in the Senate
does not enable him to devote his time
adequately to his duties in the Senate.
The Government are confident that this
Resolution will commend itself to the
Committee and, in these circumstances,
I do not propose to comment further save
to say that provision will, of course, be
made in the forthcoming Estimates for
the few payments which it is anticipated
will arise. It is proposed that the
arrangement should take effect as from
the first of next month. I beg to move.

CLAUSE 6 (Amendment as to disqualifications for receipt of benefit).
The following Sub-section shall be substituted for Sub-section (1) of Section
eight of the principal Act:-
. -
"(1) An insured contributor who has
lost employment by reason of a stoppage of work which was due to a trade
dispute at the factory, workshop or
other premises at which he was employed shall be disqualified for receiving unemployment benefit so long as
the stoppage of work continues, except
(a) in a case where he has, during the

Oral Answers to Questions.
COTTAGES AT BELFAST PRISON.
1. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Kyle)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state who is responsible
for the neglect in putting down the foundations for the prison cottages, now
in
course of erection at the Belfast Prison,
and the amount of extra expense involved
in pulling down the walls and putting in
new foundations; and whether this extra
expense is in any way attributable to the
incompetence of the old prison trades'
staff.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
question.
The hon. Member is incorrect in assuming that there has been any neglect, or
that any question of incompetence enters
into the matter. The foundations for
the cottages were put in by prison labour
before the contract for the erection of the
superstructure was made. The first tenders received for the construction of the
cottages were so high that it was decided
to re-design the cottages with a view to
the saving of public funds. As the hon.
Member will easily understand, this took
a considerable time, during which period
the foundations already laid had to be
left exposed to the elements. In consequence of the abnormal rainfall which
has occurred during the past winter the
infiltration of moisture caused the bearing
capacity of the soil under the foundations
to be diminished and a subsidence took
place.
The subsidence was first noticed on the
10th ultimo after a particularly heavy
storm which was accompanied by torrential rain. The hon. Member will recall
that this storm caused serious damage
throughout the British Isles. The extra
expense which may be involved is estimated to be in the region of £200.
ESCAPES FROM BELFAST PRISON.
2. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. Kyle)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of prisoners who have escaped from Belfast
Prison during the last four years; whether
an inquiry has been held regarding these
escapes; and, if so, on whom has the responsibility been placed and the penalty inflicted in each case; who was the Governor
of the prison on each occasion, and the number of new Governors appointed during
the same period; whether it is true that
the defence of the Governor on the recent escape of four convicts was based
on the disloyalty of the staff, and if he
considers that a Governor who has not
the confidence of his staff is a fit and
proper person to be in charge of a prison; whether he is aware that, previous
to the opening of Belfast as a convict
prison, it was reported to the Governor
by an old and experienced officer then
serving at the prison that the existing
cell locks were unsuitable for the safe
custody of convicts; what steps, if any,
were taken to remedy
to remedy this defect;
whether he is prepared to place the file
containing the Governor's report on the
matter on the Table of the House; and
L
Oral Answers

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Oral Answers
[Mr. Beattie]
whether the only punishment inflicted
on the Governor for his neglect of duty
in the matter of these escapes was to
grant him three months' leave of absence at the public expense.
the
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): During
last four years prisoners have escaped
on three occasions from Belfast Prison.
One prisoner escaped on each of the first
two occasions, but the prisoners in question were immediately recaptured. On
the last occasion four prisoners escaped,
of whom two have been recaptured.
Sworn inquiries were held in each case.
As a result of the inquiry into the first
of these escapes two warders were punished by being fined, and a principal
warder was reprimanded on the grounds.
of negligence.
In the other cases it was found impossible, after very full inquiry, to attach
blame to any particular officer connected
with the prison.
as
On the occasion of the first escape,
Captain Stephenson was acting
Governor of the Prison in the absence of
Major Long, who was seconded for special
duty at the Home Office, but at the actual
time of the escape Captain Stephenson
was absent on leave, and the chief
warder was in charge.
At the time of the subsequent escapes,
Major Long was in charge of the Prison.
With regard to the remaining part of
the question, I should like to make it clear
at once that the Governor was in no sense
called upon to make a defence, but was
in the ordinary way required to give evidence at the inquiry.
It would be impossible for me, for reasons which should be obvious, to disclose
any particulars of the evidence given at
these inquiries, but, at any rate, I cannot
for one moment admit the suggestion
made by the hon. Member that the Governor has not the confidence of his staff
or of the Ministry, or that he is unfitted
in any way for the responsible position
which he occupies.
As regards the question of the locks on
the cells, this matter as been the subject
of earnest consideration by the Ministry,
but it would not be in the public interest
to enter into any details regarding the
steps which have been taken in the
matter.
For a similar reason I am not prepared to disclose any information or to
publish any reports which have been submitted in this connection.
With regard to the last part of the
hon. Member's question, I must deprecate, in the strongest possible terms, the
suggestion in the question that any
punishment was inflicted on the Governor, or that there was any obvious neglect
of duty on his part.
The facts of the case in regard to his
leave of absence are as follow:
Prior to the recent escapes, he had
submitted to the Ministry an application for sick leave, and his application
had been approved, but, following on
the escapes, the Governor very properly intimated that he did not wish
to go on leave until all the circumstances has been fully inquired into,
and, in point of fact, he did not take
his leave until the inquiries had been
completed.
In conclusion, I must once again say
that I have entire confidence in the
Governnor of Belfast Prison, and that I
deprecate in the strongest possible terms
reflections as those contained in the question being cast on the character of this
officer, or, indeed, of the prison staff
generally.

every high-class hairdressing establishment in the city; and whether he is prepared to hold an inquiry into all the facts

workers as citizens are to be permitted to

means of handbills.

Oral Answers
26 MARCH 1928
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to
the first part of the hon. Member's question, I am advised that the police did not,
as suggested, prevent the distribution of
handbills outside the premises of Messrs.
Charley & Co.
I have no information in regard to the
second part of the question, and I see no
reason for holding an inquiry into the
case.
With reference to the last part of the
question, there is no objection to the
distribution of handbills, provided the law
is not thereby infringed.
ULSTER SPECIAL CONSTABULARY
-DEMOBILIZED MEMBERS.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
nature of the arrangements made, if any,
between the Northern Government and
Dominion or Colonial Governments, with
a view to absorbing the demobilized
members of the Special Constabulary who
are desirous of taking up occupations
overseas, and whether these arrangements
are still in force.
Sir DAWSON BATES: On the disbandment of the Special Constabulary,
in the early months of 1926, arrangements were made by my Ministry, in cooperation with the Ministry of Labour,
through the instrumentality of the
accredited shipping agents in Northern
Ireland, to draw the special attention of
disbanded members of the Force to the
facilities afforded by the British and
Dominion Governments in regard to
emigration to certain of His Majesty's
dominions.
I may also say that, at the same time,
the Australian and Canadian emigration.
authorities were approached with a view
to granting special consideration, within
the ambit of the various assisted-passages
schemes, to disbanded members of the
Special Constabulary.
These arrangements are still in force.
Sir DAWSON BATES: They had the
facilities open to the general public and
they had other facilities. By reason of
the fact that they were members of the
Special Constabulary they received special
consideration.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if the demobilized members of the
Special Constabulary had special facilities
or had they the ordinary facilities that
were open to the general public?
Colonel WOODS: How many, if any,
availed themselves of those facilities?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot tell.

Mr. POLLOCK: Again I may

here in this Bill, which is only an extension of the Bill in point of time—we are

There is only one other matter to which I
need refer, that is the point raised by the
hon. Member for County Down (Mr.
Patrick O'Neill), in regard to bank clerks.
Here again, I think there is a good deal
of misunderstanding. The Bill definitely
lays down that there shall not be contracting out in the future. The reason for that
is obvious. No insurance scheme can
exist for long if it only takes the bad lives
and does not take the good lives. For
instance, if an insurance company were
to take all the houses that were liable to
be burned and to leave out those that
were not liable to be burned, it would not
be long before that insurance company
would become bankrupt. Therefore, this
Bill lays it down that certain industries
less liable than others to unemployment
shall not be allowed to contract out.
It is rather a strange thing that these
young men or their representatives could
have asked to be permitted to contract
out of the scheme since the principal Act
was passed in 1920, but that during all
the time the door was open they never
took advantage of it. Now when the door
is going to be shut they say some injustice is being done to them. Again, the
hon. Member for County Down (Mr.
Patrick O'Neill) is under a misapprehension. He says it is not possible for those
young persons to get benefit. He will be
glad to know that some of them have got
benefit in days gone by. They can get
benefit in two ways. It is quite true that
if they are dismissed or if they leave of
their own accord they will not get benefit
for six weeks, but after six weeks they
can put in a claim, and if they can show
they are looking for work, and are qualified in other ways, they are entitled to
benefit in the same way as other people
are. Again, at the end of fifteen years
they may be paid off in the natural course
of their employment. If they get a pension from their employers, unless it brings
their income up to £250 a year, which, I
think, is very unlikely, it will not disqualify them from getting unemployment
benefit. I really fail to see how, under
this Clause any more than under any
other Clause, an injustice is being done.
to the insured persons.

if everyone had the right to make a complaint to the county council and ask the
council not only to take away their own
obstructions but to see that other obstructions were not placed on the roads.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think that
on re-consideration my hon. Friend will

surveyor himself, and either the committee or the surveyor could deal with

to their notice. It is perfectly true that
in the old Grand Jury days things were
not run on the same democratic lines as
at present. The Grand Jury met only
twice a year, but I think it would be a
mistake to place such drastic powers in
the hands of one individual to interfere
with other people's property. No delay
will take place, because the county council can delegate its powers to any of its
committees if it so desires. Therefore,
I hope the hon. Member will agree to
withdraw his Amendment.
I think the method outlined in the Clause
for bringing the matter to the notice
of the county council is a very tedious
one, and I suggest that the county surveyor should be empowered to serve the
necessary notice if he saw anything radically wrong. Suppose the county surveyor went out the day after a county
council meeting and saw a man building
a turf stack that impeded the view from
the road. The county surveyor could not
do anything until the next county council
meeting, and perhaps two months would.
pass before any action could be taken,

would continue. Therefore, I think it

was responsible to have it removed. It

for these reasons that I put down the
Amendment, which I beg to move.

CLAUSE 3 (Lopping of hedges overhanging roads)-
(1) Where any hedge overhangs any
road, street or footpath so as to obstruct
or interfere with the light from any
public lamp, or to endanger or obstruct
the passage of vehicles or foot passengers or to obstruct the view of drivers
of vehicles, the local authority may
serve a notice on the owner of the hedge
or on the occupier of the premises on
which such hedge is growing, requiring
him to cut or lop the hedge within fourteen days, so as to prevent such obstruction or interference, and in default of
compliance the local authority may
themselves carry out the requisition of
their notice, doing no unnecessary
damage, and may recover the cost in
the county court as a debt due by the
owner or occupier upon whom the
notice was served.
(2) Any person aggrieved by any requirement of a local authority under
this section may appeal to a court of
summary jurisdiction within fourteen
days after the service of the notice
aforesaid, and the following provisions
shall have effect with respect to any
such appeal:-
(a) Notice in writing of the appeal
and of the grounds thereof shall be
given by the appellant to the clerk
of the local authority;
(b) The court may make such order
in the matter as they consider
reasonable, and may award costs
to be recoverable as costs in cases
of a civil nature are recoverable
under section twenty-two of the
Petty Sessions (Ireland) Act,
1851;
(c) No proceeding shall be taken by
the local authority, or work executed, until after the determination or abandonment of the
appeal;
(d) Notice of the right of appeal
shall be endorsed on the notice
communicating the requirement of
the local authority.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
RURAL COUNCILS-CIRCULAR
LETTER, P.P. No. 84.
2. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that the recent circular letter, P.P.
No. 84, which was issued to Rural District
Councils by his Ministry, will (especially
in view of the request for the issue of bylaws dealing with factories employing
forty persons or less) throw a greatly increased volume of work upon the Councils,
necessitating the appointment of additional inspectors and increasing the burden upon the rates; and whether the
Government will introduce legislation to
amend Sections 14, 15, and 16 of the
Factory and Workshops Act, 1901, and
so place the duty of inspection of fire
escape methods upon the existing factory
inspectors, who would then be able to do
this work in the course of their ordinary
duties without unnecessary duplication of
inspection and responsibilities.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member is. I think, under a misapprehension with regard to this circular.
The circular does not throw any new
duties on local authorities, but merely
calls attention to the duties of local
authorities under the Factory and Workshops Act, 1901, an Act which has been
in force for 27 years.
It has been brought to the notice of the
Ministry that the provisions of this Act,
with regard to providing proper means of
escape from factories in case of fire were
not being enforced, and the Ministry consider it desirable, in view of the dangers
which might arise from want of proper
means of escape in case of fire, to call the
attention of local authorities to their
responsibilities in the matter.
The provision of fire escapes has to do
with the construction of the buildings, a
matter over which local authorities have
certain powers of control.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will be very
happy to discuss the matter with my hon.
Friend, and consider it still further.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I ask the
right hon. Gentleman if it is not possible
to consider an amendment of the Act?
If the local authorities are to carry out
their duties as they should be carried out,
the Act will have to be amended. Will
he consider the amendment of Sections
14 and 16? Could the duty of inspection
not possibly be placed upon the existing
factory inspectors?
ESTABLISHMENT OF CIVIL SER-
VICE MESSENGERS.
3. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether it is a fact
that the greater number of the messenger
staff of the Civil Service are still on a
temporary basis; whether most of these
men have been employed for some years;
and whether, as the number so employed
is practically stable, does he not think
that these ex-Servicemen should be placed
on a permanent basis so as to qualify
for pension rights before being debarred
by age.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the first and
second parts of the hon. Member's
question are in the affirmative.
As regards the third part, it has not
up to the present been the practice to
grant established status to manipulative
or quasi-manipulative staff other than
those performing supervisory or specially
responsible duties, and I see no adequate reason for departing from that
practice.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask if it is
not the practice of the Imperial Governnient to have the Government messengers
on a permanent basis?
Mr. POLLOCK: I understand that
is not so.
NORTHERN IRELAND LAND ACT,
1925.
4. Mr. CRAWFORD (for Mr. Lloyd
Campbell) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he can give any information regarding the large number of estates which
have not yet been dealt with under the
Northern Ireland Land Act of 1925;
whether he is aware that it seems likely
that a number of tenants will not receive
the benefits of the Act within the period
originally contemplated; and to inquire
whether the Government has brought
this matter to the notice of the Imperial
Government, and, if so,
whether any
reply has been received to these representations.
27 MARCH 1928
Oral Answers
Roads Improvement Bill-
Mr. POLLOCK : As I have so often
stated in this House, the administration
of Land Purchase is entirely a matter for
the Imperial Government, which has its
own officers in Belfast over whom we have
no jurisdiction whatever.
Our Government has for some time past
been in communication with the Imperial
Government on this subject, and has indicated that there would be a considerable
hardship inflicted on those tenants who
will not in the ordinary course receive
the benefits of the Act within the period
originally contemplated. The Imperial
Government has received these representations very sympathetically, and is at
the moment considering what steps are
possible to improve the position of those
tenants whose estates would normally be
dealt with after May, 1929. I am hopeful that the proposals of the Imperial
Government will be known shortly after
the Easter Recess.

to

CLAUSE 5 (Power of local authorities
to prohibit or restrict driving of vehicles
on roads).
(Progress
(1) A local authority may, by order,
prohibit or restrict, subject to such
exceptions or conditions as to occasional user or otherwise as may be
specified in the order, the driving of
vehicles of any specified class on any
specified road within the area of the
local authority, in any case in which it
appears to the local authority that the
road is unsuitable for use by a vehicle
of that class and would be damaged if
used by such vehicle:
Provided that a local authority shall
not make an order prohibiting or restricting the driving of any vehicle,
whose wheels are fitted with pneumatic
tyres on a road classified under subsection (2) of section seventeen of the
Ministry of Transport Act, 1919, as a
first-class or second-class road.
*
(2) A person aggrieved by an order.
made by a local authority under this
section may, within such time and in
such manner as may be prescribed by
regulations of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, appeal to that Ministry against
the order, and the decision of that
Ministry on the appeal shall be binding
upon the local authority, and shall not
be subject to appeal to any court.

powers
over third-class roads. Remember, the

they would close these roads to this particular class of traffic. I think that

It has been said that these district

great deal of attention from the local

authorities receive only 15 per cent. from
the Government. We get no reconstruction grant, and yet, if these roads are

CLAUSE 7 (Erection and use of petrol
pumps along roads).
(1) The local authority may, if
they think fit, grant to any person a
licence to erect, construct or place and
maintain, in or under any road, street
or footpath in their area, pumps, pipes
or other appliances for supplying motor
spirit to mechanically propelled vehicles
drawn up in such road or street, and
may by by-laws—
(a) prescribe the period for which,
and conditions upon which, such
licence may be granted or withdrawn,
and the conditions to be observed in
connection with the use and construction of such pumps; and
(b) require the payment, in respect of a licence, of such annual
fees as may be fixed by the by-laws;
and
(c) impose penalties for the erection or use of pumps, pipes or other
appliances without a licence under
this section.

This is an Amendment that was
brought before me by our county surveyor,
who complained of the practice of farmers,
especially on narrow roads, having their
gates opening outward. When they
bring the cows home in the evening they
leave the gates open in order to save themselves trouble when they are going back.

night and are a great danger to the
public, because cyclists, and motorists,
and even pedestrians, coming along at
night knock into the open gates. Of
course one can easily see that in certain
cases it would be impossible to have the
gates opening in any way except outward,
but then, that is provided for in the last
part of the Clause where the road authority have power to make an order to cover
such cases.
The difficulty which I foresaw in connection with the Amendment is
obviated by the latter part of the Clause.

New CLAUSE (Precautions for horse
traffic).
In the repair, remaking, resurfacing
of roads it shall be obligatory on the
local authority to make and maintain
a condition reasonably safe for horse
traffic, and in neglect of this provision
the local authority shall be liable for
damages for accidents to horse traffic
caused by the surface of the roads
being left in a slippery and unsafe
condition for such traffic.
Brought up, and read a First time
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: I beg
to move, "That the Clause be now read
a Second time."
This New Clause raises a very difficult
problem involved in the change that has
taken place in our transport system. In
their efforts to secure a solution of the
problem as to the best material to bear
motor transport, the local authorities, to
some extent, seem to have met with
ancther very big problem, that is, the
problem of making the roads reasonably
safe for horse traffic. If we had been told
four or five years ago that such a question
would arise we would not have believed it.
Roads Improvement Bill-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. G. Henderson]
Many of our main roads have been left in
a condition that they cannot be used for
horse traffic without serious danger of
accident. Now, our farmers are the men
who have largely made these roads and
largely maintained them, and the present
policy seems to be an entire disregard
of the rights of these users, and in the
reconstruction of these roads the only
interests that are being considered are
those of the motor users.
This circumstance will involve a double
tax on the farmer, because the remaking
and resurfacing has increased the upkeep
of these roads and increased the rates
to an incredible degree.
The Chairman of the County Antrim
Finance Committee this year in introducing the estimates said, even despite
the grant now made from the Road Fund,
the County Antrim Rates were £100,000
more this year than they were in 1914.
He said also, that £99,000 of that rate
was raised on agricultural land, so that
on account of creating these new roads
and resurfacing these roads, the farmers
are heavily taxed. They are taxed also
in this way, that they cannot use these
roads for their horses, and a great many
of them have to resort to paying motor
lorries to convey their produce to the
market.
conregard to their use? These roads ought to
be maintained in a reasonably safe condition for the farmer or any other person
who wants to use a horse. I know it is
possible that a comparison will be made
in this House with regard to the volume
of motor traffic and of horse traffic
at the present time. But how can there
be horse traffic when our roads are not
reasonably safe for horses? I am
tinually getting letters from a great
many parts of this Province from farmers
with regard to this grievance. Not long
ago I had a letter from the Carrickfergus
district, where a farmer stated that on one
mile of a road he passed three horses that
had fallen, two of them with loads of hay,
on account of the slippery condition of
the surface left there. I do feel that the
road authorities, at the present time,
have not given sufficient consideration to
this problem.
Now, we hear a great deal at the present time about the advisability of a more
direct service from the producer to the
consumer, but if these roads are left in
such a condition by the local authorities
that the farmers cannot use their horses
it puts the farmer more and more into
the hands of the middlemen. If they
cannot market their own produce with
their own horses they have to sell their
produce to the middlemen and cannot
get into contact directly with the consumer. Therefore, I hold by both these
counts the farmers are doubly taxed.
Besides that, they are forced to make detours from these roads and go roundabouts
that add miles to their journey. Have
these people the right of user over these
roads?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Certainly.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: They
have the right of user. They are the
people who largely made the roads. Is
there to be no consideration given with
Now everyone knows the asphalt road.
I think the greatest danger is where the
road is rounded and is left too convex.
The great danger is when the horse comes
to the bump, especially when it is a bit
damp. The horse has no chance at all;
he is nearly sure to go down. While it
is necessary in a water-bound road that
the road should be convex to throw off
the water, I hold that in the asphalt road,
being waterproof, there is not the same
necessity. A very slight fall in the road
would be sufficient, and would to some
extent obviate the danger created by
these surfaces. That is one point where
I think the local authorities might have
shown some consideration for horse traffic
in the reconstruction of these roads.
It is interesting that the Minister of
Home Affairs has taken powers under this
Bill to experiment in the remaking and
resurfacing of roads, and it surely should
not be beyond the range of science to produce material for road surface that would
bear motor traffic and be waterproof, and
at the same time not be slippery for
horses like the asphalt or cement road.
It may be said that this will involve local
authorities in lawsuits. But if it is
necessary for the community that these
roads should be left in this condition
that is unsafe for horse traffic, and if a
farmer ventures his horse on these roads
and gets his property damaged I say,
should there not be redress. I have been
told of cases where valuable horses had to
be destroyed through accidents happening on slippery roads, and I do feel that

which is a fairly steep street and very
slippery. You will find that all over
London where I do not think there is
a single street that is not slippery. The
horses have got accustomed to it and I
understand this newer method of shoeing
helps. I was struck by the remarks made
by the veterinary surgeon attached to
the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty
to Animals. With your permision I
would like to quote from some of the remarks given in the report.
Mr. Coleman, the honorary farrier
adviser to the Society, had taken much
trouble in an endeavour to persuade
farmers to abandon the old methods
of shoeing and instead to have their
horses shod in such a manner that they
can travel in perfect safety on the
smoothest surfaces. In his opinion,
the frog of the foot should take its
natural share of the road pressure, not
only to prevent slipping, but because
in other ways such conditions tend to
prolong the working life of the animal.
The frog is Nature's perfect provision
against slipping and concussion, and
too frequently the frog is deliberately
cut out to enable rubber pads to be
fitted. Mr. Coleman added that if
the Farmers' Union would take up the
matter the Society for the Prevention
of Cruelty to Animals, jointly with the
Master Farriers' Association would
gladly arrange for demonstrations of
rational shoeing to be given throughout
the country."

the drainage of the river up to the passing of the Drainage Act, 1925; whether
he is aware that the County Council is
prepared to maintain the works in good
order, but declines to involve the ratepayers in the additional expense necessary to make good the damage done
owing to past neglect; and whether the
Government will have these defects
remedied before the business of the old
Drainage Authority is transferred to the
County Council.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have seen the
correspondence between my Department
and the Antrim County Council with
reference to the transfer of the duties of
the Glenariffe Drainage Authority to the
County Council, and I have also seen a
copy of the report of the County Surveyor
with regard to the matter.
which the Government would be justified
in asking Parliament to make a grant-inaid of these works.
Section 15 of the Drainage Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925, which provides
for the transfer to county councils of the
business of drainage authorities arising
within their areas enacts that councils to
whom such business is transferred shall
have not merely the powers but also the
duties of such authorities. It is, therefore, apparent that in its application to
the present case the Act requires that the
County Council should undertake the
repair and maintenance of the Glenariffe
River drainage works which were under
the jurisdiction of the former drainage
authority. The local drainage trustees
appear to have ceased to carry out any
work or to levy any rates since 1905. It
is regrettable that the former authority
did not carry out their duties and maintain these works in a proper condition,
but I regret that I can see no ground on
Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of
the answer of the right hon. Gentleman, is it not a fact that the old
drainage authority allowed the course of
this river to get badly blocked up, that
they spent no money and did nothing in
the way of maintenance or repairs for the
last fifty years; and does he consider it
fair or reasonable that the cost of making
good the neglect of a Government Department should fall on the ratepayers of
County Antrim? Further, is it not a fact
that sub-Section (1) of Section 16 of the
Drainage Act only requires a county

Gentleman say by what authority the
Secretary of the Ministry states in his
letter of 9th March that it is the duty of

Sir DAWSON BATES: I might
correct the remark my hon. Friend made
to the effect that this drainage authority
was a Government Department.
It was
a statutory body set up with power to levy
rates from the area affected, and to maintain these works. For my part I am
really not in a position to interpret the
Act of Parliament at the present moment,
but my hon. Friend, I think, is wrong in
his interpretation of the Drainage Act.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Is a statutory
body not under the control of the Government?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, sir.
These of course were drainage authorities
created by a special Act of Parliament,
and apparently nothing has been done by
them since 1905. I quite admit that
there was neglect and that this particular
river did get silted up.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Nothing has been

Sir DAWSON BATES: I will not

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The hon. Member is wrong in

has differed from that in Great Britain,

FLOODING AT DOWNPATRICK.
Mr. P. O'NEILL (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he is aware of the serious damage
caused to property, and the possibility of
serious consequences to the public health
of Downpatrick, by reason of the recent
floods, and whether this damage is due to
the neglect of the Down County Council
in failing to take precautions suggested
by expert opinion, and whether he will
take steps to remove this great danger to
the public health.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry's
Medical Inspector has visited Downpatrick
several times during the winter, and I
am fully aware of the serious position of
the town with regard to flooding. My
Department has been in communication
with both the County Council and the
Urban District Council on the matter.
The flooding can only be remedied by
extensive drainage works, involving a
large outlay, and the matter is at present
under the consideration of the County
Council, who fully realize the seriousness
of the situation, and I am sure that the
Council will do everything in its power
to meet it. As I have pointed out, the
matter is one of considerable difficulty,
and involves a large sum of money, and
the County Council cannot be expected
to embark on a scheme of this magnitude
without careful consideration.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if he is aware that this
question of flooding in Downpatrick has
been going on for very many years, and
has been under the consideration of the
County Council? Expert opinion has
been given as to how this thing can be
abated, and will the right hon. Gentleman
draw the attention of the County Council
to the urgency of this matter, and see that
the thing is put right at once?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Down
County Council are fully alive, as I have
already stated, to the seriousness of the
question, and the Government are also
alive to it. It is to meet cases like this
that our Drainage Act was recently
passed.
Mr. GYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that the Down County Council
insisted on the Urban District Council
giving a guarantee of a sum of £1,000
before they would move in the matter,
and is he also aware that his own Department has turned down the Down County
Council on the ground that they are not
entitled to ask the Urban Council to
guarantee that sum?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon Friend
appears to know more than I do.

Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill has
for its object the amending of the Constabulary Act, 1922. Hon. Members will
recollect that under this Act we continued the old principle contained in the
Royal Irish Constabulary Acts of having
what is known as a free quota. For the
information of hon. Members, I might
tell them that the free quota is the
number of men allocated, free of all cost,
to each local authority. If any area required a number, over and above the free
quota the local authority concerned had
to pay one-half the cost of the extra men.
The free quota was to be fixed by the
Ministry of Home Affairs.
As a result of the practical working
of that principle it was found that the
free quota was never exceeded so far as regards areas outside Belfast. From this it
resulted that the Belfast Corporation felt
that they were not being treated fairly,
and a certain amount of friction arose
in regard to the matter, and they complained that, because the local authorities
were not called upon to pay anything,
that they should not be asked to pay.
As a result of negotiations which extended for some considerable time between
myself and the Belfast Corporation, an
arrangement has been arrived at which
is embodied in the present Measure.
return for that the city will be entitled
to have as many police as the circumstances may require from time to time,
without having to pay anything further.
I think hon. Members will agree with me,
that is those who have studied the question, that this is a satisfactory arrangement. It puts an end to friction that has
been going on, I venture to say, for the
last 20 or 30 years between former
Governments and the Belfast Corporation. At the same time I would also like
to point out that the other areas in the
counties will also get, without having to
pay anything, as many police as they
require, and I hope that number will be
small. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The Belfast Corporation quite properly
recognized that, as a capital city, it is
only reasonable and proper that they
should contribute a sum for the upkeep
of the force allocated in their area. The
arrangement is that Belfast should pay a
sum of £25,000 per annum for a period
of seven years, terminating in 1933. In

Sir DAWSON BATES: Another item
dealt with in this Bill has to do with
weights and measures.
As the law now
stands that work is carried out by
sergeants of the Royal Ulster Constabulary. There is a different system
in England. We appoint twelve sergeants of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
who have to undergo a similar examination to that which their colleagues
undergo in England to qualify as weights
and measures inspectors. These men
receive a bonus of £20 a year over and
above their normal pay. As against
that, fees are paid by traders whose
machines are examined from time to time.
The total amount thus received-about
£12,000 is paid into what is known as
the Reward Fund of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary.
"2
When the Special Constabulary was demobilised-of course, I am referring to
the "A" Special Constabulary, that is,
the whole-time men, and not to the "B's,'
who were only a part-time force a very
considerable sum had to be paid by the
Government by way of compensation for
the ordinary damage done to barracks.
In the case of the regular police force
that would be deducted from the pay of
the men, but we felt that it was inequitable that these men should be asked to
pay this amount for the reason that when
demobilization took place a great many
of them had not been in the barracks at
the time the damage took place.
It was
felt, therefore, that a portion of the
Reward Fund should be handed over to
the Exchequer to relieve the general
funds.
The Reward Fund is a fund into which
certain fines are paid for the purpose of
giving rewards from time to time to men
for good service, and can only be used
for the benefit of men who are actually in
the Force at the time. It is felt, however, that it is unreasonable that the
Exchequer, which bears all the cost of
the men's pay, amounting to over £4,000
a year, should not have the benefit of the '
receipts from these fees, and therefore, in
the future, after certain expenses have
been paid, the money will go into the
Exchequer as an appropriation-in-aid.
The Reward Fund was also established in
connection with the Special Constabulary.
The same remark applies to that Reward
Fund as to the Reward Fund of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. The money
only be paid out for the benefit of the
en who are actually serving at the time.
can
Another Clause in the Bill deals with
the vesting of property. A technical
difficulty has arisen as to the individual
in whom the property of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is vested. At the present
time it is vested in the Receiver, who is
the Permanent Secretary of the Ministry
of Home Affairs. I am advised that on
his death the legal ownership of the
property would pass to his personal representatives, and we propose to make it
perfectly clear that in future instead of
the property resting in an individual,
who, after all, only lives for a certain
period of years, it shall rest in the
Ministry, who have what one might call
perpetual succession, although the holders
of the office may not be perpetual.
The last Clause deals with the giving
of power to the Government to acquire
land compulsorily for barracks. In the
last Act that power was only given for
a period of five years, and it is thought
advisable that the Government should
have those powers to exercise from time
to time when erecting new barracks.
These are the main points in the Bill. I
beg to move.

£160 locomotion allowances to Royal

em-
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I propose to take

payable to officers of the R.U.C.
ployed continuously at headquarters and
at the depot under Article 3 (a) of the

With regard to the last part of the

Order, 1922, for the maintenance of
private cycles certified by the District-
Inspector of Police as being necessary for

EDUCATION AND REGIONAL
EDUCATION COMMITTEES.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether a deputation from the
Education Board of the General Assembly
recently waited on the Minister of Education, urging that ministers of religion
should be appointed to seats on the Education and Regional Education Committees; whether resolutions from Presbyteries or Committees thereof to the same
effect were received by the Ministry;
whether he is aware that, besides
ministers of religion, other persons such
as ladies interested in the welfare of the
young and retired teachers, might with
advantage be appointed to these Committees; and what steps the Ministry propose
to take in the matter.
Mr. ROBB: A deputation from the
Education Board of the General Assembly
interviewed the Minister on the question
of the desirability of appointing ministers
of religion on Regional Committees on
25th October, 1927. Resolutions on the
same subject were received from the same
Board. On every Regional Committee
except four there are lady members. I
have no information as to how many of
the members of Regional Committees are
retired teachers, but the fact of a person
being a retired teacher is not, I should
think, a disqualification for election.
by these gentlemen, both at present and
in the past, to the cause of education,
but it is by no means the case that
ministers are invariably excluded from
these committees. A number of the committees contain ministers of religion
amongst their members and the clergy are
almost always to be found on the district
sub-committees and school committees appointed under the terms of Section 3 of
the Education Act for the local management of schools. The Minister is watching carefully the administration of the
Act by the local education authorities
throughout the Province and he is not
convinced that the circumstances, as
known to him at present, would warrant
his asking Parliament to enlarge his
powers of control over the exercise by the
councils of their powers of appointment
to education committees.
The question of the individuals to be
appointed to serve on education committees is one for the county and district
councils in each area, and it is not competent for the Ministry to prescribe to
those bodies how they should exercise
their right of appointment, seeing that
Parliament has deliberately conferred
these powers on the councils so that the
control of education, so far as it is delegated to education committees, may be in
the hands of elected representatives of the
ratepayers. The Ministry would regret the
exclusion of the ministers of the various
religious denominations from the committees in view of the great services rendered
EX-SERVICEMEN IN BELFAST
WORKHOUSE.

Home Affairs whether he can state the

dependants at present in receipt of outdoor relief in Belfast.

The scheme of National Health Insurance, which is common to the whole of

National Health Insurance Act, 1924,
which was an Act of the Parliament of
the United Kingdom and applies to
Oral Answers

Written Answer
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
Northern Ireland as well as to Great
Britain. The object of the Bill recently
introduced at Westminster is to amend
that Act in certain particulars. Some
of the changes proposed by this Bill relate
to matters with respect to which the
Parliament of Northern Ireland has not
power to make laws, and others, which
affect Approved Societies operating
throughout the United Kingdom, can be
most conveniently dealt with by an Act
applying to the United Kingdom as
whole. The Government has been in
consultation with the authorities in Great
Britain on this subject, and arrangements
have been made for the inclusion of a
Clause in the British Bill providing that
the Measure shall apply to Northern Ireland, if and when provision for that
purpose is made by the Parliament of
Northern Ireland. A Bill will accordingly be laid, in due course, before this
House to achieve that object.

Written Answer.
MOTOR VEHICLES, PORTADOWN.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked
the Minister of Home Affairs whether he
can state if it is a fact that no police
prosecutions have been brought forward
for reckless driving of motor vehicles and
overcrowding of omnibuses at Portadown;
whether numerous accidents have occurred
during the past fourteen months; and,
if so, whether any action has been taken;
and whether he considers it necessary to
hold an inquiry into the whole matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a fact
that no police prosecutions have been
brought forward for reckless driving of
motor vehicles and overcrowding of omnibuses at Portadown. On the contrary,
there have been 45 prosecutions for reckless driving and 29 prosecutions for overcrowding since the 1st January, 1927.
There have been 32 accidents to motor
vehicles in the same period, and in eight
cases prosecutions were instituted. The
circumstances of the remaining cases were
fully investigated, but it was found that
they were not such as to warrant prosecutions.
I am fully satisfied that there are no
grounds whatever for the suggestion that
the police are in any way remiss in the
discharge of their duties with regard to
this matter, and I do not therefore propose to hold any inquiry.
