Superannuation and Other Trust Funds
(Validation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed :
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
877 Superannuation Funds Bill-

18 APRIL 1928
Second Reading
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): The Bill to which
I now ask the House to give a
Second Reading follows closely the
provisions of the Superannuation and
Other Trust Funds (Validation) Act
passed by the Imperial Parliament last
year. That Measure gave effect to the recommendations of a Departmental Committee appointed to inquire into the
effect of the rule of law against perpetuities in its application to certain
superannuation funds and funds with
analogous purposes. The Committee
found that many funds were placed under
disabilities by reason of the rule of law
against perpetuities, and that the only
satisfactory method of removing such disabilities was by way of legislation.
The public policy upon which the rules.
of law against perpetuities are founded
was stated by the Master of the Rolls so
far back as 1732 to be
"the mischief that would arise to the
public from estates remaining for ever
or for a long time inalienable or untransferable from one hand to another,
being a damp to industry and prejudice
to trade, to which may be added the inconvenience and distress that would be
brought on families whose estates are so
fettered."
What the Government seek to accomplish
by means of this Bill is to ensure that any
trust funds set up, or to be set up hereafter, for the purpose of providing a
superannuation to the employees of banks,
insurance companies or industrial concerns, or pensions and allowances for the
widows and orphans of such employees
shall have the means of freedom from any
disability arising out of the application of
the rule of law against perpetuities.
It will readily be appreciated that tho
success of any superannuation fund depends greatly upon its stability and permanency, and upon the existence of a
continuous stream of entrants and beneficiaries, with, of course, the necessary
safeguard of periodic actuarial valuation.
Trustees must prepare each year a state
ment of accounts and balance sheet which
must be audited by an auditor, and a
quinquennial investigation and report by
an actuary as to the financial condition of
the Fund is required to be furnished to
the Registrar.
The Bill lays down certain conditions
to be complied with, the principal one
being the registration of the Fund and its
Rules with the Registrar of Friendly
Societies, who must be satisfied that the
Fund is qualified for registration. The
I am not in a position to say how many
Funds exist in Northern Ireland which
require validation by means of this Bill
as the facts and figures concerning any
Fund are usually treated as of a somewhat
private and confidential character. I
have, however, sought the views of leading
industrial concerns, banks, and representative associations as to the desirability
of introducing legislation on similar lines.
to that recently passed in the United
Kingdom, and the replies which I have
received satisfy me they are almost
unanimous in their desire that similar
legislation should be passed for the benefit of such funds in Northern Ireland.
Question put and agreed to.
Bill read a Second time, and committed to a Committee of the whole House
for to-morrow.

Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the law
relating to certain duties of Excise and to
Stamp Duty."
Mr. BARBOUR: The above Resolution
is in general form and is designed to cover
those clauses in the Bill which, while not
effecting any change in the rate or incidence of an existing excise duty, provide
for "administrative" alterations in the
revenue laws, namely, in the first place
the delegation of powers to the Police
Authorities to enable them to act as agents
of the Ministry of Finance for the issue
of certain existing licences and the collection of the duty, namely, the gun and
game licences. Secondly, in respect of
a new method of assessment of an existing
licence duty-I refer to a provision de-

Stamp Duty is charged in certain circumstances
As is customary with Finance Bills
which do not contain any important alterations in taxation, I propose to refer at
this stage only very generally to what the

Office authorities have undertaken this
duty as an agency service for the Ministry

As regards the new system of valuation
proposed for the purposes of assessing

the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923, the
Government have recognized that under
the changed conditions introduced by that
Act the present system, whereby liquor

valuation of the entire house, etc., may
bring about hardship in certain cases.
The proposal is to give the trader
option of having his duty assessed as at

as they were before the structural alteration, or by reference to the restricted
liquor portion to be valued on a true valuation separately made on the principles of
the Valuation Act, 1852. The traders'
ordinary valuation for rating purposes
will not be affected.

SPECIAL DEALER'S LICENCE
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That as from the first day of July,
nineteen hundred and twenty-eight, there
shall be charged in respect of every
special dealer's licence to be taken out
annually under sub-section (1) of
Section five of the Intoxicating Liquor
and Licensing Act (Northern Ireland),
1927, by a wholesale dealer in spirits, an
excise duty of £5 5s."
Mr. BARBOUR: This provision is
consequential upon Section 5 of the Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing Act,
1927, which authorised a new "special
dealer's licence" to enable persons who
were already wholesale spirit dealers to
sell spirits to licensed retailers in smaller
quantities than the ordinary spirit dealer's
licence would allow. This resolution
purports to grant and impose the excise
duty on the new licence—the rate of duty
proposed being one of £5 5s per annum.
The principle underlying this proposal
having already been endorsed by Parliament, it only remains for me to point out
that the proposal does not run counter to
the intention of the 1923 legislation, as
the new licence will entitle the wholesaler
to supply the retail trade only. The cost
of the ordinary spirit dealer's wholesale.
licence is £15 15s and it is considered that
the proposed rate of £5 5s per annum
represents a fair charge for the privilege
conferred by this additional dealer's
licence. I beg to move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
SPIRITS RETAINED FOR CONSUMP-
TION IN NORTHERN IRELAND.
1. Mr. GYLE asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the number
of gallons of spirits retained for consumption in Northern Ireland in each of the
three years ending 31st March, 1926, 1927
and 1928.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I regret that, as the information
sought relates to a matter controlled by
an Imperial Department, I am not in a
position to supply particulars, but I will
endeavour to obtain the desired information, and will communicate with the hon.
Member in due course.
DOGS ACT-ADMINISTRATION
EXPENSES.
2. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will state
the reason for the increase of £1,000 in
the administration expenses under the
Dogs Act for 1926 over that of 1925.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The apparent increase of £1,000 in the administrative
expenses in 1926 as compared with the
figure shown in 1925 is due to the fact
that certain payments which were included in 1925 in the Fines and Fees
Account are more appropriately shown
under the heading Administrative expenses in the Dogs Act in 1926. Had
these expenses, however, been shown in
926 in the Fines and Fees Account, a
corresponding amount would have been
rithdrawn from the Dogs Act Account to
meet the annual deficit on the former
Account. The amount ultimately distributed to the local authorities was,
therefore, not in any way diminished by
the amount shown under the heading of
Administrative expenses.
The Administrative expenses for 1925
and 1926 were approximately the same.
BELFAST HARBOUR COMMISSION-
ERS-AGE OF EMPLOYEES.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that the
Belfast Harbour Commissioners have laid
down as a rule that no man is to be
taken on in their employment over the
age of 55 years; and whether he will use
his influence to have this rule or order
rescinded.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, to reply.
The Minister has been informed that
the rule to which the hon. Member refers
is applied to those members only of the
Commissioners' staff who are engaged for
employment of a regular nature and it
does not affect the engagement of suitable
men over 55 for ordinary day to day employment. The rule came into operation
in November, 1926, in consequence of
men who had entered the Commissioners'
employment at a late age expecting to
be pensioned after a few years' service on
reaching the retiring age of 70, and the
Commissioners feel that it is reasonable
that the service of their regular employees
should, in consequence, begin at an age
not later than 55. In these circumstances, the Minister considers that he
would not be justified in suggesting to
the Commissioners that the present
arrangement should be altered.
Mr. KYLE: Would the hon. Gentleman use his influence with the Government, in view of the fact that this very
important body in Belfast has decided
not to employ men 55 years of age, to
have the pension age reduced to that age
in order to enable these people to have
something to live on?
Mr. SPEAKER: I do not think that
arises out of the question.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
Then we come to the general question
whether the office or my salary is excessive under the circumstances. Well,
I can only repeat in this House what I
said on former occasions that no one who
has not filled the position can realize the
cost that it entails upon one's Own
private means. I can assure the House,
and I think everybody will believe me
when I say that when I lay down the
reins of office as Prime Minister I will
be an infinitely poorer man than when I
took them up.
But that is one of those
delicate matters into which one does not
care to go. I am sure nobody in the
House will press any further in the
matter. They will find out in time that
generous and all as it appears on paper,
and generous and all as Members of all
quarters of the House feel in regard to
the treatment of myself and my colleagues, there is not one of us who will
not retire from office without feeling very
much poorer in this world's goods than
when they took office. I wish that to be
quite understood in the House, so that
they will not think any one of us is
occupying the position we do for the
purpose of personal gain. I hope that is
not suggested by anyone.
This is a very costly affair. The
position is a very great one and a very
high one, and I am determined to keep
up the dignity of the office. I am not
going to allow anything to interfere with
the dignity of the Prime Minister's Department of Northern Ireland or to
allow of its sinking down in any degree
whatever. We have distinguished visitors
here from all over the world from time to
time. We are in constant communication with people of great distinction and
great weight. If we were in any way to
allow a depreciation of our own position
-if ever that came about through any
fault of our own we would be taken up
at that value. That would irretrievably
damage Ulster as a whole. By keeping
up and maintaining the high office as we
are determined to do, I believe in the
long run greater benefit will arise to
Ulster than by talking about a few
hundred pounds here or there. I hope
with that explanation the Committee will
be satisfied.
of Northern Ireland, and out of all proportion to the services rendered.

Since the Government assumed office
I think there has never been a time when
the taxpayers found it more difficult to
make ends meet than to-day. The shopkeepers in the country, the labourers and
farmers alike, have the greatest possible
difficulty in meeting their obligations and
paying their various taxes and debts. It
may be a small matter, but it will indicate in a practical way sympathy for
these people if the Prime Minister and
his colleagues will to-day consent
reduce their salaries by £1,000 each.
There will still be left sufficient for
them to carry on without feeling the
pinch of penury that falls to the lot of
so many hundreds of the taxpayers who
are obliged to foot the bill. I would
suggest, therefore, that it would be a
very practical means of showing their
sympathy with a large body of people,
many of whom are their own supporters,
who find it hard to make ends meet. In
the year 1921 when the salaries were
fixed the cost of living was a great deal
higher than it is to-day. Let the
Government take that into consideration,
and put their position side by side with
that of the people who pay their salaries.
If they do that they will agree to accept
the Amendment moved from this side of
the Committee.

Someone asked the Prime Minister to

Ulster to me is the men, women and

During the course of the late war thousands of Ulstermen went out to France
and made the supreme sacrifice, believing

Ulster is concerned.
I employed an analogy on a previous
occasion in this House. I argued that
the Ulster loaf was a certain size, and
that the citizens of Ulster got a portion
of the loaf in accordance with their income. Our Prime Minister is supposed
to be the big brother of Ulster. If the
big brother gets a large slice of the loaf,
the small brother gets too small a slice.
If we examine it from the point of view
of the home: What do we think of the
big brother who is so rapacious that he
insists on getting a large slice of the loaf,
while the small or weak brother must go
to the wall with the small slice. I know
the Prime Minister is a soldier who would
not attempt to take up the attitude that
the weaker must go to the wall. The
principle we apply to the home that I
apply to my home, as I presume every
Member of the Committee applies to hi
home-should be applied to the nation.
If we view society as we view the home,

We are very often told that the whole
thing is based on the British model. As
we have pointed out before, in some
things we follow the British Government
most carefully, but in this matter we do
not follow the British precedents very
meticulously at all, because the British
Prime Minister gets £5,000 of a salary
for controlling the destinies of about
45,000,000 people, plus the responsibility
of a far-flung Empire. We, who are
supposed meticulously to follow the
British model, pay our Prime Minister
£4.950 for being responsible for a million
and a quarter people. No one can justify
that. It cannot be justified at all, and
I think the matter should be reconsidered,
because I do not believe that the arguments used up to the moment are sufficiently strong to convince any fairminded person as to the desirability of
these things.
It is very good to argue that the

Mr. POLLOCK: Although this Vote
is the smallest Estimate presented to Parliament, it has invariably provoked very
considerable discussion. Discussion of
broad principles is in itself eminently desirable, and in moving this Estimate I
desire to refer to what is the one important principle underlying the expenditure of this money: It is that the money
must be used in the public interest.
As was stated by the Prime Minister
during a recent debate, the responsibility
for the administration of this Fund rests
upon the Minister of Finance, and I am
personally accountable to Parliament for
the payments which are made.
Hon. Members may not be aware that
the administration of the corresponding
Fund in Great Britain is similarly left.
in the hands of a Minister of the Crown,
subject only to consultation with the
Treasury in exceptional circumstances,
and that it is not customary for Parliament to question, on every possible
Supply-
Committee
19 APRIL, 1928
occasion the manner in which he discharges this public duty. I had hoped
that this House would have extended to
me the same degree of trust, but in view
of the controversy which this Estimate invariably encites, I propose to take this
opportunity of stating as succinctly as
possible the principles upon which my
decisions are based, and to allay any
doubts Hon. Members opposite may
cherish as to actions.
my
Hon. Members will not quarrel with me
in saying that it is in the interests of
our Province that its name, its products
and manufactures should be known in
every part of the globe, and that opportunities should be created for an interchange of views between representative
bodies of other areas and of this area,
whether in the realm of public affairs or
of such matters as agriculture, education
and public health. The Government
cannot directly benefit individual commercial undertakings or influence the world
of thought and research, but it can, and
I think it should, create opportunities
for visits to be paid by public men and
representative public bodies from Great
Britain and from overseas, or make use
of these visits, when arranged by other
bodies, to create an atmosphere of goodwill and friendship. A great deal of good
has already been done in this way to
further the progress of the Province.
I have no hesitation, therefore, in
authorizing the entertainment of persons
or associations whose visits here may in
some degree contribute to the material
prosperity of the people, and almost the
whole of the expenditure charged to the
Fund has been incurred in this way.
There is no secrecy about the expenditure;
the objects are all fully set out in a note
to the Appropriation Accounts when
these are published after the close of each
Financial Year. One or two examples
of contemplated expenditure in the current year will clarify the position :-

which will be holding a Session here in

race; or, again, my right hon. Friend the

Most of the expenditure from the Hospitality Fund is incurred in entertainments
such as these, and in general I restrict the
scope of the Fund to affording hospitality
on the occasion of important visits. But
instances may possibly occur when the
Fund should be used for some more local
purposes. The forthcoming ceremony of
the Laying of the Foundation Stone at
Stormont is an example of what I have
in mind. Similarly, if, in the interests
of the Province as a whole, an important
conference is summoned, I do not regard
it as improper that time should be saved,
and a friendly atmosphere created, by
arranging some slight hospitality for those
taking part.
In conclusion, I would suggest to hon.
Members that it is somewhat invidious
to bring individual entertainments under
discussion. Hospitality, whether public
or private, must be given graciously, and
anything in the nature of a public dispute concerning the recipients of the
hospitality offered by the State must defeat the end to be achieved. I beg to
move.

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
It is obvious that the display in Belfast
on Easter Sunday under such circumstances of any emblem indicating Rewas calculated
publican sympathies
gravely to imperil the peace of the city
and might well have given rise to serious
disturbances.
Instructions were, therefore, issued to
the police that persons wearing these
emblems under circumstances likely to
endanger the peace should be requested
to remove them.
Eight men who refused to do so were
arrested by the police on Easter Sunday
under the provisions of the Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Act, and were
subsequently lodged in Belfast Prison.
Their cases were carefully considered in
consultation with the Attorney-General,
and although there is no doubt that they
had been guilty of an offence by acting in
a manner prejudical to the preservation
of the peace and maintenance of order,
for which a prosecution could have been
instituted, the conclusion was finally
arrived at that in view of the serious
warning which had been given by their
arrest and detention, it was unnecessary
to take any further action against them.
Their release was accordingly affected on
the 16th instant.
I have no information as to whether
any of these men have lost their employment in consequence of arrest.

Mr. KYLE: The Local Government
(Amendment) Bill, the Second Reading
of which I am now moving, is aimed at
giving effect to that conception of the
franchise to which Mr. Baldwin gave
utterance on March 8th when he was
congratulating the women on attaining
the right to vote at the age of 21. He
said:-
The franchise does not only mean
franchise, but it means obligation and
opportunity.
It places upon us all the obligation of
taking an active part in the life of our
city, in the affairs of our country. It
confers upon us, or ought to confer upon
us, the opportunity of influencing in the
representative city or county council
the decisions that are there taken. The
reform that this Bill, which I have the
honour to present on behalf of the entire
Opposition, desires to bring about is that
the various city and county councils and
other governing bodies in our area should
be as fully representative of public
opinion in their areas as is humanly
possible, and is drafted to re-establish
the position created by the Imperial
Government in 1919.
The Bill itself is a simple one, and I
think if I put it under three headings
it would put the matter clearly before
the Members of the House. In the first
place the Bill will provide that in any
contested election of members of a local
authority in Northern Ireland each
voter shall have a single transferable vote,
and where two or more members are
elected together the election shall be by
proportional representation. That is
very necessary, as I think has been
demonstrated in the City of Belfast. At

Therefore, proportional representation

The second point is that the electoral
areas shall be the electoral areas in force
immediately before the commencement of
the Local Government Act (Northern
Ireland), 1922. Thirdly, the rules for
the election of members of a local

transferable vote was introducd, I think,
owing to a very successful experiment in
Sligo in 1919, in which town a very
serious situation had developed, owing, I
may add, to the domination of one particular party in the affairs of the town.
Real faults have been found with the administration of the town. I think it is
notorious that where a city or a country
or a part of a country gets into the hands
of one dominant party the administration
suffers accordingly. Things are done
and acts performed that would not be
possible if there was a painstaking watchful opposition. If there is not an
opposition-for oppositions do not exist in

Government bodies-acts are done which

approximately even in number I think
that cannot be gainsaid.
The facts speak for themselves. Instead
of, as at present, few contests being the

Proportional Representation was intended by the Imperial Parliament to
give a voice to minorities. The block
system favoured the large parties and the
organizations with a great deal of money,
but many people believed that there were
interests that could not find expression
under either of the two large political
parties. For that reason an experiment
was tried at Sligo, in, I believe, the year
1919. Sligo borough at that time, to my
own knowledge, had reached a pretty low
level in administrative ability. It had
come practically to the point of bankruptcy. The result of that election on
Proportional Representation lines gave a
representation to Sinn Fein of seven,
Labour five, Ratepayers eight, and Independents four, a total of 24, so that when
they came to elect a mayor they found
that there were 12 votes on one side and
12 votes on the other side. I think that
we who have some experience of local
administrative affairs find that it is not a
bad thing to have parties pretty evenly
divided in that way. The result of Proportional Representation at Sligo, where
affairs had reached the low standard I
have indicated, was that immediately
things began to look up. In the few
years that followed the rates were reduced, the services were improved, and
the people began to take a more intelligent interest altogether in the affairs of
the borough in consequence of the operation of Proportional Representation. It
is well known that many of the old
Unionist party, who under the block
system could have had no earthly chance of
sitting in the council, had a full representation of eight out of 24.
One need not stress the contrast between
what takes place in the Free State and
what takes place in Northern Ireland.
In the Free State people are satisfied to
give representation to minorities, but in
the North you are not satisfied to give
representation even to majorities. That
is a positive fact. You are not content
unless you possess the control of all offices
and public boards even where you are in
a minority. There are 28 unions in the
area known as Northern Ireland. It will
surprise many of you to know that in 14
of these 28 unions there are Nationalist
majorities. You may say that the rate.

I do not propose here, this afternoon,
to discuss the merits of P.R. as against
the demerits of P.R. I think the case
for P.R. has been completely made by
the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Kyle)
and by my hon. Friend who sits beside me
(Mr. Healy). I could detain the House
for an hour in giving cogent and irresistible reasons for the adoption of P.R. as
an effective method for proper representation in a Parliament of this character,
but I will just give this one. What do
we constantly hear from what is called
the respectable party in Northern Ireland? What is the war cry of respectability everywhere in regard to Local
Government? That it is impossible to
get independent and educated men to
come on to a public Board, because of the
bitterness of these local controversies and
because many of them are subject to
vulgar and sometimes irresponsible attack.
The one safeguard they have is that under
P.R. the area is so widened that it gives
independent and educated men a chance
of standing without being subjected to
these attacks, but because it suits a party
end and because it is against a party
interest, the one argument you are constantly advancing in favour of encouraging what is known as the better class to
come into our local bodies you completely
discard because you want to entrench
yourselves still further in power, not only
in Parliament, but in all local councils.
The necessity for this Bill is recognized,
I think, by all who believe in electoral
justice and democratic freedom. It is a
sincere, although I think a belated,
attempt to deal with a gross public evil.
Some years ago, when the minority were
not represented in this House, this
Government robbed the minority of the
representation the Imperial Government.
gave them when they accepted this Northern Parliament. No doubt you can
claim that at the end of three years you
were entitled to change the methods of
election, but to exercise a legal right,
apart from the moral obligation you assumed, is in my judgment unworthy not
only of politicians but of honourable men.
You accepted Proportional Representation because the minority accepted it, or
because it was given to the minority to
safeguard their interests, and the very
moment that you got the opportunity you
abolished that guarantee for minority
rights. We are in the fortunate position
now of being able to test the spirit of
justice with which you administered the
subsequent changes.

The ATTORNEY- GENERAL (Mr.

reality at all, centres round a question

matter of Proportional Representation.
Upon that question of principle the
Government have considered all the facts
that are known, and have come to light
in other countries and under other electoral systems with a view to seeing whether
or not this system of Proportional Representation, which was inserted in the Act
of 1920, should be allowed to continue.
Having looked around, and having considered the evidence that comes not only
from the United Kingdom itself, but also
from numbers of our great dependencies across the water, and having also
considered in the light of our own experience, what has been the result and
effect of this system in our own area.
the Government came to the conclusion
some time ago that this system should be
done away with at the earliest possible

elections, and one which they are justified
in getting rid of at no very distant date
in the case of our Parliamentary elections. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
One thing, I think, is tolerably plain, and
that is, so far as this system is concerned,
there was no demand for it in this
country. It was inserted in the Act of
1920 by the Imperial Parliament. Our
people had no say further than their representation at that time in the Imperial
House with regard to it. It was tried in
The hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) says this system is not sacrosanct. We all know that. He says that
the minority accepted it. I take it that
what he means the House to infer from
that is that they accepted it as some kind
of bargain or some kind of pledge, and
that though in law this House may be in
a position to get rid of Proportional Representation, still in honour the Government are wedded to it, and that they are
going back upon some undertaking that
they have given, and are using their
power for a purpose for which that power
was not given to them.
But when you look at the Act of 1920
it is perfectly plain that the framers of
that Measure considered that this method
of representation was only to be an experiment, because they said that this Government should not have power, for a space
of three years from the setting up of this
Parliament to do away with it in the
case of our Parliamentary representation.
Therefore, I think it is idle now to say
that there was any pledge or any bargain,
and when you consider that the party that
the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) adorns did.
not come into this House for a very considerable time after it met and held its
first deliberations, I fail to see where this
question of a pledge can arise, or in what
way the Government can be held to have
their hands tied, in the matter of abolishing Proportional Representation.
Therefore, I say that this is an open
question. It is one which the Government are entitled, and I would submit
bound, to deal with, if they are satisfied
on the matter of principle that it is the
interests of the community. They are so
satisfied, and they consider that, on the
arguments that have been put forward
and upon the experience that has been
gained in other countries, as well as in
this area, it is a most cumbersome, expensive and confusing system, and one
which should be done away with and got
rid of at the earliest possible moment.
I. in common with a great many other
people, have had considerable experience

personally of the working of this particular system, and I must say that I endorse
everything that has been said by the

I remember once, when I was a voter
in one of the constituencies in Dublin, and
a municipal election was being held under
this system of Proportional Representation, walking into a booth to record my
vote. At the table where the presiding
officer was seated there were five ladies.
who had all come in to vote together. They
were all illiterate, and they were asked
for whom they wanted to vote. They said
that they wanted to vote for the five members of a certain party, who occupied
various positions, in a list of 17 persons.
The presiding officer, according to his
duty, said, "Will you kindly tell me the
names and I will mark the ballot paper
for you." He could not tell the names
because he did not know the names of the
five gentlemen representing the party,
whom, on general grounds, they were disposed to support. So he said, “I will
read them out to you." He read out the
17 names and the five ladies made the best
shot they could to get the five members of
the party, and out of the five shots they
only got one right.
someone who, they think, represents the
principle that they adhere to, and in the

That example is one that occurred under
my own eyes, and it shows the difficulty
the ordinary citizens, especially the citizens whc, perhaps, are not very well
educated, have in recording their votes
correctly under this system of Proportional Representation. And if that be so,
what can be said with regard to the
accuracy of the results which are obtained
as a result of the elections under this system? I say that some of the results that
have been obtained under Proportional
Representation have really been grotesque,
and do not represent the true view of
the electorate in any way. We know that
it is an expensive system. We know that
it is extremely cumbersome. We know
the confusion that obtains under it. We
know the difficulty that every Member has
in one of these enormous constituencies.
He cannot possibly know more than a
fraction of his constituents, and a very
small fraction of his constituents know
him, even by appearance; and consequently the true state of feeling and
knowledge between the electorate and the
representative has completely disappeared.
People are voting not for personality at
all. They are voting for shadows, for
Now, there is another blot upon this
system. I do not know whether it has
been referred to. But we all know that
in recent times under this system we
have had very low polls at elections, not
only in this Province but in the Free
State, where Proportional Representation
is still in existence. I have always,
rightly or wrongly-and I believe rightly
--ascribed the lowness of the polls in
these enormous constituencies to the very
thing I have already referred to, namely,
the want of enthusiasm and interest of
the electorate, as a body, in the persons
who are to represent them. It is impossible to get the electorate out to record
their votes when you have a system so
cumbersome as this system of Proportional Representation, and when they are
not really acquainted with the persons on
whose behalf they are recording their
votes.
Other matters that have been raised

me last week when moving the Financial

In a Bill of this character, touching, as
it does, on various different questions
affecting the revenue of the Province and
subjects related thereto, it is, perhaps,
more convenient to consider each proposal
separately, and I think it would, therefore, meet with the wishes of hon.
Members if I proceed to consider the Bill
clause by clause.
The object of Clause I is to fix the rate
of the duty payable by those wholesale
dealers in spirits who intend to take out
the Special Dealer's Licence authorized by
the Intoxicating Liquor and Licensing
Act which was passed last year.
The circumstances which necessitated
the creation of this special class of licence
were fully explained by my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
when he moved the Second Reading of
that Bill in this House on the 1st
November last, but it will not be out of
place for me now to recapitulate briefly
the points which were brought to the
notice of the House on that occasion.
Under the law, as it then existed, a wholesale spirit dealer could not sell spirits to
a retailer at one time in quantities of less
than two gallons of each kind of spirit.
That is to say, he could not make a composite sale of, say, whisky, brandy, and
rum, but was obliged to sell at least two
gallons of each class of liquor, with the

As regards Clause 2, although this is a
very lengthy Clause and appears
tremely complicated, the object which it
seeks to achieve is really quite simple. In
accordance with the terms of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923, the licensees of
number of public-houses have been
obliged to carry out structural alterations
in order to separate that part of their
premises used for the intoxicating liquor
trade from the rest. They have then two
courses open to them in regard to valuation for licence duty purposes, namely,
either to pay on the old valuation of the
whole premises or ask for a re-valuation of
the restricted portion, and at the same
time run the risk of having their poor-law
valuation increased. The effect is that,
rather than run the latter risk, the owner
will continue to pay licence duty on the
premises as a whole. This is not desirable, and therefore the Clause proposes to
give the trader an option of having his
duty assessed as at present, that is to say,
by reference to the entire premises as they
were before the structural alterations were
made, or to have the restricted portion revalued for licence duty purposes but without affecting his poor-law valuation.
Sub-sections (2) and (3) of the Clause
are consequential and provide, respectively, for the repayment of a proportional
part of the duty where business is discontinued and for the form in which licences
are to be issued.

Before proceeding to say more on this
subject, I would like to take this opportunity of paying a high tribute to the
officers of Customs and Excise. Hon.
Members will readily understand that on
the transfer of services in 1921 it would
have been almost impossible for our
newly-constituted Departments to have
taken over the whole of the duties which
were transferred, and I refer especially
to those particular services which were
decentralized and necessitated a staff of
trained officers working throughout the
country districts. Accordingly, we found
it desirable to ask-and the Department
of Customs and Excise very readily acceded to our request-that they would act
as our agents for the administration of
various services, including, for example,
the Old-age Pensions Service, the administration of the Entertainment Duty,
and the collection of various licence duties.
With the development of our Own
Departments, however, I am glad to say
that we have at length reached the position in which we feel that we can properly
take over the administration of several of
these services, and, as hon. Members
know, an Act was passed recently, setting
up new machinery in regard to Old-age
pensions. One of the effects of that legislation will be a reduction in the number
of Customs and Excise officers operating
in the country districts of Northern Ireland, and it is felt that it would in future
be a matter of very great difficulty indeed
for the remaining officers properly to
supervise the issue of gun licences and
game certificates, since this is a work
which must essentially be carried out by
a considerable staff scattered throughout
our entire area. Accordingly, my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance, has
carefully examined the whole question in
consultation with the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and it has been agreed that, subject to Parliamentary approval, all gun
and game licences will be issued by

the Ministry of Finance.

It is felt that this change will at once
enable the police, who already
brought in touch with a much greater
number of people who must possess firearms permits and certificates, to detect
any attempts on the part of people in
their districts to evade the gun or game
licence duty. I may say that I have received persistent complaints, not only from
individuals, but also from the Game Protection Society, concerning the large
number of persons who make a practice
of shooting game without the necessary
licence. The Government is convinced
that the preservation of game is a considerable potential source of income to
the people of this Province, and it is felt
that it is in the interests of the Province
to strengthen the law, and at the same
time to take such administrative action
as may have the effect of enabling a closer
supervision to be exercised.

Capital Duty chargeable in each case at

It will be readily appreciated, even by
the most casual observer, that industries
which have suffered by recent foreign
competition, or because of other less direct
causes, may wish to strengthen their
position by a consolidation of interests,
that is to say, by amalgamating existing
companies. No doubt, such a course
carries with it many results of considerable value, and it not only enables such
companies to reduce heavy overhead
charges, but also ensures that manufactures are continued on the most up-todate lines, and that the disturbing effect
of cut-throat competition amongst individual manufacturers may be minimized.

The object of Clause 5 is, very simply,
to rectify what is evidently an omission in
existing Statutes. It is possible that by
a strict reading of the law as it stands at
present a Letter of Power of Attorney
could be charged with a 10s stamp duty
in respect of each person concerned in
giving the power. There is, however,
considerable doubt on the point, and it
has not up to the present been the practice
of the Ministry of Finance to charge more
than 10s for the stamp duty on a Power
of Attorney, irrespective of the number of
donors or the number of matters covered
by the powers thus granted. In order to
put the question beyond doubt, however,
it is considered desirable specifically to
enact that the fact of more than one person being concerned in the granting of a
power, or of more than one matter being
dealt with, should not attract a liability
to additional stamp duty. No real loss
of duty is involved, as the new Clause will
merely establish beyond doubt the legality
of an existing practice.

Mr. BARBOUR: In introducing the
Estimates for my Ministry for the financial year 1928-29 it may be useful if I
refer briefly to the activities of the
Ministry. The Department is divided
roughly into two main branches, on the
one hand Commerce, Economics and Fisheries, and on the other the Companies,
Power and Transport. I will indicate
briefly what the functions of these
branches are.
The aim of the Ministry is to assist
the development of the industries and
Supply-

Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
commerce
[Mr. Barbour]
We
overseas
of Northern Ireland.
claim, and I think not without just cause,
that there is in the Ministry a freedom
from what is known as red tape methods,
and I am glad to say that our endeavours
to assist Northern Ireland manufacturers
and exporters to extend their markets
have received the generous
recognition of a number of individual
firms. By means of the distribution of
reports on market conditions and trade
openings abroad and the provision of
lists of reputable agents in particular
markets, and by specific inquiries to the
British trade representative in the foreign
country concerned, the Ministry has encouraged the exploitation of new markets
and has contributed to the reduction of
risks normally involved in foreign
commerce.
Samples of foreign manufactured
articles enjoying considerable sale in overseas markets have been from time to time
procured by the Ministry for inspection.
in Belfast and elsewhere in the Province.
Advantage is also taken of the periodical
visits to the United Kingdom of His
Majesty's trade representatives abroad to
enable Ulster firms to interview such
representatives in Belfast. Amongst the
trade representatives who have visited
Belfast for this purpose at the instance of
the Ministry within the past few years
were the Commercial Councillors for the
United States, France and China; H.M.
Trade Commissioners for Canada, Australia and India; and the Commercial
Secretaries for Belgium, the Argentine,
and the Dutch East Indies. Hon.
Members will also recollect that recently
my Ministry was instrumental in bringing to Belfast a representative of the
Department of Overseas Trade to discuss
with local exporters the advantages of the
Imperial Government's Export Credit
Scheme in which Northern Ireland, of
course, participates.
Statistics of Northern Ireland's export
and import trade are compiled from
returns furnished periodically by the
Board of Customs and Excise in the case
of direct trade with foreign countries
and from returns furnished by the
harbour authorities in Northern Ireland
in the case of cross-Channel trade. The
collection of the statistics relative to
Northern Irish railways which, previous
to the 1st April, 1926, was undertaken
by the Imperial Ministry of Transport,
has since that date devolved upon the
Ministry. The Ministry has curtailed
the scope of these statistics to some extent
in order to afford the railway companies
some relief from the expenditure and
labour involved in furnishing returns.
Summaries of these statistics are issued
each month in the local Press.
As a complement to the Commercial
Intelligence Service which I have outlined
above, the Ministry also keeps available
up-to-date information regarding the
tariffs of British Dominions and Colonies
and foreign countries, in addition to information respecting the Customs procedure and import regulations obtaining
in such countries. As an indication of
the extent to which this service is availed
of I may mention that in a recent month
no less than 284 tariff inquiries were
addressed to the Ministry.
During the past financial year the
Ministry has participated in several
exhibitions held under the auspices of the
Empire Marketing Board, and by this
means has succeeded in obtaining, at small
expense, considerable publicity for the
agricultural and manufactured products
of the Province. During the present
financial year the Ministry proposes to
participate in a further series of these
exhibitions, approximately twelve in
number, which will be held at various
centres in Great Britain.
Examples of other activities in which
the Ministry is directly interested are to
be seen in the proposal to afford further
financial support to the Linen Industry
Publicity Campaign and to the Ulster
Tourist Development Association.
The postal service is, of course, a reserved service, but the Ministry is always.
ready to act in a liason capacity for commercial and private users in Northern
Ireland, to lay suggestions and information before the Imperial postal authorities
with a view to effecting alterations designed to improve the postal service in
Northern Ireland.
Hon. Members will remember that the
administration of the fishery services in
Northern Ireland was transferred from
the Imperial Secretary's Department to
the Ministry of Commerce on the 1st
April, 1926. Since that date close attention has been devoted by the Ministry to
the preservation and development of this
valuable asset to the Province. The immediate responsibility for the enforcement

of the fishery laws is in the hands of four
Boards of Conservators, towards the expenses of three of which Grants-in-Aid
were made during the year 1927-28.
Some months ago, in consequence of the
marked decrease in the catch of eels, a
statutory inquiry was conducted into the
times and methods of eel fishing with a
view to determining what action was required to prevent a further diminution
while permitting of the development of
the eel fisheres to their prudent limit. The
maintenance of healthy stocks of salmon
in our rivers has also received attention,
and the Ministry has assisted towards this
object by contributions to the cost of the
two largest salmon hatcheries in our area.
In the course of the two years during
which the Ministry has been responsible
for the administration of the fisheries
services a survey of the existing fishery
laws has been carried out with a view to
remedying certain defects, and to bring
the law more into conformity with requirements as indicated by the accumulated
experience of the Ministry and its predecessors. The result of this survey' will
come before the House in the form of an
Amending Bill, copies of which
already in the possession of hon. Members.

The Ministry has provided considerably

fishery. By the careful inspection of all

I should like to refer briefly to the
subject of Industrial Assurance, which
may broadly be described as the insurance of the working classes for small sums
at premiums ranging from 1d to 6d a
week. This work was initiated in the
year 1925 following upon the passing of
the Industrial Assurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1924. The Secretary of the
Ministry acts as Industrial Assurance
Commissioner and exercises judicial
powers in deciding disputes between insured persons and industrial assurance
companies and societies. An indication
of the extent of the work may be gleaned
from the fact that, apart from a large
number of verbal inquiries made and
assistance rendered, no less than 260 disputes were referred to the Commissioner s
office during the year 1927. From the
experience gained I am able to state that
the 1924 Act has conferred real benefit
upon those least able to assert their legal
rights, in providing them with the means
of assistance in relation to the many
questions and problems which arise as to
their rights, and also in providing the
means of adjudication at a low cost. The
report of the Industrial Assurance Commissioner for the year 1927 will be laid
before the House at an early date.
Supply-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee
[Mr. Barbour]
With regard to the development of
electricity, steady progress is being made,
and up to the present time it has not
been necessary to make provision in the
Estimates for public assistance. Hon.
Members will, however, recall the Lisburn Electricity (Confirmation of Agreement) Act, 1927, under which my
Ministry is empowered to grant a loan
of £1,450 so that the main transmission
line, the erection of which from Belfast
to Lisburn is now in contemplation, may
be made suitable for future development
on a larger scale. The Company has recently made an offer of shares to the
public, and the line is likely to be erected
by the autumn of the present year.
During last year generating stations
were established at Lurgan and Armagh,
both being under the control of the respective urban district councils of those
towns. Several other urban districts are
now considering schemes of electricity supply. In the establishment of local generating stations the Electricity Commissioners
have not overlooked the probability that
at a later date the industrial areas of
Northern Ireland may be linked up by
main transmission lines. When that
time comes we in Northern Ireland will
not be faced with the problem of standardizing frequencies, a problem which is
now involving heavy expenditure in the
Central Electricity Board's schemes in
Great Britain. Our problem here, as I
have remarked before, is one of demand
rather than of supply.
It will be within the knowledge of hon.
Members that we have in Northern Ireland two Royal Harbours, Ardglass and
Donaghadee. At Ardglass there has been
in recent years a welcome, though I am
sorry to say fluctuating, revival of the
herring industry which had almost disappeared during the war years. While
the bulk of this industry is still in the
hands of Scottish curers, I am glad to
say that an increasing share is being
obtained by local interests. In order to
foster and encourage the herring fishing
and curing industry, we have carried out
some useful works of improvement at
Ardglass. A section of the sea bed in
the harbour has been reclaimed and converted into curing plots which are now
being surfaced and prepared for occupation this year. A market building has
been opened for the auctioning of fish,
and ten small offices have been provided
in this building for the accommodation
of the fish salesmen and merchants.
These facilities, I am glad to say, have
been much appreciated, and to meet the
demand for additional accommodation I
have arranged to provide this year four
additional offices. The cost will be small
and the rent of £5 per office will give
ample return upon the expenditure
Apart from the Royal Harbours, I need
hardly say that I am keenly interested in
schemes for the improvement of other
harbours on our coasts. I set up a small
Departmental Committee to consider and
report upon the requirements of these
harbours and their report has now been
published.
With regard to other harbours, provision is being made in this year's Estimates for grants in aid of works of improvement in the harbours at Rathlin
Island and Portstewart. Representations
have also been made to my Ministry on
behalf of other harbours, particularly
Ballycastle and Annalong, for which
drawings have been submitted by the
county councils. These proposals will be
considered by the Government in conjunction with the Report of the Departmental Committee.
Hon. Members will recall that during
the past year a Measure consolidating all
statutory provisions relating to quarries
was placed on the Statute Book. The
question of pursuing a policy of consolidation in the matter of Fishery Laws and
Bankruptcy Legislation has been considered, but for the time being the
Measures to be brought before you will
deal with Amendments of the existing
law. The task of consolidating either the
Fishery Laws or the Bankruptcy Laws,
while & most desirable one, is of such
colossal dimensions that it must await a
more favourable opportunity.

In regard to fisheries, I may say my
Ministry and myself are very greatly interested in the possibilities of the development of the fisheries round about our coast,
but on the other hand we really do have to
take into consideration just exactly whom
we are likely to help in anything we do.
The fishery at Ardglass is carried on by
far the greatest extent by Scottish fishermen who come over here. Unfortunately
it is not a staple industry that gives employment all the year round. These men
follow the course of the herrings round the
coasts of England, Scotland and Ireland,
so that they are only present at Ardglass
for a short period of the year. I am very
sorry that the people of Ardglass, to whom
one would say the development of fishing
would mean more than to any other port
in our Province, have not done more of
themselves to help the fishermen who come
to their port. For instance, the supply
of water is so inadequate there that the
trawlers are only able to get water for
ordinary domestic purposes on board. In
order to fill their boilers they nearly always
have to go to the Isle of Man.
With regard to Killough that, of
course, is a private harbour.

with everything said in regard to Killough. It has a marvellous position.

REPORT OF DR. McDANIEL, M.D.,
CO. TYRONE.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
what steps his Department propose to take
to improve the state of affairs revealed
by the report of Dr. McDaniel, Medical
Officer for the County of Tyrone.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked to
reply to this question.
Action on the report is primarily a
matter for the Regional Education Committees in the county; and these bodies
have already obtained treatment for a
number of children whose parents were
too poor to pay, and where the necessary
treatment could not be given by the
Dispensary Doctors or in the Union
Infirmaries.
Adequate arrangements have not yet
been made for ophthalmic or dental treatment, and I am in correspondence with.
the Regional Committees on these
matters.
Mr. KYLE: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that in that Report it is stated
that some of these complaints are due to
malnutrition, and is his Department
raising the matter with the county
councils to see to the feeding of school
children?
Mr. KYLE: Will the right hon.
Gentleman give the House an assurance
that he on behalf of his Department will
send to the responsible Committees a
request that they should put into operation the matter of the feeding of necessitous school children?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course,
the primary duty falls upon the Regional
Committee, and I have not the slightest
doubt that they will pay due attention to
all recommendations contained in that
Report.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. I am not
prepared to dictate to the local councils.
Mr. KYLE: I am not asking you to
dictate to them. 1 am asking you to
send a letter requesting them to do it in
the interests of the children.

out-

door relief, and it would be impossible

operation Section 13. Owing to the

These are the major changes which hon.
Members will observe from a perusal of
the No. 1 Estimate for my Department,
and it is fitting that I should make some
observations, in passing, on the trend of
policy which they indicate. Seven years
ago, when we were first called upon to
undertake the Government of this Province, we had not the staff, nor, if I may
say so, the experience necessary to enable
us to administer several Services which
required almost specialized staffs operating not at headquarters, but over the
whole of the country. It was, therefore,
convenient, indeed, I should
say it
was necessary in the best interests of the
Province, that we should request the Imperial Authorities to continue their administration, and they, for their part,
very readily agreed to facilitate us, as
they have done from first to last.
I do not think that I have on any
previous occasion publicly acknowledged
our indebtedness to the Imperial Authorities for the services they have rendered in
respect of these details of administration.
To this extent, at least, I am afraid that
I have been guilty of a sin of omission, as
it is no reflection on the officers of my Department to say how greatly we would
have been handicapped had we been obliged
suddenly and without due notice to take
over as a going concern services such as,
for instance, the Old Age Pensions
service. Not only have the Imperial
Authorities carried out these various
duties on our behalf, but their work has
throughout been characterized by that
efficiency which we all expect from British
administration.
During the last few years legislation
passed by our Parliament has made it
more and more necessary for the work
involved by a number of other Government activities to be performed locally,
that is to say throughout the country,
and this, in turn, made it increasingly
evident that the time was rapidly approaching when we should ourselves
undertake the responsibility of administering at any rate some of the services
which were being carried on by Imperial
Departments under agency agreements.
We purpose, however, to continue to take

The division falls naturally into two

special work. The architects' division, in
particular, is, of course, responsible for

our area, in addition to the work which it
is called upon to do in regard to new
works, alterations, and purchases.

Other very heavy work has fallen on the

The second item I mentioned was Ulster
Savings Certificates. The cost of the
administration of this service is exceedingly low, and no special staff is employed
on propaganda work such as exists in
Great Britain. There they have a very
important staff engaged on this work,
where, of course, the amount of money is
so mountainous--if I may use that adjective-in comparison with ours that
they can afford, I suppose, to provide for
a very important and numerous staff to
bring before the people of the country
the advantages from the point of view of
thrift of this very important work. The
entire cost of administration in our case,
including salaries, advertising, cost of
sales by the Post Office, the commission
which we pay to bankers when certificates
are purchased through banks, the printing of forms, etc., is below 12s 6d per
£100 collected or repaid. I repeat that
I think that, in view of the value of this
great service and the work that is carried
on in connection with it, the cost of administration is on an exceptionally and a
very creditably low basis.

in this Committee would realize, or could

old traditional custom in the Imperial

said before, I never heard of such criticisms-I may say unfair, nagging, and
discourteous criticisms-as have been
made with regard to the salaries of my
right hon. Friends, being made at any
time in the Imperial House.

agreed to by both sides of the House.

old custom was not properly observed in
this new House, steps would have to be

now I have hesitated to take a step of

of that kind, I am relying upon hon.

The Charity Commissioners whom he

Henry, whom, unfortunately, we have

representing four religious denominations.
Hon. Members will realise that the great

persons' assets, and many of these are devoted to church or denominational objects.

of Ireland, and two from the Methodist

matters relating to charity. I think that
should satisfy the hon. Member in regard

WEARING OF FREE STATE
COLOURS.
4. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is regarded as
an offence against the law to wear the tricolour, the emblem of An Saorstat, in
Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, it is not
an offence against the law in Northern
Ireland to wear or display the colours of
the Irish Free State.
Mr. HEALY: Arising out of that
answer, does the right hon. Gentleman
know that practically all countries recognized the tri-colour on the recent flight
of that brave and adventurous Irishman,
Major Fitzmaurice, and that this is the
only assembly I know of that did not even
send a word of congratulation to him?
At the same time, in the case where
an organization definitely identified with
the Republican movement, or any
illegal organization, adopts and openly
displays in the furtherance of, and in
connection with, its activities any emblem
or combination of colours, and where
such display is likely to be prejudicial to
the maintenance of the peace and preservation of order, it is the duty of the
Government to prevent such
to prevent such display,
even where the colours of the emblems so
adopted and displayed happen to coincide with those of a neighbouring State.
Mr. SPEAKER: That does not arise
on this question. That is a question
about the Atlantic flight.

right hon. Gentleman has given orders
that, on mere suspicion, a man can be

of an organization of which he may not.
be a member?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No. The
position is, that if any individual does

of the peace, the Government should,

ample proof.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The number of
prosecutions in Northern Ireland in
connection with the manufacture or sale
of illicit spirits during the year ending
31st March, 1926, was 39. The average
fine imposed was £22 5s Od. The number of cases in which imprisonment was
imposed was 7.
During the year ending 31st March,
1927, there were 47 similar prosecutions,
the average fine imposed being £18
14s Od. In 19 cases imprisonment was
imposed.
For the year ending 31st March, 1928,
the number of prosecutions was 18, the
average fine £16 18s Od, and the number
of cases in which imprisonment was imposed was 3.
During the three years previous to the
31st March, 1928, no conviction was obtained against any retail licence holder
for the manufacture or sale of illici
spirits.
As regards the latter portion of the
question, I may say that in this, as in
other matters, the closest co-operation
exists between the R.U.C. and the Civic
Guard, and it is understood that the
Customs Authorities on both sides of the
Border also act in close co-operation.

LAND PRODUCE.
7. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of

The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Mr. Archdale): The Empire
Marketing Board has made a grant of
£900 per annum for a period of three
years to enable my Ministry to appoint
a Marketing Investigator, with suitable
assistance, to inquire into the conditions of
the marketing of agricultural produce.
The inquiry will in particular be addressed to the complicated methods by
which the produce of the typical small
farmer of Northern Ireland is at present
marketed, and also to the quality, packing, and grading of the agricultural commodities exported through Belfast and
Londonderry, and the conditions of transport of live stock and other produce
shipped to Great Britain. It is not proposed to set up a Committee in connection
with the inquiry and no appointments
have so far been made. The investigations conducted will be additional to
the normal activities of my Department,
and will not be directly related to the
work of the recent Committee on the
Transit, Prices and Marketing of Agricultural Produce, although the report of
that Committee will, doubtless, prove of
value in deciding upon the scheme of inquiry to be pursued.
Action has already been taken with a
view to implement certain of the recommendations of the Departmental Com-

purpose is to provide local authorities
with power for the payment of the expenses of education authorities and education committees in subscribing to the

therewith. After the constitution of the

Mr. BARBOUR: The Bill to which I
now ask the House to give a Second
reading is designed to extend and amend
the provisions of the Fisheries (Ireland)
Acts in their application to Northern
Ireland, and, by more effective regulation, to improve the stocks of fish in
Northern Irish waters, with consequent
benefit both to the wealth of the Province
generally, and to those following the calling of fishermen,
Northern Ireland is fortunate in possessing valuable inland and sea fisheries.
The salmon fisheries of the Rivers Foyle
and Bann have long been famous both as
regards the quality and the quantity of
their fish. The Lough Neagh eel fishery
is generally regarded as the most important of its kind in Europe, while the
stocks of trout and other popular inland
fish either furnish a means of livlihood to
a considerable number of fishermen or attract anglers from many parts of Great
Britain. Our sea fisheries are also valuable, considerable quantities of salmon
being caught annually off our shores, in
addition to the great catches of herring
taken each summer off the County Down
coast.
It is obvious that the conservation of
all these valuable assets constitutes a duty

which no responsible Government would
be justified in neglecting. Certainly, the
history of the Irish fisheries during the
past 80 years bears ample proof that each
successive British Government has turned
its attention in the most earnest fashion
to preserving and developing this national
asset. Only by such action has it been
possible to maintain the stocks of fish in
our rivers and around our coasts, since the
indiscriminate exploitation of any fishery,
however valuable, inevitably leads to
serious depletion and, if indefinitely continued, to practical extinction.
There are in existence some 52 Irish
Fishery Acts, starting with that of the
year 1842. The last-mentioned Act,
which still forms the main foundation of
our fishery laws, represents a great effort
on the part of the Government of the
day to regulate salmon fishing in Ireland
in such a way as would permit of the
stocks increasing and, at the same time,
allow of the discriminate exploitation of
our salmon fisheries. With growing experience, successive Governments found it
necessary to amend the 1842 Act, always
with a view of conserving and developing
the stock for the benefit of the users and
of those who should follow. As, by the
nature of the case was inevitable, some
of the restrictions imposed by these subsequent amending Acts proved unpopular
amongst fishermen at the time, and agitation for their repeal, or modification in
certain respects, has been a feature in
the history of Irish fishery legislation
even down to the present time.
To any person who applies himself to
the study of the subject, however, the
necessity for maintaining the restrictions
imposed by these various statutes is a
matter in which no reasonable doubt can
be entertained. Some of the restrictions
to which I refer were introduced after the
Fisheries Bill-
Second Reading
1 MAY 1928
most exhaustive inquiries, and were imposed as the only practical remedy of a
state of affairs which, if left unchecked,
would ultimately have resulted in the most
serious depletion of our fishery stocks.
For example, the Act of 1863 restricted
the use of bag nets at the mouths or
estuaries of Irish rivers, and in some cases
substituted permission to use only nets of
other types.
I have been approached by representatives of our sea fishermen to promote
legislation designed to undo the effects of
the 1863 Measure, but, in the interests of
all concerned, I have felt myself unable
to entertain such a proposal. Nothing
can be more mistaken in my view than to
suppose that it will benefit anyone interested in fishing to permit full unfettered
enjoyment of the fisheries without regard
to the conservation of the stocks. The
withdrawal of the 1863 Act restrictions
would inevitably lead to the return of the
serious conditions which the 1863 Act was
specifically designed to remedy, and in a
few years time the Government would be
faced with exactly the same problem as
that with which the Government
faced in 1863.

A problem of similar character has, in
fact, arisen in the case
of our Lough
Neagh eel fishery. Here we have a
fishery offering very great possibilities in
the way of development, but one which
shows a marked decline in the quantities
of mature fish caught each year. The
statutory inquiry held last winter showed,
I think beyond all reasonable doubt, that
this unsatisfactory state of affairs
mainly, if not entirely, due to the
inability of guarding against the capture
of small immature eels by the methods
of fishing at present in use. The cumulative effects of this for a number of years
inevitably showed themselves in a very
striking decrease in the quantities of the
mature eels taken at the weirs at Toome
and Kilrea. Where, as in our own case,
the physical configuration permits the
eels to be captured at a weir, any other
method, however employed, must always
be relatively uneconomic.
opinion migrates to the same waters from
when it originally came. It is apparent,
therefore, that the most economical
method of capture is by means of nets at
the weirs where only the mature-migrating eels will be caught. The great
increase in the use of long lines by the
Lough Neagh fishermen since eels became
Ach a marketable commodity in England,
about the year 1914, has inevitably prevented great numbers of eels from ever
reaching maturity, as such lines, being
hooked and baited, cannot be made selective in the matter of the weight of eel
which they take.
Eels enter our rivers as elvers, making
their way, it is believed, from the other
side of the Atlantic. Working their way
up the river they spend from 6 to 8 years
on their feeding grounds which, in the
case of the Bann, are provided by Lough
Neagh. On reaching maturity the eel
ceases feeding, and, according to scientific
The inquiry to which I have referred
showed that whereas the average weight
of a mature eel was in the region of 20
ozs. the average weight of a catch of eels
by long line was approximately between
4 and 5 ozs. It can require very little
foresight to foretell the effects of the continuance of the unrestricted use of long
lines throughout the whole of the year,
or as much of it as weather conditions
permit, in the manner practised by the
fishermen.
The Bill has been prepared after consultation between my Ministry and
representatives of fishery interests, and
most of the provisions contained in it
have received the approval, either in
principle or in detail, of those interests.
Whilst the intentions underlying the
various sections of the Bill are, I think,
sufficiently evident from the text of the
Bill itself, I propose, for the convenience
of the House, to take the different parts
of the Bill seriatim and to deal briefly
with the several provisions of each.
to
Part I of the Bill concerns the election
and membership of Beards of Comservators. As hon. Members are doubtless aware, the executive administration
of fishery matters in Northern Ireland is
a large extent entrusted to four
Boards of Conservators consisting of
members elected by the licence-holders in
each of the four districts, together with
a certain number of persons qualified to
act ex-officio. As the law at present
stands, each of these Boards holds office
for a period of three years, at the end of
which a new Board is constituted by way
of election in the manner provided by the
Acts. The restriction of the life of the
Board to a period of three years militates
against continuity of policy, and against
the fulfilment of any extended programme
of development which a Board might be
disposed to undertake.
Fisheries Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
In order to remove this difficulty the
present Bill extends the life of the
several Boards to a period of five years,
the commencing date for the first quinquennial period being fixed as 7th
December, 1930, in order to allow of the
elections under the new arrangement
being held simultaneously in each of the
four districts. The remainder of Part I
of the Bill is designed to remove a minor
difficulty which has arisen out of what
was apparently an oversight in one of the
earlier Acts, viz., the omission of any
provision for the resignation of a member
of a Board who either finds himself incapacited from acting, or is unwilling for
some reason to continue to act, as a Conservator. The Bill, accordingly, provides
for the resignation of a member in such
circumstances, and for the filling of the
vacancy so occasioned by the co-option
of a substitute by the remaining members
of the Board.
Part II of the Bill places certain restrictions on the sale, purchase, capture
and transit of salmon, trout and eels.
The provisions in the existing Acts relating to the illegal capture of salmon and
trout are numerous and stringent, but
their enforcement has been found by experience to be exceedingly difficult where,
as is frequently the case, the fish have
been removed from the place of capture
and cannot be definitely traced to a particular offender. The same difficulty, especially in regard to fish captured during
the close season, has been experienced in
Great Britain, and certain general restrictions upon the possession of salmon and
trout at certain seasons of the year were,
accordingly, enacted by the Imperial
Parliament in 1921. Legislation to the
same end, but on a much more extended
scale, was passed by the Irish Free State
legislature in 1925, the conditions of fisheries in which country are, as hon.
Members will readily understand, almost
identical with those obtaining in Northern
Ireland. Sections 4-9 of the present Bill
follow very closely the provisions embodied in the Irish Free State Measure
to which I have referred.
the present conditions of eel fishing in
Northern Ireland. The evidence obtained at that inquiry, the Report of
which was made public some
time ago,
showed clearly that, if the valuable eel
fisheries of Northern Ireland were to be
preserved and developed in a proper
manner, more effective control of the
capture and possession of eels was essential. Section 10 of the Bill is, accordingly, designed to provide such control.
In passing, it may be well to mention
here that the limitation of the weight of

Northern Irish waters to 8 ounces follows,
in principle, the limitation already existing in the Pollen Fisheries Act of 1891
on the size of pollen that may be captured
in Lough Neagh.
On one point, however, the present.
Measure is more extensive in its application, that is to say, in the case of eels.

In Part III of the Bill it will be observed that certain alterations have been
made in the rate of licence duty chargeable on different fishing engines. The
proposed increase from £1 to £2 in the
rate on single salmon rods has received
the approval of the Ministry's Fisheries
Advisory Committee, a body which may
fairly be regarded as representing all the
principal fishery interests in our area.
The increase is designed principally to
produce much-needed additional revenue
to the Boards of Conservators and, at a
later date, may also facilitate the making
of some reciprocal arrangements with the
Fishery Authorities in the Irish Free
State whereby licensees in one country
might be allowed certain concessions from
the licence issuing authorities in the other
country during the course of a visit.
Special provision to meet the case of
visiting anglers who desire to fish for only
a short period has been made in Sub-
Section (3) of Section 2, by permitting
Boards of Conservators to issue 14 day
licences at the old rate of £1. No such
provision formerly existed and visiting
anglers were, accordingly, obliged to pay
a full year's licence duty irrespective of
the length of their stay.
The increase of duty on salmon drift
nets from £3 to £6 is based on the recognition of two factors: (1) the great increase in the length of salmon drift nets
habitually used now as compared with
their length when the duty was first imposed, and (2) the catching power of drift
nets as now used being so great as to
render the contribution made by their
users towards the cost of the preservation
of salmon stocks disproportionately small

in comparison with the contributions made
by users of other engines. No change has
been made in the rate of licence duty on
draft nets in general, but in this class are
now included draft nets for the capture of
pollen which formerly were subject to the
same rate of duty as trammel nets,
namely, £1 10s. Od.
The inquiry into eel fishing called attention to the fact that a net for the
capture of eels was subject to a duty of £3
whilst exactly the same net, if stated to be
intended for the capture of pollen, was
subject to a duty of only £1 10s. Od. It
was obviously impossible to prevent abuses
in such circumstances, and the rate of £3
has, accordingly, been fixed in the Bill to
cover the use of draft nets in the capture
of pollen as well as of trout and eels. Advantage has been taken of this amendment to reduce the statutory maximum
duty on trammel nets to £1, this being the
duty charged in the Coleraine Conservancy
district, in which the majority of trammel net users reside. The fixation in Subsection (2) of Section 2 of the licence duty
for long lines for eels merely establishes
in the Coleraine and other conservancy
districts a duty already operative in the
Enniskillen district.
Section 12 is designed to remove an administrative anomaly. In the Fisheries
Act of 1848 provision was made for the
fixation by Boards of Conservators of a
licence duty on any fishing engine or device.
of a kind in respect of which a rate of

the wording of this Act. however, it was
apparently necessary, before the duty.
could be fixed, for the person proposing to

have arisen where the necessary applications were not forthcoming and where,
accordingly, the Board has been precluded from fixing a duty. The present.
Bill transfers the power of fixing duties
in such cases to the Ministry of Commerce,
and specifically eliminates the necessity
for any prior application on the part of
the prospective user.

I should like at this stage to emphasize
that, although certain of the provisions
included in the Bill may seem to some
extent onerous or restrictive upon those
engaged in the capture and marketing of
fish, the experience of those concerned elsewhere has shown that they are essentially
practical, and that members of the fishing
industry who loyally co-operate in the
carrying out of the fishery laws, including
the new provisions, derive much more
benefit from any restrictions which may
be imposed than compensates for the extra
trouble to which they may be put. To
offenders against the fishery laws, however, the new provisions are intended to be
prohibitive. Upon such class of persons
hon. Members, I am sure, will not feel
disposed to waste any sympathy.

CLAUSE 1 (Subscriptions to, and
