associations and bodies, 13 and 14 Geo.
V, c. 21).
An education authority or committee
constituted, appointed or established by
or in pursuance of section two or section
twenty-three of the Education Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923, may, subject to the approval of the Ministry
of Education, join or become a member
of any education association or body,
and may, if authorized by the Ministry of Education, and subject to
such regulations as may be made by
that Ministry for the purposes of this
Act, pay, as part of their expenses under
the first mentioned Act, such sums as
may be so authorized—
(a) by way of annual or other subscription to any such association or
body; and
(b) towards the reasonable expenses
of members or officers of the authority
or committee in attending meetings of
any such association or body:
Provided that—
(i) such authority or committee shall
not incur expenditure—
(A) in respect of more than three persons in connection with any one
meeting of an education association
or body, except with the previous
approval of the Ministry of Education; or
(B) in respect of any meeting of an education association or body held elsewhere than in the United Kingdom
or the Irish Free State;
(ii) such authority or committee shall
not pay any expenditure under this
Act, unless it has been specially authorized or ratified by resolution of the
authority or committee after special
notice has been given to members of
the authority or committee of the proposal to authorize or ratify the expenditure;
(iii) expenditure payable by such
authority or committee in respect of
the travelling and subsistence of members and officers shall be in accordance
with the scale ordinarily adopted by
the authority or committee and approved by the Ministry of Education.

The interesting feature of this return is the continued decrease in the
use of alcoholic liquors, and I
propose
to dwell on that for a moment. If last
year's decrease stood alone I should
be inclined to connect it with the exceptional industrial disturbances, but
reference to past years discloses
a consistent and regular reduction in the use both of spirits
and beer. The trade attributes
this reduction to the heavy duties and
consequent high prices of stimulants,
but whether it arises from this cause or
from a natural change in the drinking
habits of our people must remain a
matter of speculation. The striking
fact, however, remains that the people
of Ulster have consumed less alcohol
during this year, as represented by the
very considerable sum of £270,000 of
duty.
If we translate this reduction in
duty into the cost over the counter, we
find that the total reduction in the expenditure of the people on alcoholic.
drinks must have been at least £600,000
last year, and probably more.
In 1914 the consumption in Ulster was
three quarters of a gallon per head of
the population. Last year's return is
one-quarter of a gallon per head of
the population, that is to say, the
people of this Province are consuming
only one-third of the quantities used
in 1914.-(Official Report, vol. 8, col.
1316, 11th, May 1927).

Legitimacy Bill [S.].
Order for Second Reading read.
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr.
Babington): This Bill follows the
Act which came into force in England on 1st January, 1927, under the
title of the Legitimacy Act. As many
Members of this House are no doubt
aware, legitimacy by subsequent marriage
was a thing unknown to English law,
which always refused to accept the principle of legitimation by subsequent marriage, though that principle had been the
law of many civilized and Christian
countries from a very remote period and
had always been the law of Scotland,
where a child born out of wedlock is
legitimated as from the time of the
marriage of its parents. "Other times
other manners" is a rule which I think
applies to this reform, and in this presumably more enlightened age people are
beginning to realize that though the sins
of the fathers are often visited on the
children to the third and fourth generation there are good and valid reasons why
our law should be reformed so that the
innocent should not suffer for the sins of
the guilty to a greater extent than is
absolutely necessary for the welfare of the
State and the preservation of morals and
virtue. This Bill is a step in that direction. It will to some extent remove the
social stigma attaching to those born out
of wedlock, and it will also remove to
some extent the very practical disabilities
attaching to bastardy in cases to which
the Bill applies.
I think hon. Members will agree that
the word "bastard" is one of the most
Legitimacy Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Babington]
cruel words in our language. This is due
to the way in which illegitimates have
been treated socially and legally during
the course of our legal history. It is
commonly used as an expression of contempt which is partly due, as I say, to
the strength of our social conventions and
partly to the legal disabilities which unfortunately follow to the issue. This Bill
on the contrary treats bastardy with compassion, and I think the House need have
little fear that unhallowed births which
are really deplorable will either increase
or decrease as a result of this Measure.
-:
If hon. Members will take up the Bill
they will see that in Clause I children
who are born illegitimate become legitimated by the subsequent marriage of
their parents.
But Sub-clause 2 provides
that:
Nothing in this Act shall operate to
legitimate a person whose father or
mother was married to a third person
when the illegitimate person was born.
That is to say, children born of an adultrous union are not within the scope of
the Bill.
Clause 2 provides that persons claiming
that they became legitimate by the subsequent marriage of their parents may
take proceedings under the Legitimacy
Declaration (Ireland) Act, 1868, in the
courts to have that fact established. It
is not necessary that these proceedings
should be taken, because legitimation
under the Bill will follow as a matter of
fact, and as a matter of course upon the
marriage of the parents without any declaration, but, of course, there must
always be cases where there will be a
dispute, especially where property and its
devolution depends upon the legitimating of the person claiming, and
consequently the Bill provides that in
those cases they may go to the court for

and sisters born after the Bill it will
apply to all the family equally, and they
will take their ordinary seniority in the
family. The third Sub-clause of Clause
3 is a saving Clause excluding a

settled with a dignity or title of honour
where the title or honour devolves on

legitimated by the Bill, but he ranks for
Clause 4 deals with succession to a
legitimated person, and that succession
will follow as in the case of a legitimate
person. At present, as the House is probably aware, in the case of an illegitimate
child dying intestate the property passes
as bona vacantia to the Crown.
If an
illegitimate child becomes legitimate as a
result of this Bill his property will
descend to his children or pass to his
parents in the ordinary way just as if he
had been a legitimate person.
Clause 5 is also a saving Clause and
deals with the case of children dying after
the commencement of the Act, and before
the marriage of their parents.
Clause 6 deals with the general rights
and liabilities of a legitimated person.
The rights and liabilites are to be the
same rights and obligations as if he had
been born legitimate. That is only
carrying out the general principle of the
Bill to endeavour as far as possible to
put persons legitimated under the Bill on
the same focting as persons legitimate by
law at present.
Clause 7 deals with death duties. This
is also further carrying cut the principle
of the Bill.
Clause 8 deals with certain cases of
children who become legitimate by the
law of foreign countries. At the present
time if a child is legitimated by the law
of a foreign country that will not be recognized here. There are numerous
cases where children have been legitimated in Scotland who inherit property
either in Ireland or England. The legiti

macy which flows from the Scottish
marriage is not recognized by our Courts.
Now that the law of our country is being
put on the same footing as other countries

of marriage in a foreign country will be
recognized here.
Clause 9 deals with the rights of the
illegitimate child and mother to succeed
upon the intestacy of each other. That
is following out the Clause I have already
referred to which places them on the same
footing with reference to the property
of each other. Formerly when an illegitimate child died his property, as I said,
vested in the Crown. His mother or
any person dependent on him could only
acquire portion of that property by the
grace of the Crown and had no rights.
Now that has been abolished. If an
illegitimate child dies the property will
go to the mother. If the mother of an
illegitimate child dies her property will
go to the child.
That concludes the provisions of the
Bill with the exception of one or two
small saving Clauses which are really
immaterial. The Schedule to the Bill
provides that in cases where children are
legitimated under the Bill the Registrar-
General of Births and Deaths may, upon
proper evidence being produced to him,
change the original certification of birth
in order to show that the child is legitimate, so that where a child has been
legitimated by subsequent marriage he
will be able to produce a birth certificate
certified by the Registrar-General showing
that his parents were certain persons, and
that he is legitimate according to the law
of the land as it will then apply. I think
this is a Bill which very few Members
of this House will take any exception to.
I beg to move.

Dr. MORRISON: This Bill is introduced to get rid of an injustice to an
innocent helpless child. It removes
blot from the Illegitimacy Bill which we
passed in this House when there was nobody here but ourselves. In passing that
Bill we went a step further than they did
in England. We took a wise step forward. If what we wanted done had been

blot in our Illegitimacy Bill would have
been absent to-day. I think it is worse
from the view point I have than this
question of the legalisation of the marriage
of these people.
What happened was this. After full
discussion we decided in this House that
if an unmarried woman died in pregnancy the nearest relative of the child
would have the same right in seeking for
a maintenance order as if the woman were
alive. That is very clear and very distinct. After full discussion we passed
that Clause. The Bill went to the Senate
and it came back here to us with that
Clause deleted. It was just at the end of
the Session. I was pleased, as also were
other hon. Members, at getting the Illegitimacy Bill passed, and we were not
inclined to stand on little things. I protested against what had been done, but
we accepted the Measure. Sometime
after, when the Widows' and Orphans'

raised the point again by means of an

woman died during her confinement the
nearest relative of the child, the grandmother or grandfather, would have the
right to sue the putative father for a

however, at that time that the Amendment could not be introduced into that
Bill.
My colleague in the University (Mr.

He looked up the figures, and he found

unmarried mothers died every year in

When the Home Rule Act, or the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, was in

public buildings in which to carry on the
administration and the government of the

administrative purposes, and to equip

think, perfectly clear.

Mr. HEALY: I have given notice of
a matter I intend to raise on the Adjournment. I raise this matter entirely in the
public interest. On Easter Sunday morning eight men were arrested on the Falls
Road. The Minister of Home Affairs,
questioned on the matter in the House
yesterday, gave no specific reason why these
men were arrested, but indicated in a
general way in his reply that any individual who did any act likely to lead to a
breach of the peace would come within
the ban of the Home Office. These men,
I understand, were walking peacefully
along a public street. They were not in
possession of any arms, and they were not
doing anything likely to lead to a breach
of the peace. Who, then, is to determine
when a citizen or citizens may safely and
peacefully proceed along the public street,
doing no harm to anyone.
As I understand it, the kernel of the trouble seems
to be that these men were wearing rosettes
or badges of a particular colour. We know
that there is peace in the Six Counties
to-day, peace in Ireland, and indeed peace
in the whole United Kingdom. There is,
therefore, the less reason for this arbitrary
exercise of power on the part of the Home
Office
that the areas in the Six Counties that

areas from which this House decided to
arrest the largest number of people. Places

guns and canister bombs, but they
fought from street to street until the
streets were red with the blood of
British soldiers. It was with that same
spirit that the sovereign independence.
of Ireland would be attained. The

LIGHTING AND HEATING OF
SCHOOLS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
whether it is a fact that teachers of public
elementary schools, both principals and
assistants, are not financially responsible
for the cost of lighting, heating, sweeping,
cleaning, the upkeep and general sanitation of the schools, as well as the provision of furniture and equipment; and,
if not, why the Ministry of Education require details of expenditure on all or any
of the above services from the principal
teachers of such schools instead of exclusively from those who are financially
responsible according to the Ministry's
Regulations
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The answer
to the first question is in the affirmative.
As a matter of convenience the principal
teacher is required to collect and forward
the information, part of which is available
in records kept in the school account books.
AWARDING MERIT MARKS TO
TEACHERS.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education if he will state what precautions are
taken by the Ministry to ensure uniformity in the style and difficulty of
questions set in different schools, for the
purpose of awarding merit marks to
teachers.
Mr. ROBB: In order to secure uniformity in assigning efficiency ratings to
teachers in Public Elementary Schools,
the Ministry requires the concurrence of
a Senior Inspector in the first rating,
and in any alteration of rating proposed
by a Section Inspector. It also provides
for conferences and joint inspections and,
where necessary, for visits by the Chief
Inspector and Senior Chief Inspector.
As the questions set by Inspectors are
varied suit the detailed syllabus
followed by the teacher and the capacity
of the pupils, it is not desirable that the
style of questions should be uniform.

4. Mr. KYLE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether his Ministry will issue clear
definitions of the Statutory Rules and
Orders regulating salaries of elementary
teachers; whether it is a fact that the
reports furnished by inspectors are occasionally contradictory regarding the
award of merit marks to each teacher

Mr. ROBB: The regulations determining the salaries of teachers of Public
Elementary Schools are contained in
Statutory Rules and Orders of Northern
Ireland, 1925, No. 114, and are clearly
defined, although necessarily somewhat
complicated.
GRANTING OF DEPENDANTS'
BENEFIT.
The Ministry is not aware that any
contradictory reports have been furnished,
but on rare occasions differences are
observed. If these differences affect the
teacher's rating, steps are taken to determine which estimate is correct.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he is aware that, despite the passing of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, and his public declaration
that the means test has been abolished, a
number of workpeople are being denied
dependants' benefit; whether he can
issue a statement to the effect that
workers having thirty stamps to their
credit during the two years preceding the
date of their claim, or having eight
stamps during the last two years,
thirty stamps at any time, and are
genuinely seeking work will be granted
unemployment insurance.
or
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The condition known as the
"family income test" has been abolished.
To become entitled to dependants' benefit, a claimant must satisfy the conditions
laid down in the Act of 1928, which have
no relation to the means of the family,
except in so far as the question arises as
to whether a dependant is, in fact, being
maintained by the applicant.
As regards the second part of the
question, an applicant who has thirty
contributions in the two years preceding
the date of his claim, and who is seeking
work will receive benefit if he complies
with the other Statutory conditions and
is free from disqualification. The “30
contributions" condition is, during the
transitional period, waived in the case of
a claimant over 18 years of age who, in
addition to having either 8 contributions
in the preceding two years, or 30 contributions at any time, proves that he is
normally in insurable employment, and
that he has had a reasonable period of
insurable employment during the two
years preceding the date of his claim.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
Oral Answers
Estimates
3 MAY 1928
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): I have been
asked to reply to this question by my
right hon. Friend, who has been detained, but will be in the House later.
The Government has already provided
a supply of drinking water at Ardglass
Harbour, and I would draw the attention of the Hon. Member to the fact that
in the Estimates of my Ministry for the
year 1928-29, is included a sum of £600
for the provision of a water supply for
boiler purposes at the harbour.
I have delayed taking action towards
the provision of a supply of boiler water
in view of the fact that for some time
past my Ministry has been in communication with the Rural District Council
and representative residents of Ardglass,
who have been endeavouring to arrange
a comprehensive water scheme for their
town. The position at the moment is,
that the Rural District Council has carried through certain boring operations,
while the taxpayers of Ardglass are considering the extent to which they may be
able to contribute towards the cost of a
scheme undertaken by the local authority.
The hon. Member will readily appreciate
that it would be preferable for the Government to contribute towards the cost of
a comprehensive scheme of water supply
rather than to proceed immediately with
the provision of an independent supply
designed solely to meet the requirements
of fishing vessels using the harbour.
Mr. KYLE: Could the hon. Gentleman state, in the absence of the
Minister of Commerce, what grant,
if any, the Government is prepared
to make to the Rural District
Council of Ardglass, to enable them to
carry out that comprehensive scheme.
Mr. GORDON: I can give no definite
answer, only that my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Andrews) who sits on the Front
bench here has intimated that if this
scheme is put forward, so far as he is concerned, he will consider it as a relief
scheme.

Estimates-
Ministry of Education
3 MAY 1928
The transfer of schools has proceeded
steadily during the year. there are now
75 transferred schools in Belfast, and 27
in process of transfer, while outside Belfast 167 schools have been transferred,
and 154 are in process of transfer.
423-over 21 per cent-of our 1,948
public elementary schools have either
been transferred or are in course of
transfer.
Thus
If the Committee will compare these
figures of transferred schools with those
published a year ago, it will see that very
considerable progress has been made. At
that time the number of schools in which
the transfers were completed was about
90, against 242 to-day, and the number of
four-and-two committee schools has increased from 80 to 100. There are,
moreover, some 181 schools at the moment
in process of transfer, and I submit to
the Committee that it is a most encouraging sign to find that negotiations for the
transfer of schools are still proceeding
regularly as a continuous process throughout the Province, and that there is a
steady progression in the working-out of
the policy of the Education Act in respect of this important matter.
I should remind the Committee that
there is great freedom under the Act in
regard to transfer. Its provisions contemplate the existence side by side of
schools under three different forms of
management, that is to say, the provided
and fully transferred school, under the
complete control of the education authority; the voluntary school, under the socalled four-and-two committee, on which
the education authority has representation; and the voluntary school, under the
individual manager. There is no compulsion as to transfer except that compulsion which arises from the natural
desire, where the circumstances make it
expedient, to secure through transfer
better educational conditions for the
children
In estimating the progress of transfers
we are warranted in omitting from the
total number of schools those which are
under Roman Catholic clerical management as not likely to be offered for
transfer, and we then find that of the
1,200 schools remaining, 242, or 20 per
cent. are transferred, and 180, or 15 per
cent. are in process of transfer, whilst
100, or 8.3 per cent. are under four-andtwo committees--that is to say, about 43
per cent. have abandoned the individual
type of management in favour of one in
which the ratepayers have some element
of representation.
We know that, so far, the schools
managed by the Roman Catholic clergy
have not been offered for transfer, and,
whatever their motives may be, there is
no reason why we should quarrel with
them about it. The Act was framed, not
for one portion of the community but for
all, and we are satisfied that it has been,
and will be even in still greater measure
in the future, the means of enormous
improvement in the educational conditions of all classes of children.
As a considerable number of very large
schools have been transferred, particularly
in the City of Belfast, I shall not be far
wrong if I tell the Committee that probably about 50 per cent. of the children
in our Province-omitting for this purpose those taught in schools under Roman
Catholic management--are now being
educated under conditions of popular
local control. Considering that the Act
is in force in the counties only during
three years---and a year longer in the
county boroughs, and that the negotiations for transfer are, as I have pointed
out, proceding in considerable numbers,
I think we may be gratified at the progress
made.
It is pleasing to find that as soon as
schools are transferred the education
authorities at once proceed to effect improvements, and to make better provision
than has hitherto been possible in many
cases for their heating, cleaning, and
maintenance and for the comfort of the
pupils, and I am convinced that the
example of those well-kept schools will
act as an incentive to those people, who
for whatever reason have not so far
taken kindly to transfer, to imitate their
neighbours. I would urge, on the other
hand, all education authorities to deal
sympathetically with
for
proposals
transfer, to meet as far as possible the
desire for guarantees and facilities for
Bible instruction and to play a worthy
part in the great revolution in educational administration which is taking
place amongst us without the fact,
perhaps, being fully realized.

I fear, however, that it is impossible
for me or indeed for anyone else to
institute a reliable comparison between
the education now given in our schools
and that given in the past. The wellknown tendency to paint a picture of the
days of long ago in glowing colours
renders difficult a fair comparison
tween the present and the past even if
the conditions were similar. But they
are not similar. It is not only that the
school subjects which are now regarded
as essential are more numerous than a
generation ago, and that in consequence
to most of them only a reduced amount of
time can be given, but our views of the
proper scope of school education have profoundly altered in the last 20 or 30 years.
Formerly the merely literary side of edu
cation received an undue share of attention, and it was not fully recognized, if
recognized at all, that all the child's
faculties, the training of character, of the
hand and eye, of manners and tastes, as
well as attention to physical and hygienic
needs, formed the proper subject matter
of his school life and activities. A
narrow curriculum confined to religious
instruction and the three R's is nowhere
considered nowadays as sufficient. Physical training must accompany mental and
intellectual development. The observation and the manual powers must be educated through courses of drawing and
handwork, and the æsthetic taste must be
developed by lessons in singing. It cannot be tolerated that pupils should hear
nothing in school of the essential facts of
the structure and life of the world in
which they live, so that some elementary
notions of nature study--particularly important for rural schools-and physical
science have to be included in the work of
the school-day. All this means more sub-
Ministry of Education 1310
Estimates-
3 MAY 1928
jects, and therefore less attention to
meticulous details of arithmetic and English grammer, with perhaps some falling
off observable in precise knowledge of
spelling and mathematical processes.
This widening of the curriculum is, perhaps, the most remarkable phenomenon in
the modern systems of elementary education found in Great Britain and Western
Europe generally, and in the United
States, and he would indeed sin against
the light who would force upon Ulster
children a narrower course of studies and
a stunted conception of the work and outlook of the school.
To make these observations, however,
is not to admit that even in the essential
subjects there has been any loss of efficiency. The inspectors of the Ministry
are convinced that a vast improvement
has been effected in the past few years in
the power of the average pupil to read
intelligently and to convey to others in
written or spoken language the results of
his reading. And in other subjects,
while there may be a diminution in the
number of facts memorized, there has
been a great advance in the intelligent
appreciation of those facts. The Committee is, no doubt, aware that the
Ministry's inspectors make periodic estimates of the value of the work done in
the schools by individual teachers, and I
am happy to be able to say that the
result of these reports is to show that
never at any previous time were the
teachers of the Province more efficient or
more successful in the discharge of their
duties.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): Hear, hear.
In March, 1928, there were 568 fulltime and 206 part-time teachers in the
secondary schools. Of this number 399
possess university degrees, and 218 have
graduated with honours. The number of
full-time teachers with first and secondclass honour degrees has increased by 54
per cent. in the last five years. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. ROBB: I shall now give the Com-
Inittee some information in regard to the
qualifications of the teachers. Of approximately 4,500 principal and assistant
teachers in our public elementary schools
3,900-nearly 87 per cent.---have been
trained in recognized training colleges,
and about 600 are untrained-there are in
addition 627 junior assistant mistresses,
the majority of whom are untrained.
About 26 per cent. of the elementary
school teachers are rated as highly
efficient, and 67 per cent. as efficient.
The reports of the Ministry's inspectors
show a distinct improvement in the work
of the elementary schools in all parts of
the Province.
Under the secondary teachers' salary
regulations the only teachers in a school
in respect of whom the Ministry reimburses the governing body the amount
of the incremental portion of the salaries
are those who have been appointed to the
authorized staff and who have been
placed, in consequence, upon the salary
scale.
It has not been possible for the Government to accept liability for the award of
increments in respect of the entire previous service of teachers, and the existing
regulations provide that when a secondary
teacher is placed or replaced upon the
salary scale his previous secondary service
while not on the authorized staff of a
school shall be devalued by one-half, and
shall then be calculated for the award
of increments in accordance with the regulations.
The Ministry has felt that this regulation in its application to service given
since the operative date of the salary regulations bears unfairly upon secondary
teachers who have not the good fortune
to be placed upon the authorized staffs of
schools, and I am glad to be able to inform the Committee that new regulations
have just been presented to Parliament
under which all full-time secondary
service given in recognized schools in
Northern Ireland, whether on the
authorized staff or not, since 1st August,
1922, shall from the beginning of the
coming school year-1st August nextcount in full for incremental purposes
subject to the other conditions of the regulations, and existing teachers will,
where necessary, be replaced on the scales
as from that date. Preparatory teachers
are to receive a corresponding measure of
recognition for their service.
I have now told the Committee something about our machinery, but the
question put to me last year as to what
we are getting for the money we spend
required, in the answer, an estimate of
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Robb]
the products. I have said something
about our machinery, and now I will
proceed to give an estimate of what we
get out of the machinery. Frankly, I cannot pretend that without an elaborate
investigation, for which there is not the
machinery, an answer which could be
accepted as likely to be fair and accurate
can be given, but I have made some inquiries and considered some available
criteria, and, for what they are worth, I
give my conclusions.
One of the main objects of all education is to produce good citizens, men and
women of character and initiative and
industry who can do a good day's work
in the community-in agriculture, in industry, in commerce, in the professions,
in literature, scholarship, science or art.
;"
So many of the boys and girls leaving
our elementary schools go into our industries that it seemed to me natural to
make inquiries from employers as to the
calibre and equipment of those whom they
have newly employed. Without pretending that my inquiries were exhaustive,
hardly claiming for them that they were
sufficient, the conclusion I have arrived
at is that the pupils leaving our elementary schools now do not fall behind
those of former days in the amount they
know that they are nimbler of intellect,
but--and I found this a universal complaint they will not work so hard as their
fathers did. By nimbler of intellect I
mean that I got a quite definite opinion
that the modern boy or girl learns new
processes more quickly, and this I can only
attribute to the widening of the curriculum and the effort now made to develop
their powers of observation and reasoning.
The complaint that they will not work so
hard I heard from nearly every one I
asked, but when I countered this complaint with the query, "was not this a
universal symptom shown by all employees, those who made the complaint
as universally answered that it was. For
this then I do not think the schools can be
saddled with the blame. The whole
nation does not work so hard-and while
it may be said that the work of schools
should involve 3 correction of this
tendency, I think we cannot expect the
schools wholly to counteract it, though I
hope they do their best to inculcate industry and condemn the frittering away
of cnergy in idleness. We can take
encomfort in this, however, that in the
markets of the world the products of our
factories, shipbuilding yards and
gineering shops where these pupils were,
compare as well as they ever did with the
products of other countries.
So far as the pupils of our secondary
schools go into business, what I have said
about the pupils of our elementary schools
is also true. Of those who go to universities it is pleasant to note that the best
of them hold their own-perhaps in proportion to their numbers more than hold
their own-in competition with the products of English and Scottish schools for
open scholarships. But of the average,
the conclusion I have come to from what
I have been able to gather is that on the
mathematical side and on the scientific
side the product is as good as it used to
be; that in modern languages it is much
better; but on the classical side there is
a falling off. It is not only that fewer
pupils take classics, but that the standard
reached by the average pupil has fallen.
For this I do not blame the teachers; but
the demands made upon the time of
pupils for teaching in a greater variety of
scientific subjects have been met by reducing the time given to Latin and
Greek, and possibly the natural desire for
easy options has had its influence. For
myself, I regret this, though I am not
sure how best a truer at least truer from
my point of view-balance can be found
nor whether efforts in that direction can
gain the necessary support from a frankly
utilitarian public.
I turn now to school attendance.
School attendance is a little better than
last year, the percentage of average attendance to average number of pupils on
rolls being 83.8. This is, however, entirely due to improvements in Belfast and
Londonderry. Everywhere else there is
a slight drop in the attendance.
Irregular attendance, unless for a
justifiable cause, means waste not only of
the opportunities of the pupils, but waste
of the money of the taxpayer and the
ratepayer, and I earnestly hope that
magistrates at petty sessions will keep
this aspect of the question before them
and see that there is no avoidable evasion
of the Act. It is no kindness to be
lenient in this matter; the children are
bound to suffer, and not only the children
who are irregular in attendance at school,
Estimates-
MAY 1928

Ministry of Education
but other children who attend regularly
and work dilengently. Nothing so disorganizes class-work as the presence of
children who, owing to irregularity in
their attendance, are merely a drag upon
their more painstaking and hard-working
fellow pupils.
I now come to the feeding and clothing
of necessitous children, and I am pleased
again to be able to call attention to the
praiseworthy efforts which have been made
by the Belfast Education Committee in
this direction. This Committee in the
financial year just closed provided 325,326
free meals and by its energy in this direction has given a splendid lead, which I
hope will readily be followed by other
committees. The Belfast Committee, in
the estimates of its expenditure for the
current financial year, has set aside £5,500
for the feeding of needy children. County
Down follows with £400, Lisburn and
Armagh have each provided £50. For the
clothing of needy children seven committees
have provided for expenditure amounting
altogether to £500. The Omagh Committee is doing a good deal in the matter of
clothing, and numerous grants have been
made by it for this purpose. Some of the
committees, in necessitous cases, make
grants for free books. I should like to
state that in these directions the Ministry
regards what has been done as a beginning
only, and that outside Belfast it will look
for a considerable expansion in the activities of local authorities in the matter of
assistance ot necessitous children.
The feeling in favour of medical inspection is growing, and soon no part of the
Province will be without it. All the committees have made provision of some kind
in their Estimates for this purpose, and
eleven committees have their schemes in
operation.
In the present year there is an increase
of ten per cent. in the number of pupils
attending secondary schools as compared
with the year 1926-27, while that year
showed an increase of 6 per cent. over
the year 1925-26; this is very encouraging.
A part of this increase is no doubt due to
the scholarships granted by the local
education authorities, but the greater part
of it appears to be due to a growing appreciation on the part of the people of the
benefits to be derived from secondry education.
It is gratifying to note also that the
increase is by no means confined to the
lower branches of the school. There is
during the current school year an increase
of 18 per cent. in the number of pupils
following courses higher than those preparing for the junior certificate. Each
year since the institution of the certificate
examinations there has been an improvement in the percentage of passes in both
the junior and senior examinations. There
has also been a steady increase in the
number of candidates entering for these
examinations, and this year there is a considerable increase in the number of those
about to enter for the senior examination.
Technical instruction has advanced
rapidly in the course of the past year.
There has been a steady increase each year
since the Ministry came into existence, and
in the last school year the number of indidividual students enrolled was well over
23,700. And not only has the number of
students increased, but many new schools
and centres have been opened. Since
1924 fourteen new centres of technical
instruction have been added to those
formerly in existence. The greatest development in this respect has been in
County Down, where, prior to 1914, all
the technical centres were situated on the
fringes of the county.
The technical schools have in many
cases since the recent Act instituted
courses for the training of pharmaceutica!
apprentices where they can obtain instruction in botany, chemistry, physics, and
business methods. I am also pleased to be
able to record a great extension in the
number of candidates for the technical
school examinations. This greatly increased entry for the examinations which
has taken place in a couple of years is a
striking testimony to the zeal of the
principals and their staffs.
As a result of negotiations with the
Institute of Chemistry of Great Britain
and Ireland and with the Institution of
Mechanical Engineers the Ministry's Technical School examinations have been recognized as the basis of the award of National
Certificates in chemistry and in mechanical
engineering, and the Ministry is at present
negotiating with the Institute of Naval
Architects and the Worshipful Company
of Shipwrights with a view to securing
similar recognition of those examinations
as the basis of the award of National
Certificates in naval architecture.
The Committee will, I am sure, approve
of the Ministry's policy of awarding
annually trade scholarships to enable

were
When last year's Estimates
under discussion several hon. Members
appealed for the restoration of the grants
for practical instruction which had formerly been paid by the Ministry to those
committees which in technical schools
under their management gave instruction
to pupils of public elementary schools in
domestic economy and woodwork. The
Ministry was unable last year to accede to
this request, but since then the whole
question has been further considered,
with the result that I am now able to
inform the Committee that it has been
decided, with the concurrence of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Poliock), to lay before Parliament regulations for the payment of
attendance grants for classes of elementary
school pupils in domestic economy and
manual instruction held in technical
schools and centres.
I explained to the Committee last year
that we hoped to develop a new type of
Junior Technical School definitely leading
towards agriculture, but I pointed out at
the same time that for further expansion
we must look for assistance from local
sources. I am now pleased to be able to
tell the Committee that after consultation
with the Ministry of Agriculture a new
type of school suitable for pupils preparing
for an agricultural career has been started
at Lisburn for farmers' sons.
Several hon. Members in the debate on
last year's Estimates referred to the curriculum of elementary schools in rural
areas, and expressed themselves as not
quite satisfied that the programme taught
in country schools was entirely suited to
the needs of the farming community. I
should like to say that it is the view of the
Ministry that, as a rule, vocational training should not be introduced into the
school course before the pupil has attained
the age of fourteen, or at the very least
thirteen, and that his school life before
that age should be devoted entirely to a
well-balanced general education which will
serve him in after life in any profession
or occupation which he may adopt.
The education and instruction in agriculture afforded by the Ministry of Agriculture and the Committees of Agriculture
in the various counties by means of winter
classes, lectures, and courses at Greenmount Agricultural College and at the
Ulster Dairy School provide practical and
professional training for young men and
women of sixteen years and over; they do
not, however, make provision for that preliminary instruction which is desirable for
pupils between the ages of fourteen and
sixteen-for that this Ministry and the
education authorities are responsibleand it is just here that a school such as the
new Junior Technical School at Lisburn
meets a recognized need. Taking pupils.
of about fourteen years of age this school
provides a curriculum which is planned to
give the pupils some understanding of the
principles underlying agriculture, while
at the same time, continuing their general
education. This is a development which
the Ministry welcomes, and the greatest
credit is due to the Lisburn and Belfast
Regional Committee for its pioneer work
in establishing the school. I am glad to
say that three other places are considering
opening similar schools.
The Committee which was appointed by
the Minister in May, 1922, to make
arrangements for the training of teachers.
for various grades of schools in Northern
Ireland has during the past year continued
its labours with the same unremitting zeal
which has characterized all its work. I
take this opportunity of again expressing
the Ministry's indebtedness to my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, who
is Chairman of that Committee, and to the
individual members, for the self-sacrificing way in which they have devoted their
time and their energy to this very important work. The standard of entrants
at the King's Scholarship Examination is
steadily improving, and there is a corresponding improvement in the output. The
improvement may be attributed largely to
Ministry of Education 1318

the growing appreciation of the generous
scale of salaries offered to public elementary school teachers, and to the policy
of the Training Committee and the
Ministry in encouraging the system of
pupil teachers who receive a course of
education in a secondary school prior to
their admission to training colleges.
I am glad to be able to say that the
work of the three recognized training
colleges is proceeding satisfactorily. In
Stranmillis the lecture block is in course
of erection, and will, it is anticipated, be
ready for use next year. The reconditioning of Hampton House for use as a men's
hostel is approaching completion, and it
should be possible to transfer the men
students to the hostel when the college reopens after the summer vacation.
Before I close I should like to mention
that the Ministry's attention has recently
been called to the fact that much misapprehension seems to exist among certain
classes in England and Scotland regarding the political status and industrial and
commercial position of our Province-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and the
Ministry has been considering whether any
steps could usefully be taken to approach
the educational authorities in Great
Britain with a view to having the matter
ventilated through the schools. We have
been in communication with the Board of
Education in England and the Scottish
Education Department, and I am pleased
to say that both these bodies have very
willingly agreed to bring the matter to the
notice of their inspectors. We have also
made representations to publishers of textbooks in general use in the teaching of
geography and history in public elementary and secondary schools across the
Channel, and in every case our views have
been met most cordially and promises made
that in coming editions of those textbooks mistakes and omissions will be
rectified, and the situation of Northern
Ireland set forth in its proper light.
(Hon. Members: Hear. hear).
Mr. DEVLIN: What is meant by that?
Mr. ROBB: In accordance with the
actual facts.
Mr. DEVLIN: What are the actual
facts?
Mr. ROBB: Well now, I would not like
to start to tell the hon. Member that. In
concluding these remarks, which I fear
may have taxed your patience (hon.
Members: No)-I should like to say that
I know no reason why we should be downhearted or despondent as to the success of
our educational policy. Looking back at
the year that has passed I am justified in
saying that there has been a notable advance all along the line, perhaps less in
some directions than we had hoped, but
greater in others than we had dared to
expect. The material conditions in which
our elementary and secondary education.
is carried on, the schoolhouses, their
equipment, and those arrangements that
are necessary for the comfort and wellbeing of the pupils, are everywhere
gradually-in some places rapidly-being
improved. The number of our pupils
completing a full course of elementary
education by taking the leaving certificate
is steadily rising-more
rising more scholarships
are being given, and the attendance
at our secondary schools shows a substantial increase. Many new technical
schools are being built and the
facilities provided by our technical
instruction system are being appreciated
and utilized in still greater measure every
year.
Our teachers are increasing in efficiency, and their qualifications and training give evidence of a perceptible advance.
The health of the pupils is now receiving
attention in almost all parts of the country
through the setting up of medical school
inspection, and the few areas that have
not yet adopted medical inspection schemes
are now coming into line. We have made
provision for the education of afflicted
children so far as is practicable at the
moment, and suitable instruction and care
are now available for the deaf, and the
dumb, and the blind. We have still to
take up the question of the mentally deficient, and this matter will have our early
and earnest attention. If there be any
misgiving here and there as to the success
of the Act I am confident that, while
plenty remains to be done, enough has
already been accomplished through its
instrumentality to vindicate a thousand
times over the policy which inspired it.
I beg to move.

Gentleman (Mr. Robb) made a few
minutes ago about the representations
which had been made to England and
Scotland regarding the history and position of Northern Ireland one would have

It would be very interesting, I am sure,
for the pupils in the public elementary
schools of Great Britain to be taught

I presume that is the idea where
Northern Ireland is. The other day the

Ireland was in Great Britain. However,
the pupils in England and Scotland no
doubt will be made aware of the position

In regard to that matter I would like
the hon. Gentleman to let us
see the
primers that he intends to put into the

The other day at Newtownards the
Minister of Education stated that the
success of any school depended upon the
staff, it is the teacher that makes the
school, and all the inspectors in the world
could not make a bad teacher into a good
one. Has the Ministry deliberately
picked out the worst types of men and
women to make them teachers, and does
it hope to keep them in excellent teaching form by the employment of drivers
under the name of inspectors? If the
teachers have been ill-chosen or illtrained I think the fault lies at the door
of the Ministry of Education or of the
late Commissioners of National Education. Let us compare again Northern
Ireland with the West of Scotland in regard to the employment of inspectors.
We will take a division as set out by the
Scottish Education Department, including Glasgow, Bute, Lanark, Ayr, Dumfries, Dumbarton, Renfrewshire, and
Argyll, with a total population of
2,542,000. Allotted to that area there
are 23 inspectors, whereas in Northern
Ireland, according to the Estimates that
we have before us, there are no fewer
than 33 inspectors for a population of
about a million and a quarter-that is, for
a population of half the size mentioned
in Scotland we employ over 44 per cent.
more inspectors than they do in the
western division of Scotland.
I want to direct some attention to the
cost of the inspectorate department in
Northern Ireland. In this Estimate it is
set down as £20,400, and I think there
is an additional sum of £6,000 for travelling expenses. I find from "The Times"
Educational Supplement that the total
cost of elementary school education in
Great Britain is a sum of £32,000,000,
and that the total cost of the inspectorate
is £320,000 odd, which works out roughly
at £1 for inspection in every £100 that
is spent in elementary education. If we
take the total of £20,000, plus £6,000 for
travelling expenses, we find that the cost
of inspection in Northern Ireland is about
£2 for every £100 spent on elementary
education. In other words, we are
spending in this inspectorate department
about twice as much as a rich country
like England.
Looked at in another way, I may say
that the Ministry of Education employ
four times as many inspectors in our area
as the Scottish Education Board employ
in the western division of Scotland. Are
we getting better results than the Scots ?
The hon. and learned Member paid some
attention to that aspect of the question
in reply to some criticizms that were made
last year in the course of the consideration
of the Estimates. I think most of us
will agree with him that people as a rule
do not work as hard as the people of
twenty years ago. That varies of course.
I think it varies in different classes of
society. But when we say that people do
not work as hard, we do not mean that
the result of their work, the actual production, is less than it was twenty years
ago. It is very much more. In fact,
production has been doubled; in some
cases it has been more than doubled.
The actual output per man with the aid
of nachinery has very much more than
doubled in some instances, and has
doubled as a sort of general average;

Union," a non-Catholic paper, as
follows: .
The "Christian Union" has been
foremost among the journals which
have demanded an improvement in our
present public school system in this
respect. We have insisted that the
Roman Catholic critics are largely right
in saying that our present public school
system is irreligious, and that an

education is worthless, it is less than
worthless, if it does not involve the

imagination, intellect; that to develop
the latter and leave the former dwarfed
and stunted is a process not deserving
the name of education. The moral and
spiritual nature must be developed with
the intellectual.
I will now bring you to what is done
in Canada. Canada is a great model for
the Government in the Six Counties when
it comes to a question of educating our
boys and sending them out as emigrants
to that country. In Canada the school
system is denominational in the four chief
provinces of Ontario, Quebec, Alberta,
and Saskatchewan, and each denomination
that can maintain a separate school for
its children has a separate school. In
these four provinces out of a total of
27,520 schools 21,350 are separate schools
for the different religious denominations.
The Supreme Council of Education in
Quebec and Ontario consists of an equal
number of Catholics and non-Catholics,
each part controlling the schools of its
own colour. In all schools there is an
official called a commissary, which
generally corresponds to our manager.
This system has worked well in Canada,
which is a progressive country containing
nine milions of people.
I will take you now to Europe and I
will refer to the prosperous little Protestant country of Holland. Holland
with a population of seven milions,
mainly Protestant, in 1920 passed a law
putting all private, voluntary, and
church schools on a perfect equality with
the public or Government schools, giving
them equal grants from public moneys,
and the right to appoint their own
teachers and select their own text books.
Then Belgium, which we heard a lot of
during the war-gallant little Belguim-.
is about the size of Munster, and it has
always maintained the principles of religious education from the primary
school to the university. Its denomi-

OF CASES HEARD.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state the number
of cases heard before Courts of Referees
in Belfast since April 19th, and the
number of those who were refused benefits; whether it is by his instructions
that the officials of the Courts of Referees
inform the Court of the overdraft of each
applicant; and whether, in view of the
statement that has been made that all
overdrafts are wiped out, this procedure
is regular..
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): From 19th April till 5th May
inclusive, 143 appeals against the decision
of the Insurance Officer disallowing
claims to unemployment benefit were
heard by the Court of Referees at
Belfast. The Court upheld the Insurance Officer's decision in 130 cases, and
recommended the payment of benefit in
13. All these appeals related to statutory
conditions or disqualifications in force
before the passing of the Unemployment
Insurance Act, 1928.
The Umpire has laid it down that a
claimant's record of employment is a most
important consideration in determining
whether or not he satisfies the statutory
conditions. The statement of contributions paid and benefits received is therefore normally made available to the
Court, as evidence of the claimant's record of employment.
The existence of what has been known
as the overdraft is no longer, in itself, a
bar to entitlement to unemployment
benefit.
Mr. KYLE: The right hon. Gentleman
has stated in the course of debate in this
House that overdrafts were wiped out.
He now states they are not a bar to unemployment benefit being granted, and
that the officials of the Court are sup-

posed to tell the Chairman of the Court
the number of days overdrawn in the
past. Will the right hon. Gentleman
issue instructions to his Department that
the overdraft is not to be a determining

Mr. ANDREWS: Certainly.

our hopes, I undoubtedly would occupy

On this occasion, especially as the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin)
shakes his head, I am prepared to take
the risk, for I feel that if I adopted the
easier, more modest, and to me more
acceptable, course of simply dealing with
these matters which I feel to be of outstanding importance, I would be sure to
be accused by hon. Members opposite of
having treated them with scant courtesy
and having failed in my duty to give the
Committee the information which hon.
Members have the right to expect.
In dealing with the general policy of
the Department I would like to say at the
very beginning of my remarks that when
our Government was set up one of the
first things that we decided was that as
regards labour matters-those services
which my Department is charged with administering-we would keep in parity with
Great Britain both as regards legislation
and administration. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I may point out that that
policy from which we have never wavered
was decided before hon. Members opposite
came into this House at all.
On several occasions they have pressed
me to a considerable extent to yield in this
direction and in that direction, but if the
Government had been weak enough to
take their advice in connection with this
matter we undoubtedly would have done
irreparable damage to our industrial
classes in Northern Ireland. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Our policy was
the outcome of our view that there was no
reason why, because we had accepted a
Parliament of our own to help Great
Britain in her time of difficulty, our industrial classes should suffer as a consequence in their home lives and all those
things which mean so much to them.
We have, therefore, all along never recognized that there were any boundaries
*
Estimates-

Ministry of Labour
8 MAY 1928
within the United Kingdom in connection.
with social, industrial, and labour
matters. The result of our policy nas
been that our workers in Northern Ireland
have always felt quite secure in the knowledge that whatever advantages were
given to their fellow-workers in Great
Britain would also be given to them.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
It is not overstating the fact that from
the cradle to the grave these social services
bring assistance to our industrial classes
in almost every period of adversity which
may befall them. In the first place, when
the child appears maternity benefit is
paid. A little later the Ministry of Education comes along with free education,
with feeding for necessitous children, and
with inspection of all the youth of our
country attending school. A little later
if the parent-the bread winner-dies a
widow's pension is given to the mother
and an allowance to the children, and if
both parents die an orphans' pension is
given to those who are left behind.
Again, when the insurance age is reached
if sickness falls upon the insured person
he has the knowledge that he will receive
sickness benefit for a considerable time,
and if the illness is prolonged disablement
benefit until a cure is effected. Then,
again, in the case of unemployment, hon.
Members are aware that very considerable
help is given over prolonged periods.
And, last but not least, when old age
begins to fall upon the faithful worker a
pension is given either on a contributory
or non-contributory basis until the call
comes from the Greatest Ruler of all.
Surely this is a great record, a record of
which any people may feel proud; and it
cannot be denied that no Government in
the world's history has done more than
this, and that no Government, except the
British Government, has done as much.
Hear,

hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is interesting at
this stage to consider the financial effect,
or, in other words, the cost of this policy
which I have explained. Hon. Members
will observe in the Estimate that the
State's contribution for 1928-29 will be no
less a sum than £2,663,893 plus £151,752
for administration. To this must be
added the contributions of employers and
employees, namely, £1,355,000, making a
grand total-and a grand total it is--f
over four millions, all of which goes for
the benefit of our industrial classes and
is administered by the Department whica
I have the honour to be the political head.
Sometimes we are told that our Departments are over-staffed. We are told that
the cost of administration is too high.
If this charge can be brought against any
Department-I do not think it can- -it
ought to be directed against mine, because
I am responsible for employing almost
half the total staff employed in the
Government Departments. But I do not
believe the Departments are over-staffed,
and one thing I am absolutely certain of
is that the Ministry of Labour is not, and
I say here quite frankly that no one can
judge whether a Department is over.
staffed or not unless he has intimate personal knowledge of the work which the
Department is charged with performing.
But what is the cost of administration
in the Ministry of Labour? For the year
lying ahead, namely 1928-29-of course, !
refer to the financial year-the cost of the
Department's administration will be 6.6
per cent., or, if the approved societies
expenses are taken into consideration, it
will be 8.9 per cent. I venture to say
that this is a very low figure for dealing
with such important services, especially
having regard to the fact that the payments are made in comparatively small
sums. Now, the work of the Ministry of
Labour can be conveniently divided, I
think, on an occasion like this, into two
heads. First of all, there is the question
of employment in all its aspects, and,
secondly, I propose to deal with the question of insurance.
Dealing with the problems associated
with employment, I would like, in the
first instance, to say that I think it is very
gratifying that Northern Ireland continues to enjoy a reputation second to
none in the land for industrial peace.
That is mainly due to a desire on behalf
of both employers and labour to accomodate with each other, to negotiate with
each other, and to help each other to the
greatest extent that the industry will
permit. Of course, the Ministry of
Labour plays a part, as it is entitled to
do, in this connection, and when my
people I call them by that name
advisedly-hear that trouble is brewing
they immediately get into touch with one
or both parties likely to be affected. We
believe in the old saying that prevention
is better than cure, and, therefore, I am
entitled to say that in far more instances
Estimates-

Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
than are generally known through the influence of the Department matters are
adjusted before the public becomes aware
of the fact that there was any danger in
the air.
I think that at this stage I ought to
refer to those problems associated with
Trade Board legislation. I remember
when Trade Boards were very unpopular. That, I do not think, is so to-day.
I believe it is generally recognized that
in certain industries where there was not
only fierce local competition but also
national and international competition,
what is known as sweating was likely to
result, and therefore Trade Boards were
set up in eighteen of our industries. One
of the complaints against Trade Boards
in the past has been that they tended to
drive trade from the country districts into
the towns and cities. That was recognized
by the Government, and in our Trade
Board Act of 1923 a provision was inserted permitting District Trade Committees to be set up with power to recommend that wages should differentiate between town and country in such a way as
not to bring about the regrettable result
to which I have already referred. Taking
advantage of that provision there has been
established in the boot and shoe repairing
trade a District Committee, which I
understand, has brought about an agreed
result, and in the retail tailoring and
dressmaking trade a committee of the
character which I have indicated is now
being established.
rather than upon those who are engaged

Now, hon. Members may expect, as they
have expected on former occasions, that I
should say something about the prospects.
I am aware of the fact that it is always a
dangerous thing to prophesy, but I have
been particularly careful never to paint
the picture brighter than I felt I was

in our industrial life our staple trade

Now, as regards our staple trade I have
often heard many people say both in this
House and out of it that it was down and
out. I do not believe that for a moment.
I have had some personal experience of
the linen industry for over 35 years. It
has always had its ups and downs
and it has always come through. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) And that it will
do so again I feel absolutely confident.
As regards the immediate future I am
somewhat anxious, and I will tell the Committee why. Before the war we were
always dependent to a very large extent
for our raw material, namely flax,
on the supply which came from
Russia. Since the war that unfortunate
country has shipped very little. I
am not altogether surprised, because
after all in that land there is very little
incentive to effort and very little inducement to grow a crop which is a difficult
crop to grow and which is a crop that involves a very great deal of trouble. And
it is not much of an incentive to grow a
crop like that when you know you are
very likely to be deprived of the fruits of
your labour.
And therefore we have felt
the backwash of that, and to-day we are
up against somewhat of a shortage of raw
material. Flax is very much above the
normal price, and spinners are naturally
shy about buying under existing conditions. But it is gratifying to feel in this
connection that there are increased sowing
Estimates-

Ministry of Labour
8 MAY 1928
in Belgium, in France, and in Holland,
and the brairds are looking well. And
here at home it is estimated that there will
be an increased supply of about 25 per
cent. So that if the next few months had
passed away I personally feel that there
would be no reason for anxiety.
It is particularly gratifying to know
that our shipbuilding industry is improving throughout the United Kingdom, and
that our principal yard has benefited to its
full share and that its slips are occupied.
It is also gratifying to know that Messrs.
Workman & Clark's yard, which has been
passing through such difficult and trying
times, has now been reformed and that
they are now taking orders, and that it is
reasonable to hope that that yard also will
benefit in the general improvement.
Something was said about artificial silk.
the other day in this House, and I should
like briefly to refer to the position as regards this, what I may call, new industry.
With Government assistance a factory was
started at Ballymena which is now producing, I understand, an excellent article
and is giving employment to 600 persons.
I am also glad to know that inquiries are
now taking place with a view to establishing another silk factory in Londonderry.
Other new industries are gradually being
established in our midst and, therefore, as
I think I have already said, we can look
forward to our industrial future not only
with hope but with confidence.
Now in dealing with the question of unemployment we naturally think first of our
disabled ex-Servicemen, and the King's
National Roll Committees continue their
splendid public service in this connection.
All honour to them. At the beginning of
the year 1,570 disabled ex-Servicemen
were unemployed. During the year that
figure was reduced by 500, and I am sure
every hon. Member will be gratified to
know that there are at the present time
4,701 disabled ex-Servicemen working in
enrolled firms. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
and the work on which will occupy a considerable time before it is completed.
There is another matter that I wish to
take the opportunity of referring to today, because it is part of the policy of the
Government. There is a great deal of
loose thinking and loose talking about our
Richhill Training Centre. At that centre
we have trained and sent to Canada already 178 young men. We have trained
and sent to Australia 72 young men or
250 in all. And there are at the present
time in training 79 for Canada and 12
for Australia, a total of 91.
Hon. Members will naturally desire to
know a little about our relief schemes.
During the year under review 141 schemes
were sanctioned by the Department estimated to cost over £1,000,000, and the
grants sanctioned amounted to £285,000,
and, therefore, I am glad to be able to
inform the Committee that 87 schemes are
at present in hand, the estimated cost of
which will amount to over £1,400,000,
Now, I know quite well that there are
some hon. Members who take the view
that it is not desirable to send, as they
express it, the best blood of Ulster out of
the country. Well, I would like to say
that that is quite mistaken. It is not
the view of the Government that anybody
should be sent from Ulster. What the
policy of the Government is is this-to
bring within the reach of these young men
in our industrial centres the same privilege in this direction which is brought to
young men in Great Britain who, of their
own free will, desire to chance their lot
in another part of the British Empire.
It is a free choice whether they go to
Richhill or not, and the Government,
neither directly nor indirectly, puts the
smallest amount of pressure upon them in
connection with their decision. But may
I point out to the Committee the way that
I view this matter? The Dominion authorities are getting more and more particular as to whom they will accept. They
will accept no one now who has not a
knowledge of farming matters and, therefore, if the Government were not to bring
within the reach of these young persons
a knowledge of agriculture they would be
absolutely debarred from exercising the
free choice which I have referred to, and
they would have to remain here in our
cities, employed or unemployed as the
case may be, whether they liked it or not.
May I point out in this connection that
the births in Northern Ireland exceed the
deaths each year by no less a number than
7,600, and, therefore, not only have we
some leeway to make up before all our
people who are available for employment
obtain it, but if emigration were to cease
from Northern Ireland vacancies would
have to be found for 7,600 persors each
year in addition. Now the people of
Northern Ireland have always taken their
part in peopling and fashioning the

British Dominions beyond the seas.

Now, it is generally recognized that
Ulster men have risen to the very top in
the Dominions. They have helped to
make the Dominions what they are, and,
therefore, as I have already said, the
Government at Richhill is simply bringing
within the reach of these young persons
the opportunity of emigrating in case they
so desire.
The next matter that I wish to refer to
is the problem associated with the Local
Employment Committees. There is an
impression abroad that these are to cease
to function under the Blanesburgh Act.
That is not so. Under the Blanesburgh
Act it will be no longer necessary for
Rota Committees to meet because the
work which the Rota Committees did in
the past is to be transferred under that
Act to Courts of Referees. I have often
heard it stated in this House, and out of
it, that the decisions of Rota Committees
very often were very harsh, and that large
numbers of people quite wrongly were
cut off from benefit. I have always felt
that that was unfair to the Rota Committees, and I must say this to-day that I feel
deeply indebted to those committees, each
and all of them, for the valuable and
difficult services which they have rendered
to Northern Ireland since they came into
being four or five years ago.
During the past year the Rota Committees reviewed 220,500 claims, and they
actually passed 187,800 claims. I am in
a position to inform my hon. Friends that
out of every 100 claims put before the
Rota Committees, taking into consideration the rejections by headquarters, 82
persons received benefit. Surely no one
can say that that was cutting off insured
persons from the "dole," as they call it,
north, south, east and west. I think the
administration of the Act under these
Rota Committees has been very impartial
and very fair, as it ought to be.
Committee that the Department takes
care that, when cases of fraud come to

I now want to say a few words in reference to Health Insurance. The number
of people covered by our Health Insurance
Acts is 332,000. The expenditure has
risen compared with the previous year. It

Hear, hear.) I am glad to say that the
new machinery for administering noncontributory pensions has already been
set up. Forty-four pensions courts have

We are sometimes told that we have
done nothing to help our industrial
classes. "You have done nothing" are
words which frequently have been used
in this Committee, and I have given
these facts and figures to-day to prove
how untrue and unjust that statement
is. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
can scarcely imagine a time of adversity
falling on any of our industrial workers
without considerable Government aid
being brought within their reach. We
have encouraged industry in every way
possible. We have guaranteed loans to
shipowners in order to bring work into.
our shipbuilding yards. We have
assisted our linen industry in every way
in which we have been asked to assist
that great industry, and we have supported new industries wherever they
have been started and where we have
been approached in connection with the
matter.
I have frequently asked hon. Members
opposite to tell us what more we can do,
and I feel that I am really justified in
saying that I have never received from
any section of the Opposition a practical
suggestion. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It is quite true that the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. Devlin),
towards the end of last year, told me he
had written a pamphlet on the subject.
I thanked him across the floor of the
House for saying that he would send me
a copy of that pamphlet, and he immediately rose in his place and said he
would send me two. But the strange
thing is that the weeks have passed by,
the months have followed one another,
and I have never received that pamphlet
yet (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-containing as it does the solution of this unemployment problem. Then again my
hopes were raised when I read of the new
Ulster Liberal Association being started.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: That Association
issued a long manifesto, covering columns

They said it required a strong soul and

of unemployment. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) They further said that

probably issue another manifesto solving
this problem which should have been
solved long before. Again I waited to
see what this strong soul and this high
endeavour were going to produce, but
again the weeks passed and the months

Mr. ELLIOTT: And never will.
Mr. McALLISTER: Wait till the
next election.

recognize, no doubt, that when their

will hang together I do not know.

lest you might hang singly.

of us hanging.

Option?

I say that not only does that help the

administration generally, but there is an

If hon. Members will refer to Subhead K they will see that there is a substantial rise of about £11,000 odd. Of
this amount £8,800 is due to the Blanesburgh Act and for the establishment of
the courts of referees in connection therewith, and £3,000 is due to the Old-Age
Pensions Act. If hon. Members will
refer to Sub-head R they will see here a

stamps, and the provision and payment.

have already shown hon. Members, the

Just before I conclude I would like to
say this, if the Department have made
good, and I venture to think it has, the
maximum of credit is due to the officers
of the Department for the efficiency, industry and devoted services which they
have shown and given to the great problems which they have to deal with. It
is only right before I sit down that I
should pay tribute to my hon. Friend
and colleague the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon). (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). He and I have worked

Members: Hear, hear). I feel more

still remains with us. Notwithstanding

in the year 1923 to solve the problem of

Mr. DEVLIN: They do not even get
15s a week. They get coupons for their

with, in my judgment, the most tragic
and pathetic section of the unemployed
is left to the Board of Guardians. The
whole spirit in every Parliament in these
islands the whole humane spirit everywhere--is to divorce the poor-law entirely
from the question of unemployment.
That is the spirit of the age, and yet we
have men working at Whitewell for 15s
a week, given in coupons for food-a
more degrading and more humiliatng
position it would not be possible to conceive. I quite agree I have stated it
here over and over again-that Boards
of Guardians ought to have nothing to
do with the unemployment problem at all.
It is not their business. There is no
reason why the stigma of the poor-law
should be put upon these people. I think
if a man is prepared to work at Whitewell for eight hours a day on four days
in the week for 15s, it shows how anxious
the working man is to get work. And yet
when he gets that work this is the remuneration he receives.
I come now to another question, and
that is the question of poverty, as distinct from unemployment. This is a
very small area, a six-county area. It
is a rich area, rich, at all events, in the
past, and I hope it will be rich in the
future, in regard to its industries. It
is rich as a great agricultural area, and
in my opinion if we had a Government
that applied itself properly to its work
it should be possible to eradicate and, at
all events, solve this problem of preventible poverty. The insured persons get
some consideration if they are badly
treated. Their grievances can be discussed here, or in the Press, or on the
platform, but there is a seething mass of
poor people who get nothing from unemployment grants, who are not insured,
and who are struggling and trying to keep
body and soul together, and eking out
a miserable and wretched existence.
Nothing is done for them. I think there
ought to be some tribunal set up to deal
with that section of the community, so
that no one would go hungry or naked,
because many of them are practically
naked. It should be the duty of the
State to see, if they were hungry
through no fault of their own, that that
hunger should not continue. and that
these people should be allowed to live in
decent comfort in the community in
which they exist.
I come now to the question of children
leaving school. I have raised it again
and again. There are boys and girls-
12.000 of them-who leave the elementary schools every year in Northern Ireland. I confess that it amazes me that
the right hon. Gentleman made no reference to whether the Government
had given any consideration to the problem as to what is to be done with these
boys and girls when they leave school.
If they are left without occupation, and
go out into the world without anything
to do, and hang around for four or five

what is to be the future of the Northern
Ireland area, or of any community where

been glad if the right hon. Gentleman

given any serious consideration to this
question of boys and girls leaving school
at 12, 13 or 14 years of age-whether
anything had been done in that way.

There is no prescriptive right in the Opposition to be called before anybody else.
The practice in debate is, that individual
speeches are as a rule replied to from the
other side. but if no hon. Member gets
up to reply of course I call upon the only
hon. Member who does rise. But to
keep the balance of debate, if an hon.
Member does get up on the other side,
I am in fairness entitled to call him.
That is the universal and recognized rule
of procedure.
