PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): When the
Government became responsible for the
administration of National Health Insurance in Northern Ireland it was decided
that there should be no disturbance of
the administrative unity of the scheme
which, from the beginning, had been established on a broad and common basis
for the United Kingdom as a whole. The
rights and interests of insured persons in
Northern Ireland are linked up so completely with those of their fellow-members
in Great Britain that it would have been
disastrous if we had taken any step which
would have severed our connection with
the common scheme or attempted to base
our insurance system on any field less wide
than that of the United Kingdom. The
Government accordingly arranged that
the membership of Northern Ireland insured persons in Approved Societies operating here and in Great Britain should
remain unaltered, that our partnership in
the common central funds should con-
Health Insurance Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Gordon]
tinue, and that we should retain our seat
on the National Health Insurance Joint
Committee, which is the central body
charged with co-ordinating administration
throughout the United Kingdom.
Two events have taken place to which I
should now like to refer. First, the several
Acts of Parliament governing the scheme
have been consolidated by an Act passed
at Westminster in 1924 which is the basis
of the law of Northern Ireland as well
as for England, Scotland and Wales.
Secondly, the whole operation of National
Health Insurance has been exhaustively
reviewed by a Royal Commission which
reported to the Imperial Government in
1926. Generally speaking, the Commission reported that the scheme had established its position as a permanent feature
of the social system, and that it should
be continued in the main on its present
basis.
The Commission did, however, make a
number of recommendations affecting the
machinery of the system. At this stage
it has not been found feasible to adopt
two of these recommendations, namely,
the abolition of Insurance Committees
and the partial pooling of the future.
surpluses of the approved societies which
administer the system. But, whilst the
time may not be ripe for these major
structural alterations, there are other
valuable recommendations of the Commission which it is expedient to adopt at
once.
Accordingly, a Bill to amend the Act.
of 1924 in order to give effect to those
recommendations has been introduced at
Westminster. Certain of the changes
proposed to be made relate to matters
with which this Parliament has not
power to make laws, such as the powers
of the National Health Insurance
Joint Committee and charges on the
central fund which is under its
control, matters relating to the mercantile
marine and to approved societies which

Kingdom. Other changes, of which the
most important are those that deal with
the prolongation of insurance and the

was first passed. It was brought in as a

the acute unemployment crisis through
which the country has been passing.

The Act has been continued from year
to year and was amended by the Contributory Pensions Act of 1925. The effect
is to continue a person in insurance during
unemployment subject to certain conditions. The first is that he must not have
taken up work which is not of an insurable
nature. The second condition gives the
worker the choice of two alternatives. He
may either show that he has a certain
number of contributions standing to his
credit or that during every period of unemployment he has been available for but
unable to obtain work. If these conditions were fulfilled continuation as an insured person was secured however prolonged the periods of unemployment
might be.
These temporary arrangements have
proved unsatisfactory and difficult to work
in many respects. Confusion has arisen
owing to the different dates of the termination of insurance for the purposes of
Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions, and complications and uncertainties
have arisen with regard to the benefit
rights. Further, persons have been kept
in insurance for protracted periods although they have given up employment
for reasons of their own and paid no contributions for a considerable time.

The second group is the one to which
I should like to refer in more detail. It
is proposed to bring into full and equitable insurance for the first time a certain
class of people known as deposit contributors. These are people compelled to
pay the usual contributions under the Act
but who have not become members of

Once the credit is exhausted he can receive no further benefit no matter how
The persons in this class are composed
of two kinds, those whom a society refuse
to accept as members because of bad
health or for other reasons and those who
refuse or neglect to join a society for
reasons best known to themselves. With
regard to persons who can join a society
but refuse to do so, we cannot carry compulsion so far as to insist on their joining
a society. But those who would like to
join a society and get the advantage of
insurance but are not able to do so, we
propose to form into an insurance
group of their own and provide them
with the benefits of insurance at the
ordinary statutory rates. There are
about 1,000 persons of this class of contributor in Northern Ireland, and I feel
that this section of the Act will confer a
great boon upon them.
Besides these people there are persons
who are at present excluded from insurance because they are not technically employed under a contract of service. I
refer to those who are employed under a
contract for the performance of manual
labour such as market-porters, slaughtermen, stonebreakers, tree-fellers and sharefishermen. Generally speaking, there is
a desire on the part of these people for
Health Insurance and now also, of course,
for insurance for Contributory Pensions,
and the Royal Commission was of opinion
that the advantages of insurance should
not be denied them. I think this House
will agree that it is reasonable that they
should not be ruled out on a mere technicality, but that the door should be
opened to permit them to participate in
the advantages of National Health Insurance.
It is also proposed to increase the benefits payable to insured women who ceasc

I know the interest taken by Members

their insistence upon the realization of
things not as they are but as they should
be. I have taken a considerable time to

Bill without offering any explanation regarding the various Clauses. We are all
seeking to achieve the same ideal. Social
insurance is a recognition of those larger
social responsibilities, and in this Bill we
have taken a forward step to remove some
of the defects. We are here to protect
the aged and genuinely unemployed, and
to increase the benefits of those physically
unfit and, therefore, most deserving, the
deposit contributors. This Bill also embraces within our scheme further workmen who desire to make provision for
their wives and families in times of sickness and old age. I commend this Bill
and beg to move its Second Reading.

insurance there is what is known as the
central fund, and there is the joint committee, upon which we have representation, and, therefore, in this way, as I have
said, we are associated with Great Britain
to the great advantage of our insured persons.

The only matter of any importance
which was raised by the Leader of the
Opposition (Mr. Kyle) was that he rather
objected to a further burden being put
upon the approved societies due to the
charge made for medical referees. I
would point out to the hon. Member that
yesterday he said he approved of the
medical referee system, that is the wholetime men, and further he said he was
glad to know we were appointing an extra
referee. This is simply the means of
raising money in order to pay for that
service, and if the 2s 8d which is asked
for is not required it simply will not be
levied. This is not entirely a burden upon the approved societies, because most of
the approved societies, in consideration of
this service being established, have given
up employing their own referees, so that
if they spend in one way they save in
another.
The Socialist Member for West Belfast
(Mr. William McMullen) said that, because we were providing in this Bill for
the contingency that unemployment
might possibly continue for some years, we
recognized the fact that it was going to
continue for that time. Well, none of
us know, to tell the truth, but what we
are doing is this: We are providing
for the worst in the interests of our insured persons and we are hoping for the
best.
The matter raised by my hon. Friend
the Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone
(Mr. Cooper), who sits beside me, as regards the poor man who went to an
asylum, I quite agree with you, Mr.
Speaker, is more an administrative ques
tion, but I would point out that not only
did his wife fail to report that he was
not sane, but that the contributions were
not paid, and no doubt the reason why the
benefit was not paid was mainly because
of those facts.
The only point of very great inportance
which the hon. Member for Fermanagh
and Tyrone (Mr. Healy), who sits opposite me, raised was about the deposit
contributors. I do not think he quite
appreciates what the intention is. It is
simply this: At the present time we have
what are known as deposit contributors

[Mr. Andrews]

They are composed of two classes.
class is those who, for some reason best
known to themselves, could join an approved society but do not do so. That is
their own affair and we do not, therefore,
propose to interfere with them by applying compulsion. There is another class
for whom we have the greatest possible
sympathy, and those are the people who
have been rejected by the approved
societies or by their doctors. It is
those persons-about 1,000 in Northern
Ireland-for whom this Bill is going to
provide and whom it is going to place in
the same position as those who are insured
by approved societies. May I say in conclusion how gratified I am at the reception which this Measure has been
accorded?

Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL; I beg to

This Clause deals with licences for the
sale of fish, and under the Clause as it
stands the individual who requires a

Justice of the Peace before the Conservators will grant a licence. I think when
he receives this certificate from a Justice
of the Peace it should be obligatory on
the part of the Conservators to grant the
licence. Where the person engaged in
the business has received a certificate from
a magistrate, I think the licence should
forthwith be issued without the Conservators having the right to refuse especially considering that the Ministry will
have the right to refuse this licence.
The second and third Amendments, as
you see, will be consequential on this
matter, but I think the Ministry should
accept this alteration, as you have ample
power without leaving the right to refuse
the licence in the hands of a third party.
There does not seem to be any reason
why the Conservators should have the
right to refuse a licence when the magistrates have given this certificate, and
when the Ministry have a right to
annul these licences or to refuse to grant
them. It is for that reason that I propose the alteration as it appears upon the
Order Paper, and I think the Minister
should accept this Amendment.

This Amendment is moved in order to
shorten the close season so far as eel fishing
is concerned. It appears that in Lough
Neagh, which is the principal source of
eels, the present conditions are that eels
are not caught from October until 1st
April. It seems they are not to be got
during those months as they bury themselves and do not come forth till 1st April.
Anyone engaged in that particular department of fishing knows that there is thus
a close season of almost five months, and
the Ministry now propose to reduce the
time available for fishing by an additional
two months. That would be a distinct
hardship upon those engaged in the trade.
Representations have been made to the
Ministry that they should allow these men
to fish for these eels from 1st April instead
of from 1st June. A very good case was
made by the men themselves when the
Minister of Commerce was good enough
to receive deputations, but evidently they
were not able to impress him as to the
reasonableness and fairness of their claim.
Even yet I make this appeal to him, and
I think the claim can be supported with
much better arguments than I am able to
put forward. I appeal as strongly as
possible to the Minister at this stage of
the proceedings to accept the Amendment
in my name.
All men in the trade will agree that it is
absolutely necessary that the fishing industry of Lough Neagh should not be
tied up for those two months, on which
their livelihood practically depends. I
would put it to the Minister that he
He is enshould accept this alteration.
titled to our most commendatory applause
for what he has done. He has tried to

Mr. HARBISON: I second
the
Amendment for very solid and good

elose season extends at present from

should be accepted by the right hon.
Gentleman. Eels are most valuable from

these eels, when they are in season, should

these very months of April and May the

the fishermen, whose chief industry here
is the eel industry, are going to be held
up for those two months and deprived
of the benefit of the market in London.
Mr. COLLINS: I strongly support
this Amendment. I heard a statement
from the fishermen yesterday that the
close season for eels in Lough Neagh is
brought on, naturally, by the appearance
of the first frost, about October. When
the first frost appears, the eel disappears
into the mud of Lough Neagh, and will
not reappear until the temperature rises,
which is about the end of March, or the
1st of April, so that from October to
April is, at all events, an enforced close
season. These two months that we seek
to take from these men are two of the
most valuable months in the year, because, as was pointed out yesterday to
the Minister, when June and July come
large quantities of ice have to be purchased for the purpose of packing into
the boxes for these eels. These months are
not remunerative to them. Besides, the
two months taken from those who are dependent on this industry for their livelihood will simply mean they will have to
give up the industry altogether. It
seems there is a difference between the
eels in Lough Neagh and the river eels.
The eels in the river do not have this
enforced close season that the eels in
Lough Neagh have, and it is on behalf
of the fishermen of Lough Neagh we are
addressing the Minister to-day, and
urging him, as strongly as we can, to
open the close season for the wide lough,
and then if he wants to bring in other
arrangements about the close river he
can do it. We appeal to him strongly
on behalf of those men whose livelihood
depends on this eel fishing in Lough
Neagh.

I cannot pose as a technical man myself, nor can I claim to have an intimate
personal acquaintance with the conditions
attaching to this fishery, and so I am
dependant upon the advice tendered to
me by those who have been specially appointed to go into the matter. They report to me that they consider the close
time, as specified in the Bill, to be absolutely necessary in order to prevent this
stock of fish from being depleted to a
dangerous extent, in fact, it might almost
be carried to the length of extinction.
Consequently, what we want to do is not
merely to keep things as they are, but to
see some manner of protection and preservation afforded to this fishery in Lough
Neagh which would enable the stock to
he built up and so render more intensive
fishing possible in the future. Therefore,
I think it is really in the best interests
of those whose livelihood depends on this
fishing that this period of recuperation
should be granted to the fish. We cannot
accept the Amendment in consequence.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL: Hon.

The analogy of the liquor traffic that the

NEW CLAUSE (Use of nets, etc., for
capture of fish other than salmon, trout,
or eels).
Notwithstanding anything in this
Act, or in any other enactment to the
contrary, the Ministry of Commerce
may permit the use by the owner of a
several fishery, or by a person or persons authorized in writing by such
owner, of nets or other engines of such
size and description as may be prescribed for the capture of carp, tench,
bream, roach, perch, pike, and other
fresh-water fish, except salmon, trout,
or eels, in any specified fresh-water
river, lake, or pond (or any part
thereof), at any time of the year:
Provided that the said Ministry shall
not authorize the use of any engine of
a type or description the use of which
during the open season for salmon is
prohibited by any enactment or bylaw.
Brought up and read a First time.

NEW CLAUSE (Exemptions for artificial propagation and scientific purposes)
(1) The Ministry of Commerce may,
by certificate in writing, if that Ministry
thinks fit, and subject to such conditions as it may specify in the certificate,
authorize the owner of a fishery, or,
with the consent of such owner, any
other named person, to do at any
season of the year all or any of the
following things:-
(a) To catch or attempt to catch
within the limits of such fishery, and
to have in his possession, any salmon
or trout for the purpose of artificial
propagation, and the young or fry
of salmon, trout, or eels for the purpose of stocking that or any other
fishery;
(b) To buy or sell ova and fry of
salmon, trout, and eels for the purpose of artificial propagation or the
stocking of that or any other fishery;
(c) To catch or attempt to catch,
and to have in his possession for
scientific purposes, any fish of any
kind specified in the certificate.
(2) Notwithstanding anything to the
contrary contained in any of the Fisheries Acts or this Act, any person to
whom a certificate is granted under this
section may, subject to the conditions
specified in the certificate, do all or any
of the things which he is authorised by
the certificate to do.
Brought up and read a First time.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to nove,
"That the Clause be read a Second time."
The object of this Clause is to enable
owners of eel fisheries to catch young eels
for the purpose of stocking their fisheries.
I have also included the ova and fry of
salmon and trout. I will proceed to show
why this new Clause is necessary. It
appears that under the Act of 1842,
strictly speaking, it is not legal to have
in one's possession elvers and the fry of
salmon and trout, but owing to the fact
that these are an absolute necessity there
a technical infringement of this law.
going on practically the whole of the time.
It seems to me that it would be very much
better to take the opportunity provided
by this Bill to legalize the position that
exists at the present moment. I believe
the practice is for owners of fisheries to
purchase their elvers from across the

[Mrs. Chichester]
Channel and waters in Northern Ireland,
and to introduce them into their own
fisheries in order to improve the stock.
Under the Act of 1842 they are, strictly
speaking, unable to do so. Then Clause
10 of this Bill, dealing with the close
season, makes the position even more difficult, because no one can have in his
possession eels under a certain weight
and at a certain time. I hope,
therefore, that it will be possible to put
this new Clause in the Bill.
There is another point that might
arise if drainage works are carried
out in the Bann, as I very much hope
they will be at a not very distant date.
These elvers that come up to the Bann to
Lough Neagh at certain times of the year
would probably be prevented from
getting to Lough Neagh, and it might be
necessary for the owners of the fisheries
to make arrangements to bring them from
the obstruction to Lough Neagh. In
doing so they would be contravening the
law as it stands at the present moment.
The elvers come up in the early spring,
and that would be the close season. That
is an additional reason why it is necessary
that this new Clause should adopted. I
believe that so far as the ova and fry of
salmon and trout are concerned, they are
covered by the Act of 1863, but at any
rate their inclusion in this Bill with the
eels would make the whole position clear.
Mr. BARBOUR: The Government is
quite ready to accept this new Clause. We
think it is a wise provision to make.

We were told when the Ulster Government took over the fisheries that everybody expected they would deal with them
in a democratic way and would do everything to develop them. Here the Government have an opportunity by adopting
this new Clause of restoring the rights
taken from these people many years ago.
It will mean that local labour will be employed in the rural districts. It will increase the revenue for taxation from the
fishing industry, and indirectly it will help
industry in Ulster by boats being built
while the cordage and nets required will
help the flax industry, on which the Minister of Commerce is a great authority,
and it will also help the spinning industry.
There are no sound grounds on which the
Government can refuse to set right the
wrong which was created many years ago.
If the Government are sincere and want
to see fair play for the Ulster people they
will restore these rights to these people
who were the owners of the fisheries. They
are largely supporters of the Government,
and consequently when they are objecting to the Government's legislation it will
be
seen they have a grievance. I
asked the Minister of Commerce to look
into this matter and carefully consider it,
but nothing seems to have been done.
Every interest has been considered but
that of these people who are people who
would be of some advantage to employment all over the country.
You have to go across the water to get
fish for the people of Ulster simply because you will not allow some legitimate
and effective method of taking fish in
these waters. I would ask the Minister
of Commerce to consider this question. If
he likes he can hold it over for a day or so
if he cannot see his way now to accept it
in the interests of the poorer class of fishery owners in Ulster who have been fighting for these rights for many years.

NEW CLAUSE (Maintenance Orders).
Where an unmarried mother dies in
giving birth to her child, the father or
mother or other relative of the deceased,
or any public authority responsible for
the maintenance of the child, may sue
for a "maintenance order" against the
putative father, and the illegitimate
orphan child shall not be deprived of
any civil rights owing to its mother's
death.

that this is a Bill to amend the law relating to children born out of wedlock,

Clause to make a certain maintenance
provision operative and has nothing whatever to do with the question of legitimacy.
It appears to me. therefore, that the
Clause in any circumstances is not competent and may not be moved.

CATERPILLAR PLAGUE IN
CO. FERMANAGH.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether his attention has
been drawn to the caterpillar plague in
County Fermanagh, and, if so, what steps
his Department is taking to counteract the
same.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Mr. Archdale): My attention has been
directed to what the hon. Member describes as the caterpillar plague in County
Fermanagh. Immediately the visitation
was reported I sent down an inspector of
the Ministry to investigate the matter.
The inspector's report shows that this
caterpillar belongs to a comparatively
rare species of butterfly which frequents
damp waste places where the weeds known
as "Devil's Bit" Scabious is allowed to
flourish. The caterpillar in the natural
state feeds only on this weed and will not
eat grass or cultivated crops.
The report
also indicates that the caterpillars were
found only on an isolated area where the
weed mentioned was growing.
My scientific advisers tell me that by
the end of May or beginning of June the
caterpillars will have been transformed
into butterflies. To destroy these caterpillars effectively would necessitate the
use of a poisonous spray which would
later on obviously be dar gerous to live
stock grazing on the lands. In the circumstances it is not considered necessary
or desirable to take any steps to deal with
this insect.

2. Mr. KYLE (on behalf of Mr. W.
McMullen) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that the
Kilkeel Board of Guardians do not invite
public tenders for the supply of the
various commodities required by the
Guardians where the value exceeds £10;
and whether he will state what steps he
proposes to take to ensure that all those
desiring to tender shall have an equal
opportunity.
MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): So far as the
Ministry is aware, the Kilkeel Board of
Guardians and the Governors of the
Mourne District Hospital publish advertisements for tenders for supplies over
£10 in value monthly in accordance with
the Regulations; but in regard to a recent
order for coal they appear merely to have
invited quotations from local firms.
The Ministry, on a former occasion,
pointed out that advertisements for
tenders for the supply of coal should be
published, and the action of the Governors
on this occasion has been referred to the
Local Government Auditor as the lowest
quotation received was not accepted.

The successful development of this

the numbers of breeding stock, by improving quality and by producing animals

So far as beef and mutton are concerned
public taste is changing. Small joints
are now much more in demand than large
ones, and young beef and mutton of high
quality now command much higher prices
than older animals. Early maturing
stock means quicker return and considerable saving in food and thus enables
farmers to keep more breeding stock, that
is, milch cows and ewes.
Milk production is an important section
of the live-stock industry and one which
is capable of great development to the advantage both of producers and consumers.
Improvement can be brought about by
keeping more cows and by selecting
animals with high milk records and by
breeding from these cows and high-class
dairy bulls whose dams and sires also have
high milk records. Farmers who have
dairy stock almost invariably keep pigs
and poultry to consume the separated
milk and buttermilk. Consequently, by
increasing the dairy stock we automatically increase pigs and poultry.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ARCHDALE: Our milk recording work is making satisfactory progress,
although it still falls far short of what is
necessary. In 1921 we had six Societies
with 1,216 cows recorded; in 1928 sixtysix Societies with 13,365 cows recorded.
However, as there are 249,000 cows in the
country there is still much ground to be
made up.
The average yield of each recorded cow approaches 700 gallons per
annum, whereas the average yield of the
cows of the country as a whole is little

production by seventy million gallons

Mr. ARCHDALE: One aspect of our
educational schemes may be of interest to
the Members. I refer to the work of the

of these officers employed. They are
young men of sound practical knowledge,
who have attended agricultural classes,

agricultural instructors. These young
men live and work in the poorest and
most backward districts in the country.
There are, for example, six of them employed in the mountain areas in Counties
Derry and Tyrone, others are at work in
the Glens of County Antrim, in Scuth
Armagh, in the Mourne districts and also
in County Fermanagh. Very good results.
are accruing from this development of cur
work, which gives advice on manures,

assistance to the doors of a large number
of industrious small farmers who, in the

had no opportunity of keeping abreast of
modern improvements.
It is certainly the only way of getting

these parts. These people do not as a

call at the houses, and show the farmers

Our research and educational work is

Ministry of Agriculture
[Mr. Archdale]
Without going into detail it may be
desirable to indicate briefly a few of the
numerous ways in which our research and
experimental work is directly benefiting
the farmer.
Hon. Members will have realized from
my introductory remarks the vital importance of the animal side of our agricultural industry. It is natural, therefore,
that my Ministry should lay great stress
upon the development of our research
work on animal nutrition. It is essential
to realize that this work is closely related
to our live-stock improvement schemes.
Progress in breeding must go hand in
hand with progress in nutrition. Failure
to progress in one direction seriously retards any developments that may be
made in the other.
One of the Ministry's objects in placing
superior bulls throughout the country is
to improve our dairy cows. That is to
say, to make our cows capable of producing 800 or 900 gallons of milk instead of
the general average of 400 gallons. Our
farmers are breeding such cows and in
increasing numbers every year. The
feeding of 800- or 900-gallon cows is
however, a very different proposition to
the feeding of 400-gallon cows. The cows
are not proportionally greater in size, and
as it is a law of nature that something
cannot be obtained for nothing we have
had to face the problem of how to feed
these cows.
My Ministry has developed
a simple system of balanced rations which
enables farmers to feed their cows according to their milk yield. Having tested
out the system we have been rapidly
teaching our farmers how to use and
apply it. The progress that is being
made and the possibilities of this work are
well illustrated by many striking examples of increased yields which have
been brought to our notice.
Another example, which illustrates the
work of our research division, is the development which is taking place in
Northern Ireland in the production of
early-maturing or baby beef. The
first report of our experimental work
was published in 1925. Now, in
addition to the special annual sales
of baby beef cattle held at the
Belfast markets, there is a steady and
increasing supply of this type of beef
coming on to our local markets every
week. The importance of the work will
be realized from the fact that early-maturing beef or this type is the only beef
which in the English market commands
a price substantially higher than the best
imported beef. Baby beef has the
further important economic advantage of
being a product which our chief foreign
competitors cannot produce. The extent
to which the production of baby beef has
been taken up by our farmers, particularly in County Down, is a most encouraging sign and is evidence that the
farming community is not so backward
in adopting new methods as is frequently
stated.
For some time our Chemical and
Animal Nutrition Division has been exploring problems connected with the
supply of minerals, that is, lime, phosphates, etc., in the rations of farm
animals. It is too early to say much
about the work, but it may be of interest
to indicate that there is increasing evidence which shows that many of the problems, such as breeding difficulties, which
arise with highly developed cattle, are
due to inadequate supplies of mineral
salts, particularly in the winter rations.
Some practical results are already beginning to emerge. For example, we know
how to maintain large herds of breeding
sows on farms where little or no milk is
available-milk being the main source of
mineral salts for young animals. Again,
we have evidence that the size of the egg
laid by the hen is determined by the
mineral content of her rations and by altering the mineral content it has been
possible to reduce the number of secondgrade eggs from over 40 per cent, to less
than 10 per cent.
It will be of interest to hon. Members
to know that the Ministry's investigations have thrown considerable light on
the causes of sterility in cattle. Steps
have been taken by the Ministry to demonstrate to the veterinary profession in
Northern Ireland suitable methods of
treatment, and those methods have met
with a most gratifying measure of success.
In co-operation with the Animal
Diseases Research Station in Scotland,
experiments relating to braxy in sheep
were carried out in County Antrim, and
1,150 sheep were vaccinated. The subsequent death rate from braxy amongst
the unvaccinated sheep was 6.25 per
cent. as compared with .22 amongst the
Estimates-

Ministry of Agriculture
10 MAY 1928
vaccinated. The results were regarded
as very satisfactory and vaccination is
now carried out on a large scale by farmers in the Glens districts in County
Antrim.
It is notorious that the consumption
of milk in the British Isles is much less
per capita than in the countries of the
New World and in the Scandanavian
States. The low consumption in Northern Ireland and the British Isles is not
a question of price, but of keeping
qualities. Milk is one of the most difficult products to handle, because of
its poor keeping qualities. As a
consequence, purchases of milk are
reduced to a minimum. This is a
great misfortune in view of the fact
that it is one of the cheapest foodstuffs
on the market, and from a nutritional
point of view the most valuable. It is
for this reason that we have been exploring the possibilities of producing, under
our conditons, natural raw milk which
will keep sweet for several days. Under
the Sale of Milk Act which came into
operation 1st January last, a beginning has been made in the Production of
Grade A tuberculin-tested milk under
Government licence. The producers are
already taking considerable interest in
this matter, and supplies are coming into Belfast, Portadown, Limavady and
Coleraine, as well as into several of our
hospitals. It is only by placing on the
market a pure supply derived from
healthy cows free from tuberculosis, and
capable of keeping sweet for several days,
that we can hope to expand the liquid
milk trade.
relative cleanliness of the milk delivered
to them, and we hope thereby that it will
be possible for them to assist in the allimportant work by offering an inducement to the farmers to produce a cleaner
supply.

Another important problem which falls
within the survey of this new division is
the very difficult one associated with the
condition of the milk supply to our
creameries. We can only hold
butter markets if we can succeed in putting on the market a uniform and firstclass article. Scrupulous cleanliness in
the creamery is essential, but it is of little
avail if the milk itself, as it comes from
the farmer, is not a first-class article
from the point of view of cleanliness. I
venture to say that cleanliness in our milk
supply is of far greater importance today than quality. My Ministry proposes to direct its attention to this question. We hope to devise simple and
readily applied means whereby the
creameries will be able to determine the
Owing to attacks of fungus diseases, the
fruit industry in Northern Ireland, particularly apples and gooseberries, has
been in a precarious condition. Research
and experimental work on these crops has
resulted in the discovery of efficient and
cheap measures for controlling diseases
by the adoption of modern spraying
methods, thus enabling fruit growers to
prevent these diseases and to procure a
crop.

Finally, as the Committee will observe,
the Agricultural Services Estimate shows
an increase of £3,000 odd, as compared
with 1927-8. Broadly, this increase is
due to:
———
(1) An increase of £1,000 in Sub-head
F2, grants to Agricultural Societies;
and
(2) An increase of £2,000 in the three
Forestry Sub-heads, J, J1, and J2.
It will also be noticed that we have a
new division to cope with the dairying
industry, that is the dairy bacteriological
division. Otherwise there are no changes
in the Estimate list. I will endeavour
to answer any questions that may arise
as we go along. I beg to move.

I wish to raise a question with regard to
the issuing of licences in connection with
potato merchants. I think the Ministry
have taken up an attitude that is indefensible, and I will give particulars of a case
in the Newry district. Potato merchants
there have gone outside the urban district
for some time. They have gone out some
five or six miles into the rural area to a
village called Mayobridge and have
acquired stores for themselves for the purpose of buying and storing potatoes.
Another Newry firm, one of the oldest
engaged in the export of potatoes in
Northern Ireland, also desired to go to
this neighbourhood and to acquire a store
there. They applied in the usual way to
the inspector for a licence to enable them
to buy and store potatoes there, but the
application was refused.
I really cannot understand why this
firm should have been refused a licence,
considering that two others obtained
licences in the same district. I admit
that their store was not close to the other
two; it was exactly one English mile away
from the other two, but whether it was
convenient or not, I cannot understand
why the Ministry should refuse to give a
licence to this firm, or to anyone willing
to buy potatoes in a district. I understand that the difficulty of farmers up to
now was to get potato merchants to buy
their potatoes. That has occurred in
many instances even in towns. But when
merchants are willing to convenience the
farmers by taking a store in the country
districts. I cannot understand why a
licence should be refused', particularly
when two other firms were there, and it
would not be any additional inconvenience to the Ministry's inspectors to
visit the store. They have refused, in
face of the fact that the farmers themselves have appealed to the Ministry to
grant this licence. I really do not know
what the reason is, or what the policy of
the Government is in connection with
this matter.

I would also like to congratulate the
Minister of Agriculture, and the officials
of the Ministry, on the way in which they
have conducted the work in Northern
Ireland during the years since they came
into office. Friction is hardly known,
notwithstanding the fact that very revolutionary legislation has been adopted.
We have a Bull Breeding Act, which undoubtedly is of great benefit in the way
of improving our cattle, we have the Eggs
Act, and a Horse Breeding Act. Notwithstanding the new regulations and the
changes that have taken place, I should
think, on the whole, that prosecutions
have been almost nil. By the fair way
the Ministry of Agriculture met in consultation with the Farmers' Union on these
matters before they were introduced, by
the administration of their officials, and
hy letting the farmers know it would be
for their good to observe these regulations made under these Acts, they have
taken to their work in a way that is
worthy of commendation. As a result,
our Ministry of Agriculture, our magistrates, our solicitors and other lawyers in
the country, have been denied hearing
cases of this character.

reply.
As the hon. Member is aware, all
matters concerning cottages for ex-Servicemen in Ireland are under the control of
the Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust, which is an Imperial Service, and
consequently questions in respect thereof

will not be overlooked.

UNBOUGHT TENANTS—
RESULT OF NEGOTIATIONS.
5. Mr. MARK asked the Prime Minister
whether he is now in a position to announce the result of the negotiations between the British Government and the
Government of Northern Ireland regarding the unbought tenants; and
whether the representations put forward
by the Ulster Farmers' Union have been
embodied in the settlement.
The PRIME MINISTER: Through
the courtesy of the Secretary of State for
the Home Department, with whom I
have been in telegraphic communication,
I am privileged to give contemporaneously with the answer he is sending to Mr. D. D. Reid's question in the
British House of Commons this afternoon the terms of the agreement which
has been reached by the two Governments.
Briefly, it provides that all tenants
whose holdings have not been dealt with
on or before the Appointed Day (27th
May, 1929) will be placed in the same
financial position as they would be if
their holdings had been dealt with on
that date.
The arrangements to enable this to be
carried out will involve the continued
payment of the present rent till each
holding is finally vested, but a refund of
the difference between the amount of the
annuity ultimately payable to the Government and the current rent from the
27th May, 1929, till the date of vesting
will then be made to the tenants. Furthermore, the term of the land purchase
annunity will run as from 27th May,
1929.
The work of vesting holdings in the
Commission will be continued with all
possible expedition, and the outstanding
cases will be progressively disposed of
within a period of three years from the
date mentioned, by which time with certain possible exceptions which may present special difficulties, the completion
of land purchase in Northern Ireland
will be effected.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
The Government of Northern Ireland
have undertaken to bear the cost of the
refund to the tenants and of the Sinking
Fund payments during the interim
period-no inconsiderable amount. The
scheme will not, therefore, operate in
any way to the prejudice of the interests
of landlords.
Legislation is involved at Westminster, but as the two Governments are in
complete agreement it should be of a
simple and non-controversial character.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I gratefully acknowledge the
assistance rendered by the Ulster Farmets' Union and, I should add, by the
Ulster Members of the Imperial Parliament, both in regard to the original Act
and the agreement now arrived at.
I feel confident that the House will be
relieved by the knowledge that practically within a year's time every tenant
in Ulster to whom the Act is applicable
will be upon an annuity-paying basis.

ALLOTTED DAYS FOR ESTIMATES.
6. Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL (for Mr.
Devlin) asked the Prime Minister whether
he is prepared to recommend the House
to introduce changes in the Standing
Orders, so as to increase the number of
Allotted Days for the discussion of the
Estimates.
The PRIME MINISTER: I have given
this matter careful consideration and have
compared the practice prevailing at
Westminster with that adopted by this
House.
Allowing for the difference in length of
our Parliamentary day and for the totals
of the respective Estimates, the actual
number of hours allocated for the discussion of our 33 Estimates involving under
£7,000,000 is relatively twelve times as
many as are allocated at Westminster for
the dicussion of 126 Estimates involving
over £400,000,000.
It has to be borne in mind that in comparison with this House there are seventeen times the number of Members in the
British House of Commons.
It will, I think, be generally agreed that
the Committee which drafted our Standing Orders made ample, and indeed
generous, provision for the most exhaustive examination of our Estimates.
I am, therefore, not prepared to adopt
the suggestion of the hon. Member.

As the Committee are aware, the
School Sites Act enables limited owners
to make leases of land not exceeding in
extent one acre at a nominal rent for
the purposes of the erection of schools.
The purpose of Clause 1 of the present
Bill is to extend that power to enable
such limited owners to make leases of
land at a nominal rent on the same terms
where a school is already erected on
the land. It occurred to me it
be
might
useful to extend that
power to enable such limited owners
to make leases of land subject to
similar conditions for a playground
attached to the school. A case came to
my notice where a school itself was held
under a lease and where it was proposed
to take in a little piece of ground adjoining in order to provide a playground
for the school. The actual wording of
the School Sites Act did not cover that
and the actual wording of Clause 1
of this Bill did not cover it. I
thought it would be somewhat of
improvement, if I may say so,
the Clause if it were extended
to provide power to make leases of little
pieces of ground for playgrounds as well
as to make leases of ground for the
school itself. It is largely a conveyancing lawyer's Amendment, aud I suggest
to the Committee that it would be an
improvement on the Bill.

would give, I think, a convenient power

The design of the Amendment is that such

This also, I may say, is a conveyancing
lawyer's Amendment. There is just one
slight slip in the Amendment as printed
on the Paper. In the second line of the
proviso the word "rent" should be
inserted instead of "rents." The reason
I venture to suggest this Amendment to
the Committee is because of certain
technical legal difficulties in the way of
limited owners making leases of land for
schools and playgrounds. If limited
owners want to make a long lease that is
a lease for 99 years-for the purposes of
the erection of a school it is necessary,
unless there is a special power in the
settlement to apply to the Court of
Chancery. If such limited owners want
to make a lease of ground which is not
a lease for building purposes but for a
playground it cannot be done under the
existing law unless there is special power
in the settlement. My Amendment
I have not confined it to one acre.
I recognize that present day ideas are
different to what they were fifty years
ago, and it may be desirable to make
leases for a greater extent than one acre.
I have provided, just as it would be in
the case of a limited owner making a
lease under the Settled Land Acts, that
the lease should reserve the best rent
that can be obtained, so that no damage
would be done to the remainder of the
Settlement. It is further provided that
leases should only be made to the education authorities. I think the Committee will agree that this is not a case in
which any injury could be done to any
owners, especially as the Ministry of
Education have to approve every transaction which it is proposed to carry out.
The whole design of the Clause is a very
limited extension of the existing power
under the Settled Land Act, 1882, which
I think would greatly facilitate the
taking of ground for schools and playgrounds either in the country or cities.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): This Financial Resolution
arises on Sub-section 3 of Section 1 of the
Bill, a Sub-section which is designed to
give authority for the necessary Exchequer Grant-in-Aid of the expenses of
benefits and administration to be made :-
(1) in respect of increased benefits to
certain deposit contributors, and (2) In
respect of benefits to certain additional
classes of insured persons created by the
proposed new law.
——
My hon. Friend (Mr. Gordon) in his
Second Reading statement has already
touched upon the changes in the law proposed by the Imperial Bill in this connection. Shortly, the changes are
Deposit contributors who by reason of the
state of their health cannot obtain
admission to Approved Societies are
to be included in a special section,
and insured for the normal benefits
of the Act. Additional funds will
be necessary for this purpose, and it
is proposed to obtain them by diverting
certain sums forming part of the Deposit
Contributors' Fund together with the
interest on the balances in the fund,
sources which at present not available for
this purpose.
These sums will in future
be paid into the account of the special
deposit contributors' section, and as they
will enable extra benefits to be paid they
will attract a grant from the Exchequer
in aid of the cost of those benefits and
of the expenses of administration. It is
estimated that the total amount of the
new State grant on account of the special
section of deposit contributors will amount
to approximately £100 per annum.
The Bill further provides that the interest which has accumulated in the
Deposit Contributors' Fund up to 31st
December, 1927-subsequent interest is to
go to the special deposit contributors'
section as explained earlier-shall be
credited to the Reserve Suspense Fund,
the main purpose of which is to provide
credits of capital sums in respect of new
entrants into insurance. The actual expenditure of this money on benefits and
expenses of administration will not take
place immediately, but will be spread
over a considerable period in the future.
The relative Exchequer liability, in conformity with the actual expenditure, will
also be spread over a considerable number
of years, and is estimated at approximately
£1,200.
It is estimated that the addition of the
two classes of insured persons to be created
will have the effect of bringing ultimately
into compulsory insurance under Clause
17 of the British Bill about 1,000 additional persons in Northern Ireland, and
the additional Exchequer liability involved is estimated at £280 per annum,
after the expiry of the usual waiting
periods. I beg to move.

With regard to National Health Insurance generally, I think those of us who
were in the British House of Commons
at the time this Measure was passed will
realize that the inspiring motive of those
who fashioned that legislation was not
simply to give benefits to people when
they were sick, but it was to build up the
general health and stamina of the community and to fashion machinery by
which a more physically perfect race
could be maintained. One of the things
done towards that end was to give as fine
a system of medical services to the people
as it was possible to give them.
I am
quite well aware of the fact that at the
time the National Health Insurance Bill
was first introduced there was considerable hostility to it, especially from the
agricultural and rural parts of Ireland.
I differed from that view myself, although I was a member of the party.
You voted against

it.

Now, what conclusion are we to arrive at
from those figures? In considering the
economic and industrial conditions that
prevail here we must remember that large
numbers of people who are struck off the
unemployment list are people suffering
from debility. They are not necessarily
sick, but no humane doctor would refuse
to certify them, because their debility is
so great that they can make a very effective case for being placed on the list for
benefits. The result is that the approved
societies are compelled to pay health
benefits, because these people are unable
to receive unemployment benefits. That
is one of the reasons. The second reason
is that in England-and this to some
extent accounts for the figures I have recited to the Committee-there is a
complete examination of the patient when
he goes to the panel doctor. In Ireland
he can only go to the dispensary doctor,
or get a certificate for which I understand
half-a-crown is paid.
The great bulk of these people will not
go to the dispensary doctor. I understand that not twenty-five per cent. of
insured persons will go to a dispensary
doctor. They feel and rightly sothat there is a taint of pauperism about
these dispensaries and they will not go.
-
At all events their medical examination
is of such a cursory character that they
may be certified for health benefits, but
there is nothing done to improve their
health or to give them a thorough examination-in a word to cure them.
Nothing is done to cure them, and the
great object, as far as I can gather from
the speeches of those who formulated this
legislation and carried it through and,
indeed, of all reforming minds in England who are in favour of this legislation
and its character, was that this should be
a preventive Measure, a Measure to
prevent disease from growing, to build up
the physical power of the industrial
citizens, and to create a healthy and wellordered community as a consequence.
None of these things can be done as long
as our industrial community in Northern
Ireland are denied the advantages of
medical benefits which have proved such
a blessing to the industrial workers in
Great Britain.
I, of course, would prefer that we
should have a full opportunity of reconsidering this whole question of National
Health Insurance. I do not know whether
the Government intend in the near future
to introduce legislation in regard to the
Poor-law, but if they do I take it we will
have one broad and comprehensive
Measure, which will deal with the whole
question of poverty and sickness and all
the attendant evils-physical evils-that
result from our industrial life in these
large towns. But, like my hon. Friend
(Mr. Kyle), I would be glad to hear from
the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews)
whether the Government have considered
this question and what they propose.
Having departed from the step-by-step
policy by which we are to get similar
legislation to that which is enjoyed by
the English people—if it is a real step-bystep, and not a step when it suits you and
a step off the line when it does not suit
you, if there is to be anything like uniformity in the march of the dual regiment
of British and Ulster legislators surely
the worker in Northern Ireland is entitled to precisely the same advantages as
are given to industrial England and
Scotland. For these reasons- I am glad
to see the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews) taking notes-I trust he will
enlighten the Committee, because up to
this there has been a most mysterious
silence as to what the Government propose to do in regard to this matter.

17. I offer my most emphatic protest.
against the system going on in Northern

Mr. BARBOUR: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. Gentleman. I am afraid
that what the hon. Gentleman has said is
directly in conflict with the information
which I have taken the trouble to procure

Neagh had been taken away from our
fellow-country people by what some Members of this House actually consider to
be a foreign judiciary. I would like to

fact that it was in one of our own courts
here in Ireland that this matter was decided. It was brought first of all before
Judge Ross, and he held that the plaintiff's title in the whole of the Lough was
irresistible, and was not displaced by evidence of long-continued use on the part of
the public.
Of course, an appeal was taken from
that decision, and the case came before
the Supreme Court, once again in our own
country of Ireland, and an injunction was
granted in respect of Toome Bay, with
liberty to apply in respect of any further
injury to the fishery. The next step was
that an appeal was lodged in Dublin, in
the Court of Appeal, in the year 1908.
On that occasion the Lord Chancellor,
Lord Justice Fitzgibbon, and Lord Justice
Holmes unanimously approved of Judge
Ross's judgment. Therefore, here we
have these two decisions in our own Courts
in Ireland in favour of those who claim
to be the owners of the eel fisheries in
Lough Neagh. On the case being taken
to the House of Lords the judgment was
sustained.

There is, first, the appointment of arbitrators for the valuation of land taken by

Government chemist for the Province.

auditing the accounts of educational endowments, and the fourth is the appointment of officers in connection with the
probating of small estates. It is anticipated that the effect of the Bill will be not

In the first place the Bill proposes to
make a small change in the method of
appointing official arbitrators to decide
the value of land compulsorily acquired by
local authorities, where agreement has not
been reached between the acquiring authority and the owner in regard to price. Examples of the kind of compulsory acquisition to which I refer are acquisitions
under the Labourers Acts, under private
Acts of Parliament promoted by local
authorities, such as the Belfast Corporation, or the acquisition of land for road
widening purposes under the Bill which
has recently passed through this House.
The existing system of appointment of
arbitrators was set up by the Acquisition
of Land (Assessment of Compensation)
Act, 1919, under which a panel
of arbitrators was to be selected SO
far as Ireland was concerned by
the Lord Chief Justice, the Master
of the Rolls and the President of
the Surveyors' Institute in Ireland. This,
as you see, was carried into effect about a
year or a year and a half prior to the
transfer of the Parliament to ourselves.
These arbitrators were to hold office for
certain periods, and while holding office
were not to engage in private practice.
Under that Act there was set up for all
Ireland one whole-time official arbitrator,
because clearly there was insufficient work
in Ireland for a regular panel of persons.

The Bill, therefore, proposes that in

shall have power to nominate one or

of Clause 1, which I have dealt with at

15 MAY 1928
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 15th May, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
KILKEEL WORKHOUSE.
1. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. William
McMullen) asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact
that during 1926 Messrs. R. McKee &
Sons, Kilkeel, made an offer to the
Kilkeel Board of Guardians to lease
a portion of the Workhouse, at a
rent of £40 per annum and taxes:
whether this offer was refused, and, if so,
for what reason; whether it is a fact that
the portion of the workhouse in question.
has since remained vacant and has fallen
into a state of disrepair; and whether he
can state what valid reason the Guardians
had for refusing this remunerative offer
and retarding the development of a new
industry in the district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In 1927 Messrs.
R. McKee & Sons offered to take certain
portions of the Workhouse premises at
Kilkeel at a rent of £45 and taxes. The
Guardians informed Messrs. McKee's
solicitors that they were prepared to
accept this offer, but excluded from the
letting a field which Messrs. McKee desired
to include, and no further action was
taken by the firm in the matter. It,
therefore, appears that the negotations
were broken off by Messrs. McKee and not
by the Guardians.
The premises have since then remained
vacant, but it is not a fact that they have
fallen into disrepair.

2. Mr. KYLE (for Mr. William
McMullen) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that some rent
agents in Belfast are attempting to secure
from prospective tenants of houses under
£8 valuation arrears of rent alleged to
have been owing by the previous tenant;
whether he will state if this is legal, and,
if not, what steps he proposes to take to
protect the poor of the city.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not
aware that rent agents are demanding
payment of arrears of rent due by former
tenants as a condition precedent to the
granting of a new tenancy, but if they
are doing so their action is illegal and
contrary to the provisions of Section 8 of
the Increase of Rent and Mortgage
Interest (Restrictions) Act, 1920.
The tenant can recover any such payment under the terms of that Section, and
he has, therefore, full protection at the
present moment.

Civil Authorities (Special Powers) Bill,
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second

""
Sir DAWSON BATES: In moving
the Second Reading of this Bill, which
has for its object the making permanent
of the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act of 1922, I do not desire to say more
than is absolutely necessary as to the
causes which led the Government at that
time to introduce the Measure. Sufficient
to say that we were at that time faced
with an organized campaign of murder
and outrage which had for its primary
object the destruction of the Constitution
of Northern Ireland which has been conferred on the people of Ulster by the
Government of Ireland Act of 1920.
The ordinary law was found quite insufficient to deal with the situation that
had arisen, and I venture to say that if
the principles which were embodied by
us in the Civil Authorities Act of 1922
had been recognized by our predecessors
in the government of Ireland, Ireland
would not hold to-day the unenviable
reputation she does amongst civilized
countries in regard to murders.
The Government of Northern Ireland
realized to the full the futility of depending upon the ordinary law of the land to
meet that situation. The campaign of
intimidation alone prevented the ordinary
law running, and I venture to say the
passing of the Civil Authorities Act, combined with a firm but fair administration
of its provisions, brought about the peace
which, I am glad to say, we are enjoying
to-day.
The introduction of the Civil Authorities Act was in the nature of an experiment, and, for that reason, we deemed it
advisable at that stage not to make it
permanent. We realized at that time
that it might be necessary to pass an Act
of a still more drastic character. Our
experience in regard to the working of
that Act has been most satisfactory, and
we therefore find that, after that experience of its working during the last five
years, we are justified in coming to
Parliament and asking Parliament to
continue it.
con-
Some hon. Members may suggest that
because we are enjoying peace, and have
our full liberty, that now is the time to
relinquish the powers which were
ferred on the Government by that Act.
It is always a pleasant thing to forget the
unpleasant past, but people are foolish
who do not profit by the experience of the
past.
The PRIME MINISTER:
hear.
Hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I say here today that while we are living in peace
there are combined forces at work in our
Province and elsewhere that would, on the
slightest relaxation of the law, take full
advantage of the fact to plunge this
Province into a welter of bloodshed
similar to that from which we have only
recently emerged. When I make this
statement, I do so with a full sense of
responsibility.
It would serve no useful purpose to
reveal to the public the full information
which the Government possess. I propose.
with the liberty of the House, to quote
only a few examples to show the outward
activities of that organization which has
for its avowed object the overthrow of
His Majesty's Government in Northern
Ireland, as by the law established, and
the substitution therefor of an Irish
Republic.
I may be told that this organization
aims at achieving its object by so-called
constitutional means. I must confess
that I find difficulty in understanding how
a process, which has for its object the
overthrow of a Constitution, can be constitutional in its procedure.
There is, however, a section of this
organization-and it is the larger section
-which aims at attaining its end-the
establishment of an Irish Republic-by
physical force, and for this purpose,
recruits and maintains what is known as
the "Irish Republican Army." That
title is only too familiar to those who recall the past.
Mr. KYLE: How far past?
Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon.
Friend will get an opportunity of putting
his point of view afterwards. I am sure
he will forgive me if I am not to be
diverted by question and answer.

We are all anxious, and not the least
the Government, to see peace and security
as a part of the settled conditions of our
daily lives. Can anyone deny that it is
the existence of this Act and its steady
but fair administration which has brought
about peace and maintained it? No lawabiding citizen in the whole of the North
of Ireland is subject to-day to any harassment by reason of the existence of the
Act. It does not affect the law-abiding
citizen; it only operates against the lawbreakers.
There remains to be considered only
the question of what the period of the
continuance of the Act should be. This
matter has given me long and anxious
consideration. Various views have been
put forward for my consideration. In
many cases those views have come from
persons for whose ripe knowledge and
sense of responsibility and high citizenship I have the greatest respect. I am
naturally anxious, so far as I safely can,
to give effect to these views. Having
weighed up our responsibility and our
duties on the one hand, and this information and suggestions made on the the
other hand, the Government have come
to the conclusion that, while there may be,
and is, a certain amount of risk in recommending a shorter period than that indicated in the Act, yet in the hope that
it may make some appeal to the better
judgment and the moderation of those
who have uttered these threats, examples
of which I have already read, the Government are prepared to take the risk of asking the House to continue the Act for a
period of five years and not to make it
permanent.

3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Prime

early date on lines similar to those which
are at present before the Imperial House,
requiring the promoters of existing dogracing tracks, as well as those in contemplation, to receive in the first instance

Sir DAWSON BATES: As the hon.
Member is no doubt aware, the Bill at
present before the Imperial Parliament is
not a Government Measure, but was introduced by a Private Member.
a
It is open to the hon. Member, if he so
desires, and if he considers that the circumstances of dog racing in Northern
Ireland require a measure of local control,
to introduce a similar Bill, but as the
situation is not yet fully developed, even
in Great Britain, I cannot give any undertaking that the Government will automatically follow the lines of British
legislation in this respect, as it is obvious
that before the Government could accept
responsibility for similar legislation, it
would have to be satisfied after detailed
inquiry, and on consideration of representations from responsible authorities,
that the present and future conditions in
regard to dog racing were of such a
character as to justify, if not demand, a

Mr. DEVLIN: Mr. Moles, before we
proceed to the discussion of the Estimates
on the Paper I desire to call your attention to a ruling you gave in which you
said that on the first of these
Estimates we can only discuss the
general policy of the Ministry involved, and not the details. This is, I
believe, the last of the Allotted Days, and
we have not been allowed to discuss a
single detail in connection with the various
Estimates that have been presented to the
House. I want to know whether the
ruling still continues.
The CHAIRMAN: This is not, to
begin with, the last Allotted Day. The
ninth day will be the last day for Committee proceedings, and the tenth day
will be devoted to Report. My ruling
stands for the simple reason that it is
founded upon the Rules of Procedure and
the Standing Orders as adopted by this
House.
The invariable procedure is the reason
for it, I think, is obvious, and I have indicated it more than once--that the introduction by the Minister of the first
Estimate is the proper time for the discussion of policy in relation to all the
activities of that Ministry. That practice
is founded upon the fact that in the
first Estimate the Minister's salary is
found, and his salary is supposed to cover
all his activities. I did not rule that
policy only could be covered. What I
did rule was that only upon that occasion
could policy form part of the discussion.
I further ruled that the details of that
particular Estimate were open to discussion at the same period, but that
discussion of the details of the later Estimates could only be taken as and when
those Estimates were presented for consideration. That is the invariable practice founded upon our Rules of Procedure,
as I have indicated.
Mr. HEALY: Does this not mean, if
it means anything, that there are certain
Votes the details of which we cannot dis-

Sir DAWSON BATES: In introducing
this Estimate I think it desirable to remind the Committee that the Ministry of
Home Affairs comprises two self-contained
Departments, one dealing with law and
order, justice, police, prisons and ancillary
matters, and the other with local government administration. I propose to
cover as far as possible the operations of
the two Departments, but before reviewing the various activities of the Ministry
I think it well to refer in some detail to
the features of the Estimate which is now
before the Committee dealing with the
staff.
further reduction of one clerk has been
made in the Accounts Branch of the
Ministry following the disbandment of the
Special Constabulary. On the other hand
we have found it necessary to increase the
Local Government Audit Staff by two
assistant auditors.
As the Committee will see, the Estimate
shows that we are asking for a net sum for
the current financial year of £58,242, as
compared with £60,110 for last year, the
result being a net decrease of £1,868. It
will also be observed that the total staff
employed by or attached to the Ministry
as provided for in the present Estimate
is 150 as against 157 for last year. A
reduction in staff of four clerks and two
temporary inspectors has been found
possible cwing to the transfer of the administration of the non-Contributory Old
Age Pension Service from the Ministry of
Home Affairs to the Ministry of Labour
under Section 1 of the Act passed last
year. A consequential reduction in the
typing staff of two has also been made. A
Our experience during the last few
years has gone to show that the work of
Local Government Audit has been steadily
increasing in volume and importance, and
that it was nearly impossible for the Local
Government Auditors to keep up-to-date
in their work. This increase is due to a
large extent to the additional statutory
audits imposed by recent legislation, e.g.
-the audit of the accounts of County
Infirmaries and of Regional Education
Committees.
Apart from these changes there are no
other outstanding features in the Estimate
as submitted to the Committee. I might,
however, refer to Sub-head "G"-Special
Inquiries in which it will be seen that
provision has been made for a sum of
£250 to cover the expenses of the Departmental Committee of Inquiry into the
relationship between landlord and tenant
in the case of non-agricultural holdings.
Hon. Members are, no doubt, aware that
there has been in certain localities in
Northern Ireland considerable agitation
and pressure put on the Government to
inquire into the question of the leases in
urban centres, and I accordingly appointed
a Departmental Committee under the
chairmanship of Mr. Megaw to inquire
into the matter.
I propose now to deal at some little
length with the activities of the Home
Office Department of my Ministry, which,
as I have already explained, is concerned with law and order, justice, police,
prisons, etc. In the first place, as the
Committee has, no doubt, observed from
statements made by the various judges
which have appeared from time to time in
the Press, the present condition of affairs
in Northern Ireland in regard to law and
order is on the whole satisfactory. The
number of specially reported cases in 1927
was 1,434 as compared with 1,581 in 1926,
which I think
is very
satisfactory.
Although there was in some aspects a
noticeable increase in such crimes as
burglary, on the whole the figures I have
quoted show that there has been a decrease in serious crimes.

As I said yesterday, attempts to foment
trouble in our midst by disloyal elements
were apparent, but these activities have
been kept well in hand by the vigilance of
the police, and in consequence of the
wholesome effect of the powers vested in
the Government by the Civil Authorities
Act. In this connection I might also
refer to the great influence for peace
which is exercised by the presence of the
"B" Special Constabulary-a band of devoted men who have in the past rendered
valuable services, and who still for a
nominal retaining fee keep themselves in
training and hold themselves in readiness
to come to the assistance of the Government in the event of any emergency.
As regards the regular police force in
the country, we have endeavoured and
have succeeded in effecting a small but
steady decrease in strength with a corresponding saving to the Exchequer. Steps
have been taken and are being taken with
a view to effecting further economies by
closing up certain barracks in areas where
the responsible police authorities are
satisfied that effective police supervision
can be afforded by police from barracks
in adjoining areas.
As evidence of the economies which
have been and are being effected in connection with police expenditure, I think
it well to quote the following figures:-

I am asking you one
Sir DAWSON BATES: It will be
more satisfactory if the hon. Member will
put his questions all together. The only
important item of interest in connection
with our prison administration during the
past year was the escape of four prisoners
from Belfast Prison. As the Committee
is aware, two of these prisoners were
subsequently recaptured and are now in
custody; the remaining two up to the
present have succeeded in evadng recapture. Very full and exhaustive
inquiries were made at my direction into
the circumstances under which the
escapes were made, and from an examination of the various reports submitted
to me I am satisfied that no blame could
be attached to any individual officer of
the staff.
At the same time, while the experience
of all Governments is that it is extremely
difficult to make such water-tight arrangements as will rule out all possibility of
escape, it appeared to me from the reports
submitted by the officers that certain improvements both in connection with
administration as well as structural
arrangements could be effected which
would minimize the possibility of escape.
Due and proper steps have been and are
being taken in this respect. It, perhaps,
would not be out of place for me at this
stage to state that the recapture of the
two prisoners referred to reflects considerable credit on the police authorities of
Northern Ireland.
On the other hand, a convict confined
for a protracted period receives quite a
number of privileges subject to good conduct. He is allowed, for exampleand I hope I am .not wearying
the Committee by these details
to have his own shaving kit and
knife and fork. At exercise he is allowed
to associate with other convicts, and once
a week he is allowed what is called an
"hour's association" in a room specially
set apart for this purpose. He is also
allowed to receive newspapers, and after
a period of three years he is allowed to
have his meals in association with other
convicts in a specially provided dining
room.
I also think it necessary to point out
that the administration of Belfast Prison
presents exceptional difficulties owing to
the fact that, for reasons of economy, it
has been found necessary to utilize the
Prison not only for ordinary prisoners but
for convicts sentenced to penal servitude.
The latter class are those who are guilty
of serious crimes or who are old offenders.
In regard to their treatment in prison it
is necessary to make certain special
arrangements for the convict prisoners.
They are confined in a separate part of
the institution and receive separate and
distinct treatment. The ordinary prisoners confined for minor offences do not
receive any privileges beyond visits and
letters and being allowed to read newspapers after a period of six months' good
conduct.
Educational privileges are also provided not only for the local prisoners but
also for the convict prisoners, but it has
been found desirable to keep the classes
-that is the ordinary prisoners and the
convicts quite distinct. Those for the
convicts are held in the afternoons and
those for the local or ordinary prisoners
in the evenings. The convicts as a rule
prove to be a more difficult class to deal
with than the ordinary prisoners. All
that is necessary in the latter case is strict
supervision. but in dealing with the convicts the duties imposed on the prison
staff are much more onerous and exacting.
There is always, as is obvious amongst
this class, a more pronounced tendency to
escape and to give trouble, and the supervision of the convict wing of the prison
imposes a very heavy strain on the prison.
staff.
During the past year no less than 40
lectures were held in the prison, mainly
of an educational character or else dealing with history and travel. In addition
to these lectures 12 concerts were held.
As regards the educational classes, two
are held each week for the ordinary
prisoners and two for convict prisoners,
the subjects taught being mainly history,
geography, arithmetic, drawing, and so
on. These lectures are held under the
auspices of the "Toc H" Society under
the direction of Mr. W. Armour in cooperation with Mr. Foster, the principal
of the Belfast Academy, and other publicspirited ladies and gentlemen. I cannot
speak too highly of the valuable services
rendered by those who are associated in
this good work.
As I have already pointed out on a previous occasion, the prison at Londonderry

is used merely as a local prison for remand
and short-term prisoners. It has been
suggested on one or two occasions that it
might be possible for us to close this
prison altogether, but this suggestion has
been found on examination to be impracticable, owing to the difficulties in
dealing with cases from the North-West
of the Province, and the expense that
would be entailed in escorting them
to and from Beifast and Londonderry.
I may take this opportunity of mentioning that at the present time we have
no means of dealing with criminal lunatics
in Northern Ireland. The Committee
will see from the sum put down that we
have to send them to Southern Ireland
where we are charged what we consider
to be the rather extortionate amount of
£192 in respect of each criminal lunatic.
To meet that difficulty we have under con.
sideration a scheme whereby we will provide accommodation for them in Notthern Ireland. but hon. Members will
appreciate the difficulties that arise in
setting up such an institution having regard to the smallness of their numbers,
and we are only prepared to establish such
an institution provided we see that it will
mean a saving to the Exchequer.
Turning from the subject of prisons to
that of the Borstal Institution, which has
recently been established at the Malone
Training School, Belfast, I am glad to be
able to say that the establishment of this
institution has had on the whole satisfactory results, the number of Borstal
boys in confinement remaining in the
vicinity of 40. I have had the good
fortune to be able to secure as the Visiting
Committee of that institution a body of
earnest, devoted and hard-working gentlemen, some of whom are Members of this
Committee, and I am glad to take this
opportunity of expressing to them individually and collectively my appreciation
of their valuable services.
satisfactory. One or two escapes, which
are almost inevitable in an institution of
this character, have occurred during the
year, but the cases requiring disciplinary
action at the hands of the Committee
have been comparatively few.
One of the most important aspects of the
duties and responsibility of these gentlemen is in connection with the after-life
of the boys, and I think it well to say
that since their appointment they have
shown themselves most active in regard to
the raising of funds with the object of
providing each boy on leaving the institution with a fair chance of earning a living
and leading an honest life. On the whole,
having regard to the character and antecedents of the boys, their conduct has been
Consequent on representations made to
me by the Committee and my Inspectors
I have, with the approval of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance,
made arrangements for effecting structural
alterations in the institution which will
have the double object of separating more
completely the Borstal boys from the Reformatory boys, and at the same time
providing more adequate and suitable
