Turning now to the question of the
administration of justice, as the Committee is aware, the Ministry is responsible
for the local arrangements for the holding
of Petty Sessions Courts, and for the administration of duties by Clerks of Petty
Sessions.
It has been the definite policy of the
Ministry since I have had the privilege
of occupying the post I now do, to endeavour to secure for these posts the most
suitable officers, and with this object
steps have been taken where opportunity
has arisen to amalgamate Petty Sessions
Districts so as to enable larger salaries
to be offered, and to induce a better class
of men to come forward as candidates for
the appointments. This process has been
carried out in 16 cases during the last
few years with satisfactory results. I
should say, however, that before taking
action of this character the Ministry invariably consults the Resident Magistrate
of the district concerned and the police
authorities.
In this connection also I am glad to
say that there is a movement on foot for
the appointment of Probation Officers in
Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). Up to the present, outside the
City of Belfast the probation system does
not appear to have been widely utilized
or fully appreciated. For the information of hon. Members I may point out
that the appointment of a probation offi-
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs 1764
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
cer for a Petty Sessions District is in the
hands of the magistrates of that district,
but as the remuneration of these officers
is dependent on the number of cases
supervised by them, and as the rural
areas afford comparatively few of these
cases, it has hitherto been found difficult
to obtain suitable officers in these districts
owing to the limited amount of the fees
payable. The magistrates seem to have
some objection to putting individuals who
are brought before them on probation.
I do think, while it is a matter entirely
for themselves, that this Act is not
utilised in the way it might be.
In order to get over this difficulty I
issued an Order recently increasing the
remuneration payable to probation officers
and allowing for a 25 per cent. increase
to officers serving in districts outside
Belfast and Londonderry. At present
there are only 10 of these officers in
Northern Ireland, six in Belfast, two in
Londonderry, and two in rural areas.
The total number of cases dealt with by
the officers last year was 147, of which
129 occurred in Belfast. I can only
express the hope that the value of the
probation system will be more fully
realized, and that the various benches
throughout the country will give serious
consideration to the question of endeavouring to find suitable persons in
their districts to do this valuable, though
perhaps not highly paid, work. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Turning now to Local Government
Administration, I perhaps might first
make a reference to the question of
the report of the Commission which
recently sat to consider this matter. The problem is such a big
and very complicated one that I
feel that no step should be taken by the
Government or by Parliament until it is
made clear beyond all doubt that any
change made will be for the better.
Accordingly, I am having every recommendation scrutinized and examined in
the closest possible way by expert officers
with a view to having put clearly before
the Government when the time comes the
results of the various recommendations
both from a financial as well as an administrative point of view.
important question, and in this respect
I would also like to state that even after
I have, on the advice of my officers,
arrived at any particular conclusions, it
will be necessary for those conclusions to
be examined from a financial point of
view by a special expert Committee,
having regard to the desirability for ensuring that as far as possible the changes
of whatever character they may be will
not impose additional burdens on the
ratepayers. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
Under the circumstances I can hold out
no hope of very early legislation on this
The whole object of the Commission
was to endeavour to work out what would
be the most economical and efficient
system in regard to the various circumstances, and I propose before making any
suggestion to satisfy myself and this
House when the time comes that as far
as possible no more expensive arrangement is put into operation unless there
are undoubtedly satisfactory reasons for
doing so.
I would like now to deal with the question of Housing, and first of all I think
it well that the Committee should be informed of the undoubted success of the
recent Act passed by the Parliament of
Northern Ireland increasing the subsidy
on the smaller workers' houses from £80
to £100. The best means, I think, of
bringing this home to the Committee is
to quote our records for the last six
months as compared with the corresponding records for the same months in the
previous year.
Taking the last six months, that is up
to April, 1928, I find that no fewer than
2,211 houses were approved for erection
as against 715 for the corresponding six
months up to April, 1927. I think those
figures justify the action of the Government in increasing the subsidy. Let me
take the total number of houses approved
of under our own Housing Acts since the
first Housing Act was passed in 1924. I
find that the total number of houses
approved of in Northern Ireland during
these four years was as regards builders
no fewer than 9,104 houses and as regards
local authorities 1,343 houses. In other
words, during the last four years as a
result of the Housing Acts of Northern
Ireland we have had 10,447 houses approved, and 7,171 of these houses have
actually been completed.
I will now turn to the provision of
accommodation for labourers in rural
Estimates-

areas under the Labourers Acts. I think
it will interest hon. Members to see what
has been accomplished there. Those hon.
Members who take an interest in the subject are aware that the first Labourers
Act was passed in 1883. I find that
from then up to the time the
Northern Government took over this
administration only 6,118 houses were
built. That was during a period of 35
years. Since the present Government
took over the administration no fewer
than 1,590 houses have been built in
Northern Ireland under the Acts.
On the whole I consider that the
Government and Parliament of Northern
Ireland have some reason for congratulation in connection with the very rapid
development of building, due to the inception of the housing subsidy scheme in
Northern Ireland.

£120,000 already mentioned, that is, 106

Turning to the question of Road Traffic,

for some time in connection with the improvement of traffic conditions. As the
Committee is aware, these changes
followed from the passing of the Motor
Vehicles (Traffic and Regulation) Act,

1926. In the first place a new system of
penalties for motoring offences became
operative and while, no doubt, the more
stringent penalties imposed for the
serious offences have to a very considerable
extent improved the traffic conditions in
Northern Ireland, it is somewhat regrettable, as I have already stated, to
find that the toll of accidents, fatal and
otherwise, still mounts up.
As regards road accidents, the number
of accidents which occurred during the
calendar year 1927 was 1,438. This
figure includes 100 fatal accidents, the
number of persons killed being 102. The
total number of persons injured as a result of road accidents during the year referred to was 1,530. During the first
three months of the year 1927 the total
number of accidents was 268, the number
of persons killed being 12. The total
number of persons injured during this
quarter as the result of road accidents was
276.
The corresponding figures for the first
three months of the year 1928 show a total
of 269 accidents, the number of persons
killed being 28. The total number
persons injured as a result of road
accidents during this period was 270.
These figures indicate that the number of
fatal accidents is increasing in spite of the
many endeavours being made to render
the roads safer for the public. An examination of the figures would show that
the total number of serious accidents for
the year 1928 is likely to be greater than
for the year 1927.
I would like to summarize shortly our
operations in regard to this Act as regards omnibuses. The number of omnibuses in respect of which applications for
regular licences have been received (to the
end of April, 1928) is 730. Out of that
number of applications 481 of these
vehicles were found fit as a result of inspection, 85 were refused licences, and in
62 cases the applications were cancelled
at the owners' request. Apparently the
owners realized the vehicles were of such
a hopeless character that they could not
be licensed. Thus 628 of the applications
have been dealt with, leaving 102 vehicles
to be tested, or 14 per cent. of the total.
As hon. Members are aware, it takes the
inspectors time to get round all these
vehicles. Of the 481 fit vehicles satisfactory insurance policies have been produced in respect of 372, and regular, or
what we might call permanent, licences
have been issued. The remaining 109
vehicles are operating on provisional
licences pending the production of satisfactory insurance policies. Adding the
102 vehicles remaining to be tested, the
total number of vehicles operating at the
present time on provisional licences is
211.
A short time ago we introduced the
Roads Improvement Bill which has not
yet finally passed either the Senate or
this House. That Bill is for the purpose
of facilitating local authorities, for widening corners, narrow roads, and removing
obstructions to view, and make the roads
suitable to modern conditions.
I can
only express the earnest hope that this
Measure when passed, coupled with the
Act of 1926, will go a long way towards
decreasing the appalling number of motor
accidents on our public roads. As regards
the question of the licensing and control
of omnibuses which followed the passing
of the Motor Traffic Act, I am glad to be
able to say that this new system has been
put into operation without imposing any
unnecessary hardship or dislocation to the
owners of these vehicles.
I come now to Motor Hackney Carriages,
which are better known as taxicabs.. The
number of motor hackneys in respect of
which applications for regular licences
have been received up to the end of
April is 1,816. Of these vehicles 1,162
were found fit, 164 were refused licences
and in 358 cases the applications were
cancelled at the owners' request. Thus
1,684 of the applications have been dealt.
with, leaving only 132 vehicles to be
tested-about 7 per cent. of the total.
Of the 1,162 fit vehicles satisfactory insurance policies have been produced in
respect of 828, and regular licences have
accordingly been issued. Of these vehicles
334 are operating on provisional licences
pending production of insurance policies.
Adding to this figure the 132 vehicles remaining to be tested the total number
operating on provisional licences is 466.
As regards drivers, hon. Members are
aware that the driver of a public vehicle
in Northern Ireland in addition to having
a satisfactory police report must show
that he is physically fit and is capable of
driving. The number of applications received for drivers' licences up to the end
of April is 2,792. 2,175 of the drivers
Estimates-

Ministry of Home Affairs
16 MAY 1928
have been found satisfactory and in 57
cases licences were refused. In 135 cases
the applications were withdrawn at the
applicants' own request. Thus only 425
applications remain to be dealt withapproximately 15 per cent. The 425
drivers referred to are operating on provisional licences pending test.
The number of applications received for
conductors' licences up to the end of
April is 754. Licences have been granted
in 749 cases and refused in three. In
two cases the applications were withdrawn
at the applicants' own request. It will
be seen that one of the first results of the
new system was to remove from our roads
those old ramshackle machines of various
characters which were not only an eyesore
but a danger to the persons using them.
As regards Public Health Administration, there are a few points which I
would like to bring to the notice of the
Committee. Hon. Members are aware
that some time ago we passed the Milk
Bill, dealing with grade "A" tuberculin
tested milk. A start has been made, six
licences have been issued and two more
are under consideration. This may be
regarded as an encouraging commencement, seeing that the grading of milk has
been so recently brought to the notice of
producers in Northern Ireland. One or
two cases have been brought to the notice
of the Ministry where persons not licensed
have been using covers bearing the words
"Grade A-T.T. Milk," and warnings
have been issued to these persons.
In
future where a fraud of this kind is
brought home to a producer it is proposed
to institute legal proceedings.
The Dairies and Cowsheds Order of
1908 and the Bovine Tuberculosis Order,
1926, ensure a very considerable supervision of the conditions under which milk
and meat are produced and sold, but
several authorities have urged that stricter
measures are necessary, particularly in
rural areas, and the Ministry has the
matter under consideration. One of the
principal points to be determined is the
most suitable authority to administer any
Order that may be made, and in this connection the recommendations of the Local
Government Commission will be duly
considered.
The Order in force here, which is similar
to one issued in England and Scotland,
has worked smoothly except in regard to
cream. The prohibition of preservatives
in cream met with strong opposition from
the trade both here and in Great Britain
on the ground that the cream would not
keep long enough to reach the consumers,
and that it would be impossible for the
producer to carry on business.
With regard to the question of Preservatives in Food, by an Order of the
Ministry the use of preservatives and
mineral colouring matter in food has been
prohibited subject to certain exceptions.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: Hear,
hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The authorities in England and Scotland have refused to modify the Order, but in view of
strong representations made to me by the
dairying interests I decided, after consultation with the Minister of Agriculture,
to postpone its operation till the 1st
January, 1929, so as to give the trade an
opportunity of finding some method of
overcoming the difficulty I have referred
to. It should, however, be pointed out
that medical opinion is strongly against
the use of boric, which is the preservative
mainly used in cream, for the reason that
it is injurious to health, and so far as
the Ministry of Home Affairs is concerned
we cannot undertake to postpone the operation of the Order beyond the date mentioned, 1st January, 1929.
As regards the welfare of the blind,
the only complete scheme in operation is
that of the Belfast Corporation. The
Ministry has been endeavouring to get
other county councils to make a beginning, and recently County Down has
initiated a scheme. It was intimated on
a previous occasion that when the Census
figures were published, which would probably give them considerable light on the
dimensions of the problem, the Ministry
would again take up the matter with the
various local authorities. These figures
are not yet available, but the reports regarding Belfast, Armagh, and Antrim
have now been published, and it is expected that the volumes relating to the
other counties will shortly be issued.
As regards the question of Medical Inspection and Treatment of School Children, schemes are in operation or are being
made in all the areas except Londonderry
County Borough, Armagh County, and
Ballymena, but in these cases the Ministry
are pressing the education authorities to
frame schemes and to put the Act into
operation.

This Estimate gives the figure of 2,916
Within the past few weeks a Police

-
I have already twice explained to my

When I was advancing arguments against

Regarding the allocation of the Force,
I raised this question on the Police Measure to which I have referred. The Committee, I suppose, on either side of the
House will not be in sympathy with my
arguments, because I must admit that
in this House more than half the Members
either represent the City of Belfast or

not prevent me from calling the attention
of the Committee to the fact that Belfast
city gets an undue advantage, so far as
the allocation of the Force is concerned.
It has one-third of the population, and
one-third of the valuation of the Six
Counties, and it has one-half of the
Force, while it pays only an additional
additional sum of £25,000 a year, in accordance with the arrangement recently
made with the Corporation of Belfast.
If Belfast were to get the proportion that
I hold it should get, and no more, then
it would only get one-third of the Force.
I do not see why it should not be able
to do with one-third of the Force, and if

£100,000 a year. The citizens of Belfast
receive that amount by the Act to which

charge for the past five years. In addition, as this Committee knows, a sum of

Government propose to remunerate
the members of this force, it cannot
be intelligently argued that it is remuneration for loyalty. The head of that
Department is in receipt of £2,000 per
annum, and I have never heard that he
exposed himself to very great danger
during all the trouble that took place in
Belfast. If my information is correct he
encouraged other people to run risks, and
then when these other gentlemen had run
risks he compelled some of them to emigrate when the whole trouble was over.
Perhaps I am incorrectly informed, but
that is my information.
The people who actually did whatever
fighting was required to be done, the people
who bore the heat and burden of the day,
are to be remunerated to the extent of
91d per week in the case of one section,
and 13d per week in the case of another
section. Was there ever anything more
ludicrous? We have been repeatedly told
by the Prime Minister and by the spokesmen of the Government that this force
is being kept in existence as a reward for
their loyalty, and the services they rendered to the Province, and that while the
noble Lord remains as Prime Minister
this force will never be disbanded.

Now in regard to the number of accidents on the roads, when this matter was
last discussed I asked for some information

We are making what would appear to me
to be most comprehensive provision in regard to all matters except the important
things. We have improved the surfaces of
the roads and quite rightly-we have
widened the roads, we have rounded satisfactorily very dangerous corners, and we
have cleared away hedges where it has not
been possible for a driver to see clearly
round a corner. We seem to have taken
every question into consideration except
the main one.
On a number of occasions before I have
urged on the Committee that some attention should be paid to the number of hours
for which men are employed on these buses
each day.
I believe that if I had the
information at my disposal I would be able
to present an unanswerable case for the
limitation of the hours that these men
work per day. I am informed, I do not
know how reliably, that a large number
of these accidents take place when the
drivers are not in a physically fit condition, when their eyesight and physical
capabilities generally have become impaired as a result of the tension during
a very lengthy day. I would ask the
consideration of the Department to this
question. Seeing that the Roads Bill has
not finally passed this House-it is receiving the attention of the Senate at the
moment, I understand--I would ask that
the matter should have the serious consideration of the Department, that they
should take the point I have mentioned
into consideration and see how much importance it carries, and if it carries sufficient importance then the Minister would
be justified in attempting to limit the
hours per day that these drivers, particularly, work.
This would not be any departure from
precedent, because I understand that a
person must be physically fit before the
authorities will give him a certificate. He
will not be given a certificate if he is under
a certain age, so why should the Ministry
not take steps to ensure these men are not
overworked to such an extent as to impair
their fitness, and as a result of their fitness
being impaired run the risk of very
serious accidents occurring on our roads.
We want to minimize the number of accidents taking place on our roads. They are
very considerable at the present time, but
there is no reason why they should not be
substantially reduced, and I am sanguine
that if the right steps are taken a very
satisfactory reduction will be effected.
Finally I want to discuss the question
of Poor Relief. It is possibly an attempt
to anticipate the disclosures that will be
made by the Minister of Finance in regard
to this matter. That is possibly not in
order either, but Belfast has borne a very
heavy burden in regard to outdoor relief.
I understand, although I have not fully
read it up to the moment, that the intention of the Budget introduced recently in
the British Parliament by Mr. Winston
Churchill was to relieve industrial areas
that have been very heavily taxed as a

chief will be able to give us some information as to whether or not their Department propose to depart from the attitude
they have adopted on this question up to
the moment.

relieve if our rates for the city are much
higher than they will be across the water.
There will be certain commodities in which

quite wrong to think there is only two
and a half hours to complete the discussion

full outstanding days for the hon. Member.

The PRIME MINISTER: Certainly.

The PRIME MINISTER: I took as
the basis the sum of money, the number
of Votes, and the number of hours allowed
in this House as compared with those at
Westminster. If the hon. Member will
look at the amount of the Estimates there
and the amount of the Estimates here and
take the number of days and the number
of hours he will find that the time in this
House works out at exactly twelve times
the time allowed there. I do not want to
detain the Committee, because I think
more time has been wasted in discussing
this particular matter than should have
been wasted. We might have gone on
with the consideration of the Estimates.
I would like to say one thing further. One
of the difficulties, I understand, has been
that it has been impossible for the Leader
of the Opposition to arrange definitely the
important Estimates they would like to
have discussed, so that they might be put
down in order as is the custom between
the Whips on the other side.

We will do everything we can within

to fit in with the Opposition in every

The hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) knows
quite well that at Westminster at the end
of the twenty allotted days a large number,
in fact, the bulk, of the Estimates have
not been touched at. He must remember
going through the Lobby sometimes for
several hours voting against or in favour
of the Estimates for the discussion of which
no time was found in the House. That is
an old custom. A certain number of days
are allotted and the Opposition make their
plans for using that time to the best advanin
tage. That is all I have to say regard

I would like to point out in connection

There is also another reason why I want

the right hon. Gentleman presides over is

The right hon. Gentleman and his Department, it seems to me, are absolutely
incapable of running the home affairs of
this part of the country. They have
either bitten off more than they can chew,
or they are not competent, probably both.
The hon. Member for West Belfast
(Mr. Devlin) gave a list of the things the
right hon. Gentleman deals with. It
would be impossible for any man, or any
superman, to have a comprehensive grasp
of all those. I notice in reading the Press
of the Province, great criticism of the
opportunities for improving the health of
the community. In Portadown the milk
supply is being criticized. We read that
in Lurgan the same thing is happening.
We find in various parts of the Six
Counties outbreaks of scarlet fever. All
these matters are dealt with by the Ministry of Home Affairs, and, if I may say
so, are dealt with very badly. It seems
to me that they pay far
tention to the police force that the noble
Lord, the Prime Minister, talked so much
about to-day, than they do to the real

more atwhether they are the saviours of society,

and far too much money, in my opinion,

This business of law and order that has
had so much stress laid upon it to-day
and yesterday is important. One recognizes that without some form of law and
some form of order modern society cannot
get on. But, after all, to 90 out of every
100 of the population of Northern Ireland
the health services, the services for the
uplifting of the people of the Province,
are of far more importance than the payment of £66,000 or £666,000 for special
police, whether they are paid to guard the
right hon. Gentleman's political party or
Then, apparently, the activities of the
police Department are centred round the
sending of special reporters to report the
speeches in Orange Halls. The other day
a meeting was held in West Belfast Orange
Hall, and there was a special police reporter to report the speeches delivered at
that particular meeting. Last night or

and anybody who has read anything

far more attention were paid to the health

sight better off in Northern Ireland than

That is all I want to criticize with regard to the Ministry of Home Affairs. It
seems to me the Ministry of Home Affairs
or the Minister-I do not want to make it a
personal attack upon him-but I do want
to say that it is my honest opinion they
are trying to do more than they can do,
and more than they are competent or
capable of doing. I think the sooner the
right hon. Gentleman and his Department
resign or probably it would be better
for the Government to resign and go to
the country, and let us get more attention
paid to the things that really matter.
After all, the life of a child, or the life
of a woman, or the life of a man in the
Province would be far more important
than the subjects the right hon. Gentleman has dilated so much about. These
are the things that, in my opinion, affect
us in this Parliament far more than the
points that have been raised by the noble
Lord, the Prime Minister, in regard to
the saviours of society.

Specials in Northern Ireland as the militia

accurate in his figures when he compared
the cost of the police in Northern Ireland
with the cost of the police in Glasgow. As
the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh pointed out, the gross total as
quoted by the Prime Minister was not
correct. The total for the Royal Ulster
Constabulary is £833,251, and if you add
to that £68,734 which the Special Constabulary costs you get a grand total of
£902,035 that our police force costs.
Another item that was pointed out by
the Comptroller and Auditor-General was
an allowance to the police of £3 per
annum for the upkeep and renewals of
bicycles. The Public Accounts Committee asked if there was any check at all
as to the necessity for this allowance, and
I think the answer they received was that
there was no check at the present time.
I notice that a great proportion of the
men who receive this allowance are in
the city of Belfast, where one would think
the allowance was less needed than anywhere else. One can understand that
such an allowance might be very necessary
in the country. With regard to the Special
Constabulary, so far as I am able to make
out from this Vote, the pay which the
members of the "B" force receive amounts
to £27,075, and the administration costs
amount to £39,709. I do not know how
this can be justified, and I do feel that
the Royal Ulster Constabulary alone
should be sufficient to maintain law and
order in Northern Ireland.
I think there is also room for great
economies in respect of prisons. The
right hon. Gentleman quoted the average
cost of prisons as being £112 in 1925,
£108 in 1926, and £96 in 1927. I am
sure we are glad to see that the scale is
decreasing, but I think it is largely
accounted for by the drop in the cost of
living. There is also the point raised by
my colleague for County Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) that while the average cost of
maintenance of a prisoner is £96 5s 8d,
the average gross cost to the country of a
prisoner is £151. Salaries and administration absorb more than one-third of this
Vote if I was right in the figures that I
took down as the right hon. Gentleman
gave them to us.
There is one other point in connection
with this. The right hon. Gentleman said
that the policy of the Government at the
present time, in the interests of economy,
was to amalgamate petty sessions districts
one with another in connection with the
appointment of petty sessions clerks, and
that in these cases before making an
appointment they consulted the R.M. I
do not know whether the right hon.
Gentleman said they consulted the local
magistrates or not. In connection with cre
of those amalgamations that have taken
place, namely, the amalgamation of Randalstown and Toome petty sessions
districts, I would like to ask if they consulted the police, if the police advised
against the amalgamation, and if even
against that advice they did amalgamate
these districts. I think both the local
magistrates and the police were against
the amalgamation. Of course, I may be
wrongly informed, but that is the information I have received.
I think it is rather discouraging that,
despite the Motor Vehicles Act that we
passed last year, accidents should have increased on our roads. I certainly would
support the hon. Member for Derry (Mr.
Leeke) with regard to the way in which
these prosecutions have been carried out.
I think it is up to the Government to be
a little more generous in the administration of that Act, for I am afraid the
prosecutions have increased a good deal.
There was a general outcry against the administration of the Act, and I think it had
some effect. Take, for instance, the
method for testing speed at the present
time. I find myself on these buses because
they are a democratic mode of travel and
suit my purse very well. What do I find?

There was a very famous admiral at one

Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON asked
the Prime Minister whether the Opposition Chief Whip received an invitation
to the luncheon to be held at Stormont
on the 19th instant, prior to the laying
of the foundation stone of the Parliament
Buildings; if not, can he state the
specific reason why the invitation was not
issued; and, if the answer to the first
part of the question is in the negative,
can he state why the Government Chief
Whip was invited.
The PRIME MINISTER: The answer
to the first part of the question is in the
negative; as to the second, I was under
the impression that the Socialists were
the only party in opposition which had
appointed a Whip. As that party consists of only three members I felt that the
Leader of the Opposition could adequately
represent it at the official function referred to. With regard to the last part
of the question, the Chief Government
Whip was, of course, included on account
of his high official position.

Members on the Opposition benches are
prepared to accept the Whip of this individual-even the Independent Unionists?

luncheon as an insult.

closing day there was only one tender in
for the contract. The tender was opened,
and I presume the tenderer's price was
noted. Fifteen minutes after the closing
hour another tender, which was about
£140 less, was handed in. Naturally the
first tender was rejected, and the second
tender was accepted.
Just about the same period there was
another contract for the sale of clothing.
You will remember that on the first occasion the Government accepted the lowest
tender although it came in late. In connection with the second contract there
was a late tender which was the highest.
The other three were lower in price. Did
they act consistently in this case? No,
they rejected the late tender although it
was the highest and we would have benefited from it, and accepted the first tender
it being the lowest. What sort of consistency is there in such a business transaction? Surely to goodness the ordinary
man in the street cannot be blamed if he
comes to the conclusion that there is
something gone astray at the Home Office.
Such a thing in itself warrants the
presence of the Minister here.

Take up an Irish history, and you will
find there was an insurrection in 1798,
another in 1847, another in 1867, and
another in 1916. The periods between
all those insurrections were peaceful and
quiet. What brought about peace in
Northern Ireland, as it brought about
peace in Southern Ireland was the "Dump
Arms" order of the Republicans' commander. Do not have any humbug about
it. The moment that order was put into
operation peace spread over the land,
North and South, and we have had it
since.

The hon. Member (Mr. Collins)
opposite adopted a very peculiar criticism in connection with Londonderry
Prison. He says the money we are
spending on that prison is too much for
the return we are getting. Of course,
being a lawyer, I suppose he would
rather the prison was full of inmates.
Mr. COLLINS: No. I would rather
keep them out of prison. They are no
good to me if they go in.
Mr. GRANT: It is a tribute to his
profession that they have been able to
keep these people out of prison. But
he does not surely suggest that after we
set up a prison with warders and all that,
and supply them with uniforms, then,
because he and his colleagues
are
so able defenders of these people that
they do not get into prison, we ought to
close the prison altogether. We all rejoice that there are so few people in these
particular establishments, and we hope
they will continue to have few inhabitants, but at the same time it is absolutely
necessary to have these places, and I
think under the circumstances the criticism of the hon. Gentleman was not
justified.
In conclusion, I just want to say that
I am delighted that the Minister has seen
his way to increase the grant in aid of
the Borstal Institution. The Leader of
the Opposition (Mr. Kyle), the hon. and
gallant Member for Armagh (Major
Shillington), the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. McAllister), who sits on
the opposite benches, and myself are
members of the Committee of this
institution. We take a very lively
interest in it, and we are very glad to
pay a tribute to the Minister of Home
Affairs for the help he has given to this

institution for Northern Ireland.

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON: There is
just one point in the reply of the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Hanna) to which
I wish to refer. I feel that the Committee
appreciates the very careful manner in
which the Parliamentary Secretary endeavoured to reply to the points raised on this
Estimate, but he seemed to convey to me
the idea that his Ministry was not responsible for inefficiency in the Departments
over which they have control. He cited
three or four cases that had been raised
by hon. Members of the Committee as to
the efficiency of his Department, and he
seemed to repudiate on behalf of the
Ministry responsibility for this inefficiency.
Now I hold that if the Ministry is to
justify itself at all the hon. Gentleman
must see that its Departments are efficient.
That is the only justification he can make
to this Committee and to the country for
the money spent in the Ministry. We may
be blamed for raising questions that are
not important, but we have not raised any
question that the Comptroller and
Auditor-General did not find it necessary
to raise before the Public Accounts Committee. I say that in some of the Departments under the control of the Ministry,
Departments for which the Parliamentary
Secretary seemed to repudiate responsibility, the Reports of the Public Accounts
Committee and of the Auditor-General reveal a slackness which would not be tolerated in any business community. I feel
that the Parliamentary Secretary should
not lay it down as a dictum that his
Ministry should not be responsible in
every degree for the inefficiency of the
Departments they control.
fact that at least one Department has been

The PRIME MINISTER: I will discuss it outside the House, but I do not
think it is in order to go back to that time
and to discuss whether the Ulster people
were rebels or gallant men defending their
liberties. I do not think that would be
in order at the present moment. I am
only going to say that I believe it was
the worst day's work that was ever done
in the Imperial House of Commons when
they dropped the Arms Act and cleared
the way for all the agony and trouble aud
disorder that have taken place in Ireland.
Looking back, no one can tell what might
have happened in regard to the peace and
quietude of this country of ours if that
Act had not been taken off the Statute
Book. Are we as responsible Ministers
to do the right thing because it is difficult,
or the wrong thing because it is easy?
One of the arguments used just now
was that it was a stain upon the escutcheon
of Ulster that this Act should be on the
Statute Book at all. It was in order to
remove a little of the stain that my colleagues and I considered it was better to
have this Statute continued for some
time longer rather than to have this sort
of discussion year after year. I would
point out to hon. Members that it does
no good in time of peace-which I am
glad to say we are enjoying at presentto raise this question year after year.
You may have four years of absolute
peace, in which case this Act will be
practically shelved. If it is practically
put away, and never taken off the shelf
at all, what harm will it do to anybody?
It has done nothing but secure peace in
our country. Extending the operation of
this Measure for some five years means
that we will not have this annual discussion. It has almost become part of the
law of the land. It has been in operation, I think, for some six years.
Remember that from time to time acts
of a very dangerous character are carried
out in our area which my two right hon.
Friends beside me have to treat under
this Act. If we were to take this Act off
the Statute Book and if there was going
to be a recrudescence of the difficulties we
had a few years ago let hon. Members
think of the long-drawn-out, tedious and
painful work it is to get powers given to
a Government again to deal with an outbreak of that kind. Suppose Parliament
is not sitting. Imagine the first shots of
rifles at the Border or elsewhere, or any
other depredation that might take place.
Suppose those young men in Derry my
right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
spoke about the other day were to take
it into their heads to start a difficulty such
as we had before, it would mean calling
Parliament together, and going through
the tedium of getting powers again to
deal with an extraordinary situation-and
what might happen in the meantime?
Some hon. Member said that we should
think of the life of even one child in Ulster
before we should do some particular act
in connection with the Home Office
when the Estimate was being considered
yesterday. Is it not far more important
for us that we should take every precaution and that we should have the full
machinery lying to our hand in order that
we may deal with any unexpected or untoward happening in our midst?
I would like to raise one other point.
Are we certain that the Republican forces
have ceased to wish to overawe Ulster or
to compel her to go with the rest of Ireland into a Republic? I ask myself that
question constantly. I observe what is
going on, even in London. I follow reports that reach me from time to time and
which are of a confidential character. I
say the Republican party have not by
any means ceased to hope that at some
time or other they will be able to coerce
Ulster into the rest of Ireland. I would
be false to my trust and my colleagues
would not be doing their duty to the
country unless in a matter of this kind
they not only took up but retained the
full powers they considered necessary in
order to defend Ulster as it was defended
before. Therefore, I do not mind admitting quite frankly to the Committee
that I was in favour from the very beginning of making this Measure one that
would be part and parcel of our law for
all time.
I was in favour of making it perpetual
from the very beginning, but out of
respect to representations which my right
hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) received
from sources he has confidence in we
agreed that we would get this Measure
continued for another five years. If at
the end of five years anyone standing at
the this box in my place is satisfied that
no further attacks upon the liberties of
the subject in Ulster are going to take
place, if he is satisfied there will be no
further attempt by the Irish Republican

TRACTS FOR MATERIALS.
1. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
foreign produced materials are being used
in road construction in five out of the Six
Counties in Northern Ireland, and
whether, in view of the fact that the Road
Fund is being paid by the people of Northern Ireland, he is prepared to circularise the various authorities to the
effect that they should use material produced in Northern Ireland, and thereby
increase employment for local workmen.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I would refer the
hon. Member to the reply given by me in
this House to the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) on the
29th March last, in which it was
pointed out that the Ministry of
Home Affairs has already sent
every road authority in Northern Ireland a circular letter indicating that all
contracts for or incidental to road works,
including contracts for materials, are to be
placed preferably in Northern Ireland,
but in any event not outside the United
Kingdom, and that where possible
to
materials of Northern Ireland or British
manufacture or origin are to be specified.
I am not aware that the road authorities
in Northern Ireland are disregarding the
terms of this circular letter, which was
issued on the 20th July, 1926.
HAIRDRESSING TRADE REGISthern Ireland, and whether the Government is prepared to introduce legislation
to meet the requirements of this business.
TRATION.
2. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received representations from employers and employees engaged in the hairdressing
business to the end that a system of
registration should be established in Nor-
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have received
representation from members of the hairdressing trade advocating the establishment of a system of registration in
Northern Ireland, but I am not in a
position to state that the Government is
prepared to introduce legislation on the
lines suggested.
The hon. Member will doubtless realize
that it would be a dangerous precedent for
the Government to establish by accepting
the responsibility of introducing legislation which would have the effect of
conferring vested interests on a class of
employers and employees for which there
is no justifiable reason.
A reference to the Acts on the Statute
Book dealing with the registration of
members of the various professions will
show that Parliament in the past has
only conferred such privileges in cases
where the activities of the members of
those professions affected the general
health or well-being of the community.
It would be difficult to establish the
principle that hairdressing can be regarded
as a profession affecting either the health
or the well-being of the community, and it
will also be obvious that if the principle
were accepted in connection with this
trade it would be impossible to refuse
similar recognition to other trades of a
similar character.

THE BUDGET.
FINANCIAL STATEMENT, 1928-29.
Mr. Pollock's Speech.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House approves the proposals
of the Government for meeting the financial requirements of the year.'
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I would remind the House that
this is the seventh annual Budget of Northern Ireland which I am privileged to
present to the House to-day.
may be that as we have experienced seven
lean years, we may now hope to enter
seven years of peace, prosperity and contentment.
I do not know whether hon. Members
attach any of the traditional significance
to the mystical number. If they do, it
When presenting my Annual Statement of Revenue Expenditure in the past,
I have avoided embellishments, as is befitting when prosaic financial questions
are under discussion.
But in view of the completion of seven
years of Ulster's autonomy, and having
regard to the coincidence of Saturday's
remarkable function, I feel, if I may be
pardoned for a few moments, that I
should indulge in a short retrospect of our
progress during the period of our local
responsibility.
It will be remembered that it was on the
threshold of the year 1921 that the British Parliament decreed that the Six Northern Counties of Ireland should be constituted an autonomous State, with federal
relationship to the Kingdom. This was
a new and startling experiment unprecendented and unknown in British history.
It ran counter to all our preconceived
ideas of the political and economic unity
of these islands, and it was, therefore,
with much misgiving and many doubts
and fears that we undertook the responsibility of conducting the affairs of a selfgoverning State within the ambit of the
Kingdom.
All this, of course, is well-known to the
world. But what is not so well-known,
perhaps, or so fully appreciated is the
initial encouragement and material help
given by the British Government-
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK and especially by
British Departmental Officers, to aid our
faltering footsteps.
Apart from the Statutory obligations
of the Government to provide our public
buildings, we were given the help of
British financial guarantees in respect of
some of our earlier obligations, such as
Ulster Savings Certificates.
And perhaps, most important of all, we
are under great obligation to Mr.
Baldwin-
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK--when, as Chancellor
of the Exchequer, he agreed to the creation of an Arbitration Committee,
whom the duty was assigned of providing
to

a formula for the annual adjustment of
our Accounts with the Central Authority.
And now at the end of seven years of
self-government, some of them anxious
years but all of them years of effort, it is
pertinent to inquire whether we have justified the hopes of those who trusted us,
and believed in us, or belied the vaticinations of those who directly and covertly
worked for our undoing.
My answer to such an inquiry is that
we have internal peace firmly established.
Further, speaking with full knowledge
and authority, I can assure the House
and the country that the financial credit
of Ulster is unassailable.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: Proof of this lies in
the fact that bankers are eager to bid for
our Treasury Bills at rates closely approximating to those of Britain." Again,
under our Loans Guarantee Act, London
issuing houses accept our Government
guarantee on terms that differ only by the
merest fraction from those of the Imperial
guarantee.
But our surest safeguard is the fact
that not only have we paid our way, but
out of our savings have accumulated
Sinking Funds and Reserves, as well as
one-third of our National Revenue, and
I have to express my obligation to Mr.
Churchill for his appreciation of this fact
in his recent Budget Statement.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: Finally, during the
period under review, we have contributed
to the Imperial Services sums amounting
to £22,000,000, and our great ambition
is to be able, with returning trade recovery to contribute in larger measure.

In speaking of Death Duties, I would

curities: We are entitled to collect duty

Before leaving the subject of Death
Duties I would like to take this opportunity of making a brief reference to life
insurance policies. It has been decided
that the moneys payable under a policy of
insurance taken out by a person domiciled
in Northern Ireland with a company
having his head office in Great Britain are
to be regarded as a British asset. Unless
specific provision is made on the face of
the policy for payment in Northern Ireland, the Death Duties do not accrue to
our Exchequer. As the result of discussion with the Association of Life Insurance Companies, future policies issued
in Northern Ireland will be payable here,
but various complex questions of mortgages and so forth prevent the companies
from initiating any general action so far
as existing policies are concerned, and so
I would appeal to all patriotic persons
holding life insurance policies to
approach the company concerned, with a
view, if possible, of having them endorsed so as to provide that on maturity
they should be paid here. There is quite
a substantial amount of revenue involved.

Before proceeding further with my
Statement I would pause for a
few
moments to consider a question of some
interest. The inauguration in the Irish
Free State of a new currency system has
not excited very much comment in our
Province, but it has had the direct result
of raising a currency question of no little
importance here, especially in relation to
the ordinary banking operations of the
country.
cover, and "excess issue," against which
the bank must hold gold and silver coin
or Treasury notes. The fiduciary issue,
which requires no cover, was determined
by the Irish Bank Act of 1845, allocating
to each bank a fixed amount and totalling
in the agregate £6,354,000 for all the
banks then in Ireland. The reason for
fixing definite amounts was the undesirability of leaving the banks free to issue
as many notes as they wished.
There are at present six banks operating in Ireland who have the right of
issuing bank notes. Three of them have
their head offices in Ulster and two in
London, the remaining one being domiciled in the Free State, Now, there are
two portions of the note issue of each
bank, namely, "fiduciary issue," against
which no legal tender need be held as
The privilege of these fiduciary or free
note issues has been of material value to
the banks, and has probably facilitated
the opening of branches in many rural
places where the volume of business is not
sufficiently large in the ordinary way to
justify the expense involved in providing
banking facilities. Moreover, the note
issues are very useful to the agricultural
community, which, as is well known,
deals with bank notes rather than with
cheques.
So long as a common currency system
obtained in the whole of Ireland, these
arrangements proceeded in their normal
way, but on the creation of a new currency
system by the Free State powers were
taken by that Government to create a new
fiduciary issue for the banks operating in
the South. This is called the Consolidated Bank Note Issue. The total issue
of all such banks was fixed at £6,000,000,
but notes may not now be issued in excess
of the fiduciary issue except in very special
circumstances. This sum is divided
among the banks roughly according to
the scope of their business in the Free
State. Previous to the Free State
Currency Act of 1927, the total free, or
fiduciary, issue which had been allocated
to all the Irish Banks of Issue amounted
to £6,354,000, and it is clear that we
could not expect the whole of that sum
to become available for banking purposes
in Northern Ireland, by reason of the fact
that a separate fiduciary issue of
£6,000,000 had been created by the Free
State for the use of banks in their area.
The problem which confronted the
British Government was, therefore, to
determine upon an approximate amount
of fiduciary issues for the banks of issue
operating in Ulster, and although the
question of currency remains an Imperial
matter under the Government of Ireland
Act, yet at the request of the banks and,
indeed at the request of the Treasury,

my Ministry interested itself with negotations which have extended over a period
of approximately two years and have only
now been concluded.
I am happy to be able to say that
although the difficulties in the way of a
settlement at one time appeared to be
very formidable, yet unanimous agreement has now
been reached-(hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-between the
British Governinent and all the Banks of
Issue in Northern Ireland. I am satisfied
that as the result we are now assured of
a sufficient supply of currency to meet
trading requirements, and that the banks
themselves have not suffered any loss as
the result of the readjustment. The
agreement, however, requires statutory
confirmation, and a Bill with that object
in view is now before the Imperial
Parliament.
We have also been obliged to give careful consideration to the question of the
circulation in Northern Ireland of Free
State currency.
As hon. Members will
doubtless be aware, the Free State
Government has taken every precaution
to ensure that British currency shall not
circulate in the Free State, and indeed the
banks in that area are expressly forbidden
to pay out to the public any currency
other than their own notes and Free State
legal tender. Similar steps will be taken
here. The necessary statutory authority
is now being sought by the Imperial
Government. Although there is bound to
be a small interchange of British and
Free State currency between individuals
residing near the border, yet the existence
of Free State currency should, I think,
cause no embarrassment in the various
trading centres of our area, especially as
I understand that the banks will be able
to issue notes for the use of bona fide
travellers going across the Border, in the
same way that French and other foreign
notes are issued.
A short time ago I entered upon a discussion with the Treasury in order to see
whether arrangements could not be made
to ensure a more satisfactory circulation of
clean currency notes in Northern Ireland,
but the matter was not pursued to a conclusion, since the impending transfer of
the issue to the Bank of England will, it
is hoped, achieve the result I had in view.

While on the subject of Entertainment
Tax, I desire to touch on a small matter
in which agriculture is interested As we
all know, Ireland has long been famed for
its horses, and considerable profit has
accrued to farmers and others directly
engaged in the industry of horse-breeding
as a result of the fine specimens of
thoroughbreads which have and still are
being produced. This is a section of the
agricultural industry which in the past
has received little or no encouragement
from the Government, and I think that
it is desirable that we should, if at all
possible, do something, however small, to
stimulate the industry in view of the
material benefit which it confers on the
Province.

that in 1685 James II granted a Charter
to a body of public-spirited people who

The Budget-
Finance Minister's Statement 1944
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
by Mr. Churchill will have on our

Firstly, it will be remembered that the
Imperial Chancellor proposes to alter the
law relating to relief from Income Tax
in respect of children, in order to increase
the allowance to £60 for the first child
and £50 for each subsequent child. It is
expected that this concession will cost
£30,000 this year in Northern Ireland
and £70,000 in a full year. May I give
an example of the practical results of this
change? In the case of a person whose
household consists of a wife and three
children, and who has an income of £600
a year, there will be, first the reduction
of £100 because of the standard, the marriage allowance reduction of £225, rebate
for children £160. His taxable income
will be only £115, and the rate at which
he will be expected to pay is 2/-. Therefore, his total income tax on an income of
£600 will be £11 10s Od.
Next, turning to the changes made in
Customs and Excise Duties, the reduction
in the duty on sugar will diminish our
revenue to the extent of £51,000 this
year and £66,000 in a full year.
The duty on mechanical lighters will
yield £1,000 this year and the same in a
full year
The duty on buttons is estimated to
produce £2,000 this year and £3,000 in a
full year
Lastly, we have the duty of 4d per
gallon on oils, which is estimated by the
Imperial Chancellor to produce in Northern Ireland £160,000 this year and
£200,000 in a complete year. I feel it is
a source of satisfaction that the Chancellor
has agreed to withdraw his proposed tax
on paraffin. From the figures of consumption in Ulster, I feel that the burden
of a tax on paraffin would have fallen
more heavily on our people than on
Britain, where this article is not used so
generally as in Ulster.
As there is evidently a considerable
degree of general misunderstanding in
regard to the application of the proceeds
of the duty on petrol, it is desirable that
I should take this opportunity of stating
the position occupied by Northern Ireland
vis-a-vis Great Britain.
The net effect of these various changes
is estimated at an increase in revenue of
£84,000 this year and £70,000 in a full
year. Therefore, to sum up, our total
revenue in respect of the current year is
estimated at the sum of £10,842,000.
against which we have expenditure
totalling £10,770,000, so that the surplus
I budget for amounts to £72,000.
The petrol duty in great Britain is not,
as seems to be commonly supposed,
specifically appropriated to the scheme for
granting relief from local rates. In the
first place, I apprehend that the revenue
thus raised will be by no means equal to
the burden of the Rating Relief Scheme.
In fact, the revenue from the tax on oils
in Britain is estimated to produce in a full
year about £13,300,000, allowing for the
abandonment of the tax on paraffin, while
the Rating Relief Scheme will cost up to
£30,000,000. That scheme has in Great
Britain been adopted as a part of the
Government's programme for the assistance of agriculture and of the basic industries of the State, and the duty on
petrol merges in the general body of taxation which will meet the general
expenditure of the country.
Pursuing this matter a little further,
hon. Members will recollect that the
Rating Relief Scheme is not intended to
come into operation in Britain until the
autumn of 1929, with the result that the
imposition of the petrol duty this year
provides the Chancellor with a very useful
addition to the surplus which he intends
placing to a Suspensory Fund, presumably
in order to lighten the charge of the
Rating Relief Scheme in its initial years.
I have explained this subject at some
length, because of the fact that I have on
several occasions been asked whether the
revenue which we will derive from the
petrol duty (estimated by the Imperial
Chancellor to amount to £200,000) will
be adequate for the purposes of any
Rating Relief Scheme which may be introduced here. If I endeavour to answer
these questions, I find two important
difficulties.
First: The Statement of the Chancellor
in his remarkable Budget outline was confined to Britain and, therefore, did not
afford us any knowledge as to how such a
scheme would work out here, where conditions are not identical.
Second: Important changes have
already been made in the original pro-

further changes may not develop before

But assuming that the main features

the scheme does not begin to operate
until October, 1929, I propose to follow
the Chancellor's programme of forming a

definite provision for this until we know
our exact position in relation to the
project.
This tax should produce in Northern
Ireland the sum of £200,000 in a full
year, an amount which, so far as I have
been able to make a forecast, would be
quite insufficient to give relief to agriculture and industry on the scale outlined.
by the Chancellor.
I am, however, investigating the whole.
question of the incidence of rates in the
Province in order to reach some conclusion
as to the benefits which our basic industries, including agriculture, may
expect to derive from the application of
the scheme, but I may say at once that
it is the intention of the Government to
ensure that our farmers will not be placed
in a position less favourable than those
in Great Britain. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
As regards our basic industries, the
burden of rates falls on them with even
greater weight than the rates on farming
land.
The Chancellor gave an example of the
crushing nature of this burden on the
cost of the production of steel and ships.
Let me apply the same reasoning to our
linen trade.
First, the farmer pays his rates to produce flax; the scutcher follows with rates
on his mill; then comes the spinner's
rating on his large buildings, the weaver
on his factory, the bleachers, finishers,
etc., on their works. All this accumulation of charges means that every yard of
linen is charged with rates on at least six
different processes before the final stage
of marketing is reached.
force, so that the same measure of relief
should be afforded.
Therefore, it is the Government's view
the arguments which apply to
British industries apply here with like
I expect that many hon. Members are
impatiently awaiting an opportunity of
assailing me with conundrums concerning
the implications of this very important
subject. But it is so intricate and so
many interests are involved that I cannot
do more at the present time than state
the general policy and intentions of the
Government, and this I have already
done.
In order that the subject may receive
the mature and detailed consideration it
requires, I have appointed a small and
efficient inter-departmental committee to
inquire into all its aspects, and I hope,
by the autumn, to be in a position to
deal with it more comprehensively.
I have now finished my Statement of
the present financial position of our State,
and although the future cannot be said
to be free from financial care and grave
responsibilities, I am persuaded that if
we should be blessed with the return of
trade prosperity, we can face these responsibilities, not, perhaps, with a light heart,
but at any rate with confidence borne on
the courage and fortitude which so far
have carried us safely through. I beg to
move. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

governed by the simple elementary rule
of book-keeping, that "In" is debtor and
"Out" is creditor. For that reason I will
try here to-day to confine myself to dealing with the "Ins" as carefully as I can.
I have knowledge of the fact that the
right hon. Gentleman's hands are tied by
Section 32 of the Act which constituted
this Parliament. That Section created a
Joint Exchequer Board and it says:
--
For the purposes of the financial
provisions of this Act, there shall be
established a Board, to be called the
Joint Exchequer Board, consisting of
two members appointed by the Treasury, one member appointed by the
Treasury of Southern Ireland, one member appointed by the Treasury of
Northern Ireland, and a chairman appointed by His Majesty.
Assuming that Southern Ireland has gone
out altogether as she has done, the position we find is that on this so-called Joint
Exchequer Board the big brother on the
far side of the water has two representatives to our one, so that we may take it
that when the Minister of Finance gets

Message from the Senate.
I would like to emphasize the point made
by the Leader of the Opposition that it
is a grave reflection on the Government
to pass legislation of this character. It
means, first of all, that your Parliament
is not respected and that the laws of your
Parliament are not observed, because you
have got to employ force and to retain on
the Statute Book the Civil Authorities
(Special Powers) Act. If British public
opinion was definitely informed that the
Parliament of Northern Ireland could only
be maintained because the Government
had special and extraordinary legislation
on the Statute Book I wonder how many
subscriptions the Minister of Finance
would get when he floated a loan in England. I should imagine that under those
circumstances the response would be
neither very prompt nor generous. Having
regard to the fact that this legislation is
not necessary and would be used in a
partisan way, if it was of any use appealing to the Government or to their sense
or idea of fair play I would do so, but
the Government have neither sense nor
idea of fair play, and therefore I hesitate
to appeal to them. I consider I shall have
discharged my duty satisfactorily by voting
against the Third Reading of this Bill.

part. No doubt it gives to the widows

the advantages of the Act, but why should
not all widows-I mean all necessitous
widows and children get this pension?
We know what the value of it is. We
have described it before. I would like to
describe it again, although I know this
House does not like sentiment. I would
like to describe it again, because, great and
beneficent as the Old Age Pensions Act
was as a service to humanity, it was not, in
my judgment, comparable to the value of
the Widows' and Orphans' Pensions' Act.
Old people sometimes have the advantage.
of having their relatives to maintain them
-and sometimes they are not hard to
maintain—but there is no more tragic
situation than that of the mother of little
children with the bread-winner gone and
with no future before them-a woman
with four or five children, the eldest of
whom is perhaps twelve years of age.

She and those children are cast out in the
world without a friend or anyone to help
them.

I must say that I cannot see why he
continues to keep this tax on cinemas and
theatres, because everybody knows that
the competition among those places is so
great that hardly any of them are able to
make ends meet. That is their business?
It is their business to make ends meet,
and it is your business to let them make
ends meet; but how are they to do it if
you impose a tax of this character upon
them. These picture houses are of tremendous value to the public. I do not
know whether the right hon. Gentleman
ever goes to one of them or not. I used
to be a constant visitor to them for three
years. When I was an absentee from this
House I used to go there twice a week.
Then I came here, not for your entertainment, but for my own. I do not go to
places of entertainment for other people's
entertainment; I go to them for my own.
Very well, then, I have a great appreciation of these institutions, because they are
the poor man's theatre. Poor people can
drop into them and at a small charge they
can get a pleasant two and a half hours.
In this period of trade depression, with
people living in wretched slums, and not
able to make ends meet, it is a great thing
that even the little entertainment they do
get should be got in these picture houses.
I come to the Entertainment Tax.
Again, the right hon. Gentleman has
dealt with this tax in a very piecemeal
way. We tried to move him. In fact
I have been standing behind him pushing
him with more than ordinary agility for
the last three years. I think he described
me as one of the battalions of deputations
that waited upon him last year, but I
cannot for the life of me see how he can
defend the continuance of this tax. He
has taken off the tax here, and he has
taken it off there. He has taken a little
bit off the tax in one place, and a little
bit off in another, but what we want here
is the glorious British policy of equality
of treatment. We have heard of step-bystep, of equal conditions for the people of
Great Britain and Ulster. Well, we
want in relation to the Entertainment
Tax precisely the same conditions as prevail in Great Britain.
The right hon. Gentleman admitted
last year that he had seen the balance
sheets of these cinemas, and I think the
one or two theatres that are in existence
in Belfast are in a similar position. He
had the balance sheets before him, and
he knows that these places do not pay.
I object to the tax for that reason, and I
object to it for another reason. I object.
to the incidence of this tax, because it is
a tax upon receipts and not a tax upon
profits. On every ticket that is sold to any
member of the public going into a theatre
or picture house there is a tax. It is the
only tax I know of that is indefensible
from that point of view. If you are going
to maintain a tax upon entertainments or
amusements, whatever you choose to call
them tax the profits. You will not get
any tax by taxing the profits. Shortly
you will get no tax by taxing them as
you are taxing them, because there are no
profits, and I think that is unfair. I do
not think there exists a condition of things
in any part of the world where a business
concern that is not paying has to pay a
big tribute to the State for carrying on
an unpaying business. There might be

That in the opinion of this House the

This Motion which I have put down
relates to the dismissal of an official by
the Ministry of Agriculture in the month
of January, 1927. I endeavoured to

Vote, but the Minister objected and the
Chairman held that his objection was in

I think in this instance it will be shown
that the action of the Government is, to
say the least, not at all creditable. I
suppose that in itself it would not make

official a serious financial and personal

was indicted for a most grave and indefensible action towards a Civil Servant,

ordinary member of the public is to defend himself. I do not know this man;
I never saw him, and I take it that he

He comes before this tribunal. From his

Here is the result, after a complete and

As you are aware, the Civil Service
Committee for Northern Ireland, at

Mr. LEEKE: Congratulations on his
Budget have been showered upon the
Minister of Finance, but there is one thing
I must say I am very disappointed about,
and that is the question of the Bann
drainage. That has been a burning question-it is a national question, not a local
question-for many years. As long as I
can remember in every election that took
place in County Derry after you stated
your political views on Home Rule the
next thing you put in was "I am in
favour of the Bann drainage." It was
recognized by the then Chief Secretary for
Ireland as a question which should be
dealt with nationally, but the Minister of
Finance here with that cleverness he has
always shown in shoving as much as possible of what should be national taxation
on to local taxation has managed to get
the Bann drainage partly out of the question. He told us he gave 75 per cent.
as against 50 per cent. given in England.
I am not sufficiently versed in what the
English Act covers, but the flooding of the
Bann effects every one of the Six Counties
with the exception of Fermanagh. That
a matter that affects the whole nation---
for we are a nation now-should be made
a local charge is to me ridiculous. You
must remember that the agriculturists
have to bear this.
public service of Mr. John McAlonan, an
official employed in the Ministry of Agriculture, inflicted a grave injustice on this
public servant.

With regard to the taxation of motors
I want to raise a point. I have raised
this question again and again—in fact I
think the Minister of Finance himself took
the matter up. The Derry hackney motorowners are in a worse position than any
other people in Ulster. They have to pay
double taxation for operating in Northern
Ireland and in the Free State. They do
no trade towards what I may call the
Belfast end of County Derry at all. It
is all through to the Free State, for they
are only five or six miles from the Border.
All their business is done there, and if they
cannot afford to pay the double licence
duty they are unable to run these motors.
I think a special case should be made, and

I would like to explain, if I am not

No, no)-that the conditions in Great
Britain are entirely different. There is
no relationship between the conditions on
a farm in England and a farm here, especially in regard to valuation. Valuations in England comprise the land and
buildings; and the houses of the farmers
are valued separately. Here, on the
contrary, our farm land is valued as one
item, and the farm houses and farm buildings as a second item in the valuation
lists. Thus we have two valuations-the
houses and the farm buildings in the one
case, and the farm lands in the other.
This implies that if we have to carry out
literally the proposal that has been outlined by the Chancellor of the Exchequer
it will be necessary for us to institute a
revaluation of the entire Province, with
a view to discovering the rateable value
of the land and the farm buildings.

is so determined by a Committee which

at our request, and known as the Colwyn
Committee. The formula by which that
adjustment is carried out is laid down in
the finding of the Colwyn Committee by
which the Joint Exchequer Board is
bound to be guided, so that it is rather the
law laid down by an independent
authority which guides the Joint Exchequer Board in the matter of adjustment. Let me say frankly that we have
been fairly, honestly and honourably

(Hon Members: Hear, hear). I cannot

able to relate in my Budget Statement
yesterday bear out clearly the financial
condition in which the State finds itself
at the end of seven years.

somewhat jocularly by the Member for
Derry (Mr. Leeke) on the question of the
small allowance given to horse-racing.
As I stated, I have no direct connection
with horse-racing.

After all is said and done the consumption of liquor in Northern Ireland is a
very small quantity when it is put over

head per year. I wish to draw the hon.
Member's attention to the fact that there
are only four bottles of stout or beer per
month consumed by the working-class
people in Northern Ireland.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
•
EX-SERVICEMEN AS TEMPORARY
CLERKS.
1. Mr. P. O'NEILL (on behalf of Mr.
Devlin) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he can state how many disabled
ex-Servicemen are at present serving as
temporary clerks in the various Ministries
under the Northern Government, and
what steps have been taken or are being
taken by the Ministry of Finance to absorb
all these men in permanent posts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): There are at present 72 disabled
ex-Servicemen employed as temporary
clerks in the various Departments in the
Government of Northern Ireland. These
men will have an opportunity of competing
for such permanent clerical vacancies as
are reserved for ex-Servicemen.
PREFERENTIAL
APPOINTMENT
OF EX-SERVICEMEN.
2. Mr. P. O'NEILL (on behalf of Mr.
Devlin) asked the Minister of Finance
whether it is a fact that a number of ex-
Servicemen are still serving in a temporary capacity since 1921, notwithstanding the guarantee made that all posts must
be filled by ex Servicemen, preference being given to disabled ex-Servicemen.
explained in my replies to the hon. Member's previous question.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is a fact that a
number of ex-Servicemen are still serving
in a temporary capacity, having been
transferred from the Imperial Service to
the Service of the Government of Northern Ireland in the same capacity on the
transfer of Services in the years 1921 and
1922. No guarantee has ever been given
that all Government posts in the Northern
Ireland Service must be filled by ex-Servicemen, because, obviously, any limitation of that nature in respect of the
method of filling public appointments
would be fatal to the present and future
efficiency of the public service. The
Government, however, has always been
fully alive to its responsibilities to ex-Servicemen, and has fulfilled them to the utmost possible extent compatible with efficiency, and, at the outset, all appointments to clerical posts not filled by
officers transferred from the Imperial Service were reserved for ex-Servicemen.
The more recent arrangements in regard
to recruitment from this class have been
APPOINTMENT OF BOY CLERKS.
3. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Devlin)
asked the Minister of Finance whether it
is a fact that boy clerks are being brought
into the Civil Service, and are absorbing
all these posts which should be given to
the disabled ex-Servicemen who have been
serving since 1921.
Mr. POLLOCK: For the last four or
five years a system of open competition
into the Northern Ireland Civil Service
for youths between the ages of 17 and 19
has been in operation. As indicated,
however, in my reply to the previous
question of the hon. Member, a proportion of clerical vacancies has always been
and is still being reserved for ex-Service
temporary clerks, both disabled and not
disabled.
TRANSFERRED EX-SERVICEMEN.
4. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Devlin)
asked the Minister of Finance whether
he can state what steps the Ministry of
Finance have taken in respect of five ex-
Servicemen (one of whom was badly
disabled) to safeguard these men who
transferred to a Government Department
under the jurisdiction of the Imperial
Government in November, 1925; and
whether these men are on loan to this
Department or actually transferred to
the Imperial Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: I regret that from the
particulars supplied I
am unable to
identify with precision the five cases to
which the hon. Member refers, but I am
aware that in the year 1925 several ex-
Servicemen who had previously been employed as temporary clerks in Northern
Ireland Departments obtained similar
work in Imperial Departments in Belfast,
a number of them on the direct recommendation of my Ministry.
No question arose as to the loan or transfer of
these men to the Imperial Departments,
because they were, in any event, due for
retrenchment in the several Ministries
in which they were serving, their appointments in those Departments having been
of a purely temporary character.

CLASS VI.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
First Resolution read a Second time.
Mr. KYLE: I beg to move a reduction of £1,000. I want to do so as a
protest against the action of the
Ministry of Agriculture in making
a grant of £1,300 to the Ulster
Farmers' Union. In my opinion this
is a case of subsidizing that particular organization to an extent that is not
warranted. This organization consists
of farmers who are well able to maintain
their own trade union without the assistance of the Government. I cannot see
at all that these farmers should be in the
position to take £1,300 of public money
to enable them to maintain their organization in the country. I do not think there
is in the world another country where a
grant similar to this is made to an
organization which exists specifically for
the purpose of benefiting one particular
class of the community. It is just the
same thing as if the trade union I have
the honour to belong to made application
to the Government, holding meetings as
we do for educational purposes, for a
grant of £1,300 to enable it to carry on
its activities. Apparently this Farmers'
Union, despite their activities, have not
been able to convince the farmers of
Northern Ireland of the necessity of cooperation to that extent which, in my
opinion, is necessary to enable the farmers
to get decent prices for their produce.
Nor do they see to it that the agricultural labourers, who are employed on the
farms, are paid a reasonable wage for the
work they do. I think that until the
Farmers' Union or the Ministry of Agriculture they are synonymous are able
to convince the farmers in Northern Ireland of the necessity of co-operation, particularly as regards the purchase of seed,
the use of machinery, and co-operative
marketing, no grant should be made to
this organization.
CLASS I.

be granted to His Majesty to complete.
the sum necessary to defray the charge
