I want also to take the opportunity
afforded me on the Report stage to complain about the lines that the Ministry of
Agriculture seem to be going on in regard to agricultural research. Further,
I want to mention what I think is very
necessary in the interests of one of our
staple industries--I refer to the linen
trade. I suggest that the Government
should take a number of acres of land as
an experimental farm to grow flax. The
Estimates-
Ministry of Agriculture
23 MAY 1928
Ministry could in conjunction with the
Ministry of Commerce set up a central retting plant with the new machinery that is
now available for scutching purposes. I
think if they did so it would probably
mean a fixed price for the farmer for a
period of say five years. It would further
mean that the flax would be bought on
the field by the Government and so save
the farmers any further trouble as far as
the retting and scutching of flax are concerned. I am strengthened in that view
by the Report of the Departmental Committee on the transit, prices, and marketing of agricultural produce which was set
up by the Ministry. Paragraph 45 on
page 17 says:—
We are particularly interested to receive evidence regarding a contemplated
revolution in the manner of dealing
with the flax crop. In brief, the proposed scheme, which is at present under
trial, would substitute a direct sale by
the farmer to the spinner of his flax
un-retted and in the field for the existing system under which the flax must
be retted and scutched before purchase
by the spinner.
The only difference in the suggestion
I am making and the suggestion of the
Departmental Committee is that instead
of the spinner coming in it should be the
Government that should purchase the
flax on the field and that the Ministry in
conjunction with the Ministry of Commerce should establish a station for retting and scutching the flax. This would
enable spinners to get flax even of a better quality than they can get at present.
I think the Ministry of Agriculture have
been very negligent in their duties in
regard to this particular matter which
concerns one of the staple industries of
Northern Ireland. It is worthy of comment also that this Committee I have already referred to on page 7 of this Report refers to the enormous transport
charges which our farmers are compelled
to pay.
It says:
Apples in barrels are carried from
New York, Boston, Nova Scotia, etc.,
to any port in the United Kingdom for
3s 9d per barrel; while apples in barrels from many stations in the County
Armagh cost 4s 5d per barrel to London.
carrying companies to the end that our
farmers may be put on an equal footing
with the farmers in any other part of
the world. Take eggs. They say:
That is a thing that the Ministry of Agriculture could very well take up with the
Eggs from Enniskillen to Liverpool
cost 65s per ton, whereas eggs from
Hamburg to Liverpool cost 50s per ton.
I think those figures are enough to warrant criticizm of the right hon. Gentleman who has control of the Ministry of
Agriculture. I think more important
than either of the matters I have mentioned is the matter of marketing. Every
party in the State has been investigating
the question of the marketing of produce.
They have all said this question is one of
the most important if not the most important. This Committee was, I think,
primarily set up to bring about, if possible,
some adjustment of the prices paid by the
consumers and the prices received by the
producer, but apparently very little if
anything has been done in that respect.
It seems to me as an ordinary observer
that the question of the prices received by
the cultivator for his produce is probably
the most important factor in determining
whether the industry is prosperous or the
reverse. I think that the farmers cannot
be held primarily responsible for this, for
it seems to me that the farmers' chief concern is and ought to be with the actual
work on the farm itself, and that after
that all the facilities possible to be
afforded should be afforded by any Government that take any interest in the
affairs of the country.
It is to be borne in mind that the farmers and agricultural labourers represent
60 per cent. of the entire working population of Northern Ireland. It is, I
think, something well worth the consideration of the Government. The party to
which I have the honour to belong issued
a Report in which it states that co-operation, transport facilities and stabilization
of prices are the three things that could
be tackled by any Government that were
really in earnest on this particular subject.
There are other reforms which will probably take a longer time and which if carried into effect would be of tremendous
importance, but if these three things were
attempted and brought into being in
Northern Ireland it would enable this
basic industry to be in a more prosperous
condition than it is to-day. It is for that
reason I draw the attenton of the House
to what I would call the lack of intelligent

There is another matter I want to mention and that is with regard to the amount
of relief the farmers are getting in agricultural rates. It seems to me that there
should be some line drawn between those
farmers who are really producing foodstuffs and those who have their land in
grass. I am strengthened in that view
by the report of the Irish Labour Party
on Labour and Agriculture in which they
state and most people will agree with
it-
The farmer who tills his land and improves his holding ought to be recognized by the State as worthy of more
generous consideration than the farmer
who leaves his land in grass; and the
sparsely populated areas of rich land
ought to be made to bear a share of
the undue burden now borne by the
thickly populated areas of poor land.
In regard to thickly populated areas, it
is interesting to note that in Northern
Ireland we have a higher percentage of
small farmers than they have in any
other country. In Northern Ireland in
1924 eighty-six per cent of the holdings.
were under fifty acres; Irish Free State,
78.5 per cent; England and Wales, 65.5
per cent.; and Scotland, 66.3 per cent.
It will be seen that the small holders are
greater in number in Northern Ireland
than they are in any other country. It
seems to me to add weight to the opinion
I have expressed that the Department of
Agriculture should be more easily accessible to the small farmers of our Province.
It should not be through the agency of
the Farmers' Union, which is more or
less a political organization, and exists
to bolster up the Government in any
action they may think fit to take, however wrong that action. It is through
the Department itself that these small
holdings should be assisted. I think
additional assistance also should be given
to the agricultural labourers who should
be paid a living wage. The wages paid
in Northern Ireland, in regard to farm
dislabourers, are nothing short of
graceful.

Mr. MARK: I gladly avail myself of
the opportunity of speaking generally on
the very important subject of agriculture
and Government agricultural policy. It
is admitted that agriculture has passed,
and is passing, through a very depressing
time. This depression is world wide. The
farmers of the United States are as hard
hit as those of Great Britain. Germany
and the British Dominions overseas are
making similar complaints, but, notwithstanding this those who are able to study
the situation and who take an unselfish
and unprejudiced view must admit that,
on the whole, great progress has been
made towards the development of the
agricultural industry in Northern Ireland. Whether we take the Horse Breeding Act; the Live Stock Act or the Eggs
Act, in each and all of these we find enshrined a policy and a principle which.
when they have fully fructified, will assist
very materially in placing Northern Ireland in the forefront of countries which
are, with foresight, developing their agriculture. In promoting these Measures,
some of which, as I stated in the House
last week, might be described as revolutionary, it was inevitable that imperfections would arise in their administration, but I have to admit from personal
experience that where such cases
brought to the notice of the Ministry
every effort was made to mitigate any
temporary injustice. The Live Stock
Breeding Act has undoubtedly brought
about a marked improvement in the
class and quality of cattle produced in
Northern Ireland; and so far as the Eggs
Act is concerned, even those who were
opposed to this Measure in the first instance are now compelled to admit that
were
it has re-established our important egg industry in the Cross-Channel markets,
where, before the passing of the Act, this
trade was almost threatened with extinction.
In connection with both these Measures
it will stand to the credit of the Government that they have shown themselves in
many respects to be pioneers in promoting
agricultural legislation, and have displayed a vision which, as I have said, must
ultimately, to a very great extent, promote the prosperity of the farming community in Northern Ireland. Notwithstanding that I think I can claim, in all
modesty, to have as an extensive and
practical experience of actual farming as
any Member of this House. It has been
stated that I, and the organization of
which I have the honour to be President
this year, have been always too subservient
to Government policy. It would be impossible to conceive a more unfair statement. It is true that, generally speaking,
the Farmers' Union have supported
Government policy, but only when, after
consideration and investigation, we have
decided that the Measure or Measures
were in the best interests of agriculture.
We have not hesitated, as occasion arose,
both to criticize and oppose, and as a
result of our representations we have, on
not a few occasions, succeeded in securing
amendments of policy which we felt to be
essential. If we have not, like others
who lay claim to a deeper knowledge of
the farmers' interests and more practical
sympathy with their welfare, been bellowing from public platforms, like Bulls of
Bashan, it does not follow that in our own
way we have not been able to accomplish
much more by conference and negotiations
than by breathing out fire and slaughter,
although, as I have already said, we have
not hesitated-nor shall we hesitate
when occasion arises, strongly to
oppose any Measure or policy which we
think inimical to the best interests of the
farmers.

ciations?

There is another matter I want to mention in connection with the Ministry of
Home Affairs. I want to draw public
attention to the fact that in Northern
Ireland it costs £126 14s to keep a
prisoner in jail for twelve months. The
Minister of Labour in the Northern
Government thinks £46 16s is enough to
keep an unemployed man. I do not want
to suggest that all the unemployed would
be better in jail, but that at least would
cost the Government more money.
Certainly, they would be better fed and
better housed than a great many of them
are to-day. It is true to say that the
Government of Northern Ireland believe
in keeping prisoners who have committed
an offence against the law in a better condition than those men who have done so
much in the creation of the huge ships
we are never done boasting about, and the
magnificent linen we prate so
much
about, and who carry on the industries,
generally speaking, of Northern Ireland.
While those men are being starved the
Government apparently stand by and are
not prepared to take action.
Another matter I want to draw attention to is the exorbitant legal charges.
If hon. Members will turn to page 68 of
the Estimates they will see legal charges
which are, I think, indefensible. The
Attorney-General for Northern Ireland
gets £2,500 a year; the legal adviser
(part-time) gets £50 a month or £600 a
year; the Chief Crown Solicitor £1,405 a
year, the Assistant Chief Crown Solicitor
£1,096 a year, the Crown Solicitor for
Londonderry, Armagh and Tyrone sums
varying from £540 to £330. In addition
to all these legal officers, despite the fact
that the Parliamentary Secretary himself
is a very competent lawyer, there are fees
for additional counsel amounting to
£2,650. I cannot understand why we
should pay the Attorney-General to conduct prosecutions at the instance of the

I come now to the matter of some adjustment or arrangement that has been made

proper, and amicable arrangement has

protection during troublesome times.
The hon. Member then dealt with the
question of rent restriction. You have
ruled, Mr. Speaker, that we must not
duscuss further at this stage the matter

valuation. Working-class dwellings are

Acts, and there is not the slightest intention that that protection should be
withheld from them until such time as it

The hon. Member also points out that
there are some estate agents who have

hon. Member would put me in possession

do such things, I will consider the matter

very much difficulty in discovering a way
to put an end to treatment that is not
only indecent but immoral, and that
would get no sanction or support from
any Member of the Government. As a
matter of fact, all their activities as far as

the Opposition mentioned and I am
hearing about it myself for the first time
some complaint from people who lived

The hon. Member draws a great distinction between the cost of a prisoner, an
unemployed man, and a lawyer. Well,
they all have their relative values. We
regret exceedingly that the cost of a
prisoner is as much as £126 14s per head
per annum. We would like if we could
reduce that, but it would be impossible
and inhuman, and hon. Members opposite
themselves would not tolerate it if we
attempted to reduce the cost at the expense of the prisoner himself. We must
keep up a great institution. We are all
very glad when we have a small number
of prisoners, but the smaller the number
the greater the cost, not that I am anxious
to have control of any more than we have
at the moment. However, I do not take
it that the hon. Member makes any very
serious charge against us on the score of
not running our prisons satisfactorily and
efficiently.
In my Department, of course, I have
nothing to do with the amount of money
that is given to unemployed persons, but

tremendous discrepancy between the
figures as quoted by the Minister of Finance and the figures as given in the Estimates. I also find an extraordinary disparity between the sums of mony devoted
to police purposes and the sums given by
way of grants to local authorities. On
the Estimates grants to local authorities
are set down as £474,383, less than half a
million- and that is to all the authorities
in the Six Counties-and I find that the
total grant for relief of agricultural land
is £128,000. That, however, was supplemented during the year by an additional sum of £128,000, making a total
of £256,000. But anybody can see that
the grants in aid of agricultural land and
the grants to local authorities when
totalled together do not come any way
near the amount that is spent on what
may be described as law and order.
It ought not to be difficult in times like
these to preserve law and order on a far
less sum than £1,000,000. Surely, if the
right hon. Gentleman and his Friends are
sincere in stating that we have peace in
Northern Ireland, he does not want a
police force costing £1,000,000 to preserve
that peace. Besides, a police force primarily is not for preserving law and order.
It is for a different purpose altogether.
You have all the resources of the British

trouble occurring such as the Minister of
Home Affairs indicated was possible recently. You have the British Army to
place along the Border if that happens,

FINES ON BOOKMAKERS.
1. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
the number of bookmakers who were fined
during the year 1927 in the City of
Belfast; the amount of such fines, and in
what
way such
sums accruing were
utilized.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
to reply to this question.
During the year 1927 there were 612
prosecutions under the Betting Houses
Act, 1853, for offences in the City of
Belfast. The total fines imposed amounted
to £3,526, of which, in accordance with
Section 9 of the above-mentioned Act,
one-half was paid to the Belfast Corporation, and one-half to the informers. In
all cases the informers were the police, and
the proportion of the fines awarded to
them was credited to the R.U.C. Reward
Fund, in accordance with Section 4 (5)
of the Constabulary Act (Northern Ireland), 1922.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like
to ask the right hon. Gentleman as to
whether the police are under instructions
to visit bookmakers in Belfast periodically
for the purpose of enforcing those fines.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The general
instructions to the police are to enforce
the law.

5. Mr. MCMULLEN: To ask the
Minister of Home Affairs whether Mr. E.
McGonigle, Chairman of Kilkeel Board
of Guardians and Chief Governor of the
Sir DAWSON BATES: With the hon.
Member's permission I will answer this
question and question No. 5 standing in
his name together.
No official information has as yet been
received as to the specific transaction referred to, but in any event the Ministry
has no jurisdiction to interfere in a matter
of this character.
Under the
Regulations governing
the administration of Workhouses and
District Hospitals, the Guardians or
Governors as the case may be are required
to advertize for tenders for supplies where
the requirements are estimated to exceed
ten pounds per month, and if the
Guardians neglect without the express
sanction of the Ministry to follow the prescribed procedure, their action is likely to
be reviewed and questioned by the Local
Government Auditor, and any ratepayer
in the district is entitled to appear before
the auditor and to object to any payments being made in respect of such
contracts.
With regard to the suggestion that
members of the Board of Guardians or
Board of Governors have entered into contracts with the Guardians or Governors,
as the case may be, I desire to state that
under the Application of Enactments.
Order, 1898, any member of a local
authority who so interests himself in any
bargain or contract with the local authority of wihch he is a member becomes thereby disqualified, and if he acts or votes
when so disqualified he is liable on summary coviction to a penalty not exceeding
£20.
It is no part of the duty of the
Ministry of Home Affairs to take any
action in regard to initiating the appropriate legal preceedings, but it is open to
any interested person to do so.
At the same time the matter is being
investigated by the Ministry, and the
papers will be referred to the Local
Government Auditor for such action as he
may deem fit in regard to the method of
accepting tenders and entering into contracts.

RENTS OF COTTAGES IN BALLY-
MENA RURAL DISTRICT.
4. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether it is a
fact that at a meeting of the Ballymena
Rural District Council, held on the 12th
instant, it was decided to increase the
rents of the cottages under the control of
the Council by 50 per cent.; and whether
it is a fact that the existing rents cover
all charges against the cottages; and, if
so, what steps he proposes to take to prevent the occupiers being rack-rented.
Sir DAWSON BATES: At a recent
meeting of the Ballymena Rural District
Council, a Resolution was passed increasing the rents of existing cottages in the
rural district by varying amounts. This
Resolution which must receive the sanction of the Ministry before becoming
operative, is at present under the
sideration of my Department.
con-
It is not a fact that the existing rents
cover all charges against the cottages, and
there is at present a deficit on the account.
All applications for sanction to inincreases of rents under the Labourers
Acts are carefully scrutinized by the
Ministry, and increases are only allowed
where the existing rents are low and cast
an undue burden upon the rates. The
present application will receive the same
careful scrutiny, and the hon. Member
may rest assured that no increase which
cannot be fully justified will be sanctioned.

mentioned.

because we say that one of the reasons

In addition to that, up-to-date machinery is being installed in every department,

of industrial depression such as we have
been enduring. It is very hard for craftsmen and labourers to get employment. I

As a matter of fact, in normal times
Harland & Wolff's employ 300 plumbers.
To-day they are employing 60. There

Southampton, and 20 joiners have also
been sent there.
During the last two years many unemployed shipyard workers went voluntarily
to England and Scotland to work, but

nast two months the joiners' trade union
have had as many as 1,000 men unemployed out of a total membership of 3,000.
Therefore, I think it is true to say that
SO far as craftsmen and labourers are

Clause in regard to their being employed

men employed for years in the engineering

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Kyle]
I only want to deal with the matter as
it seems to me it is of importance in
connection with the administration of the
Home Office, and to deal with it in a very
cursory fashion. I was going to say that
two prominent members of the legal profession in Northern Ireland have been
holding meetings, one in Belfast, one in
Dromore, and one, I understand, in some
other part of the Six Counties, to rouse
public opinion as to an injustice that has
been done to a woman called Mrs. Whan.
I think they are perfectly entitled to
arouse public interest in this matter.
About two years ago I myself asked a
question in this House as to whether it
would be possible for the Minister of Home
Affairs to lay on the Table of the House
the report of District-Inspector Allen, of
Banbridge, who was put on to investigate
this case.
The Minister stated on that
occasion that this was a secret document
and, therefore, could not be laid on the
Table of the House. If it was a secret
document obviously it could not be laid
on the Table, but apparently this document was not secret, because at a public
meeting the document was referred to,
and in the report of that meeting it is
alleged that District-Inspector Allen was
perfectly satisfied that the charges
made against Mrs. Whan were bogus
charges.
I want to submit to the House that
that is a most damning indictment
of the Ministry of Home Affairs if
it is true, and it is up to the
right hon. Gentleman to state whether it
is true or not in the interests of law and
order of which he is the champion in this
House. It is also stated that this District-Inspector Allen asked the Home
Office or his superiors who really are
the people in the Home Office-to take
a certain course of action, and, despite
the fact that this District-Inspector who
was put on to prove this woman's guilt,
and who himself says that when he went
into the case in the first instance, went
into it believing the woman was guilty, but
owing to the evidence which he had collected he submttted a report in which
he stated that he was satisfied that the
charges were bogus charges, that course
of action was not followed. That being
the case it is surely the obvious thing now
for the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) and his Department to come
forward and say that their Detective
Office made a mistake for which they are
responsible in this House, that is if they
do the right and proper thing by this
woman, who has been so cruelly wronged
by the neglect of the right hon. Gentleman and his Department in not paying
the attention they should have paid to
that report of the District-Inspector.
Now, if that is right and if that does
appear in the report--and apparently
these legal gentlemen have had the
privilege of seeing it; and a certain prominent arm of solicitors in town here
actually threatened to serve a writ for
libel against District-Inspector Allen for
something alleged to be contained in that
report. I have never seen it up to now,
but apparently other people have seen it,
despite the fact that the right hon.
Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) stated that
it was a secret document. District-Inspector Allen stated in his report that the
evidence on which this lady was convicted
was bogus evidence, and that the Belfast
Detective Office had not given to the case
the care, attention, and thorough investigation which it demanded. But that
was not all. When the lady was before
a judge and jury on a charge of assault
and robbery the Belfast Detective Office
had evidence-and this is the serious part
of our charge against the Ministry of
Home Affairs--which, had they disclosed
it, would have had an altogether different
effect on the proceedings.
Further than that, not only did this
District-Inspector issue a report proving,
or asserting, this woman's innocence but
other officers of the Crown, who were put
on for exactly the same reason, also investigated the charges that were made
against her, and apparently were convinced of her innocence. Despite all this,
the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Game Preservation Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time.'
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I do not think
that it is necessary to offer any
excuse for the introduction of the
present Measure, which has, for its object the better preservation of game. If
the present poaching and shooting out-ofseason is allowed to continue at its present
rate, it is only a question of time until
game will become practically extinct in
Northern Ireland.
¡
Game Preservation Bill--
: 220
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
The intensity of poaching appears to
be due to a variety of reasons, and it is
a fact that large numbers of the general
public look with a comparatively lenient
eye on poaching offences. Undoubtedly
the unpopularity of the old Landlord
system, and the general impression that
Game Rights were the property of the
leisured and wealthy classes alone contributed much to bring this unsatisfactory condition of affairs about. Much
water, however, has flowed under
bridges since the first Game Act was
introduced, and it is a fact that while
in the old days Game Rights only vested
in a comparative few, Game Rights to-day
belong to very many thousands.
the
This is due to a variety of circumstances, but principally to the operations
of the Land Purchase Acts. Under the
old Acts, the voluntary purchase Acts, in
many cases the Game Rights passed to the
purchasing tenants, and under the recent
Land Act of 1925, under which we hope
the balance of all agricultural tenancies
will before long, become vested in the
occupying tenant, it is expressly provided
that, in the absence of a voluntary agreement between the landlord and the
tenant, the rights pass to the Land Commission who can make whatever arrangements they think right, either with the
landlord or the occupying tenants.
Therefore, instead of, as I said before,
this being a matter that only interests a
few landlords, it is of vital interest to
the purchasing tenants. Looking at it
from that point of view when we were
considering the form of the Bill, I set up
a small Committee to advise me in regard
to these matters. I had the advantage of
the presence on that Committee of Mr.
Jackson, the President of the Farmers'
Union, who is in a position to speak from
the tenants' point of view. I might say
here that I appreciate greatly the help
which I received from this Committee,
whose practical knowledge of the subject.
and of the rather complicated code of
Game Laws was of great assistance to
me.
One may look with a certain amount of
leniency on the poacher who may have an
odd shot at game when it does not belong
to him, but I think no one can have any
patience with the individuals who, for
the sake of gain, shoot out of season, and
sell birds at a large profit to themselves.
The damage done by poachers is not by
any means confined to the destruction of
game. I have received from time to time
numerous complaints from farmers concerning the damage done by poachers to
their fences when trespassing on their
lands.
We read in the
papers every
Twelfth that birds that were supposed to be shot early in the
Highlands were conveyed by aeroplane
in order to supply the tables in
some of the big restaurants in London,
but we do not hear of the enormous
number of birds that are shot in Northern
Ireland days before the 12th and sent
surreptitiously over to be used on the
night of the 12th August, and, therefore,
as I said before, unless something is done
to tighten up the Game Laws, game will
become extinct in Northern Ireland.
I do not think it necessary to dwell on
what must be obvious to every hon.
Member, and that is, the value of game
as a national asset.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: You have
only to go to Scotland and see the numbers of visitors and amount of employment that follows through the preservation of game, to realise that in no
sense can Game be regarded as a matter
of purely private interest.
Coming now to the Clauses of the Bill.
I think the first Clause is perhaps the
most important one, and requires some
explanation. The Constabulary Act of
1836 definitely provides that the Constabulary should not be used in any way
whatever for the purpose of enforcing
the game rights. It is doubtful why such
a prohibition was inserted in the Act,
and I think it was felt by the powers
that be in those days that if such a
power was not definitely taken away
from the police that it would be the subject of much abuse at the hands of the
game owners who were in those days
the landlords in Ireland, and who would
seek to use their influence to utilise the
police as gamekeepers. However, whatever the cause may have been it, would
be out of place now to continue this prohibition if we are to do anything to
preserve the game as a National asset in
Northern Ireland, and while we propose
to remove this limitation, we have inserted a proviso to ensure that we do
2221 Game Preservation Bill-
9 OCTOBER 1928

Second Reading.
not in any way intend to turn the police
into gamekeepers, or relieve those who
have Game Rights of their own responsibility of protecting their rights. But
what we do propose to do is to give the
police wider powers in the ordinary
course of their duty to ensure that the
Game Laws are enforced.
May I give an example of what I
mean?-If a Constable sees an individual shooting out of season, it would be
his duty to enter those lands and take
the necessary steps to see that the individual was dealt with by law.

I point out that at the present time the
law enables the constable to enter private
land if he actually sees a person carrying a gun and demand the gun licence.
At the same time he has no power to
demand to see the game licence. If the
gun licence which the constable is entitled to demand is not forthcoming, and
if the individual does not give his name,
the constable has power to arrest him.
Under Clause 2, we propose to extend
this power to enable the constable to demand the game licence, and it also enables the constable to search the bag, or
motor car, or, generally, the premises in
which the individual may be. Hitherto,
the right to demand the game licence was
confined to the Excise Authorities, but
this is quite impracticable now, and the
result is, to a very large extent, the Reis defrauded by individuals
shooting without game licences.

that has been illegally
illegally shot.. This
Clause simply provides for the keeping

With regard to Clause 5, as I have already indicated, it is a known fact that
a great many birds are shot in Northern
Ireland out of season and sold at high
prices in England. With a view of trying to stop this practice, this Clause provides that all boxes and packages containing game shall be so labelled with
the address of the consignor.
Coming now to Clause 6, the constable,
under the law as it now stands, can only
search a person if that individual is on a
highway, a street, or public place, and if
he has good reason to believe that he is
coming from land where he has been unlawfully in search of game. In the event
of a refusal on the part of the individual
to give his name, he has only the right to
summon the individual. I think hon.
Members will appreciate how useless these
particular powers are, as an individual,
the moment he saw the constable, could
step into an adjoining field, and the
constable would be powerless. The effect,
briefly, of Clause 6 is to extend these
the
powers which the police have at
present time to practically any places,
but I think it right to point out that no
power of arrest is given under this
Clause.

As I have pointed out, poaching is, in
many districts, regarded as a very mild
offence, and sometimes local farmers do

Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON:
think in so far as this Bill is likely to

I think the right hon. Gentleman in his

as to the quantity of game that is exported from and sold in this country.
He said that the purchasing tenants were

district I come from the purchasing
tenants do not attach much importance
to the game rights. Of course, I come
from a district where there is not much

thought, an asset to them but a liability.

I think that the Bill is very remarkable
in some ways. One very remarkable
thing about the Bill is the almost unlimited power it puts in the hands of the
police over the personal property of the
people in Northern Ireland. If the Bill
had stopped at the first Clause that, is
taking away the restrictions from the

Act of 1836-would it not have been

Bill? This gives a police constable
power to arrest a person on the very
slightest suspicion-if he refuses to give
his name and address.
In the low lying parts of the Northern area I do not think the game
rights are of very vital importance to
anybody at all. I cannot speak for the
more hilly districts where the grouse
may be of considerable value. I think
if the rght, hon. Gentleman had wanted
to impress the House with the importance of this Measure and the necessity
I see that under Clause 4 in the case
of a holder of a licence to deal in game
who is convicted for the second time, the
magistrate has no option at all with regard to the offence that may have been
committed. As I understand this
Clause he must suspend the licence.
The magistrates in the case of a second
conviction have no option to deal with
it on its merits, or to mete out, a sentence that they may think was equal to
the offence. It may be possible under
the complicated rules to be made under
this Bill that an honest dealer carrying
on his business with the best intentions
of keeping within the law may fall into
a technical error. If that should happen a second time the court has absolutely no discretion left in its power but
to suspend the man's licence for five years.
That might be a very serious loss.
It used to be said that an Englishman's house was his castle, but if the
Government go on enacting Measures like
this Bill and the Fisheries Act the saying will have to be changed and it will
be said that an Englishman's house is
not his castle when the police go and inspect it. The Government should not
unduly interfere with trade. Traders
at the present time are in a very difficult position, and with all these enactments it, seems to me that trading will be
carried on in very difficult circumstances,
while this will also add to the expense.
As I said before. this Bill seems to give
almost unlimited powers to the police.
It gives them power of search which
they never had before, except under

are in favour of such legislation.
Standardization of agricultural produce
has the same advantages as in any other
line of production. It enables the importer to order without inspection, because he knows he can rely on receiving
an article of uniform excellence. He can,

In the case of ungraded produce the
British distributor has to make due allowance for wastage, re-handling and disorganization of business. All these costs
must ultimately be borne by the Irish producer. These facts have been recognized
by British Dominions and foreign

bulk of agricultural produce from abroad

British market.
The Marketing of Eggs Act passed by

Hear, hear). Moreover all progressive

that is increased demand and increased

merchants have told us that now is our

and to get higher prices because

The chief features of the measure are:
(1). All merchants exporting potatoes
to Great Britain must be licensed and in
the first instance every person applying
for a license will obtain one-its continuance depending on compliance with the
Regulations. The fee of £1 will be
charged for each licence.
(2). Potatoes exported to Great Britain,
must, with certain minor exceptions, be
accompanied by a certificate of an inspector that they are of the prescribed
standard of quality and have been graded
and packed in a proper manner.
In
order to help to cover the cost of administering the Act a fee of 6d per ton will
be charged for all potatoes inspected.
(3). It is also proposed to grant permits for potatoes coming within certain
categories, such as lots grown by the exporters, lots sent for experimental demonstration, or similar purposes, and lots
of less than, say, one ton.
Licences will
not be required in these cases but consignments may be inspected.
(4). Where, for the purpose of issuing
a permit, inspection of a consignment is
necessary fees at the rate of 6d per ton
will be charged but for the permit itself
no fee will be charged.
The Bill provides that at present its
provisions shall not apply to potatoes sent
to the Irish Free State but later on an
arrangement can be made to have such
exports inspected if considered desirable.
At the Border there is considerable trade
done in potatoes and it would not do if
we did anything to stop that at present
until the Bill gets into working order.
We have been written to over and over
again by almost every agricultural district urging this grading and we have had
meetings with the leading potato exporters, and although I honestly say they are
not in agreement still the majority of
them are in favour of the Bill. They
all say something is necessary. I do not
know that there is anything further I
can say about the Bill. I can go into
the various clauses or not according to
the wish of the House.
The intention is that the Act shall
come into force on the first day of February next-the period intervening between
the passage of the measure and its coming
into operation being devoted to the
training of the necessary staff and the
education of the farmer and the merchant
in the provisions of the Act.

Hon. Members will recollect that
during the past two years the Government.
has contributed approximately £18,000
towards the campaign organised by the
linen industry for advertising damasks
in the United States of America. That
contribution was made on the basis of a
Government grant of 10s for every £1
contributed by trade interests in Northern
Ireland during each of the years 1926 and
1927, subject to a maximum contribution
of £10,000 in each year.
As hon. Members are aware, the organisation of the advertising campaign is
carried out by a Committee in New York,
composed largely of the local representatives of Northern Ireland firms. I have
had the advantage of personal contact
with this Committee during my visits to
the United States and I am glad to be
able to tell the Committee that their
meetings are animated by keenness and
harmony which are reflected in the undoubted vigour with which the campaign
has been, and is being, waged.
wireless has been pressed into the service
of linen by the Committee, and, coincident
with the lectures and broadcast talks,
special displays of linen are arranged in
the different localities.
In order to interest traders in linen
damask a trade magazine entitled "The
Linen Guildsman" has been published
each month since October, 1926, some
3,000 copies being circulated each month
to the buying departments of retail establishments throughout the length and
breadth of the United States, while advertising in trade journals has also been
undertaken. Lecturers have been appointed to visit all the leading cities and
to give public demonstrations of the
merits and artistic qualities of linen as an
article of universal household use. The
A large number of advertisements have
been inserted in American newspapers
and magazines with a view to reaching
the actual consumer.
From October 1st,
1927, to January 1st, 1928, no less than
350 articles appeared in American newspapers and magazines, covering a circulation of over 25 million readers.
The success of this publicity campaign
has encouraged the linen industry to extend its scope, and it has been decided to
advertise not only damasks but other
linens as well and, further, to extend the
campaign to the home market and to the
Dominions. Although the United States
is still the most important individual overseas market, the British Empire is becoming year by year a larger consumer of
linen goods. In 1913 the United States
bought 47.6% of the total United
Kingdom exports of linen goods, but in
1926, the latest year for which detailed
statistics are available, the per centage had
fallen to 42. Shipments to the Empire,
on the other hand, had grown from
25.6% in 1913 to 36% in 1926.
The Irish Linen Guild has been formed
for the purpose of carrying out this extended campaign, and encouraging support to the new project has been forthcoming from the trade. The Government
originally agreed to make a contribution
to the new campaign on the basis of 10/-
for each £1 raised by the local industry,
subject to a maximum contribution of
£17,500. It is now proposed to increase
the basis of the Government's contribution
to 15/- for each £1 raised by the trade,
but I may say, as hon Members will have
observed from the Supplementary Estimate, that it is not intended to increase
the amount of the Government's contribution but merely to vary the basis. For
that reason the estimate now put forward
is only for a token sum of £10 in order
to call the attention of the Committee to
the proposed alteration in the basis of the
contribution. The object of this proposed
increase in the rate of contribution is to
enable the campaign to be maintained at
its present degree of intensity in the
United States and to be extended to the
home and Dominion markets at a time
when the resources of the trade itself are

The remaining item in respect of which
provision is now sought is a grant-in-aid
of the Londonderry and Lough Swilly
Railway Company Limited towards the
loss on working during the current calendar
year. In the three previous financial
years grants amounting in all to £20,000
have been made from Northern Ireland
Government Funds and a similar amount
has been provided by the Government of
the Irish Free State to enable the Company to keep its lines open for traffic.
A sum similar to that included in the
Estimate now before the Committee,
namely £5,000, has already been voted by
the Government of the Irish Free State
in respect of losses during the current
calendar year.
As hon. Members are already aware, this railway has, since the
date on which the period of Government
Control terminated, been unable to balance its working receipts with expenditure. In the absence of financial assistance from the two Governments undoubtedly the line would long ago have
been compelled to close down.
The loss on working in 1923 amounted
to £14,932 which was reduced to £8,953
in 1924 and to £9,499 in 1925. In 1926
owing to the stoppage in the Coal Industry
and the consequent high cost of fuel the
loss amounted to £13,312. In 1927 the
loss was £11,178. The loss for the first
eight months of the current year amounts
to £5,069, which would on the average
work out at £7,604 for the full year. It
is anticipated, however, that the loss during the remaining four months will be
considerably increased as compared with
the previous period of the year as during
the winter months the receipts from passenger traffic in common with those of
similar undertakings normally show a reduction in comparison with the summer
months.
It may be anticipated with confidence,

State have got. I refer to the employment of men on this railway. Before the

Swilly Railway Company have discharged

their own administration of the railway.
The administration of the Londonderry
and Lough Swilly Railway is a byword.
The chairman of the directors supplies
the company with coal. There is no contract. There are no tenders asked for
in connection with the supply of this coal,
with the result that some of the directors
of this company supply the railway with
coal at a higher price than that at which
coal could be obtained in the open market. Of course, that is part of the grand
capitalist game that our Friends on the
Government Front Bench have been playing for the past number of years, bolstering up a system that is gradually
crumbling away before their very eyes,
although they refuse to admit it. We
grant them credit facilities. We guarantee their loans. We are now giving
£5,000 to bolster up this rotten concern.
We are giving £1,263 to enable another
set of capitalists to get concessions for
their particular trade, and so it goes on.
These honourable and right hon. Gentlemen do this in the name and in the
interest of private enterprise, private enterprise at the public expense for private
profit. That is the order of the day now.
I want to protest against it, and to move
a reduction of this Estimate by £5,000.

REVENUE.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state the
total amount collected by his Department
during the season 1927-1928 for the
inspection of potatoes in stores, and
whether, as this amount indirectly comes
out of the pocket of the producers, he will
consider the advisability of abandoning
the said charge.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): The
total amount received in respect of the
inspection of potatoes for export during
the year ended 31st August, 1928, was
£2,277 15s Od.
PRICES OF FLOUR, MEAT, AND
BACON.
It is not proposed to abandon this
charge which has been in force for a
number of years without causing any
hardship.
2. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Commerce whether he is aware of the
fact that whilst a considerable reduction
in the price of flour has taken place
during the past six months, no proportionate reduction has taken place in the
price of bread; whether he is aware of the
fact that flour is being retailed in the City
of Belfast at a much higher price than in
most rural districts which have higher
freight charges to pay; whether he is.
also aware of the fact that meat and
bacon are being sold throughout the City
of Belfast and many other places at prices
out of all proportion to what is being
paid to the farmers for their cattle and
pigs; and whether in view of all these
facts he will seriously consider the
advisability of setting up a Food Council
for Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am informed that the
current price of bread in Belfast is 94d
per quartern loaf, as compared with 9d
in Glasgow, where, as the hon. Members
will be aware, the price of bread is
regulated by a sliding scale based upon
the current price of flour. At the same
time I am informed that the consumer
in Belfast is allowed a discount which has
recently been increased to 1/2d in the £.
There would appear, accordingly, to be
an approximate parity between the Belfast and Glasgow rates. The current
price of bread in Dublin is 10d and in
Cork 10d to 11d per quartern loaf and no
discount is allowed.
I am, nevertheless, aware that, as
stated by the hon. Member, there has
been a considerable reduction in the price
of flour during recent months, and I am
glad to have been given this opportunity
of expressing the hope in this House that
the master bakers of the city may find it
possible to accord to the consumer further
relief in the price of bread at an early
date.
With regard to the comparative price
of flour in the city of Belfast and country
districts, no representations have hitherto been made to me on this subject, and
the hon. Member will appreciate that a
proper investigation of this matter would
take a considerable time.

[Mr. Barbour]
Similarly with regard to the prices of
meat and bacon, the hon. Member will
have gathered from the reports issued to
the Press from time to time of the proceedings of the Food Council that this is
a matter of the greatest complexity upon
which no arbitrary pronouncement can be

in the report on the transit, prices and
marketing of agricultural produce presented to Parliament by the Committee
over which my hon. Friend the Member
for Derry (Mr. Mark) so ably presided, a

affecting retail prices. As I informed the
hon. Member. in my reply to his question
on the 24th November last, my Department is keeping in close touch with the
proceedings of the Food Council in Great
Britain. That Council, as the hon. Member will be aware, has at present no statutory powers, but should steps be taken
in Great Britain to create a statutory
body, and should representations on the
subject of food prices be made to the
Government by organised bodies of public
opinion, the Government will be prepared
to consider, in the light of such representations, the advisability of taking
similar steps in Northern Ireland.
WAGES OF LINEN TRADE
WORKERS.
3. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is aware that workers in the linen trade are paid lower
wages than workers in the cotton and
woollen textiles trades; and whether he
is prepared to take steps to remedy this
state of affairs before granting any additional public money in advertising Irish
linen.
In reply to the latter part of the question I would inform the hon. Member that
there is no ground upon which the Government would conceive itself justified in
withholding at this stage assistance towards the linen advertising campaign.
On the contrary, it is the opinion of the
Government that in helping to stimulate
the demand for Ulster linen the Government is taking the most effective steps
possible in the interests of all connected
with the trade.
Mr. BARBOUR: I am aware of the
relative rates of wages operative in the
linen, cotton and woollen industries, but
I would remind the hon. Member that the
rates of wages at present ruling in the
linen trade were, for the most part, fixed
under agreements made through the
medium of collective bargaining between
representatives of employers and workers,
agreements in the promotion of which the
hon. Member has always taken an active
and helpful part.
Mr. KYLE: Would the right hon.
Gentleman state whether it is the intention of the Government that the wages
paid the linen workers should compare
favourably with the wages paid in the
woollen and worsted trades?
Mr.
BARBOUR: If I be in order
in answering a question of this kind I
think it must be obvious to hon. Members
of this House that the rate of wages paid
in one industry does not necessarily react
on the rate of wages paid in another industry. In the linen industry we have
to take into consideration the rates of
wages paid in other countries in producing
the article concerned. It might be well
for the hon. Member to know that the
rates of wages paid in the linen trade in
the North of Ireland are, I think, with
the exception of only the United States,
higher than in any other country. I may
quote one or two instances to reassure him
on that point. The most striking differences are in the cases of skilled artisans.
Now, in the case of sorters—I have to
use these technical terms, but they will
be perfectly understood by a great number
of hon. Members-the rate paid in the
North of Ireland is 133d per hour. In
France, which is more concerned with internal trade than with export trade, the
rate is only from 7d to 7.16d per hour.
In Belgium, a very formidable competitor,
from which a large amount of yarn comes,
the wages are from 5.42d to 5.61d per
hour.
When we come to mechanics, who are
the most highly paid employees in
the flax spinning industry, we see that the
rate in Northern Ireland is 15.84d per
hour and in France 7.04d to 7.74d. In
Czecho Slovakia, which has recently become a formidable competitor in the linen
trade, I am informed that the rate is 31d,
but I am really so surprised at that figure
that I give it with reservation.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
16 OCTOBER 1928
Then we come to women labour, which,
of course is most numerous in flax spinning. We find that drawers in the North
of Ireland receive 5.31d per hour, in
France 4.7d to 4.9d, in Belgium 2.59d to
31d, and in Czecho Slovakia 24d to 2.85d.
Carders, who perform another important operation, come next. In Northern
Ireland they are paid 5d per hour, in
Belgium 32d, and in Czecho Slovakia 24d
to 3 d.
Rovers in the North of Ireland are paid
5.31d per hour, in Belgium 3.69d to
4.55d, and in Czecho Slovakia 2.93d.
I think these figures will illustrate that
our spinners in the North of Ireland, who
are carrying on trade under immense difficulties owing to the competition of this
low-priced labour in foreign countries, are
worthy of being encouraged in every way
in order that we may help the trade to get
on a better footing, and in this improvement the working class will undoubtedly
share.

The Ministry is aware of the lack of

that with that object there will be general

This is not at all a political question. It

can all
irrespective of any political question emphatically get our legs under the table and
discuss what is best in the interests of this
very important branch of agricultural industry. The right hon. Gentleman the
Minister of Agriculture, in introducing

our potato crop. It is the centre round
which all our tillage farming revolves.

can enlarge and expand the area under

and expand tillage farming in every direction. Therefore there is no branch of our

I do not claim that sometimes there is

the potatoes that are shipped. There is
probably cause for some of the

was able to tell me yesterday that he had
not received a single complaint last year.
I say, therefore, that the proportion must
be small. We can grow the best potatoes
in the world, or at least they are as good
as the potatoes that can be produced anywhere else.
Of course there is this difficulty
about making a hard and fast standard
for potatoes in Northern Ireland. We
have a great diversity of soil. On the
farm that I had at Randalstown for a
great number of years, I could have got
potatoes out of red soil at one end of a
field, and out of black soil at the other
end. I understand that some of our
agricultural competitors on the Continent have not that difficulty to contend
with, because they can get hundreds and
thousands of acres of almost the same
texture. But there is a great diversity
of land in Northern Ireland; there is a
great diversity to be found even on one
farm.
Then there is another factor: This is
largely a country of small holdings. Even.
if you had general inspection to-morrow,
I do not believe you would eliminate all
complaints so far as the export trade is
concerned, because when a shipper exports potatoes, the market on the other
side may turn against the importer, and
he may have to keep those potatoes lying
for two or three weeks on a wharf or at a
station. Even if the potatoes were inspected before they left Northern Ireland it is possible that when they reached
the man that the importer would sell
them to they would be in an unsatisfactory condition. So, even with general
inspection, you are not going to eliminate entirely causes of complaint, because
you are dealing with what is, to some extent, a perishable article, and with an
article which fluctuates a great deal in
price, with the result that the buyer has
to store the potatoes before he can market them.

Mr. ELLIOTT: Since this Bill was introduced by the Minister of Agriculture last
week I have studied it most carefully.
While I may be permitted to say that it
could be altered I am not, having regard
to the interests of the whole potato industry, prepared to support the rejection
of the Measure. I recognize that the
potato industry is of paramount importance to Northern Ireland, and while we
hear from the Opposition that we on the
Government side are not, in unity on this
Bill I say that the Members on the Opposition side did not agree in their arguments.
The first question I ask myself about this
Bill is, is it going to do anything to enable the farmers to get better prices for
their produce? If it is going to help the
farmers to get a fairer proportion of the
amount the consumers are paying then I
am for the Bill heart and soul. I recognise that to-day in Northern Ireland
potatoes are being sold by farmers at
about £2 per ton, and in this city of
Belfast potatoes are being sold retail to
consumers at 8d a stone or 5/4 a cwt.
It is not at all fair that the man who
has the most trouble in growing the potatoes should have only 2/- when the people
who are going to consume the produce
have to pay 5/4. If this Bill will do
something to get the farmer better and
fairer prices for his produce I will be
entirely in favour of it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I would like to say I am
altogether in favour of the inspection of
potatoes and of the licensing of potato
merchants. The inspection of potatoes
is absolutely necessary, and if we are to
put our potatoes on the market in the
condition in which the consumer wishes
to get them we must have them inspected
and we must have them going forth from
Northern Ireland bearing the hall mark
of genuineness.
Unfortunately, a great
deal of harm has been done to our potato
trade by farmers who put their stuff on
the market in a condition that did not
obtain for it the best possible price. That
also did a great deal of harm to the potato
trade in general.
I live in an area where potato inspection
is already in force and I am in entire
agreement with it. I hold that inspection has done a great deal to improve the
potato industry. I am confirmed in my
opinion by the fact that at the meeting
of the County Committee of Agriculture
at Omagh a short time ago farmers proposed and seconded a resolution asking
the Government to enforce inspection all
over. Therefore, it is not fair to say
that the inspection of the potato crop has
proved a failure. It has been a great success. I hold that if the Government instead of putting this very drastic Measure into operation would only enlarge the
present system of potato inspection everything that is necessary would be done.
I would like to say in reply to what
the hon. Member for Down (Mr. P.
O'Neill) has stated that the inspection of
potatoes has done a great deal of good.
I would also like to say that I believe
in the licensing of potato exporters and
that only men who know their business
and are prepared to do justice not only
to the consumers but also to the producers should be licensed. A great deal
of harm has been done to the potato industry in Northern Ireland by people who
know nothing whatever about the business dabbling in it. I think the worst
offenders have been the Ulster Farmers'
Produce Company who dabbled in the
potato trade to the detriment of the
whole industry and who, according to
their balance sheet, have lost more than
all the potato merchants of Northern
Ireland put together. I hope that when
he comes to issue the licences the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Agriculture, will see to it that such people as the
Ulster Farmers' Produce Company will
not be licensed to export potatoes, and
that only men who know something about
the business and are prepared to do it in
an honourable way and without any financial aid from the Government will be allowed to carry on the potato trade from
Northern Ireland.
We have lost a great many of our
potato markets. Hon. Members have
heard that the United States of America
have closed down their market against us.
That is not, the fault of the Northern
Government, who have done what they
could to keep the market open. As the
hon. Member for Derry (Mr. Leeke)
said, it was the farmers of the West of
America who wanted to protect their own
produce who brought pressure to bear on
the Government and got them to close
the ports against the import of our Irish
potatoes.

Poor Relief Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Poor Relief Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second time.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of
this Bill is to remedy the defects in, and
to improve the machinery of, the existing
law in regard to the granting by Boards
of Guardians in Northern Ireland of what
is known as special Outdoor Relief in cases
where exceptional distress prevails in any
particular area. In order to understand
what the existing difficulties are, and how
this Bill will operate, I think it desirable
that I should explain in detail the law in
regard to the general question of Poor
Relief, and particularly the question of
Outdoor Relief.
Most hon. Members are aware that the
fundamental Act on which our present
system of Poor Relief is based is the Poor
Relief Act of 1838. The underlying
principle of that Act was that Poor Relief
should be afforded in the Workhouse, and
that Outdoor Relief should only be
granted under the most exceptional circumstances, which I propose to explain
later.
Following the passing of the 1838 Act,
Ireland was divided into Unions in which
workhouses were established. Hon.
Members will realise that at the time the
Act was possed, the social conditions of
the people in Ireland were very different
from those which exist to-day. Destitution was rife, and the standard of living,
particularly in regard to the working
classes, was far below that which exists today. Pestilence and famine were of
common occurrence, and, accordingly,
carrying out their policy, the Government
of the day felt constrained to build a great
chain of institutions known as workhouses,
in which hundreds of people could be accommodated under circumstances which
would not be tolerated to-day.
Now I might point out shortly the conditions under which Outdoor Relief could
be granted, as distinct from Indoor Relief.
First of all it only applied to destitute
poor persons permanently disabled from
labour by reason of old age, infirmity, or
bodily or mental defect. I am speaking
now of outdoor relief. Another qualification was that of destitute persons being
disabled from labour by reason of severe
sickness or serious accident whereby their
families were deprived of the means of obtaining subsistence. A third condition
made it applicable to destitute widows,
having two or more legitimate children
dependent upon them. But in addition.
to this, no person in occupation of more
than one quarter of an acre could receive
Outdoor Relief.
It was intended by the Authorities in
those days that the conditions under which
Poor Relief was given in workhouses
should not be made of too attractive a
character, and, as a natural consequence
of the carrying out of this policy, the Act
also prescribed, within very narrow limits,
the conditions under which Outdoor Relief
should be given.
These were the limitations under the
Act of 1838 and subsequent amending
enactments under which Outdoor Relief
could be given, and hon. Members will
appreciate how very narrow these limitations are. I do not propose to say anything as to whether those conditions were
appropriate in those days, but I do say
this, that these conditions are not suitable
to modern ideas or standards.
(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
To diverge rather from the main question-I refer to workhouses-it might be
interesting to the House to know that in
Northern Ireland there were formerly 27
workhouses. This number I am glad to
say has been reduced to 15 and the process of reduction is still proceeding, and
personally I am in great hopes that progress will be made along these lines and
that workhouses as we know them will
soon be a thing of the past and that
county homes as recommended by the
Poor-Law Commission will take their
place.
However, coming back to the main
point, I come to the Act of 1898, which
was the first Act to extend the benefit of
out-door relief. At the time when the
1898 Act was passed, it is perfectly obvious, the framers of that Measure felt
as we do to-day that the time had come
when the terms on which Outdoor Relief should be granted should be made
more elastic, and accordingly, in that
Act the Section known as Section 13 with
which I think hon. Members are familiar.
was inserted. This enabled Boards of
Guardians, under certain conditions, in
Poor Relief Bill-
Second Reading
17 OCTOBER 1928
cases of exceptional distress to grant outdoor relief to able-bodied persons with
the approval of the Local Government
Board, and here we have, for the first
time under the Poor Law Code, the recognition of the principle that under
modern industrial conditions, provision
must be made for the hard-working industrious worker, who, through no fault
of his own, finds himself and his family
at the point of destitution, and for whom
the workhouse would be most inappropriate relief.
At the same time, I do not think the
framers of that Act had before their
minds the conditions which prevail to-day.
It is probable that those legislators had
more in their minds the conditions which
prevailed in some of the outlying
districts of Ireland where, owing to the
failure of the crop or other causes, waves
of destitution were continually occurring.
At all events, whatever was the cause of
the insertion of this Section, it has, since
that date, been utilised from time to time
by Boards of Guardians, and by the old
Local Government Board for the purpose
of relieving the exceptional distress which
prevailed from time to time in the poor
parts of Ireland.
the
Following the establishment of
Government of Northern Ireland, it was
found that as in other industrial centres
in the United Kingdom, a state of affairs
had arisen out of the industrial depression which cailed for special measures of
relief. The Belfast Board of Guardians
found themselves faced with a serious
situation and, finally, in December, 1923,
they represented the facts to the Home
Office in Belfast, and an Order was issued
authorizing them to grant Outdoor Relief to able-bodied persons.
provided, therefore, was that application
should be made through the local rating
authority. Then having applied to the
local rating authority the application had
to come before the Ministry of Home
Affairs. I think hon. Members will see
afterwards one of the defects where there
is a conflict of interest between the board
of guardians and the rating authority.
It might be convenient to hon. Members if I was to explain the machinery
under which the Application for the
Order is made, because I think Hon.
Members will agree with me that the
method prescribed by the Act is of a most
cumbersome character. Section 13 of the
Act of 1898 provides that where a Board
of Guardians is satisfied that exceptional
distress prevails, they may apply through
the County Council or the County
Borough Council according to the situation. Hon. Members will appreciate that
boards of guardians are not rating authorities, but county councils and county
borough councils are. The machinery
The Act expressly limits the operation
of the Order to a period of two months,
and accordingly, if, at the end of that
period, the Guardians still find the same
conditions of destitution prevailing, they
have again to apply for a further Order,
and the application has again to go before
the County Council or the County Borough
Council concerned, and again the Ministry
of Home Affairs has to make a new Order,
and the new Order can in no case be made
for period longer than two months.
Therefore, I think all hon. Members will
agree with me that this machinery is
entirely out of date.
Apart altogether from the Act of 1898
where an Order is made under the Clause
in question half the cost is to be borne by
the union and the other half is to be borne
as a county-at-large charge by either the
county council or the county borough
council. Hon. Members will realise that
this particular aspect of the question
operates adversely against destitute ablebodied persons in particular localities
where the county council refuse to endorse
the action of the board of guardians, because, after all, the guardians have a local
knowledge which the county council cannot have and they have also a sense of responsibility which I am glad to think
boards of guardians in Northern Ireland
are prepared to shoulder.
The effect of this Clause is, that if the
county council refuses to acquiesce in the
application made by the board of guardians, the matter can go no further. I know
of one or two cases in Northern Ireland
where boards of guardians have applied to
the local rating authority to put the Section into operation, and have met with a
refusal. Therefore the application could
go no further. To deal with these particular cases these boards applied to the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and, ultimately, as a temporary expedient, we
were enabled to do something to
help those unfortunate inviduals. Hon.
Members will, therefore, I think, agree
with me that the machinery, as pro-
Pocr Relief Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
vided by the law as it now stands, is both
unnecessarily cumbersome and to a large
extent ineffective.
The present Bill proposes to repeal the
Section in question, and to substitute what
I may describe as a straightforward and
simple procedure, and it is proposed that
where the Ministry of Home Affairs is
satisfied that in any area exceptional distress prevails, the Ministry will be enabled, under the Bill, to make a simple
order authorizing the guardians for any
period of one month, or two months, or six
months, as the case may be, to administer
outdoor relief to able-bodied persons who
are destitute through no fault of their
own, and who are obviously not fit subjects
for relief inside the workhouse. It may
be asked by hon. Members on what
grounds the Ministry of Home Affairs may
consider itself satisfied that such a condition of affairs exists, but a glance at the
Bill will show that it is open to any board
of guardians to make representations to
this effect.
My experience of boards of guardians in
Northern Ireland is that representations
made by them should not be lightly turned
down, but, independent altogether of
that, I might explain that the inspectors
of the Ministry are in the closest possible
touch with the social conditions which prevail throughout Northern Ireland. It is
their constant duty to keep themselves
closely informed, through the relieving
officers, and other machinery, of the state
of affairs in every area, but, in addition to
this I think my hon. Friends below the
gangway will appreciate this—most valuable information could be and is obtained
from time to time from the Ministry of
Labour through the various unemployment committees, which are only too well
aware of the condition of affairs that
exists.
Therefore, I suggest to this House,
that this Bill will afford machinery that
is both elastic and more in accordance
with modern requirements, and once an
order is issued, it will empower the
guardians, with their own local knowledge, and their sense of responsibility
to the ratepayers, to consider the various
claims which may be made to them, and
to deal with them in not alone a practical but a sympathetic manner.
For some time past the situation in
Belfast has been the subject of constant
correspondence and discussions between
the Belfast Board of Guardians and the
Ministry of Home Affairs. The Guardians
have undoubtedly realised the seriousness
of the situation, and I find from the returns which I have received that the
numbers of persons who received special
outdoor relief increased from 65 at the
end of 1924 to 5,629 in September 1927.
Recently, however, the Guardians, acting no doubt as they considered proper in
the interests of the ratepayers, have endeavoured to relieve themselves of this
responsibility. They have pointed out
that the Government should assume financial responsibility for the class of persons
who were claiming special outdoor relief.
The Guardians have been informed over
and over again that the Government has
assumed, in regard to the workers of our
community, an enormous financial burden, and that it would be impossible for
the Government to accept further liability.
May I refer to the increase of the benefits under the Acts passed by this House?
There have been the Old Age Pensions
Acts, the Contributory Pensions Act, the
Widows' and Orphans' Act, and
th

Government have made it clear that once

State benefit, and that man or woman, as

dians at that stage to assume responsibility for the necessary assistance to be

Guardians have admitted that they are

but only in the form that the individual

Under that Act all food for the poor was
supplied by the landlords. The Act of
1838 made provision for the people to be

to law they are entitled to be housed and

it entitled the people to be fed outside
the workhouse. That Act is wider in its
scope than the Bill now presented.
Times have progressed between the years
1898 and 1928, and that being the case,
I ask you to delete that section from the
poor law altogether.

Mr. POLLOCK: I am aware of the

Act is the granting of facilities for longterm loans to enable farmers to purchase

INDUSTRIAL WORKERS AND AG-
RICULTURAL LABOUR.
4. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of Labour whether he is aware that, according
to recent decisions of the Umpire, skilled
workmen are expected, and compelled, to
compete with thousands of unemployed
labourers for work ordinarily done by
agricultural labourers, and if these skilled
workmen are unable to prove that they
have got work on the land they are denied Unemployment Insurance benefit;
and whether he will take the necessary
steps to remedy this state of affairs.
Mr. ANDREWS: The decisions of the
Umpire to which the hon. Member refers
are based on the provision in the last
Unemployment Insurance Act in Northern Ireland whereby Parliament laid
down that it was reasonable that an applicant for unemployment benefit should
be expected to seek suitable employment
in some other occupation, if, after a reasonable period of unemployment, he had
no prospect, within a reasonable time, of
obtaining re-employment in his own
trade with sufficent regularity. The
principle of this decision met with the
unanimous approval of the members of the
recent Blanesburgh Committee on Unemployment Insurance and is embodied in
the Unemployment Insurance Codes both
here and in Great Britain by recent legislation.

Gentleman state whether in his opinion
it is reasonable for a tradesman who has
been put out on short time to be compelled to seek work on the land or be

want is what is a reasonable amount of
time for a tradesman to be out of work
before he is compelled to take work as an
agricultural labourer.
Mr. ANDREWS: The authorities who
are charged with the responsibility of
administering the law in this respect take
into consideration all the circumstances
of the case which they are considering at
the time it is brought before them.

that tradesmen have been compelled after

Mr. ANDREWS: No, Sir. I do not

they are.

hon. Gentleman actual cases of men who
