The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): The Bill
which I have the honour of presenting
2461 Rent Restrictions Bill-

18 OCTOBER 1928
Second Reading
to this House is very short. The object,
of it is apparent on the face of the Bill,
and in these circumstances it will be unnecessary for me to trouble the House
with any detailed explanation. The
position at the moment is that, under the
Rent and Mortgage Restriction Act of
1925, dwellinghouses of which the rateable valuation does not exceed £26 will
become decontrolled on the 1st May,
1930, and in these circumstances, it is
necessary for the Government, to consider very carefully as to whether the
enforcement of this Act will inflict undue
hardship on any particular class.
It
is also the duty of the Government not
to wait until the last moment before
giving a decision. It is only equitable
that if, in our judgment, the circumstances are such as to warrant the continuance of control for a further period,
that early intimation should be given to
all parties concerned.
The Government has given this matter
for some time past very grave consideration, and in reply to a question which I
think was put to me by my hon. Friend
the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) in April of last year, I then
stated in respect of houses of the valuation I have mentioned that the Government was prepared to ask for Parliamentary sanction at an early date for the
introduction of a Bill further postponing
the decontrol of these houses unless by
that time we were fully satisfied that an
ample number of small dwellings had
been erected. That was the attitude and
the policy of the Government at that
time.
during the war, and the subsequent inflation of the price of building materials
brought about an acute shortage, with the
result that the price of houses to be sold
and the rents of houses which were let increased by leaps and bounds.
I desire to emphasise what must be apparent to most hon. Members that the
system of control of rents can culy be regarded as a temporary expedient, and can
only be justified on the ground that the
shortage of houses has been brought about
by a national emergency. Until the outbreak of war in 1914, houses in Northern
Ireland were both abundant and cheap,
and it is often said that the citizens of
Belfast were better housed and more
cheaply housed than those of any place in
the United Kingdom. If, however, the
supply of houses is to equal the demand,
it is necessary that there should be a constant and a steady stream of building to
take the place of houses that are worn
out, and to meet an increasing population.
The restriction in the building of houses
To meet these circumstances, various
Rent Restriction Acts were passed, but
these Acts are only a palliative, and not
a remedy, and should be removed so soon
as it is possible without inflicting an undue hardship on any portion of the community. That is the policy of the
Government. The only remedy for the
present condition of affairs is obviously to
provide a sufficient number of houses in
order that the ordinary economic laws can
again operate. This I propose to refer to
later.
Dealing with the present object of this
Bill, that is, to extend the period of decontrol in regard to the houses which are
at present under control, namely, houses
of a valuation of £26 and under, may I
tell the House that in Belfast alone there
are approximately 79,000 houses of this
category, and, therefore, I think hon.
Members will fully appreciate the extent
and importance of the problem that we
have got to face. This class of house is
inhabited for the most part by a portion.
of the community who are least able to
provide houses for themselves, and who
are people of very moderate means, principally the artisan and labouring classes,
who certainly, in these difficult times
through which we are passing, deserve the
greatest consideration from the community.
Had the Government been convinced
that in 1930 the supply of houses then
existing would be sufficient to meet
the demands of the people, they
would not have hesitated to carry out the
policy laid down in the 1925 Acts. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) As I have already stated, it is, in the opinion of the
Government, against the public interest
that control should be continued for one
moment longer than is absolutely necessary.
The Government, after surveying the
whole situation, have come to the conclusion that in spite of the increasing
number of houses which have been, and
are being, built, with the aid of the subsidy which the Government is affording,
the supply of houses of the valuation
Rent Restrictions Bill-

Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
which I have mentioned will be inadequate to meet the demands at 1st May,
1930. Therefore, the Government propose to implement the undertaking which
I gave to this House in April last, and
propose, under this Bill, to extend the
period of control which would otherwise
terminate on 1st May, 1930, to 1st May,
1933. If the Government was simply to
continue rent control, and take no steps
to see that a sufficient number of houses
are being built, they would be failing in
their duty. From the time that, the
Government took office, they have never
lost sight of this question. Our State
subsidy scheme has worked, and is working, most satisfactorily, and the success
of our policy may be gauged from the
fact that under these schemes 15,000
houses have been approved.

when one contrasts these figures with

the Government is satisfied that the control should not be taken off until May,

vacancy occurs the control should be continued. One knows why the £8 to £22
provision was included in the 1925 Act.
The reason is that the original design of
the Increase of Rent Acts was not to
stereotype the rent upon all houses. The
original design was to protect the sitting
occupier. The idea was that you were
protecting the man in the possession of a
house at a fair rent, but when that house
fell vacant there was no man to protect
and there was no reason to stereotype the
rent on the house. I am afraid that the
Government will, through the policy
which they have carried out in the last
year, be faced with a considerable and
not ill-founded demand for some such
amendment as has been suggested by the
Opposition. What you have got now to
consider is that a large number of people
are not voluntarily leaving houses, but
are being forcibly dispossessed of houses.

Of course, at the present stage we cannot
do other than support the Bill, but on the

take a wider and larger view. (Hon.

CLAUSE 9.-(Offences, prosecutions.
and application of sums.)
(1) Any person who sends, or attempts
to send, potatoes out of Northern Ireland in contravention of any provision of
this Act or rule made thereunder, or in
breach of any condition of a licence, certificate of an inspector, or permit granted
or issued to such person under this Act,
shall be liable on conviction for the first
offence to a fine of five pounds, or any
greater sum not exceeding ten pounds,
and for the second offence to a fine of ten
pounds or any greater sum not exceeding
twenty pounds, and for the third or any
subsequent offence to a fine of twenty
pounds or any greater sum not exceeding
fifty pounds.

23 OCTOBER 1928
PART VIII.
JOINT COMMITTEES ON BILLS.
108. (Hour of meeting, &c., of Committees on opposed Bills).
Every Joint Committee on opposed
Bills shall meet not later than eleven
o'clock every morning, and shall sit
till four, and shall not meet at a later
hour nor adjourn at an earlier hour
without leave of both Houses or without reporting to both Houses the cause
of such later meeting or earlier adjournment. No Committee shall adjourn over any day except Saturday,
Sunday, Christmas Day, and Good
Friday, without leave of both Houses,
or without reporting to both Houses
the cause of such adjournment, but
should a Committee meet on
Saturday the sitting is to be in conformity with this Order.

Bills be amended as follows:-
Order No. 108, line 6, after the word
"except" ("except Saturday") to insert

The object of this Amendment may be
stated very shortly to the House. It will
allow a Committee to adjourn from
Thursday until the following Tuesday, if
it thinks fit. That is, to confine its
sittings to days on which the House is
sitting.

the education authority was entered into
by the school trustees, the manager and
the education authority early last year
and approved by the Ministry. Owing
to unexpected difficulties, however, the
conveyance of the school buildings has
not yet been completed and pending the
completion of this conveyance the Regional Education Committee has carried
on the management of the school.
It may, however, point out that,
according to the Ministry's regulations,
a teacher who has not obtained his training diploma is not eligible for recognition
as principal of a school such as the school
referred to in which the average attendance is about 50 pupils.
The Ministry has no information in regard to the steps taken by the Regional
Education Committee to appoint a new
principal in the school, nor is it aware
to what extent the Secretary has been
authorized to act in the manner stated in
the question.
Teachers have adequate opportunities
of obtaining their diplomas as assistants
or as principals of small schools.
KING'S SCHOLARS.
2. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether he will state how many King's
Scholars completed their course of training and passed satisfactorily in July,
1927, and in July, 1928, respectively;
how many of the former and how many
of the latter respectively have been appointed to teacherships in Northern Ireland; how many in each case have
migrated to Great Britain; how many in
each case have migrated to the British
Dominions and other countries; how
many in each case have gone to other
employments in Northern Ireland; how
many in each case are unemployed; and
whether he will take steps to ensure that
the supply of trained teachers will be
only equal to the demand.
Mr. ROBB: 177 teachers successfully
completed their training in 1927, and of
this number 162 have secured employment in Public Elementary Schools in
Northern Ireland, 8 are continuing their
studies at the university for a degree, and
7 have not yet secured appointments.
154 teachers successfully completed
their training in 1928. Up to the
present the appointments of 58 of these
teachers have been approved by the Ministry, and it is anticipated that employment will be available for the remainder
before the termination of the present
training session.
The Ministry has no information that
any teachers trained in 1927 or 1928 have
gone to Great Britain or the British
Dominions or have taken up other employment, with the exception of
woman teacher who, it is understood, is
entering upon missionary work abroad.

I can assure the hon. Member that it

LONDONDERRY BOYS' EVENING
CLASS.
3. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Beattie) asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether an unemployed, though qualified, teacher was a candidate for the
teachership of a boys' evening class for
unemployed juveniles under the control
of the Education Committee of Londonderry City; whether a principal of a day
public elementary school, enjoying a
salary of £600 per annum, was appointed; and what steps he proposed to
take, if any, to ease the unemployment
situation by abolishing cases of pluralism.
Mr. ROBB: The Ministry is aware
that the principal teacher of a day public
elementary school has been appointed
teacher of a boys' evening class for unemployed juveniles under the control of
the Education Committee of the city of
Londonderry. It appears from their
minutes that the Committee had under
consideration the appointment of another
teacher whose name is not on the list of
teachers serving in a permanent capacity
in a public elementary school.
Teachers of evening elementary schools
are appointed by the school managers,
and the Ministry does not interfere with
their discretion in the selection of qualified teachers. It is, therefore, open to
a manager to select the candidate who
appears to be best qualified for the work.
With regard to the last part of the
question, I may say that it would not be
in the interest of the pupils attending
evening schools to prohibit the employment in this part-time work of experienced teachers serving in day schools.
STATE TREASURY
NOTES.
IRISH FREE
4. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Kyle) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he is aware of the inconvenience
caused to citizens of Northern Ireland in
cashing Free State Treasury Notes which
they receive from their relatives working
in the Free State; and can he state
whether these notes are legal tender in
Northern Ireland; and if they are not
legal tender can he make a public declaration as to the availability of these bank
notes in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am not aware of any such
inconvenience as is referred to by the hon.
Member. I have ascertained that all
banks operating in Northern Ireland
facilitate their clients by exchanging without charge Irish Free State notes for notes
current in Northern Ireland. Should
difficulties occur in the case of persons
unable to avail themselves of these facilities, the proper and indeed, in any event,
the safer course appears to be for persons
despatching money from the Free State
to relatives in Northern Ireland to make
use of the Postal or Money Order system.
Free State Treasury notes are not legal
tender in Northern Ireland, and I see no
reason for making any public announcement in regard to any informal arrangements which may exist in Banks or elsewhere for their acceptance.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN : Can
the right hon. Gentleman say whether
this is the exact position in regard to
Free State currency in Great Britain, or
whether it is another attempt on the part
of Northern Ireland to discriminate
against the Free State?
Mr. POLLOCK: No, Sir, I emphatically dissent from any such assumption.
The conditions that govern the circulation
of Free State currency in Great Britain
apply here in all particulars.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would
the right hon. Gentleman say whether
that is the position taken up by the
British Government-perhaps he will
give the House that information?
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman not aware that the public of Northern Ireland are very glad to get notes
from any State?

Mr. POLLOCK: Last year in discussion
with the British Legion, I undertook to

in the Civil Service with a view to ascertaining whether further steps could be
taken to absorb a larger number in our
permanent establishment. In pursuance
of this undertaking, consultations have
taken place with the Civil Service Representative Council in Northern Irelandwhich is recognised by the Government
as the appropriate body for consultation.
in connection with such matters-and investigation has been made into the present and prospective requirements of our
Departments. As a result, I am satisfied that justification exists for providing
definite established and pensionable posts
for seventy-five of those ex-Service Temporary Clerks who have not up to now

grade. This is the utmost extension of
our permanent establishment which can be

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE
CERTIFICATES.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Kyle) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he is aware of the practice of dispensary doctors in Belfast of
compelling poor patients to attend their
own private houses to issue certificates for
National Health Insurance purposes, and
charging these patients one shilling for
them; and whether he will issue instructions to the Belfast Poor Law Guardians
that dispensary doctors are not to charge
a fee for the issuing of these certificates.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The matter referred to in the hon. Member's question
is one over which I have very little
control.
It is no part of the duty of a dispensary
medical officer as such, to issue certificates to dispensary patients for National
Health Insurance purposes. If a certificate is required it is a personal matter
between the doctor and the patient, so
far as the administration of the Poor
Relief Acts is concerned.
I should, however, add that if a dispensary medical officer were to exact any
substantial fee for such a certificate, I
should regard it as a colourable device
to obtain payment for his medical services from a dispensary patient, and take
action accordingly.
It was brought to the notice of the
Ministry some time ago that fees were
being charged by some medical officers for
the issue of certificates in maternity
cases, and it was thought desirable to
issue a circular to boards of guardians
stating that while the Ministry could not
prevent a nominal fee being charged it
could not countenance anything beyond
this.
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend will give me any facts I will certainly inquire into them.
Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN: Would
the right hon. Gentleman give an undertaking to inquire into the allegation contained in this question and find
whether there is any substance in it?

1930.

MATERNAL MORTALITY.
10. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN (for
Mr. Kyle) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether, in view of the exceptionally high maternal mortality rate in Northern Ireland, the Government proposes
to take any steps to keep in line with the
Governments of Great Britain, Australia,
and the United States, not to mention the
League of Nations, all of which have instituted inquiries into the cause of this
blot on our civilisation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The matter
referred to by the hon. Member has been
engaging the attention of the Ministry of
Home Affairs for several years, and the
Ministry has been working on practically
parallel lines with the Ministry of Health
and other Government Departments responsible for public health administration.
Ireland, and as the hon. Member is aware,
one of the first Acts passed by the Government of Northern Ireland at my instigation provided for the setting up in Northern Ireland of a Joint Midwives Board,
whose functions are to co-ordinate and
improve the training of midwives for the
public service in Northern Ireland.
As the hon. Member is
aware, the
Ministry has been encouraging in every
possible fashion the establishment and the
administration of Maternity and Child
Welfare Schemes throughout Northern
Ireland. The Ministry has also
couraged the appointment of fully
trained and qualified midwives in the
various districts throughout Northern
en-
The Ministry is at the same time taking
steps to collect and collate information
regarding maternal mortality and the
causes of death, and it is hoped that from
the information so collected it will be possible to ascertain more fully the causes
of the high maternal mortality in certain
areas, and to make suitable provision for
dealing with the problem.
I should, at the same time, mention
that it is the intention of the Government at a very early date to introduce
legislation into Parliament providing for
the control and inspection of Nursing and
Maternity Homes.
PORK CURING-NEW PROCESS.
12. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he has seen the
statement of the President of the Armour
Packing Company of America, that owing
to the abundance of the corn crop and the
discovery of a new process in the curing
of pig meat for long distance exportation,
the American shippers have perfected
plans for capturing the British trade, and
if he has considered what the effect will
be upon the farmers of Northern Ireland,
and what action he proposes to take.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have seen the
statement referred to. As the hon. Member for Fermanagh is aware, the bacon
trade is a fluctuating trade and there is
no doubt that a bumper harvest in the
U.S.A. would probably be reflected in increased exports of bacon to the British
markets. At the same time the chief
factors in capturing a market are quality
and price and my Ministry will not relax
any efforts to focus the attention of Northern Ireland producers on these points.
In any event it remains to be seen whether
the new process referred to will have the
effect claimed for it.

CLAUSE 1 (Powers of Ministry of
Home Affairs and Guardians as to exceptional distress).
Mr. WM. McMULLEN: There is
one portion of this Clause I desire to
speak against, and it will be found on
page 2, Sub-section 3. This is in connection with the area of charge so far as
outdoor relief is concerned. I am of
opinion that the charge should not be.
localised at all, and that the financial
responsibilities in regard to relief disbursed in Belfast should be borne by the
entire area of Northern Ireland. The
Committee will remember that when this
Bill was being given a Second reading I
directed attention to this aspect of the
matter, and I then gave reasons why in
my opinion the charge should not fall
directly upon the ratepayers of Belfast,
but that on the contrary it should be
borne by the entire taxpayers of Northern
Ireland.
I suppose I will not be permitted to
anticipate the legislation that is likely to
be introduced in this Parliament during
the present Session, but if the derating
proposals, which I understand are to be
introduced by the Minister of Finance,
are similar to the proposals to be introduced in the British Parliament, I believe
it is the intention in cases of this kind
that the charge should be borne by a large
and not by a local area at all. In view
of this circumstance and in view also of
the fact that Belfast is not responsible
for the degree of unemployment that
exists I am of opinion that the ratepayers of Belfast should not be saddled
with this responsibility.
I should point out that Belfast like
every other industrial centre is suffering
as a result of the world war. Forces were
let loose which have been responsible for
an increase in the National Debt from
seven hundred millions as it stood in 1914
until I think the figure at the moment
is approximately seven thousand five
hundred millions. In other words, the
National Debt has increased by about ten
times since 1914. And the war has been
directly responsible for that. In my
judgment that factor together with the
hurried deflation policy followed by the
British Government is responsible in a
large measure for the industrial situation
that we are experiencing in Belfast at the
present time.
Having regard to the fact that the
Belfast citizens were not responsible for
the policy that has brought about this
unfortunate situation and that the Board
of Guardians may be expected to disburse
outdoor relief to a considerable number
of people as they were doing before
they took their recent action to discontinue the payment of outdoor relief, I
am of opinion that it would be a more
equitable burden if the charge were distributed over the entire area rather than
being put on the ratepayers of Belfast.
I am going to oppose this Clause, and I
hope, though the right hon. Gentleman
will not agree to its deletion, he will make
some alteration in it.

My Motion is put down with a specific
object. It is to the effect that this
House views with grave concern the unchallenged statements made on the public.
platform in Belfast and Dromore, County
Down, and widely reported in the Press
in Northern Ireland, that District Inspector Allen, in July, 1924, accused
Head Constable Slacke of the Belfast
Detective Department, of concealing evidence at the trial of Mrs. Whan in January, 1923, which in the interests of Justice
Head Constable Slacke should have disclosed, and which if disclosed in his
--District Inspector Allen's opinion

who have made, and are still making,
the said false statements as will vindicate
Head Constable Slacke and the honour

the settled conviction in the public mind
that, owing to the reprehensible conduct
of responsible servants of the Crown, Mrs.
Whan has been cruelly victimised by a
serious miscarriage of justice.
District Inspector Allen satisfied himself that Mrs. Whan's convictions were
obtained on perjured evidence. He reported to his superiors in July, 1924, that
Head Constable Slacke concealed evidence favourable to Mrs. Whan at her
trial in January, 1923. District Inspector Allen asked permission to take proceedings at once against the Walkers for
criminal conspiracy; failing that permission he asked to be allowed to hand over
to Mr. Watters, solicitor, his report, to
enable Mr. Watters to obtain the evidence
to institute civil proceedings against the

Loans Guarantee [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair].
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922
to 1928, by increasing from ten million
five hundred thousand pounds to eleven
million five hundred thousand pounds
the limit on the aggregate capital amount
of the Loans, the principal or interest of
which may be guaranteed by the Ministry
of Finance under the Loans Guarantee
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922; and by
extending to the thirty-first day of March,
nineteen hundred and thirty the period
within which guarantees may be given
thereunder; and to charge on the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland any
moneys required for fulfilling any such
guarantees. -Governor's Recommendation signified-(Mr. Barbour).
..
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY of
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE
(Mr. Barbour): The
The policy recommended by this resolution is the extension of the operation of the Loans
Guarantee machinery for a furthur period
of one year and the increasing by a sum
of one million pounds of the statutory
maximum within which guarantees may
be given by the Ministry of Finance.
Unless extended by furthur legislation.
the Loans Guarantee Acts will automatically come to an end on 31st March
next, and although it has been the
Government's intention to leave the question of extending legislation in abeyance
nutil next spring, the activities of the
Ministry in this conection during the last
few months have so reduced the cash
margin within the existing statutory
maximum of ten million five hundred
thousand pounds laid down by the Act of
1927, that the Government has decided to
seek furthur
powers at the present
juncture.
The position at the present time is that
guarantees have been issued or are about
to issue aggregating a sum of £9,680,657,
leaving a margin of approximately seven
hundred thousand pounds for further
undertakings. It is proposed to increase
this existing margin by a further one
million pounds, thus giving the Ministry
power to issue new guarantees aggregating
one million seven hundred thousand
pounds. The actual outstanding liability
of the State in respect of the guarantees
which have been issued is £8,632,530.
It is encouraging to know that very
important orders have been secured in the
course of last year by our Belfast shipyards without recourse being had to these
Government facilities; yet hon. Members

That brings in a very important
aspect of this whole question of rent and
rent restrictions. In the days when rent
restriction was working under the 1915
Act rents did bear some relation to the

Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member seems to have entirely overlooked the intention and effect of the Bill.
Under the Act of 1925 the houses of
a valuation of £26 and under become subject to decontrol on 1st May, 1930, and
this Bill has for its sole object the
lengthening of that period so that those
houses will remain under control until 1st
May, 1933. I am rather astonished that
my hon. Friend should move this Amendment because if it was carried it would in
my opinion remove all protection from
the tenants whose interests he professes
to represent. The Amendment states
that control shall continue until such
time as a sufficient number of houses are
available to house the people. Who is to
determine that? The only thing I can
suggest is that the hon. Member has now
got so much confidence in the Government that he wishes to leave to the
Government the decision as to how long
control is to continue.
The intention of this Bill is to give a
longer period of security to the tenants
than would be given if the Amendment
moved by the hon. Member was carried.
I would remind the hon. Member that in
the course of my Second Reading speech
on this Bill I stated that if the circumstances warranted we would prolong the
period of control until after 1st May,
1933. He taunts the Government with
having increased the period fixed in the
Act of 1925, but we afterwards all became aware of certain things and I hope
that when 1st May, 1933, comes there will
be a sufficient number of houses for the
people who require them. For these
reasons the Government cannot accept
the Amendment.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY of
the MINISTRY of FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The Bill, the Second Reading of
which I am now privileged to move, makes
provision for the payment of additional
grants to the Queen's University of Belfast; secondly, it gives Parliamentary
approval to the arrangement already
entered into between the Queen's University authorities and the Ministry of
Agriculture whereby the expenses of the
Agricultural Faculty of the University
are defrayed by the State: and thirdly,
it contains a Clause empowering the Governing Body of the University to borrow
money. I propose to refer to the three
Clauses of the Bill in some detail.
Under Clause 1, which will require to
form the subject of a Financial Resolution, it is proposed to increase the existing annual Parliamentary grant to the
i'niversity by a sum of £4,000 per annum.
The present annual Parliamentary grant,
which is contained in the Estimates for
'Educational Services-it is mentioned on
page 115 of the Estimates-amounts to
£36,000 per annum and is made up of
£10,000 which was formerly paid out of
the Church Temporalities Fund-a fund
which no longer exists, having been
merged in the Exchequer £18,000
[5-30 p.m.
McMullan, Thomas Wallace
Parker, Mrs. Dehra
Pollock, Rt. Hon. Hugh MacDowell
Robb, John Hanna
Shillington, Major David Graham
TELLER FOR THE AYES-

Mr. Beattie.
which was the original grant under the
Irish Universities Act, 1908, to which
must be added the sum of £8,000 conferred by the Government of Ireland Act,
1920. The present proposed addition of
£4,000 will bring the total State assistance to the University to a figure of
£40,000 per annum.
In putting forward this proposal I may
state that the Minister has very carefully
considered the present circumstances of
the University and has satisfied himself
that this additional grant is fully justified
having regard to the changes in economic
conditions, the normal growth of the
University, particularly since the Government of Northern Ireland was established, and the needs of the University.
The Government are further satisfied that
had the University remained subject to
the University Grants Committee, upon
whose recommendations Government
grants are made to the British Universities, the Queen's University might have
expected to receive supplementary annual
assistance from State sources of at least
the equivalent of the grant of £4,000 now
proposed. It will be noted that this increased grant is to date from 1st October
of the present year, so that a sum of
£2,000 will be payable in the current
financial year. If this Bill meets with the
approval of the House, a supplementary
Estimate will be introduced in due course
to enable the payment of this sum to be
made in the present financial year.
Clause 2 deals with the new Agricultural Faculty, the necessary accommodation for which has been recently provided
-partly at the expense of the State and
nartly out of the resources of the University--for the teaching of applied agricultural sciences in connection with the Agri-
2641 Queen's University Bill-

Second Reading.
cultural Faculty of the University and for
the agricultural research and experimental work of the Ministry of Agriculture
and of the University. The running expenses of this Faculty have been voted
from year to year in recoupment to the
University authorities, and if hon. Members will refer to page 125 of the Estimates they will see therein set out the
estimated payments for the current year.
It has been felt, however, that now that
the Faculty has been moved to its permanent home, which was declared open
by His Grace the Governor during the
summer of this year, a continuing liability of this kind should be set upon a
more definite statutory basis than the
annual Estimates and the Appropriation
Act. Consequently Clause 2 of the Bill
provides for the desired record being
placed on the Statute Book. The detailed
expenditure will, of course, continue to be
shown in the annual Estimates.
No reference is made in Sub-section (b).
of this Clause to the professors and
lecturers of this Faculty. These gentlemen are, in fact, the chiefs and their
assistants in the Ministry's Research Division, on whom the University for academic purposes conferred the titles of
professors and lecturers, but without any
salary payment from University funds,
that is to say the professorial and lecturing work of the Faculty is performed by
civil servants whose salaries are already
borne in their primary capacity as such
on the estimates of the Ministry of Agriculture.
Clause 3 of the Bill has been framed
so as to meet the express wishes of the
Governing Body of the University that
they may be given the power to borrow
money for certain capital purposes, which
are enumerated under four heads in the
Clause itself. The present buildings have
been provided in the main from State
funds supplied to the University before
1908 or under the Universities Act of that
year, but modern requirements in the
matter of laboratories and so forth render
it necessary that further construction
shall take place at no distant date, and
it is to ease the burden of the resultant
expenditure that this borrowing power is
being given. I beg to move.
It will be noted that, in addition to the
payment of the subordinate staff and of
the general maintenance costs, provision
is made for an increase in the amount of
the Capital Construction Grant from the
sum of £34,500, which was laid down in
sub-section (1) of section 13 of the Government Loans and Exchequer Provisions
Act (Northern Ireland), 1925, to a sum
not exceeding £35,500, that is to say an
increase in the maximum grant of £1,000.
It is not expected that the full amount of
£1,000 will be required in connection with
this capital work, but it is known that
supplementary works and fittings will
make some
further limited provision
necessary. I would remind hon. Members that this expenditure finally comes
out of the Capital Fund No. 2, which was
provided by the the Imperial Exchequer
to enable counterparts of certain buildings
situated in Dublin to be erected in
Northern Ireland.

25 OCTOBER 1928
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 25th October, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
BALLYMONEY MODEL SCHOOL-
WAGES OF JANITORS.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
amount of money spent for the year ended
31st March last in wages of janitors in
the Ballymoney Model School; the number of other transferred schools in the
North Antrim region; the number of
which have janitors, and the money expended on their wages; and the arrangements made for lighting fires and cleaning school rooms where no janitors are
retained.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb.): The wages of the
janitor in Ballymoney Model School
amount to £68 18 0 per annum. There
are 11 other transferred schools in the
area of the North Antrim Regional Education Committee. The Ministry has no
information in regard to the wages paid
to janitors of any other transferred school
in the area, with the exception of Bushmills, the janitor of which receives 25/-
per week.
The only schools in which the Ministry
does not require the employment of hired
help to discharge the duties of lighting
the fires and daily cleansing of the school
premises are small country schools with
not more than two rooms. In these
schools, provided that there is no objection on the part of the parents, the
Ministry does not interfere with the
practice which has been hitherto in force of
arranging for the carrying out of the
trifling work involved in the lighting of
fires and the daily sweeping and dusting
of the rooms by the voluntary assistance
of the pupils.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the hon. and
learned Gentleman make arrangements
whereby the pupils in the small schools
would not be charged with this upkeep?
I think he should see that this is carried
out in the smaller schools.
Mr. ROBB: If there is any objection
on the part of parents they can make it
to the education authority.
Mr. BEATTIE: Surely the hon. and
learned Gentleman is aware that the
parents will not make any objection to
the small contribution, although they
are unable to bear it. It is the poorer
class of children that go to the small
schools.
NEWRY TEACHERS' ASSOCIATION
---TEACHING OF IRISH.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he has seen the resolution passed by the Newry Teachers'
Association expressing their disappointment that "Irish" is virtually excluded
from the public schools of Northern Ireland; and whether he will agree to consult
the wishes of the parents in this matter.
Mr. ROBB: I am aware of the resolution regarding the teaching of the Irish
language in public and
and elementary
schools to which the hon. Member
refers. I cannot agree that the
regulations of the Ministry virtually
exclude the teaching of this subject from
the schools. In the larger schools Irish
may be taken in the senior standards in
place of one of the compulsory subjects.
In smaller schools where the prescribed
curriculum is naturally less extensive
Irish may be taught as an additional
subject at the option of the school
manager. I will not take up the time of
the House with the detailed regulations,
but I shall be happy to send the hon.
Member a copy of the official regulations.
The Ministry considers that the facilities
provided for the teaching of Irish are
fully adequate to meet all the legitimate
desires of parents and others interested,
and it is not prepared to extend them.

-FREIGHT REDUCTION.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of

first instalment of de-rating legislation,
viz., freight reduction, is to take effect

relief will become effective in Northern

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Relief to railways in respect of
rates will, it is understood, operate in
Great Britain from 1st December next,
and, subject to the necessary money provision being made by this House, the
Government proposes that the date from
which the corresponding relief will operate
in Northern Ireland will be identical
with that adopted in Great Britain.

MATERNITY NURSES' FEES.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
some dispensary medical officers and dispensary district maternity nurses charge
fees to mothers for signing the certificates
which entitle them to maternity benefits;
whether other dispensary district maternity nurses charge mothers for cost of
motor cars, and, if so, does the Minister
approve of these deductions from the
maternity benefit; and can he state what
is the maximum charge for signing certificates and for car fares.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In reply to
the first part of the question, I would
refer the hon. Member to the answer I
gave to a similar question put by the hon.
Member for North Belfast on the 23rd
instant.
The answer applies equally to dispensary midwives.
With regard to the second part of the
question, no dispensary midwife has any
power to demand any remuneration for,
or payment of, expenses incurred in
connection with the treatment of a dispensary patient.
If the hon. Member will furnish me
with particulars of any specific case where.
a midwife has demanded the payment of
travelling expenses from a dispensary
patient, I shall have the matter fully
investigated.

It reads.
For the purpose of this part of this
Section the expression "tenanted land"
means land held for a statutory term or
under any contract of tenancy other
than a fee-farm grant, or lease for
lives or years renewable for ever or
lease for a term of years of which sixty
or more are unexpired:
In view of the limitation imposed by this
Section it is quite obvious we have no
power to determine what occupant of land
comes within the purview of the Act. It
is a matter for the Land Purchase Commission, and I have no doubt at all that
if we
interfered with the operation of
that Commission the Imperial Authorities
associated with the carrying out of the
work would resent it very much.
Provided that land which has become
tenanted land as above defined by

entered into on or after the sixteenth

Part of the Act.

OLD AGE CONTRIBUTORY

10. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state why
Mr. Patton, of Rugby Avenue, Belfast,
is refused the Old Age Contributory
Pension; whether it is a fact that this
man worked all his life in Northern Ireland, but owing to depression in trade he
was compelled to take up a position in the
Free State, and had he refused to do so
he would not have received unemployment benefit; whether, after working for
two years in the Free State he returned
to his home in Northern Ireland, and
was then refused his Old Age Contributory Pension on the ground that he was
not five years insured although he had
been insured since 1920; and whether he
will re-consider this case in view of the
hardship imposed, as during the time that
he was employed in the Free State his
home was still in Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I regret that Mr. Patton's
absence in the Irish Free State for 24
years during which time he did not contribute to the Northern Ireland Pensions
Fund disentitles him to a contributory
pension. I may add that as there is no
Contributory Pensions Scheme in the
Irish Free State no reciprocal arrangement would overcome this difficulty. The
hon. Member is incorrect in his suggestion
that Mr. Patton would have been refused
unemployment benefit solely on the
ground that he had refused to accept employment in the Irish Free State.

he had in Northern Ireland for the pur

UNEMPLOYMENT BENEFIT-"NOT
GENUINELY SEEKING WORK."
11. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

number of applicants for unemployment
benefit are being turned down for "not

employment; whether it is a fact that
men have been known to be out six days
per week looking for work, and, after receiving a Court, were turned down for
"not genuinely seeking work."
Mr. ANDREWS: It is no longer any
function of mine to interpret the
Statutes; but I can assure the hon. Member that no claimant who satisfies the
Insurance Authorities that he is really
seeking work is refused benefit on the
ground of the condition mentioned.
Mr. BEATTIE: I require no assurance from the Ministry of Labour. The
facts speak for themselves. Is the Minister aware that during the last twelve
months workers in the shipyards and engineering works have been attending regularly every morning at engineering and
shipbuilding yards and yet have been
turned down for not genuinely seeking
work, notwithstanding the satisfactory information given by the applicants to the
courts? Will he have this system more
thoroughly gone into and interpret what
is meant by not genuinely seeking work?
The answer is in
Mr. ANDREWS:

Mr. BEATTIE: Of course.
COURTS OF REFEREES-NUMBER
OF CASES HEARD.
12. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the number of cases heard before the Courts of
Referees in Northern Ireland since the
5th of May last, and the number who
were refused benefit; whether it is by his
instructions that the official of the Court
of Referees informs the Court whether
the applicant is "genuinely seeking
work," and, if so, whether he is prepared
to allow all cases to go before the Court
without prejudice.
Mr. ANDREWS: Between 15th May
and 8th October, 15,163 applications for
unemployment benefit have been reviewed
by Courts of Referees. Of these, there
were 1,610 recommended for disallowance.
In addition, the Courts upheld on appeal
5,198 disallowances of the chief insurance
officer.
I have given no instructions to appeals
officers of the nature indicated by the
hon. Member. Such facts as are in the
Department's possession are placed before
the Court, whether for or against the
applicant; and the claimant is given
every opportunity of putting forward
fresh evidence to further his own case.
Mr. BEATTIE: Surely the Minister
is aware of the procedure adopted. Is
he not aware that prior to the sitting of
the Court of Referees two interviewing
officers approach the applicant and put
certain questions to him? The decision
of the court is based on their information.
I claim that is not putting the case before
the court without prejudice. I ask the
Minister if he is not prepared to allow
cases to go before the court without prejudice.
Mr. ANDREWS: It is quite right to
say that claimants are interviewed by an
officer of the Department. The claimant
is asked to state his views as regards his
particular case. He is then permitted to
read over that statement or it is read over
to him and he signs it. The decision of
the court is in no way unfairly influenced

IMPORTATION OF FOREIGN
LINEN.
14. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Commerce whether
it is a fact that large consignments of
foreign linen goods are being imported
into Northern Ireland and are being sold
as Irish linen, and, if so, what steps he
proposes to take to safeguard real Irish
linen.
buyers of linen goods may occasionally
purchase such goods under the impression.
that they are Irish linens. A remedy
for such abuse is, however, provided by
the provisions of the Merchandise Marks
Act, 1926, whereby application may be
made to a Standing Committee of the
Board of Trade for an Order in Council
requiring the compulsory marking of
imported linens at the time of sale, or
exposure for sale, with an indication of
origin. My Ministry has called the
attention of the Associations connected
with the linen trade to this remedy, but
the latter hold the view that a more
satisfactory solution of the difficulty
would be for Irish merchants to mark
their products "Irish linen." In many
instances this is being done at the present
time.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I am aware that considerable quantities of foreign linen
goods are unfortunately imported into
Northern Ireland and it is possible that
I am glad that the hon. Member has

on being supplied with the manufactures
of our own people.

Deanta i-nEireann-that is Irish.

677 Game Preservation Bill-

Committee.
Any officer or constable of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary (in this Act
referred to as an "officer or constable')
may enforce the Acts relating to the
laws for the preservation of game, notwithstanding anything in section fifteen
of the Constabulary (Ireland) Act,
1836, as it applies to the said Coustabulary:
Provided that no officer or constable
shall enter upon any lands for the sole
purpose of enforcing the game rights
of any owner or occupier of such lands,
or of any person to whom such owner
or occupier may have granted the
game rights over such lands.
Mr. COOPER: I beg to move in Clause
1, line 12, to omit the word "sole" ("for
the sole purpose"). The section reads:
"Provided that no officer or constable
shall enter upon any lands for the sole
purpose of enforcing the game rights of
any owner or occupier of such lands, or
of any person to whom such owner or
occupier may have granted the game
rights over such lands."
Now this Section may lead to very remarkable results. I may say that I am
not in any way opposed to the preservation of game.
(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) In fact I am one of those who
would like to see game preserved. But in
the constituency which I represent the
game rights are reserved on practically
every holding in the county to the landlord. I would like to give an instance to
show you what my objection is. I happen
to own two pieces of land. One is in a
townland called Relagh, and the landlord,
Lord Enniskillen, has the game rights. I
own another piece of land of which
Colonel Archdale has the game rights reserved. Both these lands are excellent
shooting lands. There are numbers of
pheasants, woodcock, snipe and so forth.
Neither landlord ever interferes with my
shooting nor does either landlord ever put
his foot on the lands nor does he in any
way try to preserve the game. I am not
able, because the game rights are vested in
another, to preserve the game myself. The
result is that instead of these reservations
preserving the game they have the opposite effect and the lands are open to every
poacher in the country. If either of these
gentlemen wished to come and shoot the
lands he would be heartily welcome. He
would be welcomed on the adjoining lands
belonging to his tenants. They never
shoot them, and if this Section is allowed
to remain as it is any policeman could go
upon either of these lands for the purpose
of enforcing the game rights of the owner,
who does not wish him to do it, who never
looks after his game, and never looks after
his game rights. Therefore I beg to move
that the word "sole" should be left out.

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government from the very first, as I explained
on the Second Reading, felt that this
Measure would confer a great benefit particularly on the agricultural community.
I referred particularly to the farming
community. That being so the Government came to the conclusion that this being
essentially a non-political Measure there
was no reason why the Whips should not
be taken off. I hope the Committee will
now try, instead of asking for amendments
which will have the effect of making the
Bill useless to everybody, to consider each
amendment on its merits and combine together to bring about a good Bill. I think
everybody in this House will agree with
me that if we can bring about a condition
of affairs where we will have game preserved much good will result to the community as a whole. With regard to the
amendment which has been moved by my
hon. Friend, personally I see no objection.
The only thing I do say is this that in debating the passing or rejection of these
amendments hon. Members will give due
weight to the purpose of the Bill.

Mr. DAVISON: I beg to move in
page 1, line 14, leave out from "person"
("of any person to whom') to the end of
line 15, and insert "in whom the game
rights over such lands are vested."
This Clause generally extends to police
officers and constables the power of enforcing the game laws, but the proviso, to
which I am now moving an Amendment,
limits those powers. The intention of it
is to forbid the police entering upon lands
for the sole purpose of enforcing game
rights. There is an enumeration there of
the persons interested in game rights, and
it is intended to be, I think, an exhaustive
enumeration, but the police could enter
lands for the purpose of challenging the
game rights of any persons who are not
subject to the proviso.
The enumeration
at present in the Clause is:
No officer or constable shall enter upon
any lands for the sole purpose of enforcing the game rights of any owner
or occupier of such lands, or of any
person to whom such owner or occupier
may have granted the game rights over
such lands.
That would exclude landlords who had
reserved the game rights to themselves.
I now move the Amendment for the purpose of including these and forbidding a
constable entering lands for the purpose
of enforcing such game rights. I move to
strike out:
"to whom such owner or occupier may
have granted the game rights over such
lands'
and in place of that to insert:
"in whom the game rights over such
lands are vested."
These words would be wide enough to
cover all persons who are interested in the
game rights of any lands, and so carry
out what I believe is the intention of the
proviso.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Government feel that this is an Amendment
that should be accepted as it clarifies the
the Clause and will improve it.

farm shooting upon it until he satisfied

NEW CLAUSE (Close season
woodcock and snipe.)
for
No person shall, on any pretence
whatsoever, kill or destroy any woodcock or snipe, between the fifteenth
day of February and the twelfth day
of August in any year, or wilfully
destroy the eggs or nest of any woodcock; and any person offending against
this section shall be liable to the same
penalty as is imposed by an Act passed
by the Irish Parliament in the session
held in the twenty-seventh year of the
reign of His Majesty King George the
Third, chapter thirty-five, intituled,
An Act for the Preservation of the
Game, upon persons offending against
that Act. The provisions of the Wild
Birds Protection Acts, 1880 to 1908,
shall cease to apply with respect to
woodcock and snipe or the eggs of
woodcock and snipe.
Brought up, and read a First time.
I beg to
Major SHILLINGTON:
move, "That the Clause be now read a
Second time." As this matter stands at
present the close season varies in different
counties in Northern Ireland. The present close season begins on the 1st March
and it ends on the 1st September in
some counties, and on the 1st October in
others. It is proposed in this New Clause
that the close season for woodcock and
snipe shall begin on the 15th February
and end on the 12th August. I think
hon. Members will realize that it will be
an advantage to have uniformity in regard to the close season. I do not know
whether any changes will be necessary
owing to the Amendments already accepted in connection with snipe, but I

CONDITION OF THE SHORE ROAD.
3. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether his attention has been drawn to
the dangerous and unsanitary condition of
the Shore Road, outside the city
boundary and, if so, whether he is prepared to take action to remedy these evils.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No complaints
have reached the Ministry with regard to
the condition of the Shore Road outside
the City Boundary. I have, however,
made inquiries, and find that there has
been some temporary flooding due to the
bursting of a culvert under the road, and
that some sewers have been obstructed by
the debris carried into them by the overflow.
I understand that the culvert has been
repaired by the County Council, and that
the Sanitary Authority concerned is
having the sewers cleaned out. This
action on the part of the local authorities
should remedy any nuisance that may have
been temporarily caused.

FORTNIGHTLY PAY FOR R.U.C.
5. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs

of paying the members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary fortnightly instead

are married and have families.
Sir DAWSON BATES: An alteration
such as that suggested by the hon. Member would cause a very heavy increase in
the work involved in the payment of
salaries, etc., and corresponding additional expenses. I do not think that we

PAY DAY.
6. Mr. WILLIAM MCMULLEN asked
the Minister of Labour whether he is
aware that the pay-day for a large
number of recipients of Unemployed Insurance benefit has been changed from
Friday to Tuesday; whether this means
that on each pay-day recipients have five
days' benefit owing to them; and whether.
in view of the hardship caused, he will
endeavour to have all benefit paid on
Fridays, or failing this, to have payment
made up to Saturday where payment is
made on a Tuesday.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers
30 OCTOBER 1928
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In order to avoid congestion,
it was found necessary to distribute the
payment of unemployment insurance
benefit over three days in the week-
Tuesday, Thursday and Friday-instead
of the normal arrangement to pay on
Friday for the week ending on Wednesday.
As the claimant receives his benefit in
weekly periods, any hardship which may
be involved by the temporary re-arrangement of the pay days only occurs in connection with the first payment.
I regret that at present it would not
be practicable to pay all benefit on
Fridays nor to arrange for the Tuesday
payments to be made up to Saturday as
suggested, but I can assure the hon. Member that I am anxious to revert to the
normal arrangement as soon as, through
a fall in unemployment, it can be done
without causing congestion.

In dealing with this matter, I think it
might be of interest to this House to state
briefly the various Acts that have been
passed dealing with the Housing problem,
particularly those relating to the question
of "subsidy," and I think hon. Members,
when they look at the results which
followed the passing of these various

which has been fully justified by the

Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of
this Bill is to extend the time for the
operation of Section 1 of the Housing
Act of 1927, and if this House passes the
The first attempt which appears to have
been made by the British Government to
deal with the acute shortage of houses in
Ireland following the War was the Act of
1919, under which power was given to
urban authorities to erect houses, the
Government providing £1 5s Od in respect
of every £1 of rent collected by the
authority. The Act lapsed in 1922, and
the figures I have, go to show that during
the 3 years in which the Act was in operation, only 502 houses were provided. Of
these, 459 were built in Belfast, most of
them being entirely unsuitable to the resources of the working man.
I might remind the House that the
Government, some years ago, commuted
the huge liability that they were under in
respect of the Belfast houses by a lump
sum payment of no less than £220,000.
A later Act was passed in 1919, and
this Act, for the first time, introduced
the principle of paying a subsidy to a
private builder, but the great defect of
this Act was was that it provided for a
maximum of 1,400 superficial feet, and
builders concentrated on this type, and
I think that hon. Members opposite will
agree that a house of that description
could not possibly come within the resources of the working man. This Act
was also a failure. as I find that only
533 houses were built under it within
a period of 3 years.
Now I come to the first of the subsidy
Acts passed by the Parliament of Northern Ireland, that is, the Act of 1923.
The Act, the scope of which was limited
to urban areas, provided that a subsidy
should be given of £60 for each house
built in urban areas. whether by the
urban authorities or by private owners,
Housing Bill-
Second Reading

and limited the house to an area of between 600 and 950 superficial feet. The
Act also allowed the urban authorities to
supplement the grants by grants not exceeding £40, or if they preferred they
could give loans of £100 free of interest
for 25 years. That Act operated up to
1st April, 1925. As a result of the working of this Act, I find that at the date
when it lapsed, no fewer than 2,530
houses had been approved, and 850
actually built.
The next Act was the Act of 1925 which
extended the scope of the Act to rural
districts. The old Act had applied only
to urban districts. It also increased the
Government subsidy to £80 where a house
was completed within six months, and it
further provided that local authorities
could, if they so desired, exempt houses
from rates for a period of 10

It must be remembered that we began
our policy in respect of the employment
of ex-Service men almost from the time
we began to function, and, therefore, it
is desirable that I should inform the
House exactly what we have done, the
difficulties we have had to encounter, and

(Col. Woods) opposite, that we have done
more for the ex-service men in Northern
Ireland than the British Government
have done for the ex-Service men in Great
Britain. That is the basis of my whole
argument, but at the same time it is
necessary I should give the material and
evidence of my submission. In the first
place it will be understood that we were
very badly handicapped as compared
with the Imperial Government at the
start, and, indeed, from that time
on wards.
The hon. and gallant Member (Colonel
Woods) opposite and the hon. and gallant
Member (Major Shillington) behind me.
have referred to the numbers employed
by the Imperial Government. There are
227,000 men employed there as against
our 1,600. With such an enormous staff
as this and such an amount of routine
work as is found in many Imperial
Departments, such as the Post Office, the
Excise, and a great many other services,
it will be seen that the opportunities in
the Imperial Service for the absorption
of ex-Service men were undoubtedly
greater than anything we possessed here
in view of the very limited number of
services open to our selection for these
men. That is the first difficulty we were
faced with.
In the second place, we were under a
statutory obligation to take a considerable number of civil servants from the
central government in Dublin. We
could not, of course, avoid that. The
great majority of those were men who had
not military service, I suppose, because
there was no conscription in Ireland; but
from whatever cause, it is a fact that the
great majority of those we were compelled
to absorb into our services were not ex-
Service men. The House will understand from this that a large proportion of
our civil servants was fixed before we
began our operations at all, and that that
necessarily limited the number of ex-
Service men that could be absorbed into
our own Departments. Notwithstanding
these handicaps I am out at this morient
to show that we have done better for our
ex-Service men relatively than the British Government have done for the ex-
Service men in Britain. This, I may
say, is the basis of my argument from
beginning to end, and I will give evidence
to prove it.

the present 353 temporaries have received.
permanent appointments. At this stage

and the result would be that by-and-by,

2815 Ex-Servicemen in Civil Service HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 31st October, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
EX-SERVICE MEN IN THE CIVIL
SERVICE.
Major SHILLINGTON (by Private
Notice) asked the Prime Minister whether
in view of yesterday's proceedings he is in
a position to make any statement regarding the Government's intentions.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I have been in consultation
with my right hon. friend the Minister
of Finance and am convinced that the
Cabinet's proposals regarding the staffing
of the Civil Service as outlined by him
yesterday afternoon secured more advantageous terms to ex-Servicemen as a class,
than would be the case were the British
Govenment method to be adopted, and
further, that the introduction of a new
class of any description between permanent and temporary clerks would not be
conducive to the smooth working of our
Civil Service as a whole.
As, however, a difference of opinion appears to exist regarding the figures upon
which this conclusion is arrived at he is
having a memorandum prepared setting
forth the actual circumstances in full detail, which will be embodied in a White
Paper and circulated to hon. Members,
and if as the result of this meticulous reexamination any new salient facts should
be revealed he will be pleased sympathetically to consider the possibility of absorbing a larger number of ex-Service men
into the permanent ranks of the pensionable Civil Service.

debtedness and obligations to the ex-Service men of Ulster as are those who yesterday had an opportunity of voicing their
views in the matter.
I think it right to sound a note of
warning that false hopes should not be
raised by this statement, but the House
ay be assured that every member of the
Government is as fully alive to their in-
Major SHILLINGTON: I thank the
noble Lord for that statement.
Mr. BEATTIE. I would like to ask

The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): Hon Members will appreciate that this Bill only
deals with the franchise of our local Parliament, and the franchise for local
government elections in Northern Ireland. The main object of it is to confer
upon the women of Northern Ireland the
same rights which have been excerised
hitherto by men; in other words, to assimilate the franchise for men and women.
Hon. Members are aware that recently a
similar Act was passed by the Imperial Parliament dealing with the elections to that
Parliament, but of course hon. Members
will appreciate that the Imperial Act did
not in any way deal with elections either
to our own Parliament or for local authorities.
As this is a somewhat complicated
matter I hope hon. Members will not
think I am dealing with the question at
too great length, but it is desirable that
I should deal in some detail with
the qualifications for men and women for
our own parliamentary and local government elections. May I explain what are
the qualifications for men in regard to
our own Parliament, that is, the qualifi-
2817 Representation of People Bill-
31 OCTOBER 1928

Second Reading
cations that exist to-day! First of all,
the individual must be twenty-one years
of age and not subject to any disability
such as being a lunatic, an alien, or, say,
a Peer of the Realm. He must also have
what is known as a residence qualification;
or, if he has not that, he must qualify as
regards a business qualification. I should
explain that a "residence" qualification
means that the individual must be ordinarily resident in Northern Ireland for a
period of six months before the qualifying
date; while a "business premises' qualification implies that the individual must
be in occupation for a similar period of
business premises the valuation of which
must be at least £10.
Under the Bill I would refer hon.
Members to Clause 1—we propose an alternative qualification, in addition to those I
have mentioned above, namely, that the
man is the husband of a woman who is
registered in virtue of business premises
qualification of £10. But, apart altogether
from this alternative qualification, we intend to impose an overriding qualification
under which the individual must have
been ordinarily resident in the United
Kingdom for a period of three years.

Coming now to the existing qualifications for women for our local Parliamentary franchise, those which exist at present
are as follow:-A woman must be 30
years of age and upwards and not subject to the legal disability I have referred
to, and she must be the occupier or the
tenant of a dwelling-house for a period of
six months before the qualifying date; or
she must be 30 years of age and be the
occupier, as owner or tenant, of the lands
or premises other than a dwelling-house
of a valuation of at least £5, for a period
of six months before the qualifying date.
There is a third qualification. She must
be at least 30 years of age and be the
wife of a man who is entitled to be on
the local government register, and with
whom she resides. Those are the three
qualifications that exist at the present
time to enable a woman to vote for our
own local Parliament.
The new conditions which will be imposed on women will be of a much simpler
kind, because we propose that they will
be precisely those I have already indicated
as regards the men. In addition, a woman
will be entitled by virtue of being married
to have a vote in respect of her husband's
business premises qualification. In other
words, we give a man a vote by virtue of
his wife's qualification, and we give a wife
a vote by reason of the husband's qualification.
Let me come now to the franchise for

Sir DAWSON BATES: To suggest
that a girl who earns her living by her
hands and by her brains cannot be entrusted to decide who should represent
her, is an idea that has long since been
exploded. Before I leave the question
of local government franchise I would
direct the attention of Members of the
House to Clause 3 of the Bill, and now my
hon. Friend (Mr. Beattie) will have a
chance of hearing something on the subject of directors.
Mr. HEALY: Splendid.
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Clause
introduces an entirely new principle. It
introduces the principle of according to
directors of limited companies, whose
company pays local rates, the right of
exercising the franchise-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)--and affords them the
opportunity, not alone of exercising
the franchise, but of becoming members of local authorities, which
at present they cannot do. As the law
now stands, a director of a firm paying
large rates is deprived of having any voice.
in the expenditure of that money. May
I say here and now that I regard that as
a most undemocratic condition of affairs.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Hon.
Members are aware that every year there
is a tendency for the sake of convenience
to turn businesses with perhaps two or
three partners into what are known as
private limited companies, and the effect
of doing so was that while these partners
had a right of voting, the right of becoming members of a local authority and
of voting was by their action in forming
the company taken away from them.
For years past, this principle which I
set forth in the Bill has been urged upon
the Government from the most responsible organisations representing commerce,
trade and industry. It has often been
cast up in the face of many of the great
pioneers of industry in Northern Ireland
that they do not take an interest in local
government administration, but the real
truth is this, that in the large majority
of cases they have not the right nor the
opportunity of doing so.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
least to my hon. Friends on the Government Benches.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Therefore, I
do suggest that a democratic principle
such as I put forward will commend itself,
if not to my hon. Friends opposite at
Hon. Members will observe that we are
strictly limiting the number of directors,
or other representatives of the board, who
can qualify as electors. But under it we
provide that while the valuation is £10
only one director or representative can
obtain a vote. Where the valuation is
high, the directors can qualify at the rate
of one for each £10, but not exceeding on
the whole six representatives.
Mr. BEATTIE: Six votes.

draw the attention of hon. Members to

certainly used to in the old days-that

all the partners, even more than six, were

qualification of three years' residence in
the United Kingdom will apply not only
to our local parliamentary franchise, but

I think it is quite obvious that those of

House for that purpose. But I cannot
understand for the life of me how any
man, even a director, even the Minister

In what way do they differ from us?
Simply because they have more money

Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. KYLE: It is obvious. There is

have more money they are going to get
more votes. That is a state of affairs I
think we ought not to tolerate in these
days. I would like to say in regard to
this Representation of the People Bill as
it is called-I think it is rather a misnomer. It should be as well as Representation of the People, Representation
of Companies Bill. I should like to say
also that a Clause should be introduced
into this Bill making it illegal for any
party to use their country's flag so far
as party use is concerned.
Another point I think my colleague the
Member for East Belfast referred to was
the fact that there is nothing in this Bill
apparently to attempt to put an end to
impersonation of other people's votes. I
think that, strictly speaking, comes under
the heading of Representation of the
People. What has been the practice,
which has been the subject of comment by
Lord Justice Andrews, in our courts?
What has been this practice, which has
been the subject of very drastic remarks
by very prominent people in the Party
opposite as well as here, in regard to this
question of impersonation? Surely something should be done to see that in a
Measure like this that purports to be a
Representation of the People Bill that
should be put a stop to by reasonable
penalties being put on.
Another matter is in regard to the
question of the machinery which is to be
set up to administer this Act, and the
rather complicated references in Clause 7
of the Bill that:
-:
Nothing in this Act shall affect the
right of any person, or confer on any
person any right, to be registered in
the register of electors to be made in
the year nineteen hundred and twentyeight, or to vote at any time before the
register of electors to be made in the
year nineteen hundred and twentynine comes into operation.
Well, I have heard of jig-saw puzzles
and legislation by reference, but I think
that nothing more involved has ever been
offered for the consideration of this
House. I beg to support the amendment
moved by my colleague for East Belfast.

If a man

CLAUSE 7 (Close season for snipe and
woodcock).
No person shall, on any pretence
whatsoever, kill or destroy any woodcock or snipe, between the fifteenth day
of February and the twelfth day of
August in any year, or wilfully destroy
the eggs or nest of any woodcock; and
any person offending against this section shall be liable to the same penalty
as is imposed by an Act passed by the
Irish Parliament in the session held in
the twenty-seventh year of the reign of
His Majesty King George the Third,
chapter thirty-five, intituled, An Act
for the Preservation of the Game, upon
persons offending against that Act.
The provisions of the Wild Birds Protection Acts, 1880 to 1908, shall cease
to apply with respect to woodcock and
snipe or the eggs of woodcock and snipe.

It is quite true to say that workers are

would be that all the conditions for the

benefit would be paid to all comers.
That would be disastrous. It would

it would be quite improper of me to presume to criticize the umpire's decision
just as it would be improper for the Minister of Home Affairs to criticize the decision of a judge of the High Court.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DANCE HALLS IN EAST BELFAST.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
number of licensed dance halls in East
Belfast and the number of unlicensed
ones; and what supervision is exercised
over the unlicensed halls in order to see
that the Public Health Act of 1890 is
not violated.
The MINISTER OF HOME AF-
FAIRS (Sir Dawson Bates): There are
four premises in East Belfast licensed
under the Public Health Acts for music
and dancing.
The attention of the Belfast Corporation-who are the appropriate authority
for instituting proceedings in such caseshas been drawn to these cases by the
police, and prosecutions have been,
accordingly, instituted; or are being
instituted, for breaches of the Acts referred to above.
According to reports received from the
police two cases have come under notice
where premises not so licensed have been
used for public dancing.
PAYMENT OF PETTY SESSIONS
CLERKS' SALARIES.
2. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if it
is a fact that Petty Sessions Clerks have
to make monthly returns of their financial
accounts to his Department, and when
they have £10 and upwards on hands to
lodge it to the credit of the Ministry; and
whether, if this is so, the Minister will
consider paying Petty Sessions Clerks'
salaries monthly instead of quarterly, as
at present.
accounts.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is not a
fact that the Petty Sessions Clerks make
monthly returns of their financial
Their financial accounts are
rendered quarterly to the Ministry of
Home Affairs, but at the same time they
are required to inform us monthly as to
the sums they have on hands, and if these
sums amount to £10 or upwards to lodge
the sum to the credit of the Ministry.
As regards the latter part of the
question, I have not received any representations from the Petty Sessions Clerks
in regard to the suggestion that their
salaries should be paid monthly, and in
these circumstances, and as the suggested
change would involve considerable extra
work and consequential expense, I do not
consider that it would be justifiable to
adopt the suggestion made by the hon.
Member.

6 NOVEMBER 1928
Home Affairs to make grants under
Section one of the Housing Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, being grants chargeable
upon the Consolidated Fund of Northern
Ireland or the growing produce thereof,
in respect of the construction of houses

one thousand nine hundred and thirty,

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): My right hon. Friend (Sir
Dawson Bates) in moving the Second
Reading of the Housing Bill, indicated
the very considerable increase in the
numbers of houses which are being built
with the aid of the State subsidy,
especially since, under the Housing Act
of last year, the amount of the subsidy
in respect of the smaller type of house
(namely, of less than 650 superficial feet)
was increased to £100 for houses completed within six months, the subsidy on
the larger type being discontinued.
As the object of the Resolution now before the Committee is to secure authority
for the continuance of these grants for a
further year, I think the Committee may
wish to know what the cost of the grants
has been up to date, and to have some
indication of the probable expenditure
during the year covered by this Resolution.
In the period from the passing of the
Housing Act of 1923 up to the 31st March
last the total payments by the Government in respect of housing grants were as
follows:-By private builders, 5,184
houses built; £382,840 grants paid;
by Local Authorities, 1,157 houses built;
£76,320 grants paid; or a total payment
by the Government of £459,160 in respect
of 6.341 houses.
I think that these figures are sufficient
to show that under the scheme which is
now in operation and for the continuance
of which the Government seeks the approval of the Committee, we are rapidly
moving towards a solution of the difficulties caused by the shortage of houses
which can be let at a rent within the
means of the average working man.
In the six months ended 30th September last a total sum of £157,180 was paid,
that is to say, more than one-third of
the total amount paid in the five years up
to the 31st March, 1928. This amount
was almost wholly in respect of the
smaller type of house. It is estimated
that in the full year up to the 31st March
next a total sum of no less than £323,000
will have been paid, representing grants
for 3,350 additional houses.
It is, of course, difficult to forecast with
any close degree of accuracy what the cost
of the scheme will be in the year beginning on the 1st April, next, but in the
light of the figures I have already given
it seems possible that as many as 4,000
additional houses qualifying for the grant
will be built during the year, the grants
for which would amount to £400,000. By
the year 1930 therefore this Government
will have spent not less than one million
pounds on housing subsidies, a record
which shows the Government's care and
forethought for the needs of the working
classes of the community. I beg to move.
Mr. KYLE: I want to speak on this

was satisfied that the work was not being

was bound to fall off within a very short

technical details of building in connection
with this Money Resolution, but I do
think that the right hon. Gentleman
should give us some assurance in the first
place that there are specifications, and,
in the second place, that the specifications
are fulfilled by the building contractor.
