Sir DAWSON BATES: In respect to
the two points raised by my hon. Friend
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Kyle)
last night and which you, Mr. Moles,
ruled out of order on the Financial Resolution, I would just like to draw the attention of my hon. Friend to the system
which is adopted in regard to the payment
of subsidies. First of all, the plans must
be drawn up and inspected by the local
authority and passed by them. They have
also to be submitted to the Ministry and
passed by them, and the building operations afterwards must all comply with
the specifications laid down. If my hon.
Friend wishes I will be only too glad to
give him the specification from which he
will see that the utmost care is taken to
ensure that the bricks, timber and other
material used in the building are of a suitable quality. In addition to that, during
the progress of the building the house is
liable to be inspected by the local authority just like any other house and also by
our inspector. Before a subsidy can be
granted the house has to pass an official
inspection, not alone by the surveyor of
the local authority but by the inspector
of the Ministry. It does not follow that
because a house is built the subsidy is
given.
In regard to the question of town.
planning, I quite admit there is necessity
to extend the powers of the local authorities. My hon. Friend knows that in
England the local authority is also the
planning authority. The great object of
town planning is to try to avoid undue
congestion in towns and big areas. We
have been in consultation-I only mention this to show the matter is not overlooked by the Government-with the
Municipal Association which is the association connected with all the municipal
authorities. We have been in touch with
them and also with the Belfast Corporation. At the present time we are actually
awaiting suggestions from them. When
we do produce a. Measure we want to try
to produce one that will meet the situation. I think those are the few points I
desired to mention
I have before me the figures which show
that in at least 32 cases no subsidy was
given on the ground that the house was
imperfectly built, and in hundreds of
other cases the builders were informed that
having regard to the way in which the
houses had been built no subsidy would be
paid unless the defects were remedied. If
I may quote an example, that applies particularly to the houses in connection with
the scandal over the housing question in
the Belfast Corporation. No subsidy was
given in connection with those houses until
the defects complained of had been
remedied. From time to time we have
found it better to alter the specification.
For example, in regard to timber some
time ago we altered the specification to
meet the very case that arose then, and we
have specified that in future the timber
used in those houses should be a class of
timber certainly not of that quality that
we heard so much about. Then there was
the case my hon. Friend referred to.
There we had the Board of Works engineers on to those houses to see whether
or not they complied with the conditions
laid down.

The first essential, in my opinion, ought
to be for decent houses to be erected for
the people to live in, as near decency and
comfort as possible, instead of the first
essential being to enable someone to make
a profit out of the erection of these houses.
Simply because we are allowing the making

Now, it is obvious that if we are to
increase the area of these houses we must
inevitably restrict the number that are
built. In other words, we are able to
build more houses of 650 feet than if we
were to increase the area to 750 or 800
feet. I think it is obvious to everybody
in the House that we cannot take
more out of a pint pot than is in a pint
pot. We have a certain sum which my
right hon. Friend is able to allocate to
help the working classes. These houses
are being snapped up. sought after and
occupied. I hear myself from people
from time to time, very often indeed, how
satisfied they are with these small houses.
I spoke on this subject more than once.
I take a great personal interest in it. I
have visited many of these houses. I
have been in Newry, Ballymena and other
parts of Ulster in order to examine for
myself the houses that are being built
under the various Government schemes,
and I feel that we are on the right lines.
There are 14,708 houses already approved, and the Committee is to-day
asked to pass this Clause in order that a
beneficent Act may be continued until
the 1st April, 1930. If the Committee
were to say to us, "You ought to increase
the size of the houses" we might possibly
get into the awkward position which
we were in in 1923 when houses were
being built for a different class than the
very poor. I am determined that I will
suit the requirements of the very needy
first of all. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
What do I hear? I hear that in some
parts of Ulster houses are let at say 10s
and 129 a week. Those that have got
these house are charging families as much
as 8s and 9s a week for a room inside the
house. Surely it is obvious to all that
the first thing we have to do is to get
these families that are cramped up and
being charged these rents in other
people's houses under a little cover of
their own. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It seems to me to be quite obvious. I
cannot understand what is going on. I
cannot understand this quarrelling with
the Government for finding money to
build what will amount probably to some
20,000 new houses before we are finished
with our scheme, because if there are
14,708 houses now approved I am sure
there will be something nearer 20,000
when we get to the 1st April, 1930. And
we are charged with not doing our duty!
I feel, and my colleagues feel, especially
the Minister of Home Affairs, that this
Act is proving a success and is meeting a
crying need for the very needy. In some
places that I visited in order to study the
position on the spot I found it was impossible to let the houses that had been
built under the earlier subsidies of the
Government. They are let at a rent
that the working classes were not able to
pay, and, therefore, they were of no
advantage to the working classes. I Ι
heard of houses on which subsidies had
been paid not being occupied by the type
they were intended for but being occupied
by people who under ordinary circumstances would have brought in an architect and said to him, "I want you to
build a house of such and such a size for
me."
In other words, advantage was
being taken of these houses by the wrong
class of people.
This Act is, in my opinion, proving
such a success that it would be a cruel
thing to run the slightest risk of breaking
it down. The builders know where they
are, and the people themselves know

and thousands of people who are single.

comfortable and happy, far more so than
under the old conditions which, unfortuately, many of them suffer under at
the present day. Is there any proof that
the demand for this type of houses is
falling off? When these houses are built
is there any indication whatever that the

I hear that when it is proposed to develop a site for the erection of 20, 30 or
40 houses there is immediately an overwhelming number of applications for
them. Only twenty can be granted, and
out of 60 applications 40 applicants are
disappointed. What the Government is
in favour of to-day is to go on and
encourage sixty more being built so that
nobody will be disappointed in the long
run. I think myself when the demand
for these houses begins to fall off, when
we find that as soon as a row is built they
are not occupied and unable to be let,
then it will be time enough for the Government to consider some other scheme.
In the meantime my colleagues and myself feel satisfied we are on the right lines,
and it would be a mistake, either on the
ground that the houses should be a little
larger or on the ground that they should
be very much larger, if we should do
anything whatever that would interfere
with the steady flow of some 500 houses a
month going on. Everybody is accustomed to the idea that the building is
going ahead, and for goodness sake do not
put an end to what is one of the most
beneficent Acts the Government has
undertaken.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
AMENDMENT OF LAW.
1. That it is expedient to amend the
law relating to Stamp Duty and a Duty
of Excise.
STAMP DUTY ON BANKERS'
LICENCES.
II. That as from the twenty-fifth day
of March, nineteen hundred and twentynine, there shall be charged in respect of
every licence to be taken out annually by
a banker under an Act of the present
Session a Stamp Duty of thirty pounds.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): It would, perhaps, be convenient if the two Resolutions on the
Order Paper-one being the usual general
Resolution and the other a specific
Resolution covering the grant of a new
duty-were to be dealt with in the same
speech. In moving their adoption I am
constrained to think that my task will be
an easy one inasmuch as the Bill to be
introduced upon them is not likely to be
regarded as contentious, its subject matter being only minor in character.
The main proposal, which is the subject
of the second Resolution, is the creation
of a banker's licence as such to replace
the present licence which is a licence to
issue unstamped promissory notes, or, as
we more familiarly term them, bank notes.
A bank will in future pay a licence duty
for the privilege of carrying on the business of banking instead of paying for the
privilege of issuing unstamped documents.
Under the old arrangement two banks
operating in Northern Ireland, which
are non-note issuing banks, and a third
bank, which was specifically exempted
under old Imperial legislation, escaped
payment of licence duty in Northern Ireland in any form, and it is now proposed
to correct these anomalies by substituting
a new form of licence duty which will
place all banks on a par. The rate of
duty proposed, namely, £30 for each
licence with a maximum of £120, is the
same as the present duty.
Bankers' Licences

Committee
7 NOVEMBER 1928
A second amendment of the law
relating to Stamp Duty in its relation to
the business of banking, and which is independent of the licence duty provision
to which I have just referred, is covered
by the general Resolution which appears
first on the Order Paper. It relates to
the payment of composition duty on unstamped bills of exchange and bank post
bills which, I may say for the information
of hon. Members, are the technical terms
for bank documents passing between
the several offices in connection with
"Clearing House" activities. It is
rather in the nature of a re-enactment
than an amendment, being designed to
replace a couple of scattered sections of
existing Acts. It leaves undisturbed the
present arrangement with regard to composition duty on these bills of exchange
and bank post bills, the double taxation
relief arrangements between Northern
Ireland and the Irish Free State making
it more convenient that each bank should
continue to compound and pay according
to the location of its head office in Ireland; that is to say, the Irish Free State
Exchequer will receive composition duty
on such documents in the case of banks
whose Irish head offices are located in the
Irish Free State, while the duty will
accrue to the Northern Ireland Exchequer
in the case of banks whose head offices are
situate in Northern Ireland. Although
the provisions of the Bill will be found to
be somewhat technical, hon. Members
will doubtless be satisfied at this stage
with my assurance that they have already
been brought to the notice of the banks
concerned and they have raised ro objection to them.
The general Resolution also refers to
an amendment of the law relating to a
duty of Excise, the duty in question being
Entertainments Duty. It is now proposed
to give effect to the undertaking given by
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) in the course of
his Budget statement, namely, that as
from the 1st day of June last an entertainment consisting solely of one or more
horse-races will be exempt from the duty.
It is also proposed to include provisions
of a minor character designed to clear up
some points of doubt or alleviate cases of
hardship that have arisen under the administration of the present law relating
to Entertainments Duty.
Question, "That it is expedient to
amend the law relating to Stamp Duty
and a Duty of Excise," put, and agreed
to.

Questions separately.
Mr. KYLE: Did I gather the right
hon. Gentleman rightly when he stated
that an arrangement had been entered
into between the banks with head offices
in the Irish Free State and those that
have their head offices in Northern Ireland, a reciprocal arrangement
garding this £30 that is to be paid in
Stamp Duty? Did I gather the right
hon. Gentleman rightly? Did he say
rethat, or is it the case that there is a reciprocal arrangement between our Government and the Government of the Irish
Free State in regard to this matter, that
is, that, in the case of banks having head
offices, say, in Belfast and branch
establishments in towns in the Irish Free
State, we will remit to the Irish Free
State a certain amount, and they will do
similarly to us in the corresponding case
of banks with head offices in the Irish Free
State? Is that the system?
Mr. BARBOUR: The hon. Member is
almost right, but not quite. It arises
out of the working out of the double taxation relief, under which persons, say,
living in Northern Ireland and having
income arising in the Free State, are
only required to pay one income tax,
namely, the larger amount payable in
either of those two places. So in this
arrangement it is obviously undesirable
that a bank should pay duty in both
places, and, as a way of arriving at an
equitable distribution of the taxation.
arising from this licence to carry on
banking business, this is a mutual
arrangement that those banks which have
their head offices in Northern Ireland
will pay their duty to the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland, and those having their
head offices in the Irish Free State will
pay their licence duty to the Exchequer
of the Irish Free State.

RETIREMENT AND RESIGNATION
OF TEACHERS.
3. Mr. PATRICK O'NEILL asked
the Parliamentary Secretary of the
Ministry of Education whether he can
state the number of circuits with their
sub-divisions into which Northern Ireland is divided for the purpose
of
elementary education, and can he give a
return for the past three years showing
for each circuit and its sub-divisions the
following particulars:-(1) The number
of teachers who retired with less than 40
years' service; (2) the number of teachers
who resigned through ill-health; (3) the
number of teachers who died while in the
actual service of the Ministry.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The number
of circuits into which elementary schools
in Northern Ireland are divided for inspection purposes is four, and the number
of sub-divisions is thirteen.
The particulars in the return sought in
the latter portion of the question are not
available in the form in which they are
asked for, and their preparation in this
form would cause such an interruption of
work that the Ministry thinks that the
time and labour involved would be entirely disproportionate to any educational
usefulness of the return when obtained.
Mr. P. O'NEILL: May I ask the hon.
Gentleman as this is a matter of considerable importance, not alone to the teachers
but to many people sympathetically
engaged in educational work, is an hon.
Member not entitled to information when
he asks for it?
turn and if the House, after having been
informed of the cost of the answer,
sanctions it, the Ministry will readily
undertake the work of preparing it.
Mr. ROBB: If the hon. Member will
put down a Motion asking for this re-
Mr. P. O'NEILL: In view of the
answer given is it necessary for an hon.
Member to put down a specific Motion
when he asks for a specific answer to a
specific question, which should be within.
the reach of the Ministry of the hon.
Gentleman?
Mr. SPEAKER: The proper course,
and really the one that should have been
taken where a question asks for statistics,
is to put down a Motion for an unopposed
return, and, assuming, that is, that the
Government agree to give the information, that Motion could be put down any
day before Questions as an unopposed
Motion and taken formally and passed.
If it was opposed, of course, I do not
know quite when he would get an opportunity of moving it. Unopposed Motions
asking for statistics of this kind are
generally granted by the Government,
and the proper way is to put down the
Motion on the Paper before Questions.
Mr. O'NEILL: Surely to ask for a
return of the number of teachers who
have retired in a certain district in
Northern Ireland does not involve such a
huge amount of labour that the Ministry
could not give it when a Member asks a
question?
Mr. ROBB: I do not know whether
this is the proper time for me to say that
this would involve one Department investigating 755 cases. When they had
investigated these, each five would have
to be segregated into one of three categories, and each category would have to
be sub-divided into thirteen divisions.
I am informed by the officials of my
Department-part of the information is
in our Department-that the least estimate of time which it would take our
Department to compile this return is the
time of 33 men for two days. After we
had finished with it, it would then have to
go to the Department of Finance, who would
have to go through the same performance,
and what time it would take them I do
not know. Whether the return is worth
that is a matter for the House. The
Ministry has no objection to give this
information, but if the information is not
available without excessive trouble and
cost, it is for the House to say.

UNEMPLOYED GRADUATE SECON
DARY TEACHERS.
4. Mr. McMULLEN asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he can state how many
graduate secondary teachers are out of
employment; how many are males and
how many females; how many Ulster
graduates have got teaching posts in England and Scotland; whether means can be
found to get work for those unemployed
in Ulster; and whether future aspirants
cannot be kept in smaller numbers until
those at present unemployed are placed.
Mr. ROBB: The Ministry has no information nor means of information as
to the number of graduate secondary
teachers out of employment, nor as to how
many Ulster graduates are teaching in
England and Scotland. Further employment for secondary teachers could only
be provided by the establishment of new
schools or the extension of existing
schools. The Ministry has no control over
the aspirations of graduates.
ARRANGEMENT WITH BUS
COMPANIES.
5. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
arrangement entered into between the
Government and the omnibus companies:
whether it is a fact that the Government
have offered some of the larger omnibus
companies a monoply of certain roads,
and what compensation the Government
proposes to give to workmen who have
lost their employment as a consequence
of this arrangement.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): A provisional arrangement has been entered into between
the Belfast Corporation and the principal
omnibus proprietors who have been
operating within the City precincts.
This arrangement has not yet been formally ratified by the Corporation, but
the Ministry has undertaken that it is
prepared to accept the arrangement.
Pending formal ratification, it would be
premature for me to make any formal
statement in the matter, but the hon.
Member may rest assured that during the
discussions which took place in connection
with the matter, the interests of the employees of the omnibus proprietors have
not been lost sight of.

KILKEEL AND NEWRY-SUBSIDY
HOUSES.
11. Mr. BEATTIE (for Mr. William
McMullen) asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether it is a fact that builders
and contractors in the Kilkeel and Newry
district are using seashore gravel and
sand in the erection of subsidy houses;
whether this is a contravention of the
specifications issued by his Department;
and, if so, what action he proposes to take
in the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am aware
that seashore gravel and sand is used in
making mortar in Kilkeel and elsewhere,
and its use for this purpose is not a contravention of the Ministry's specification.
I am informed that most architects
prefer this sand to inferior pit sand, and
that the shore sand obtained at Kilkeel
is particularly good, being sharp and free
from loam.
It would be contrary to the Ministry's
rules, however, to use this sand in the
making of concrete as the sand used for
this purpose must be free from salt.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Minister whether he is aware that
seashore sand has a certain effect on the
bricks going into the building, whether
he is aware that the face of the brick is
destroyed by this class of sand being used,
and does he approve of sand being used
as described by my hon. Colleague?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Of course
this is a very technical matter, and.
therefore, I must be guided by my
technical officers. I understand that this
sand is quite useful and quite good for
the purpose of making mortar, but not
for the purpose of making cement. If
the sand is to be used for concrete it can
be washed and made suitable in that way.
PLASTERERS' ASSOCIATION AND
HOUSING SCHEMES.
12. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the
results of the inquiries instituted at the
request of the Plasterers' Association into
the housing schemes at present in operation; whether he is satisfied that builders
Oral Answers.
Housing Bill -
8 NOVEMBER 1928
receiving the subsidy are carrying out the
work in a proper manner, and can he
state whether it is a fact that subsidies
are given to builders of houses without
specifications being produced.
Sir DAWSON BATES: An Inspector
of the Ministry accompanied by two representatives of the Plasterers' Association visited a number of houses which
were complained of, and found that in
some cases cracks have developed in the
skimming or final coat of plaster. In one
case only had these defects developed to
any extent.
This cracking is caused by the final
coat being applied before the second coat
was sufficiently dry, and the defect would
only become apparent after there had
been fires in the houses for some time. If
the houses were left unoccupied for some
time after completion, and the plaster
work allowed to dry out naturally, it is
unlikely that cracks would develop.
In all cases the defects have been or are
being remedied by the contractor.
I am satisfied that so far as can be
ascertained from inspection, builders receiving the subsidies are carrying out the
work in a proper manner.
No subsidy is paid on any house until
the inspectors of the Ministry are satisfied
that it complies with the specification
laid down in the Ministry's Rules.

Mr. HANNA: Local option meeting.
Therefore, I say, apart altogether from
the inconveniences which are incidental to
the lives of working men living in these
small houses, the housing problem constitutes the biggest and most important,
and, in my judgment, the most transcendant of our problems next to the question
of employment for our people. I say then
that it was a grave blunder on the part
of the Government to start out on this
policy of perpetuating slums and wretched
houses. I stated yesterday I repeat it
to-day-that I was a member of the Housing Committee which the British Parliament set up, and there was not a member
upon that Committee who would agree to
this policy of two small rooms and a little
room of which the hon. and learned Member (Mr. Hanna) has reminded me.
There was not one member in favour of
that.
They recognised, and we must all recog
nise, that it is not simply a question of
giving some place to sleep in at night
and to be hunted out of in the daytime,
but a question of creating comfortable,
comparatively happy homes for the toiling
masses of our people in our large industrial centres. Therefore, when the Prime
Minister asked us to place a laurel wreath

8 NOVEMBER 1928
A Point of Order.
Adjournment.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps I
should explain that there is a double safeguard against anything such as the hon.
Member (Mr. Devlin) fears occurring. Not
only has my right hon. and learned
Friend, the Attorney-General, to certify
that our Acts, whatever they may be, fall
within the ambit of the powers given to
us under the Act of 1920, but all the
Acts are submitted to the Home Office on
the other side, and there the Secretary
of State, if at any time he considers we
are exceeding our powers in any Bill we
introduce, has power of withholding the
Assent to it, and in that case, of course,
we would not be able to proceed with the
Measure. So that there is a double check.
Not only has my right hon. and learned
Friend, the Attorney-General, to give
his certificate, but also the British
Government, through the Law Officers on
the other side, have a right to object if
they see anything in our proposed legislation that is ultra vires.
Mr. DEVLIN: Might I suggest that
it would be well, as a matter of convention, that these Bills should be sent over
to whoever is the authority on the
other side to declare whether we are within our legal powers before they are discussed in this House?
The PRIME MINISTER: They are
sent over.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did they sanction this?
The PRIME MINISTER: Certainly.
Mr. DEVLIN: I will write to Joynson-
Hicks. (Laughter).

Government employment (as outlined in
connection with the Imperial Civil Service
in Treasury Memorandum E. 3797, dated
12th November, 1923); and, if such temporary civilian service has not previously
been so reckoned, does the Minister propose retrospectively to revise the existing
regulations on the lines indicated in the
Treasury Memorandum already quoted.
Mr. POLLOCK: The answer to the first
part of the hon. Member's question is in
the affirmative, save that as regards temporary staff whose present term of reemployment commenced earlier than the
1st June, 1927, previous service ceased to
be reckonable where the break in employment lasted for over three months instead
of over twelve months as laid down in the
Treasury circular. In all other cases
the terms of that circular have been
adopted in full.
The second part of the question arises
in respect only of those clerks affected by
the foregoing qualification.

ductors, employees of firms plying for hire

end to the exploiting of these workers,
and thus help to reduce unemployment.
:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to answer this question. If
on occasions omnibus drivers and conductors are working the hours indicated
by the hon. Member, I am inclined to
think that the circumstances are exceptional. I hope the hon. Member will
agree that, for the present at any rate,
the matter may reasonably be left with
the responsible Trade Union leaders.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: Failing
the Trades Union leaders taking action
will the right hon. Gentleman, as representing the Minister of Home Affairs, take
action to put a stop to this slavery, and
so reduce the number of unemployed on
the streets?
Mr. ANDREWS: Whenever such a
question arises as suggested by my hon.
Friend, the Government will consider the
matter.
Mr. DEVLIN: Is it the argument of
the right hon. Gentleman that these conditions ought to continue simply because
these men have not got an effective trade

Mr. ANDREWS: I am not aware of
the fact that these men have not an
effective trade union.
Mr. DEVLIN: An effective trade
union?
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes.
Mr. DEVLIN: Why should these men
not have the same rights and privileges as

should these men have to work longer

Mr. ANDREWS: The conditions of
employment of railway workers. are
arranged between the trade union and

support it?
Mr. KYLE: He did not support it
before.
CLOSING OF MONKSTOWN MILL.
5. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON asked
the Minister of Commerce whether he can
state if it is a fact that Monkstown mill
and factory have been closed for the past
fourteen years, causing considerable hardship in that district, and whether he will
state if his Department has made any
effort to re-open the factory.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Barbour): I am sorry that the factory to
which the hon. Member refers was closed
down some years prior to the establishment of the Parliament of Northern Ireland. It is also unfortunately the case
that many active concerns are unable at
the present time to maintain full-time
production.
In regard to the latter part of the question, I think the hon. Member will appreciate that, while my Ministry is ready
at all times to take steps towards assisting
an industry as a whole or towards attracting new industries to the locality, it cannot carry its efforts to the point of reopening a particular mill or factory which
has been closed down on account of trading
difficulties of one kind or another.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am; and I
may say I am extremely glad to have this.
opportunity of making a full statement on
this matter, as it will, I hope, be the means
of removing a great deal of misapprehension which has arisen, partly as a result of
an imperfect knowledge of the arrangements actually arrived at and the reasons
which led to these arrangements, and
partly, I regret to say, as the result of
deliberate misrepresentation of the facts
by those who are personally interested.
The matter is of such importance that I
am sure I will be forgiven if I take the
up
time of the House at some length.
I would, first of all, ask the House to
consider carefully the problems with which
the Government is faced, and to appreciate
them fully. I think it is necessary to ask
the House to allow me to show the attitude
that all Governments have had to take up
for generations past in regard to the
traffic problem.
It has long been an established principle
that there was a duty imposed on the State
to ensure that passenger traffic, whether it
is by road, rail or sea, is properly conducted. It has always been recognised
that where a privilege has been conferred
on companies or individuals of carrying
passengers for hire it is the bounden duty
of the State to see that such obligations
are imposed on the bodies or persons enjoying these privileges; first of all, to provide for the safety of the public and, at
the same time, to give the public reasonable facilities at reasonable fares.
It cannot be disputed that the tendency
is for transport that is left to itself to
become practically a monopoly, and if you
have that tendency it is absolutely
essential that the State should interfere
to protect the public. And therefore we
have to consider what should be the principles which should guide the State in
interfering in the case of road passenger
traffic.
I can mention several other factors, but
there is one factor that must not be lost
sight of, and that is, that due regard must
be paid to the wear and tear of our roads,
which, at the present time, is a matter of
concern, not alone to the Government, but
to the various local authorities.
I suggest that the first essential is that
this traffic should be conducted with due regard to the safety of the ordinary users of
the road. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I further suggest that it must also be conducted with due regard to the safety of
the passengers; and third, that it must be
conducted with due regard to the convenience of the travelling public. That is
to say, that the public are entitled to be
provided with reasonable facilities at
reasonable fares.
I have said that these principles have
Even
been recognised for many years.
the old stage coach was not free from regulation, and when we come to the days of
the railways, the Parliaments of those
days, realising the added danger to the
travelling public by this form of transport, imposed restrictions solely in the
interests of the travelling and the general
public. If hon. Members will take the
trouble of reading the history of any of
the great English railways they will see
that there was much resentment felt at
the restrictions which were then imposed
on the railways, as it was felt that these
restrictions were imposed, not in the interests of the general public, but in the
interests of other competing transport
systems, such as canals. So far as railways are concerned these restrictions, instead of being lessened, have been increased from year to year in view of the
increasing dangers following the
increased speeds at which passengers were
carried.
on
But the State took a further step. In
return for the concessions given to the
railways they imposed conditions as to
the maximum fares and minimum services, and the result to-day is that every
railway must provide for the benefit of
the public a certain number of trains
every day and at certain fares-fares
which they could not increase without the
authority of the State.
What was said of the railway restrictions by the superficial critic in those days
is very similar to what is being said by
the ill-informed critic of our proposals
to-day, but looking back everyone can
appreciate that the restrictions and obligations imposed were both reasonable and
necessary.
Coming now to tramways, we find a
similar state of affairs. We find that
where Parliament has given an exclusive
right to a tramway undertaking to work
a service within a certain area, that it has.
in return for that, imposed on the undertaking heavy obligations compelling the
3225 Traffic Regulations-

Bus-Tramway Agreement.
tramways to carry workmen at cheaper
fares, and compelling them also to provide
convenient services on all sections of the
roads in that area whether they were paying routes or the reverse.
We come now to the ordinary hackney
vehicle. From time immemorial the
local authority had the right to license and
limit the number of hackney vehicles plying in any particular area, and also to
provide for the fares that these vehicles,
which are limited in number, should
charge to the public, and that they were
constructed and maintained in a suitable
manner.
This Parliament itself has dealt with
this matter. In 1926, as hon. Members
are aware, the Motor Traffic Act was
passed. That Act required that all public service vehicles must comply with the
conditions which were designed to secure
that the vehicles were of proper construction, and that the drivers were physically
fit, and were otherwise qualified to drive
the machine, and, above all, that the
owners would be in a position to meet all
legal claims for compensation for injury
caused by their vehicles. It also subjected the drivers of road passenger vehicles, in common with other forms of motor
transport, to very heavy penalties for
breaches of the law which would endanger the lives of either their passengers
or the general public. Parliament again
showed its concern in the problem of road
transport when it passed the Roads Improvement Act, which had for its object
the making of the roads more safe for
motor users and for the public.
While these Measures have proved most
useful, motor transport has increased with
such rapidity that they cannot be regarded as, in any sense, a final solution
of the problem. The House might be interested to know that the number of public service motor vehicles of the omnibus
type has more than doubled in four years.
When I quote these figures, I do not
wish to place the responsibility for these
accidents on the buses. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). That responsibility must be
shared, not alone by them, but by other
motor users, and even by pedestrains. 1
only quote these figures to get the House
to realise the seriousness of the problem,
and the heavy responsibility which lies
upon my shoulders-a responsibility which
I am entitled to ask the House to share
with me. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
No one in this House can contemplate
with equanimity that last year, in this
small Province of ours, with a population
of 1 million, there were no fewer than
1,436 accidents, involving injury to no
fewer than 1,530 persons and the death
of 102, while up to October of this year,
a period of only seven months, there were
no fewer than 1,217 accidents, involving
injury to 1,320 people and the death of
93.
The question of the traffic problem in
Belfast has been prominently before the
public for some time, and it is perhaps
well that I should refer to it first, but I
would ask the House not to lose sight of
the fact that it is really only part of a
larger problem. It is examined at very
considerable length in the report of the
inspectors whom I appointed to hold an
inquiry into the application for confirmation of by-laws submitted for approval
by the Belfast Corporation. The matter
is dealt with at very considerable length,
both on general principles and with particular regard to the situation in Belfast
itself. This report and the correspondence following upon it are now in the
hands of hon. Members.
I cannot hope in the time at my disposal to go into the matter at the same
length to-day, but I propose to endeavour
to give the House a summary of the situa
tion that presented itself to me. May I
first of all point out that by the Belfast
Tramway Acts the Imperial Parliament.
conferred on the Corporation what was,
in practice, the exclusive right to road
transport within the city, and under that
authority the Corporation, on behalf of
the citizens, invested very large sums of
money, and acting upon that authority
the Corporation constructed the present
tramway system. But Parliament also
conferred on the Corporation the means
of preserving their exclusive right by enabling them to endorse conditions on
licences issued by them, without which no
omnibus could ply in the city.
In 1926 this Parliament realised that
the time had come when, in place of each
local authority in Northern Ireland having the power to issue licences with or
without examination, there should be a
centralised system for the purpose of ensuring better inspection of the vehicles
and uniformity in regard to the terms in
which they were issued, and if no other

[Sir Dawson Bates]
provision had been made in the 1926 Act,
the Corporation, and indeed any other
local authority placed in the same position, would have been deprived of any
means of regulating the traffic in their
area in any way. But, while that Act
took away the power of the local authority to issue licences, it conferred on them
express powers to regulate traffic and to
impose on omnibuses a minimum fare.
This Section enables local authorities to
make by-laws to carry out these purposes, but, in the absence of such bylaws, it is open to any omnibus to ply for
hire in the city without restriction.
The Act was passed in November,
1926, and in order to give ample opportunity to every local authority, such as
the Belfast Corporation, to frame the
by-laws to give effect to the powers that
were conferred on them of regulating the
traffic, we did not bring the Act into
operation until the 1st July, 1927, which,
in effect, gave ample opportunity to any
local authority to frame and present their
by-laws for confirmation. Unfortunately, the Belfast Corporation were dilatory in the matter and did not present
any by-laws for confirmation until nearly
a year afterwards.
But, owing to the procedure which is
prescribed by Act of Parliament, before
the by-laws can be confirmed, involving
the holding of a public inquiry, it would
have been impossible for the Ministry to
have given a decision on the by-laws until
a very short time ago. In the meantime
the omnibus proprietors seized the opportunity in the early part of June last to
put services into the streets of Belfast,
and entered into an intensive competition
with the tramway undertaking.
sums
Under the Acts, the Belfast Tramway
undertaking has to pay rates on its
permanent way, which forms part of the
city streets. It has to make and maintain this permanent way out of its earnings. It has to pay substantial
every year to the general funds of the
Corporation by way of rent, and it must,
above all, maintain convenient services for
the public whether those routes are paying or not, and if there are losses in any

The evidence at the inquiry was conclusive. It showed first that unrestricted
competition by motor omnibuses must result in the closing down of the Tramway
undertaking with disastrous results from
a financial point of view to the city, and
heavy financial burdens. on the ratepayers. It showed secondly that it produced great congestion of the traffic, and
consequent danger to the public.
further showed that this unrestricted
competition must in the end place the

undertaking, are not under any obligation as regards either the fares to be
charged or the services to be provided.
It is also bound to carry workmen during
certain hours at half the ordinary fare, a
traffic which naturally results in a loss
which has to be borne out of the general
profits of the undertaking. It has been
estimated that whereas the tax payable
by an omnibus amounts to approximately
£2 per seat per annum, the obligations
cast on the tramway undertaking are
equivalent to at least £4 a seat. It must
be obvious to every Member of this House
that, with the advent of unrestricted and
uncontrolled motor omnibus competition,
a state of chaos was produced in the city
of Belfast which was dangerous to the
safety of the public.
The central streets of Belfast at the
present time cannot be crossed by the
ordinary pedestrian without considerable
danger to life or limb, and therefore I
think hon. Members will agree with me
that no one could contemplate a continuance of that condition of affairs. The
position was sufficiently bad in this respect
at the date of the inquiry, which was
commenced on the 27th August last, but
within a day or two afterwards it was
stated that negotiations for a settlement
were proceeding during the inquiry involving a payment of a sum of money to
those omnibus proprietors who were plying in Belfast.
The effect of this was that omnibus
proprietors either purchased new vehicles,
or brought their vehicles in from the
country, to ply in the streets of Belfast
with a view of sharing in the spoil, and
eight new services were placed on the
streets within a few days. Some of these
services were not ordinary omnibuses.
Some of them were chars-a-bancs which had
been used during the summer, and which,
for the time being, had been converted
into improvised omnibuses of a wholly
unsuitable character. I do not think
anyone can suggest that any of these vchi-

In return for the sale of an artificial and

The position was sufficiently bad from

see the situation continue. May I point

and in no town of any size in Great Britain
is unrestricted competition allowed?
The position, therefore, in Belfast may
be summed up very shortly:-
(1) The traffic was reduced to a condition of chaos, constituting a menace to
the safety of the public;
(2) The municipal undertaking was
being driven into a state of bankruptcy;
(3) The omnibuses were carrying on a
cut-throat competition, not alone with the
tramway undertaking, but with each
other, and confining their energies to the
profitable streets in the city of Belfast,
leaving the trams the privilege of looking
after the non-paying routes and sparsely
populated areas.
It is unquestionable that, as a result of
this omnibus competition, the public were,
for the moment, being carried at cheaper
rates than hitherto. They were getting
greatly improved facilities, but I am satisfied that this advantage was entirely of a
temporary character and could not possibly be maintained without driving both
forms of transport into bankruptcy. But
there was a further development of the
situation which was bound to arise at a
very early date. Indeed, steps had already been taken in that direction.
using to the full the powers which they

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
The hon. Member for West Belfast suggested that in relation to what took place
in the city of Belfast, Home Affairs might
have acted more than a year ago. We
had acted, but the statutory obligation
imposed on Belfast Corporation was a
matter that only they themselves could
fulfil. They did not produce the by-laws. I
think it was a great pity that the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Mr. William
McMullen) was taken away from the Corporation. I understand that if he had
remained there he would have had the bylaws presented in good time, and all this
thing would have been avoided.
There is one other thing I want to say.
I have been in very close association, as
hon. Members know, with the Minister of
Home Affairs in regard to this matter,
and I would like to take this opportunity
of paying my tribute to the single purpose
and honesty with which he approached
this difficult matter and carried it out.
If ever there was a situation where there
was no shadow of leaning on one side or
another here is a case. There was no
leaning towards the railway companies,
or towards the big bus owners as against
the small bus owners, or towards the
small bus owners as against the big ones.
The one matter that was kept in the
forefront by the right hon. Gentlemanand I had the honour to help him with
the assistance of the very able staff we
have at the Home Office-was the safety
and convenience of the public, and because we have kept that so closely
before us and followed it so rigidly
practically for the first time in this House
there has been unanimous approval of the
action taken by the Minister of Home
Affairs in connection with this matter.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The word monopoly has been mentioned.
I cannot understand its use in regard to
this matter. The word monopoly suggests
having power, complete control. There
is nothing of the kind here. If you have
a monopoly of something it is something
you can sell. There is nothing here that
anybody can sell or keep except on the
strictest of strict conditions.
How anybody who appreciates the meaning of
English words, and particularly the word
monopoly, can suggest that there is anything in the nature of monopoly here is a
matter that gives me a wonderful amount
of concern. On the whole there has been
nothing but praise and support of the
action taken by the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates).

DEATH OF MRS. A. CASSIDY,
BELFAST.
4. Mr. W. McMULLEN asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he will
order an inquiry into all the circumstances
governing the death of Mrs. A. Cassidy,
of 52 Sultan Street, who died in childbirth
on the 28th October last.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As promised by me
on the 8th instant, I have made inquiries
into this matter, and I find that the
woman in question was not a Dispensary
patient, but was attended as a private
patient by a doctor and midwife.
In these circumstances I have no jurisdiction to make formal inquiry, but, on
the other hand, under the provisions of
the Midwives (Ireland) Act, 1918, the
Belfast Corporation acts as the supervising
authority over midwives, and any question
as to the treatment of the patient by the
midwife concerned should be dealt with
by the Corporation.
At the same time I have received a report on the matter from the Public Health
Department of the Belfast Corporation,
from which it appears that that Department has been fully alive to the circumstances of the woman's confinement, and
subsequent death, and that it is not considered that there was any neglect or incompetence on the part of the midwife
who attended on the patient.
It is also understood that the cause of
death in this case was really kidney
disease.
Mr. W. McMULLEN: I would like to
ask the right hon. Gentleman whether he
is aware that this lady suffered for five
hours and a half from hemorrhage, and
during that time it was not possible to
get proper medical skill and attention.
Having regard to that unsatisfactory state
of affairs does he not think it is a duty

Minister of Health in Great Britain proposes to have an inquiry into every case
of maternal mortality in childbirth in
Great Britain; and whether he is prepared to follow this example in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member appears to be under a misapprehension as to the action being taken by
the Minister of Health in Great Britain
in this matter, as I understand that the
proposal in Great Britain is to obtain
reports in such cases from the Local
Medical Officers of Health, in order to
obtain statistics and medical information
as to the cause of death in each case.
In this connection I would refer the
hon. Member to the reply given to him by
me on the 23rd ultimo, to the effect that
the Ministry of Home Affairs is taking
all steps within its power to collect and
collate information regarding maternal
mortality and the causes of death.

appointed in Great Britain to make inquiries into all deaths arising out of

is chairman of that committee, and is he
prepared to set up a similar committee in
Northern Ireland in view of the fact that
deaths from this cause are higher in
Northern Ireland than in the Free State
or in Great Britain?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As a committee has been appointed by the Minister
of Health in England for the purpose of
collecting this particular information I
might inform the hon. Member that the

setting up of the English Committee had
already taken steps to collect and collate
the information.

object of obtaining this information.

collected would not warrant some action

take steps on the basis of that
information?

Representation of the People Bill.
Considered in Committee (Third Day).
CLAUSE 2 (Assimilation of local
franchise of men
government
and
women).
(1) For the purpose of providing that
the local government franchise in Northern Ireland shall be the same for men
and women, sub-section (3) of section
four of the princpal Act shall be repealed in its application to the said
franchise, and the following section
shall be substituted for section three of
that Act in its application as aforesaid:
:-
"A person shall be entitled to be registered as a local government elector
for a local government electoral area if
he or she is of full age and not subject
to any legal incapacity, and-
(a) is on the last day of the qualifying period occupying in that area,
as owner or tenant, any land or premises (not being a dwelling-house) of
a yearly value of not less than five
pounds, or a dwelling house; and
(b) has during the whole of the
qualifying period so occupied, either
in that area or, if that area is not
an administrative county or a county
borough, in any adminstrative county
or county borough in which the area
is wholly or partly situate, any land
or premises (not being a dwellinghouse) of such yearly value as aforesaid, or a dwelling-house; or
*
*
*
(ii) for the purposes of this section
the word 'tenant' shall include a person who occupies a room or rooms as
a lodger only where the room or rooms
is or are let to that person in an unfurnished state; and
(iii) for the purpose of paragraph
(c) of this section, a naval or military
voter who is registered in respect of a
residence qualification which he or
she would have had but for his or her
service shall be deemed to be resident
in accordance with that qualification."
(2) The Local Government (Franchise) Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, is
hereby repealed.

Mr. COOPER: I beg to move, in
Clause 2, page 4, line 13, at the end to
insert:-
--
"Provided that no person shall be
entitled to a Local Government vote
as a sub-tenant who occupies a room
or rooms in a house of which the Poor
Law valuation is £7 10s 0d or under."
I mentioned on the Second Reading of
this Bill that there is a great number of
houses in the various towns that have a
valuation of £3, £4, £5, £6. and £7 10s.
The father and the mother of a household
take one of these houses. This Amendment does not aim in any way at the
tenant of the house; the tenant of the
house will still have a vote as formerly,
and if the tenant is married his wife will
have a vote as formerly. Unfortunately
the practice has sprung up of, say, two
sons of the father and of the tenant
coming to the Revision Court and saying
that they are sub-tenants of rooms in
that house under their father. They will
come and say that they own the furniture
in the room, that they cook their own
meals in their own room, and that the
room is their house. As soon as those
two sons have been disposed of, probably
two daughters will get up, and they will
claim to be joint tenants of another house
which is another room in the same house.
They will come in and say that they own
the furniture in their own rooms, and
that they cook their meals in their own
rooms. The Amendment that I am proposing does not in any way disentitle the
tenant of the house or his wife, no matter
what the valuation may be, to get a vote;
it only aims at preventing the local
government franchise being extended
sometimes to ten or twelve persons in
these small houses who are only members
of the family, and who really are only
lodgers in that house.
Mr. COOPER: The question that the
hon. Member has asked more or less
proves just what I am going to say. In
houses which are over £7 10s and over
£8 there is often a great number of
lodgers. There are often people who
come along and take a furnished room.
Some of them take the room as joint
tenants, and some of these rooms are
rooms for which they pay a considerable
sum of money, but none of those people
are entitled to votes at all, because if
you sub-let a room with furniture the law
is that the lodger cannot get a vote. The
result is that in a great number of these
small houses there are people who are
franchise experts; they can manufacture
nearly as many votes as they like, and the
result is that in streets which have small
valuations we have often a very large
number of local government votes. I
have taken a very small valuation-a
valuation of £7 10s-and I propose to insert the words on the Paper.
Mr. BEATTIE: Perhaps the hon.
Member will pardon me for a moment.

this stand in regard to the Rent Restriction Act, under which no such thing as
a sub-tenant exists?

4, line 20, insert as a new sub-section--
After listening very carefully to the
reply of the Parliamentary Secretary I
have come to the conclusion that this is
an Amendment which he can accept.
This Amendment deals with another class
of case altogether. It is well known that
where a man in the country dies leaving
a farm of land, even if he makes a will
and the will is not proved the next-of-kin
in possession can come in and claim the
vote. I will show you exactly how that
works out. We will say a man owns a
farm and he dies leaving his son and two
daughters or two sons and two daughters.
He leaves the farm by his will to one of
his sons, and that son then becomes the
owner of the farm. No probate of the
will is taken out and the two daughters
come to the next revision sessions and
they claim local government votes as
owners and occupiers of that farm.
Mr. McHUGH: What age are they?
"(iv) No person shall be entitled to
be registered in respect of land, a

other person under a Will or intestacy,
unless and until Probate of the Will
(if any) of the said deceased person
has been granted, or in the case of an
Intestate Letters of Administration
have been granted."
Mr. COOPER: Aged 21 years and upor
wards. The result of that is that two
persons are registered as local government
electors for that farm although they have
no interest whatever either in law
equity in the farm. The same thing
happens where a man dies without a will
at all and where no administration is taken
out, because in that case the same two
daughters come and claim to be owners and
occupiers of he farm. They say no administration has been taken out, and
therefore both are registered as local
government electors. Those people were
given votes by a decision of the Court of
Appeal in Dublin some years ago. The
decision was that where a will had not
been proved or letters of administration
had not been taken out these people were
the next-of-kin in possession. It led to
very extraordinary results in the revision
courts. One of the results is that a number of people will come up one after the
other. They are asked if probate of the
will has been taken out and they say no.
They are asked if letters of administration
have been taken out and they say no. It
is very well known that letters of administration or probate have been taken out in
those particular cases. It leads to another
very extraordinary result. A man who
has taken out probate, paid his estate duty
to the Government and helped to run the
country will only get one vote. If he defrauds the Government by not taking out
probate and does not pay any estate duty
the Government reward him by giving him
two votes.

CLAUSE 3 (Local Government Franchise (Companies) ).
The principal Act as amended by
this Act shall, in its application to the
local government franchise in Northern
Ireland, have effect as if the following
section were inserted therein after section three:
"4.-(1) Where any company has,
during the whole of the twelve months
ending on the last day of the qualifying period, occupied as owner or
tenant any land or premises of the
yearly value of not less than ten
pounds in a local government electoral
area in Northern Ireland, and is rated
for the relief of the poor in respect of
such land or premises, then, subject
to the provisions of this section, such
company may make a claim to have
such person as is specified in the claim.
registered as a local government elector in respect of the said land or
premises, and the said person shall be
entitled to be registered accordingly.
Such occupation of land or premises
by a company as complies with the
requirements aforesaid is hereinafter
referred to as a company qualifica-
"
tion.'

of a yearly value greater than ten

Mr. DAVISON: This Clause makes
provision for giving votes to companies
for local government elections. The
ground for that is that these companies
have an interest both in property and in
employment in the local government area,

its present form the Clause gives the right
to a company which has, during the qualifying period, occupied certain premises
and which is rated for the relief of the
poor. Now, a company is rather a peculiar thing. It is what we call in law an
artificial person.
You can have a number
of companies occupying the same premises. Indeed, you very often see it.
Anyone who takes the trouble to go to
some of the offices in Belfast will see a
number of companies having their registered address in the one set of offices.
It would be possible under this section
as it stands for, say, five or six companies
to occupy the same premises, to be jointly
rated, and, if the premises were of an
annual value of £10, each one of those
companies would have the vote. It,
therefore, appears to me that this Clause
requires some Amendment. I had intended to propose to put in the word "exclusively" before "occupied" in line 29,
but I understand the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) in charge of the
Bill prefers to make the Amendment in
a different way, and, instead of limiting
the occupation, to limit the rating.
That, I think, would have the same effect,
and on that understanding I do not propose to press this Amendment.

he was the biggest ratepayer in the city of
Belfast. It happened that this man collected the rents of hundreds, if not of
thousands, of small houses in Belfast, and
all the rates were paid by him. The rates
were not really paid by him at all. He
was only the vehicle through which those
rates were paid. It was the small tenants
who were the ratepayers. They paid the
rates indirectly to this rent agent in the
rents they paid to him. That is a fallacy
that is constantly being presented here by
rich people, that, because the rates happen
to pass through their hands they are the
ratepayers and not the people who indirectly pay the rates and make them the
vehicles through which those rates pass.

THE EXPORT TRADE IN PORK.
1. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he has seen the report of the
Coleraine Chamber of Commerce, in
which it is stated that the export trade
in pork from the Free State has increased
from 4,000 hundredweight in 1925 to
16,000 in the present year; and whether
he can give the figures for Northern Ireland for the same period.
The MINISTER OF AGRICUL-
TURE (Sir Edward Archdale): My
attention has been drawn to a Press report of a meeting of the Coleraine
Chamber of Commerce, at which certain
figures were quoted regarding the increase in the export of pork from the
Irish Free State between 1925 and 1928.
A similar increase has been recorded in
the case of exports from Northern Ireland ports as follows:-
January-September.


8,580 cwt.
2,466 cwt.
20,092 cwt.
48,747 cwt.
from 153,150 cwt. during the first nine
months of 1926 to 242,855 cwt. during
the corresponding period of this year, an
increase of 58.6 per cent.
I may add that there has also been
an increase in the export of bacon and
hams through Northern Ireland ports
THE DERRY MILK SUPPLY.
2. Mr. P. O'NEILL (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether his attention has been drawn to
the proceedings of the Public Health
Committee of the Derry Corporation,
in which it is stated that under
the existing law there is great difficulty in securing convictions against
offenders; and, if so, whether the Government will amend the law in that respect,
in order to secure to the public a pure
supply of milk.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to answer this question. I am
aware that a number of cases against milk
vendors in Londonderry City have been
dismissed by the magistrates on the
ground that the milk was sold as it came
from the cow. Under the existing law, if
the milk falls below the prescribed standard, the onus of showing that it has not
been tampered with rests upon the vendor,
and if he is able to satisfy the magistrates
on this point he is entitled to have the
case against him dismissed.
The question of the sufficiency of the
evidence is a matter for the magistrates,
and the Ministry has no function in this
respect.
I may add, however, that the law relating to the milk standards has been the
subject of discussion for a considerable
time by those concerned in the production
of milk, and by the experts of the local
authorities concerned, both as regards the
agricultural point of view and the point
of view of the consumer, and I am following the discussions carefully with a view
to taking whatever action may appear
most suitable.

the British Government is liable. Prior
to the passing of the Importation of
Animals Act, 1922, by the Imperial Parliament, the British Government was
liable, even when animals were slaughtered
in landing places. By that Act, however, the British Government relieved
itself of this liability, and it is this landing place gap that now remains to be
bridged. This unsatisfactory position
has been frequently stressed by the cattle
trade. A number of animals have already been slaughtered in British lairages
and the owners have received no compensation, but this Bill gives the power to
pay, even in these retrospective cases.
This retrospective clause must not be lost
sight of when considering the proposal to
extend the scope of the Measure. Losses
due to slaughter are definitely known and
can be checked. Clearly, however, it
would, after a lapse of time, be difficult,
if not impossible, to verify claims in respect of vague losses due to detention.
It is, therefore, clear that even if the demand for an extension of the measure as
However, the fundamental objection to
widening the scope of the Bill is that such
a course must involve higher insurance
fees at Northern Ireland ports than at
Free State ports. In this connection it
may be remarked that a scheme similar
to the one embodied in this Bill, and with
corresponding contributions, has already
been put into operation in the Irish Free
State.
It is essential that nothing should be
done which might have the effect of
jeopardising the trade of our ports, and
it seems obvious that higher insurance
contributions might have such an effect.
I am not, therefore, prepared, on the information at present before me, to recommend any scheme involving higher contributions than those embodied in this
Bill.
Experience of the actual working of
the Measure will, doubtless, suggest ways
in which it can be improved, and if a
reasonable case can be made out to have
risks, other than slaughter, included
without at the same time jeopardising
trade through Northern Ireland ports the
question of extension can be reconsidered
at a future date.
Difficulties arising out of the wording
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
have heretofore prevented this matter
being dealt with in a satisfactory way in
this Parliament. Any doubts as to our
powers have, however, now been removed by the Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act recently passed
by the Imperial Parliament, so that the
way is clear to deal with the matter.
The sum of money we propose is verv

worked by the parties concerned and no
money at all will be paid by the Government. I beg to move.

confidence, and seek the co-operation of

will go on slowly but surely down and
down until, when this Government no

do, but if you do not create industries,

in a few years you will have no population
left. People will not be able to live in
the area. Our expenses are still high.
The running expenses in connection with
this Government are still costly. Even
the salaries in connection with the different
Ministries amount to about half a million
a year, and in this time of serious trade
depression and unemployment, could the
Government not consider the question of
reducing those salaries by, say, 50 per
cent.?
The only cure for unemployment in my
opinion is the creation of new industries.
That would leave a quarter of a million
pounds to support old industries or to start
new ones. I notice that the Minister of
Finance smiles at that suggestion.
should have thought that in a community
like this, a quarter of a million a year to
establish new industries, to assist the
new silk industry and various other industries, would go a long way. As a
matter of fact, it would go a long way in
reviving the old industries.
The spending of £10,000 a year in advertising linen seems to have been useless.
So far as I can see, and so far as I can
hear, there has been practically no improvement in the linen trade. It would
seem to be a lost industry, and that money
has been lost with it, but if it can be restored it seems to me to be necessary to
use more money in restoring it. I suggest
that there is one way in which you can
have more money for restoring that industry. Reduce the salaries in connection
with Government offices, and have a
quarter of a million a year for additional
advertising of old industries or for the
starting of new ones. The Government
must tackle the problem in that way.
There is no use in coming to the House and
telling us year after year that the unemployment numbers are larger, and that
you have spent so much in relief schemes,
schemes that will not give any return in
employment when they are finished.
While they may be useful and necessary
and desirable, they are not schemes that
will cure unemployment, and unless you
revive some of the old industries and start
new ones you will never solve this problem
of unemployment.
Question put, "That the words proposed
to be left out stand part of the Question."
The House divided: Ayes, 11; Noes, 20.

Committee
[Mr. Miller]
Local Government Act was passed, without changing the electoral divisions. The
result was that 100 voters in one district
have as much power as 1,800 in another.
Then Proportional Representation came
in, I think the year 1918; that was when
the real gerrymandering took place. The
Government in Dublin Castle at that time
was in the hands of a nominal Chief
Secretary, but the real Chief Secretary
was a gentleman well known to everybody.
The Local Government Board sent down
proposals for grouping the electoral
divisions, in order to form constituencies
for the system of Proportional Representation. Those proposals were put before
the various boards-the county councils
and the district councils-and they were
approved of by both. They went back to
Dublin Castle, and we all wondered why
they were not sent out in the form of an
Order. That went on until within a
fortnight of the election, and then these
provisions were sprung on us suddenly.
In the meantime, someone had gone in by
the back door and had changed them
slightly, but in such a way that they
turned Unionist divisions into Nationalist
divisions. Then when the election took
place it was found that for the first time
in history the Nationalists had got
command.

. day or to-morrow they would naturally

I ask why is this provision in the Bill.
I think that the hon. Member who has just
sat down has very likely given the answer
to that question. This provision is in the
Bill because the Government think they
will get some party advantage out of it.
It is just in line with their whole policy,
which seems to me to be a life-saving
policy. They are trying every means,
artificial and otherwise, to dig themselves
in as an ascendency in this country, and
to keep themselves in power for ever and
a day. Why is it necessary that people
coming from other parts of Ireland should
have to live here for three years before

who have votes on account of their being

qualification for one place should apply
in the other, and I think the very fact
that this dual qualification is set up
proves beyond doubt that this provision
is in this Bill simply because the Government think it is going to be a party advantage to them. There is another reason
why I think the Government would
be well advised to accept this Amendment, and it is this: This proposal
has an anti-Irish bias about it. I do not
see why we cannot be good Ulstermen
and good Irishmen at the same time. I
do not think the two things are incompatible. It would not be suggested to a
Canadian that he could not be a good
Canadian and be loyal to the Empire of
which he is a citizen. It would remove
the suspicion of an anti-Irish bias if the
Government would accept this Amendment and put the franchise for the Northern Parliament on exactly the same
footing as the franchise for the Imperial
Parliament.

Its object is to ensure that a soldier or
sailor will be entitled to vote notwithstanding the fact that he may not have
been a resident in Northern Ireland or
the United Kingdom for three years.

What is the position?
The Prime Minister says he has made a
concession. I could never visualise the
Frime Minister in the role of a concessionist. I have been in this House for
four or five years and I never knew him
to make a concession to anybody on this
side. That is not the kind of concession
we ask for. We ask him to clear the Paper
of all these Amendments. There will be

There ought to be a concession to the

to the Clause as it stands I cannot agree
to it.

In looking into the matter further we
found that a soldier who had been demobilized during the period would be deprived of a vote unless we inserted these
words. It is for that object, and to ensure
that if he was serving His Majesty either
in the Army or Navy, he would not be
disqualified from voting by reason of the

Amendment is to ensure that any soldier
or sailor will be entitled to vote whether

been demobilized during the three years,

if technically they have not the three
years' residence qualification.

may not be moved.

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 22nd November, 1928.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
PUBLIC ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS-
INSPECTION SYSTEM.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education whether he is aware that all
the unions of public elementary school
teachers functioning in Northern Ireland
have expressed the utmost dissatisfaction
with the present system of inspection;
whether some inspectors consult managers
regarding the rating which they should
give instead of passing an impartial judgment on the work done by the teachers,
and that before visiting a school for the
first time some inspectors invite local persons to state their opinion regarding the
teachers; whether facts regarding the
schools which they learned as inspectors
and which are supposed to be treated as
confidential are divulged to outsiders;
whether inspectors adversely report upon
teachers within a few years of retiring on
full pension with a view to inducing them
to resign, and also on teachers of schools
with declining averages with a view to
having them removed and grants withdrawn from their schools, and refrain
from giving teachers a higher rating than
their predecessors did; and whether he
will consider the propriety of holding a
searching inquiry into inspection methods.
generally.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Dissatisfaction with the present system of inspection
of public elementary schools has been expressed in varying degrees by some of the
teachers' unions in Northern Ireland, but
it is by no means the case that these
opinions have been expressed by all the
unions or in emphatic terms. I would
remind the hon. Member that only three
of the five elementary teachers who were
members of the Lynn Committee joined
in a reservation expressing dissatisfaction.
with the system.
The Ministry does not believe that there
is any foundation for the allegations contained in the remaining part of the question, and action of the kind suggested, if
such took place, would meet with strong
disapproval. The hon. Member will find
on reference to the table on page 58 of
the Ministry's Annual Report for 1927-
28 that the number of teachers rated as
"highly efficient" and "efficient" respectively shows a well-marked progressive increase since 1922, while the number of
those not so rated has decreased from 14.9
to 5.8 per cent.
It is not proposed to hold an inquiry
as suggested in the question.
SMALL SCHOOLS-PRINCIPAL-
SHIPS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry has
decided that teachers, after they leave
the training college, and before they
receive their diplomas, are ineligible for
principalships save those of one-teacher
schools with an average attendance below
thirty; whether he is aware that it is
more difficult to conduct such schools and
to bring them up to and keep them in a
state of efficiency than schools with
larger attendances and staffs of teachers:
whether the same efficiency is expected in
these small schools as in schools with
much larger attendances and full staffs;
and whether he is aware that for this
reason many young teachers of skill and
zeal are deprived of their diplomas.
Mr. ROBB: The answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative:
the Ministry does not encourage exstudents of the training colleges who are
necessarily without actual experience of
school work, except such as may be
obtained during the training course, to
take up positions as principals, and these
posts are open to such persons only in
very small schools with an attendance of
less than thirty pupils.

MINISTRY OF EDUCATION---
REGULATIONS AND STATUTORY
ORDERS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry of
Education has issued in book form its
Regulations and Statutory Orders, and, if
not, whether it proposes to do so; and
how may those who are not teachers, but
interested in education, obtain copies of
the circular not on sale.
Mr. ROBB: The Ministry has not
issued its Regulations or Statutory Rules
and Orders in book form and does not
propose to do so as it is much less expensive to the majority of purchasers to
obtain separately those regulations in
which they are interested. Copies of the
Ministry's circulars are sent to all
school managers and governing bodies
concerned. Applications from other persons interested in education for copies of
particular circulars may be made to the
Ministry.

4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state how many
teachers in the triennium ended the 31st
March, 1928, have been dismissed on
account of not having received their
diplomas; how many have voluntarily re-
Mr ROBB: Within the period
mentioned by the hon. Member recognition has been withdrawn from two
teachers on account of failure to obtain
their diplomas. In ten other cases recognition in a particular position has
been withdrawn, but the persons concerned have been allowed to seek appointments in a less responsible capacity.
The Ministry is not aware that any
teacher has resigned voluntarily on
account of not having received his diploma.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.
