HOUSE OF COMMONS
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
FUND.
6. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of Finance whether the actuarial
investigation into the pension fund for
secondary school teachers, promised for
this year, has been held, and, if so, with
what result; and whether any revision of
the pension scheme is to be made in consequence.
7. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of Finance whether any portion of the
money paid by secondary school teachers
and schools towards the pension fund is
absorbed by the pension fund for primary
school teachers, and, if so, in what
proportion.
8. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of Finance whether any of the moneys
contributed by secondary schools and
teachers are invested in interest bearing
securities, and, if so, whether the increment is likely to be sufficent to provide
better pensions in the future, when larger
numbers of secondary teachers qualify
for pension.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As Questions 6, 7, and 8 are
concerned with the same subject, perhaps
my hon. Friend (Mr. Johnstone), will
pardon me if I deal with them all in a
single answer.
By Section 1 of the Teachers' Superannuation Act, 1926, all teachers' superannuation funds were amalgamated under
the name of the Teachers' Superannuation Fund, and all income and expenditure
in respect of secondary teachers is incorporated in the transactions on this
fund.
SUPERVISION OF PRIVATE
SLAUGHTER HOUSES.
The Government actuary, who is conducting the actuarial investigation of the
Teachers' Superannuation Fund, has indicated that he is nearing the completion
of his work, and it is hoped that his report will be received before the end of
this calendar year. The report of this
investigation will in due course be laid
before the House, but until then it would
be premature to make any statement in
regard to any one class of teacher. Each
class will, of course, be treated separately
according to Sub-section (3) of Section 2
of the Teachers' Superannuation Act.
9. Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON
asked the Minister of Home Affairs
whether he can state the number of
private slaughter houses in Northern Ireland, and whether the Government are
taking any steps to have those places put
under official supervision in order to protect the health of the citizens of Northern
Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): According to the
latest return available there are 178
private slaughter houses in Northern Ireland. All of these, which are situated in
County Boroughs and Urban Districts, are
registered and subject to regulation
and inspection by the local Sanitary
Authority.
Some rural district councils have
acquired similar powers of regulation and
inspection of slaughter houses in their
respective areas, and with regard to those
other rural district councils where the
power does not exist the Ministry is at
present considering whether any, and, if
so, what steps should be taken to extend
the principle of inspection and regulation
generally, but the hon. Member must appreciate that it would be inappropriate
without careful consideration of the circumstances which obtain in these various
areas to apply rigid uniform rules, having
regard to the fact that in the rural areas
ia Northern Ireland a considerable number
of animals are slaughtered for the dead
meat trade in farm buildings which could
not be otherwise regarded as slaughter
houses.
Certain recommendations, however, in
this regard have been made by the Local
Government Commission, and these recommendations are being carefully
followed up.
Mr. THOMAS HENDERSON: I
wonder is the Minister aware that there
are a good many instances of where tubercular cattle are killed in these private
slaughter-houses and sold to the citizens
for human consumption. I am delighted
that the Minister has taken action, but
would the right hon. Gentleman tell me
if any other people have drawn his attention to this very serious matter?

COST-OF-LIVING COMMITTEE'S
REPORT.
11. Mr. KYLE asked the Minister of
Labour whether he can state when the
recommendation contained in the Cost-of-
Living Committee's Report (1922), which
suggested that a quarterly return should.
be issued setting out the fluctuations in
the cost of living in Northern Ireland,
will be carried out.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Committee on the cost
of living in Northern Ireland recommended that no attempt should be made
to publish a separate cost-of-living index
number for Northern Ireland. In
these circumstances I do not feel that
the quarterly return mentioned in the
hon. Member's question would serve a
purpose which would, at the present
time, justify the expenditure involved
by the collection and publication of the
data.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Finance (No. 2) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. POLLOCK: The details of this
small Measure were given, in fact, by my
hon. Friend who usually sits beside me on
the Money Resolution which was submitted to the Committee last week. It
is concerned especially with small matters
in regard to our arrangement with the
business of banks and entertainment duty.
In fact it is divided into two parts, one
relating as I have said to the business of
bankers, and the other to some comparatively unimportant changes and relief
in respect of the entertainment duty.
In respect of banking business, hitherto
the banker has paid licence duty for the
privilege of issuing unstamped notes.
But since 1828, exactly 100 years ago,
when the first imposition of a licence duty
was made in the Imperial Parliament, the
Bank of Ireland was exempt from the payment of any licence duty. I suppose that
was largely because it was the official
Government bank and it had close relations with Government matters. In
addition to that there are two banks at
present operating in Northern Ireland
that were not in existence at that time.
They did not issue any notes, and so escaped any payment, although they paid a
special duty in lieu of licence duty to
cover unstamped notes.
Finance Bill-

Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
It is now proposed in this small Measure to alter the system by relating the
licence to the business of banks so that
all banks operating in Northern Ireland
will require to be licensed and placed on
the same basis. The first Clause of the
Measure provides for the payment of
stamp duty to the amount of £30 for a
branch and a maximum of £120, that is
a bank operating with four branches.
Clauses 1 and 2 make provision for these
matters and also that the licence will remain in force for one year and will be
renewed in the ordinary way from year
to year. In the carrying out of this system it is provided that three licences are
issued for the three principal offices and
all the remaining branches are named in
the fourth licence so that the maximum
of £120, being four thirties, will be provided for.
Then the old Act of 1828, to which I
have referred, laid down certain conditions in respect of banks taking out
licences to issue unstamped notes. At
that time security by bond was required,
but the question of the continuity of this
matter is of no great importance. These
conditions are still continued in the case
of note-issuing banks, and the new licence
will be recognised as a licence granted
under the Act of 1828. The special
exemption from the payment of licence
duty which the Bank of Ireland has enjoyed is now withdrawn, and the Bank
of Ireland will be in the same position as
all other banks operating in Northern
Ireland.
Up to the present, note-issuing banks
have been obliged to give bonds for the
proper performance of the conditions
imposed on them. The Ministry of
Finance should be able to dispense with
this security if it sees fit. Of course, I
think it is not necessary in the case of
banks of such standing as are operating
in Northern Ireland and no bonds are
to be required. Therefore, that part of
the conditions of the Act of 1828 may be
withdrawn. The remaining two Subsections deal with fines and definitions,
and are of no importance.
peals two Sections of the provisions

The
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE:
object of this Bill is to provide that when
cattle, sheep, and swine shipped through
Northern Ireland ports are slaughtered
in British landing-places on account of
foot-and-mouth disease compensation will
be available. The Bill provides that a
small levy per head will be made on
animals exported and these contributions
will form an Insurance fund out of which
compensation will be payable in the
circumstances mentioned.
The intention is that the administration of the Act should be in the hands of
trustees appointed by the trade interests
concerned, and the scheme will be selfsupporting, no expenditure from public
funds being involved.
The Bill has had a generally favourable reception, and the only complaint is
that it does not go far enough. It has
been suggested that its scope should be
widened so as to cover losses due to
detention in lairages. In order to appreciate fully the problem to be dealt with
it seems desirable to set out the existing
position in regard to slaughter and compensation.
At present when animals are slaughtered in Ireland by official order on
account of foot-and-mouth disease the
appropriate Irish Government is responsible for compensation. Similarly when
animals are slaughtered in Great Britain,
otherwise than in a landing place, the
British Government is liable. Prior to
the passing of the Importation of Animals
Act, 1922, by the Imperial Parliament,
the British Government was liable, even
when animals were slaughtered in landing
places. By that Act, however, the
British Government relieved itself of this
liability and it is this landing place gap
that now remains to be bridged. This
unsatisfactory position has been frequently
stressed by the cattle trade. A number
of animals have already been slaughtered
in British lairages and the owners have
received no compensation, but this Bill
gives the power to pay, even in these
retrospective cases.

and it seems obvious that higher insurance contributions might have such an
effect. I am not, therefore, prepared, on

Bill.
Experience of the actual working of the

Northern Ireland ports the question
of extension can be re-considered at a
future date.
Difficulties arising out of the wording
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
have heretofore prevented this matter
being dealt with in a satisfactory way in
this Parliament. Any doubts as to our
powers have, however, now been removed
by the Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous
Provisions) Act recently passed by the
Imperial Parliament, so that the way is
clear to deal with the matter.

The present Bill takes us a long step
further. In many of the large consuming
centres in Great Britain the transfer of
foreign eggs to Irish cases before exposure
for sale has become almost a trade practice,
and the mixing of foreign and home eggs
is more or less openly done. Detection is
well-nigh impossible since there is no
means of determining the country of
origin of particular eggs. The reputation

Under the Merchandise Marks Act, 1926,
provision is made for the marking, in
certain cases, of imported produce, and it
has been agreed to prescribe that all imported eggs shall, at the time of landing
in the United Kingdom of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland be individually
marked with an indication of the country
of origin. This arrangement was
reached subject to the proviso that preserved eggs, whatever their origin, and
home-produced cold-stored eggs, are also
marked to indicate that they have been
submitted to such process. The Bill is
thus part of the machinery for ensuring
that any egg, other than a home-produced
fresh egg, must bear a mark which will
let the consumer know the sort of egg he
is buying. In the whole matter we have
been in the closest touch with the appropriate Imperial Departments, and the
present Bill follows very closely on the
lines of the special provisions as to eggs
contained in the Agricultural Produce
(Grading and Marking) Act, 1928, which
received the Roval Assent on the 3rd

Funds (Ireland) Act, 1888, certain local
authorities can use their funds for promoting a Bill in Parliament, but the Act,
in the interests of the electors, prescribed
certain procedure for the purpose of ascertaining the wishes of the electors so as to
ensure that any Bill that was promoted
in Parliament had the goodwill of the
electors. I desire, first of all, to impress
on hon. Members that this Bill does not
propose in any way to interfere with the
principle contained in the Act of 1888.
The local authority will still be under the
control of the electors as regards the desirability of putting forward a Bill, and
that principle, I suggest, is an excellent
one and one which should be preserved.
At the same time the experience of years
past has shown that there are several defects in the machinery for giving effect to
this principle, and it is desirable that these
defects should be removed.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill which
I now have the honour to ask the House
to give a Second Reading to is one which
I think will commend itself to hon. Members. It is designed to remove certain
inconveniences which local authorities are
put to before they can promote a private
Bill in Parliament. Under the Borough
I propose to deal very shortly with what
these defects are. Under Section 7 of the
Borough Funds Act, 1888, when a local
authority desires to promote a Bill in Parliament and it has passed the necessary
resolution to that effect it must call a
meeting of local government electors in
order to obtain their approval of the proposed Measure. At this meeting a resolution is put in favour of the promotion
of the Bill. That resolution must be put
in favour of the Bill as a whole, and it
cannot be put in favour of different parts
of the Bill, such as Part 1, Part 2, or
Part 3. The Bill must be submitted to
the meeting as a whole, and if the resolution is defeated the Bill is killed, and
nothing further can be done. If, on the
other hand, the promoters of the Bill succeed in carrying the resolution approving
of the Bill it is still open for any five
electors present at the meeting to demand
a plebiscite of the electors, and this
plebiscite must be taken.
Notice taken, that ten Members were

Sir DAWSON BATES: As I was
pointing out, any five electors can demand
a plebiscite, and the electors must subsequently vote either for the Bill as a
whole or against it. I might point out
that this is a one-sided agreement, because
while a local authority might be defeated

in a resolution to obtain the approval of
the electors it is not open to the local
authority itself to demand a plebescite.
In recent times we have had a very striking illustration showing the inconvenience
which may result from what I might
describe as a rather antiquated procedure.
Hon. Members will remember that last
year the Belfast Corporation took steps
to promote an omnibus Bill containing a
highly controversial provision in regard
to the Corporation running buses outside
their own area. But the Bill also dealt
with several very useful and desirable
matters. For example, it proposed to incorporate power to hand over certain land
for the purpose of building a hospital.
But the vote was taken at the meeting
called by the Belfast Corporation and the
vote at that meeting was unfavourable
to the Bill. Five electors present
then demanded a plebiscite. While the
only contentious matter in the Bill was
the question of the buses at the same time
the electors at that plebiscite had to decide
whether or not they approved of the Bill
as a whole. They were in the position
that they had either to lose some part
they desired or to swallow a part they did
not desire.
As the law now stands it is not necessary
for the local authority to print the Bill
before submitting it for the approval of
the electors. The result is that at these
meetings called the only information the
electors have is a statement put forward
by the local authority which might be a
biassed statement and even inaccurate.
At all events it puts the electors in a very
difficult position in thoroughly understanding what they are asked to vote
about. In this Bill we propose that the
Bill must be printed before the meeting
is called and that a copy will be available
for anyone who desires it.
In Bangor
Bangor also an omnibus Bill
was promoted in 1926. It contained
amongst other things a Clause under
which Bangor Urban Council could erect
baths. There were several other very
useful provisions, but there was a very
strong feeling as to whether or not the
inhabitants of Bangor needed baths and
when a plebiscite was taken the Bill was
thrown out. I might point out that a
similar condition of affairs existed in
England until 1903 when a Bill was
passed called the Borough Funds Act,
1903, which amended the procedure, and
we propose to adopt in this Bill similar
procedure. Now the Bill provides that
at the meeting called by the local authority the Measure which the local authority
intends to promote may be voted on in
parts or in Clauses instead of the Bill
being put to the electors as a whole, and
we also propose it will be open either to
the local authority or to the electors within a period of seven days to demand a
plebiscite, but in order to save the electors
expense it is provided that if the electors
wish a plebiscite the requisition shall be
signed by at least 100 electors or onetwentieth of the electors whichever is
smaller. Then there is another objection.
Then there is another difficulty. There
is some doubt at the present time whether
in the event of the local authority being
beaten on the question whether or not
they should promote a Bill, they have
the right to pay for the expenses of promoting the Bill up to the time it was
rejected by the electors. We propose to
remedy this difficulty. There is another
point which I am sure will appeal to my
hon. Friend from Antrim. At the present time county councils and county
boroughs have the right to use the funds
of the local authority to oppose any Bill
which they think may adversely affect the
electors. There is no power in urban
councils to oppose any Measure. As a result they are very seriously affected in
having no locus standi to use the funds
of the ratepayers to oppose a Bill which,
if it passed, might adversely affect the
ratepayers. I might point out at the
same time that we propose to safeguard
the electors to this extent that before
urban councils will be in a position to
spend the ratepayers' money in opposing
any Bill they must obtain the sanction of
the Ministry of Home Affars. These are
the main points of the Bill, and I beg to
move.

PRIME MINISTER: Mr.
Speaker, before we enter upon to-day's
business I think I would be voicing the
feelings of everyone on this side of the
House if I were to tender to you our deepest sympathy in the loss which you have
recently sustained. In speaking of the
late Lord O'Neill I need hardly say that
ever since I became acquainted with him
I always felt that I was a mere boy and,
therefore, I cannot claim that close intimacy with him that one can associate with
a person with whom one has grown up.
Ulster has sustained a serious and severe
loss (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—of a
kindly Ulster gentleman, one who to me
always extended great courtesy, and who
at the outbreak of the Great War placed
his magnificent park entirely at the disposal of the authorities. From time to
time he has evinced in a similar way his
desire to help Ulster in every way that lay
in his power.
I know, Sir, that you personally feel his loss very, very acutely,
and I cannot say more than that the whole
House tenders to you its deepest sympathy
in the loss you have incurred.

you
as Members of this House. Mr. Speaker,

hear).

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): For some time past it has been
apparent that many of the industries of
the Kingdom had reached a condition of
depression which promised to become
chronic unless some steps were taken to
reach the root of the disease. The causes
of the trouble were not difficult of diagnosis, but the remedy was not so obvious.
The great basic industries of the country,
such as agriculture, coal, textiles and the
important steel trade were all affected by
a multiplicity of adverse conditions both
internal and external. The trade situation had reached the point that foreign
competitors, favoured by labour conditions of lower wages, longer hours and
the depreciation of international exchanges, where able to outbid us in most
of the markets of the world where British
goods were formerly dominant. To add
to the acuteness of the position, the home
market, by reason of the traditional freetrade policy of the country, was invaded
to such a serious extent that many industries were threatened with extinction.
Many statesmen and eminent economists
favoured a policy of limited protection of
those industries which had to face the full
blast of foreign competition, but the acute
differences of political opinion which prevailed on this great question paralyzed
the defensive powers of the country
and left us open and unarmed against invasion. Without attemping to analyze
here how far a protective policy might
prove the salvation of the economic life
of the country, I may say it was obvious
to all who had studied the situation that
I

active measures must be taken to assist industry in meeting its many difficulties and
so to remove the dreadful load of unemployment which was the natural corollary of these conditions and which
threatened to gain a stranglehold on the

It was not unnatural, therefore, and
hardly caused any surprise, that the Chancellor of the Exchequer, in submitting the
Financial Budget of the Kingdom, announced that the Government had determined to ask Parliament to adopt a farreaching scheme by which the heavy burden of rating should in great part be
removed from the productive industries
of the country; that agricultural land and
buildings, which were probably the
greatest sufferers by foreign competition,
should be entirely relieved from the payment of all rates; and that the contraction
of the sources of revenue of the local
authorities resulting from such a policy
should be made good from the national
purse. All this is, of course, common
knowledge, and I need not enlarge upon
it further than to state that as the Province under our control is being affected
by trade depression identical with that
existing in Great Britain, our Government had no hesitation in deciding to ask
Parliament to follow the British lead in
respect of this important matter.
In view of this decision, I established
a small Departmental Technical Committee to investigate the problem in so far
as it affected our Northern area. Whilst
our general policy was expected naturally
to follow the British lead, the local conditions in Ulster differed so materially
from those existing in Britain that it was
necessary that the working of the measure
of relief should be closely investigated so
that the matter might be dealt with in a
way suitable to conditions obtaining in the
Province. Following this investigation,
we are now able, in the Measure which I
am submitting to the House, to offer a first
instalment of the legislation which will be
necessary to give effect to the proposed
relief.
Before proceeding to consider the Bill,
I should like to express a sense of obligation to Members on all sides of the
House for the consideration they have
shown in not pressing me for details of
this far-reaching scheme of rating reform
during the time I was engaged in making

It is proposed to give relief from rates;
Firstly, to agricultural land and buildings;
Secondly, to productive industry; and
Lastly, in respect of freight-transport.
Of course, the relief will entail a deficiency in the budgets of local authorities.
This will be made good by the Exchequer,
so that the ratepayers who do not get
relief will incur no additional burden by
the relief being given to farmers and industrialists in their own districts. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The present Bill
does not deal with these payments from
the Exchequer to local authorities or the
method and principles on which they will
be assessed; that will be the subject matter
of a separate Measure to be introduced in
the spring. In order that every aspect
of this question may receive the fullest
consideration I have set up a small Inter-
Departmental Committee to investigate
the subject very carefully and to consult
local authorities on the many points of
detail which are bound to arise out of a
comprehensive scheme of this character.
I come first to agriculture. The rating
of agricultural land has engaged the attention of successive Governments for the
last generation. At first the relief was
very small; it has been gradually increased, until at the present day our State
is annually contributing over a quarter of
a million, which amounts roughly to onethird of the rates chargeable on agricultural land.
The idea of partial derating for agriculture is thus not new, but the step
which is now being taken represents not
only finality, but a remarkable advance
on anything which had previously been
thought of. The additional relief is estimated at £457,000.
In addition to land we propose to go
a step further, and farm offices will be ex-

We propose to give industrial hereditaments relief to the extent of 75 per cent.
of all rates, whether county-at-large,

I estimate that the total relief to industry will be £120,000 a year. In comparison with turnover, for instance, the
figure assumes very small proportions, and
I do not pretend that this direct relief
will work any startling transformation in
the condition of trade. The fact remains
that we are largely relieving industry of
a charge which, to say the least, was not
created on a scientific basis and which,
moreover, never had any relation to industry's taxable capacity. Rates in industrial areas move in a vicious circle;
bad trade brings with it unemployment,
and thus creates charges which fall partly
on the very factories which, because of
the condition of affairs, are literally
struggling for existence.
The relief which it is proposed to give
will therefore serve to place rating on a
sounder basis. It may not mean very
much to individual manufacturers, but it
may, however small, make just the difference to a factory on the point of closing
down or to the placing of an important
order or contract. The first step, however, is to determine what are industrial
hereditaments for the purposes of this
relief, and Clauses 4 and 5 of the Bill are
designed to achieve this object.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): I beg to move in page 3, lines
27 and 28, to leave out the words "having
his head office in Northern Ireland."
In moving the Amendment which stands
in the name of my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock), it is necessary that I
should explain what is, I am afraid, a
very technical matter. The words which
it is now proposed to omit were inserted
in the original draft Clause as it was intended at the time the Clause was framed
to continue as regards Bills of Exchange
and Bank Post Bills, the present informal arrangement whereby the Northern
Ireland Exchequer collected the composition duty on Bills made or drawn by the
three Northern Ireland Banks, irrespective of the area in which the Bills were
drawn, and conversely the remaining
Banks paid the full composition duty to
the Irish Free State Exchequer.
After further examination of the problem, however, it seems likely that the
Banks will experience no difficulty in arranging for such Bills to be segregated as
between the two areas, and, as the new
currency conditions have made it necessary to discontinue this informal basis of
apportioning the composition duty on
ordinary Bank notes between the two Exchequers, it is thought only logical to
arrange if it can be conveniently done
for the segregation of duty in the minor
case of Bills of Exchange and Bank Post
Bills. As hon. Members will be aware
the Clause is permissive, but as it stands
at the moment it would preclude the
Ministry of Finance from agreeing with
the Irish Free State Revenue authorities
to any revision in the system. Any
action on the lines I have suggested would
only be taken after consultation with the
Banks and the Free State Revenue Commission. I may add that the duty involved is trifling in comparison with the
composition duty payable on ordinary
Bank notes.
Amendment agreed to.
Clause, as amended, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

NORTHERN IRELAND CIVIL

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): My attention
has been drawn to the statements in the
Press, to which the hon. Member refers.
This question of the facilities for the shipment of live stock from Belfast is at
present being investigated by my Ministry, and I hope, in due course, to let the
hon. Member know the result. I may say
that so far as our inquiries have gone they
indicate that the difficulty is the shipment
of sheep and lambs on Monday night.
EMPLOYMENT OF EX-SERVICE-
MEN.
2. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
when it is the intention of the Government to issue a White Paper dealing with
the question of the employment of ex-
Servicemen in the Northern Ireland Civil
Service.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): A White Paper dealing with
the employment of temporary ex-Servicemen will be circulated to Members to-day.
In it the 75 additional permanent posts
which I have already announced have been
included.
In addition, I have pleasure in announcing that, after further discussion with my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour,
whose Department is principally concerned, as a further evidence of the
Government's anxiety to deal generously
in this matter, an additional 25 temporary
ex-Service clerks will shortly be given
permanent and pensionable status, making
a total of 100 instead of the 75 first proposed.
Colonel WOODS: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he thinks this
is the last concession he can give to these
ex-Service temporary civil servants?
Mr. POLLOCK: At the present time
I should say the answer is in the affirmative, that is to say, while it would be impossible for me or anyone standing at this
Table to enter into any obligation in regard to the future, the Government at
present think they have gone to the very
limit of safety in the action they have
taken and in the spirit of generosity they
have displayed towards the ex-Servicemen.
Colonel WOODS: Then may I take it
there is hope of an improvement in the
future?
Mr. POLLOCK : Anything may
happen in this world.
Oral Answers.

Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
SELECTION OF ADDITIONAL
APPOINTMENTS.
3. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the method
to be adopted in the selection of the additional appointments of ex-Servicemen to
the permanent ranks of the Civil Service.
Mr. POLLOCK : The Civil Service
Commission has decided to select the men
to fill the 100 permanent clerical posts to
which I have referred in my previous
reply by means of a Selection Board comprised of higher officials of the Departments concerned, who themselves will all
be ex-Servicemen. This Board will have
before them reports furnished by the immediate superiors of each of the ex-
Servicemen who come before them.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if he has consulted the
Association of Ex-Service Temporary Civi!
Servants? If not, can he give any valid
reason why that was not done as it was
done in the Imperial Service?
Mr. POLLOCK: No. I can only repeat what I have just said, namely, that
this matter will be carried out and completed by those who are ex-Service men,
and, therefore, in my judgment it is not
necessary that any other tribunal should
be consulted.
Colonel WOODS: Does the right hon.
Gentleman consider that the Imperial
Service were misguided when they consulted, and consulted alone, the Association of Ex-Service Temporary Civil Servants; is he not aware that they have been
in correspondence with the Government.
on this particular subject; and is it not
right that they should be recognized and
consulted regarding a subject of which
they have expert knowledge?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Imperial Government is necessarily a law to itself. So far
as our own local arrangements are concerned I am quite satisfied that we have
taken every possible step to obtain the
views of the ex-Servicemen.
Mr. POLLOCK: In a selection where
efficiency is necessary one of the features
of the investigation or examination, it is
perfectly obvious, is that those officials.
who have had relation with those temporary servants must necessarily have a larger
experience of their fitness than others.
Colonel WOODS: Will there be nobody
on this Committee that is to be set up
representing the actual men concerned
and not the higher officials of the Departments? It is the men themselves who are
to be considered and not the higher
officials.
NORTHERN IRELAND LAND ACT,

ing Bill to the 1925 Northern Ireland
Land Act, which has been introduced in
the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
take this question.
The answer to the hon. Member's question is in the affirmative. He will recollect that in reply to the hon. Member
for Derry, the Prime Minister announced
in this House on the 14th May last the
terms of an agreement which had been
reached between this Government and the
Imperial Government in regard to tennants whose holdings will not have been
dealt with on or before the 27th May of
next year. The Amending Bill which has
now been introduced in the Imperial
Parliament is designed to give effect to
that arrangement.
Mr. COOPER: May I ask the Minister
if anything can be put into this Bill to
provide for the cases of fee farm grantees
and leases renewable for ever?
Mr. SPEAKER: What can be put in a
Bill in the Imperial Parliament is not
a question for this House.

Government so that this matter might be
dealt with in the Amending Bill? I

Gentleman if he is aware that there is an
urgent demand and necessity for further
Amendments to this 1925 Act and if he
will give time for this House to discuss
this Measure so that these Amendments
may be suggested to the Government?

Motion made and Question proposed:

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Supplementary Estimates.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY (Mr.
Barbour): I am glad to have the opportunity of presenting this Supplementary
Estimate to the Committee. The object
of the Estimate, which requires no
apology, is, as explained on the paper
itself, to establish a Fund to provide in
perpetuity for the maintenance of the
Thiepval Memorial.
This memorial, it is hardly necessary
to say, was erected some years ago on the
Somme battlefield and is a tribute in
particular to the men of the Ulster
Division who fought there in 1916, but it
may also be regarded as a monument
erected by Ulster to the memory of all
those of her sons who fought in the Great
War. I dare say some hon. Members
present may have actually visited this
Memorial, but for those who have not
had that privilege I may read the inscription that stands on it:
This Tower is dedicated to the Glory
of God, in grateful memory of the
officers, non-commissioned officers and
men of the 36th (Ulster) Division, and
of the sons of Ulster in other forces who
laid down their lives in the Great War,
and of all their comrades-in-arms who,
by Divine grace, were spared to testify
to their glorious deeds.
Hon. Members are, of course, aware
that this Memorial stands on the site of
the famous advance of the Ulster Division
on the 1st July, 1916. The Memorial
was erected by means of public subscription and it is considered only right and
proper that the maintenance of the
Memorial should, as in the case of the
Memorials erected in France by Newfoundland, Canada and Australia, be a
charge upon the Government of the
people by whom the Memorial was
erected.
Accordingly, the Committee is asked to
vote a sum sufficient in the first place to
recoup to the Patriotic Fund the costs of
maintenance for the last seven years, and
in the second place to provide a capital
sum which, when invested in trustee
securities, will yield a yearly income suflicient for the payment of the caretaker's
wages and other expenses incidental to the
upkeep of the Memorial and its surroundings. I may mention that the Patriotic
Fund, which it is now proposed to recoup
for its expenses in looking after the
Memorial for the last seven years, was
I
raised mainly for the purpose of assisting
ex-Service men belonging to the Ulster
Division and their dependants. Part of
the Vote will thus go to make good to that
Fund expenditure incurred from it on an
object which, though allied, is not perhaps
strictly within the original scheme of the
Fund, and thereby a sum of £1,255 will
be released and made available for the
original purpose, namely, the relief of
distress among these ex-Service men.
It has not yet been possible to estimate
the exact annual sum required to carry
out the work, but while it is not expected
to exceed a sum of £250 per annum, it
is possible that a capital sum producing
a lesser amount may be sufficient, and the
wording of the Estimate provides for this
contingency.
The note refers to a small balance of
£231 remaining over from the original
building account. There are one or two
alterations needed at the present moment
in connection with the Memorial which
may absorb about £100 or £150 of this
money, and the balance will be retained
by the Ministry of Finance and will be
available at any time in the event of any
unusual item of expenditure arising on
upkeep.
Some reference should perhaps be made
as regards the body upon which the responsibility for the proper care of the
memorial will rest, and hon. Members
will observe from the descriptive matter
on the Estimate itself that the Minister of
Finance, the Secretary or an Assistant
Secretary of the Ministry, and a representative of the trustees of the Patriotic
Fund will form a Committee for this purpose. I beg to move.

This Clause is really giving effect to the
last part of Clause 2; that is, it proposes
to derate what is defined in Clause 2 as
agricultural buildings. I would like to
congratulate the right hon. Gentleman
on the manner in which he has approached this question, namely, that there
should be an automatic adjustment with
regard to the valuation of these hereditaments, because at the present time, as the
Committee have been informed and
as most hon. Members are well aware,
the dwelling house and agricultural
buildings on farms are valued together.
There is not a separate valuation as between the dwelling house and the agricultural buildings. The right hon.
Gentleman, I think, at first thought it
would be necessary in this case to have a
revaluation of the two hereditaments.
However, he has adopted the suggestion that instead of a revaluation, which
would be expensive and cause a good deal
of delay, there should be an automatic
adjustment of these hereditaments.
The Amendment standing in my
name proposes that the automatic adjustment should be on a fifty-fifty basis.
Fifty per cent. of the valuation now on
the total buildings should be credited as
on the agricultural houses and fifty per
cent on the dwelling house. The effect
of that would be that fifty per cent. of the
present valuation on agricultural buildings
would be derated. Of course, the right
hon. Gentleman will no doubt say that
anybody who feels aggrieved has the
right to appeal against this one-third.
At the same time I think the Committee
should be concerned, in the first instance,
to have this apportionment as fair as possible. I do not think the State would
lose anything if this Amendment standing in my name were passed. Really,
the apportionment would, if anything, be
in favour of the State as against the
farmer, because if we take the average
farm over the Six County area you will
find, I think, that the agricultural buildings are really much more extensive than
the dwelling house. In a great many instances these dwelling houses are very unpretentious buildings, and with regard to
the agricultural buildings the tenants
have been compelled in recent years in a
good many cases by Act of Parliament to
improve them. Under the Dairies and
Cowsheds Order they have been compelled, in some cases, to improve the
agricultural buildings so as to comply
with the requirements of the law. They
have also been compelled, from the
economic standpoint, to erect haysheds
and piggeries on more modern lines than
what used to prevail.
I think the Amendment I put forward
would provide for a fairer proportionment of the values. While we still retain the right for any man who feels
aggrieved to appeal, yet I think this
Committee would be striking a fair apportionment. It may be said that in
asking for this we are very ungenerous,
but the proposal in this Bill is to derate
entirely agricultural land and what is described as agricultural buildings. I think
instead of one-third being the proportion
for agricultural buildings it should be
one-half. I do not wish to detain the
Committee any further. In adopting
this Amendment the Committee will be
dealing fairly with the agricultural community. I hope it will not be said that
in asking for this we are asking for something that is outlandish. In England the
dwelling house and farm houses, I understand, are separately valued, and the
farm buildings under their Bill entirely
derated, and I do hold that if we want to
derate entirely what are defined in this
Bill as farm buildings we will not be
going anything too far in derating onehalf of the entire valuation of the buildings on agricultural holdings.

as to what constituted a fair, and equitable, and just apportionment of houses

that the very efficient Commissioner of
Valuations had investigations over no
less than 300 holdings taken at hazard,
that is to say, there was no selection;
there was no attempt to take one particular class of farm or another particular

that on the average-perhaps before I
give the average I should say in certain

so on, taking various counties. These
selections are made from different
counties and the average comes to exactly
33 per cent., that is to say, that taking
the valuation of the farm buildings as
33 per cent. over the whole Six Counties,
as a result of this investigation, that is
proved to be a fair and just separation of

the houses, buildings and land shall be

of the house and building is equal to or
greater than the value of the land, so that
very small farmers are likely to get practically relief from the payment of rates.
This sub-clause (b), which includes the
matter to which hon. Members have referred, is really instructions to the Commissioner of Valuations as to the method
by which these agricultural buildings can
be separated from the valuation of the
dwelling houses. I think it is so clear
that it does not require very much explanation. In sub-paragraph (c) when
any revision arises by reason of any
changes that may have taken place in the
character of the buildings, then the local
authorities, presumably, would call for a
revaluation of the holding and in that
case there would be no question of any
percentage because the value of the house
and lands would be separated on that
valuation. That makes that position
perfectly clear, and I think if hon. Members will give the Clause full consideration
they will see that every effort is being
made to produce a fair and equitable adjustment between the various interests
as human ingenuity can effect.

Agricultural land which is situate

nor land used mainly or exclusively for

One very important matter in connection with this Measure is that it should as

two about this particular Appropriation
Bill. I see it is the intention of the
Government to supplement certain funds
that were subscribed by certain gentlemen to erect a war memorial. It seems

up an illegality which apparently has
taken place. I understand that this
Patriotic Fund was subscribed to help ex-
Servicemen and their dependants, and it
was used for the purpose of erecting or
helping to erect a memorial. If right
hon. Gentlemen had been at the back of
the City Hall opposite the offices of the
Minister of Finance last week they would
have seen a tremendous queue of ex-
Servicemen or their dependants waiting
for assistance from charitable sources.
Now we are going to vote £1,255 to reimburse the Patriotic Fund for doing
something with their money which they
were not entitled to do. In other words,
to cover up an illegality the Government
are prepared to compel the ex-Servicemen
of Belfast to pay in taxation to keep up
a war memorial.
It would be far more to the point if the
Government would keep ex-Servicemen in
the way they were led to believe they
would be kept when the war commenced
and shortly after the war was over. The
statement was then made that a grateful
country would reward them, that a grateful country would never forget them.
There are thousands of ex-Servicemen
roaming the streets of Belfast and in the
Six Counties and the Government quietly
say they have nothing to do with it, that
it is a matter for the British Government.
Therefore these men starve or go to the
workhouse or do whatever they jolly well
please, so far as the Government of Northern Ireland is concerned.
I think it is nothing short of a
monstrous proposal that the Government

should be no discussion, because the percentage of Members in the Imperial Parliament who have any special knowledge
of this question or who take any interest
in it must be very small. I have always
thought the common-sense thing would
be to have this service transferred to this
Parliament where there are Members who
have some knowledge of the subject and
take some interest in it; where there is
plenty of time to discuss the matter, and
where the people have to foot the Bill.
That is a sound business proposition. I
am quite sure that if the Government of
Northern Ireland put that proposition
before the Imperial Parliament they
would only be too glad to get rid of the
service like a great many other Irish.
questions.
I have always held that a very much
simpler way of dealing with these cases
would be that on the 27th May, 1929,
there should be arrangements made
whereby the tenants left outside the
ambit of the Bill at that time should begin to pay interest in lieu of rent to the
Land Commission, the Government also
paying a sufficient amount to the Land
Commission to meet the interest necessary
for the bonus. This, in fact, should have
been done when the 1925 Act was passed,
because if that Act had been made operative from the gale day preceding the
passing of that Act it would have placed
all tenants and all landlords in Northern
Ireland in exactly the same position.
Surely there can be no hardships done now
if, after the 27th May, 1929, all landlords
should be asked and should be compelled
by this Amending Bill to accept the same
income as they were entitled to previously.
I may be told that is impossible. I do
not believe it is.
Just before making some suggestions
that, I think, should be included in this
Bill, or, if too late for this Bill, to be included in what the Prime Minister visualises as another Bill, I would like to
say in my opinion if the Government had
consulted this House before initiating and
approving of the plan embodied in the
Amending Bill now before the Imperial
Parliament, we could, in this House have
hammered out a simpler and easier plan
of dealing with tenants who will be left
out after the date fixed by the Bill. I
refer to those tenants whose cases will not
be dealt with on the 27th May, 1929. I
feel that the arrangement that has been
initiated and approved of by our Government is a very roundabout, very cumbrous and very expensive way of dealing
with these cases. We hardly know where
we are with regard to the expense-what
this arrangement is going to cost.
I am
speaking entirely from memory and I can
be corrected if I am not right. I think
when the Minister of Finance made the
statement this year in the House with
regard to this new arrangement he said
it was estimated it would cost the taxpayers of Northern Ireland £9,000. I
have not verified that, but I think that
is what he said. According to the financial memorandum issued in connection
with the Bill in the Imperial Parliament
it is estimated it is going to take £50,000
to cover the expenses whch will be incurred
and which will have to come off the Northern Ireland taxpayers.
The Irish Free State Act, 1923, was
made applicable from the gale day preceding the passing of that Act. A similar
provision in the Amending Bill could
make such a system and plan applicable
in this case. That is one suggestion I
would make in dealing with this question.
If that is not acceptable I will give another: That the Land Commission should
before that date publish provisional lists
-they must have particulars in their
office sufficient to do this-and that all
judicial cases where there is no objection
should on that date come in. The
Government may say that is not possible.
I say if the Government say that this job
must be done in that way the officials
will find a way to do it. It will save the
Ulster taxpayers many thousands of
pounds, because a great deal of the money
that is going to fall on the Ulster taxpayers in connection with this arrangement will only be to provide larger incomes for a few favoured landlords for a
few years longer.
It may be said that you could not do
this because it would necessitate some revision. This plan may necessitate revision. I want to face the difficulties of
the question. I do not say there are not

cases where they are really bona fide

in the 1903 Act, after the exclusions, a

There is another point. By a recent

practice of the Land Commission up to
the present time has been reversed.
this particular case before the Appeal

The practice of the Land Commission up

the tenants.
Now, this decision of the Appeal
Court has reversed that practice, and in
future the Land Commission will be compelled to make their
their basis of purchase the rents that prevailed before these

think that in this Amending Bill it

Then picture the difference. Under the

In every

to round off the whole of those vast transactions you immediately introduce a
completely fresh factor, and that is the
factor of compulsion, where the elasticity.
of voluntary sales and purchase is nonexistent.
Now the Act of compulsion reigns,
and we on these Benches quite frankly
admit that it has thrown up a certain
number of hardships. But I would have
the House understand this matter. Are
we done with them? One difficulty that
we had to deal with was this: That if, say

Sir DAWSON BATES: My hon. Friend
can read them any time he wishes. That
is only a sample of the resolutions that I
have received. I might have let the matter drift, and of course the result of that
would have been that my hon. Friend
would have accused me of lacking foresight. If a condition of affairs similar to
that which exists in England to-day had
been allowed to develop here, I know that
the hon. Member would have been the
first to put down a question on behalf of
the local road authorities demanding that
something should be done to protect the
downtrodden people. But because I
advance perhaps a little ahead of public
opinion, as represented by my hon. Friend.
he makes this attack upon me. I have
been accused of being both a monopolist
and a Socialist, and I certainly find great
difficulty in reconciling the two titles that
I apparently possess.
The bus business is not in a satisfactory
condition. The hon. Member has referred
to some facts. I can quote him a case
where a person can travel 36 miles for twopence. All I can say is that people who
think they can continue to travel for ever
at a fare that is below cost price are living
in a fool's paradise. To suggest for one
moment, as my hon. Friend has done, that
I am taking away any of the powers of the
road authorities is entirely wrong. The
powers of the road authorities are going to
remain exactly the same. They have
power, as my hon. Friend knows, to close
third-class roads. I think he is one of
those that advocate that power should be
given to them under the Roads Act to close
first- and second-class roads also. That is
a proposition that the Government could
not accede to.
In regard to the conditions under which
these licences are going to be issued, the
arrangement that has been made in regard
to the country was not contingent on what
we did in regard to Belfast. They are
abs lutely separate and distinct problems.
But when I was faced with the problem of
dealing with the Belfast traffic, I felt that
that was a suitable time to deal with the
problem in the country. After all, my
hon. Friend must realize that Belfast has
practically one-third of the population of
Northern Ireland, and I venture to say
that if I had done nothing in regard to
dealing with the bus traffic in the country
he would have been the first to get up in
this House and to say "Now that you are
dealing with the Belfast problem, why do
you not deal with the country problem?"
In fact, I think that in one of his speeches
my hon. Friend suggested that I had been
rather dilatory in regard to the issue of
those licences.
I have now come across the paper that
I was looking for, showing the cities that
have complete control over their own
traffic. I find here Manchester, Plymouth,
Sheffield, and Leeds, and they are only
samples. They have complete control over
their own traffic, without being controlled
from any higher quarter. In future, however, Belfast Corporation, while they will
have control over the traffic in the city, will
have to provide a service that will meet
the needs of the public. As regards the
issue of licences, we intend at present not
to issue any more licences unless we find
that the needs of the public require them.
My hon. Friend behind me quoted
Clause of the Agreement:—
That no further licences will be issued
in respect of any route so long as the
Ministry are satisfied that an adequate
and satisfactory service is being maintained by the proprietors concerned; but
if objection is taken by the Ministry to
the service which has been provided and

of the Ministry, it shall be open to the

other operator.
As I have said before, the people are
entirely wrong who think that the

continue. What happens? I know of my

increased bevond what they had been

and to ensure that in the future the

Oral Answers to Questions.
RETIRED CERTIFICATED
TEACHERS ON PENSION ROLL.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the number of retired certificated teachers of
Public Elementary Schools who were on
the roll of pensioned teachers of the Ministry of Finance for Northern Ireland on
31st March, 1928, and whose pensions are
less than fifty pounds per annum; and
whether he will state how much would be
required to bring these pensions up to the
standard of fifty pounds per annum.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In the unavoidable absence of
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) I
have been asked to reply. In reply to the
first part of the hon. and gallant Member's question, there were on the 31st
March, 1928, 186 retired Public Elementary School teachers out of a total of
1,071 in receipt of pensions of less than
£50 per annum.
As regards the second part, the annual
cost of increasing these pensions to £50
per annum would be £2,970.

CULAR TEACHERS DIPLOMAS.
Mr. GEORGE HENDERSON (by
private notice) asked the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education
would he say on what date the circular
was issued declaring that teachers who
have not received their diplomas are ineligible for the principalship of schools
with an average attendance of thirty or
upwards; how many such principals were
then in charge of such schools, and has the
Ministry directed that all such principals
shall be dismissed.
Mr. HANNA: The regulation referred
to in the question is contained in Statutory Rules and Orders of Northern
Ireland, 1928, No. 41. This document
was issued to all managers of public elementary schools and to all principal
teachers of public elementary schoolswith the exception of schools in the
County Borough of Belfast-on 3rd July,
1928; its issue to principals of schools in
Belfast County Borough was delayed
until 13th August, 1928, as the schools
were closed for vacation up to that date.
The Ministry has not withdrawn recognition under the regulation referred to
from any teacher recognized prior to 1st
July, 1928, as principal teacher of a
school with an average attendance above
thirty.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

CATION (Mr. Robb): In two cases
schools which until recently have been
staffed by a principal teacher and a junior
assistant mistress are staffed at present
only by a junior assistant mistress. In
one of these the principal has just died
and a successor has not yet been appointed; in the other (in which the

is only temporairly recognized and the
average attendance is small.
It is only in quite exceptional circumstances that the Ministry would sanction
the conduct of a school under a junior assistant mistress, and this would be only
for a limited period pending the appointment of a new principal.

PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod as follows:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned.
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to acquaint
the House that the House has this day
attended in the Senate, where His Grace
the Governor, on behalf of His Majesty
the King, delivered in his speech to both
Houses of Parliament as follows:
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I congratulate you upon the result
of your labours during the session now
concluded.
I feel that widespread satisfaction will
be occasioned by the extension of the
Franchise to women of 21 years of age.
I am glad that the powers of Local
Authorities in connection with the widening and improving of our road systems
have been extended. Every step in this
direction safeguards users of our highways
by minimising the risk of accident.
The decision of my Government to
postpone till 1933 decontrol of rents of
the smaller type of dwellings and to
continue the housing subsidy for a
further year causes me profound gratification, as I feel that if the present rate
of building is maintained one at least of
the many difficulties facing the working
classes will be rapidly overcome.
The necessary preliminaries in connection with the drainage of Lough Neagh
and the River Bann have been initiated.
I earnestly hope that when the scheme
is completed relief from flooding so long
looked forward to and so urgently required will be amply afforded.
It is satisfactory to note the passage of
further legislation remedying difficulties
and removing anomalies in the laws
dealing with the sale and consumption
of intoxicating liquors; and that in
particular steps have been taken, with
beneficial results, enabling a stricter
control to be exercised over the sale and
consumption of noxious beverages.
A National Health Insurance Measure
has passed into law which will extend
the usefulness and simplify the machinery of that scheme, and an Unemployment Insurance Act has been passed
placing on a simpler and more equitable
basis the conditions governing the distribution of benefit to unemployed workers.
The administrative changes in connection
with the Non-Contributory Old Age
Pensions were smoothly and satisfactorily
effected.
increase of activity in the shipbuilding
industry with consequent additional employment. The operation of the Loans
Guarantee Acts has been a very important
contributory factor in this improvement.
The limit within which guarantees may
be issued has been extended from ten and
a half million pounds to eleven and a half
million pounds.
I am glad to observe that during the
present year there has been a welcome
I note that additional support to the
Linen Publicity Campaign has been
afforded, but I regret that owing mainly
to international causes, this trade is still
in a depressed condition.
ment.
My Government has continued its policy
of subsidising schemes beneficial to the
community which are promoted by public
bodies for the purpose of giving employ-
During the present year grants
amounting to two hundred and fifty-four
thousand pounds have facilitated the initiation of one hundred such schemes on
which the expenditure on wages alone
will, it is estimated, amount to three
hundred and forty-one thousand pounds.
The placing upon the Statute Book of
the first of the measures designed to give
effect to the Government's proposals for
de-rating of Agriculture and productive
industry is a very satisfactory feature of
your labours. The operation of the provisions relating to freight and other transport charges will provide a measure of
immediate relief.
Legislation has been passed to regulate
the sale of fish and to secure the better
preservation of the inland fisheries. This
Act comes into full operation at the
beginning of next year, and it is hoped
that the benefits which are expected to
accrue therefrom will manifest themselves
within the coming season.
It is gratifying to observe the success
that has attended legislation already
passed in the interests of the egg industry.
This augurs well for the third Marketing
of Eggs Act that has so recently been
added to the Statute Book to advance
yet further the interests of that most
important branch of agricultural activity.
Regard has also been paid to the potato
trade, and you have satisfied progressive
agriculturists by passing the Marketing
of Potatoes Act, kindred in principle ani
purpose to the enactments relating to the
marketing of eggs.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
I am glad that it has been found
possible to make provision for additional
financial assistance to meet the needs of
Queen's University. I trust this will be
of value in furthering the educational
requirements of the community.
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank you for the provision of
supplies for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the House
of Commons.
I note with great satisfaction that
good order generally prevails throughout
Northern Ireland and that there has been
a diminution of serious crime.
A gratifying feature of the industrial
life of Northern Ireland is its continued
immunity, save in very rare instances,
from trade disputes, and the maintenance
of harmonious relations between
ployers and employed.
em-
It is my earnest prayer that the blessing
of Almighty God may rest upon all your
past and coming labours.
After which the Proclamation proroguing Parliament was read as followeth:
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said
Act, that the Governor of Northern
Ireland shall in His Majesty's name
summon, prorogue and dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern Ireland should be prorogued to the twentysixth day of February, One Thousand
Nine Hundred and Twenty-nine:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT ED-
WARD, DUKE OF ABERCORN,
KNIGHT OF THE MOST NOBLE
ORDER OF THE GARTER, KNIGHT
OF THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS OR-
DER OF ST. PATRICK, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation
do publish and declare His Majesty's
Pleasure that the said Parliament be, as
from the reading of this Proclamation in
the Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued to Tuesday, the twenty-sixth day
of February, One Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-nine.
AND I do hereby further declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
twenty-sixth day of February, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twentynine, assemble and be holden for the despatch of divers urgent and important
affairs, and the Senators and Members of
the House of Commons of Northern
Ireland are hereby required to give their
attendance accordingly.
Given at the Council Chamber, Belfast,
the seventeeth day of December, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twentyeight.
Signed by his own hand.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday, 6th March, 1928), of the Second
Parliament of Northern Ireland, in the
Nineteenth year of the Reign of His
Majesty King George the Fifth.
